content.article_text:
On Monday, before the eyes of Washington, D.C., water once again filled the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool .

A sign, posted by National Park Service on the premises, reads : “The Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool is being refilled as the National Park Service and contractors put the final touches on a historic effort to clean, repair, and beautify this iconic national landmark. As part of the normal refilling process, the water may temporarily appear cloudy before clearing.”

Earlier this year, after a restoration that involved painting the bottom of the reflecting pool—a color described by President Donald Trump as “American Flag Blue”—the new coating began to peel, prompting a second round of repairs even as Trump declared the work “totally complete.”

Related Articles

Pope Leo Addresses Global Museum Directors, Who 'Safeguard a Heritage That Belongs to All Humanity'

A $25 M. Tribeca Apartment Is Being Sold with a Keith Haring Mural

Atlantic Industrial Coatings, which was awarded a no-bid contract to renovate the pool, announced on its website that warranty repairs had been completed on October 2, adding, “It has been an honor to serve our great nation!”

The fenced-off, slate-blue basin had sat exposed through the summer, a stark reminder of the project’s other protracted troubles: a major algae bloom, controversial contract awards, and most recently, flaking paint. The Trump administration initially attributed the pool’s peeling coating to vandalism, leading to criminal charges against several people, including former Olympic canoeist David Hearn. The Justice Department dropped the case against Hearn in July, after a determination that the coating’s installation was “botched.”

Despite evidence contradicting the vandalism claims and a ruling barring Hearn from being prosecuted again, President Donald Trump reiterated at a Tuesday press conference that vandals had cut pieces out of the basin.

“We had vandalism there, and we have it about as vandal-proof as you can get,” he said. “But only sick people do that, and we have their pictures.”

The project has also faced a legal challenge. In May, the Cultural Landscape Foundation (TCLF), a nonprofit education and advocacy organization, sued the NPS; its acting director, Jessica Bowron; the Department of the Interior; and Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, alleging that they bypassed required historic-preservation review in pursuit of a poorly planned renovation.

Of the basin’s new color, “American Flag Blue,” the suit noted that the pool’s original gray coloring helped preserve the visual cohesion between the Lincoln Memorial and the Washington Monument.

“A blue-tinted basin is more appropriate to a resort or theme park,” Charles A. Birnbaum, TCLF’s president and chief executive, said in a statement.

content.article_text:
Black Bear has acquired the rights to a comedy spec script from up-and-coming writing duo Cassidy Alla and Read Masino, Variety can reveal exclusively

According to an official logline, the untitled film “tells the story of when a mother and daughter inadvertently start dating the same man; the whole family – each at their own crossroad in life and love – must deal with the chaotic fallout.”

Related Stories

Emmys Move to Prime Video in Six-Year, Global Deal Worth Around $15 Million a Year

Amazon Launches Faster Fire TV Stick 4K and Redesigned Remote, Adds Alexa+ Hub to Fire TV Interface

Alla and Masino, both working toward their feature breakouts, have a movie in development at Netflix with Berlanti/Schechter producing and Nahnatchka Khan (“Totally Killer”) directing. The duo met while working as assistants at Apatow Productions. Masino worked as a writers’ assistant on Amazon’s “Spider-Noir” and Apple’s “Brothers” and “The Muppet Show,” while Alla worked for showrunner Justin Noble, co-creator of “The Sex Lives of College Girls.”

Popular on Variety

“This script is one of the funniest and most poignant scripts we have seen in years about romance, family and the dysfunction so often associated with both,” said Michael Heimler, Partner, President of Production & Operations at Black Bear. “Cassidy and Read are two of the most exciting voices we’ve read in some time, and we can’t wait to bring this story to life.”

Alla is represented by UTA and Mosaic. Masino is represented by UTA and Artists First.

content.article_text:
Pope Leo XIV addressed a group of directors of globally renowned museums on Saturday at the Apostolic Palace at the Vatican, underlining the Catholic Church’s “special affinity with the arts.”

The pontiff spoke to members of the Bizot group, also known as the International Group of Organizers of Major Exhibitions, whose member institutions include the Louvre in Paris, the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York, the National Gallery of Singapore, the Hermitage Museum in St. Petersburg, the Art Gallery of Ontario, the British Museum in London, and the Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam, among other world-class institutions.

Related Articles

Pope Leo XIV Blesses 20,000-Year-Old Greenland Ice in Rome

A $25 M. Tribeca Apartment Is Being Sold with a Keith Haring Mural

Founded in 1992, the group takes its name from Irène Bizot, former director of France’s Réunion des Musées Nationaux, who was instrumental in its establishment. Rijksmuseum director Taco Dibbits is its current president. The organization’s members met in Rome and Vatican City, including at the Vatican Museums, for a meeting devoted to the theme of materiality.

“Art is the means by which persons, through their ingenuity, enhance and transfigure matter—that is, the creation in which they dwell as made in the image and likeness of God,” Pope Leo said in his address on Saturday. “The theme of your meeting, ‘Materiality,’ is therefore of particular interest, not only for exploring the relationship between an object and the interpretation of a work of art, but also for reflecting on the distinctive quality of matter as the place in which God chose to reveal himself.”

Quoting a 2015 letter from Pope Francis, the current head of the Catholic Church compared artists with Jesus, saying that Christ “worked with his hands, in daily contact with the matter created by God, to which he gave form by his craftsmanship.” Matter is also memory, said Leo, adding, “The works preserved in museums bear witness to a history that speaks to every person, from one generation to the next. Museum objects thus offer to the present the wisdom of the past.”

“I therefore congratulate all of you for your efforts in directing and administering the museums to which you devote yourselves, safeguarding a heritage that belongs to all humanity,” he concluded his remarks.

The address to museum directors came just days after the pope spoke to artists and curators , saying that the Church needs them, adding, “This is especially true in this age of artificial intelligence, in which we urgently need to distinguish human art from what is produced by machines.”
content.excerpt_original: Leo spoke to members of the Bizot group, which brings together leaders of some of the world’s largest museums.

content.article_text:
Long Long Night (2026) by Youm Kyu-bock, film review

From Ru Ri’s bestseller, an animated coming-of-age journey through fatherhood and grief, with the voices of Park Ki-wook and Suzy

The only animated film in the competition section of the 31st Busan International Film Festival, Youm Kyu-bock’s “Long Long Night” is based on the book of the same name by Ru Ri, a celebrated tale with over 800,000 copies sold. Director Youm approached the story together with his daughter. The book had already inspired a musical and a pansori version, so bringing it to the big screen was, as the director himself rightly pointed out, a truly long night .

Long Long Night is screening at Busan International Film Festival

The film arrives after some very famous productions, and it won’t be hard to feel transported to the landscapes of “Flow”, the Latvian hit of 2024, or to recall the humor of the penguins in “Madagascar”, the DreamWorks franchise with fans all over the world. Here too, the penguins are hilarious.

The film features the voices of Kim Kyu-na and Suzy, who bring the little penguin to life, while Park Ki-wook, with his dense timbre, voices Norden.

The story is very simple and moving but never loses its cheerfulness, and follows the unusual life of Norden, a white rhino rescued from poachers and taken to an elephant reserve, where he learns, first of all, how to be an elephant. Just as he nestles into what he believes is his world, he is offered the freedom and the identity that are rightfully his. Running “faster than the wind,” he meets another white rhino and, with her, a family. The last of their kind.

Once again, just when he thinks he has found happiness, a tragedy forces him back into solitude and confinement. Norden is transported to a zoo and manages to escape only because war breaks out among his own jailers, who are, of course, human beings. Having survived, he sets off once more, this time with Chiku, a grumpy penguin who walks carrying a precious bucket in his beak, in which he keeps his egg, still waiting to hatch. When the egg hatches, the second part of the film begins: the second, greater voyage of Norden and the newborn, toward the sea.

“Long Long Night” is an animation made with contemporary techniques, namely Unreal Engine, a video game graphics engine, much lighter and cheaper than better-known animation software such as Maya. If technically it is an experimental undertaking, from a narrative standpoint, the film follows a classic arc. The hero’s journey, as Campbell would have it.

And yet Norden is not a traditional hero. He is a survivor, who processes multiple traumas and who channels his mission into fatherhood. It is touching to consider how closely the “Long Long Night” project itself aligns with the film’s theme, since it was born from a father (the director himself) reading a story to his daughter. That bond and the theme of parenthood find an echo in the characters who, animated though they are, show an emotional depth that leaves no one indifferent.

The film is neatly divided into sequences, or perhaps it is better to say into stages of life: youth, adulthood and old age. Norden matures through his experiences, which, once acquired, are ready to be passed on. Even to a penguin. This blend of species nods to unconventional families, and the solutions the film proposes are plainly, lovingly successful.

There is nothing this rhino won’t come up with to make the penguin appreciate his “penguinness” and to nurture in him the desire to reach an ocean he has never seen, but toward which he must head all the same. Norden wields the magic of storytelling, which educates, reassures, comforts and energizes. It is a poetic dynamic that points back to cinema itself: a film about the power of stories, folding back on itself. We are both outside and inside the screen without even knowing it.

Drawing on the freedom the digital environment has given him, Youm Kyu-bock plays festively with the action scenes. He doesn’t necessarily make the film adrenaline-fueled; he offers them as fitting entertainment for the viewer. A herd of wildebeest migrates, enraged and out of control, and not even a rhino can withstand its force. From this pitiless surge comes a thrilling scene in the waters of a raging river, where a rhino father’s desperation becomes the will to survive. It is also the scene where the software’s technical limits, especially in the rendering of water, are most visible, though in the emotional whirlwind they vanish.

The director deliberately chooses not to describe certain moments precisely: the protagonist’s thoughts, most of the time reserved and taciturn, are told by the starry sky. Likewise, some memories and emotions return and are reworked as bedtime stories. “Long Long Night” is truly rich in ideas that are not handed over gratuitously but revealed gradually. It allows us to embrace the natural course of loss and to accept the impermanence of existence, though not without a few tears. Vulnerabilities evolve into acceptance and perseverance, thus revealing themselves as strength.

Confident in his background in advertising, Youm Kyu-bock cuts the film at a frenetic rhythm where needed and slows it down when we need rest, a gathered, introspective moment. This wise alternation fosters the fullest immersion in, and involvement with, the challenges Norden and his extended family face.

It is a family film, and one that draws viewers toward the environmental cause without growing rigid on the theme. Above all, it breathes infinite landscapes, saturated colors and long shots, daring point-of-view shots and carefully worked details, not so common in traditional animation. Purists will notice a certain “robotic” stiffness in the movements and video-game pacing. But in front of a rhino teaching a penguin to believe in an ocean he has never seen, that detail can be overlooked.

Feature

“Cornell 7” Case Sparks Fury and Protests in Solidarity With Jane Doe

A Nationwide Day of Action on October 8 gathered artists, activists, and survivors in a collective call for institutions to hold abusers accountable.

Washington, DC — Approximately 250 protesters gathered beside the Washington Monument on the National Mall on October 8 as part of a National Day of Action event calling for accountability and justice for sexual assault survivors. The protest was just one of more than a dozen “I Am Jane Doe” demonstrations held across the country last week, “from the frat house to the White House,” as described by the Women’s March.

The National Day of Action was largely organized in response to allegations that seven Cornell University men, now known as the “Cornell 7,” gang raped a female student and advertised it in a fraternity Snapchat group. When the woman, known as Jane Doe, reported the incident two years ago, two of the men she accused were expelled, while the rest were required to write essays . Two years after the university’s response, Jane Doe’s lawyer filed another suit .

“We are in a moment of reckoning,” Dani Bensky, a vocal Jeffrey Epstein survivor and victims’ advocate, thundered into the microphone. She was one of six speakers who called for the passage of legislation to hold abusers accountable, including Alva Johnson, a 2016 campaign staffer who publicly accused Trump of sexual assault, and Claire Barnett, a JD candidate and president of Advocates Against Sexual Violence at Georgetown Law.

Protestors cheered them on and lifted signs reading “History Has Its Eyes on Us” and “Give Me Back My Girlhood, I Had It First.”

Hyperallergic )

Among them was activist and curator Nadine Seiler, known for her work on the preservation of artworks in the Black Lives Matter memorial fence. She held a poster that with the words “I Am Jane Doe” spray-painted on one side and “rapists are not victims” on the other, a response to criticism from the Cornell 7 and their supporters that these men’s lives were disrupted when their photos and names were shared online as part of calls for justice. Seiler told Hyperallergic that she was deeply offended by these arguments.

“I am a victim of sexual assault, and so are many people. Our experiences are important and life-changing,” Seiler said, adding that the argument that “boys will be boys is old.”

In New York's Foley Square, protesters dressed up as characters from The Handmaid's Tale and carried signs calling out systemic violence. (photo Bonnie Biess/Getty Images for Women's March)

Days earlier, on October 5, hundreds of Cornell students staged a campus rally against the Ivy League school’s administration , expressing solidarity with Jane Doe and calling out what many view as a toxic and openly sexist fraternity culture.

When asked about the choice of location for the action, protest organizer Riley Reed told Hyperallergic that they wanted to situate survivors and advocates against the backdrop of recognizable DC emblems, with the Washington Monument obelisk behind them and the White House in sight.

“It’s a big statement [that] we will not accept sexual abusers in the White House, and we have one currently in the White House,” Reed said, referring to the multiple sexual assault allegations against President Trump.

“We want to hold the leaders at the top accountable for their actions, and this is a pretty poetic and powerful spot between the Monument and the White House, which are symbols of power,” Reed continued.

Hyperallergic )

The protest lasted two hours with speeches, chants, and eventually music performed by two singers with guitars that called on Americans, in Johnson’s words, to “vote the rape regime out of office.”

As the group marched towards the White House and dispersed, Johnson’s words still hung in the air: “I am not afraid. They feed off fear, so we starve them with courage.”

E XCLUSIVE : The Black List has named the six writers and projects chosen for its 2026 Writers Lab. They are Elton de Almeida ( A Mark of Kin ), Yasmin DeWinter ( Guillaume ), Scott Leddy (Nightwatch) , Marcelle Pallais ( One Last Summer ), Alexander Seltzer and Kyle Jutkiewicz ( Depths ) and Emma Taylor Stock ( Denial ).

The program, now in its 13th year, provides creative mentorship and professional support to promising feature writers as they further develop their selected project during a weeklong workshop in Ojai, CA.

The Black List’s Annual Lab program supports two distinct cohorts: writers and ﬁlmmakers. The Writers Lab focuses on developing feature scripts to be sold in the studio system and/or used as voice samples. The Projects Lab, which will be announced in November, offers writer-directors the chance to develop a screenplay that they intend to direct.

Watch on Deadline

Related Stories

Spiegel & Grau's Full Catalog Available On The Black List Online Platform

Deadline's L.A. Law Summit: Nina Shaw & Patricia Glaser Honored On Day Of Big Ideas, Big Insights; Watch The Video Presentations

During the Lab, each writer will develop their screenplay through peer workshops and one-on-one sessions with working professional screenwriters, including returning mentors Travis Braun ( One Night Only ), Stephany Folsom ( Toy Story 4, The Lord of the Rings: Rings of Power ), Katie Silberman ( Set It Up, Don’t Worry Darling ), Victoria Strouse ( Seekers of Infinite Love, Finding Dory ) and Christina Hodson ( Birds of Prey, Bumblebee ).

Black List Annual Lab alumna Savion Einstein ( A Cuban Girl’s Guide To Tea and Tomorrow ) will also join as a session mentor. After the lab concludes, the writers cohort will participate in a yearlong support program involving monthly meetings with screenwriters, agents, managers, producers, and executives. Pitching and peer workshop sessions will be led by Scott Myers ( The Protagonist’s Journey , Spec Script Deals: 1991-2025) who has been a part of every single annual Black List Lab so far.

“We’re excited to welcome the latest cohort of screenwriters to the Black List Lab fold. At a time when the industry can seem particularly challenging and harder than ever to break into, we’re thrilled to be able to support projects that make us excited to go to the movies. These writers are bringing distinctive voices, bold points of view, and stories that deserve to be heard to the Lab and we’re privileged to be able to give them space to take risks, challenge themselves, and build community with other writers, in Ojai and beyond,” said Megan Halpern, Black List SVP.

Submissions for the 2027 Labs are now open on the Black List website .

Previous Black List Lab alumni include Claire Ayoub ( Empire Waist ), Minhal Baig ( We Grown Now ), Tom Dean ( Carolina, Caroline ), Gia Gordon ( Law and Order ), Danny Hogan ( The Pitt ), Jimmy Keyrouz ( Broken Keys ), Dagny Looper ( The Resort) , Alexandra Qin ( ThirstyGirl) , Michelle Steffes ( For When You Get Lost ), and Jason Young ( The Magic Flute) .

Learn more about the 2026 Writers Lab projects, and the creatives behind them, below.

2026 Writers Lab Projects:

Elton de Almeida – A MARK OF KIN

Haunted by her family’s tragic past, a cunning scammer seeks revenge on the uncle who abandoned her decades ago — only to be trapped by a demonic curse that feeds off her bloodline.

Yasmin DeWinter – GUILLAUME

Paris, 1898. Two American brothers walk into a brothel. One vomits on a girl. The other pulls a knife. Within the hour, they owe a madam five thousand francs they don’t have. Their ship sails at dawn. The elder just had a seizure in a piss-soaked alley – and if anyone finds out, he loses his wife, his childen, and his name.

Scott Leddy – NIGHTWATCH

In the midst of an apparent nuclear attack on NATO and the US, a communications blackout with the President places the Defense Secretary in the hot seat on America’s Doomsday Plane, but with the minutes ticking down, a comms expert discovers an anomaly that could change everything.

Marcelle Pallais – ONE LAST SUMMER

A restless, sharp-witted teen aching for meaning and adventure escapes to a wealthy beach town, only to be pulled toward a charming boy and his family’s deadly secret. Adapted from NORTHANGER ABBEY by Jane Austen.

Alexander Seltzer and Kyle Jutkiewicz – DEPTHS

Trapped aboard a US nuclear submarine, a former priest turned navy engineer must stop a demon-possessed Soviet defector before she turns the Cold War hot.

Emma Taylor Stock – DENIAL

When a health insurance giant denies their bestie’s cancer treatment, three friends attempt to approve the claim themselves. But their plan spirals when they accidentally kidnap the CEO and must expose his fraud to save themselves.

Preview

Art Films We Look Forward to Watching at DOC NYC

Documentaries on a giant pencil that became a local watering hole, the afterlife of Frida Kahlo through her image, and collagist Romare Bearden are among the festival’s most enticing offerings.

Frida: The Girl Just Doesn't Go Away (2026), directed by Trisha Ziff (all images courtesy DOC NYC)

I’ve never put much thought into how I want to be portrayed after I die. Perhaps I’d opt to be plastered on Etsy mugs, tea sets, and journal covers, à la Frida Kahlo (though I doubt I’d have many buyers, or that Kahlo would’ve enjoyed how her self-image is often nowadays detached from the politics and life behind it), or I would begin things early by enlisting an artist to paint their best guess at my posthumous body. Maybe I'd like to be dipped in ink and stamped onto rice paper, as Molly Tenzer does with the roadkill she finds on New York City streets.

The lineup at this year’s DOC NYC, which returns to venues throughout the city from November 11 through November 29, offers many reflections on this question — and more regarding documentary's capacity to sensitively portray communities currently under threat, examine artists' legacies, and narrate some of art's most idiosyncratic stories. We’ve selected 13 films we’re looking forward to seeing in-person or online at the festival's 17th edition.

Frida: The Girl Just Doesn't Go Away

Village East by Angelika , 181-189 2nd Ave, East Village Nov. 14 & 16

Go to any gift shop in an art museum, and there’s a decent chance you’ll find Frida Kahlo’s image draped over mugs, t-shirts, or decorative tapestries. Simultaneously a political icon, feminist celebrity, and a global household brand, Kahlo presents an interesting case study about how artists’ images define their legacy long after their deaths. Director Trisha Ziff taps into the commercial fascination with Kahlo and how her image has taken on a distinct life from her motivations and work.

The Hummingbird Paints Fragrant Songs

SVA Theatre , 333 W 23rd St, Chelsea Nov. 11

The Hummingbird Paints Fragrant Songs (2026), directed by Èlia Gasull Balada and Matteo Norzi

Èlia Gasull Balada’s and Matteo Norzi’s documentary on Indigenous artist Sara Flores (Shipibo-Konibo) was born out of a decade-long collaboration during which the painter began to receive international recognition. Using natural dyes sourced from her home in the Peruvian Amazon, Flores paints intricate geometric patterns with striking symmetry. Equally channeling the visual and matrilineal language of the Shipibo-Konibo practice of Kené, Flores creates works as a form of resistance against environmental, political, and social ills.

content.article_text:
Feature

Sara Flores Paints What the World Stands to Lose

“Every opportunity to show my work is a platform to raise attention on the struggle for self-determination and cultural resistance of the Shipibo people,” the artist told Hyperallergic.

The Hummingbird Paints Fragrant Songs (2026) (all images courtesy Shipibo Conibo Center)

A long canoe floats onscreen to the throbbing hum of insects; a frail woman expertly strips bark from a tree. She boils it slowly, a small tamarin monkey curled on her head like a crown. Dipping a blade into a bowl of tree juice, the woman free-hands a series of geometric shapes. Her nails are stained with age and ink, her grip remarkably steady.

Directed by Èlia Gasull Balada and Matteo Norzi, The Hummingbird Paints Fragrant Songs (2026) follows artist Sara Flores throughout her rapid ascendance to art world fame as the representing artist of the Peruvian pavilion at the current Venice Biennale . The film will screen at the 50th annual São Paulo International Film Festival starting on October 19, and will make its United States premiere as the opening night selection at DOC NYC on Wednesday, November 11, streaming online as part of the festival from November 12–29.

After an opening sequence set deep in the Amazon rainforest, we encounter Flores smiling at a flute of champagne on a first-class flight to New York. At her exhibition at the now-defunct Clearing gallery on the Bowery, she stands proud in a crimson blouse, admiring the admirers. In Central Park, she feeds the pigeons after watching a man extend acorns to the squirrels.

The Hummingbird Paints Fragrant Songs (2026)

content.article_text:
T here is a tender sweetness to this silver-years romance of new experiences and new ideas – and also some sugary sentimentality, an autumnal woodwind score telling us how to feel, and a bit of sitcom-cartoony characterisation in the all-star gallery of supporting turns. Sometimes that works and sometimes it doesn’t. But the movie’s easy-going good nature wins out – and there’s a terrific contribution from Joanna Lumley, playing Belinda, an elegant woman poignantly suffering from early onset dementia. Screenwriter Martin Sherman adapts the two-hander stage-play by Ben Weatherill in which Roger Allam and Ian McKellen originally starred. They return here for the expanded movie version and Sean Mathias once again directs.

Allam plays Frank, a retired history teacher whose wife died of cancer a few short years ago (Belinda is his sister-in-law) and who now likes to walk his dog Toffee on Hampstead Heath. McKellen is Percy, an academic sociologist and climate scientist who can be found there too, with his dog Bruno. Percy is rather acrimoniously separated from his now ex-partner, a waspish and querulously self-pitying figure gamely played by Stephen Fry .

In their differing ways, the men are lonely; Frank has nothing to do but mope around the garden centre, brooding over memories from his marriage, and volunteering at a charity shop where he has to stand, and Derek Jacobi , as a salaried employee, is allowed to sit. Percy goes in for age-gap dates from a niche website called Papa Search – some broad comedy cameos here for Ncuti Gatwa and Hugh Skinner – but he’s not satisfied. His friendship with Frank grows, his mischievous donnish sense of fun vibing unexpectedly with Frank’s stolid northern common sense. Then one day over a drink, Percy asks if it might be quite all right if he kissed Frank. Wonderingly, Frank agrees – and it is the start of something new; he says: “I felt like I did when I had a cataract removed.”

This leads Frank to ponder if he is bisexual – but perhaps it is more that he is simply sexual, and sexual in a way that he never expected to be at this time of life, or any time of life, and could only have been with this individual person. We get some bittersweet comedy as Frank and Percy realise that their social life consists of funerals, and Percy has a startling Yorick moment looking at the churchyard’s headstones. “Oh my God! I’ve had him!”

Naturally, the course of true love, or any sort of love, does not run smooth and at one stage Belinda, in a moment of lucidity, tells Frank: “How lucky you are to have a broken heart at 77!” True enough. It’s a love story as comforting as the cups of tea and slices of cake to which the characters are partial.

Rockefeller 展翼，并组建专家团队照料藏品所涉及的三个地区的艺术。此前，我只是一名资深非洲艺术专家。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Adam：你出生在非洲。你的成长经历如何影响你研究非洲艺术的兴趣？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alisa：我父亲是美国外交官，职业生涯在非洲和欧洲度过。他深爱自己在撒哈拉以南非洲工作过的许多地方。我出生于刚果民主共和国卢本巴希，成长关键时期在赞比亚、科特迪瓦和多哥度过。我读大学和研究生期间，家人住在塞内加尔、尼日利亚和南非；那也是我逐渐把关注点转向艺术史和非洲艺术的时期。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Adam：最近，我们和一群大都会的朋友一同参加了巴黎一年一度的非洲与大洋洲艺术博览会 Parcours du Monde（“环游世界”）。在那里我们看了所有参展商，也去了卢浮宫的“五大洲”展翼以及布朗利河岸博物馆的世界艺术展。我觉得此行最有意思、也最发人深省的一站，是布鲁塞尔特尔菲伦的比利时皇家中非博物馆。我从 20 多岁后期起就一直喜欢非洲艺术，也读过 Adam Hochschild 写的《利奥波德国王的鬼魂》，了解比利时暴力的殖民历史。不过，直到那时我才突然意识到，如今已是 2026 年，他们仍然占有数千件物品——这些东西是在当地被称为“刚果自由邦”时期由利奥波德二世国王的私人武装夺走或盗取的。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alisa：特尔菲伦是欧洲殖民势力在非洲存在的独特遗迹，也是那段历史中最黑暗的篇章之一。这个机构基本上是为展示中非广袤领土的财富和丰富自然资源而建立的；比利时国王利奥波德曾宣称对这片土地拥有主权。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Adam：这是哪一年？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alisa：1800 年代末，具体说是 1898 年，在 1897 年布鲁塞尔国际博览会举办临时殖民展之后。它是利奥波德宣传机器的一部分。它不是艺术博物馆，也从未被设想为艺术博物馆。它真正展示的是矿产、木材、野生动物，以及那里资源的惊人财富。特尔菲伦的文物反映了比利时人在该地区数十年的存在。其中许多是比利时人在服役期满后带回的物品，随后卖给特尔菲伦或作为礼物转交。许多不同的人从刚果回来：有传教士，也有参加过军事行动的人；有些人纯粹是行政官员。因此，这批文物汇集了比利时人在该地区长期活动的痕迹，也记录了比利时人与中非当地居民之间不同的互动。有些互动极为暴力残酷，有些则相对温和，但这段历史尤其令人创伤。Joseph Conrad 曾亲历刚果自由邦建立初期，他把所见写进《黑暗之心》，有力批判了欧洲殖民主义。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://news.artnet.com/app/news-upload/2026/10/Commemorative-portrait_Edo-812x1024.jpg", "alt": "一件埃多人的纪念肖像作品。", "caption": "", "credit": "Artnet News", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Ùhúnmwèlaò（纪念肖像），约 16 世纪作品，由 Ìgùn Ẹ́rọ̀nwwọ̀n（青铜铸造行会）为埃多人创作；由尼日利亚国家博物馆委员会借展给大都会艺术博物馆。照片：大都会艺术博物馆。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Adam：我们看到那件令人惊叹的刚果权力像，上面缠着许多绶带，面容也十分摄人。它是一件非凡杰作，背后还有一段故事。军事掠夺者 Alexandre Delcommune 因货物经过当地时欠缴关税而袭击首领 Ne Kuko。争端涉及通行费的收取金额。当地人的神圣护符被没收了。Ne Kuko 想要拿回来，Delcommune 拒绝归还，最后它落入特尔菲伦手中。他夺走了他们的神像，可为什么把它交给特尔菲伦？为什么不自己留下？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alisa：他是个不受监管的商人，面对即将出台、并向他征收的关税，便自行其是。他对此愤怒不已，想要仗势压人。他曾在当地生活，知道那件物品确有力量，也知道它在案件仲裁和裁决中发挥着重要的心理作用；夺走它，是削弱地方官员权威的极端手段。我无法想象那样的人会在意把这件作品留在自己手里。对他而言，重要的是把它夺走。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "特尔菲伦这样的机构有一种讽刺之处：我们保存着这些故事，详细记录了特定作品在原生社群中发挥的作用。我们对这件雕塑被移走之前的身份了解很多；这本身就是极其重要的历史文献。这件作品在视觉上令人叹为观止，同时也是一场冲突的物质见证。因此，特尔菲伦的藏品能让我们学到许多。它们是非常珍贵的记录，不该被埋没。相关材料理应更广泛地向公众开放，让我们更深入理解历史上发生的一切。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Adam：这就引出了显而易见的问题：接下来会怎样？博物馆该如何处置这些藏品？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alisa：这正是来源研究以及与相关同行和社群持续对话至关重要的地方。大都会长期将这类研究纳入策展实践，相关领域的专业能力已积累逾 25 年。并非每件物品或每批藏品都适用同一个答案。比利时已就现有国有藏品通过立法，并正与刚果民主共和国积极讨论文化遗产与归还问题；这些讨论引出了更广泛的问题，包括公众如何接触作品、如何保护、如何研究，以及在哪里才能最有意义地欣赏作品。关键在于调查并公开这些历史，并让与相关物件联系最密切的机构和社群参与决定下一步。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://news.artnet.com/app/news-upload/2026/10/Queen-Mother_Edo-768x1024.jpg", "alt": "一件埃多人王母像。", "caption": "", "credit": "Artnet News", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Iyọ́bà（王母像），约 18 世纪作品，由 Ìgùn Ẹ́rọ̀nwwọ̀n（青铜铸造行会）为埃多人创作；由尼日利亚国家博物馆委员会借展给大都会艺术博物馆。照片：大都会艺术博物馆。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Adam：简单说一句“全部送回去”，并不能涵盖其中的复杂性与现实情况。你谈的是一个幅员辽阔的国家、不同的社群、不同的历史，以及数以千计各不相同的物件。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alisa：这些问题需要通过合作逐一厘清，而不是抽象地给出答案。在这个过程中，我们不应忽略作品本身作为文化成就的重要性；我们应该尊重并珍视这些成就。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "从某种意义上说，这又让我们回到刚才谈的 Rockefeller 展翼。博物馆继承了特定历史时期形成的收藏、分类和展示方式。如今我们的责任是公开审视这些历史，深化研究，进一步阐明具体作品的意义，并加强与作品来源地同行及社群的关系。博物馆不应掩盖复杂性，而应帮助人们理解它。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Adam：如今人们确实在努力正视这些物件的历史，并在适当情况下将其归还。对于这些问题以及更多相关议题，我的看法是，我们无法让时间倒流，必须找到前进的办法。接下来该怎么做？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alisa：我们都需要想出富有创意的解决方案。本月我们宣布达成一项三方协议：一位长期支持大都会非洲艺术项目的美国慈善家，将三件历史杰作的法律所有权转让给尼日利亚国家博物馆与纪念物委员会；该委员会再将作品借给大都会，至少 25 年，以便它们能在纽约得到研究和欣赏。这些作品现正陈列在 Rockefeller 展翼。今年秋天，我们也期待有机会再次迎来该委员会总干事 Olugbile Holloway。他去年参加了展翼开幕仪式，一直是我们这项合作中坚定的伙伴。", "links": [{"text": "three-way agreement", "url": "https://www.metmuseum.org/press-releases/ncmm-landmark-agreement"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "物件在流转，人也在迁徙，共同塑造了我们今天生活的世界。自 19 世纪末这些物件被交易或从原属地移走以来，离散迁徙从根本上改变了世界。我们的社群高度国际化，由来自各地的人组成；我们的机构也体现了这一点。艺术品的流传历程中可能包含许多历史悲剧，我们不该回避这些故事。我们无法扭转既成事实，但可以帮助人们理解发生过什么。根据我的经验，我们有机会呈现其文化的社群，对参与其中感到无比自豪。讲述这些故事应当提高我们对既有不公的敏感度，让我们更有同理心，并坚定不再造成新的伤害。博物馆可以是人们单纯来看美丽事物的地方，也应当让人们了解传统教育课堂上可能接触不到的人类历史面向。它们是一扇窗口，让我们看到彼此在过去和现在如何相互连结。", "credit": "Artnet News", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Asmat 艺术家的身体面具，20 世纪中叶。照片：大都会艺术博物馆。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Adam：再谈谈著名的贝宁青铜器。Andrea Emelife 是尼日利亚新建的西非艺术博物馆策展人。许多贝宁青铜器于 1897 年在所谓的“惩罚性远征”中被英国军队掠走。该博物馆希望让许多作品回到尼日利亚，并为它们及其他艺术品建造了博物馆。国际博物馆开始归还部分作品时，贝宁国王奥巴出面主张这些作品的所有权。考虑到他的家族对这些物件拥有祖传所有权，事情就更难厘清了。贝宁的这段故事产生了什么影响？接下来会怎样？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "贝宁艺术是世界伟大的艺术传统之一。它与欧洲文艺复兴时期的作品同时创作，创作者掌握的技术与 Donatello、Brunelleschi、Ghiberti 和 Cellini 同样精湛。贝宁艺术讲述了其他撒哈拉以南非洲传统难以讲述的故事：由于作品以耐久的铸造金属和雕刻象牙制成，我们得以看到这一传统可追溯至 14 世纪的作品范例；非洲大陆其他许多地区并没有这样的留存。对于 Alain Locke 和 W.E.B. Du Bois 等非裔美国文化史学家而言，认识到贝宁艺术的存在，对于理解自身身份及书写非洲文化遗产都至关重要。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我们收藏了非常重要的贝宁艺术品。20 世纪 1950 年代末至 1960 年代，Nelson Rockefeller 想要建立一批杰作收藏。他在艺术市场上从经销商处及拍卖会上购入这些作品；如今它们已成为大都会非洲艺术收藏的标志。这些作品历经数代流转。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Adam：是的，不过我记得大都会归还过几件。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alisa：2021 年，大都会主动将两件贝宁作品归还尼日利亚，并协助一位外部收藏家归还第三件作品；合作研究认定，大都会并未（或无法）取得有效所有权。这项工作促成大都会与尼日利亚国家博物馆与纪念物委员会的伙伴关系迅速发展。此后双方签署谅解备忘录，建立持续合作，其中包括一项长期计划：由尼日利亚团队参与，为该委员会的藏品进行数字化和编目。我前面提到的新借展协议，也在这一基础上迈出了意义深远的一步。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Adam：Calder 的经销商 Klaus Perls 曾把许多这类作品捐给大都会。它们是从哪里来的？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alisa：是的，我们收藏的贝宁宫廷作品大多由 Klaus Perls 捐赠。他是一位重要的现代艺术经销商，从德国移居纽约，个人特别热衷于收藏贝宁王国艺术。他于 1991 年将收藏捐给大都会。当时，大都会对其进行了来源研究；这一研究领域在过去几十年中持续大幅发展。博物馆还举办了展览、在国际巡展，并在线发布作品及其历史。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "如今，我们的新展翼展出这些作品，并将它们置于对非洲大陆各地主要艺术运动及活态传统的整体梳理之中。新的展示以当代研究为基础，也融入了大都会及世界各地专家网络的交流成果，其中尤为重要的是尼日利亚专家的声音和意见。观众可在展厅中直接阅读和聆听这些内容。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "展翼开放当天，是疫情前以来博物馆单日参观人数最多的一天。这些作品不仅能被每年逾 600 万名到馆观众看到，也能通过网站向更多人开放，最终触达全球观众。重新开放时，我们迎来了总干事 Holloway，以及许多参与展陈工作的地区伙伴和学者；那是一个庆祝文化、社群与合作的有力时刻。我们还听到许多纽约人——他们的文化遗产正是这些作品所代表的文化——表达了深切感谢，因为他们的文化在纽约得到了礼赞。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://news.artnet.com/app/news-upload/2026/10/Chief-Omas_Drum-768x1024.jpg", "alt": "一面鼓。", "caption": "", "credit": "Artnet News", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Chief Omas，鼓，20 世纪中叶。照片：大都会艺术博物馆。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Adam：这里存在一种结构性的不公：这些东西都在博物馆里，可如果你回到创造它们的国家，却找不到它们。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alisa：在近几年这些作品转移之前，尼日利亚拥有的贝宁艺术藏品就已位居世界前列。该国有规模庞大的国家收藏，只是由于博物馆基础设施方面的问题，这些藏品一直未能展出。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我们与尼日利亚合作的很大一部分，是支持其能力建设。五年前，我们曾与尼日利亚同行坦诚交流，询问他们认为我们最能在哪些方面提供帮助。他们说自己没有数字藏品数据库。于是我们开始共同投资开发一个试点数据库，并着手进行摄影记录，同时建立藏品登记档案。我们的目标是让他们收藏的数万件无可比拟的重要作品，逐步纳入这个数据库。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我们有责任成为真正的伙伴，通过支持博物馆专业人员培训和开展有意义的交流来提供帮助。例如，我所在的部门会接待驻访人员，也会定期与拉各斯、哈博罗内和达累斯萨拉姆等地机构的同行共同举办工作坊。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Adam：美国博物馆与欧洲博物馆很不一样。艺术界的每种情况都各有特殊之处。例如，一些欧洲收藏是殖民势力搜集的作品构成的；美国博物馆则是由在公开市场上购买物件的收藏家建立。我想多数人不知道，欧洲第一次非洲艺术展是什么时候举办的。1920 年是非洲艺术首次在卢浮宫办展吗？当我得知这件事时，我觉得博物馆承认非洲抽象艺术和非洲艺术对当时当代艺术的影响，真是太好了。后来我才知道，那不过是一次殖民炫耀，目的是显示法国有多强大，拥有多少异国珍宝。大英博物馆也是如此。“大英帝国的太阳永不落下”，他们收集其他地方的文化象征、纪念物和珍宝，就是为了彰显自己的强大。一方面，这些行为是错误的；另一方面，若非如此，或许这些东西都无法保存下来。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alisa：我认为我们常常把这些机构的性质过度简化。一方面，它们是某些历史时期的遗产，那时人们挪用、盗窃和掠夺他人财物；另一方面，它们也属于人们拓展交流网络、努力认识自身之外世界的历史时期。那是欧洲以外传统的学术好奇心和研究的开端。今天我们之所以如此了解过去，很大程度上是因为 18、19 世纪的收藏。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我们不想过度美化启蒙运动时期，但世界的确因此变得更小。这一点也体现在各种不断丰富和扩大的博物馆收藏上。博物馆是鲜活的机构，反映着社会的热情。1870 年，纽约人决定创建一所可以通过汇集藏品了解广阔世界的机构，并由此建立了今天的大都会；这令人惊叹。它体现了人们对熟悉范围之外世界的好奇，以及亲身体验的愿望。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这种初衷非常值得尊重，不该被轻易搁置。真正重要的是让人们意识到，世界比他们眼前所见复杂得多。在我们生活的这个时代，这一点尤其重要：我们身处多元文化社会，也生活在全球相互依存的世界中。理解多样性以及构成我们身份的众多传统，既重要又不可替代。博物馆有责任启发我们去了解并尊重那些看似陌生、相对难以接近的文化。理想情况下，它们也能成为起点，鼓励我们走出馆舍，亲自前往文化源头。", "translated": true}]

content.article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alisa LaGamma is the Ceil and Michael E. Pulitzer Curator of the Department of the Arts of Africa, Oceania, and the Americas at the Metropolitan Museum of Art . As a lifelong collector of African art myself, I have seen many of her shows and also served on her committee for years, more recently as chairman. The history of these objects is a fascinating one, from the painful colonial era to the struggle to have this art broadly accepted in the art world. Few people realize that it wasn’t until the ’80s that the Met exhibited these artworks, and before that, many saw them as little more than artifacts. This field is currently the subject of ongoing debate regarding the politics of restitution and the complex realities of repatriation. On our return from Parcours du Monde , the classic African and Oceanic art fair in Paris, last month, and not long after the one-year anniversary of the $70 million rebuild of the entire wing, it felt timely to explore a few topics in the zeitgeist."}, {"type": "heading", "text": "The best of Artnet News in your inbox."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Sign up for our daily newsletter."}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "The best of Artnet News in your inbox. Sign up for our daily newsletter. Please enter a valid email address Signup failed. Please try again later. Thank you! You have successfully subscribed to Artnet News."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Adam: What is the Michael C. Rockefeller Wing? Can you explain the Met’s relationship to classic African, Oceanic, and Ancient American art?"}, {"type": "heading", "text": "The best of Artnet News in your inbox."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Sign up for our daily newsletter."}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "The best of Artnet News in your inbox. Sign up for our daily newsletter. Please enter a valid email address Signup failed. Please try again later. Thank you! You have successfully subscribed to Artnet News."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alisa: Sure—it’s a fascinating story. In 1969 New York’s Governor Nelson Aldrich Rockefeller and the Metropolitan Museum of Art announced that a new wing of the museum would be built in order to accept the gift of his collection of sub-Saharan Africa, Oceania, and the Ancient Americas. The collection had until then been housed at his Museum for Primitive Art."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "This development fundamentally redefined the mission of the Met, which was then, as it is today, one of America’s leading museums. The move established that suddenly artistic traditions of three-quarters of the world, previously relegated to natural history museums, were to be recognized shoulder to shoulder with the then pinnacle of art history—the Old Masters of Western European art. Overnight the Met’s identity became that of a global institution whose aspiration was to represent all cultures."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Adam: It was a pretty radical move at the time—a major shift that changed the way we in the West see art from these huge regions of the world, and had a big impact on collectors, galleries, and museums by expanding notions of what is considered fine art. But people might not realize that the Met wasn’t on board with it at first."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alisa: That’s right—that transformation led by Rockefeller was a hard-fought one. His enthusiasm for non-Western art was not originally shared by the Metropolitan, so actually in 1954 he established his own private institution across from the Museum of Modern Art. He was being advised by the leading specialists in what were then very young branches of art history, as he sought to assemble a survey of the major traditions absent from the Met."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://news.artnet.com/app/news-upload/2026/10/TWO-PANEL-SPLIT-WITH-BACKGROUND-2-1024x819.png", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Artnet News"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alisa LaGamma and Adam Lindemann. Photos: The Met and the author"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Adam: Here’s this politician from one of the wealthiest families in the U.S., as close to American royalty as we get, and he’s asking for these objects, which were considered ethnographic material from what was then the farthest reaches of the world, to be recognized as fine art. What drove this passion of his?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alisa: In 1930, the year Nelson graduated from Dartmouth he was made a Met trustee. The son of John D. and Abby Rockefeller, his mother had instilled in him an awareness of the important role that African and Ancient American art had played in the transformation of 20th-century art. As an internationalist and a statesman, in the years that followed he embraced learning about less familiar parts of the world through their artistic traditions. This led to his conviction that “all people have art.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Nelson’s son, Michael, shared his father’s passion for that mission and majored in anthropology at Harvard. He was deeply and personally inspired by the cultures and art of the Pacific and pursued new avenues of inquiry into artistic practice during his travels there. We have incredibly striking Asmat sculptures he researched and collected in southwest New Guinea on view in the wing. In 1961, during his second trip to research, collect, and document the works of artists in Papua New Guinea he was in a small craft at the mouth of the Betsj River that ran out of gas and was drifting into the Arafura Sea. In attempt to swim to shore he tragically drowned."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Adam: And this is all happening in the ’60s and ’70s, when so much of the world, including the U.S., was undergoing major shifts in culture and society. How did that play into these collections coming to the Met?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alisa: Major developments at home and abroad over the course of the 1960s relating to Civil Rights and the coming of age of new nation states across Africa were such that by 1969, Rockefeller’s campaign to incorporate non-Western art within the Met finally succeeded. In addition to the significance of the timing, the process of absorbing an existing pioneering institution into the Met was a complex one."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "On a logistical level it might be considered comparable to the recent announcement of Ronald Lauder’s Neue Galerie merger . The prior Rockefeller development, however, was not simply the addition of a major private institution and epic infusion of art but one that fundamentally redefined the mission of one of America’s leading museums. It was decided that the new Met Wing would be named for Michael Rockefeller’s quest to deepen his understanding of Asmat art and over the next decade, the staff, collection, archives, and library of what had been known as the Museum of Primitive Art was transferred into the footprint of what is today the MCR Wing.", "links": [{"text": "merger", "url": "https://news.artnet.com/art-world/met-museum-neue-galerie-merger-2773237"}]}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://news.artnet.com/app/news-upload/2026/10/Installation-view-of-the-Arts-of-Africa-Galleries_Bruce-Schwarz-33-1024x621.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Artnet News"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Installation view of the Arts of Africa Galleries. Photo: Bruce Schwarz"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Adam: And now you’ve just last year reopened the wing after a complete renovation and rethinking of it. Of course, scholarship on art from these regions has evolved dramatically over the last few decades. But why the full renovation?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alisa: For much of the time that the wing was under construction, Nelson Rockefeller was vice president. He died before its completion in 1982. Encompassing 40,000 square feet of galleries at what was then the southernmost frontier of the Met campus, its inaugural state-of-the-art display made minimal reference to the original cultural contexts of the works featured. Its success was such that their study blossomed in the academy and the museum’s collection expanded in new directions."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "This was increasingly evident in a growing contrast between the permanent collection galleries and the groundbreaking research that we directed toward temporary exhibitions organized by the Met’s curators. It was a priority for me that those special projects that advanced deeper understanding of major traditions represented in our collection and that developed meaningful partnerships with institutions and colleagues in the regions of the world from which the works originated be reflected in the permanent collection galleries. This led me to propose a capital project to renew the Rockefeller Wing over a decade ago. A priority for my curatorial team was to reenvision our section of the museum and reintroduce the permanent collection within three independent surveys of world art that were at once grounded in history and many layers of content enriched by engagement with experts in source countries."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "This is reflected in an infusion of digital content we developed to afford greater context that includes a series of three audio guides highlighting the perspectives of an international cohort of leading public intellectuals in the arts and humanities based in centers ranging from Bamako to Bogota. We also hired filmmaker Sosena Solomon to document interviews and landmarks at a dozen sites across sub-Saharan Africa featured in a series of critically acclaimed short documentaries that widen the lens on major cultural centers relevant to deeper engagement with the decontextualized works on display. That project has created all kinds of new bridges between the Met and regional partners some of which have led to signing of new memoranda of understanding, and we have followed up with a series of workshops held at museums from Gaborone to Zanzibar in which we screen the films with regional audiences.", "links": [{"text": "series", "url": "https://www.metmuseum.org/perspectives/series/africa-cultural-landmarks"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Another important dimension of this reset is that we have leveraged the adjacencies of neighboring sections of the museum to be more meaningful. For example, the interface of the Africa galleries and those devoted to European Renaissance sculpture and decorative arts highlights works created along the coast of West Africa from the 15th century for the earliest European traders. Completed at the end of May 2025, the reinvigorated MCR Wing has shifted from its original design as a museum within a museum to a major crossroads of the museum that is at once physically and intellectually illuminated and in dialogue with adjacent galleries of Greek and Roman, European sculpture and decorative arts, and modern and contemporary art."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://news.artnet.com/app/news-upload/2026/10/Horse-head_Yoruba-768x1024.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Artnet News"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "A horse head by a Yoruba artist from the 12th century–15th century on loan to the Met from the Nigerian National Commission for Museums. Photo: Met"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Adam: Alisa, how long have you worked at the Metropolitan Museum?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alisa: I have been at the museum since I was a graduate student some 31 years ago. For the last 12 of those I’ve overseen the Michael C. Rockefeller Wing and its team of specialists that I recruited to care for the three areas of the world covered by its collections. Prior to that I was simply a senior African art specialist."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Adam: You were born in Africa. Tell me how that shaped your interest in studying African art?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alisa: My father was an American diplomat who spent his career in both Africa and Europe. He had a deep love for the many places he worked in across sub-Saharan Africa and I was born in Lubumbashi in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and spent formative years in Zambia, Côte d’Ivoire, and Togo. My family was living in Senegal, Nigeria, and South Africa when I was in college and graduate school, the period I was myself increasingly turning my focus to art history and African art."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Adam: We recently attended the annual African and Oceanic Art Fair in Paris called Parcours du Monde (“Trip Around the World”) along with a group of friends of the Met. While there we saw all the dealers and went to both the Louvre’s Cinq Continents wing and the Quai Branly Museum for world art. I thought the most interesting and provocative part of the trip was when we went to Brussels to the Royal Museum for Central Africa at Tervuren. I’ve been enjoying African art since my late 20s, and I’ve read about Belgium’s violent colonial history in King Leopold’s Ghost by Adam Hochschild. Still, only then did it strike me that we’re in 2026, and they’re still sitting on thousands of objects, things taken or stolen by King Leopold II’s privateers when it was the “Congo Free State.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alisa: Tervuren is a unique vestige of the European colonial presence in Africa and one of its darkest chapters. It is an institution that was essentially created as a showcase for the wealth and rich natural resources of the vast territory of Central Africa to which King Leopold of the Belgians had laid claim."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Adam: In what year was this?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alisa: This was in the late 1800s, 1898 following the temporary colonial exhibition featured at the 1897 Brussels International Exposition. It was a branch of Leopold’s propaganda. It’s not, and was never conceived of, as an art museum. It was really an institution that showcased the minerals, the woods, the wildlife, the sheer wealth of its resources. The artifacts at Tervuren reflect decades and decades of Belgian presence in that region. Many of them were things that Belgians brought back with them, after their tours of duty and then either sold to Tervuren or transferred as gifts. There were all kinds of people coming back from the Congo. You had missionaries as well as individuals who had been part of military campaigns. Some were just pure administrators, so it’s an assemblage of artifacts that reflect the Belgian presence there over an extended period of time and the result of different interactions between Belgians and residents of this region of Central Africa. Many were very violent and brutal, some of them were more benign, but it’s an especially traumatic past. Joseph Conrad was witness to the early years of the Congo Free State and he channeled his observations in the powerful critique of European colonialism that is Heart of Darkness ."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://news.artnet.com/app/news-upload/2026/10/Commemorative-portrait_Edo-812x1024.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Artnet News"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Ùhúnmwèlaò (commemorative portrait) by Ìgùn Ẹ́rọ̀nwwọ̀n (brass-casting guild), Edo peoples, ca. 16th century on loan to the Met from the Nigerian National Commission for Museums. Photo: The Met"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Adam: We were looking at that amazing Kongo power figure with all those ribbons on it and that gripping face. It’s an incredible masterpiece, with a story. The military privateer Alexandre Delcommune attacked chief Ne Kuko over tariffs owed when goods were coming through their regions. The dispute was about the amount charged for passage. The people’s magical fetish was confiscated. Ne Kuko wanted it back. Delcommune refused to give it back, and eventually it ends up at Tervuren. He had seized their idol, but why did he give it to Tervuren? Why didn’t he just keep it?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alisa: He was an unregulated tradesman taking the law into his own hands in response to tariffs that were going to be introduced and levied against him. He was outraged by that and he wanted to throw his weight around. Having spent time in the region, understanding the efficacy of that object and that it had a very important psychological role in the arbitration and adjudication of cases, his seizure of it was the ultimate way of diminishing the authority of local officials. I can’t imagine that somebody like that cared about holding on to the work. It was the removal that counted as far as he was concerned."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "One of the ironies of an institution like Tervuren is that we have these stories, very detailed histories of the role specific works performed in their original communities. We know a lot about the identity of this sculpture before it was removed and that in and of itself is an incredibly important piece of historical documentation. This work which is such an incredible tour de force visually is also the materialization of a conflict. The Tervuren collection can teach us so many lessons as a result of this. These are very, very precious records that shouldn’t sit in obscurity. It really should be material that is more widely accessible, and that gives us a deeper understanding of what unfolded historically."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Adam: And that raises the obvious question: What happens now? What should museums do with these collections?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alisa: That is precisely where provenance research and sustained dialogue with colleagues and communities connected to these works become so important. At the Met, that research has long been embedded in our curatorial practice, with specialist expertise in the field developed over more than 25 years. There isn’t necessarily a single answer that applies to every object or every collection. Belgium has passed legislation concerning existing state collections and is in active discussions with the Democratic Republic of the Congo around cultural heritage and restitution that raise larger questions about access, conservation, scholarship and where works can be most meaningfully encountered. What is essential is that these histories are researched and made transparent, and that the institutions and communities most closely connected to the material are part of determining what comes next."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://news.artnet.com/app/news-upload/2026/10/Queen-Mother_Edo-768x1024.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Artnet News"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Iyọ́bà (queen mother) figure by Ìgùn Ẹ́rọ̀nwwọ̀n (brass-casting guild), Edo peoples, ca. 18th century, on loan to the Met from the Nigerian National Commission for Museums. Photo: The Met"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Adam: Simply saying “send everything back” doesn’t capture the complexity nor the realities. You’re talking about an enormous country, different communities, different histories and thousands of individual objects."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alisa: Those questions need to be worked through collaboratively rather than answered abstractly. In doing so we should not lose sight of the importance of the works themselves as cultural achievements to be respected and honored as cultural achievements."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "And in a way, that brings us back to what we were talking about with the Rockefeller Wing. Museums inherited ways of collecting, categorizing and presenting works that were products of particular moments in history. Our responsibility now is to examine those histories openly, to deepen the scholarship, to deepen the presentation of the significance of specific works, and to strengthen relationships with colleagues and communities in the places where these works originated. The museum shouldn’t obscure complexity. It should help people understand it."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Adam: There’s a real effort now to reckon with the histories of these objects and, where appropriate, to return them. My view on all these things and more is that we can’t wind back the clock—we have to find a way forward. Where do we go from here?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alisa: We all need to come up with imaginative solutions moving forward. This month we announced a three-way agreement in which an American philanthropist who has been a longtime supporter of African art at the Met is transferring her legal title to three historical masterpieces created in what is today Nigeria to its National Commission of Museums and Monuments, which is in turn loaning the works to the Met for at least 25 years so they may be studied and experienced here in New York City. These are now on view in the Rockefeller Wing, and this fall we’re looking forward to hopefully welcoming back the director general of the NCMM, Olugbile Holloway, who joined us for the opening of the wing last year and has been a steadfast partner in this work together.", "links": [{"text": "three-way agreement", "url": "https://www.metmuseum.org/press-releases/ncmm-landmark-agreement"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Objects have circulated, and people have circulated to define the world that we live in today. Since the end of the 19th century when these objects were traded or removed from their places of origin, the world has fundamentally changed by diasporas. Our communities are highly cosmopolitan and comprised of people from all over. And so, our institutions also reflect that. There are many historically tragic events that may be a part of the path of works of art. We shouldn’t shy away from those stories. We’re not going to reverse what happened, but we can help people understand what unfolded. In my experience, communities we have had the opportunity to represent are enormously proud of their participation. Telling those stories should heighten our sensitivity to wrongs that were done and should equip us to be more compassionate and committed to not perpetuating further damage. Museums can be places where you just go to look at beautiful things, but they should also be places where you learn about dimensions of human history that you might not be exposed to in the classroom as part of your traditional education. They’re a portal to other dimensions of how interconnected we all are, both in the past and in the present."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://news.artnet.com/app/news-upload/2026/10/Asmat-artists_Body-Mask.-Mid-20th-century-661x1024.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Artnet News"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Body mask by Asmat artist(s), mid-20th century. Photo: The Met"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Adam: How about the famous Benin bronzes. Andrea Emelife is the curator of the new Museum of West African Art in Nigeria. Many of the Benin bronzes were taken by the British army in 1897 in what is called the “Punitive Expedition.” The museum sought to get many of them back to Nigeria and built a museum for them as well as other Art. When international museums started sending back certain works, the Oba (king) of Benin appeared and sought ownership of the works. Given his family’s ancestral ownership of the objects, it becomes even more complicated to unwind the situation. What’s the fallout of that Benin story and what happens now?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alisa: Benin art is one of the world’s great art traditions. Those works were produced in parallel to works that were created in Europe during the Renaissance. They were created by artists who had a mastery of the same technology as Donatello, Brunelleschi, Ghiberti, and Cellini. They tell a story that you cannot tell with other traditions from sub-Saharan Africa because, given that they were composed of durable materials of cast metal and carved ivory, we have exemplars of creations from this tradition going back to the 14th century, which is not the case for much of the rest of the sub-continent. For African American cultural historians like Alain Locke and W.E.B. Du Bois, an awakening to the existence of Benin art was critical to their understanding of what defined their identity, and to their writing about an African heritage."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "We have very important holdings of that material because, during the late 1950s through 1960s, Nelson Rockefeller wanted to put together a collection of masterpieces. He bought the works that are now icons of the Met’s African art collection on the art market—from art dealers and at auctions. These were works that had circulated over the past generations."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Adam: Yes, but the Met gave back a few, I recall."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alisa: In 2021, the Met voluntarily returned two Benin works from the collection to Nigeria and helped facilitate the return of a third work from an outside collector, after our collaborative research determined that the Met did not (or could not) have proper title. And that effort led to a real blossoming of partnership between the Met and Nigeria’s National Commission for Museums and Monuments. We have since entered into an ongoing collaboration outlined in a memorandum of understanding that now includes the long-term project to facilitate the digitization and cataloguing of the NCMM’s collections together with a Nigerian team. And the new loan agreement I mentioned earlier builds on this foundation in a really powerful way."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Adam: Klaus Perls, Calder’s dealer, gave a lot of these works to the Met. Where did he get them from?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alisa: Yes, the majority of the works in our collection from the Court of Benin were given by Klaus Perls. He was a major dealer of modern art who had immigrated to New York from Germany and his private passion was collecting art from the Kingdom of Benin. He gave his collection to the Metropolitan in 1991. At that time, the Metropolitan did provenance research, which is an area of research that has continued to advance significantly over the past few decades; exhibited the collection; toured it internationally; and published the works and their histories online."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The works in our collection are now displayed in our new wing, contextualized within our survey of major artistic movements and living traditions from across the subcontinent. The new presentation is grounded in contemporary research and exchanges with a network of experts at the Met and around the world, including, importantly, the voices and input of experts from Nigeria, which can all be read and heard by visitors right in the galleries alongside these works."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The day we opened the wing was the museum’s highest single-day attendance since before the pandemic. And the works are widely available not just to our more than six million yearly visitors, but also to an even larger number of people on our website and ultimately, they’re accessible to a global audience. When we reopened, we welcomed General Director Holloway and many partners and scholars from across the regions who we worked with on the display, and it was an incredibly powerful moment to celebrate culture, community, and collaboration. And we’ve also heard from many, many New Yorkers whose heritage this is who deeply appreciated seeing their culture celebrated here in New York City."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://news.artnet.com/app/news-upload/2026/10/Chief-Omas_Drum-768x1024.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Artnet News"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Chief Omas, Drum, mid-20th century. Photo: The Met"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Adam: There’s a built-in injustice because all these things are in museums, but if you go back to the country that actually created them, you can’t find them."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alisa: Nigeria has had among the largest holdings of Benin art even before all this transfer of works in the last couple of years. It has enormous national collections. They have not been visible because of issues with the museum’s infrastructure."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "A huge part of our work together with Nigeria has been around supporting their capacity needs. Five years ago, we had a heart to heart with our counterparts in Nigeria and we asked them what is it that they felt we could be most helpful with. They responded that they didn’t have a digital collection database. So, we’ve been investing in creating a pilot for one with them and beginning the process of photographic documentation accompanied with accession records—the goal will be for the tens of thousands of works of incomparable importance in their collection to become part of that database over time."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "We have the responsibility to help by being true partners, supporting the training of museum professionals and engaging in meaningful exchanges. For example, we host residencies in my department and periodically co-organize workshops with colleagues in institutions from Lagos to Gaborone and Dar es Salaam."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Adam: American museums are very different from European museums. Every situation in the art world is kind of a unique situation. For example, some of these European collections were built with works collected by the colonizing forces—unlike U.S. museums, which were built by collectors buying objects on the open market. I don’t think most people are aware when the first African show in Europe happened. Was 1920 the first time that African art had a show in the Louvre? When I learned this, I thought it was wonderful that the museum was acknowledging the influence of African abstraction and African art in the contemporary art of that time. I later found out this was just a colonial flex. This was to show how powerful France was, and that they possess all these exotic trophies. That’s the same with the British Museum. The sun never sets on the British Empire, and so for them to collect these cultural talismans, and monuments, and treasures from other places just showed how powerful they were. On the one hand, those actions are wrong, but on the other hand, perhaps if not for them, none of these things would have been preserved."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alisa: I think we tend to oversimplify the nature of those institutions. On the one hand they are a legacy of periods in history when things were being appropriated, stolen, and looted. They’re also a part of the period in history when people are engaged in expanded networks of exchanges and trying to understand the world outside themselves. It’s the start of intellectual curiosity and scholarship concerning traditions outside of Europe, and we know so much today about what came before because of what was collected in the 18th and 19th centuries."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "We don’t want to over glorify the Enlightenment period, but it is a fact that the world became a smaller place as a result. This is true with all kinds of museum collections that are diversifying and expanding. Museums are living institutions that reflect the passions of their societies. It’s incredible that in 1870 people in New York City decided to create an institution where they could learn about the world at large by assembling what is today the Metropolitan. It’s a reflection of people’s curiosity about the world outside of what they’re immediately familiar with, and their desire to experience it."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "This is a very honorable intention that we shouldn’t just put to the side. It really is about sensitizing people to a more complicated world than the one that they’re immediately aware of. That’s an important thing, especially in the moment that we are living in, where we are a multicultural society in a globally interdependent world. It’s important and invaluable for us to understand diversity and the many traditions that define us. Museums have a responsibility to inspire us to learn about and respect cultures that appear to be foreign and relatively inaccessible to us. Ideally they are a springboard to venture beyond their walls and go to the source ourselves."}]
content.article_text:
Alisa LaGamma is the Ceil and Michael E. Pulitzer Curator of the Department of the Arts of Africa, Oceania, and the Americas at the Metropolitan Museum of Art . As a lifelong collector of African art myself, I have seen many of her shows and also served on her committee for years, more recently as chairman. The history of these objects is a fascinating one, from the painful colonial era to the struggle to have this art broadly accepted in the art world. Few people realize that it wasn’t until the ’80s that the Met exhibited these artworks, and before that, many saw them as little more than artifacts. This field is currently the subject of ongoing debate regarding the politics of restitution and the complex realities of repatriation. On our return from Parcours du Monde , the classic African and Oceanic art fair in Paris, last month, and not long after the one-year anniversary of the $70 million rebuild of the entire wing, it felt timely to explore a few topics in the zeitgeist.
