Nathan Fielder now wears the uncomprehending stare. He’s directing it at Elizabeth Holmes in the days before her 11-year imprisonment over a nine-figure defrauding for her blood-testing project Theranos, a scam orchestrated at such uncommon size that it must be made into the harshest example. Why she and her husband have trusted Fielder, a constant chronicler of errant human behavior, to craft a sympathetic portrayal of her ostensible plight is never quite clear. Holmes, resembling a Chuck Jones cartoon and sounding like she’s just overcome airway constriction, returns a stare that’s not so much uncomprehending as it is incomprehensible . Her vague visage creates an organizing principle: not just for the basic film-grammar question of when to cut between hers and Fielder’s, but how this face, even once cut from, seems to echo and radiate across the scene.

I was thinking about the ping-ponging point-counterpoint between people’s faces—Fielder and Holmes and her husband and some others who show up—through many of the 174 minutes comprising You Can See Everything , his often-extraordinary feature-filmmaking debut during which nearly every expression that can be made with a person’s eyes will occur and recur to our amusement, if not knowledge. A camera has seldom fixated so hard on expressions to crack what is (or might be) resting beneath the surface. It stares and stares and stares : at faces, their musculature, at eyes, their shifts through smiles or frowns, the device like an interrogator forcing a confession or a psychic trying to explode a head. You Can See Everything is vertiginous in its staticity, a concentric circle that expands or contracts by the smallest brush of discomfort; it operates through an inability to manage its own tasks, entering a cocktail-napkin-sized pantheon of films that succeed so brilliantly on the basis of failure.

Though co-directed by Lance Oppenheim—whose involvement Fielder obviously did nothing to discount during a post-screening Q&A, and which one can connect to nothing less than a film du jour —it’s nigh impossible envisioning You Can See Everything as (co-)made by anyone else (or, pending availability, the ghost of Abbas Kiarostami). It is also, by all counts, Fielder’s inaugural time playing straight. This is evident quickly, if not quite instantly: the first laugh earned at a beyond-sold-out New York Film Festival premiere was not from Holmes’ several appearances throughout the opening minute, but from Fielder, and just part of him—an obscured face making what any neophyte would naturally read as a resting expression. It’s a fair-enough response when taken hand-in-hand with the serious-documentary form (slightly overbearing music, greyscale color-grading) this movie wears like an odd suit, and one from which we see the paradox in being a major artist: the deeper one goes to establish their own style, the less a devotee’s willing to let them turn elsewhere.

But it can be hard, once an admirer, to discuss Nathan Fielder without lapsing into overly fawning, even obsequious tones. Yet Nathan for You is replete with Fielder seeming to possess some frightening, Dr. Mabuse-esque capacity for bending reality to his will; it’s no exaggeration to say turning these powers for persuasion and problem-solving towards evil could engender global catastrophe. The authorities exhibited therein haven’t burned quite as bright in the nine years since: The Rehearsal , for whatever honest greatness it has achieved, can suffer in comparison—a tad too strong the sense of controlled experiment, a tad too many seams visible in its editorial practice. You Can See Everything left me considering Fielder’s genius as choosing when or when not to engineer. Acknowledging that this film simply couldn’t have been made in real time or without certain stretches built on careful organization, it’s also his first project since Nathan for You that has the quality and danger of open-air experiment. The camera is not just turned on, we know full well; but once it is and allowed to rest on a subject facing direct, difficult questions, Fielder’s skills for social manipulation thrives on a Rick Rubin-like let-them-be-them philosophy. In a world where everyone, including himself, is totally nuts, Elizabeth Holmes and her husband, Billy Evans, just happen to be so on another level. Who inches the other out is a question you may be asking while reading this, then will continue asking after You Can See Everything .

I’ve been less fascinated with Elizabeth Holmes, whom I only knew to identify circa The Dropout , a 2022 miniseries that starred Amanda Seyfried as the turtleneck-wearing, mottle-throated scammer. Clips and contextualizing detail were sufficient; I’ve found it more telling that our culture’s awful habit of eventually affording every cretin actually-they’re-cool plaudits has never been afforded her. I say this to establish a personal bias—likely less than many will bring—that shapes my sense You Can See Everything ’s first stretch lacks much of its own. What these scenes (some built on candid conversation, some a tad more structured) instead exemplify is Fielder’s genius for the open-air investigation—often through his own failure to explain why he’s in Holmes’ seaside house to begin with, and from the contradiction borne of respecting those who have opened their doors but, in so doing, expose habits for which respect is an uneasy match.

Holmes, facing an incredibly harsh future on the basis of her mendacity, stands by the remarkable insistence that she’s never lied. Evans, amidst postures as a nice and caring husband, quickly steps in when his wife can’t whisk eggs fast enough, forcing Fielder to break his interrogation mid-sentence. Holmes claims ignorance towards the notion that words might have more than one direct meaning, leaving her equal parts helpless to explain Theranos’ failure or understand “Who’s on First?” while nevertheless—or for this?—grasping the depth of her situation. Evans downplays the extent of his family’s wealth when Fielder suggests it’s attractive to an erstwhile-billionaire wife. Holmes sends Fielder a text that is both the source for this film’s title and, despite my best efforts to parse, completely incoherent to the conversation they’ve just had or anything I might tether to greater happenings. Evans insists he’s prioritizing spousal care, a performance that spurs disturbing questions amidst his resistance to cooperate during the film’s second half. Or a second half that blooms exclusively through his cooperation and willingness to share (for his sake, for the film’s, for nothing’s) revelation after revelation.

These and many such perplexities abound until we witness Holmes enter prison from behind and afar, vanishing at You Can See Everything near-exact halftime. Whether Fielder and Oppenheim knew where to go next isn’t so obvious. A “Two Years Later” title card launches us from the spring 2023 to late 2025, and subjects now viewing the material we’ve sat through certainly implies thorough editing in that interim. What then ensues deserves discussion and, I’m sorry to say, is highly discouraged from such. The NYFF Q&A began with a notice that it a) should not be recorded by us and b) would not be made public until after the film’s release, a two-factor security system that still found Fielder and Oppenheim cautious to name any person or thing relevant to their movie’s second half.

Suffice to say, Fielder’s career-long investigation-through-recreation method is a more-than-suitable tool for You Can See Everything ’s well-established perspective on duplicity and sycophancy. Nor is it some deep spoiler to note that other figures will, almost by necessity of length, enter the frame. How that front-and-centering alters alchemy is a deeper quandary. Certainly it’s a means for turning inside-out to increasingly uncomfortable degrees, yet at turns I suspected the audience was forming their own obsequious attitude towards new players who, like Holmes, have an inability to articulate what’s directly before them while, unlike the convicted felon, avoiding derisive laughs.

Such ground-shifting choices beget queries about a project so concerned with the way questions can sublimate doubt. Is You Can See Everything ’s somewhat rote soundtrack—notes that get loud and louder until hush , dialogue—and solid but functional palette (often from DP David Bolen’s nevertheless impressive ability to work with a single light source) their play on stock doc form, or a dribbling-out of imagination? Am I talking in circles and making excuses to buttress my intense admiration for this, otherwise a surplus of imagination? Should I not suspect editorial tinkering whenever a conversation “starts” just as the scene begins? How effectively do the recreations parody prestige-TV style without falling into its traps? Am I convinced by its bigger gestures because I want to believe in Fielder’s larger project—which can often seem designed to showcase his genius—thus rendering me a dupe? Why is there not only an image of Evans’ penis, but one that lingers?

I can assert a minimal fascination with Elizabeth Holmes’ inner workings; I can tell you it did nothing to stop my leaning forward during a brief hitch in Nathan Fielder recalling a conversation with her, how this film then hinges on if she once said it or something ; I can voice admiration for his and Oppenheim’s patience to let us ponder that question deep into an extensive runtime as well as I appreciate the sustained reenactment interpolated throughout. You Can See Everything is replete with such tenacity, with a desire to sit as those in frame proceed per their truest selves or wobbly projections, their deficiencies or my own judgements, their charms or a dubious copy. The whole operation suggests being let in on a wild secret told by a person you have no reason to trust. Whether I’m talking about the auteur or subjects is one question; whether the subjects are the auteurs stands to review. This movie could be a dead rabbit pulled from a frayed hat or a benchmark or Fielder and Oppenheim fusing both into something altogether new. I don’t know the answer, I don’t want to tell myself, and I do not trust you to do the same.

You Can See Everything opens in theaters on Friday, October 16.

content.article_text:
N othing is safe from the scourge of immersification. They’ve turned Gustav Klimt and Vincent Van Gogh into vast, projection-mapped digital environments; they’ve told the stories of the moon landings and the dinosaurs and David Bowie as floor-to-ceiling electronic spectacles; and now they’ve come for Aardman . For Wallace and Gromit and Shaun the Sheep, our national treasures. Is nothing sacred?

The latest immersive cinematic experience at Lightroom is a big, eye-popping celebration of Aardman Animations, the company behind the world’s favourite claymation films and TV shows. It moves between documentary storytelling, behind-the-scenes insight and dazzling immersive renderings of all your wide-grinned, cheeky northern favourites.

We get to hear about how Peter Lord and David Sproxton met in suburban Surrey and started messing around with clay, before joining forces with Nick Park and setting in motion a series of events that would take them from Woking to the stars. We get to hear about how they first made Morph out of a ball of clay, how the animators hilariously act out all the scenes to camera themselves before moving over to puppets, how they make the mouths form the “eeee” sound of the word cheese, all interspersed with Shaun the Sheep doing a barn-based talent show and clips from their biggest cinematic triumphs.

And it makes a pretty convincing argument for why Aardman is so important, so beloved by so many people. Early on, it cuts to a clip from 1989’s A Grand Day Out, the first Wallace & Gromit film. At this huge scale you see every lump and bump in the clay, every finger print and smudge. It looks so real, so human. Director Lucy Izzard says in a voiceover: “I think people still crave imperfection,” and you think yes, that’s it, that’s why Aardman matters. It’s something incredibly human in an age when things feel so amazingly non-human so much of the time.

Does that hand-made, imperfect, homely aesthetic rub up awkwardly against the technological wizardry of immersive cinema? Sure does. But the bigger issue is that this experience doesn’t really know what it wants to be.

It ends up as half-documentary, half-clip show, becoming sort of neither in the process, and a bit hard to follow too. It doesn’t even take full advantage of Lightroom’s capabilities. It could be bolder, more fun, it could play with the immersive format a bit more.

One good use of the tech are the side screens, which make you feel like you are inside various environments: Shaun the Sheep’s barn, Gromit’s cardboard box as he spies on Feathers McGraw, behind the recording desk as actors do their vocal takes. But it’s not quite enough.

There’s some fun stuff here. It’s great seeing Creature Comforts recreated in living rooms and gardens, it’s nice to see all the concept art and storyboards come to life, it’s pretty joyful watching the amazing video for Peter Gabriel’s Sledgehammer at such an enormous scale. It just lacks the crowd-pleasing immersive thrills of Lightroom’s recent Prehistoric Planet: Discovering Dinosaurs.

As a jaded, tired contemporary art critic, I may not be the target audience, so I brought along someone called Solomon. What are his qualifications? Well, he’s four, and yesterday he went to the cinema to see the latest Shaun the Sheep movie , so you could say he’s something of a young cinephile. Also, his father (me) is a critic, so he is probably genetically predisposed to have opinions about this.

Halfway through, I ask what he thinks. He says: “When is the movie starting? This is just ads.” He’s right – the whole thing just feels like an advert for Aardman. “When is the movie starting?” he asks again, more impatient this time, almost pleading. “This is it,” I say. “It’s sort of a documentary.” He stares at me, uncomprehending, and then yawns. Ouch, he really is a critic.

It doesn’t really have enough for kids, and the storytelling isn’t strong enough for adults. It’s gimmick over narrative, as if they didn’t ask: “How can we make an amazing immersive experience?” but instead asked: “How can we tell our story in an immersive-ish way?” And those are two different propositions.

This show doesn’t tarnish Aardman’s stellar reputation, nor detract from all the amazing, quirky, quaint, funny work that they’ve done, but it doesn’t add a huge amount to it either. More of a rubber glove on the head than a crowning achievement.

content.article_text:
It is 50 years since cultural historian Naseem Khan’s challenge to the British arts establishment was first published, and the question of who and what counts as British continues to be contested.

The Arts Britain Ignores – Khan’s groundbreaking 1976 report, commissioned by organisations including the then Arts Council of Great Britain, presented a vision of a pluralistic national culture, in which the creativity of Britons of diverse ethnic backgrounds – from bhangra music, to black painters and Ukrainian dance – should be recognised, supported and respected.

Today, when polls, debates and cultural and political moments present differing notions of British identity – whether it is the diversity of the England football team , or how political figures choose to define their own identities – Khan’s work retains its relevance.

On Wednesday, Dawn Airey, the new chair of cultural funding and development agency Arts Council England , will give her inaugural speech at a conference celebrating Khan’s legacy – The Arts Britain Ignores: 50 Years On – at Serendipity Institute for Black Arts and Heritage in Leicester.

Today, the work of black and Asian British visual artists, such as Frank Bowling, Sonia Boyce and Anish Kapoor is critically acclaimed and in demand. But in 1976, Khan documented how grassroot arts and cultural practices that thrived in UK ethnic minority communities were largely ignored by funders and critics.

This week’s conference, bringing together artists, organisations, experts and policymakers, will explore how much progress has been made in 50 years and comes at a time when community and independent cultural spaces face pressures over finances, redevelopment and gentrification.

Contributors to Wednesday’s conference include Khan’s daughter, Amelia Torode, the theatre director Jatinder Verma, the broadcaster Brenda Emmanus and the crossbench peer and chancellor of the University of Nottingham, Lola Young.

The conference also marks the launch of a new book, The Arts Britain Ignores at 50, published by Serendipity Institute , including essays and new research.

Pawlet Brookes, the chief executive and artistic director of Serendipity Institute, said: “We had Cool Britannia, we’ve had the ‘ain’t no black in the union jack’. We’ve had all of that narrative. But the reality is British is diverse – whether that diversity is layered with colour or layered in other ways. We can go down a negative road, or we can celebrate what we have, which is fantastic, the best in Europe – although we still have some way to go.”

Describing Khan’s work as “seminal”, Brookes said it was time to “see how far we’ve travelled, and what we need to do for the next 50 years.”

She added: “We did a timeline investigation [for the new book] and what it shows is that, there has been funding for culturally diverse organisations, but what there hasn’t been is sustainability and growth.

“We also need recognition for dance and theatre, in the way that progress has been made in the visual arts.”

In her speech, Airey is expected to say: “The journey Khan set us on remains one of the most important our sector is undertaking … [it] will sit at the centre of my work.”

She praises Khan as having told institutions such as the Arts Council that “you have built an entire cultural establishment – its funding structures, its buildings, its critics, its canon – around a definition of British art that leaves whole swathes of it out.”

Airey is also expected to say: “It a hard time to be an artist in this country, whatever your background – but for many people in this room it is harder still.

“Racism, Islamophobia and antisemitism are part of daily life for too many people in our sector: sometimes in crude and obvious ways, sometimes in subtle and deniable ones, but constantly there … So let me be emphatic. Those of us who don’t experience this – and I include myself – have a responsibility to stand with you: to stand up for the work you want to make, and to back that with action, not just words.”

content.article_text:
Two films have won five of the prizes at the Busan Asian Project Market (APM).

Indonesian director Aditya Ahmad’s “ Goldfish ” took three and Indian filmmaker Tribeny Rai’s “ A Chronicle of Minor Things ” (working title) took two. The awards were part of the Asian Contents & Film Market’s (ACFM) first combined ceremony.

“Goldfish” won the QCinema Special Award, the Kongchak Studio Award and the VIPO Award. Ahmad’s first feature is set in South Sulawesi, where he grew up, and centers on a boy who flees his father. Muhammad Zaidy and Meiske Taurisia are producing. The project also received money from this year’s ACF Script Development Fund. It was selected for APM, where it took part in business meetings.

Related Stories

Danny Trejo Had ‘Never Heard’ of Ben Shapiro Before Signing On for Daily Wire’s ‘Pawn Shop,’ Says His Son: ‘It’s F---ed Up. He’s Handcuffed to This Stupid Project’

How 'Ink' Production Designers Recreated The Sun Newsroom Using Functional Linotype Machines, Working Rotary Phones and Old Typewriters

Rai’s project is produced by Kislay and took the Sørfond Award and the APM Busan Award. The APM Busan Award recognized its original story and structure, and the way Rai works a social issue quietly into the narrative. The citation also said its setting and themes could appeal to audiences outside India.

Popular on Variety

Six other projects also won APM awards. Actor-director Reza Rahadian’s “Casparina” is a family drama built from a personal story. It won the CJ ENM Award. Kim Jinyeong’s “Red Hunger” won the Kantana Picture Award, and Panu Aree’s “Fātimah” won the Kantana Virtual Production Award. Yen Hao-hsuan’s “Uncle” draws on the director’s own life to look at family, shame and belonging as Taiwan changes fast. It took the CathayPlay Award and was praised for giving a character with an intellectual disability full depth and dignity. Park Syeyoung’s “Satellite of Love” won the Songwon Award, and E Del Mundo’s “Once Upon a Time in the Philippines” won the ArteKino International Award.

APM’s submissions hit a record 604 this year, from 48 countries. Its official selection had 30 projects from 17 countries, and eight of them shared prizes across 11 categories.

“Today’s awards recognize the promise of these projects and the stories they have yet to bring to life. ACFM’s awards do not end in Busan. They travel on to Jakarta, Manila, Oslo and Bangkok,” said ACFM director Ellen Y.D. Kim.

At the ceremony, ACFM also honored three international co-productions with Korean involvement that won the ACF Co-Production Support Fund in August. Fukada Koji’s “Grateful” gets KRW60 million ($41,700). Jakrawal Nilthamrong’s “Rhizome” and Boo Junfeng’s “Trinity” get KRW40 million ($27,800) each.

Doc Square gave out two new prizes at its documentary work-in-progress showcase. Three projects won the Impact Asia Award, and each receives $5,000. They were Ma Chi Hang’s “Moon Is Watching You,” Jang Minkyung’s “Our Waves,” and “Restless Farewell,” directed by Yang Nan and He Peiyun. “Restless Farewell” is about young migrant workers in precarious jobs in Shanghai, and it also won the Newstapa Award. That prize includes KRW10 million ($6,900) for production. Once the film is complete, it will also have the chance to screen a 60-minute cut on the Newstapa Foundation’s channels.

From the Busan Story Market, “My Upstairs Neighbors” from Clayhouse and “Friend Request” from Ryoung Studio won the JAFF Market IP Connection Award. Both will go to Indonesia’s Jogja-NETPAC Asian Film Festival for its JAFF IP Connection program. At InnoAsia, Taiwan’s imCore Corp. won the MPS Award, chosen by industry votes. Korean startups Lumicraft and Reproduction took the AWS Award, which comes with KRW10 million ($6,900) in AWS cloud vouchers. Lumicraft makes an AI casting platform called Castlink. Reproduction makes Pre-Flow, a tool for screenplay analysis and sharing production data.

APM hosted 746 business meetings with 133 companies. The Busan Story Market held 520 meetings with 136 companies. ACFM ran Oct. 10–13, and the Busan International Film Festival continues through Oct. 15.

content.article_text:
La muerte de RJ Mitte , reconocido mundialmente por interpretar a Walter White Jr. en Breaking Bad , conmocionó a Hollywood y especialmente a quienes compartieron con él los años de rodaje de la exitosa serie.

El actor falleció el lunes 12 de octubre a los 34 años, según confirmó su representante. Entre las numerosas despedidas, una de las más emotivas fue la de Bryan Cranston , quien interpretó a su padre en la ficción y mantuvo una relación cercana con él incluso después del final de la producción.

A través de su cuenta de Instagram, Cranston publicó una extensa carta en la que recordó sus primeros encuentros con Mitte, su crecimiento profesional y el vínculo que construyeron durante más de una década.

La emotiva despedida de Bryan Cranston

Cranston comenzó su mensaje expresando el profundo dolor que le provocó la noticia. El actor recordó que conoció a Mitte cuando tenía apenas 14 años, después de que fuera seleccionado para interpretar a Walter White Jr., el hijo adolescente de Walter y Skyler White.

Desde el comienzo, destacó su entusiasmo por la actuación y la determinación con la que enfrentaba las exigencias de una producción televisiva de semejante magnitud. También recordó cómo él y Anna Gunn, quien interpretaba a Skyler, intentaban aconsejarlo durante los rodajes, aunque el joven actor, como cualquier adolescente, no siempre seguía sus recomendaciones.

Te puede interesar

Bryan Cranston habló sobre su retiro de la actuación

Bryan Cranston y Aaron Paul juntos en una nueva serie

Con el paso de las temporadas, Cranston fue testigo de su transformación en un intérprete cada vez más experimentado.

El encuentro que nunca llegó a concretarse

Uno de los momentos más conmovedores de la publicación llegó cuando Cranston reveló que ambos habían intercambiado mensajes apenas unas semanas antes de la muerte de Mitte. Los actores estaban intentando organizar un almuerzo para reencontrarse, pero ese encuentro nunca llegó a concretarse.

Cranston se preguntó si aquella reunión podría haber cambiado algo, aunque reconoció que nunca tendrá una respuesta. El actor cerró su despedida con un:

“Te voy a extrañar, hijo”.

Sus palabras reflejan un vínculo que trascendió la pantalla y continuó mucho después de que Breaking Bad emitiera su último episodio en 2013.

¿Quién era RJ Mitte?

Nacido el 21 de agosto de 1992, Roy Frank Mitte III , conocido artísticamente como RJ Mitte, alcanzó la fama internacional gracias a su interpretación de Walter White Jr., también llamado Flynn, en Breaking Bad .

El personaje era el hijo de Walter White, interpretado por Cranston, y Skyler White, interpretada por Anna Gunn.

Mitte participó en las cinco temporadas de la serie creada por Vince Gilligan, que se emitió entre 2008 y 2013 y se convirtió en una de las producciones más aclamadas de la historia de la televisión.

Al igual que su personaje, Mitte tenía parálisis cerebral, una condición que lo llevó a involucrarse activamente en la defensa de los derechos de las personas con discapacidad.

Después del final de Breaking Bad , continuó trabajando en cine y televisión y participó en producciones como Switched at Birth , Triumph y Standing Up for Sunny .

Además, desarrolló una importante actividad como defensor de la inclusión y la representación de las personas con discapacidad dentro de la industria audiovisual.

La despedida del elenco de Breaking Bad

Cranston no fue el único integrante de la serie que expresó su tristeza. Aaron Paul , quien interpretó a Jesse Pinkman, y Dean Norris , recordado por su papel de Hank Schrader, también compartieron mensajes en memoria de su compañero.

La muerte de Mitte generó numerosas reacciones entre los seguidores de Breaking Bad , una serie que, a más de una década de su final, continúa ocupando un lugar fundamental en la cultura popular.

Según confirmó su representante, el actor murió por suicidio. En su despedida, Cranston también hizo un llamado a quienes atraviesan situaciones de sufrimiento emocional para que busquen acompañamiento y ayuda profesional.

Más allá de su recordado papel como Walter White Jr., RJ Mitte deja un legado vinculado a la actuación, la inclusión y la representación de las personas con discapacidad .

Y para Bryan Cranston, además de un compañero de trabajo, siempre será aquel adolescente al que vio crecer durante cinco temporadas y al que todavía recordaba como su hijo.

content.article_text:
“The Batman” star Robert Pattinson has offered his first comments after the highly anticipated DC superhero sequel had to pause production last week . Matt Reeves , who is returning to direct the follow-up, had to step away from production due to a “family matter.”

“We’re pausing for a little bit and then we’re going to figure it all out,” Pattinson told the Official Pop Drop at the London Film Festival’s U.K. premiere of his new film “Primetime.”

Related Stories

Whistleblowing Portal Launches in U.K. for Entertainment Industry Workers to Report Abuse, Harassment and Discrimination

Ethan Hawke Stars in Supernatural Horror Podcast 'Midnight Radio': 'There’s an Intimacy to the Audio-Only Medium'

On Oct. 5, news broke that Reeves needed to take a step back from filming; no reason has been given for his leave nor has there been any update on if “The Batman Part II” will need to shift its release date from Feb. 18, 2028.

Popular on Variety

“Production on ‘The Batman Part II’ has been temporarily paused while Matt Reeves focuses on a family matter,” a rep said in a statement last Monday. “Matt has the full support of DC Studios and we look forward to continuing the journey soon.”

Along with Pattinson, other cast members for “The Batman Part II” include Scarlett Johansson, Sebastian Stan, Charles Dance, Brian Tyree Henry, Colin Farrell as the Penguin, Andy Serkis as Alfred Pennyworth and Jeffrey Wright as Commissioner Gordon.

It’s been a long journey for “The Batman” sequel, with several delays along the way. The movie was first slated to release on Oct. 2, 2026, before Warner Bros. delayed it a year to Oct. 1, 2027. Then, the studio pushed the film to February 2028. Reeves and Pattinson’s first “Batman” was released on March 4, 2022, meaning the sequel will land six years after the original.

See Pattinson’s full interview below.

content.article_text:
Over the past few years, museums have increasingly spotlighted women artists whose practices extend into printmaking. The Philadelphia Museum of Art presented “ Julie Mehretu : In Focus” in 2025, following its acquisition of two monumental print series by the artist. The attention on women printmakers has also been seen at art fairs. The 2025 IFPDA Print Fair commissioned Mickalene Thomas to create a site-specific installation exploring the possibilities of printmaking at the Park Avenue Armory in New York, and artists like Laura Owens , Joan Hall , and Louise Bourgeois took center stage across the fair’s booths this year .

Mickalene Thomas, Interior: Fireplace with Blackbird , 2016. Mixed media collage with screenprint, woodcut, digital print, etching, gold leaf, wood veneer, and flocking on Saunders Waterford paper. Courtesy of Artnet Auctions.

But is the market for women printmakers keeping pace with this institutional attention? To find out, we examined auction results from the Artnet Price Database , and the findings are more complicated than a simple price comparison suggests.

Prints and multiples by women artists account for just 7 percent of the $2.18 billion in combined editions sales between 2022 and 2026, but that gap is driven by volume, not value. In that period, 286,970 editioned works by male artists came to auction, compared with 24,144 by women. On price alone, women’s prints sell for only slightly less on average than men’s, with a higher sell-through rate and more frequent results above high estimate. The market is clearly there for women artists who make it to auction; representation and availability remain the real obstacles.

Helen Frankenthaler, Contentment Island , 2004. Screenprint in colors on Rives BFK paper. Courtesy of Artnet Auctions

A more complicated picture of the gender gap

Published research has documented a significant gender price gap in the broader art auction market. A 2021 study by Renée Adams , Roman Kräussl , Marco Navone , and Patrick Verwijmeren , based on 1.9 million auction transactions across 49 countries, found that paintings by female artists sold for 42.1 percent less, on average, than paintings by male artists. But does the same disparity hold for prints and editions?

Artnet Price Database data covering 2022–2026 suggests that the answer is not that straightforward. Over this period, the median auction price for prints and multiples by women artists was approximately $2,016, including buyer’s premium, just above the $1,937 median for prints and multiples by men.

Women’s prints also performed slightly better on other measures. Over the same period, 78.8 percent of lots by women artists sold, compared with 75.2 percent of those by men. And 43.1 percent of women’s lots sold above their high estimates, versus 41.1 percent of men’s.

These figures complicate the assumption that women’s prints consistently lag men’s in the secondary market. They suggest that women’s works are performing competitively on several measures, even as differences in average prices and overall sales volume persist.

Who is leading the women’s prints market?

Looking more closely at which women artists are driving the prints market reveals another layer to the story. From 2022 through 2026, Yayoi Kusama remained the clear leader by total auction sales value, underscoring both the strength of demand for her work and the extraordinary prolificacy of her printmaking practice.

But total sales value is also a measure of market volume: Artists with large bodies of prints and multiples appearing regularly at auction have more opportunities to accumulate sales than those whose editions are produced or traded less frequently. For that reason, the rankings offer a picture of the size and activity of an artist’s market rather than a direct comparison of the value of individual works.

Julie Mehretu, Unclosed , 2007. Etching with aquatint and drypoint in colors on Somerset paper. Courtesy of Artnet Auctions

Beyond Kusama, the recent data shows a mix of established printmakers and contemporary artists attracting significant activity. Helen Frankenthaler , Käthe Kollwitz , Bridget Riley , Vija Celmins , and Barbara Kruger remain among the market’s established names, while Julie Mehretu , Kara Walker , and Tracey Emin have emerged as particularly notable presences in recent years. Between them, they generated approximately $6.7 million in prints and multiples sales between 2022 and 2026, placing them among the leading contemporary women artists in recent years.

The data also points to a deeper historical imbalance. Of the 15 top-performing women printmakers by auction value, only three were born before 1900, and none before 1867. This isn’t necessarily evidence that women weren’t making prints earlier; rather, it reflects how much work may still be needed to bring this material to the market. Over half of these top-performing printmakers are also American, pointing to the democratization efforts of printmaking studios during the Postwar Print Renaissance in the U.S., especially after Tatyana Grosman founded Universal Limited Art Editions in 1957, setting the standard for printmaking in the country.

Taken together, the rankings point to a market that is both concentrated and evolving. Long-established names continue to account for substantial sales, while artists such as Mehretu and Emin are gaining ground, suggesting that the hierarchy of the women’s prints market is not necessarily fixed. The market, though, remains firmly anchored to 20 th- and 21 st- century production.

What publishers see before works reach auction

Auction results tell only part of the story. The primary market for prints and editions begins with artists, publishers, and printers, whose decisions about edition size, release prices, and production can shape the market long before works reach the auction block.

Conner Williams , head of prints and multiples at Artnet Auctions , notes that, “in recent years, women artists working in print have, to far less fanfare than public auction, produced editions made available directly for purchase through various print-publishers and at prices that would be noteworthy if only public. Julie Mehretu, Elizabeth Peyton , Cecily Brown , and Dana Schutz , to name a few, have collaborated with leading international publishers including BORCH Editions , Gemini G.E.L. , and Two Palms , to regularly sell their prints at prices exceeding $100,000. In many cases, these new releases outperform those of their contemporary male counterparts. Because sales in this segment of the market are often private and less transparent than public auctions, these achievements are not widely known, leaving many collectors unaware of the extraordinary demand and value these artists have generated through printmaking.”

The publishers’ perspectives can help illuminate a dimension that auction data alone cannot capture: whether interest in women artists is broadening among collectors, how publishers approach pricing, and whether strong demand at release translates into sustained secondary-market performance.

Elizabeth Peyton, Kiss (Jackson + Ally, Bradley + Stephanie, A Star is Born) #1 , 2019. Monotype on Twinrocker handmade paper. Courtesy of Artnet Auctions

A market still taking shape

The growing visibility of women artists in printmaking is also reflected in Artnet Auctions’ current “Premier Prints & Multiples” sale, which includes works by Julie Mehretu, Elizabeth Peyton, Vija Celmins, Mickalene Thomas, Helen Frankenthaler, Beatriz Milhazes , and Katherine Bernhardt . Spanning generations and approaches to the medium, the works offer a snapshot of the breadth of contemporary collecting of women artists in the medium.

Ultimately, the question may not be whether women artists are having a moment in prints. Museum acquisitions, institutional programming, fairs, and the auction data all point to meaningful activity. The harder question is how broadly that momentum is being felt, and whether increased visibility is translating into lasting market value across generations of women artists.

The data suggests that the relationship between gender and auction performance is more nuanced in prints and multiples than a single price-gap figure might imply.

For now, the results offer a reason to look beyond headline prices, and to ask not only which women artists are selling, but how the market for their work is evolving.

content.editorial_title_zh: 《理智与情感》影评：乔治亚·奥克利以敏锐视角改编简·奥斯汀
content.editorial_excerpt_zh: 奥斯汀改编总让人想与前作比较，尤其李安的版本为艾玛·汤普森赢得了第二座奥斯卡。乔治亚·奥克利明白这一点，没有试图重新发明轮子……
content.editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "谈论简·奥斯汀作品的影视改编时，总让人忍不住拿它与先前版本比较。尤其在这里，最著名的前作是李安的版本，艾玛·汤普森也凭它赢得了自己的第二座奥斯卡。乔治亚·奥克利明白这一点；她没有试图重新发明轮子或颠覆文本，而是交出了一部出色的改编，足以证明这个故事值得再讲一次。我们固然渴望原创故事，但扎实地转译一部经得起考验的作品，同样能带来乐趣。这也确认了《蓝色珍妮》的导演是一位重要人才：她拥有出众的眼光，能在外来的素材上留下鲜明印记，又不会用力过度。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "影片几乎不在铺垫上耗费时间：片头字幕叠在一名女孩躺在田野里的画面上；接着，我们得知达什伍德家的父亲已经去世，除非大女儿埃莉诺（黛西·埃德加-琼斯）或二女儿玛丽安（埃斯梅·克里德-迈尔斯）嫁给一个有钱人，否则母亲和女儿们便可能失去住宅及上流社会的位置，将这一切让给他的儿子约翰和妻子范妮（斯泰西·马汀）。性格内敛的埃莉诺，与范妮的哥哥爱德华·费拉斯（乔治·麦凯）试探着建立某种……关系；而玛丽安更愿意追随情感，简直可以说是“跌入”了对约翰·威洛比（弗兰克·迪兰）的爱恋。一位年长、疏离的家庭友人布兰登上校（赫伯特·诺德鲁姆）一直在旁，暗示她也许会走向一条更出人意料的道路。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "故事的发展并没有多少特别的惊喜。即使你是第一次接触这个故事的任何版本，奥斯汀搭建的爱情结构也如此稳固，以至于结尾故弄悬念时，难免让人稍感不耐。好在她也是一位机智的作家，而这一版充分体现了这一点。埃德加-琼斯与克里德-迈尔斯饰演姐妹，配合极佳，在典型的手足针锋相对与真诚的深厚情谊之间取得平衡。凯特芮娜·巴尔夫演绎的母亲颇为讨喜，只希望女儿们过得好——尽管她显然更希望她们赶快结婚——并经常运用奥斯汀式的冷幽默。博迪·蕾·布雷思纳奇饰演小女儿玛格丽特，补全了这个家庭，也制造了不少笑声。菲奥娜·肖饰演粗鲁的詹宁斯太太，登场不错，却很快就显得戏份过多，虽还不至于打乱整部电影的节奏。几位男演员的表现都相当得体。麦凯的面容与气质仿佛天生适合年代片，尤其演出了英雄人物的潇洒；迪兰既有机会展现更温暖的一面，也演出了他在《Urchin》中所饰演的有害男性角色的一种变奏；诺德鲁姆则说出了一口颇不错的英语口音，只是受角色本身限制，似乎没得到更深入挖掘的机会。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "真正的主角，是奥克利的导演功力。她拥有极佳的视觉眼光，再加上阿诺·波蒂埃丰润的摄影，足以跻身年度最佳之列。有时，影片采用泰伦斯·马利克式的游移手持镜头，甚至连画外音也一并出现；这种拍法，比《Hamnet》耗费大量篇幅描绘自然世界所取得的效果还要好。室内对话场景中，她偏爱镜面，并在餐桌上的谈话者之间微妙地转移焦点。手法只有一点点炫技，却让人看到，一位熟练掌握电影技艺的导演终于得到了舒展身手的机会。舞蹈段落尤其能体现这一点：她捕捉身体移动的方式，单是看着就令人愉悦。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "如同《蓝色珍妮》，这归根结底也是一个关于压抑、以及女性在世界上处于何种位置的故事。影片节奏轻快，却巧妙而细腻地展开了这些主题。达什伍德一家从相当体面的中产住宅搬进简陋小屋；对她们而言，婚姻意味着生存，那一时代几乎所有女性都如此。她们必须摸清前来求婚的男人的心意，不只是为了爱情，也为了判断对方的意图是否真诚、是否值得信赖。最终，这是一部关于情感必须得到表达的电影，奥克利将这些情感自如地传递给观众。它也许不会取代你最爱的版本，却是一部有趣、制作精良、足以独立成立的改编：既能成为参与者事业的新起点，也让观影本身充满愉悦。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "《理智与情感》将于10月16日、星期五上映。", "translated": true}]

content.article_text:
It’s always tempting to discuss Jane Austen adaptations in comparison with their predecessors, especially when the most famous example here is Ang Lee’s version that earned Emma Thompson her second Oscar. Georgia Oakley recognizes this; rather than trying to reinvent the wheel or subvert this text, she instead delivers a sublime take that more than justifies returning to the well once more. For as much as we desire original stories, there’s just as much pleasure to be taken from a solid translation of sturdy material. And it confirms the Blue Jean director as a major talent—a great eye who can put a definite stamp on outside sources without going overboard.

Very little time is wasted on setup: the credits play over images of a girl lounging in a field; we then learn that the Dashwood patriarch has died and his wife and daughters are in danger of losing their house (and their place in the upper class) to his son John and his wife Fanny (Stacey Martin), unless either eldest stepdaughter Elinor (Daisy Edgar-Jones) or middle child Marianne (Esmé Creed-Miles) gets hitched to someone of means. The former, more reserved, starts up a tentative… something with Fanny’s brother Edward Ferrars (George MacKay) while the latter, prone to feeling her feelings, quite literally falls for John Willoughby (Frank Dillane). An older, aloof family friend named Colonel Brandon (Herbert Nordrum) hovering in the background suggests a more unexpected path for her.

There are no particular surprises for where this turns. Even if it’s your first time engaging with any version of her story, Austen created such a sturdy romantic structure that it’s easy to get a tad annoyed towards the end as it springs for the fakeout. Luckily, she was also a writer of wit, and this iteration embodies that in spades. Edgar-Jones and Creed-Miles are perfectly matched as sisters, balancing classic sibling antagonism with true, heartfelt devotion. Caitríona Balfe does pleasant business as the matriarch who simply wants the best for her daughters (though she clearly would prefer they get married soon), often utilizing the dry wit so associated with Austen, while Bodhi Rae Breathnach rounds out the family as youngest daughter Margaret and gets a lot of laughs. Fiona Shaw, meanwhile, has a good intro as the boorish Mrs. Jennings, but rapidly overstays her welcome (though not quite enough to throw off proceedings). The men all acquit themselves rather well. MacKay, with a face and presence built for a period piece, makes a particularly dashing hero; Dillane gets a chance to show off a warmer register as well as a variation of the toxic man he played in Urchin ; and Nordrum pulls off a pretty good English accent, though one feels he doesn’t quite get the chance to burrow as deep just by the nature of his character.

The real star is Oakley’s direction. She possesses a fantastic eye, aided by Arnaud Potier’s lush cinematography, that surely ranks with the year’s best. At times it adopts the roving, handheld Malickian style (complete with voiceover!) and does so far better than Hamnet ever achieved with all the time it spent in the natural world. When indoors, she favors mirrors while characters are in conversation, subtly shifting focus between speakers at a dinner. It’s only a little showy, but demonstrates someone with a command of craft getting the chance to stretch herself—perhaps best seen in the way she captures bodies moving during dance sequences that simply look so pleasing.

Much like Blue Jean , this is also, in the end, a story about repression and a woman’s place in the world, themes that are drawn out deftly and subtly during a brisk runtime. For the Dashwoods—moved as they are from a rather nice middle-class house to a shabby cottage—marriage is survival, as it is for basically every woman in the period; they must suss out the whims of the men who come courting them not just for love, but whether they can actually be counted on to be honest with their intentions. In the end, this is a movie about feelings needing to be expressed, and Oakley translates them to the viewer with aplomb. Maybe it won’t supplant your favorite version, but it’s an entertaining, well-crafted take that more than stands on its own, as much a springboard for those involved as it is a delight to watch.

Sense and Sensibility opens on Friday, October 16.

content.article_text:
The International Documentary Film Festival Amsterdam, the world’s leading documentary festival, has unveiled the main competition lineups for the 39th edition, which runs from Nov. 12 to 22. “White Tiger Column” opens the event, at which 253 titles from 80 countries will screen.

Newly unveiled selections include the International and Envision Competitions, Luminous, Frontlight and the IDFA DocLab competition selections, and the nominations for all cross-section awards.

Related Stories

BBC, ZDF Cold War Thriller ‘Honey’ Offers Sex, Lies – and Prosthetic Testicles: ‘There’s an Innate Comedy and Absurdity to Spying’

Katherine Mallen Kupferer, Audrey Grace Marshall, Dean Norris, Jordan Ladd Join ‘The Attentionist’ from Caroline Kepnes (EXCLUSIVE)

Opening film IDFA opens with the world premiere of “White Tiger Column” by Robert Mentov, Dwight Jantzi and Bryan Dickie, following a group of recruits through 45 days of training with Myanmar ’s resistance movement. In a training camp deep in the jungle, the filmmakers capture the daily lives of young volunteers as they prepare to fight for their freedom.

Popular on Variety

“White Tiger Column” has been selected for the International Competition and nominated for the IDFA Award for Best First Feature.

International Competition The International Competition brings together works that “invite curiosity and critical reflection on our world today,” IDFA said. The selection of 13 titles brings together established veteran voices next to first-time filmmakers, with 12 films presenting their world or international premieres.

Bardi, dir. Tala Hadid (Morocco), 108’ – European Premiere

Crack in the Head, Crack in the Sky, dir. Mehran Tamadon (France), 120’ – World Premiere

Down the River, dir. Ruslan Fedotov (Germany), 79’ – World Premiere

Hazara Town, dir. Khadim Dai (Belgium/Australia/Germany), 103’ – World Premiere

Here Where the Fire Burns, dir. Juan Manuel Sepúlveda (Mexico), 97’ – World Premiere

An Incomplete Day in the History of Georgia 10.06.93, dir. Salomé Jashi (Georgia), 100’ – World Premiere

Lonan Tché, dir. Joël Richmond Mathieu Akafou (France/Italy/Ivory Coast/Senegal), 95’ – World Premiere

Mangabangabaka, dir. Michaël Andrianaly (France/Madagascar/Burkina Faso), 92’ – World Premiere

Morro Grande, dir. Isabel Joffily, Rita Toledo (Brazil/Netherlands), 88’ – World Premiere

Still Night, Burning House, dir. Carol Nguyen (Canada), 76’ – International Premiere

White Tiger Column, dir. Robert Mentov, Dwight Jantzi, Bryan Dickie (Canada), 95’ – World Premiere

Women and War, dir. Elwira Niewiera (Germany/Poland/Ukraine), 103’ – World Premiere

The Year of the Ghost, dir. Louis Hothothot (Netherlands/China), 95’ – World Premiere

Envision Competition The Envision Competition offers “13 unparalleled films, each of them stylistically arresting, as visionary filmmakers forge new cinematic languages,” the festival said.

“The selection brings together titles in which form drives the narrative. Through distinctive visual approaches and formal choices, the filmmakers deconstruct and reframe the complexities of our world, offering new ways of seeing and understanding the subjects they explore.”

Bahía Honda, dir. Alejandro Alonso Estrella (Cuba/France/Norway), 85’ – World Premiere

Between Revolutions, dir. Ruben Desiere (Belgium/Netherlands), 78’ – World Premiere

The Black Box Is Orange, dir. Yuula Benivolski (Canada), 89’ – International Premiere

Drop! Cover! Hold On!, dir. Stéphanie Roland (Belgium/France), 77’ – World Premiere

Lyrical Vengeance, dir. wendelien van oldenborgh (Netherlands), 111’ – World Premiere

Memories, dir. Anna Falguères (Belgium/France), 78’ – World Premiere

Memories of Lightning, dir. Riccardo Giacconi (France/Italy), 73’ – International Premiere

My Own Personal Gulag, dir. Lina Gorbaneva (Spain), 84’ – World Premiere

Radiant Mountain, dir. Miguel Moraes Cabral (Belgium/Portugal/France), 75’ – World Premiere

Ragazzi al fiume, dir. Pablo Briones (Switzerland), 75’ – World Premiere

Rivers of Memory, dir. Shishir Jha (India), 72’ – World Premiere

Vertigo Garden, dir. Lei Lei (Hong Kong / SAR /China), 73’ – World Premiere

You Don’t Die Two Times, dir. Ager Oueslati (Algeria/Germany/Netherlands), 90’ – World Premiere

Luminous The premiere-only section Luminous presents “a wide range of styles and formalist approaches, from observational to personal to experimental. Across both feature-length and short films, the titles grapple with big questions of life through deeply personal, lived experiences,” IDFA said.

Among the selection of 21 films, 19 titles are world or international premieres, including nine debut feature films.

In the immersive and poetic “Where the Sun Is Born” by Laura Bermúdez and Jorge García, a dancer leaves the city in Honduras to travel back to the Afro-Caribbean Garifuna community of his youth—in search of his roots and a sense of community.

The IDFA Bertha Fund-supported “She Was Not Alone” by Hussein Al-asadi closely follows Zaira, an elderly woman living in close communion with nature in the marshlands of southern Iraq—meditatively illuminating an idyllic place, increasingly under threat.

In the IDFA Project Space NL alumni Raluca Lupaşcu’s “A Modern Roma Fairytale,” 10-year-old Nicoleta, granddaughter of a Roma king, grows up dreaming of a life in a marble palace—while watching the women around her navigate the restrictions of the patriarchal traditions that will shape her future.

In “Every Death Diminishes Me,” Sergii Bazhenov trains as a medic to join the front lines, documenting his colleagues as they treat the wounded and confront the human cost of war.

Frontlight The premiere-only section Frontlight showcases 16 films, from “critically examinations of the truth and urgent issues of our time to portraits of artists and their work.” Fifteen of the selected titles are world or international premieres.

“Several films offer immediate responses to critical current events, while others take time to reflect, examining the social realities and challenges shaping people’s lives,” IDFA said.

“The Big Boom!” by Gabriel Tejedor explores a Bulgarian arms manufacturer in Kazanlak, rife with contradictions and simmering tension, where the machine guns and rockets are destined for Ukraine while many of its employees are pro-Putin.

In “No Man’s Air” by Peter Delpeut and Gerco de Ruijter, a pilot recalls the last flight to Nicosia Airport in July 1974, as a Turkish invasion of Cyprus loomed.

Afsaneh Salari’s “Tehran, Under the Skin” enters Tehran’s cosmetic clinics to explore the pressures behind Iran’s widespread culture of cosmetic surgery in pursuit of physical perfection, in a conservative society that seeks to control women’s beauty.

In “Jenin & the Nakba Between Us,” Serene Husni returns to her parents’ hometown in the occupied West Bank, weaving family archive and conversations with residents into a portrait of a place shaped by displacement, occupation and memory.

Additions to the program Tuesday’s program announcement also included additions to the Signed, Dead Angle: Common Ground, IDFA DocLab Spotlight, Best of Fests and Special Screenings selections.

Recent additions to Signed include Alex Gibney’s “Musk,” an incisive look at the power and influence of Elon Musk; Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s “You Can See Everything,” a complex portrait of notorious Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes; and “Sixteen Moments of My Life” by Albert Serra, spotlighting Ingrid Caven singing live at the Théâtre des Bouffes du Nord in Paris.

The Special Screenings section brings an Eye Filmmuseum restoration of John Leerdam’s “30 mei, 1969 (gritu di un pueblo),” that revisits the historic uprising in Curaçao and the colonial inequalities and racial discrimination that fuelled it.

The IDFA DocLab Spotlight selection announces several titles, including “In Pursuit of Repetitive Beats,” Darren Emerson’s landmark VR experience (IDFA, 2022) revisiting Britain’s late-1980s rave scene, presented in a new collective, multi-user format for DocLab’s 20th anniversary.

IDFA DocLab Competition for Immersive Non-Fiction With 10 titles, the IDFA DocLab Competition for Immersive Non-Fiction boldly expands the horizons of the documentary genre, pushing immersive media beyond conventional boundaries. Across VR, live theater performances, full-dome experiences, and multisensory works, the selection “explores how immersive art can alter the way we encounter reality—offering unexpected perspectives and opening up new possibilities for agency and resistance,” IDFA said.

“Several artists use immersive experiences to bring audiences into close, embodied encounters with realities that may otherwise feel distant. Other works deal with the corporeal and the body, from digitally altering our perception of ourselves and inviting our microbiomes to a feast, to examining grief through magnifying the decomposition of a loved one’s body—turning grief and death into a profound reflection on how humans are but a part of a larger ecosystem,” the festival said.

IDFA DocLab Competition for Digital Storytelling The nine-title IDFA DocLab Competition for Digital Storytelling expands the possibilities of documentary through digital art, games, interactive installations, and live performance. With artists from across disciplines bringing traditional forms into dialogue with new media, the selection showcases a new wave of cross-disciplinary experimentation.

“Several works confront the digital systems shaping contemporary life, subverting algorithms and finding room for human error and agency. Other works invite audiences into interactive open worlds, adapting game and world-building technologies to create participatory experiences that radically depart from everyday reality. Elsewhere, artists explore the ever-evolving relationship between the physical and digital, investigating how technology fundamentally shapes our experience of intimacy, desire, and connection,” IDFA said.

Cross-section awards IDFA has also announced the nominations for the cross-section awards—distinct awards that “transcend the program sections to recognize outstanding artistic achievement across the festival program.”

The IDFA Award for Best First Feature “celebrates the most remarkable debut feature-length films, recognizing works that reveal a distinctive creative voice and the promise of an evolving signature.”

Drawn from the International Competition, Envision Competition, Luminous and Frontlight, the award is accompanied by a €5,000 prize, awarded by an international jury.

The films nominated for the IDFA Award for Best First Feature are also eligible for the FIPRESCI Award, chosen by an international jury of film critics.

The IDFA Award for Best Dutch Film highlights exceptional Dutch filmmaking talent across the International Competition, Envision Competition, Luminous and Frontlight selections. The winning filmmaker with receive €5,000, awarded by an international jury.

The Beeld & Geluid IDFA ReFrame Award for Best Creative Use of Archive honors outstanding archival film, selected from across the film program. The winning film will receive a €5,000 prize, awarded by an international jury.

The winners will be announced during the IDFA awards ceremony on Nov. 19.

content.article_text:
Yaza Takenoshin Talks “Hinotama”, Family, Silence, Fantasy and Learning to Direct Through Space

Yaza Takenoshin discusses “Hinotama”, Japanese family dynamics, fantasy, silence and turning space and movement into cinematic language.

For Yaza Takenoshin, the premiere of “Hinotama: Ball of Fire” came with a particular kind of nervousness. Everything surrounding his first feature felt new, from working with experienced collaborators to presenting the completed film at a major festival. Yet nervousness had accompanied almost every stage of the production, to the point where the young filmmaker joked that he was gradually becoming accustomed to it.

Hinotama: Ball of Fire is screening at Busan International Film Festival

At the center of “Hinotama” is a 16-year-old boy living within a family that is gradually falling apart. He reconnects with a childhood friend he has not seen for eight years, and she tells him about a strange encounter with a ball of fire. Their search for this mysterious object becomes a means of escape, but fantasy eventually assumes a broader function within the film, helping connect the different fractures appearing inside the family.

One of Takenoshin’s main concerns was ensuring that the father did not become a straightforward villain. The character frequently behaves badly and says things that can make him easy to dislike, but the director wanted to understand where that behavior comes from. The family’s deterioration, in his view, cannot simply be attributed to one individual, while many of the father’s attitudes are also connected to the culture and social expectations in which he was raised. His words and behavior are recognizable as things that many Japanese men of his generation might say or believe.

Takenoshin is critical of some of those traditional values, particularly certain expectations surrounding etiquette and proper behavior, but he does not see direct criticism as his primary task. Instead, he wants to depict such attitudes precisely enough that audiences become aware of things they might hear every day without really noticing. Once familiar behavior is placed on a cinema screen and isolated from everyday routine, people can examine it differently and decide for themselves whether they want to continue living according to those ideas.

Check the review of the film

Nature became another means of expressing what is happening inside the household. The main house has extensive glass surfaces, meaning that leaves and other natural movement are constantly visible behind the characters. Takenoshin initially found this useful for creating continuity and flow between scenes, but gradually began thinking of nature as a larger force surrounding the family. Since their separation feels increasingly inevitable, the environment creates an impression that something larger is pushing them toward a destination they may be unable to avoid. The fireball functions similarly as an unexplained, almost supernatural presence.

Despite being the director, Takenoshin did not approach the production as though he needed to establish himself as “the man in charge”. He was the youngest person on set in terms of professional experience, even though some of the young actors were younger in age, having already worked in the industry since childhood. What allowed him to function comfortably was the collaborative atmosphere created around the production. Once filming began, he no longer felt particularly conscious of being the least experienced person there.

The extensive silence in “Hinotama” developed naturally from Takenoshin’s writing and preparation process. His first screenplay drafts tend to contain a great deal of dialogue. Once locations and actors are established, however, he begins constructing shots and often realizes that dialogue can be replaced by a camera movement, a person crossing a room or simply the relationship between bodies and space. The original screenplay ran approximately 130 pages, but after he spent around a week living inside the house where the film would be shot, it had fallen to about 110, with much of the missing material consisting of dialogue.

That interest in space is closely connected to his cinematic influences. Michael Haneke and Michelangelo Antonioni were particularly important when Takenoshin was younger, especially in teaching him how to organize figures within a frame and use architecture dramatically. However, when he initially tried to reproduce their formal qualities in his college films, he found that his own work became excessively cold and dry. He subsequently began looking toward filmmakers whose work, in his view, contained a stronger human element.

Ryusuke Hamaguchi became particularly important in that respect and remains one of Takenoshin’s major cinematic heroes, while Eric Rohmer is another favorite. The challenge for “Hinotama” was therefore not simply to construct carefully controlled compositions, but to find a way for formal precision and human emotion to coexist.

The house itself helped determine much of the cinematography. Its large windows and strongly geometric architecture immediately attracted Takenoshin, who noticed the abundance of straight lines and ordered spaces. Those characteristics could visually reflect both the father’s insistence on particular forms of behavior and the broader sense of suppression inside the household. The windows also allowed the camera to occupy a variety of positions while retaining connections between the interiors and the natural world outside.

Finding such a location was partly fortunate. The building had previously operated as a café but was no longer being used, while its owners lived elsewhere. This gave the production access to an interesting architectural space without having to displace residents for a month or rely on a comparatively expensive and visually less distinctive studio house. More importantly, it allowed Takenoshin to actually live there before filming and understand how people might move through it.

Casting the younger characters was done through auditions, while most of the adult roles were offered directly. Takenoshin first selected the actor playing Takeshi and then organized the rest of the younger cast around him. What immediately attracted him was the difficulty of reading the young actor’s face. There was an opacity to his expression that suggested something was happening internally without revealing exactly what, a quality Takenoshin compares with actors such as Alain Delon and Kyle MacLachlan.

Takenoshin’s own filmmaking journey began unusually early. At 16, he started making documentaries about nuclear power, motivated initially more by an interest in nuclear energy than cinema. After the 2011 Fukushima nuclear disaster, he had become fascinated by how polarized discussions surrounding the subject were and thought documentary might provide a means of communicating across those divisions. Over approximately three years and two documentaries, however, his interest gradually shifted. Shooting, editing and studying films became increasingly compelling until filmmaking itself overtook nuclear energy as his central concern.

Getting “Hinotama” made involved another unlikely development. Takenoshin wrote the screenplay during his junior year of college and originally imagined shooting it with a very small student crew. Unsure how even a basic feature production should be budgeted and scheduled, he contacted an established cinematographer Yoshio Kitagawa, through Instagram simply to ask practical questions. After they met for coffee, Takenoshin gave him the screenplay in the hope of receiving some comments. Around two weeks later, the cinematographer called and told him that he wanted to make the film. He subsequently helped connect Takenoshin with the producer who would bring the project together.

Post-production remained suitably modest. Takenoshin edited “Hinotama” in his bedroom using two monitors his mother borrowed from her office. The first cut took roughly two or three months. Composer Gabriel Brady, a friend from college who had scored all of Takenoshin’s previous films, came to Japan and worked in the same small room, allowing editing and music to develop almost simultaneously through constant conversation.

The film’s silences also reflect Takenoshin’s observations of communication within Japanese families. Conflict does not necessarily involve people continually shouting or explaining what is wrong. He describes Japanese communication as frequently passive-aggressive, with frustration remaining beneath the surface instead of being confronted directly. Too much dialogue or constant sound would have weakened the atmosphere of quiet suppression he wanted to maintain. …

That does not mean Takenoshin considers “Hinotama” an attack on the family itself. He points toward Japan’s long tradition of family cinema, particularly Yasujiro Ozu, whose films neither condemn nor romanticize the institution but instead record its structures, etiquette and changing values. Takenoshin hopes “Hinotama” can function in a similar way: a personal story that also records something recognizable about the contemporary Japanese family and, eventually, the particular period in which it was made.

Takenoshin is already writing new scripts, although he is not yet ready to discuss them. For now, “Hinotama: Ball of Fire” represents the culmination of a journey that began with teenage documentaries and developed through film study, chance encounters and a highly collaborative first feature. Its combination of controlled space, silence, nature and fantasy suggests a filmmaker interested not in telling audiences exactly what is wrong with his characters, but in placing familiar behavior inside a frame and allowing us to finally notice it.
content.excerpt_original: Yaza Takenoshin discusses “Hinotama”, Japanese family dynamics, fantasy, silence and turning space and movement into cinematic language.

content.article_text:
With the hope of catching Modigliani momentum evident at auctions in Europe over the past couple years, Phillips is bringing a rare sculpture by the Italian-born modernist to the marquee New York sales in November with a hefty price tag.

Modigliani’s Tête (1911–12) will hit the block with a $28 million–$35 million estimate. If it sells, the sculpture will be one of the most expensive three-dimensional works ever sold at auction by the artist, who is best known as a painter of female nudes with almond-shaped eyes. Related Articles At the Fall's First Major Auctions, Buyers Spent Carefully but Competed for the Right Works Strong Hong Kong Evening Sales, Totaling a Combined $223.6 M., Mask Key Hurdles in Asia's Art Market

The sculpture belongs to a larger series of heads, examples of which are generally held by major institutions, from the Metropolitan Museum of Art to the Tate museum network. This one was carved from a block of limestone and features a slender face with a long nose and a tiny, smiling mouth.

Modigliani is thought to have produced around 28 sculptures during his short lifetime. Twenty-six of them survive.

Calling Tête a “masterpiece,” Phillips deputy chairman of the Americas and senior international specialist Jeremiah Evarts said in a statement, “Fresh to the market after over half a century in the same important private collection, Tête embodies everything that makes Modigliani’s sculpture so revered, including its profound art historical importance.” (The house did not identify who had previously owned the work, which last changed hands in 1972.)

Tête is not likely to become the most expensive Modligiani sculpture ever sold, however. In 2010, Christie’s sold another stone head for $52.8 million, in what was then Modigliani’s overall record. The same auction house sold another Tête in 2019 for $34.3 million.

Modigliani’s current record, it is worth noting, is far higher than the upper end of Phillips’s estimate for its Tête . That benchmark stands at $170.4 million, as minted by the 2015 sale of his 1918 painting Nu couché , which remains one of the most expensive artworks ever brought to auction .

Still, Phillips is likely hoping to catch a wave of market interest in Modigliani evident in auctions staged over the past two years. In 2025, at Christie’s in Paris, a portrait by the artist sold for $31.3 million, tripling its estimate and setting a new record for the artist in France. Then, earlier this year, a painting of a nude woman from the collection of Joe Lewis sold for $63.5 million at Sotheby’s in London, creating a new record for Modigliani in Europe.

content.article_text:
T his small-town police thriller sets its stall out intriguingly, with a murder that seems actively begging to be solved. The perp chose to dump his victim – the 14-year-old daughter of a local political bigwig – into a part of the Mississippi River where she was likely to resurface, and from a highly visible bridge. When veteran detective Alan Kramer (Devon Sawa) and rookie forensic psychologist Amelia Pembrock (Maggie Grace) show up to investigate, they are immediately alerted to a gun in the bushes just yards away. As a colleague observes: “This isn’t a clean-up. It’s a message.”

But Brando Benetton’s debut film sadly fails to capitalise on the misdirection at play in this open-goal crime scene. Instead of using it to pry open community secrets, he gives us a ropey and implausible manhunt. As Kramer and Pembrock race to locate the girl’s twin, who is presumably still in the killer’s clutches, they zero in on local butcher Boris (Darron Dunbar). He has a sex-pest rap sheet and lives with his mother – which apparently ticks all the boxes for a profiling genius such as Pembrock. Kramer pulls her up for being unbothered by the lack of actual prosecutable evidence. But carping is about the only investigative contribution this seasoned criminologist makes here (and what’s a criminologist – a crime sociologist – doing out in the field anyway?).

If the killer leaves behind a parody of a crime scene, The Girl in the River offers up its own parody noir, though in a cliche-strewn and far less careful fashion. We have the obsessive desk jockey, the boozy, trauma-harbouring vet halfway out the retirement door, Tiffany Haddish’s angry black captain (as satirised in the Jump Street franchise), and the affable town coroner (The Karate Kid’s Ralph Macchio). Whenever the detectives are floundering, the over-directed script is always on hand to put them back on the rails. The local media seem strangely willing to share their voluminous stash of damning evidence; a transparently staged mutiny among the townsfolk fires up Kramer and Pembrock just as they’re out of leads.

Grace, with her twitchy defensiveness, and the frazzled Sawa manage to half-ballast this dubious sleuthing, and Benetton keeps the film moving fast enough so the many infelicities don’t register too horrifically. But with no time to accumulate any proper gravitas, Kramer’s capstone speech about universal corruption is, like the victim, dead in the water.

content.title_original: Our Bodies Have Been Bridges review – riveting portraits and the story of the first woman on Earth
content.article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "I n the 1990s, the late Chicana artist Laura Aguilar was living with depression. A friend took her on a road trip to New Mexico, where Aguilar made some nude self-portraits in the mystical landscapes. Those photographs evolved into a pivotal series shot in desert environments across the American south-west, Aguilar’s notable 1996 Nature Self-Portrait – considered an early work of intersectional feminist art, before the word had entered academic discourse."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "London gallery Autograph first worked on an exhibition of Aguilar’s in 1997, the year after she made Nature Self-Portrait, so this is something of a homecoming, a generation on. Aguilar’s contours, folds, and crevices sometimes disappear into the barren desert landscapes, assimilating the shapes of boulders or trees; at other times, her body is incongruous, soft flesh that can’t be held by the harsh, barren conditions. These images capture the paradox of a body that is both hypervisible and ignored."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Several works from Nature Self-Portrait appear at the beginning of Our Bodies Have Been Bridges, Autograph’s new three-person headline show. content.article_text:
I n the 1990s, the late Chicana artist Laura Aguilar was living with depression. A friend took her on a road trip to New Mexico, where Aguilar made some nude self-portraits in the mystical landscapes. Those photographs evolved into a pivotal series shot in desert environments across the American south-west, Aguilar’s notable 1996 Nature Self-Portrait – considered an early work of intersectional feminist art, before the word had entered academic discourse.

London gallery Autograph first worked on an exhibition of Aguilar’s in 1997, the year after she made Nature Self-Portrait, so this is something of a homecoming, a generation on. Aguilar’s contours, folds, and crevices sometimes disappear into the barren desert landscapes, assimilating the shapes of boulders or trees; at other times, her body is incongruous, soft flesh that can’t be held by the harsh, barren conditions. These images capture the paradox of a body that is both hypervisible and ignored.

Several works from Nature Self-Portrait appear at the beginning of Our Bodies Have Been Bridges, Autograph’s new three-person headline show. They’re so quiet and minimal, shot in black and white, they’d be easy to coast past – which is partly Aguilar’s point. Bodies like hers – large, queer, Chicana – had no visibility in culture at the time Aguilar made these works, while in real life her experiences were of an uncomfortable, scrutinised presence. Out here in the terrain of nowhere, Aguilar returns her body to the earth – a body wanting to just be a body, to not ache to fit in. A body with the same cracks, dents and curves as the land; hardy, wild and free. They’re photographs about rejection, but also embrace.

This is the beginning of three concurrent exhibitions at Autograph about rebellious bodies. In the first and largest, Our Bodies Have Been Bridges, Aguilar’s story continues through two younger artists who also use their bodies as anchors, in pursuit of healing, truth and connection to ancestral female knowledge. In a diaristic, family album-style account of matriarchy and ritual, Other Stories/Historias Bravas, the artist Koyoltzintli re-enacts remembered scenes from her childhood in the Andean mountains of Ecuador.

Her bare breasts are blessed by her aunt, for protection. In another picture, her mother braids her hair tenderly, the same way, the caption tells us, her grandmother had once done for her. Her mum takes her to sit among the iguanas at the local park, to cure her of her phobia of the reptiles. Routines of care passed down generations of women, through their bodies. Tangible, physical, felt knowledge and history is reflected in Koyoltzintli’s very direct, intimate approach to photography. In a group of works from the series Meda – indebted to Aguilar’s self-portraits – Koyoltzintli asked women to interact with the land as their ancestors might have, to trace a collective, imagined, silent story of the first woman on Earth. An alternative origin story.

These works appear with Peruvian Tarrah Krajnak’s grainy, photocopied, archival images that focus on 1979 – the year the military regime ended in Peru, and also the year of the artist’s birth. The works explore the dissonance between women’s bodies portrayed in the country’s media and the private, personal experiences of living as a woman through that time and the years of armed conflict that followed. She takes images cribbed from newspapers and magazines published that year, and to query their veracity, photocopies, rephotographs, and interrupts them with her own image. The bodies here are agitated, unstable and unresolved.

Upstairs, this dovetails seamlessly into Charan Singh’s Your Tongue in My Mouth. As the unforgettable title promises, Singh’s work is a joyful provocation, but also a serious meditation on desirability, sexuality and reciprocity – when certain bodies are seen by some as a burden, a threat.

Singh’s lucid colour portraits of Hijra, Kothi and trans people combine a realist sensibility and theatricality – the subjects’ authenticity contrasts with choreographed poses; beautiful hand-painted backdrops behind them evoke a world of fantasy and escape. Riveting, regal portraits such as Umrao and Sonu have a timeless elegance: the subjects’ decision to wear traditional salwar kameez or anarkali-style dress, ornate brocade fabrics, their bodies adorned with henna and bindi, are intentional gestures that they also belong to a longer history in south Asia. These portraits are statements of dignity that claim their right to that place without words or apology.

after newsletter promotion

The subtle tension between realism and artifice takes on a particular urgency against the backdrop of India’s deteriorating trans rights. In March 2026, legislative amendments to the country’s Transgender Persons Act 2019 rolled back protections for gender self-identification, raising profound questions about bodily autonomy, recognition and the right to define oneself. A timeline of transgender history and rights, displayed on a table at the centre of Singh’s exhibition, situates these intimate portraits within a longer struggle for visibility and legal recognition, grounding their gestures of self-fashioning and self-expression in a shifting and often hostile political reality.
