content.article_text:
The Artnet Bulletin is our daily digest of five items from around the art world that are worth knowing. A different writer takes over each morning.

The best of Artnet News in your inbox.

Sign up for our daily newsletter.

A Personal Note Re: Kelly Clarkson’s Feud With a Brooklyn Magic Shop…

OK, here’s a very silly but very big story: “Miss Independent” singer Kelly Clarkson is in a furious internet dispute with tiny Brooklyn magic shop the Art of Play over whether or not its staff was rude to her when she inquired about buying a certain singing bird sculpture. Seriously, look it up. Huge story . I’m here to say: I’m team Art of Play all the way. It sells incredible puzzles sourced from around the world, and I saw the best magic show of my life—by the incomparable David Williamson —in the hidden theater behind the bookshelf in the back. While I was there, I also happened to ask about the magic wind-up bird sculpture, which the owners show off before each performance. It’s by an artist named Bliss Kolb from Seattle. Being from Seattle myself and having a dad who loves clocks and other wind-up gizmos, I also, like Clarkson, wanted more details, and I will say the staff seemed mildly cagey. But I simply interpreted this as them maintaining an air of mystery. The bird in question is like the mascot for the store! And the entire wonder of the store is that it feels full of secrets!

The best of Artnet News in your inbox.

Sign up for our daily newsletter.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Art of Play (@artofplay)

A Random List of Culture’s ‘Free Thinkers’…

For some reason, for its 40th birthday, the Independent has dropped the “Independent’s Free Thinkers List,” featuring “people who have exhibited free thinking” during the paper’s lifetime. The 40 chosen Free Thinkers include artists Ai Weiwei (“changing the possibilities of politically engaged contemporary art“) and Tracey Emin (“helped make confession, vulnerability and autobiography legitimate subjects for contemporary art”). These picks do not exactly symbolize “radical free-thinking”; they are pretty familiar. The rest of the list’s grab bag includes the likes of Virgil Abloh , Richard Dawkins , Deng Xiaoping , Elon Musk , Shonda Rhimes , Margaret Thatcher , and Donald J. Trump . What a head-scratcher.

A Second Opinion on Mark Fisher…

The late theorist Mark Fisher , author of Capitalist Realism (2009), remains one of the major theory references in an art writing world that has largely replaced theory with attitude. Writer and researcher Rômulo Moraes has a scathing, attitude- and theory-filled dissent at his blog Ear Vortex . The one-line summary is this: Fisher was “a producer of false urgencies and chewed-up thought processes lifted and resized from the better work of others.” I happen to agree that Fisher’s cultural pessimism has outlived its sell-by date, reprocessed into the dull work of a commentator like W. David Marx in Blank Space (2025). To Moraes’s credit, the bulk of his essay is devoted to proposing thinkers he sees as better than Fisher.

Bad at Sports turned 21 with a tailgate party at the Museum of Contemporary Art Chicago. Image courtesy Bad at Sports.

An Anniversary-of-Note for the Art-Pod-Sphere…

The OG art podcast, Chicago-based weekly Bad at Sports , celebrated 999 episodes at the beginning of this month, with a big live onstage conversation at the Museum of Contemporary Art Chicago featuring New York mag’s critic, Jerry Saltz . That’s just one shy of 1,000 episodes! An accomplishment worth celebrating! I’ve been on B@S twice, and both times (episode # 767 , in 2021, and # 912 , last year), the chatty informal style let us get both weirder and more personal than almost anywhere else. The Saltz ep, which goes up online and on Lumpen Radio , will come out later in 2026. Congrats!

Something Not to Miss…

“ The Bowery: Devil’s Mile ” is an unexpected crowd-pleaser at the New Museum , not to be lost in the furor over Arthur Jafa , which opened at the same time (odd habit, that—almost guaranteeing things get lost in the mix). Surveying the long, long history of the Bowery as a creative site, the show serves as former New Museum director Lisa Phillips ’s final show, as if to put her legacy in context, and is co-curated by up-and-comer Thalia Stefaniuk . (At the press conference, Phillips affectionately compared their dynamic to the show Hacks ). Art highlights range from portraits of Bowery characters by Billy Sullivan and a suite of engaging sculptures by contemporary artist Brad Kahlhamer , whose studio is on the Bowery, to Jacob Riis ’s formative social documentary work How the Other Half Lives (1890) and Nan Goldin ’s incomparably moving The Ballad of Sexual Dependency (1985). But—surprisingly or unsurprisingly—the copious well-chosen non-art artifacts pack just as much punch, fleshing out the New York neighborhood’s history as a site of creative experimentation in the fullest popular sense. A civic-minded, serious, and seriously delightful exhibition.

The “Feejee Mermaid,” displayed in “The Bowery: Devil’s Mile.” Photo by Ben Davis.

“The Bowery: Devil’s Mile” 2026. Exhibition view: New Museum, New York. Courtesy New Museum. Photo: Dario Lasagni.

Works by Billy Sullivan and Bradley Kahlhamer in “The Bowery: Devil’s Mile.” Courtesy New Museum. Photo: Dario Lasagni.

July Jung, Kim Do-yeon and Song Sae-byeok on “Dora”

A film inspired by Freud’s Dora, two decades in the making

July Jung returns to Busan with “Dora”, her third feature after “A Girl at My Door” (2014) and “Next Sohee” (2022). All three have premiered at Cannes, and “Dora” arrives at the Busan International Film Festival, in the Gala Presentation section, after its world premiere in the Directors’ Fortnight in May. Inspired by Freud’s case study of Dora, the film follows an eighteen-year-old girl suffering from a mysterious illness who experiences a summer full of changes.

July Jung was joined by lead actress Kim Do-yeon, a former Weki Meki member who won Best New Actress at the Blue Dragon Film Awards for Kim Min-ha’s “Idiot Girls and School Ghost: School Anniversary”, and by Song Sae-byeok, who reunited with her for this new film, twelve years after “A Girl at My Door”.

They discussed an idea the director first had in her twenties, the long road to making it and the casting of Japanese actress Sakura Ando as Nami.

Dora is screening at Busan International Film Festival

The titles of your films are the names of their characters, from Dohee-ya (“A Girl at My Door”) to “Next Sohee” and now “Dora”, and they are all films with powerful female characters. How did Dora start?

As you say, it may well be the starting point for the films that carry their protagonists’ names. In my twenties I came across Freud’s case study of Dora and her hysteria, and I was fascinated by it. I thought that if I ever made films, I would like to make one from this story. When I first tried to write a screenplay, this was the story that came to mind. But I had never written a screenplay before, and it didn’t work.

I kept it in the back of my mind and made “A Girl at My Door” first. When that was finished, the story came back to me, and I worked hard on a screenplay. I completed a first draft and tried to get the film produced, but it didn’t happen. People who read it said they couldn’t tell what was going on, and the investors in particular said it was too difficult. I pushed for a long time and then abandoned it. After that I made “Next Sohee”, and only then did I go back to where I had started and made “Dora”.

So this may be a film you made after a long wait. What should the audience pay attention to if they want to enjoy it, or see it differently?

When this story first came to me, I was around Dora’s age. Time has passed, and by the time I was making the film I felt I had grown much closer to Nami. So two things now coexist in me: the young person I was then and the adult of an older generation I am today. If viewers wonder why I made this film, I hope they will keep that in mind as they watch.

Kim Do-yeon, you portrayed Dora wonderfully. What joy did you find in playing her, and what was most rewarding about the process?

When I first read the script, I thought Dora and I were very different. I wondered how I was supposed to understand her, because her choices were so unlike what I would have chosen, and at first she felt very far away. But as I kept talking with the director, I gradually grew closer to her. While reading the script I even sent the director a text message saying that every sentence grew more beautiful the more I read, layer by layer. So the process of understanding this story was happy and moving for me, and shooting was a joy as well.

It was an intense and difficult summer, and everyone worked hard. But it was a kind of work I had never done before. We had a Japanese actor with us, and the cinematographer and camera team came from France. All of it was new and fun, and I learned a great deal. Being able to immerse myself so deeply in a role was a precious experience for me.

Song Sae-byeok, those who saw “A Girl at My Door” will remember you, and you have come back to the director’s world, perhaps as one of its essential figures. You play Yeon-su, who becomes a catalyst for events in the film. What was it like to work with her again?

Yesterday the director sent me a few photos. They were stills from “A Girl at My Door”, a film we made twelve years ago. It’s awkward to say it myself, but we both looked rather cute. I thought, has it really been twelve years? Time passes. Now that we have worked together again after twelve years, what I felt on set, personally, was that the director is just the same as ever: the delicacy of her direction in shaping each character, and the depth of her world. She leaves things open for a long time, and then at the decisive moment she points the way. That freedom in her approach is very attractive to me, and it helped me get closer to my character.

Your young female characters often find themselves in a world of adults who dismiss their feelings and are unable to listen to them or understand them. Could you elaborate on your intention in portraying this dynamic?

Yes, Dora clearly keeps experiencing discomfort. The world Dora sets out from includes her parents and friends of her father, and the adults spend time together there, but there are also their children, including twins, and friends of her own age. It may look like a world of adults because the people with whom she exchanges emotions, forms relationships, and influences and is influenced are adults. But I don’t think her youth is what creates the root of her discomfort. She is simply the most vulnerable being in that situation.

At first the people around her are a great driving force in restoring her fragile, ill state. Then she gradually recovers and reaches the point where she can stand entirely on her own, and at that point things change abruptly. One may wonder whether they did not actually want her to recover, and I think the confusion that arises from there dominates the second half of the film. What I most wanted to explore was how Dora acts in that confusion, what choices she makes, and how she heads toward the end.

You said earlier that you first worked on a screenplay in your twenties. Is that first screenplay similar to the finished film? And what were your thoughts about the ending?

At the beginning, what interested me in Freud’s account was the relationships and psychological forces that surround the girl. But when I looked at it again after many years, wanting to make it into a film, it struck me that all of it was what that man had seen, and that was a shock. I felt almost overpowered by it. I asked myself: is Dora’s voice here? Does it really grasp what she wants? Haven’t we only ever seen her through him? From there I thought the film should overcome that account, and I wondered what would happen if I told the story entirely in Dora’s own voice. That is the big difference from Freud’s original report, and it became the driving force of the film. In his case, she never recovered, and it ended with her ill and untreated. I kept thinking about how it could become another kind of case, one in which she recovers by herself and stands up whole.

The ending was something I had already written in the first draft. But the steps leading to that ending were not sufficient, so the work kept stalling, and some parts never fell into place. In the end, the finished screenplay is not very different from the first draft. The major developments are the same, but the relationships between characters and their actions, woven in tightly, changed little by little, and that is how I was able to reach the ending as it is now.

Dora expresses very subtle emotions. Kim Do-yeon, how did you prepare for the role, and how was the rapport with the other actors?

It grew as we got to know one another, and I value that process, which the actors built together. The most important process for me, and the most difficult but necessary one, was in a way similar to what I said at the start.

I remember it was probably at my first audition. I had received only excerpts, and I found it very hard. It was a scene with the doctor, with a senior actor in the other role. I read only that part without knowing the rest of the story, and I asked the director whether Dora was lying at that moment. She told me that Dora keeps telling the truth. At that moment I thought how lonely and difficult it must be for her to be telling the truth while everyone treats it as a lie. I was auditioning for her role and even I doubted her. That first audition came back to me again and again while I was preparing. I needed to keep switching perspectives, as a third party and as Dora, until I could come to know her heart. It was a process I needed, and I worked hard at it.

How did the casting of Sakura Ando come about?

One thing did change from the first draft, and this is it: the character was originally Korean. I had never imagined making a film with a foreign actor, and I had never really thought of people from other countries. Then at some point I wondered whether I could ever fully understand the depth of Nami’s emptiness and loneliness. Even if I made the film, wrote it and played the part myself, there would be parts I did not know. That realization was a big one for me. At the same time I wondered: what if she were Japanese rather than Korean? And almost in the same moment, I thought: then it would be Sakura Ando.

That was my train of thought that day. But I only knew Sakura Ando as a member of the audience. I had no personal connection and no way to contact her, so I was just thinking about it by myself. Then I decided to try. I contacted her through her management and asked whether she would be interested in a film in Korea. She said she would like to hear more and see the script. I had the screenplay translated into Japanese and sent it about a month later.

Why Japanese, and why Sakura Ando? It may be because I am a great admirer of Japanese cinema. When I watch her performances across many films, I find it astonishing that every role is a completely different person, and yet there is also a sense that this is simply Sakura. I thought that in whatever part of Nami I did not yet know, or could not know, an actor like her might make it possible for a person called Nami to exist between me and the actor, and that we could build this character together. I kept thinking about it, and then I reached out. Fortunately, she read the script and said she wanted to meet, and we met.

At first she agonized a great deal over the Korean dialogue; she had never spoken Korean before. Nevertheless, she wanted to bring this film, the character of Nami, and Nami’s story with Dora to life, and that is how we came to work together. I was very lucky.

The film is rated for adults only and includes intimate scenes, a first for you. Kim Do-yeon, did you have any concerns before taking the role, and how did you feel after shooting them?

Honestly, I hardly felt such concerns at first. Even though it was my first time shooting an intimate scene, I accepted it naturally when I read the script, so I wasn’t troubled by it. In the process, the director and I talked in more detail about how we would shoot it, and she asked me many times whether I was comfortable and listened carefully to what I said. The more she did, the more I tried to understand the script: how the scene is written and why it is needed. I asked the director, and I came to see that this scene is very important in our film. Nami and Dora each carry their own wounds, and showing them fully to each other for the first time, and connecting through that, is essential to the film.

As an actor I had to shoot it, and as a person it could not be nothing to me, so I was curious how it would be expressed, and the director had very firm thoughts about it. Because she understands the female body, and therefore the feelings that go with it, so well, I came to trust that I didn’t need to worry, and that trust let me throw myself into the character. On set, my scene partner helped me a great deal and checked on how I was doing, and I relied on her. The staff were very considerate as well. We also had an intimacy coordinator. It was my first time working with one, and I came to feel it is truly necessary. Thanks to that, I was able to shoot with peace of mind.

July Jung closed the conference by saying she hopes the film will move those who watch it and draw a wide range of reactions and opinions.

content.article_text:
B ack in the 90s and 00s, Japanese horror (or “J-horror” if you want to save on syllables) was much admired , reasonably widely distributed and sometimes remade in other languages . They never actually stopped making them in Japan, but the results don’t seem to get as much crossover exposure as they used to. That may be because we have quite enough horror getting made closer to home, especially since it’s so remunerative at the box office.

Nevertheless, it’s good to see evidence that the genre keeps evolving in Japan just as it does everywhere else, and there is something tangibly fresh and kicky about this low-budget horror-comedy amalgam. Made by comedian Yuriyan Retriever , an irrepressible character whose dadaist shtick got her on America’s Got Talent twice, makes her directorial debut with this satirical ghost story which sends up male misogyny and women’s obsession with romance alike.

Told in a series of interrelated chapters, the plot explores encounters with Mag Mag, a female ghost notable for her height (two metres), wild mane of hair, and generous proportions that go against Japan’s petite female beauty norms. When Mag Mag falls in love with a cute guy, he’s done for, because she will pursue him to the death – a passion that is finally consummated with fatal throttling and sucking out the limerent object’s eyes (a step beyond merely boiling the family bunny à la Fatal Attraction).

Mag Mag’s backstory doesn’t get fully fleshed out until the last section, but Yuriyan rather implies she was a fat high school girl bullied into killing herself by mean classmates who therefore deserve persecution. (There’s a twist in store, however – one that really upends viewers’ assumptions about bullying victims.) Meanwhile, the obsessions of another young woman called Sanae (played by Sara Minami, delivering a truly crazed comic performance), who is also in love with one of Mag Mag’s victims, shows that women are just as capable of toxicity as men if they put their minds to it.

There’s a bizarre sequence in which Sanae slathers her entire body in lubricant and forces her way through a sphincter-like orifice located where the mouth should be in a giant portrait of the guy that she is obsessed with, which is worthy of cult Japanese trash auteur Takashi Miike at his most deranged. Somehow it’s not surprising to learn that Miike is one of the backers of Mag Mag, a sign that the older generation of Japanese horrormeisters are passing on the torch.

content.article_text:
I n the early 1950s, Alvar Aalto built a boat to get to his remote summer residence on an island in Lake Päijänne, about 200km north of Helsinki . But the celebrated Finnish architect was not a happy skipper. He named the boat – a title as cumbersome as his buildings were elegant – Nemo propheta in patria: “No man is a prophet in his own land”.

The name was a dig at Finland , which the architectural maestro believed had taken him for granted. Other nations, he moaned, recognised his talent more than his own. Today, arriving in Helsinki, I find that Finland doesn’t just love Aalto, he’s a national treasure.

Last month, 13 Alvar sites dotted around Finland gained Unesco world heritage status. In addition to this international honour, vast quantities of Finnish public funding are being spent on the restoration of his buildings, and his designs are currently being celebrated in the Aalto Design – Shapes of Wellbeing exhibition at Helsinki’s Architecture & Design Museum. Norman Foster could but dream of such public adoration. For many Finns today, Aalto’s buildings – light-filled, harmonious habitats created from the mid-1920s to his death in 1976 – speak of national pride at a time of geopolitical tension with Russia and, further afield, connect to global considerations about “wellness” in the built environment.

But was it true that Aalto was once underappreciated at home? “The boat’s name wasn’t entirely in jest,” notes Sofia Nivarti, author of Studio Aalto, a new survey of his work to be published later this month. “The more he succeeded internationally, the more a local audience turned against him – steeped in a social-democratic ethos of egalitarianism, Finnish architectural circles worried about the dominance of one name over all others.”

In the first half of the 1950s, Aalto “wasn’t able to get a professorship from his alma mater, the Helsinki University of Technology,” explains Tommi Lindh, CEO of the Alvar Aalto Foundation. And a starchitect’s ego is a fragile thing, even in the cool egalitarian north.

In Helsinki, Lindh gives me a tour of the National Pensions Institute – now home to the Finns’ social security system – a vast brick building designed by Aalto between 1953 and 1957. It is perfectly preserved, right down to its ingenious overhead heating panels, angled skylights and working paternoster lift. This monumental brick building is one of five Aalto sites in Helsinki to gain Unesco recognition, alongside the House of Culture (commissioned by the Finnish Communist party in 1952, with the goal of “making culture the property of the entire nation”), Finlandia Hall, the vast, glacier-like concert and conference centre, and both Aalto’s home and his studio.

At the Shapes of Wellbeing exhibition, curators have broadened out the Aalto story to include the work of Alvar’s first wife, Aino, and second wife, Elissa, both skilled architects in their own right. It also shows that the experiential – and nature-loving – considerations Aalto brought to buildings also shaped his approach to furniture and lighting systems: his pendant lights recall beehives and jellyfish, his wooden chairs look as if they have been bent by the wind. “As we reconsider our relationship with nature and seek more sustainable ways of living, Aalto Studio’s work offers a valuable perspective,” says Pilvi Kalhama, director of the Architecture & Design Museum.

Naturally, Aalto’s domestic flourishes can also be found at his home in Munkkiniemi, Helsinki’s leafy, classy, equivalent of Hampstead. Completed in 1936, the Aalto House is a series of light-boxes overlooking a sports field, quiet but for birdsong and rippling with daylight. Aalto’s monochromatic abstract paintings still hang on the walls, his Homburg still sits in a wardrobe.

In contrast, Finlandia Hall – completed in 1971 and arguably his greatest masterpiece – introduces visitors to Aalto at his most symphonic. Standing in its concert hall – a jagged collection of white-on-white geometric planes – is like being inside an ice cube. A €136m renovation between 2022 and 2024 saw the building’s facade reclad in pristine Lasa Bianco Nuvolato marble and the opening of a permanent exhibition space dedicated to Aalto’s life and times.

Following Finland’s independence from Russia in 1917, the built environment – and Aalto’s mark on it – played a significant role in the shaping a new national identity. “Aalto did not set out simply to create a national style, but through his work he expressed values that became closely associated with modern Finland,” says Pilvi Kalhama. “Functionality, purpose, aesthetic quality and a progressive outlook were all central to his architecture and design. These qualities still reflect a broader Finnish attitude towards everyday life.”

As his compatriots once feared, Aalto’s international success has largely overshadowed the achievements of other Finnish architects. But these days, Finns seem less oppressed by his legacy. “You can’t really grow up as a Finnish architect without Aalto being part of your thinking. But that doesn’t mean we all want to design like him,” says Asmo Jaaksi, founding partner of JKMM Architects, which refurbished and restored Aalto’s House of Culture and has won the international competition to design a new Museum of Architecture and Design on Helsinki’s South Harbour (planned to open in 2030). “What I admire most is Aalto’s independence of thought, his willingness to experiment and his instinct for putting people and nature first. I think he’d be rather disappointed if we were all still copying him.”

At the height of Aalto’s career in the mid-20th century, he may have been sore at perceived slights, but his disgruntled state proved short-lived. “Aalto was a chameleonic persona,” says Sofia Nivarti. “Grumpy at times, yet bubbly and joyful to his core; moody and hilarious in turn; at times egotistical and at others deeply self-sacrificing and generous.” He was impossible to pigeonhole and his buildings embraced the contradictions of the human experience.

Soon enough, the Finns acknowledged his vision. In 1955, just as he launched his scornfully named boat, Aalto was elected as a member of the Finnish Academy. “He is the only architect in Finland to have received this position,” says Lindh. “Meaning the nemo propheta in patria days were over.”

Aalto Design – Shapes of Wellbeing is at the Architecture and Design Museum Helsinki until 3 January 2027. Studio Aalto by Sofia Nivarti is published by Yale University Press on 27 October 2026

content.article_text:
Swann Galleries Fall offering of Fine Photographs is set for Thursday, October 15, 2026.

Notable works from the nineteenth century include Francis Frith’s The Pyramids of Dahshoor, from the East , 1857 ($6,000-9,000); and a rare daguerreotype by Felix Jacques Moulin, Two Prodigal Women , 1860s ($7,000-10,000). The auction further features a significant constructivist composition by Alexander Rodchenko, Pushkin Square , 1932 ($20,000-30,000), and a rare portfolio by Todd Webb previously unoffered on the market ($18,000-22,000).

Further highlights include imagery of the American West with Ansel Adams’ Winter Sunrise, Sierra Nevada from Lone Pine, California , 1944, printed April 1978 ($30,000-45,000), and Moonrise, Hernandez, New Mexico , 1941, printed 1963-70 ($30,000-45,000); and abstraction studies, including ten photographs from the Seaweed Martha’s Vineyard Portfolio , 1943-53, printed 1982, by Aaron Siskind ($7,000-10,000).

The auction also features works associated with the Kamoinge Workshop, including Gordon Parks’ American Gothic , 1942, printed circa 1970 ($6,000-9,000), and Roy DeCarava’s Man Coming Up Subway Stairs , 1952 ($12,000-18,000).

Street photography features Fan Ho, Three Men Walking, Hong Kong , 1962, printed 2006 ($7,000-10,000); and Elliott Erwitt’s oversized Arc de Triomphe, Paris , 1956, printed 2000s ($10,000-15,000). Contemporary highlights feature Peter Hujar’s Keith, N.Y. , 1981 ($10,000-15,000), and Vik Muniz’s Aftermath (Emerson) , from the Children of Brazil project, 1998 ($8,000-12,000). Fashion photography includes images by Richard Avedon, Bruce Weber, Helmut Newton and more.

A selection of press photographs documenting civil rights by Bob Adelman with No Man is an Island, Kelly Ingram Park, Birmingham, Alabama (Civil Rights demonstrators) , 1963, printed 1970s ($4,000-6,000), and Fred McDarrah with George McGovern and Coretta King, Political Campaign , 1972 ($700-1,000), along with examples of vernacular photography, will further enrich the dynamic sale.

Bidding is available through online platforms, absentee, the phone, and live in-person. Live online bidding platforms will be the Swann Galleries website, Invaluable, and LiveAuctioneers.

Swann Auction Galleries is a third-generation family business as well as the world’s largest auction house for works on paper. In the last 80 years, Swann has repeatedly revolutionized the trade with such innovations as the first U.S. auction dedicated to photographs and the world’s only department of African American Art. More than 40 auctions and previews are held annually in Swann Galleries’ two-floor exhibition space in Midtown Manhattan and online worldwide. Visit swanngalleries.com for more information.

content.article_text:
Huis Marseille presents a premiere of Adolphe de Meyer ’s rediscovered collection of photographs of Venice.

From 24 October 2026 until 7 February 2027 Huis Marseille will be hosting Adolphe de Meyer. The Substance of a Venetian Dream , the first ever European museum exhibition devoted to the photographer Adolphe de Meyer (1868–1946). This follows the remarkable discovery in 2019 in the municipal library of Tours: a series of 75 photographs documenting his life and photographic work in Venice. This collection is being displayed in its entirety for the first time, and offers an exceptional glimpse into his personal and artistic world.

A pioneer of fashion photography Adolphe de Meyer was born in Paris in 1868 and enjoyed a fascinating and ground-breaking career in both Europe and the United States. Historians recognise him today principally as a pictorialist photographer (a movement that approached photography as an art form), as a virtuoso portraitist, and above all as a fashion photographer. He was one of the first to elevate fashion photography to artistic heights, creating elegant images for the pages of Vogue , Vanity Fair and Harper’s Bazaar . It is less well known that he was also an interior decorator, designer, art collector, journalist and writer. He turned his whole life into a work of art, in which photography, clothing, interiors and stagings expressed a coherent artistic vision: that of a man continuously reinventing himself and his surroundings.

Globetrotter His travels were a constant and invaluable source of inspiration, usually in the company of his wife and creative partner Olga. Japan was an early love, followed by China, India and South America. De Meyer made the world his field of experimentation, and he also proved able to apply the meticulous precision of his studio to the photographic work done outside his atelier. Despite a remarkably successful and influential career he was almost unknown when he died in Los Angeles in 1946.

A Venetian dream Venice had a special place in his heart. Between 1904 and 1908/09 Adolphe and Olga rented the Palazzo Balbi-Valier, an opulent 17th-century palace surrounded by gardens, that De Meyer transformed from a dilapidated building into a landmark attraction that was pointed out to tourists by tour guides and gondoliers. The Palazzo was a vibrant cultural centre, whose guests included the photographers Gertrude Käsebier and Frances Benjamin Johnston and the art collector Isabella Gardner; De Meyer also invited Auguste Rodin to come and work there. Palazzo Balbi-Valier was first and foremost an extension of his studio, where he experimented with light, staging, and early colour photography, developing an aesthetic that would strongly influence his work and fashion vision.

Through eight different themes the exhibition explores his life, work, artistic network, and the many facets of his work, from fashion photography and interior design to art collection, as well as his special relationship with Olga. Visitors will have a rare opportunity to discover some of the secrets behind this ground-breaking fashion photographer, as well as the city that fired his imagination throughout his life.

The title of the exhibition is derived from an article that De Meyer published in Vogue in 1916, ‘The Substance of a Venetian Dream’, in which he reflects on his years in the city. A copy of this particular edition of Vogue , which Huis Marseille recently acquired, is also on show in the exhibition.

Olga: partner and myth No woman played a more important role in De Meyer’s life and work than his wife Olga, born Donna Maria Beatrice Olga Alberta Caracciolo (1871–1931). She was one of the most charismatic and idiosyncratic women of her generation, who inspired artists such as John Singer Sargent, James McNeill Whistler and the writer Henry James. Their unconventional marriage, which lasted for more than three decades, was regarded by their contemporaries with fascination and admiration. Both were homosexual, and their union was considered a marriage of convenience: it offered social legitimacy and protection in an age when homosexuality was a social taboo. Olga constantly modelled for De Meyer’s camera, wore his designs, and co-organised the social and cultural events that cemented their reputations. Driven by creativity and self-invention they built a shared identity together, thereby creating a myth. De Meyer never fully recovered from Olga’s death in 1931: although he later sold a great deal of work, he always kept her portraits, and she continued to inspire him. She was a central figure in his writings, particularly in his unpublished autobiographical work of fiction Of Passion and Tenderness .

A remarkable discovery In 2019, while conducting an inventory of the estate of local collector Paul Caron (1918–1988), Anaïs Arlot of the Bibliothèque municipale de Tours uncovered a collection of seventy-five photographs that appeared to be attributable to Adolphe de Meyer. Camille Mona Paysant, who had recently published a book on the artist’s travel photography, was subsequently invited to establish the photographs’ attribution and conduct a study of the corpus.

Publication The exhibition is accompanied by a new book, Adolphe de Meyer. The Substance of a Venetian Dream , containing an article by Camille Mona Paysant, who also curated the exhibition in Huis Marseille. The publication was designed by Ernst Georg Kuehle (of Kuehle und Moser) in a bilingual (English/French) edition.

Curated by Camille Mona Paysant

content.article_text:
Jackson Fine Art presents She Was I , a survey of career-defining work by Sam Taylor-Johnson , one of Britain’s most internationally celebrated artists, photographers, and filmmakers. This extensive solo exhibition coincides with the publication of the artist’s major new monograph, Sam Taylor-Johnson: The Self and the Portrait , published by Rizzoli .

The exhibition She Was I traces Taylor-Johnson’s psychologically rich explorations of the self through portraiture in her photography and film work.

Focusing on the self-portraits that are central to Taylor-Johnson’s practice, the selection begins with the early black and white photographs taken in London in the 1990s when she was a student. Then, more than a decade later, the artist returned to self-portraiture with images of herself suspended in her London studio, her body appearing weightless, seemingly held aloft by balloons. In Wired , shot in 2020 in Joshua Tree, Taylor-Johnson now reveals and makes integral to the composition the fragile support mechanisms that elevate her body above the ground in the California desert. Taylor-Johnson’s powerful new series Self Portrait in Dark Water , in which she relies on water to hold her body in otherworldly suspension, will be presented to US audiences for the first time.

The exhibition will also feature a selection of works from the series Crying Men . Created between 2002 and 2004, Taylor-Johnson invited leading male actors to appear before her camera, sat in a moment of intimate reflection, their vulnerability exposed through the act of crying. In parallel to these recognizable individuals, the portraits of the artist’s family and friends captured in the most familial of private settings possess a semi-autobiographical quality.

Seen together, the works in She Was I reveal Taylor-Johnson’s career-long inquiry into the nature of the self and how our individual and complex psyche can be, simultaneously, revealed and concealed.

About the book:

Sam Taylor-Johnson: The Self and the Portrait (Rizzoli, October 6, 2026) is the first comprehensive monograph on the artist, including new writing by Sam Taylor-Johnson alongside texts contributed by Lynsey Addario—award-winning photojournalist and New York Times bestselling author of It’s What I Do —and Tracey Emin, the acclaimed British artist whose work has been exhibited internationally, including at Tate Modern, London; the Musée d’Orsay, Paris; and the Stedelijk Museum, Amsterdam.

Sam Taylor-Johnson: The Self and the Portrait draws imagery from the artist’s extensive archive. The 224-page volume captures the evolution of her vision from early floating self-portraits through to the quiet intensity of Crying Men and the behind-the-scenes imagery of her cinematic work. The book will be available to purchase at the gallery.

Born in 1967 in London, Taylor-Johnson studied sculpture at Goldsmiths College, emerging alongside the generation of artists who came to prominence in the 1990s and was included in the groundbreaking exhibition Sensation (1997) at the Royal Academy of Arts, London. She turned from sculpture to photography and video early on, merging a cinematic sensibility with the still image. Encouraged toward filmmaking by Anthony Minghella, who produced her Palme d’Or-nominated short Love You More (2008), Taylor-Johnson went on to direct Nowhere Boy (2009), Fifty Shades of Grey (2015), A Million Little Pieces (2018), and Back to Black (2024), earning numerous BAFTA nominations.

Taylor-Johnson’s studio practice has been documented in monographs published by Steidl, including a 2002 volume produced for her Hayward Gallery retrospective and Still Lives (Steidl/BALTIC, 2006). Her editorial and commissioned work ranges from the 2014 series Second Floor , photographing Coco Chanel’s private Paris apartment, to an artist-book edition of F. Scott Fitzgerald’s Tender Is the Night . She won the Illy Café Prize at the 1997 Venice Biennale, was nominated for the Turner Prize in 1998, and was appointed OBE (Officer of the Order of the British Empire) in 2011 for her contributions to British arts and culture.

Taylor-Johnson’s work is held in major public collections including the Museum of Modern Art, New York; the Art Institute of Chicago; the Walker Art Center, Minneapolis; Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum; and National Galleries of Scotland, Edinburgh. She has held solo museum exhibitions at Kunsthalle Zürich (1997), the Louisiana Museum of Modern Art, Humlebæk (1997), Fondazione Prada, Milan (1998), Museo Nacional Centro de Arte Reina Sofía, Madrid (2000), Hayward Gallery, London (2002), and BALTIC Centre for Contemporary Art, Gateshead (2006). She Was I is Sam Taylor-Johnson’s second solo exhibition with Jackson Fine Art.

Sam Taylor-Johnson : She Was I Exhibition Dates: October 22, 2026 – January 23, 2027 Opening Reception: October 22 | 6-8 PM Jackson Fine Art 3122 East Shadowlawn Ave. NE Atlanta, GA 30305 www.jacksonfineart.com

Opening hours: Tuesday – Saturday, 10AM – 5PM.

content.article_text:
Kehrer Verlag releases José Antonio Rosas : Somewhere We Feel Free .

For a decade, José Antonio Rosas has photographed from deep inside the crowds at some of the world’s great gatherings. From music festivals and religious pilgrimages to cultural rites, he found a common impulse: the desire to step outside everyday life and experience a sense of connection and release.

In 2015, standing in a crowd at Glastonbury Festival, José Antonio Rosas experienced a sense of collective euphoria that stayed with him. Over the next ten years, he followed this feeling across four continents, photographing seven of the world’s great gatherings—from the explosion of colour at India’s Holi, the candlelit devotion of Christmas in Lalibela, the vibrant dances of Peru’s Candelaria, the icy pilgrimage to Qoyllur Rit’i in the Andes, the vast human tide of Kumbh Mela and the unrestrained joy of Brazil’s Carnaval.

Though separated by culture, geography and purpose, these gatherings share a powerful common thread: the suspension of ordinary life and the collective release of uninhibited emotion. Within the press of bodies and the roar of music or prayer, individuality does not disappear, it transforms. Closed eyes, open mouths and gestures of serenity or ecstasy become expressions of freedom, connection and transcendence.

Somewhere We Feel Free moves across cultures, faiths and continents, revealing the shared human impulse to gather, to surrender and, somewhere within the crowd, to feel free.

With an essay by art critic Jean Dykstra and an interview with José Antonio Rosas by artist Janelle Lynch, the publication brings together this powerful decade-long body of work in the photographer’s second monograph.

José Antonio Rosas is a documentary photographer based in Lima, Peru. He has built his work through repeated visits and sustained attention to mass celebrations, religious pilgrimages, remote wildlife, and communities far from home. His award-winning work has been exhibited and published internationally.

Jean Dykstra is an arts writer and editor. The former editor of photograph magazine, she writes The Photosphere , a Substack publication about contemporary photography. She’s contributed to numerous publications, including The New York Review of Books , The Brooklyn Rail , and Dear Dave .

Janelle Lynch is an artist, writer, and educator, based in New York City. She is represented by Flowers Gallery and has three monographs published by Radius Books. Lynch teaches at the International Center of Photography and writes for LensCulture and The Brooklyn Rail .

José Antonio Rosas : Somewhere We Feel Free Kehrer Verlag Texts by Jean Dykstra, Janelle Lynch, José Antonio Rosas Designed by Kehrer Design (Susan Greszta, Laura Pecoroni) Cloth hardcover 23,3 x 32 cm 152 pages 60 duplex ills. English / Spanish ISBN 978-3-96900-245-2 Euro 58,00 / US$ 68.00 www.kehrerverlag.com

Exhibitions: Caelum Gallery, New York, US 15–21 Oct 2026 Book presentation on 17th October 202

Centro Cultural Inca Garcilaso, Lima, PE 03 Dec 2026 – 13 Mar 2027

content.title_original: Galerie Frank Elbaz : Kunié Sugiura : Ubiquitous Conjunction
content.article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "Galerie Frank Elbaz announces Ubiquitous Conjunction , the first solo exhibition of Kunié Sugiura in Paris, presented at the gallery from October 19 to December 31, 2026, and curated by Ryo Sawayama. The exhibition is part of the celebrations of the Bicentennial of Photography, which in 2026 mark 200 years since the invention of photography."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The exhibition is accompanied by this essay by Ryo Sawayama on the artist’s work."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In 1963, at the age of twenty, Kunié Sugiura moved from Japan to the United States and enrolled at the School of the Art Institute of Chicago—an institution which descends from the New Bauhaus lineage. It was in Chicago that Sugiura first encountered photography as a medium and began her career as an artist. From that point on, Sugiura has consistently worked with photography as her primary medium."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "At the time, photography was still regarded within the art world as a secondary field, subordinate to painting and sculpture. It was only later that a number of women artists—such as Cindy Sherman, Francesca Woodman, Ana Mendieta, Laurie Simmons, Barbara Kruger, among others—would take up photography as an important medium. Sugiura’s work anticipated this shift (a contemporary parallel can be found in Betty Hahn)."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Photography came to be actively taken up by women artists precisely because it had long been dismissed as a secondary mode of expression. Unlike painting and sculpture, traditional fields largely occupied by male artists, photography was seen as a democratic field open to those on the margins. Therefore, Sugiura—a foreigner and a woman—turning to photography as her medium was a conscious and theoretical choice bound up in these very issues."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Although Sugiura embraced photography as her primary medium, she has distanced herself from presenting so-called “photographic works” associated with straight photography, and likewise from being regarded as a “photographer.” Instead, Sugiura has continued to pursue and expand the latent plasticity inherent in photography, experimenting with how photography might become a means of expression equal to painting and sculpture. Sugiura’s work does not treat photography as a privileged medium in itself; it engages photography through hybridization and its conjunction with other media."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The use of hybridization can be seen in Sugiura’s Photocanvas Island 2 (1971), where photography conjoins with painting. Here, acrylic paint is layered over a photograph of the surface of the Coney Island breakwater, where the rough “ground” of the photographed breakwater is superimposed onto the “ground” of the painting, and the brushstrokes are combined with the pre-existing pattern of the rock surface. The three-dimensional object of the breakwater and the two-dimensional picture plane, the figurative and the abstract, are brought into conjunction. Here, rather than placing the brushstrokes freely, Sugiura arranges them along the textures and patterns already formed by the rocks."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "For Sugiura, the conjunction of photography and painting meant collaborating with an already-existing nature: creating a superposition of nature and artifice."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "This kind of conjunction can be found throughout Sugiura’s work: the conjunction of photography and painting in Island 2 (1971), Christmas Lights (1979) and Hossawa (2022); the conjunction of multiple frames in Arita and Miyazaki (both 2023); the connection of different sequences in Story of Catfish (1993); the linking of skeletal structure and joints through X-ray photography in Vertebra (2021) and Racks (1994), in which a photo rack holding postcard-sized X-ray photographs recalls the connective structure of bones, or the structure of DNA. This conjunction can also be seen where Sugiura binds flowers together with thread, or in the large photocanvas of a couple having sex. In Sugiura’s work, photography is a plastic material that carries out endless operations of severance and conjunction with everything it touches. Through these conjunctions, new forms are produced. By staging these encounters, conjunctions, and hybridizations, Sugiura turned photography into a site of experimentation, revealing its open, transversal, and mediating nature."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Sugiura was also known in Japan as a writer, with a regular column in Bijutsu Techō . Before the widespread use of the internet, the information she sent from New York, from the 1980s onward, was extremely valuable. Sugiura introduced the New York art scene to Japan, welcomed and looked after many Japanese visitors in her studio, and connected them with people on the ground in the local art community—she was herself a mediator in every sense. Sugiura understood, better than anyone, that the encounter between two things generates a new form, and that chance encounters give rise to new events. In a sense, Sugiura’s stance as a mediator resembles the very attitude she takes toward photography as a medium."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Sugiura’s work carries forward a New Bauhaus mode of thinking that crosses and conjoins photography with a variety of other media, in parallel with her treatment of photography as a site of formal experimentation. What characterizes her practice is its continuity with early experimental and avant-garde photography—through the use of photograms, X-ray photographs and the material and fluid use of photographic emulsion. Sugiura treats photography not simply as a means of reproducing an existing scene, but as an experimental field for formal invention."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Experimental and avant-garde photography explored precisely this plastic potential inherent in photography, and such experiments were themselves preceded by occult photography, including early spirit photography. Notably, the birth of photography and the rise of spiritualism were historically contemporaneous. Multiple exposures on wet and dry plates, stains, chemical unevenness, and irregular reduction reactions during development often produced unexpected double images or hazy forms. This made it possible for different moments in time to coexist within the same pictorial space, as in Futurist painting (although, more precisely, Futurist painting was influenced by experimental photography, rather than the reverse). These photographic processes and their unpredictable effects all served to expand photography’s plastic potential."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "At the time, photography was believed to reveal the presence of spirits automatically and objectively, without human intervention. Avant-garde and experimental photography consciously and aesthetically repurposed techniques first seen in early spirit photography: multiple exposure, solarization and the photogram. Therefore, it could be said that spirit photography had already realized photography’s chemical plasticity, preceding experimental photography and the avant-garde."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "One could say that photography announces the existence of another “nature”—a parallel world. Photography reveals that the perceivable world runs parallel to a supernatural world, and to a world beyond human perception, that includes electromagnetic waves such as ultraviolet light and X-rays. X-ray photography visualizes precisely that behind the visible lies a reality beyond human perception. By chemically combining multiple substances, photography demonstrates that the world is a superimposition and conjunction of multiple universes, exceeding what human beings can coherently grasp. Through developments in contemporary science and early photography, it became clear that the way human beings had grasped the world was no more than a contingently generated pattern—a subjective convenience."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Early photography served as evidence in police records and as a form of historical documentation. At the same time, however, its chemical process of mixing volatile substances and its capacity to reveal what would otherwise be invisible gave early photography a magical, even suspect quality. Photography and spirit photography were bound together by this same unpredictable process of development. The word “occult” carries the meaning of “hidden knowledge.” In this sense, occult photography sought to make visible an invisible, hidden world—the latent plasticity of the world and its hidden creativity."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "It was this expectation—that photography possessed an automatism capable of revealing a hidden, surreal world, an automatic productive force independent of human agency—that drew the Surrealists, who placed automatism at the center of their methodology, so intensely to photography. The emergence of an image through chemical reactions in photography shares the same structure as a spirit medium, who similarly makes the invisible visible. Photography is thus the perfect medium, in both senses of the word. Through its chemical plasticity, photography binds together different worlds and reveals another, invisible nature."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In this way, photography transmits a hidden world into the here and now. For example, Sugiura’s The Kitten Papers (1992) was made by leaving two kittens alone in a darkroom for a week and turning the traces they left—their footprints and movements—into the work itself. The traces are made not by the artist but by cats moving of their own will; they record the cats’ unpredictable movements, which are beyond human intention. This device—a cat in a darkroom—recalls the thought experiment in quantum mechanics known as “Schrödinger’s cat”, in which a cat sealed inside a box is described as simultaneously alive and dead—an object in quantum superposition. Here the contents of the box constitute a literal “black box”, and whether the cat is alive or dead cannot be known until the box is opened."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Although Schrödinger’s cat is a thought experiment modeling the indeterminacy of measurement in quantum mechanics, Sugiura’s The Kitten Papers is an experiment actually carried out in a darkroom. Among the works exhibited in this exhibition, Story of Catfish , made by Sugiura during the same period, belongs to the same artistic trajectory. In both The Kitten Papers and Story of Catfish , the accumulation of uncontrollable, probabilistic deviations produced by the behavior of animals in the darkroom appears as material traces fixed onto photographic paper."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "An important point to note is that the word “Papers” in The Kitten Papers evokes the documentary practice of reconstructing an event after the fact from its material traces—a movement of nature that no one observed. Here, Sugiura functions simultaneously as the maker and observer."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Sugiura’s photograms, in dealing with the physical movement of living creatures in the darkroom, reveal the countless deviations possible within nature—the superposition of multiple worlds. The unrestrained movement and energy of these creatures arise not because the world is fixed and static, but because countless possibilities remain latent and open within it. content.article_text:
Galerie Frank Elbaz announces Ubiquitous Conjunction , the first solo exhibition of Kunié Sugiura in Paris, presented at the gallery from October 19 to December 31, 2026, and curated by Ryo Sawayama. The exhibition is part of the celebrations of the Bicentennial of Photography, which in 2026 mark 200 years since the invention of photography.

The exhibition is accompanied by this essay by Ryo Sawayama on the artist’s work.

In 1963, at the age of twenty, Kunié Sugiura moved from Japan to the United States and enrolled at the School of the Art Institute of Chicago—an institution which descends from the New Bauhaus lineage. It was in Chicago that Sugiura first encountered photography as a medium and began her career as an artist. From that point on, Sugiura has consistently worked with photography as her primary medium.

At the time, photography was still regarded within the art world as a secondary field, subordinate to painting and sculpture. It was only later that a number of women artists—such as Cindy Sherman, Francesca Woodman, Ana Mendieta, Laurie Simmons, Barbara Kruger, among others—would take up photography as an important medium. Sugiura’s work anticipated this shift (a contemporary parallel can be found in Betty Hahn).

Photography came to be actively taken up by women artists precisely because it had long been dismissed as a secondary mode of expression. Unlike painting and sculpture, traditional fields largely occupied by male artists, photography was seen as a democratic field open to those on the margins. Therefore, Sugiura—a foreigner and a woman—turning to photography as her medium was a conscious and theoretical choice bound up in these very issues.

Although Sugiura embraced photography as her primary medium, she has distanced herself from presenting so-called “photographic works” associated with straight photography, and likewise from being regarded as a “photographer.” Instead, Sugiura has continued to pursue and expand the latent plasticity inherent in photography, experimenting with how photography might become a means of expression equal to painting and sculpture. Sugiura’s work does not treat photography as a privileged medium in itself; it engages photography through hybridization and its conjunction with other media.

The use of hybridization can be seen in Sugiura’s Photocanvas Island 2 (1971), where photography conjoins with painting. Here, acrylic paint is layered over a photograph of the surface of the Coney Island breakwater, where the rough “ground” of the photographed breakwater is superimposed onto the “ground” of the painting, and the brushstrokes are combined with the pre-existing pattern of the rock surface. The three-dimensional object of the breakwater and the two-dimensional picture plane, the figurative and the abstract, are brought into conjunction. Here, rather than placing the brushstrokes freely, Sugiura arranges them along the textures and patterns already formed by the rocks.

For Sugiura, the conjunction of photography and painting meant collaborating with an already-existing nature: creating a superposition of nature and artifice.

This kind of conjunction can be found throughout Sugiura’s work: the conjunction of photography and painting in Island 2 (1971), Christmas Lights (1979) and Hossawa (2022); the conjunction of multiple frames in Arita and Miyazaki (both 2023); the connection of different sequences in Story of Catfish (1993); the linking of skeletal structure and joints through X-ray photography in Vertebra (2021) and Racks (1994), in which a photo rack holding postcard-sized X-ray photographs recalls the connective structure of bones, or the structure of DNA. This conjunction can also be seen where Sugiura binds flowers together with thread, or in the large photocanvas of a couple having sex. In Sugiura’s work, photography is a plastic material that carries out endless operations of severance and conjunction with everything it touches. Through these conjunctions, new forms are produced. By staging these encounters, conjunctions, and hybridizations, Sugiura turned photography into a site of experimentation, revealing its open, transversal, and mediating nature.

Sugiura was also known in Japan as a writer, with a regular column in Bijutsu Techō . Before the widespread use of the internet, the information she sent from New York, from the 1980s onward, was extremely valuable. Sugiura introduced the New York art scene to Japan, welcomed and looked after many Japanese visitors in her studio, and connected them with people on the ground in the local art community—she was herself a mediator in every sense. Sugiura understood, better than anyone, that the encounter between two things generates a new form, and that chance encounters give rise to new events. In a sense, Sugiura’s stance as a mediator resembles the very attitude she takes toward photography as a medium.

Sugiura’s work carries forward a New Bauhaus mode of thinking that crosses and conjoins photography with a variety of other media, in parallel with her treatment of photography as a site of formal experimentation. What characterizes her practice is its continuity with early experimental and avant-garde photography—through the use of photograms, X-ray photographs and the material and fluid use of photographic emulsion. Sugiura treats photography not simply as a means of reproducing an existing scene, but as an experimental field for formal invention.

Experimental and avant-garde photography explored precisely this plastic potential inherent in photography, and such experiments were themselves preceded by occult photography, including early spirit photography. Notably, the birth of photography and the rise of spiritualism were historically contemporaneous. Multiple exposures on wet and dry plates, stains, chemical unevenness, and irregular reduction reactions during development often produced unexpected double images or hazy forms. This made it possible for different moments in time to coexist within the same pictorial space, as in Futurist painting (although, more precisely, Futurist painting was influenced by experimental photography, rather than the reverse). These photographic processes and their unpredictable effects all served to expand photography’s plastic potential.

At the time, photography was believed to reveal the presence of spirits automatically and objectively, without human intervention. Avant-garde and experimental photography consciously and aesthetically repurposed techniques first seen in early spirit photography: multiple exposure, solarization and the photogram. Therefore, it could be said that spirit photography had already realized photography’s chemical plasticity, preceding experimental photography and the avant-garde.

One could say that photography announces the existence of another “nature”—a parallel world. Photography reveals that the perceivable world runs parallel to a supernatural world, and to a world beyond human perception, that includes electromagnetic waves such as ultraviolet light and X-rays. X-ray photography visualizes precisely that behind the visible lies a reality beyond human perception. By chemically combining multiple substances, photography demonstrates that the world is a superimposition and conjunction of multiple universes, exceeding what human beings can coherently grasp. Through developments in contemporary science and early photography, it became clear that the way human beings had grasped the world was no more than a contingently generated pattern—a subjective convenience.

Early photography served as evidence in police records and as a form of historical documentation. At the same time, however, its chemical process of mixing volatile substances and its capacity to reveal what would otherwise be invisible gave early photography a magical, even suspect quality. Photography and spirit photography were bound together by this same unpredictable process of development. The word “occult” carries the meaning of “hidden knowledge.” In this sense, occult photography sought to make visible an invisible, hidden world—the latent plasticity of the world and its hidden creativity.

It was this expectation—that photography possessed an automatism capable of revealing a hidden, surreal world, an automatic productive force independent of human agency—that drew the Surrealists, who placed automatism at the center of their methodology, so intensely to photography. The emergence of an image through chemical reactions in photography shares the same structure as a spirit medium, who similarly makes the invisible visible. Photography is thus the perfect medium, in both senses of the word. Through its chemical plasticity, photography binds together different worlds and reveals another, invisible nature.

In this way, photography transmits a hidden world into the here and now. For example, Sugiura’s The Kitten Papers (1992) was made by leaving two kittens alone in a darkroom for a week and turning the traces they left—their footprints and movements—into the work itself. The traces are made not by the artist but by cats moving of their own will; they record the cats’ unpredictable movements, which are beyond human intention. This device—a cat in a darkroom—recalls the thought experiment in quantum mechanics known as “Schrödinger’s cat”, in which a cat sealed inside a box is described as simultaneously alive and dead—an object in quantum superposition. Here the contents of the box constitute a literal “black box”, and whether the cat is alive or dead cannot be known until the box is opened.

Although Schrödinger’s cat is a thought experiment modeling the indeterminacy of measurement in quantum mechanics, Sugiura’s The Kitten Papers is an experiment actually carried out in a darkroom. Among the works exhibited in this exhibition, Story of Catfish , made by Sugiura during the same period, belongs to the same artistic trajectory. In both The Kitten Papers and Story of Catfish , the accumulation of uncontrollable, probabilistic deviations produced by the behavior of animals in the darkroom appears as material traces fixed onto photographic paper.

An important point to note is that the word “Papers” in The Kitten Papers evokes the documentary practice of reconstructing an event after the fact from its material traces—a movement of nature that no one observed. Here, Sugiura functions simultaneously as the maker and observer.

Sugiura’s photograms, in dealing with the physical movement of living creatures in the darkroom, reveal the countless deviations possible within nature—the superposition of multiple worlds. The unrestrained movement and energy of these creatures arise not because the world is fixed and static, but because countless possibilities remain latent and open within it. It is because these innumerable worlds are superimposed simultaneously, that the world possesses creativity. Here, the living creature is not merely an object being photographed, but it is itself the subject that produces the image.

The fact that Sugiura has repeatedly chosen living things—such as humans, animals, and flowers—as her subjects is congruous with her interest in the formation of natural forms. A living creature, which produces its own form through its own agency, is structurally similar to photography, which also produces an image automatically (for example, a flower grows by its own power and forms its own shape as a flower, entirely by its own power). As Sugiura herself has said, a flower is a reproductive organ: the stamen produces pollen, and the pistil receives that pollen to create a new life that ultimately becomes the seed.

Sugiura’s works that bind flowers together with thread appear to show, quite literally, the conjunction of male and female—pollination and fertilization—within a process of biological reproduction. Here, photography’s automatism responds to nature’s process of self-formation.

The photographic emulsion itself is, materially, a forced homogeneous dispersion and suspension of substances that do not naturally dissolve into one another—a mixture of water-based gelatin and fine particles of silver salts. The very support of a photograph embodies, at the material level, the conjunction between heterogeneous elements, as photography arises through an operation—emulsification—that binds together things that are chemically unmixable by nature. This operation recalls the Hindu creation myth of the Churning of the Ocean of Milk, in which every manner of plant and seed is placed into the ocean of milk and churned, and from that churning, the sun, the moon, the gods, and all animals are born.

This conjunction in reproduction and photography can also be linked to the alchemical term coniunctio . In the alchemical process, the chymical wedding—the chemical marriage of opposites, sulfur (the male principle) and mercury (the female principle)—was said to produce a new substance: the philosopher’s stone. Coniunctio meant a chemical conjunction, while at the same time serving as a metaphor for the conjunction of the sexes.

The mixing and blending of heterogeneous elements—emulsification—could be thought of as the emergence of life itself. The human body, living creatures, flowers, and the earth itself—subjects that Sugiura has persistently captured—belong precisely to this realm of nature and living things, onto which she superimposes the chemical process of photography’s own formation, together with her own acts of painting and image-making. Photography, rather than serving as a means of reproduction, can be understood as a self-generating movement that, through acts of conjunction, generates new forms—releasing a creative productive force inherent in the world itself. Sugiura’s work reveals the ubiquity of an automatic creative power that permeates the world.

Born in Japan and based in New York since 1967, Kunié Sugiura has spent more than six decades developing a body of work at the crossroads of photography, painting, and sculpture. Through a selection of works made over the past sixty years, Ubiquitous Conjunction looks back at a practice that has never ceased to push the boundaries of the photographic medium and to explore the possibilities of its dialogue with other art forms.

Ryo Sawayama

Curated by Ryo Sawayama

content.article_text:
Photographer and filmmaker Neal Slavin returns to his alma mater for a conversation with artist and author M. Leona Godin . Their conversation will explore perception and what it truly means to see.

Neal Slavin met M. Leona Godin at the New York Public Library, where Godin was the 2025–26 Jean Strouse Fellow in the Cullman Center for Scholars and Writers. As a fellow, Godin was working on a book about blindness, photography, and image description. Their first encounter sparked many long conversations on the ways perception shapes how we experience the world through photography.

This evening’s conversation will explore the phenomenon of synesthesia, where the boundaries among the senses dissolve and the languages of music, poetry, painting, and photography intermingle. Together, they will discuss how perception moves beyond eyesight alone, and how photography continues to expand our understanding of what it means to see.

Slavin’s portraits have been published in several books, including Portugal , Britons , and When Two or More Are Gathered Together , recently republished and expanded with new photographs that bring together portraits taken over a span of 50 years (1974–2023). He was the recipient of a Fulbright Fellowship in Photography and of Cooper Union’s highest honor, the President’s Citation. Slavin’s photographs are in numerous permanent collections, including The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Centre Pompidou, and the New York Public Library, where Godin first encountered his work.

M. Leona Godin is a blind writer, artist, and the author of There Plant Eyes: A Personal and Cultural History of Blindness . She is currently working on a project about photography, blindness, and what it means to see, which received recent support from an NYPL Cullman Center Fellowship.

THURSDAY, OCTOBER 15, 2026, 6 – 8PM The Cooper Union Located at 7 East 7th Street, between Third and Fourth Avenues

content.article_text:
Archives – October 13, 2011

The second portfolio, which Jean-François Jonvelle began for Photo in the 1980s, is devoted to French actresses. The book features a lovely preface by Frédéric Beigbeder, followed by a short biography:

Jean-François Jonvelle was snatched by the hand of death with a suddenness to match the photographs that were his life. Just as that life was dedicated to capturing these stolen moments, so death followed suit, carrying him off in the midst of life. A tumour discovered in early January, a final farewell just a fortnight later. He was gone in a flash. As I turn the pages of my friend’s last book my eyes mist over. My tears dissolve Jonvelle’s photographs into the soft focus of a David Hamilton.

Jonvelle’s work is often described as being – in the time-honoured formula – ‘sexy but not vulgar’. I prefer his own description of what he sought out: ‘la poésie du quotidien’, ‘the poetry of the everyday’. Photographs freeze moments of truth, all you have to do is choose the ones that do it best. ‘I tell myself that the present and the future don’t exist,’ he also used to say. ‘Everyone, every day, creates their own past.’

The quality that makes his images more moving than the rest is their vulnerability. Jonvelle taught me one crucial lesson: in photography, as in literature, what counts is feeling. Eroticism and tenderness are not sworn enemies. A downy arm, the frail nape of a neck, an uptilted breast, the curve of a back beneath the sheets, damp hair, closed eyelids, the trace of a kiss on the neck all these can be arousing.

Jonvelle’s women are fresh and natural because they are unaware of our gaze. Jonvelle makes adoring voyeurs of us all. He shows us why heterosexuality can be so painful: everywhere, in every house and every bathroom, paradise lurks. Paradise delicately removes her T-shirt, brushes her teeth, buttocks pert, the curve of her breasts taut, timeless. Suddenly paradise parts her legs in silence, biting her fin- gernails as she looks you straight in the eye, teasing you as she waits for you on the sheets. Jonvelle is in paradise now, but for him nothing has changed: he was already there in his lifetime.

As I gaze in wonder, the way I always do, at these images, so far removed from the familiar clichés, my thoughts turn to the beautiful women he immortalized. Photographs fix the fleeting, immortalize the ephemeral. Many of the women Jonvelle photographed are now old or dead, but – thanks to this photographer who is now also dead – their perfection will never fade.

Every one of Jonvelle’s photographs is a declaration of love. One day, at my request, he photographed Delphine Vallette, the mother of my daughter. I wanted to give this brunette whom I loved a portrait. Never have I felt such a cuckold – though in the most erotic of ways.

Beauty is an evanescent mystery that some artists have the ability to capture. As I look again at these wonderful images, I’m reminded of the title of that American comedy Drop Dead Gorgeous. Jonvelle’s work as a whole is not an ode to femininity; the story it tells is of the battle to vanquish death by means of the celebration of desire. All these shoulders caught by surprise, these half-seen breasts, these finely- arched insteps, these flawless backs, this sensual solitude, this calm between two storms, all these beautiful women who don’t give a damn are simply doors softly opened, through which we may catch a glimpse of eternal life.

Frédéric Beigbeder

Jean-François Jonvelle was born in 1943 in Cavaillon, south of France. Soon he will sell famous melons to buy Hasselblad. Its inspirations will come from the painting of Balthus, Bacon, of Schiele, but the true influence comes from films from Mankiewicz, Lubitsch, Fritz Lang, Orson Welles, Arthur PEN, Minnelli and more recently of Terry Gillian of which it acknowledges to have seen eleven times the film Brazil ; Finally its preferred film: Jules and Jim of François Truffaut.

In 1959, it is the photographer George Glasberg who initiates him with photography while making him make the turn of France of the cathedrals. It is a photographic revelation which will leave it never again.

content.article_text:
Archives – October 13, 2020

Opening on November, Tate Modern hosts the the first major exhibition in the United Kingdom of Zanele Muholi . The show gathers about 260 photographs presenting the full breadth of their career to date. Muholi often describes their* work not as a photographer or a videast but as a “visual activist”. From the early 2000s, the artist documented and celebrated the lives of South Africa’s black lesbian, gay, trans, queer and intersex communities. The following videos, produced by Tate Modern, explores Muholis various aspects of her arts and describer their series.

“In the early series Only Half the Picture , Muholi captures moments of love and intimacy as well as intense images alluding to traumatic events – despite the equality promised by South Africa’s 1996 constitution, its LGBTQIA+ community remains a target for violence and prejudice.

In Faces and Phases each participant looks directly at the camera, challenging the viewer to hold their gaze. These images and the accompanying testimonies form a growing archive of a community of people who are risking their lives by living authentically in the face of oppression and discrimination.

Other key series of works, include Brave Beauties , which celebrates empowered non-binary people and trans women, many of whom have won Miss Gay Beauty pageants, and Being, a series of tender images of couples which challenge stereotypes and taboos.

Muholi turns the camera on themself in the ongoing series Somnyama Ngonyama – translated as ‘Hail the Dark Lioness’. These powerful and reflective images explore themes including labour, racism, Eurocentrism and sexual politics.​”

Zanele Muholi – In My World, Every Human Is Beautiful 5 November 2020 – 7 March 2021 Tate Modern Bankside, London SE1 9TG, United Kingdom

The exhibition is organised by Tate Modern in collaboration with the Maison Européenne de la Photographie, Paris, Gropius Bau, Berlin and Bildmuseet at Umeå Universit

*Zanele Muholi sees theirself as a non-binary person, and therefore uses the pronoum “their”. The Eye of Photography wishes to respect this use.a
