content.article_text:
P rem Sahib turns the city inside out, twists it around and rips it apart. His show at the De La Warr Pavilion in Bexhill, a sort of mid-career survey for the 44-year-old English artist, is full of private spaces and urban nightmares that have been gutted and left on display. It’s minimal, claustrophobic, intense stuff.

A sodium street lamp hangs upside down from the ceiling, casting its sickly pale orange glow across the gallery. You feel like you’ve stumbled into some urban back alley where physics has been flipped, it has all the threat of an underpass, but surreal and inverted. Nearby, three puffer jackets have been squeezed between sheets of glass – are these the blokes who were waiting for you in the underpass? Or are they three strangers who you’ve caught mid-embrace?

That’s what Sahib does, over and over: he plays with the line between terror and pleasure, threat and intimacy, public and private.

So much here is geared towards an atmosphere of discomfort. There’s a deep bass throb echoing out of one space, its tone eventually rising to an ear-piercing squeal, before settling back into a chest-rattling sub. A table has been made out of a grossly overgrown flea’s body, a street sign has been left blank but its light is still on. Two space heaters constantly flick on and ramp up the temperature. It is liminal, weird, uncomfortable.

Queerness is central to Sahib’s work. The double doors you pass as you walk in were taken from a Mile End leather bar that closed in 2022, the water fountain encased in resin is from Chariots sauna in Shoreditch which closed in 2016. Private spaces, places of intimate pleasure, that have been erased from the city.

In one of his signature resin panels, clear droplets have accumulated on a sheet of black aluminium, like sweat gathering on a nightclub wall. You can almost smell it, almost feel hot, damp, writhing people coming together somewhere nearby. Hung up high, two acrylic discs nod to the visual results of rapid HIV tests. There’s intimacy here, but risk too.

Risk, and threat: an obsidian mirror hangs cracked on the wall, burbling out discordant sounds, a slowed down recording of a homophobic rant sent to Sahib on a gay chat room.

Is this all about architecture, as the wall text here insists? I don’t know. Architecture is already about architecture – I don’t need art to make me think deep thoughts about buildings. This feels way more intimate than that description coldly implies. It’s about bodies being pressed together, sweat dripping down a wall, and feeling like it’s all about to be torn away from you.

The whole way through, it’s as if Sahib is asking: what happens when the places that matter to me, where I express myself, are destroyed? What is left for me, for us? Who decides which spaces can survive, who decides what communities are worth preserving, who decides where bodies get to exist?

after newsletter promotion

I don’t think it all works. The recording of Suella Braverman hatefully talking about the migrant crisis that you listen to while looking out at the sea is a bit on the nose, and the little dotty images of the horizon that line one wall don’t really add a huge amount.

But for the most part, Sahib is brilliant, with an incredible knack for crushingly intense minimalist atmospherics. He’s been one of the most interesting artists working in this country for more than a decade now, and a big institutional show like this feels long overdue.

Prem Sahib: Chamber is at De La Warr Pavilion, Bexhill, from 10 October 2026 to 3 January 2027

content.article_text:
The Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has ordered the country’s attorney general and the head of the Shin Bet security service to reveal the identities of soldiers and officers interviewed in the investigative documentary NAZA and prosecute them for causing “harm to Israel’s diplomatic and security interests”.

The award-winning documentary, directed by the Oscar-winning film-makers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor and produced by the Guardian, details Israel’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza. The film is in cinemas, including in the UK and the US, and will be shown in more than 50 countries.

In a letter addressed to the attorney general, Gali Baharav-Miara, the IDF chief of staff, Lt Gen Eyal Zamir, and the Shin Bet head, David Zini, the Israeli prime minister demanded they “act urgently to uncover the identity of all those who are involved or appear in the libel film”.

Netanyahu also called for “the opening of a criminal investigation and prosecution for serious information security offences, criminal defamation, and harming Israel’s diplomatic and security interests”.

NAZA premiered last month at the Venice international film festival, where it won the special jury prize after receiving the longest ovation in the event’s history. It takes its name from an acronym used euphemistically by Israeli intelligence to indicate how many civilians it expects to be killed in an airstrike .

The Israeli government has fiercely attacked Abraham and Szor, threatening to strip them of their citizenship and accusing them of treason. Government supporters have vowed to hound the film-makers on their return to Israel and picketed Szor’s parents’ home in Savyon, chanting: “Death sentence to traitors.”

Zamir denounced the film as an “attack on the state of Israel”, accusing it of spreading “lies and blood libels” . He had earlier ordered military and legal officials to identify the soldiers featured and examine possible legal action against them. However, the military advocate general, Itai Ofir, said criminal prosecution would require evidence of security violations or disclosure of classified material, although disciplinary measures remained possible.

The protection of journalistic sources is a cornerstone of press freedom under international human rights standards and disclosure orders are permitted only under stringent conditions.

Ricardo Gutiérrez, the general secretary of the European Federation of Journalists, representing over 320,000 journalists, said: “These threats constitute a blatant act of intimidation against journalists who have simply been doing their job, in strict accordance with ethical standards and in the public interest. I am not surprised by this outburst, which confirms that this regime is prepared to do anything to cover up its crimes against humanity and the ongoing genocide in Gaza.”

A Guardian spokesperson said: “After first threatening to strip NAZA’s directors of their Israeli citizenship, the Israeli government is now calling for an investigation into their journalistic sources. These moves are all attempts to distract from the urgent questions the film asks about the mass killings of Palestinian civilians in Gaza. Journalists should be free to pursue public interest investigations without threats or harassment.”

NAZA builds on revelations first published by the Israeli-Palestinian publication +972 Magazine, the Hebrew-language outlet Local Call and the Guardian between 2023 and 2025. Earlier this month, a Guardian spokesperson said the “process of assessing the credibility of the testimonies was rigorous. It included leaked classified documents, detailed verification of specific strikes and corroboration via a wider pool of confidential journalistic sources who did not appear on camera in the film.”

In the past three years the team behind the film has “ interviewed more than 100 sources familiar with IDF systems used in the war in Gaza, including senior-ranking commanders directly involved in the authorisation of strikes”, the Guardian spokesperson added.

In recent days, the Israeli government has promoted an online film project that mimics the style of NAZA, in an attempt to challenge the real film’s findings. Ariel Averbuch, an Israeli attorney and army reservist who made NAZA: The Real Story, described it as an “offensive move” intended to shift the world’s focus from allegations about the Israeli military’s killing of civilians.

Film industry heavyweights across the globe, including the heads of the Locarno film festival, have expressed solidarity with Abraham and Szor , saying they stood “firmly in support of film-makers’ rights to pursue difficult and urgent subjects without fear of reprisal”.

content.article_text:
Digger, the ambitious eco-fable starring Tom Cruise and directed by Alejandro G Iñárritu, is heading for an even worse financial outcome than previously thought , with reports suggesting it will lose around $245m (£185m), placing it among the biggest disasters in movie history.

According to a report in Variety , Digger’s estimated second weekend revenue in North America of $3.2m is a 60% drop on its opening weekend figure of $8m, meaning its current domestic gross is $14.4m, for a global total of $35.3m , with a projected final box office total of around $50m worldwide.

Though precise figures are not available, Variety estimates that Digger’s production costs are $160m-180m (well over the original budget of $125m), with another $100m spent on marketing the film. Another $15m was potentially on hand for awards-season marketing, but this is likely to be scaled back after the film’s failure. Given that cinemas keep around half the revenue of ticket sales, Variety estimates the film would need to make around $350m to cover costs. (A spokesperson for Digger’s producing studio Warner Bros, says that break-even point is $300m, suggesting a production spend of $150m.)

A $245m loss would put Digger on a par with such legendary turkeys as Cutthroat Island ($222m loss, adjusted for inflation), Mortal Engines ($224m adjusted) and The Marvels ($205-$250m adjusted).

Reaction to the film has likely played a key role in its underperformance, with critical opinion radically divided. In the Guardian, chief film critic Peter Bradshaw called it “an exasperatingly shallow, laborious, self-congratulatory satire” in a two-star review , while Guardian Australia’s deputy culture editor Sian Cain took the opposite position, describing it as “a masterpiece” . Warner Bros, whose last release this is before its takeover by David Ellison’s Skydance , tried to play into the controversy with a post-release advertising campaign quoting its negative notices , but it seems to have had little effect.

So far, 2026 has been a disappointing year for Warner Bros, as it prepares for new ownership, with poorly performing releases such as Supergirl and The Bride! and co-chairs Michael De Luca and Pamela Abdy due to leave ahead of the takeover. This contrasts with a successful 2025, in which releases such as A Minecraft Movie, Sinners and F1 propelled it to the second most successful studio, behind Disney.

Elsewhere, the Aaron Sorkin-directed The Social Reckoning also failed to live up to expectations on its first weekend, taking an estimated $5.5m at the North American box office and $9m globally . The sequel to The Social Network, which stars Jeremy Strong as Facebook founder Mark Zuckerberg and Mikey Madison as whistleblower Frances Haugen, was comprehensively beaten by Jessica Chastain horror The Other Mommy, which led the North American box office with an estimated $27.5m, part of a global take of $45.2m.

Reza Rahadian, Eva Celia and Christine Hakim Talk “The Sea Speaks His Name”, 1998, Political Memory and Finding Truth in Performance

Reza Rahadian, Eva Celia and Christine Hakim discuss “The Sea Speaks His Name”, Indonesia’s political past, acting and memory.

“The Sea Speaks His Name” brings together Reza Rahadian , Eva Celia and Christine Hakim in a story rooted in Indonesia’s political upheaval of the late 1990s, following young activists whose lives, relationships and families are changed by the violence surrounding the period. Based on the work of Leila S. Chudori, the film also marks another collaboration between Rahadian and director Yosep Anggi Noen , while giving Celia one of her first major acting roles after spending much of the previous decade concentrating on music.

The Sea Speaks His Name is screening at Busan International Film Festival

For Rahadian, the project actually began many years earlier. He had already played the character in a short film made around eight years ago for the launch of the book, giving him an early understanding of Laut and the world around him. Returning to the character for the feature therefore felt less like starting from zero than revisiting someone he had already encountered. As for playing a university student despite his current age, Rahadian joked that this was not particularly difficult since “most of the students” in the 1990s looked considerably older anyway.

Celia plays Rati Anjani, an art student involved in the movement and its organization. She meets Laut during a protest and the two gradually fall in love. Celia describes the relationship as one based strongly on intellectual intimacy and equality, with the pair sharing similar hopes for the future and a common understanding of the political work around them. Having known Rahadian for approximately 12 years, she felt that their existing familiarity also made the collaboration particularly natural.

Rahadian refers to a phrase associated with the period, “cinta bersemi setelah aksi” — love that grows after a demonstration. For him, this mixture of political commitment and romance is one of the most human aspects of the story. Two people can be participating in a movement driven by larger ideals while simultaneously discovering someone with whom they share those same convictions. He was also particularly pleased to work with Celia again, describing her as an actress he had wanted to collaborate with for some time.

His own memories of the 1998 period are fragmented but vivid. Rahadian was still in his final year of elementary school, but remembers his mother returning from work and telling him that she had travelled through the Sudirman area on a tank because roads and public transportation were blocked. He also remembers unrest reaching his own neighborhood and people taking goods from a store. At the time, he did not understand why any of it was happening. Only later, through books, news reports and his growing interest in politics, did he begin to understand the scale of what he had witnessed as a child.

Those memories helped him approach Laut, whose personality is more complicated than that of the stereotypically vocal activist. Rahadian describes him as contemplative and relatively quiet, carrying fear and courage at the same time. That contradiction became important because Laut is participating in a political struggle while not necessarily possessing the extroverted temperament people might associate with a movement leader. Even his attraction toward another senior figure within the organization remains restrained by hierarchy and his own reluctance to confront his feelings openly.

The character’s disappearance halfway through the film presented another challenge. Rahadian realized that his voice would have to continue carrying Laut’s presence after his physical absence from the screen. Narration consequently became essential, not simply as exposition but as another form of performance. He wanted the emotion behind the words to preserve the character’s presence and allow audiences to continue feeling him even after he was no longer visible.

For Celia, the emotional consequences of that disappearance become particularly demanding. Anjani initially refuses to accept that Laut has been kidnapped and begins interpreting signs and superstitions as evidence that he may still communicate with her. Celia describes this as a coping mechanism, a way for someone overwhelmed by loss and uncertainty to create an alternative explanation she can emotionally survive. Many of her scenes were therefore less physically difficult than psychologically exhausting.

Christine Hakim approaches the same absence from another direction, playing Laut’s mother, a photographer whose son leaves and simply does not return. For Hakim, the difficulty lies in portraying a parent forced to continue living without certainty. She sees the role as another example of the very different women she has been offered at this stage of her career, following characters including the woman she played in “Four Seasons in Java”. She expressed particular gratitude that younger directors continue trusting her with demanding parts and considers supporting younger filmmakers one of her responsibilities as an established figure in Indonesian cinema.

Hakim and Rahadian have already played mother and son several times, something that makes establishing their connection relatively easy even though the characters themselves are always different. Hakim considers him a “brilliant actor” and feels that their existing chemistry allows them to concentrate on adapting to the specific circumstances of each new story rather than having to manufacture familiarity from the beginning. She also points toward another upcoming project in which they again play mother and son, illustrating how differently the same pairing can function depending on the characters.

Aging has not made Hakim less interested in difficult roles. Quite the opposite: she says she now has to work five or even ten times harder than when she was younger. Physical preparation, diet, concentration and maintaining enough energy on set all require greater discipline. She rejects the idea of trying to remain permanently associated with the romantic roles of her youth, arguing simply that time cannot be stopped and an actor has to continue adapting along with life.

That adaptation also means participating actively in the construction of a character. Hakim speaks of performance through the combination of body, soul and mind. Costume, makeup and visual design may provide the physical exterior, but an actor must still discover how to give that exterior a soul. She is comfortable offering directors suggestions when they emerge from this process, citing her character in Four Seasons in Java, for whom she proposed having a chicken as a companion because it better reflected the woman’s isolated existence than a more conventional pet would have.

Rahadian and Celia describe Anggi Noen’s directing style as precise without being rigid. The director knows exactly what he needs from a scene, but creates enough space for the actors to explore how to reach it. Celia particularly appreciates that he establishes an environment and context rather than ordering an actor to produce a specific emotion. Rahadian summarizes the method even more directly: Anggi “never directs the feeling. He directs the motive.” Instead of asking someone to cry, he gives them the reason that might eventually produce tears.

The production could nevertheless be demanding. Rahadian remembers a major nighttime sequence in a cornfield as one of the most difficult, involving a large cast, rain, mud and filming into the early hours of the morning. The corn itself had been planted specifically for the production, requiring the filmmakers to wait around three months until the location was ready. Other scenes worked precisely because the production refused to artificially enlarge its spaces. A small family kitchen, for example, forced the actors to constantly move around and bump into one another, creating an intimacy and everyday busyness that Rahadian felt worked beautifully.

The political context inevitably led the conversation toward contemporary Indonesia. Rahadian believes civil space today is “a little bit shrinking”, although he emphasizes that conditions remain considerably better than in the 1990s. People can read, criticize the government and speak openly in ways that were previously far more dangerous, but new forms of intimidation have appeared, including anonymous cyberattacks and attempts to provoke conflict between citizens. The methods may have changed, but he feels some of the tensions explored in the film remain relevant.

At the same time, he is optimistic about Indonesian cinema itself. The range of Indonesian titles appearing internationally reflects what he sees as an increasingly diverse industry willing to engage with different social realities through very different genres and styles. Celia, meanwhile, is particularly grateful simply to have returned to acting. After her first feature around 12 years ago, she spent roughly a decade concentrating primarily on music before moving back toward cinema. “The Sea Speaks His Name” has now brought her to her first international film festival, something she describes with considerable gratitude.

Rahadian is also continuing to balance acting and directing. He is currently developing his second feature, “Casparina”, which he was pitching at the Asian Project Market. Based on his own family history, the film concerns the absence of a mother during the political upheaval surrounding 1965. His grandmother was exiled in Utrecht and returned to Indonesia 32 years later, after the fall of Suharto, attempting to reconnect with children who had grown up without her. Rahadian witnessed that homecoming himself as a teenager and now considers it the story he wants to tell next.

Hakim is expected to play the grandmother and has already begun turning down other projects so she can prepare properly for the role. Celia, meanwhile, is preparing for an action film whose details she cannot yet reveal. Their future projects may move in very different directions, but “The Sea Speaks His Name” brings all three together around a subject that continues to resonate: how personal lives absorb political history, and how love, memory and family persist even when someone is suddenly removed from them.

Excerpt: Reza Rahadian, Eva Celia and Christine Hakim discuss political memory, acting, loss and “The Sea Speaks His Name”.

Galerie von Vertes is staging a major survey of Pop art, debuting in London before making its way to Zurich. The new exhibition, “ Pop-ism ,” brings together work from across more than six decades—from 1946 through 2008—and by some of the movement’s most recognized names, including Andy Warhol, Keith Haring, Robert Rauschenberg, Niki de Saint Phalle, Tom Wesselmann, Robert Indiana, and John Chamberlain.

London specifically is an apropos backdrop for “Pop-ism,” as Pop art first emerged in the English capital in the mid-1950s, pioneered by artists like Richard Hamilton and Eduardo Paolozzi. The exhibition premieres alongside PAD London, which runs October 13–18. Following that first week, it will travel to Zurich and continue through December 4. It is a coincidental boon for Pop art fans around the globe, as the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum is also running a Pop retrospective in New York, on view through January 2027.

The best of Artnet News in your inbox.

Sign up for our daily newsletter.

Claes Oldenburg, Tea Bag (1966). Courtesy of Galerie von Vertes.

The title of the Galerie von Vertes show comes from Warhol himself, who used the term to describe the moment the long run of insular, theory-driven art movements gave way to something looser and more accessible. The show traces the shift toward approachability through a wide lens, presenting Chamberlain’s sculptures built from crushed automobile parts; Haring’s graphic, energetic cityscapes; Saint Phalle’s voluptuous Nana figures; Rauschenberg’s layered collages; and Wesselmann’s flattened, boldly colored compositions.

Complementing pieces from Pop icons are works by artists who paved the way for the then-burgeoning movement: The exhibition features Alexander Calder’s stabiles, Fernand Léger’s industrial still lifes, and Yayoi Kusama’s early soft sculptures, to name a few. Together, they illuminate a through line from Pop’s immediate predecessors to its heyday.

John Chamberlain, Potatopoultry (2008). Courtesy of Galerie von Vertes.

What Galerie von Vertes’s exhibition makes apparent is that Pop artists share more than a visual style; they share an instinct, an openness to abandoning the serious and rarefied materials, motifs, and techniques of generations prior in favor of accessible, mass imagery, commercial processes, and materials from everyday life. Instead of approaching art as something precious and exclusive, each artist approached art-making first and foremost as a conduit for ideas, borrowing the strategies and logic of advertising, embracing repetition, and finding new aesthetic potentials from within consumer and mass culture, rather than attempting to stand outside of it. In doing so, many of the artists took on the same attributes as celebrities or brands in their own right—a phenomenon that is treated within the exhibition as an indispensable facet of the work rather than an extraneous historical fact.

Tom Wesselmann, Daytime Still Life with Blonde and Goldfish (1999). Courtesy of Galerie von Vertes.

Galerie von Vertes also makes a case for Pop art’s long reach—both geographic and temporal—as it provided the fertile ground for successive movements, such as Neo-Pop, Minimalism, Conceptual art, and Political Pop. Accompanied by an exhibition catalog featuring a selection of important works by influential Pop artists and texts by art historian Dr. Quirine Verlinde, “Pop-ism” is a cogent exploration of what remains one of the most influential movements of the past century.

“ Pop-ism ” is on view at Galerie von Vertes through December 4, 2026.

content.article_text:
B ritish influencer/singer/content creator Chiara King stars as influencer/singer/content creator Chiara King, or some kind of parafictional version of herself, in this quease-inducing thriller exercise. The ick gets generated not necessarily by the eventual gore that erupts in the last reel, but by the tacky weirdness of the way the film apes the mannerisms of social media reels and streaming nonsense to both satirise the ugly side of the business but also exploit and profit off it at the same time. On one level, it’s an eerily clever exercise in bad faith, like a poor Michael Haneke film (think Funny Games) for gen-Z kicks; on another, maybe it’s just a crappy ripoff of online tropes that have been way overexposed already. Or both.

Anyway, here’s what happens: influencer Chiara gets invited to visit Copenhagen by a tourist organisation, a deal set up by her avaricious manager Alice (Jazmine Summer). Of course, this means practically every moment of her time awake in the city will be filmed, both by Chiara herself on her trusty smartphone, or a camera crew led by director Mike (played by Mike Nybroe, who is also director of The Influencer Project, ha ha); Mike is supported by sound man Daniel (Daniel Parmo) and cameraman Victor (Luca Storm). The early sections turn in all the influence-slop you would expect, with shopping trips to trendy merch vendors such as Baum und Pferdgarten, and meals at fancy local restaurants, and then a livestreamed visit to a “haunted house,” which is the big thing on Instagram and TikTok these days.

But the product placement is somewhat interrupted by moments of real fear (or “real fear”) when Chiara starts getting threatening direct messages (from someone calling themselves KingSlayer) who wants her to stop talking for reasons not clearly explained at first, otherwise he will kill and rape her, not necessarily in that order. This unsurprisingly creates a pall over Chiara’s trip, but if she just quits and goes home she’ll miss out on $100k in deals, so that’s not an option.

So are we supposed to despise Chiara for her greed or applaud her girl-boss fortitude in not being intimidated by a stalker? And what to make of the film’s claims that this was partly inspired by real incidents of stalking? Nybroe and co work the debate into the endless stream of comments we see scrolling alongside Chiara’s livestream – a river of chat that doesn’t let up even when the credits start to roll, ersatz dialectics for an age of digital proliferation.

content.article_text:
The Artnet Bulletin is our daily digest of five items from around the art world that are worth knowing. A different writer takes over each morning.

The best of Artnet News in your inbox.

Sign up for our daily newsletter.

A Papal Audience

Pope Leo XIV continues his campaign to champion and protect art. On Saturday, the pontiff welcomed the Bizot Group , the international network of directors from the world’s largest museums, to the Vatican for an audience. Speaking on the meeting’s theme of “materiality,” he described matter as a gift entrusted to human care, shaped by artists into expressions of transcendent meaning, and as a form of memory that museums carry across generations. He closed by praising the group, currently led by the Rijksmuseum ‘s director, Taco Dibbits , for safeguarding heritage that “belongs to all humanity,” according to a transcript of his remarks. The meeting came just days after the pontiff announced plans to bolster the church’s alliance with artists and cultural institutions, citing rising threats of censorship and homogenization posed by A.I.

The best of Artnet News in your inbox.

Sign up for our daily newsletter.

Pope Leo XIV meets with directors of museums around the world during an audience at the Apostolic Palace on October 10, 2026 in Vatican City, Vatican. Photo: Simone Risoluti – Vatican Media via Vatican Pool/ Getty Images.

More Kennedy Center Developments

It’s impossible to guess what could happen next with the Trump-run Kennedy Center . The embattled arts complex, currently closed to the public, has appointed a new artistic director, according to NPR , Rick Canny has been serving as a consultant to the center since April 2025, through his talent-management firm Favor the Artist , during which time staff have lodged complaints about his business practices. His previous clients have included ZZ Top , Whitesnake , and Tommy Lee .

Meanwhile, the Financial Times reported that Gaurav Srivastava , a major donor to the center, was a secret FBI informant from 2019 to 2024. Unsealed court documents show that the bureau had flagged concerns about his “reliability and honesty.” The disclosure emerges from a lawsuit by sanctioned Dutch oil trader Niels Troost, who accuses Srivastava of defrauding him of more than $43 million, an allegation that Srivastava denies.

Brotherly Love

Tondo of the Two Brothers (Antinoopolis Tondo), second century. Courtesy of the Egyptian Museum.

Egypt unveiled a restored Tondo of the Two Brothers , a prized second-century Fayoum portrait. Specialists from Rome and conservators from the Egyptian Museum in Tahrir spent three weeks patching up the work, according to the Associated Press . Notable for its circular shape and double subject, the wax-based painting had suffered termite damage to its wooden support, and restorers recovered the features of the brother on the right. Egypt will lend a major part of the Fayoum collection to a Rome exhibition running from November 2026 to May 2027, marking the first time the work will travel abroad.

Backlash Over Smashed Porcelain

The British Museum is facing criticism after a Qing dynasty porcelain bowl and a ceramic box from the Sir Percival David Collection were smashed on October 4, provoking anger in Chinese national media and on social media. The bowl fell from its mount in a display cabinet in Room 95 and landed on the box below. Staff who reviewed CCTV can’t explain why: The mount was undamaged and the room was empty. A museum spokesperson told the South China Morning Post that the objects are already with the conservation team for repair.

Frieze Week Potpourri

Happy Frieze Week, London!

Among the countless gallery openings, one I wasn’t counting on: Harry Blain , formerly of Blain Southern , which shuttered abruptly in 2020 and allegedly left many of its artists financially in the lurch, is hosting a private view today at 23 Bruton Street for his new venture, Blain . The show, titled “The Best Way Out Is Always Through,” features works by Felix Gonzalez-Torres and Bruce Nauman. If you want to see Gagosian ’s blockbuster Magritte show , “This Is Still Not a Pipe,” leave extra time: When I went on Saturday, the line to get in snaked around the corner and down Mount Street. (I admit I used my press credentials to skip it.) It simply wouldn’t be Frieze without a big ol’ dino from David Aaron , which is bringing a remarkably complete 150-million-year-old Camarasaurus supremus skull to Frieze Masters. Priced at £1 million ($1.3 million), it has an Allosaurus tooth still embedded in its lower jaw, evidence of a Late Jurassic encounter. Plus, Wyclef Jean will headline the second annual British Museum Ball on October 17.

The wrap-around line to get into Gagosian’s “This Is Still Not a Pipe” show on October 10. Photo: Margaret Carrigan.

Tune in tomorrow when my colleague Ben Davis is in the driver’s seat.

content.article_text:
T he sound of mourning spills out into the streets. A single, endless wailing note echoes out of the basement of Ibraaz, a relatively new cultural centre in London’s Fitzrovia. This is Gabrielle Goliath’s heart-wrenching Elegy, each of its three films featuring a woman singing just one note until their lungs falter and another woman steps up to fill in for her. Just as a note is about to die, it is sustained. It’s a haunting, shocking act of mourning for murder, injustice and genocide.

And it almost never made it.

A panel of five leading South African cultural voices picked Goliath’s work to represent their nation at this summer’s Venice Biennale. Goliath has been working on the project for a decade, collecting voices, collecting stories. This was a work about femicide and the murder of LGBTQ+ people in South Africa, but it had expanded. The latest iteration dealt with the Ovaherero and Nama genocide in Namibia , and the death of a Palestinian poet in 2023. It was a step too far for Gayton McKenzie, South Africa’s sport, arts and culture minister.

McKenzie is the president of the far-right Patriotic Alliance party, and has been vocal in his support of Israel in recent years. He wrote a letter describing the work as “highly divisive”. He called for the work to be edited, for the offending passage about the Palestinian poet to be removed. Goliath refused, so McKenzie put a stop to the whole thing, cancelling her Venice pavilion. She fought it tooth and nail , taking her case to South Africa’s high court, but the case was dismissed. The South Africa pavilion at the biennale sat embarrassingly empty, a big, glaring visual metaphor for the global reach of the culture wars and a symbol of censorship in the face of violence.

Goliath instead found a home for the work in a nearby church , which is where I first saw it. It was devastating then, an almost overwhelmingly emotional piece of art in a beautiful setting. Ibraaz lacks the ornate, quiet atmosphere of that Venetian church, but has made up for it with absolute sombre darkness. The space is pitch black save for the screens. One film is in commemoration of Ipeleng Christine Moholane, a woman who was strangled and left for dead in a field near Johannesburg in 2015. Another is in honour of two women who died at the hands of German colonial oppressors during the genocide in Namibia between 1904 and 1908. The third is for the poet Hiba Abu Nada and the thousands of Palestinians who have died in Gaza since 2023.

This is not a soft, plaintive lament – the room is a discordant, uncomfortable place, filled with a wailing cacophony of clashing vibrato and just out of tune notes. It sounds angry, vicious, furious, because it is. It’s not just an act of commemoration, it’s a call to action, a demand for change and justice.

While it’s incredibly emotional and deeply moving, the main feeling you get is frustration and hopelessness, not sadness. What makes Elegy so powerful is the endless proliferation of horrifying images we have to deal with on a daily basis. If you want to see images of death and genocide, you just have to look at social media or the news. We have more access to shocking, real imagery of awful current events than ever before. But Goliath has stripped the imagery away and left you with only the emotion, so just the anger and heartache remains.

It’s an act of resistance against the image economy, against murder and femicide, against violence and genocide. It’s a feminist lament, a scream against it all.

But it’s also a significant modern artwork, a symbol of our times, of our wars and cultural frictions, and its sound lingers in your ears long after you’ve walked away.

content.article_text:
Sur le papier, j’aurais dû résister. J’ai passé l’âge canonique, j’ai deux filles bientôt adolescentes et un esprit critique aiguisé par une mauvaise humeur chronique. Rien, rationnellement, ne devrait m’exciter dans une série comme The Shards . Et pourtant, je l’ai bingée avec la dévotion embarrassante d’une groupie d’un soir. La série de Ryan Murphy et Bret Easton Ellis coche toutes les cases du plaisir coupable : un tueur qui rôde autour d’un lycée ; des ados scandaleusement friqués et cocaïnés ; les mots d’Ellis, enveloppant comme la fumée d’une clope froide un lendemain de sexe débridé. Dès le premier épisode, tout m’emballe honteusement : les brushings, les piscines, la moquette même. Prendre la pilule bleue, replonger dans la matrice rassurante des nineties, redevenir celle qui découvrait Ellis dans sa chambre, sur du Kurt Cobain.

Sauf que la matrice était fucked up. Pour ma génération, l’entrée dans la sexualité et la terreur du sida allaient de pair. Désirer, c’était déjà côtoyer la mort. Ajoutez-y une culture qui érotisait l’abus, le prédateur en figure romantique, le danger en préliminaire, et vous obtenez un imaginaire bâti, malgré nous, sur une équation : sexe = péril = mort. Vingt ans à la déconstruire, mais le câblage, lui, tient toujours. C’est cette équation que The Shards remet sous tension. Le désir adolescent et le tueur qui rôde ne font qu’un. Ellis n’a jamais écrit autre chose, la prédation comme horizon du désir. Le coup de génie est dans le casting. Susan, c’est Kaia Gerber, affichant le visage de sa mère, Cindy Crawford. Robert Mallory, c’est Homer Gere, fils de Richard.

Le sourire de Kaia est une uncanny valley, « das Unheimliche » (« l’inquiétante étrangeté ») disait Freud : le refoulé qui fait retour. Nous ne regardons pas des acteurs mais nos idoles ressuscitées, et tout ce que leur époque avait implanté en nous. Le philosophe britannique Mark Fisher appelait cela la « lente annulation du futur » : une époque qui, ne sachant plus tracer son désir vers l’avant, en refait indéfiniment la boucle. Jusque derrière la caméra, où Max Winkler, fils du Fonzie de la série Happy Days, filme les héritiers d’un âge d’or qu’il a connu de l’intérieur. Voilà peut-être pourquoi je l’ai bingée sans oser l’avouer. Pas par nostalgie d’une esthétique, mais par fidélité honteuse à l’ado que j’étais, celle qui confondait l’excitation et le péril.

The Shards , disponible sur Disney+

content.article_text:
Hier comme aujourd’hui, la tentation est grande pour qui vit dans un régime autoritaire d’y faire face en se ménageant un espace privé, où l’on pourrait continuer à vivre sa vie comme si de rien n’était. Gleb, le protagoniste du brillant Minotaure d’Andreï Zviaguintsev , est un de ceux-là. Patron d’une entreprise de transport dans une ville moyenne russe, au quotidien partagé entre le travail et sa vie de famille avec sa femme, Galina, et son fils adolescent, Gleb ne parle jamais de politique ni ne mentionne l’invasion de l’Ukraine, survenue quelque mois plus tôt.

Pourtant, derrière ce quotidien de bon père de famille, aussi propre que le SUV neuf qu’il conduit dans une imagerie presque publicitaire, l’illusion vacille. Sa relation avec Galina se réduit à se faire servir son repas et à lui déléguer l’ensemble des tâches domestiques, tandis que la guerre s’infiltre partout en arrière-plan : un groupe de soldats en uniforme traverse la rue ; une de ses salariées regarde des vidéos de bombardements de villes ukrainiennes sur YouTube ; une affiche incite les jeunes hommes à s’engager pour défendre la mère patrie ; plusieurs de ses salariés émigrent pendant le week-end ; un train chargé de tanks estampillés d’un « Z » blanc roule devant lui à un passage à niveau. L’intrigue s’emballe lorsque le maire de sa ville lui ordonne d’établir une liste de salariés qui seront mobilisés et envoyés au front, et que sa femme décide de ne plus tolérer cette situation. Il est confronté à un choix.

Andreï Zviaguintsev : « L’enjeu principal, c’est celui du choix »

À l’inverse d’un de ses amis, qui abandonne tout vernis de moralité pour se complaire cyniquement dans une vie de plaisirs sans lendemain, Gleb ne veut pas voir ce dont son pays se rend coupable ni ce que son couple est devenu, et passe le reste du film à tenter de reconstruire l’illusion de sa vie d’avant. En fin de compte, Minotaure montre qu’il est impossible de dresser une frontière entre morale privée et morale publique. En cela, le film emprunte son argument à La République de Platon. À travers son analogie entre la psychologie de l’individu et l’organisation de la cité, Socrate y développe l’idée que justice individuelle et justice collective sont une seule et même chose, à deux échelles différentes, et que l’on peut difficilement avoir l’une sans l’autre. De fait, tous les efforts de Gleb pour restaurer son quotidien d’avant la guerre ne font que le pousser plus loin dans la compromission et l’immoralité. En cherchant à ignorer la corruption et la violence latente du régime, il en devient complice, et Zviaguintsev montre crûment les conséquences de ses actions. Le dernier plan, glaçant, résume l’avertissement que le réalisateur exilé adresse à ses spectateurs en Russie et au-delà : se préserver un espace de moralité dans une société injuste est voué à l’échec.

content.article_text:
In 1962, the then French culture minister, André Malraux, reportedly bored by the ballet he was watching at Paris’s opera house, raised his eyes to the classical ceiling and decided it needed a makeover.

In his ennui, Malraux thought his friend and artist Marc Chagall , sitting next to him at the Palais Garnier at the time, was the man for the job and commissioned him to make a new ceiling.

Over the next two years, Chagall worked in secret and for free to produce 24 enormous and colourful wedge-shaped canvases, that were installed over the original 19th-century classical ceiling by the now forgotten artist Jules-Eugène Lenepveu.

Today, more than four decades after Chagall’s death, one of Lenepveu’s descendants is planning legal action to have the original ceiling uncovered and restored.

Arnaud Carayon says he has “asked nicely” for this to happen for three years, including writing two letters to France’s president, Emmanuel Macron. Now he has instructed a lawyer to take the fight to court.

“The Lenepveu ceiling is classified as a historic monument and yet it hasn’t been seen for 60 years and we have no idea what state it is in,” Carayon said.

“Today, everyone has forgotten Lenepveu. Unfortunately, he was swept away by the wave of impressionism, but in his time he was really a star. More importantly, he was specifically chosen to decorate the opera ceiling by Charles Garnier, who designed everything in the opera house right down to the last door knob.

“But on a whim, Malraux decided he did not agree with Garnier’s choice.”

Garnier’s opera house was commissioned by Napoleon III and opened in January 1875 in the presence of European royals and political figures including the then lord mayor of London, Sir William Cotton.

Lenepveu, who was Garnier’s friend and artistic collaborator, produced a classical and allegorical work painted in oil directly on the copper plates of the dome. The work, called The Muses and the Hours of Day and Night, and given historic listing in 1923, was considered perfectly in keeping with the ornate Second Empire style of Garnier’s palace.

Lenepveu, who went on to lead the French Academy in Rome, later produced a series of Joan of Arc frescoes in the Paris Panthéon, but his name is little known today.

Malraux is said to have wanted to give the fusty opera house a more modern, edgy feel. Chagall’s 24 cake-slice shaped canvases were spliced together around the central chandelier covering 220 sq metres (2,368 sq ft) of the dome. The work is divided into separate colours: red, blue, green, yellow and white; and features dancers, angels, musicians and the names of composers.

Even before Chagall’s work was installed, the row between traditionalists and modernists erupted and reached the other side of the Channel.

The Royal Institute of British Architects in London wrote to the culture minister asking him to abandon his plans to cover the original ceiling. “The unique character of this edifice [the opera house] is based on the fact that all its elements: architecture, paintings, sculptures and mosaics work together in harmony,” Riba wrote. Its plea was ignored.

The Palais Garnier will be closed for renovation between 2027-32, and Carayon, the president of the Friends of Lenepveu Society, said he had written to Macron to suggest alternating the Lenepveu and Chagall ceilings after it reopens, with each being shown for a decade. He said the Élysée Palace replied only that the president was “particularly attentive” to the subject.

“From the beginning, the Chagall ceiling was designed to be removable. It can be taken down without any damage. We thought the idea of alternating ceilings was very positive and promising, but it seems nobody has the guts to touch the Chagall ceiling,” Carayon said.

At a 2023-24 Chagall exhibition at the Pompidou Centre, the curator, Anne Montfort-Tanguy, said: “The ceiling [of the opera house] is Chagall: it’s his autobiography, his vision of Paris. All the artists he loved are represented as well as what he considered the most important Paris monuments like the Eiffel Tower … It’s a moving, fluid almost cinematic work. The ceiling is a complete work of art.

“It was Chagall’s gift to the country that welcomed him; an homage to France and to Paris,” Montfort-Tanguy added.

Alexander Neef, the director of the Paris Opera, told Le Monde : “The debate over the Chagall ceiling has gone on for more than 60 years. The Lenepveu ceiling has been listed as a historic monument since 1923 so its heritage value is recognised. That his [Lenepveu’s] descendants wish to defend his memory is legitimate.”

content.article_text:
H ome Alone meets Mad Max in this atmospheric seasonal chiller, named for Halloween and not a cheery greeting. A disease has wiped out most of humanity, leaving 16-year-old Pumpkin (Milly Shapiro) stranded alone in her rural family home in the middle of nowhere for the best part of four years. This classic American clapboard house has always been the perfect quaint yet unsettling place to celebrate Halloween, and she determines to uphold the family tradition and do just that, sending a radio broadcast to anyone listening to invite them to celebrate spooky season with her. Unfortunately, the message is picked up by some less than wholesome types, led by Thalia (Shannyn Sossamon), thus setting the stage for the proverbial to hit the fan.

It’s the first major screen role for Shapiro since her memorable debut as the little sister in Ari Aster’s Hereditary , and she is in almost every scene here, making for quite the showcase. It’s good casting: Pumpkin is an intriguing presence – at once young and old, presumably because she’s been fending for herself during such a key stage of her development. She’s not had any adult guidance since the age of 12 – arresting her development in some ways, while having to survive, be totally independent and grieve her entire family alone has simultaneously made her unusually tough in others.

This turns out to be invaluable in a horror film; it gives the script plenty of room to have her make naive decisions which are wholly justified, as well as to prove surprisingly resilient in ways that the character’s backstory supports. This gives a plausible, grounded core to the story’s more outlandish trappings, and the splendid production design – ranging from cosy cottagecore Halloween to a timeless Bates motel aesthetic – makes for an appealing storyworld. Hallowarrior is the feature debut of Ben Sottak, an experienced short film-maker, and on this evidence he’s likely to be worth keeping an eye out for.

content.article_text:
The Burkina Faso artist’s later work reveals the changing ethos and sociopolitical shifts in West African photography

When asked why The Photographers’ Gallery is displaying later colour works by the Burkinabe studio photographer Sanlé Sory – and why now – TPG curator Taous Dahmani’s answer is clear and direct: “Because I’m here now.”

“I had always wanted to think about the long tradition of West African studio photography as a global surface,” she adds. Fed up with dominant readings, Dahmani argues that these photographs require a relocation of function if they are to be understood in more generative, restorative ways. The job of photographer is political, artistic, often polemic and gestural; it is also, fundamentally, a job. It is labour. It is a means to get paid and a way to live one’s life, void of a punch card and with freedom to roam. Photography is a history of grafting, of making ends meet, of waking up and going to work. Dahmani looks away from the recent landscape of “revived” West African photographic exhibitions, literally blown up for the Western art powers that be, and instead sees them as they are: small and intimate. And that is enough.

Perhaps ‘fine art’ – whatever that means – is a poisoned chalice, a trapdoored pedestal, a gilded cage. Instead, Sory is here a master craftsman, but one looking to get paid rather than necessarily disrupt the canon. This curse of fine art, which fixes Sory’s oeuvre and character into something discovered, demanding recontextualisation, and subsequent elevation, in turn shuts a door into the modern world.

“[Sory’s later colour work] holds quite a significant shift in what we know about the history of West African practice” – Taous Dahmani, curator

Reductive readings often position this sort of photographer, and by extent photography, as a historical event over a living being. Dahmani says this limited reading “refuses entry into contemporality”, and perpetuates Western art narratives as “acceptable forms of nostalgia about this past of liberation, a call to the time ‘when we liberated poor Africans’”. On the two far sides of the Atlantic, and deep in the white cube, when we see West African studio portraits, it is always revolutionary times. Nothing ever changes, Africa is Africa, and the West is the West.

But Sory’s archive holds “thousands and thousands” of later colour negatives, many of which have never been printed beyond their original commission. Dahmani asks why and steers towards a relocation, a “re-anchoring” in her terms. Perhaps these colour works, a move on from the earlier black-and-white work of the 1960s and 70s, were deemed harder to digest for Western audiences, something less fixed than the story we know (or have been told). To Dahmani, Burkina Faso, and the wider African stage, is not a fixed event but a site to examine universal photographic systems, alongside the specificities of 20th-century African histories. “[Sory’s later colour work] holds quite a significant shift in what we know about the history of West African practice,” she says.

She reads the practice as both ubiquitous and unique; closer to the functional, political and social histories caught within the portraits, and understood as wholly commissioned artefacts. Yet by curating the show in London there is an awareness that home is not always a place one can return to, that there is perhaps no true contextual providence left. Instead there is a possibility to seek out new lands, ways of being and seeing, ones which bring the photographs to audiences new and old, but allow all those looking to see for themselves.

The Western art reading has a tendency to turn African nations into islands, dislocating them from neighbouring, concurrent histories. Dahmani refers to this as a “dictated, fetishised history”, one the market embraces with ease but which brings us no closer to understanding these images or people. “For me, colour became the starting point,” she says. “Can we think critically about this history through the lens of colour? Can we think of it as a form of politics? Most of the pictures we know are from the 1960s and 70s. Postcolonial moments of aspiration, of joy… at least that’s how it’s sold. Moments of ‘Finally, the freedom of the African people!’ But it stops there. No one wonders what happens after.”

Sory’s later portraits of street vendors, personable and direct, grew out of a slowing appetite for commissioned portraits. Cameraphones had arrived and times were changing. Dahmani also stresses the desires of the later sitters he was commissioned to record, commenting on their input into the images. “Sory printed in black-and-white, but when colour became more accessible, clients asked for it. It was more expensive, and he suddenly couldn’t work alone.” For Dahmani, both sitter and printer become producer and collaborator.

Dahmani traces stories of the sitters through historical relocations; every now and then you notice someone dressed fancifully for the camera, who is “wearing a suit slightly too small, their shoes maybe unvarnished”. Through these images Dahmani moves away from a fashion-first reading towards something more akin to socially informed style studies, an analysis of hand-me-downs and counterfeit designerwear. This becomes part of the re-anchoring, and perhaps a new type of non-hierarchical photographic kinship. It aids an understanding of universality, not exotic idiosyncrasy, though a story that is also deeply African.

Sory had to negotiate and barter with his subjects, as ultimately the images existed off their payments. He had to follow trends, keep up with the changing times. Suddenly people did not want his famed illustrated backdrops any longer. “They wanted to be part of a new technology, and a new capacity of being seen,” Dahmani explains. Sory, as with many West African portraitists, is rarely discussed within the contexts of an emerging contemporary. Entry into the modern world, with colour, Nike, Obama T-shirts, and iPhones, has not been curatorially permitted.

“I now don’t have to prove that photography is an art form,” Dahmani states. “But I do want to get back to the fact that actually, historically, there were things that we were too quick to put into one category, instead of allowing them to be a multiplicity of things. And I don’t think we often allow African artists to be a multiplicity of things.”

Sanlé Sory: Colour Years is at The Photographers’ Gallery , London, from 14 October 2026 to 21 February 2027. The accompanying book is published by GOST, priced £45 https://gostbooks.com/products/volta-colour

Isaac Huxtable is a Yorkshire-born, London-based writer and curator. He works across the photographic medium with a central focus on race and realism. Isaac is currently an Assistant Curator in Photography at the Victoria and Albert Museum. He studied at the Courtauld Institute of Art, followed by roles at the British Journal of Photography, the Photographers' Gallery, and the art agency Artiq. His words have featured in the British Journal of Photography, Elephant Magazine, Galerie Peter Sillem, The Photographers' Gallery, and The South London Gallery. He is particularly interested in documentary practices, gender, class, and the body.

Daily Newsletter

Raven Chacon’s Echoes on Park Avenue

The Pulitzer Prize-winning Diné artist on latest projects, art in NYC for Indigenous Peoples’ Day, and a Felix Gonzalez-Torres show misses the mark.

It’s a beautiful Monday to celebrate Indigenous Peoples’ Day, no matter what the federal government says. In a conversation with Associate Editor Phillip Pyle, Diné musician Raven Chacon discusses his recent improvised performances at the Park Avenue Armory, the “collision” at the heart of all music, and reclaiming the technologies of colonial violence through sound.

Read on for a guide to shows centering Native art around New York City — including Shelley Niro and Sarah Sense, two of my favorite artists — and a critique of a Felix Gonzalez-Torres exhibition that bizarrely glosses over the late artist’s AIDS advocacy and political spirit.

—Lakshmi Rivera Amin, associate editor

Raven Chacon Sounds the History of the Land

On Wednesday and Thursday night, sound mixers, synthesizers, pedals, speakers, whistles, a turkey call, and a ceramic horn sat on a table at the center of the Veterans Room in Manhattan’s Park Avenue Armory. Serving as the stage for Raven Chacon’s hour-long improvisation sessions for the Armory’s Artists Studio series, the table also offered audiences the rare opportunity to see the prolific artist at play. | Phillip Pyle

content.article_blocks_json: [{"type": "image", "url": "https://www.troiscouleurs.fr/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/LE-JOUR-DE-SON-RETOUR_Kim-Sunjin_Song-Sunmi-1024x576.jpg", "alt": "LE JOUR DE SON RETOUR Kim Sunjin Song Sunmi", "caption": "", "credit": "Trois Couleurs"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Ce film-là n’est pas flou. Ici, l’image est en noir et blanc, nette, et le cadre tellement fixe dans un premier temps que l’on se demande s’il s’agit d’une nouvelle performance formelle. Presque. content.article_text:
Ce film-là n’est pas flou. On avait laissé Hong Sang-soo sur In Water (2024), où le point jamais fait à l’image donnait aux paysages des couleurs délavées, rappelant les œuvres de Mark Rothko ; et Ce que cette nature te dit (2025), qui jouait aussi d’une photographie nébuleuse. Ici, l’image est en noir et blanc, nette, et le cadre tellement fixe dans un premier temps que l’on se demande s’il s’agit d’une nouvelle performance formelle. Presque. Le réalisateur sud-coréen utilise ici la répétition : trois jeunes journalistes se succèdent pour interviewer Bae Jeongsu, une actrice sur le retour.

Elle vient de tourner dans un film d’auteur et répond différemment à chacun en fonction de microévénements de contexte – accepter une bière en plein milieu de l’après-midi peut tout changer. Plus tard, lors d’un cours de théâtre, l’actrice tente de rejouer ces entrevues pour mieux les revisiter… On pense à Hotel by the River (2018), à ce Hong Sang-soo qu’on aime, architecte de la parole qu’on a connu plus filou. Ce film aussi se tient bien, sans prétention dans sa réflexion sur la nature des échanges professionnels. Il y a bien quelques piques sur les journalistes, mais ce n’est pas un pamphlet satirique, et l’écriture ne rate pas le personnage de l’actrice non plus. Le film lui rend plutôt un hommage, et offre un dialogue réussi sur les choix et les chemins de vie.

Le Jour de son retour de Hong Sang-soo , Carlotta Films (1 h 24) sortie le 14 octobre

content.excerpt_original: Avec ce long métrage moins aventureux en matière d’image (plus nette) que ses deux précédents, Hong Sang-soo revient à une formule qu’il maîtrise : un petit dialogue drôle et introspectif.

content.title_original: Dans « Low Expectations » d’Eivind Landsvik, girl in red trouve un premier rôle touchant
content.article_blocks_json: [{"type": "image", "url": "https://www.troiscouleurs.fr/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/496be15830c801e2260f290261bff31c-1024x510.webp", "alt": "496be15830c801e2260f290261bff31c", "caption": "", "credit": "Trois Couleurs"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Sa dépression consume tout, alors autant ne pas le montrer. Élément secondaire de ce film norvégien qui exclut de sa mise en scène bien des gimmicks du drame psychologique, l’état psychique de Maja ponctuera plutôt ses élans de vie. La jeune femme est de retour chez sa mère avec un petit boulot de surveillante de lycée, après une carrière explosive dans la musique (sous le nom de Vongole, projet que l’on devine fun et hype) et un burn-out créatif – plus des excès de consommations diversement illicites."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Habile vertige, Maja est jouée par Marie Ulven Ringheim, que l’on connaît plutôt sous son nom de scène : girl in red. Mais le film a le bon goût de ne pas tout confondre et tient sa musique à distance – même si Low Expectations sonne déjà comme un morceau de l’intéressée : doux et puissant. L’ensemble est bien sûr à l’image de ce cinéma norvégien éthéré et mélancolique à la mode Dag Johan Haugerud (les tourbillonnants Rêves, Amour, Désir de 2025) ou Joachim Trier ( Low Expectations devient presque méta quand on voit la manière dont est filmé, vieilli, l’Anders Danielsen Lie d’ Oslo, 31 août ), mais reste plus terre à terre, dans l’air du temps. Glosant autour de cette question conventionnelle mais fondamentale : peut-on, à 29 ans, se demander si on a raté sa vie ?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Low Expectations d’Eivind Landsvik , UFO (1 h 45) , sortie le 14 octobre"}, {"type": "heading", "text": "Retrouvez-nous sur"}]
content.article_text:
Sa dépression consume tout, alors autant ne pas le montrer. Élément secondaire de ce film norvégien qui exclut de sa mise en scène bien des gimmicks du drame psychologique, l’état psychique de Maja ponctuera plutôt ses élans de vie. La jeune femme est de retour chez sa mère avec un petit boulot de surveillante de lycée, après une carrière explosive dans la musique (sous le nom de Vongole, projet que l’on devine fun et hype) et un burn-out créatif – plus des excès de consommations diversement illicites.

Habile vertige, Maja est jouée par Marie Ulven Ringheim, que l’on connaît plutôt sous son nom de scène : girl in red. Mais le film a le bon goût de ne pas tout confondre et tient sa musique à distance – même si Low Expectations sonne déjà comme un morceau de l’intéressée : doux et puissant. L’ensemble est bien sûr à l’image de ce cinéma norvégien éthéré et mélancolique à la mode Dag Johan Haugerud (les tourbillonnants Rêves, Amour, Désir de 2025) ou Joachim Trier ( Low Expectations devient presque méta quand on voit la manière dont est filmé, vieilli, l’Anders Danielsen Lie d’ Oslo, 31 août ), mais reste plus terre à terre, dans l’air du temps. Glosant autour de cette question conventionnelle mais fondamentale : peut-on, à 29 ans, se demander si on a raté sa vie ?

Low Expectations d’Eivind Landsvik , UFO (1 h 45) , sortie le 14 octobre

content.excerpt_original: Ce drame, sur la dépression d’une jeune musicienne et vêtu des atours du cinéma norvégien moderne (réalisme et mélancolie pop), sonne juste. La musicienne girl in red y trouve un premier rôle cinématographique de choix.

content.title_original: The Most Expensive Works by Gustav Klimt Sold at Auction
content.article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "In recent decades, Gustav Klimt has become one of the most sought-after artists on the international art market, with his paintings achieving record-breaking prices at auction. From the gilded elegance of his celebrated portraits to the richly patterned views of Lake Attersee completed during his summer retreats, Klimt’s oeuvre embodies the decorative brilliance and artistic innovation that defined Viennese Modernism. The rarity and enduring appeal of these works among collectors have made them some of the most valuable examples of early 20th-century art ever offered for sale."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The market for Klimt reached new heights with landmark sales of such works as Lady with a Fan in 2023, Blooming Meadow in 2025, and Portrait of Elisabeth Lederer in 2025, each reaffirming the extraordinary demand for his masterpieces. Today, some rank among the most expensive artworks ever sold at auction, including the 10 paintings discussed below."}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "Landhaus am Attersee (Country House by the Attersee), 1914 Image Credit: Sotheby’s. Landhaus am Attersee (Country House by the Attersee) depicts the forester’s house at the entrance to Austria’s Weißenbach Valley, where Gustav Klimt stayed during his summers on the southern shore of Lake Attersee. In this secluded setting, near members of the Flöge family—including his companion Emilie Flöge—the artist refined his mature approach to landscape painting. With oil on canvas, the artist transformed the humble building and surrounding vegetation into a richly patterned composition of vibrant foliage, vivid color, and mosaic-like brushwork. Unlike his meticulously prepared portraits, Klimt’s landscapes were executed with few preparatory studies, lending them a greater sense of immediacy and spontaneity. Created during the final phase of Klimt’s Attersee period, the work reflects his fascination with nature as a space of visual intensity. Offered at Sotheby’s New York on November 5, 2003, with an estimate of $18–25 million, the painting achieved $29.1 million. The result confirmed the growing appreciation of Klimt’s landscapes, now regarded as some of the artist’s most personal and innovative achievements."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Sothebys_Landhaus.jpeg?w=400", "alt": "Gustav Klimt, Landhaus am Attersee (Country House by the Attersee), 1914", "caption": "Image Credit: Sotheby’s.", "credit": "ARTnews"}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "Apple Tree I , 1912 Image Credit: Christie’s. Klimt’s Apple Tree I is a luminous example of his mature landscapes, depicting a single apple tree rising above a dense carpet of flowers and foliage. This oil on canvas is distinguished by its vibrant palette, shimmering brushwork, and richly decorative surface, reflecting Klimt’s interest in nature during his summers at Lake Attersee and the influence of Vincent van Gogh’s expressive approach to color and movement. First exhibited at the Große Kunstausstellung in Dresden in 1912, the work demonstrates Klimt’s ability to turn a simple natural motif into a striking decorative composition. Its provenance includes ownership by Adele and Ferdinand Bloch-Bauer and its restitution to their heirs in 2006. Offered at Christie’s New York with an estimate of $15–25 million, Apple Tree I sold for $33 million on November 9 of that same year. The sale underscored the enduring appeal of Klimt’s garden landscapes."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Christies_Apple-Tree.jpg?w=400", "alt": "Gustav Klimt, Apple Tree I, 1912", "caption": "Image Credit: Christie’s.", "credit": "ARTnews"}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "Portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer II , 1912 Image Credit: Christie’s. Klimt’s Portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer II is an oil on canvas depicting the eponymous Viennese socialite and salonnière , who was one of Klimt’s most important patrons and the only sitter to whom he devoted two paintings. The first, Portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer I (1907), is now held by the Neue Galerie New York. The second, along with works such as Apple Tree I (see above), belonged to the Bloch-Bauer family collection that was looted by Nazi authorities after the annexation of Austria in 1938. After a prolonged legal battle, these paintings were returned in 2006 to Maria Altmann and the other heirs of Ferdinand Bloch-Bauer in a landmark restitution case. On November 8 of that year, Portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer II was sold at Christie’s New York as part of an Impressionist and Modern Art Evening Sale. The painting achieved $87.9 million, setting a new auction record for Klimt at the time. In 2016 the work was sold privately by its owner, Oprah Winfrey, who had purchased it at Christie’s, to an anonymous Chinese buyer for a reported $150 million, making it one of the most significant private art transactions of the decade."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Christies_Adele.jpg?w=400", "alt": "Gustav Klimt, Portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer II, 1912", "caption": "Image Credit: Christie’s.", "credit": "ARTnews"}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "Birch Forest , 1903 Image Credit: Christie’s. “I get up early in the morning, usually around 6 am, sometimes earlier, sometimes later. If I get up and the weather is fine, I go into the nearby forest. I am painting a small beech grove, mixed with a few conifers,” wrote Klimt in a letter to M. Zimmerman in August 1903. It was during his summers in Litzlberg, on the shores of Lake Attersee, that the artist developed his profound connection with the natural world. In Birch Forest (Buchenwald) , he captured a secluded grove with precision. The elegant silver trunks rise like “columns in a cathedral created by nature.” Their intricate patterns contrast with the deep green foliage, creating a richly textured surface. Landscape occupied a significant place in Klimt’s mature oeuvre, reflecting his search for harmony and visual rhythm. With each tree trunk bearing its own unique markings, the painting shows extreme attention to detail. Acquired by Adele and Ferdinand Bloch-Bauer and confiscated by Nazi forces, Birch Forest was returned to their heirs in 2006 before appearing at Christie’s New York on two occasions. In November 2006, the lot achieved $40.3 million against an estimate of $20−30 million. Returning to the auction house as part of the Paul G. Allen Collection in 2022, it realized $104.6 million, becoming the most expensive Klimt landscape ever sold at auction at the time."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Christies_Birch.jpg?w=400", "alt": "Gustav Klimt, Birch Forest, 1903", "caption": "Image Credit: Christie’s.", "credit": "ARTnews"}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "Litzlberg am Attersee (Litzlberg on the Attersee), 1914 Image Credit: Sotheby’s. Litzlberg am Attersee depicts the shoreline of Lake Attersee, with houses nestled beneath a densely wooded hillside and a narrow stretch of water in the foreground. Recent scholarship suggests the painting was executed in the second half of 1914. Its vibrant palette, flattened perspective, and densely layered brushwork exemplify Klimt’s decorative approach to landscape. The composition is believed to have drawn in part on a postcard photograph of the lake that the artist sent to his nephew in August 1914. Acquired directly from Klimt by Viennese patrons Viktor and Paula Zuckerkandl, the painting later entered the collection of Viktor’s sister, Amalie Redlich, a Jewish collector who was dispossessed following the Nazi annexation of Austria and deported to Łódź in 1941. After decades in the collection of the Museum der Moderne Salzburg, the work was restituted to Redlich’s heir in 2011. Later that year, it sold for $40.4 million at Sotheby’s New York, surpassing its $25–30 million estimate. A portion of the sale proceeds was donated to the Museum der Moderne Salzburg to support an extension named in Redlich’s honor."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Sothebys_Litzlbert.jpeg?w=400", "alt": "Gustav Klimt, Litzlberg am Attersee (Litzlberg on the Attersee), 1914", "caption": "Image Credit: Sotheby’s.", "credit": "ARTnews"}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "Bauerngarten (Flower Garden), 1907 Image Credit: Sotheby’s. Klimt’s Bauerngarten (Blumengarten) (Flower Garden), one of the artist’s most celebrated landscapes, presents an informal profusion of poppies, daisies, zinnias, and roses arranged into a riot of color and pattern. This oil on canvas gives a sense of Klimt’s summers at Lake Attersee and of his evolving approach to landscape, rooted in the symbolic ambitions of the Viennese avant-garde. Painted in the garden of the Mayr-Hof, his summer retreat in Litzlberg, the work shows how the natural and decorative worlds converged under his brush. First exhibited at the Kunstschau in Vienna in 1908, the painting attracted attention for its innovative composition and almost mystical treatment of nature. Offered at Sotheby’s London in 2017 with an estimate in excess of $45 million, Bauerngarten sold for approximately $59.3 million, becoming the most expensive Klimt landscape ever sold at auction at the time. The sale underscored the rarity of major Klimt landscapes appearing on the market, with many works of this caliber held in museum collections."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Sothebys_Bauerngarten.jpeg?w=400", "alt": "Gustav Klimt, Bauerngarten (Flower Garden), 1907", "caption": "Image Credit: Sotheby’s.", "credit": "ARTnews"}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "Portrait of Fräulein Lieser , 1918 Image Credit: Wikimedia Commons. A young woman clad in a flower-patterned cape sits in a frontal pose against a vivid red background. Her face is rendered with delicate, precise details that contrast with the looser, more expressive brushwork characteristic of Klimt’s late style. The identity of the sitter remains uncertain. Earlier catalogues identified her as Margarethe Constance Lieser (1899−1965), while more recent research has suggested that she may have been either Helene Lieser (1898−1962) or Annie Lieser (1901−1972), daughters of the Viennese patrons Henriette and Justus Lieser. Klimt began working on the portrait in 1917, with the model visiting his studio in Hietzing nine times during April and May of that year. The portrait was unfinished when he died of a stroke on February 6, 1918. The painting was known to scholars only through a black-and-white photograph, and its whereabouts remained uncertain for decades before it was discovered in Austrian private hands. On April 24, 2024, it was auctioned by Vienna’s im Kinsky, Austria’s second-largest auction house, recognized for its expertise in Klimt’s works and its experience handling restitution-related art sales. Portrait of Fräulein Lieser sold for approximately $41 million including fees, setting a record as the highest price ever achieved for an artwork at auction in Austria. The sale was conducted on behalf of the owners at the time and the legal successors of the Liester family, following an agreement based on the 1998 Washington Principles. The work was purchased by Patti Wong & Associates for an anonymous buyer."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Wikimedia_Gustav_Klimt_Fraulein_Lieser.jpg?w=395", "alt": "Gustav Klimt, Portrait of Fräulein Lieser, 1918", "caption": "Image Credit: Wikimedia Commons.", "credit": "ARTnews"}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "Dame mit Fächer (Lady with a Fan), 1917−1918 Image Credit: Sotheby’s. Dame mit Fächer is thought to be the last portrait Klimt worked on before his death in 1918; it was still on the easel in his Vienna studio at the time of his passing. The work represents the culmination of the artist’s late portraiture, combining the human presence of the unidentified sitter with the rich patterns and decorative experimentation that defined his last years. Returning to the square format he first employed in Portrait of Sonja Knips (1898), Klimt placed the figure at the center of the composition and surrounded her with motifs drawn from Asian art, including the phoenix and lotus blossoms. The sitter’s elaborate robe also evokes Klimt’s long-standing interest in textiles and fashion, an area closely connected to his companion Emilie Flöge, an influential Viennese fashion designer.
