content.article_text:
In recent decades, Gustav Klimt has become one of the most sought-after artists on the international art market, with his paintings achieving record-breaking prices at auction. From the gilded elegance of his celebrated portraits to the richly patterned views of Lake Attersee completed during his summer retreats, Klimt’s oeuvre embodies the decorative brilliance and artistic innovation that defined Viennese Modernism. The rarity and enduring appeal of these works among collectors have made them some of the most valuable examples of early 20th-century art ever offered for sale.

The market for Klimt reached new heights with landmark sales of such works as Lady with a Fan in 2023, Blooming Meadow in 2025, and Portrait of Elisabeth Lederer in 2025, each reaffirming the extraordinary demand for his masterpieces. Today, some rank among the most expensive artworks ever sold at auction, including the 10 paintings discussed below.

Landhaus am Attersee (Country House by the Attersee), 1914 Image Credit: Sotheby’s. Landhaus am Attersee (Country House by the Attersee) depicts the forester’s house at the entrance to Austria’s Weißenbach Valley, where Gustav Klimt stayed during his summers on the southern shore of Lake Attersee. In this secluded setting, near members of the Flöge family—including his companion Emilie Flöge—the artist refined his mature approach to landscape painting. With oil on canvas, the artist transformed the humble building and surrounding vegetation into a richly patterned composition of vibrant foliage, vivid color, and mosaic-like brushwork. Unlike his meticulously prepared portraits, Klimt’s landscapes were executed with few preparatory studies, lending them a greater sense of immediacy and spontaneity. Created during the final phase of Klimt’s Attersee period, the work reflects his fascination with nature as a space of visual intensity. Offered at Sotheby’s New York on November 5, 2003, with an estimate of $18–25 million, the painting achieved $29.1 million. The result confirmed the growing appreciation of Klimt’s landscapes, now regarded as some of the artist’s most personal and innovative achievements.

Apple Tree I , 1912 Image Credit: Christie’s. Klimt’s Apple Tree I is a luminous example of his mature landscapes, depicting a single apple tree rising above a dense carpet of flowers and foliage. This oil on canvas is distinguished by its vibrant palette, shimmering brushwork, and richly decorative surface, reflecting Klimt’s interest in nature during his summers at Lake Attersee and the influence of Vincent van Gogh’s expressive approach to color and movement. First exhibited at the Große Kunstausstellung in Dresden in 1912, the work demonstrates Klimt’s ability to turn a simple natural motif into a striking decorative composition. Its provenance includes ownership by Adele and Ferdinand Bloch-Bauer and its restitution to their heirs in 2006. Offered at Christie’s New York with an estimate of $15–25 million, Apple Tree I sold for $33 million on November 9 of that same year. The sale underscored the enduring appeal of Klimt’s garden landscapes.

Portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer II , 1912 Image Credit: Christie’s. Klimt’s Portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer II is an oil on canvas depicting the eponymous Viennese socialite and salonnière , who was one of Klimt’s most important patrons and the only sitter to whom he devoted two paintings. The first, Portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer I (1907), is now held by the Neue Galerie New York. The second, along with works such as Apple Tree I (see above), belonged to the Bloch-Bauer family collection that was looted by Nazi authorities after the annexation of Austria in 1938. After a prolonged legal battle, these paintings were returned in 2006 to Maria Altmann and the other heirs of Ferdinand Bloch-Bauer in a landmark restitution case. On November 8 of that year, Portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer II was sold at Christie’s New York as part of an Impressionist and Modern Art Evening Sale. The painting achieved $87.9 million, setting a new auction record for Klimt at the time. In 2016 the work was sold privately by its owner, Oprah Winfrey, who had purchased it at Christie’s, to an anonymous Chinese buyer for a reported $150 million, making it one of the most significant private art transactions of the decade.

Birch Forest , 1903 Image Credit: Christie’s. “I get up early in the morning, usually around 6 am, sometimes earlier, sometimes later. If I get up and the weather is fine, I go into the nearby forest. I am painting a small beech grove, mixed with a few conifers,” wrote Klimt in a letter to M. Zimmerman in August 1903. It was during his summers in Litzlberg, on the shores of Lake Attersee, that the artist developed his profound connection with the natural world. In Birch Forest (Buchenwald) , he captured a secluded grove with precision. The elegant silver trunks rise like “columns in a cathedral created by nature.” Their intricate patterns contrast with the deep green foliage, creating a richly textured surface. Landscape occupied a significant place in Klimt’s mature oeuvre, reflecting his search for harmony and visual rhythm. With each tree trunk bearing its own unique markings, the painting shows extreme attention to detail. Acquired by Adele and Ferdinand Bloch-Bauer and confiscated by Nazi forces, Birch Forest was returned to their heirs in 2006 before appearing at Christie’s New York on two occasions. In November 2006, the lot achieved $40.3 million against an estimate of $20−30 million. Returning to the auction house as part of the Paul G. Allen Collection in 2022, it realized $104.6 million, becoming the most expensive Klimt landscape ever sold at auction at the time.

Litzlberg am Attersee (Litzlberg on the Attersee), 1914 Image Credit: Sotheby’s. Litzlberg am Attersee depicts the shoreline of Lake Attersee, with houses nestled beneath a densely wooded hillside and a narrow stretch of water in the foreground. Recent scholarship suggests the painting was executed in the second half of 1914. Its vibrant palette, flattened perspective, and densely layered brushwork exemplify Klimt’s decorative approach to landscape. The composition is believed to have drawn in part on a postcard photograph of the lake that the artist sent to his nephew in August 1914. Acquired directly from Klimt by Viennese patrons Viktor and Paula Zuckerkandl, the painting later entered the collection of Viktor’s sister, Amalie Redlich, a Jewish collector who was dispossessed following the Nazi annexation of Austria and deported to Łódź in 1941. After decades in the collection of the Museum der Moderne Salzburg, the work was restituted to Redlich’s heir in 2011. Later that year, it sold for $40.4 million at Sotheby’s New York, surpassing its $25–30 million estimate. A portion of the sale proceeds was donated to the Museum der Moderne Salzburg to support an extension named in Redlich’s honor.

Bauerngarten (Flower Garden), 1907 Image Credit: Sotheby’s. Klimt’s Bauerngarten (Blumengarten) (Flower Garden), one of the artist’s most celebrated landscapes, presents an informal profusion of poppies, daisies, zinnias, and roses arranged into a riot of color and pattern. This oil on canvas gives a sense of Klimt’s summers at Lake Attersee and of his evolving approach to landscape, rooted in the symbolic ambitions of the Viennese avant-garde. Painted in the garden of the Mayr-Hof, his summer retreat in Litzlberg, the work shows how the natural and decorative worlds converged under his brush. First exhibited at the Kunstschau in Vienna in 1908, the painting attracted attention for its innovative composition and almost mystical treatment of nature. Offered at Sotheby’s London in 2017 with an estimate in excess of $45 million, Bauerngarten sold for approximately $59.3 million, becoming the most expensive Klimt landscape ever sold at auction at the time. The sale underscored the rarity of major Klimt landscapes appearing on the market, with many works of this caliber held in museum collections.

Portrait of Fräulein Lieser , 1918 Image Credit: Wikimedia Commons. A young woman clad in a flower-patterned cape sits in a frontal pose against a vivid red background. Her face is rendered with delicate, precise details that contrast with the looser, more expressive brushwork characteristic of Klimt’s late style. The identity of the sitter remains uncertain. Earlier catalogues identified her as Margarethe Constance Lieser (1899−1965), while more recent research has suggested that she may have been either Helene Lieser (1898−1962) or Annie Lieser (1901−1972), daughters of the Viennese patrons Henriette and Justus Lieser. Klimt began working on the portrait in 1917, with the model visiting his studio in Hietzing nine times during April and May of that year. The portrait was unfinished when he died of a stroke on February 6, 1918. The painting was known to scholars only through a black-and-white photograph, and its whereabouts remained uncertain for decades before it was discovered in Austrian private hands. On April 24, 2024, it was auctioned by Vienna’s im Kinsky, Austria’s second-largest auction house, recognized for its expertise in Klimt’s works and its experience handling restitution-related art sales. Portrait of Fräulein Lieser sold for approximately $41 million including fees, setting a record as the highest price ever achieved for an artwork at auction in Austria. The sale was conducted on behalf of the owners at the time and the legal successors of the Liester family, following an agreement based on the 1998 Washington Principles. The work was purchased by Patti Wong & Associates for an anonymous buyer.

Dame mit Fächer (Lady with a Fan), 1917−1918 Image Credit: Sotheby’s. Dame mit Fächer is thought to be the last portrait Klimt worked on before his death in 1918; it was still on the easel in his Vienna studio at the time of his passing. The work represents the culmination of the artist’s late portraiture, combining the human presence of the unidentified sitter with the rich patterns and decorative experimentation that defined his last years. Returning to the square format he first employed in Portrait of Sonja Knips (1898), Klimt placed the figure at the center of the composition and surrounded her with motifs drawn from Asian art, including the phoenix and lotus blossoms. The sitter’s elaborate robe also evokes Klimt’s long-standing interest in textiles and fashion, an area closely connected to his companion Emilie Flöge, an influential Viennese fashion designer. At Sotheby’s London in June 2023, Dame mit Fächer carried an estimate of more than £65 million ($80 million) and was backed by a third-party guarantee. The painting was hammered in at $93.5 million, reaching $108.4 million with fees and establishing a new auction record for Klimt. The result surpassed the previous record of $104.6 million held by Birch Forest , highlighting the extraordinary demand for Klimt’s late masterpieces in the international market.

Blumenwiese (Blooming Meadow), 1908 Image Credit: Sotheby’s. In this painting of the meadows surrounding Lake Attersee, Klimt moves away from a traditional landscape format to offer a dazzling carpet of wildflowers—bellflowers buttercups, daisies, cornflowers, clover, and dandelions—that fills the canvas, Here, the horizonless view, square composition, and flattened pictorial space show the influence of late Claude Monet, Japanese art, and emerging Modernist photography. Executed likely in the summer of 1908, Blumenwiese represents a pivotal moment in Klimt’s landscape painting, when he pushed the genre toward greater abstraction. The radical composition was so unconventional that some contemporary critics dismissed Klimt’s style as the work of a “madman.” Its distinguished provenance, including ownership by Austro-Galician painter Broncia Koller-Pinell and her husband, Hugo Koller, further enhances its historical significance. The painting sold at Sotheby’s in 2025 for $86 million (including fees), becoming the second-most expensive Klimt landscape ever auctioned and reaffirming its rarity and enduring appeal among collectors.

Portrait of Elisabeth Lederer , 1914-1916 Image Credit: Sotheby’s. Portrait of Elisabeth Lederer (1914−16) exemplifies Klimt’s mature portrait style, where realism and decoration meet seamlessly. The subject emerges from an elaborate costume that blurs the boundary between figure and background. Completed after nearly three years of revisions, the painting demonstrates Klimt’s meticulous working process and extraordinary feeling for ornamentation. Commissioned by the Lederer family, among Klimt’s most important patrons, the painting is one of only two full-length portraits by the artist remaining in private hands. It survived Nazi confiscation during the Second World War and was restituted in 1948. Its provenance, later including a time in the collection of Leonard A. Lauder, makes it one of Klimt’s most significant surviving mature portraits. Estimated at $150 million, the painting was the centerpiece of Sotheby’s November 2025 sales. After a dramatic 20-minute contest between two telephone bidders, it realized $236.4 million (including fees), eclipsing Klimt’s previous record and becoming the second-most expensive work ever sold at auction, behind Leonardo da Vinci’s Salvator Mundi .

content.article_text:
Arthur Jafa is such a star these days that most art lovers know his story. It wasn’t always so.

Until about a decade ago, he was basically an artist’s artist, working between the cinema and art worlds. His reputation only exploded in 2016, when he was in his mid-50s, in the immediate aftermath of Donald J. Trump ’s shock defeat of Hillary Clinton .

The best of Artnet News in your inbox.

Sign up for our daily newsletter.

His video Love Is the Message, The Message Is Death (2016) drew crowds to Gavin Brown’s Enterprise in Harlem in the days after the election, and emotional reactions from visitors and critics . Jafa has been treated as a sage ever since, receiving honor after honor. The New Museum ‘s recently opened retrospective of his work, curated by the museum’s director, Massimiliano Gioni , and its senior curator, Gary Carrion-Murayari , is only the latest.

The Gavin Brown tale has been so often recited that it’s almost not worth revisiting. I mention it to stress that the conversation around Jafa has been shaped by a very particular cultural moment: the post-2016 Reckoning and Resistance period, what writer Molly Fischer called “ Pop Culture’s Great Awokening .” Some now term it “Woke 1.0.”

Installation view of “Arthur Jafa: I Am Tony” at the New Museum. Photo by Ben Davis.

That phrase was popularized recently by Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez . Disavowing some of her previous statements, the Democratic congresswoman alluded to a new common sense among progressive politicians: “Woke 1.0 was crazy.”

Is social justice washed? Or just moving on to something more practical? Is the culture trending post-woke, or anti-woke, or “dark woke,” or entering some kind of Woke 2.0 era? Anna Kornbluh ’s Immediacy , Olúfẹ́mi O. Táíwò’ s Elite Capture , Catherine Liu ’s Traumatized , and Anton Jäger ’s Hyperpolitics are all recent works of cultural theory, of varying degrees of acuity, that try to find a way to say that the liberal symbolic politics of the post-2016 period were reductive and destructive. (Big parts of my last book, Art in the After-Culture , were trying to work out some kind of non-reactionary critique of this era of culture as well.)

The museum world has so far shown only the most desultory interest in engaging that issue. Here, we can just ask how Arthur Jafa’s work lands now, in this new cultural climate—whatever we call it.

Installation view of “Arthur Jafa: I Am Tony” at the New Museum. Photo by Ben Davis.

The Message, Revisited

Love Is the Message, The Message Is Death began as a personal project, composed of clips that Jafa had on his computer that he strung together to screen for intimates. It’s a tough, hard-to-watch work, a harrowing montage of violence against Black people, alternating with joyous and stylish clips of Black celebrities.

Yet when I returned to it at the New Museum, what struck me about it now is that it is unusually direct for Jafa. Perhaps that is what its origin as a personal project let it be, actually: not unusually experimental, but abnormally blunt.

Arthur Jafa, Love is the Message, The Message is Death (2016). Photo by Ben Davis.

You get a moment with 16-year-old Hunger Games actress Amandla Stenberg , clipped from a viral 2015 video about cultural appropriation, “ Don’t Cash Crop My Cornrows. ” Stenberg gives the audience the one-line way to read the film’s upsetting juxtapositions: “What would America be like if we loved Black people as much as we love Black culture?”

And just like that, an artwork that was personal, shockingly violent, and full of tortured, unresolved feelings was distilled into something that could be read in a very simple way: as a teaching tool. Which is how it was used. In 2020, in the full flush of the George Floyd uprising, museums teamed up to show the work online, as if exposure to Jafa’s vision, somehow, would heal America’s soul.

A decade of cultural politics has shifted the meaning of the work’s imagery. Protests rose and fell. Corporate America responded by leaning on Black culture to insulate itself from those protests and to capture the cachet that only a righteous cause brings (including in mortifying ways: Kendall Jenner ’s “Black Lives Matter” Pepsi ad ; the Gushers brand tweeting solidarity with BLM; Jeff Bezos sending Amoako Boafo art into space to honor “Black joy”).

Arthur Jafa, Notebooks (1988–2007). Photo by Ben Davis.

Stenberg was elevated as high as you can go in pop culture: Disney made her the star of a Star Wars show. Critics praised The Acolyte for diverse casting and queer themes. But it was a turkey; Stenberg blamed its cancellation on racist online trolls.

Barack Obama ’s presence in Love Is the Message , singing “Amazing Grace,” was unifying and cathartic for the liberal audience at the time. A decade on, the millennial-and-younger left has defined itself against Obama’s brand of professorial centrism.

Kanye West ’s halting, lachrymose “Ultralight Beam” on the soundtrack granted Love Is the Message a lot of emotional punch. West spent the next decade becoming a more and more unnerving public figure (though Jafa still defends him ). He went on to stump for Trump and sell swastika merchandise .

All these developments trouble any use of Love Is the Message that turns on the simplest reading of that Stenberg line from 2015. But for Jafa himself, the shifting, complicated meanings of his subjects can be easily absorbed into his artistic project as a whole.

“My drive is to make things that are epic, and dense, and knotty, and Black—but at the same time completely refuse any sort of reductive idea of what Blackness is,” he has said . Jafa keeps saying things like that, and he keeps making works that are edgy, and uncomfortable, and hard to read; the audience keeps wanting to read him as offering clear-cut lessons.

Installation view of “Arthur Jafa: I Am Tony” featuring APEX (2013). Photo by Ben Davis.

Ultra-Violent Thoughts

You can see the wires of interpretation cross in the case of Jafa’s most recent major work, BEN GAZARRA (2024), more or less the grisly climax of the New Museum show.

It edits the final ultra-violent showdown of Martin Scorsese ’s Taxi Driver (1976) into multiple alternate versions, with subtle and not-so-subtle variations. But, always, you see a young, mohawked Robert De Niro storm a tenement to save a preteen Jodie Foster , who is in thrall to a pimp. We watch, over and over, fingers blown off, daggers gouging through hands, blown-out brains scattering across the wall. The twist is that Jafa has seamlessly reedited the film so that the pimp and his henchmen are Black.

The backstory is this: When he was in high school, Jafa saw Taxi Driver and had the idea that something was off, that these characters felt like they were meant to be Black. Later, he found out that Paul Schrader ‘s original Taxi Driver script had the pimp character as a Black man. According to film lore, Scorsese and the studio worried about charges of racism and changed the role. Harvey Keitel ended up playing the pimp.

Arthur Jafa, BEN GAZARRA (2024). Photo by Ben Davis.

In its accompanying explanation, the New Museum gently nudges the work back toward a moral reading, suggesting vaguely that it is “deconstructing the narrative faults of the scene,” and that the Jafa version holds up a mirror to contemporary racism by rendering De Niro’s avenging skinhead, Travis Bickle , in a way that reveals the film’s parallels to present-day white supremacist violence. This is the easiest hook for justifying such shocking imagery, and an almost automatic reflex of the discourse : “Black filmmaker corrects white filmmaker’s racism.”

Jafa has compared the Bickle character to Dylann Roof . But Roof slaughtered Black churchgoers, not child sex traffickers. The original film’s decision to cast the characters as white was meant to avoid staging stereotypes of Black thugs preying on innocent white girls that have always fueled white supremacist violence. Even critics who have long celebrated Jafa as a truth-teller scolded him for BEN GAZARRA , when the work debuted, finding its intention murky.

But if anything, Jafa seems drawn to the idea of the reedited Taxi Driver exactly because he doesn’t quite know what to do with the thought, because it is disturbing. (He told me that it “began as a joke,” like many of his works.) The many repeating versions of the Bickle killing spree read as Jafa trying to figure out what to do with a haunting, ugly idea, while always being pinned to the historical object.

Minor Works

Back in 2017, as the intensely moralizing period of #Resistance culture set in, art writer and now-dealer Chris Sharp penned an essay called “ Theory of the Minor. ”

Sharp was writing against the tendency—always active, but injected with steroids after 2016—of curators to favor art that flattened out into neat little homilies. This is what Sharp calls “major art,” art meant for public communication. (In recent history, I’d say Hank Willis Thomas is the epitome of “major art.”) Against it, Sharp defended art that is idiosyncratic, that comes from a distinctly personal place, that has no clear purpose or use. That’s what he called “minor art.”

Arthur Jafa, Picture Unit (Structures) II (2024). Photo by Ben Davis.

After seeing this New Museum show, my feeling is that if you can see Jafa’s work removed from the hyper-charged 2010s political and media moment that made his reputation, he looks very much like what he was before his 2016 breakout: an artist’s artist. This show is even organized more as a labyrinth than as a clear-cut career retrospective, as if to emphasize the fact of his difficulty.

Art historian Darby English has decried how the art industry tends to frame all Black contemporary artists alike, as communicators of moral truths about race and racism. Viewed clearly, outside these stock ideas, Jafa’s art is much more drawn to messiness than message; it starts from a place of personal psychodrama; and it is probably more for an art audience than a mass audience. It feels, in Sharp’s sense, minor.

Arthur Jafa, Townshend (2025). Photo by Ben Davis.

This means, also, that the work doesn’t always land. I do not personally believe that being hermetic is an end in itself. There’s a 2025 video in the show that is a wonky A.I.-animated image of the face of Pete Townshend , cofounder of the rock band the Who . The soundtrack is snippets of Who hits, punctuating silence. Whatever is going on here for Jafa doesn’t register, though I admire, sort of, how obdurate the work is.

The Texture of the Present

Then, on the other hand, there’s AGHDRA (2021). The heart of the show, for me.

Shown on a giant screen here, it is a digital video of a sun above a vast extraterrestrial ocean. The surface of this sea is some inexplicable form of black stone, like a mixture of tar and asphalt, seething up and down, somewhat crudely animated.

Fragments of distorted soul music come in and out of the soundtrack, as if we are picking up the last transmissions from Earth. Sometimes it is as if a storm picks up. The rolling berms of liquid rock become intense and threatening, filling the sky, blocking out the sun. Your head spins.

Arthur Jafa, AGHDRA (2021). Photo by Ben Davis.

Clearly, there is a symbolic association between this black ocean and Blackness. How striking that this work emerged in 2021, amid the Black Lives Matter protests that coursed through the culture, when the demands on Black artists—and on Jafa very specifically—to offer a righteous message were at their peak.

If Jafa’s mission is to make work that is “epic, and dense, and knotty, and Black,” but that “refuses any sort of reductive idea of what Blackness is,” AGHDRA takes that mission to its eerily abstract climax. It quite literally puts texture over meaning. It is sublime, and artificial, and bleak, personal and impersonal at once, and probably useless for teaching anyone anything.

It is an almost perfect work of contemporary art. And, incidentally, probably a good image for the unsettling period we are in right now, which no one seems to have the words to navigate.

“Arthur Jafa: I Am Tony” is on view at the New Museum, New York, through January 3, 2027.
content.excerpt_original: His New Museum retrospective offers a chance to make sense of a cultural shift.

content.article_text:
With a world in crisis and an art market spinning out of control, ace art-world consultants Chen & Lampert deliver a quiz full of hard choices for Art in America readers from far and wide.

Fall is traditionally a time to reflect, so we hereby offer up this Hard Choices quiz as a chance for you to evaluate the advice we’ve been offering Art in America readers since 2019. Have we helped? How have we hurt? Are things better today than they were before you considered our counsel? Answer the following questions to let us know how we’re doing and where we can improve. Please send your responses to hardtruths@artinamericamag.com or share them with us on social media.

Related Articles

Hard Truths: Can Senior Citizens Be Sage Social-Media Ambassadors?

Hard Choices: Should You Donate to Institutions Getting Gutted by Trump?

1. Reading Chen & Lampert makes me feel: a) Seen b) Peeped c) Stalked 2. The best description of Hard Truths is: a) Satirical but earnest advice column b) Ethical North Star c) Art world snitch sheet

3. My favorite part of taking the Hard Choices quiz is always: a) Tallying the score b) Learning new words c) Renewing my pledge to “never do this again” 4. Following Chen & Lampert’s advice has made me into: a) A stronger artist and all-around better person b) An incurable troll c) A GOD

5. Reading Chen & Lampert over the years has convinced me to: a) Pursue my master’s degree b) Finish my PhD c) Flee the art world to become a therapist who treats artists who become therapists 6. Chen & Lampert have proven to me that: a) Others wrestle with similar professional and personal dilemmas b) I am completely alone in this world c) Art problems are for coastal elites 7. The thing I like least about reading Chen & Lampert is: a) Their snide tone b) Their mercy for sinners c) The rest of the magazine 8. If Art in America stopped publishing Hard Choices and Hard Truths, I would: a) Immediately unsubscribe b) Initiate a boycott c) Finally be free of the mind goblins they gave me

9. Another Penske Media publication I would like to see Chen & Lampert write for is: a) Robb Report b) Women’s Wear Daily c) Vibe d) All the above—and they should also headline an event at SXSW

10. Chen & Lampert are people I could imagine: a) Hiring as consultants b) Having a beer with at my local bar c) Avoiding at public functions because of the shame they induce

SCORES

10–16: While doomscrolling Hyperallergic and fuming over Timothée Chalamet’s disdain for the slow arts, you inform social media that “art criticism is dead” because Chen & Lampert are besmirching the hallowed legacy of Art in America with hooliganism and puerile jokes.

17–23: Your love of Chen & Lampert is heroic. You are there for our merch drops and cannot wait to subscribe to our future Substack, which we’ll be forced to make if/when they fire us. But you won’t let that happen, and neither will the Pulitzer committee.

24–30: Deep down you’ve always known that Chen & Lampert’s uncomfortable sociological tour of the art world is actually a bighearted ploy to shape a society where artists and art will flourish and save humanity. You look forward to making their dream a reality.

content.article_text:
At the 61st Venice Biennale, Senegalese artist Caroline Gueye transforms Palazzo Navagero into an immersive exploration of perception, using gold to question how value is constructed and how our understanding of the world shifts depending on where we stand.

Gold has shaped economies, political power, and cultural histories for centuries, yet its value remains inseparable from the belief systems and perceptions through which we understand it. At the Senegal Pavilion of the 61st Venice Biennale, Caroline Gueye approaches this familiar material from an unexpected perspective. Her exhibition, WURUS , meaning ‘gold’ in Wolof, is less concerned with the precious metal itself than with the conditions that determine what we see, how we interpret it and what we consider valuable. Caroline Gueye, WURUS , ‘Structural Field’ detail. Image © Courtesy Caroline Gueye.

Curated by Massamba Mbaye, WURUS transforms the historic building into an immersive environment where architecture and sculpture become inseparable. Darkness gives way to unexpected reflections, intricate brass-and-bronze polymer forms emerge from concealed spaces, and visitors navigate an installation in which their physical position continually alters what becomes visible. Drawing on her background in fundamental physics and astrophysics, Gueye approaches space as an active system of relationships rather than a neutral setting for objects. In conversation with ART AFRICA at the Senegal Pavilion, she reflects on representing her country, her unusual ability to visualise entire installations before they exist, and how movement, material, and perception can challenge established ideas of value.

ART AFRICA : Gold has long been associated with wealth, power and possession. What drew you to it as the starting point for WURUS, and how does the exhibition challenge our understanding of value?

Caroline Gueye: It is an honour to represent Senegal at the Venice Biennale, but it is also a big responsibility. For this exhibition, we chose the title WURUS , which means ‘gold’ in Wolof. Gold symbolises desire, power, wealth and history, but we wanted to approach it from a different perspective: the question of value.

Gold is a material whose value appears self-evident, yet that value is constructed through the meanings and systems we associate with it. In WURUS , we are not presenting gold itself. Instead, I wanted to create an experience that encourages visitors to question how they perceive something and how that perception influences the value they assign to it. Caroline Gueye, WURUS , ‘After Collision’ detail. Image © Courtesy Caroline Gueye.

You have completely transformed the interior of Palazzo Navagero. How did you approach the architecture as an integral part of the artwork, rather than simply a space to exhibit sculptures?

We rebuilt the entire exhibition space, constructing walls and changing the room configuration because I wanted visitors to become part of the experience. Depending on where you stand and how you look at a work, your perception changes.

From the beginning, I conceived the transformation of the palazzo as an artwork in itself. The walls, passages, openings and viewpoints were not simply exhibition design but part of the artistic composition.

Working within a historic building required careful planning and collaboration with the local production team. We had to translate my vision into architectural drawings while respecting the building’s restrictions. For me, the exhibition is not a collection of separate artworks placed in a room. Everything is connected, and the space is as important as the sculptures themselves. Caroline Gueye, WURUS , Installation detail. Image © Alice Sartori.

Visitors encounter your sculptures through darkness, reflections and unexpected viewpoints. What interests you about disrupting the relationship between what we see and what we believe we are seeing?

When you enter the exhibition, you find yourself in a relatively dark space with very little light. Mirrors and reflective surfaces are everywhere, and sometimes you get a little lost. You see artworks reflected in different places, and you are not always certain whether you are looking at an object or its reflection.

I wanted to create this experience because perception depends on the conditions in which something becomes visible. Some sculptures appear immediately, while others are partially concealed or revealed only from particular positions.

Seeing something directly, from a distance or through a reflection produces different experiences. This connects to the question of value because how something appears influences how we perceive it. Caroline Gueye, WURUS , “Structural Field “Element’ detail. Image © Courtesy Caroline Gueye.

Movement is fundamental to the WURUS experience. How does the visitor’s physical position influence what becomes visible, and what does this reveal about the relationship between perception and value?

In French, we have the word parcours, which describes a path or journey. That is how I imagined this exhibition. You have to walk through it because you cannot understand the installation from a single position.

The visitor becomes an actor within the exhibition rather than simply an observer. A sculpture might be visible from one angle, disappear from another or reappear through a reflection. Movement changes the conditions in which the work is perceived.

We tend to think that what we see is fixed, but it depends on our position, distance and movement. I do not expect visitors to arrive at one particular interpretation. What matters is that they experience this shift and become aware that what they see depends on where they stand. Caroline Gueye, WURUS , ‘Structural Field’Resonance’ detail. Image © Courtesy Caroline Gueye.

Your background in fundamental physics and astrophysics informs your understanding of space and the relationships between objects. How has this scientific training shaped your artistic thinking and the development of WURUS?

I think my background in fundamental physics and astrophysics shapes the way I work with three-dimensional forms and space. It may also explain why my sculptures are often quite intricate and complex.

My scientific background influences the questions I ask. With WURUS , for example, I became interested in where gold comes from. In astrophysics, gold is produced through extreme cosmic events, including neutron star collisions. I was also interested in its scientific and technological applications, where its electrical, thermal and optical properties are particularly valuable.

But science is not something I want to illustrate. It is a way of thinking, questioning and understanding relationships. For me, space is not simply an empty container but something active, shaped by the relationships between objects, bodies and positions. Caroline Gueye, WURUS , ‘Structural Field’ detail. Image © Courtesy Caroline Gueye.

You have described an unusual creative process in which you can visualise an entire installation before producing drawings or models. How does this process unfold, and what challenges arise when translating these mental constructions into physical form?

My process is quite particular because I see everything in my head. It is so clear that I can walk through an entire exhibition in my imagination before it exists.

I discovered that this was perhaps unusual during the Dakar Biennale in 2022, where I received a prize for an immersive installation. People asked how I had created it, and I explained that I could see everything in my head. Through those conversations, I realised that not everybody works this way.

For WURUS , the process was the same. I could imagine the rooms, the sculptures, their positions and how visitors would move through the space. I do not necessarily need drawings to understand how something should look, although translating that vision into architectural plans and explaining it to the production team is another matter.

With individual sculptures, the process can require more experimentation, particularly when working with unfamiliar materials. Even a small change in scale or form can affect how a work is perceived. Caroline Gueye, WURUS , installation detail. Image © Courtesy Caroline Gueye.

Your sculptures are made from brass and bronze polymer, materials that resemble gold without possessing its material identity. How do these choices, together with light and reflective surfaces, contribute to your exploration of perceived value?

I like to have freedom when I create because the shapes I imagine are often intricate and technically difficult. I need materials that allow me to achieve those forms.

For WURUS , I used brass and bronze polymer, which can resemble gold without actually being gold. This distinction is important because the exhibition is about shifting perceptions of value. You look at something that appears to be gold, but it is not, which raises questions about how appearance influences what we think something is worth.

The mirrors, reflective surfaces and lighting are equally important. They are not simply atmospheric elements but part of the concept, influencing how the sculptures appear and how visitors experience them. Everything contributes to the uncertainty between what something is and what we perceive it to be. Caroline Gueye and Massamba Mbaye. Image © Courtesy Caroline Gueye.

At a time when economic, cultural, and symbolic values are increasingly contested, what broader questions does WURUS raise about how we construct meaning, assign value, and understand the world around us?

We are living in a moment when value is becoming increasingly abstract and detached from materiality. WURUS does not address this directly as a commentary, but it creates a situation in which people can experience how value is constructed.

The exhibition is about changing the conditions through which we perceive something. The objects themselves do not necessarily change, but the way we encounter them does. Their appearance depends on our position, movement, the light and the surrounding space.

I wanted visitors to become part of the installation because their presence contributes to what becomes visible. Something that appears obvious from one perspective may become quite different from another. I am not asking people to arrive at a particular conclusion, but to experience how changing their position can change their perception.

The best of Artnet News in your inbox.

Sign up for our daily newsletter.

For a decade, the Art Basel and UBS Art Market Report has been one of the most widely cited surveys about the market. In this extended episode of Art Market Minute, host Margaret Carrigan sits down with Clare McAndrew , founder of Arts Economics and the economist behind the report.

The best of Artnet News in your inbox.

Sign up for our daily newsletter.

McAndrew traces her path from studying cultural economics to measuring the global art market, and explains what 10 years of data have taught her about how it behaves under pressure. The episode also digs into her latest research on collectors, published in the Art Basel and UBS Survey of Global Collecting , which finds that Gen Z is spending the most on fine art, more collectors are using A.I. tools for art-buying advice, and buyers are playing it safe with their purchases.
content.excerpt_original: The economist behind the Art Basel and UBS market report on 10 years of data analysis, Gen Z spending, and why collectors are playing it safe.

content.article_text:
Après Faute d’amour (2017), qui sondait la déliquescence d’un couple à travers les yeux de son enfant, le cinéaste revient à ce modèle familial pour mieux le dévisager, le défigurer, le dé­construire. Parfaitement lisse, le trio formé par Gleb (Dmitri Mazourov), Galina (Iris Lebedeva) et leur fils unique adolescent apparaît déjà comme une utopie décharnée, isolée du monde et de ses vices.

Andreï Zviaguintsev : « L’enjeu principal, c’est celui du choix »

À ceci près que le couple se rend chaque jour en ville : Gleb pour se voir intimer d’envoyer ses salariés sur le front en Ukraine ; Galina pour rejoindre en secret l’homme qu’elle aime. Le cinéaste ne cherche pas à sauver moralement les apparences du masque social, autrement dit la vie de famille dans cette maison filmée comme un panoptique, où chacun des personnages se surveille et se contrôle. L’extérieur se lit alors comme l’envers du masque, le lieu d’une vérité inavouable à l’un et à l’autre et sans doute pour eux-mêmes.

À l’instar de Chabrol en son temps, Minotaure soulève une question glaçante : jusqu’où peut-on aller pour préserver le masque ? Jusqu’à quel degré d’aliénation ? Appliquée au contexte de la guerre en Ukraine, la réponse – tout aussi glaçante – n’en est que plus frontalement politique, car, enfin, Gleb fait partie des puissants de ce monde. Les pauvres, les chômeurs, les artistes, dont le « troisième homme » du récit en est une forme de synthèse, sont sacrifiés sur l’autel de l’indifférence. Un constat d’autant plus noir qu’il est filmé avec ce sens de la tragédie cher à Andreï Zviaguintsev, réduit à son essence muette : l’image d’un couple qui s’enlace dans l’obscurité, rien que l’obscurité.

Minotaure d’Andreï Zviaguintsev (Les Films du Losange, 2h15), sortie le 14 octobre

content.excerpt_original: Remake audacieux d’un des plus grands films de Claude Chabrol, "Minotaure" transpose l’austère sinuosité du cinéaste français dans la Russie contemporaine, mais se veut avant tout une dénonciation de l’hypocrisie des puissants de ce monde.

content.article_text:
Two Pierre-Auguste Renoir paintings stolen from a museum in the French Riviera last month have been recovered, local officials said. Six suspects were arrested.

The best of Artnet News in your inbox.

Sign up for our daily newsletter.

The mayor of Cagnes-sur-Mer, where Renoir lived out his final days, described the news as “a source of immense joy and a great relief.” He added that the paintings were “part of our city’s history, our cultural heritage.”

The best of Artnet News in your inbox.

Sign up for our daily newsletter.

Two thieves broke into the artist’s former home, the city’s Renoir Museum , early on September 8. They attempted to take four paintings before dropping two in the garden as they rushed to escape. The value of the two stolen works, Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano (1910) and Young Woman at the Well (1886), was reported at a combined $10 million. Both belong to the Musée d’Orsay in Paris and were on loan.

The Marseille public prosecutor’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment on how the Renoir paintings were recovered. A press conference that would have given more details about the recovery was canceled so as not to interfere with the ongoing investigation.

France’s culture minister, Catherine Pégard , commended “the efficiency and determination” of the investigators in a post on social media. She also praised the “swift response” of local police, “from the moment the alarm was triggered,” as “remarkable.”

France has suffered a spate of museum heists in recent years. The highest-profile one occurred at the Louvre in Paris last October. Investigators uncovered various security failings that left the institution vulnerable to the shock $102 million theft, and the Louvre announced a $92 million master security plan .

Though Renoir continues to divide opinion , the Impressionist just broke box-office records at the National Gallery in London, with the museum selling over 22,000 tickets for its “Renoir and Love” exhibition, which is on view through January 31.

content.article_text:
I n Arabic, “fidai” means someone willing to sacrifice themselves for the greater good. Borrowing this word, which is at times used in a military context, for his collage film, Palestinian film-maker Kamal Aljafari stages a potent uprising of images against the tide of propaganda and historical erasure. Much of the film draws on archive materials once housed in the Palestine Research Centre in Beirut. In 1982, during the Lebanese civil war, Israeli forces raided the centre and seized the archive. Most of these documents on Palestinian history – books, newspapers, audiovisual artefacts – are believed to still be in the hands of the Israeli army.

Obtained through clandestine means, the footage that resurfaces in Aljafari’s film bears the physical traces of political suppression. The images are scratched, grainy and pixelated, yet through the power of montage they evoke startling visual parallels that point to the relentless violence endured by Palestinians through the decades. Black-and-white film taken during the British mandate show soldiers patrolling the streets and inflicting violence upon the Indigenous population; similar acts then committed by Israeli forces. In place of a chronological order, the editing builds a sense of continuity through recurring images. Time and time again, we see torn-down houses, terrorised children and the bodies of Palestinians murdered by occupation forces.

More than simply a work of compilation, the film also performs its own historical intervention. Many of the reels are imprinted with pejorative captions added by Israeli authorities, which Aljafari covers in streaks of red paint. In their place are excerpts from poems by Palestinian authors such as Ghassan Kanafani, whose words return a sense of humanity to these past images. Through these strategies of reclamation, Aljafari’s film brings liberation, if only momentarily, to a captive archive.

content.article_text:
F ilmed in Taiwan and set entirely inside a prestigious high school, Kiwi Chow’s gripping drama frames educational systems not merely as a preparation for the real world but as a microcosm of society at large. At this elite private institute, pupils studiously march in lines like obedient soldiers, their purple uniforms the only pop of colour in a grey building of glass and steel. The school’s operations have a touch of dystopian sci-fi: students check in with AI recognition panels, which also display their class standing and disciplinary scores. In this sterile environment where human worth is measured by standardised metrics, the breathing room for individuality is nil.

This panopticon atmosphere of surveillance and cut-throat competition is punctured by a shocking incident: an anonymous student drops a flurry of leaflets announcing their intent to take their own life on the day of the final exam, unless the school changes its authoritarian ways. The note sends tremors through both the administration and the students; intersecting narrative lines weave through a group of characters that include a model student, a dedicated but ambivalent teacher and a righteous slacker. Each carries a heavy secret that points to the moral rot beneath the facade of academic excellence.

Though grappling with heavy subjects such as self-harm, bullying and drug use, Chow treats these youthful foibles as evidence of a systemic malaise rather than individual failings. A staunch anti-authoritarian message is smuggled in the conventions of a whodunnit thriller; it parallels Chow’s previous films, including the 2021 documentary Revolution of Our Times , about the 2019-2020 Hong Kong protests . Like the rebellion in Deadline, that movement also began on campuses and was led by students. That both titles are banned in Hong Kong only underscores the urgency and importance of Chow’s film-making.

content.title_original: ‘We’re in a brotherhood now’: the Bill Pickett rodeo – photo essay
content.article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "T he image of the cowboy widely portrayed in westerns and popular culture has long been almost exclusively white. Yet Black cowboys hold an important place in the history of the American west. After the civil war and the abolition of slavery, many African Americans found work on ranches and on the great cattle drives westward. By the late 19th century, historians estimate about one in four cowboys were Black."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Among the Black figures who shaped this history was Bill Pickett . Born in Texas in 1870, he became one of the most celebrated Black cowboys and rodeo performers of his time, known in particular for popularising bulldogging, which would eventually give rise to modern steer wrestling.", "links": [{"text": "Bill Pickett", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/culture/ng-interactive/2024/may/19/black-cowboys-cowgirls-rodeos"}]}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/a407bd0a481f4acbe6ae3c77a58facdac3de9f42/0_0_7330_4929/master/7330.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "A man in a cowboy hat rides a horse in an arena", "caption": "After the national anthem, Josh, a member of the Outlaws Most Wanted, rides around the arena to a pounding hip-hop track as his teammates cheer him on at the Bill Pickett invitational rodeo in Conyers, near Atlanta , Georgia, on 2 August 2026", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture"}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "After the national anthem, Josh, a member of the Outlaws Most Wanted, rides around the arena to a pounding hip-hop track as his teammates cheer him on at the Bill Pickett invitational rodeo in Conyers, near Atlanta , Georgia, on 2 August 2026", "links": [{"text": "Atlanta", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/atlanta"}]}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/9f7908403f44c350716dce75fb5522712e186ff4/0_0_7728_5152/master/7728.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "A group of men in cowboy hats joke with each other", "caption": "Members of the Outlaws Most Wanted joke and playfully challenge other riders, some of whom have travelled long distances to compete, backstage at the rodeo", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture"}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "Members of the Outlaws Most Wanted joke and playfully challenge other riders, some of whom have travelled long distances to compete, backstage at the rodeo"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "His name was chosen by the promoter Lu Vason when he created the Bill Pickett invitational rodeo. In 1977, Vason attended Cheyenne frontier days and was struck by the absence of Black cowboys in the arena. His research led him to the Black American West Museum in Denver, where he discovered the story of Pickett and the history of African Americans in the American west. In 1984, he created a rodeo designed to give Black cowboys and cowgirls a platform and bring greater visibility to this heritage."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "More than 40 years later, that mission remains at the heart of the Bill Pickett invitational rodeo. Part sporting competition, part spectacle and part space for passing on history and culture, its 2026 tour crosses the US from February to October, with stops including Memphis, Atlanta, Oakland and Los Angeles."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "This year, I decided to join the tour in Atlanta."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/77dac485df3bc3853c0ffa53454e3ba935ab1508/0_0_7728_5152/master/7728.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "A man with three young children in cowboy hats sit atop horses", "caption": "A family on horseback waits to enter the arena at therodeo, reflecting the intergenerational nature of a cowboy culture passed down through families. 1 August 2026", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture"}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "A family on horseback waits to enter the arena at therodeo, reflecting the intergenerational nature of a cowboy culture passed down through families. 1 August 2026"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "While there, I met for the first time a contact I had been speaking with before my trip. He runs Diamondcut Ranch, where he works with and trains horses, and around which a wider community of riders has formed. It was there that I met the Outlaws Most Wanted, a team of “bronc riders” competing at the Bill Pickett."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The organisers allowed me behind the barriers on the condition that I stayed with them. I found myself in the space just behind the arena, where the riders wait for their turn and prepare their equipment."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Music is everywhere. The riders joke around, encourage one another and build each other up. The energy and adrenaline rise as their turn approaches, until each rider has to move away from that collective excitement and focus on the few seconds waiting for him in the arena."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/c0342ddb8e4062be0b85b7586e637926f2fc81bb/643_0_6442_5152/master/6442.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "A man in a cowboy hat at night", "caption": "Rachied Robins, AKA Django, a member of the Outlaws Most Wanted bronc-riding team, who became my main contact and a key voice in telling the group’s story during the Bill Pickett invitational rodeo. 1/08/2026", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture"}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "Rachied Robins, AKA Django, a member of the Outlaws Most Wanted bronc-riding team, who became my main contact and a key voice in telling the group’s story during the Bill Pickett invitational rodeo. 1/08/2026"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "One of them, Rachied Robins, AKA Django, describes the Outlaws Most Wanted as a group of Caribbean men, some of whom have come from difficult backgrounds, brought together by their love of horses. Some, he says, found “refuge in this horse world”. Over time, their bonds grew stronger: “We’re in a brotherhood now.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Django grew up in Kissimmee, Florida, surrounded by rodeo culture. He started out in bull riding before changing disciplines after a bull stomped on his face. He now competes in ranch bronc riding and laughingly describes himself as an “adrenaline junkie”."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "But behind the adrenaline, there is also fear. Before he gets on the horse, thoughts of the danger and all the “what ifs” run through his mind. Then he has to find a way to clear his head."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/e85111002152c3812ec5312cebd645b10fa41d42/0_0_6530_4414/master/6530.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "A group of men and young boy in cowboy hats point towards the distance", "caption": "The Outlaws Most Wanted bronc-riding team at the Bill Pickett rodeo", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture"}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "The Outlaws Most Wanted bronc-riding team at the Bill Pickett rodeo"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“You just gotta clear your mind and leave it in God’s hands.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "He has to trust his technique and make it through eight seconds. And even once the ride is over, the danger is not: Django tells me that getting off the horse can be one of the most dangerous moments."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "There is also a financial side to competing. Django tells me that the Bill Pickett is not among the rodeos offering the largest purses: at the April event he competed in, he says a rider could win up to about $1,500 (£1,135), compared with as much as $10,000 at some other rodeos. But money is only part of what is at stake."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“It’s not just the money, but also your name, the respect, ranking.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "What struck me most about the Bill Pickett, however, perhaps happens beyond the competition itself."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/a11f430efc106c98549db2bece215fbe6265620a/0_0_7725_4765/master/7725.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "People on horses wait outside an arena", "caption": "Riders wait to enter the arena in a solemn moment, hats held over their hearts, as The Star-Spangled Banner is sung a cappella at sunset before the start of the rodeo", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture"}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "Riders wait to enter the arena in a solemn moment, hats held over their hearts, as The Star-Spangled Banner is sung a cappella at sunset before the start of the rodeo"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Before the events begin, The Star-Spangled Banner is sung a cappella. Hats are placed over hearts, the riders stand still, and silence falls across the stands and the arena. I remember getting goosebumps and tears in my eyes."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Then, almost without transition, the atmosphere shifts completely and the adrenaline takes over."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "All the riders enter the arena to a powerful hip-hop track. The volume rises, the horses come in, and the crowd shouts, applauds and dances. Within moments, the atmosphere moves from solemn stillness to an almost explosive energy."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "That contrast captures much of what I felt at the Bill Pickett. History and memory are central to the event, but they are not frozen in the past. They coexist with hip-hop, fashion, competition and a deeply contemporary Black cowboy culture."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/42a2ae2b2683708bfff46961dc194be95320b181/20_0_6220_3919/master/6220.jpg?width=465&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "A cowboy stands at the edge of an arena as the crowd cheers him on from the stands", "caption": "After his ride, a cowboy walks along the edge of the arena as the crowd cheers him on at the Bill Pickett", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture"}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "After his ride, a cowboy walks along the edge of the arena as the crowd cheers him on at the Bill Pickett"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The audience is very much part of the spectacle. Western shirts, cowboy hats and boots fill the stands: people come to watch the rodeo, but also to gather, dance, show their style and celebrate a shared culture. Throughout the event, the announcers return again and again to the history of Black cowboys and the values the Bill Pickett seeks to pass on. That history is not confined to a few lines in a programme: it is an integral part of the event."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "When I ask Django what the Bill Pickett means to him, he tells me that it is about more than just rodeo: “Bill Pickett means a lot to me personally. Not just because it’s a rodeo, but because it’s a platform for us minorities to come together.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "He talks about being able to show what they can do “as a group, as a unit”, but also about having a place where he can be himself and where he feels at home."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The Outlaws Most Wanted do not compete only at Black rodeos. Django tells me they compete wherever they have the opportunity and rejects the idea that these events are a form of separation. For him, they are above all about making a heritage visible: “We just want to bring out our heritage and bring out our history and show that we are part of this history, and this is part of our history.”"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/937f91083cf285ff45c40279c05b1fc3565845b0/0_0_7728_5054/master/7728.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "Members of the Outlaws Most Wanted bronc riding team gather behind the arena", "caption": "Members of the Outlaws Most Wanted bronc riding team gather behind the arena", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture"}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "Members of the Outlaws Most Wanted bronc riding team gather behind the arena"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "It is also about passing something on. T he image of the cowboy widely portrayed in westerns and popular culture has long been almost exclusively white. Yet Black cowboys hold an important place in the history of the American west. After the civil war and the abolition of slavery, many African Americans found work on ranches and on the great cattle drives westward. By the late 19th century, historians estimate about one in four cowboys were Black.

Among the Black figures who shaped this history was Bill Pickett . Born in Texas in 1870, he became one of the most celebrated Black cowboys and rodeo performers of his time, known in particular for popularising bulldogging, which would eventually give rise to modern steer wrestling.

After the national anthem, Josh, a member of the Outlaws Most Wanted, rides around the arena to a pounding hip-hop track as his teammates cheer him on at the Bill Pickett invitational rodeo in Conyers, near Atlanta , Georgia, on 2 August 2026

Members of the Outlaws Most Wanted joke and playfully challenge other riders, some of whom have travelled long distances to compete, backstage at the rodeo

His name was chosen by the promoter Lu Vason when he created the Bill Pickett invitational rodeo. In 1977, Vason attended Cheyenne frontier days and was struck by the absence of Black cowboys in the arena. His research led him to the Black American West Museum in Denver, where he discovered the story of Pickett and the history of African Americans in the American west. In 1984, he created a rodeo designed to give Black cowboys and cowgirls a platform and bring greater visibility to this heritage.

More than 40 years later, that mission remains at the heart of the Bill Pickett invitational rodeo. Part sporting competition, part spectacle and part space for passing on history and culture, its 2026 tour crosses the US from February to October, with stops including Memphis, Atlanta, Oakland and Los Angeles.

This year, I decided to join the tour in Atlanta.

A family on horseback waits to enter the arena at therodeo, reflecting the intergenerational nature of a cowboy culture passed down through families. 1 August 2026

While there, I met for the first time a contact I had been speaking with before my trip. He runs Diamondcut Ranch, where he works with and trains horses, and around which a wider community of riders has formed. It was there that I met the Outlaws Most Wanted, a team of “bronc riders” competing at the Bill Pickett.

The organisers allowed me behind the barriers on the condition that I stayed with them. I found myself in the space just behind the arena, where the riders wait for their turn and prepare their equipment.

Music is everywhere. The riders joke around, encourage one another and build each other up. The energy and adrenaline rise as their turn approaches, until each rider has to move away from that collective excitement and focus on the few seconds waiting for him in the arena.

Rachied Robins, AKA Django, a member of the Outlaws Most Wanted bronc-riding team, who became my main contact and a key voice in telling the group’s story during the Bill Pickett invitational rodeo. 1/08/2026

One of them, Rachied Robins, AKA Django, describes the Outlaws Most Wanted as a group of Caribbean men, some of whom have come from difficult backgrounds, brought together by their love of horses. Some, he says, found “refuge in this horse world”. Over time, their bonds grew stronger: “We’re in a brotherhood now.”

Django grew up in Kissimmee, Florida, surrounded by rodeo culture. He started out in bull riding before changing disciplines after a bull stomped on his face. He now competes in ranch bronc riding and laughingly describes himself as an “adrenaline junkie”.

But behind the adrenaline, there is also fear. Before he gets on the horse, thoughts of the danger and all the “what ifs” run through his mind. Then he has to find a way to clear his head.

The Outlaws Most Wanted bronc-riding team at the Bill Pickett rodeo

“You just gotta clear your mind and leave it in God’s hands.”

He has to trust his technique and make it through eight seconds. And even once the ride is over, the danger is not: Django tells me that getting off the horse can be one of the most dangerous moments.

There is also a financial side to competing. Django tells me that the Bill Pickett is not among the rodeos offering the largest purses: at the April event he competed in, he says a rider could win up to about $1,500 (£1,135), compared with as much as $10,000 at some other rodeos. But money is only part of what is at stake.

“It’s not just the money, but also your name, the respect, ranking.”

What struck me most about the Bill Pickett, however, perhaps happens beyond the competition itself.

Riders wait to enter the arena in a solemn moment, hats held over their hearts, as The Star-Spangled Banner is sung a cappella at sunset before the start of the rodeo

Before the events begin, The Star-Spangled Banner is sung a cappella. Hats are placed over hearts, the riders stand still, and silence falls across the stands and the arena. I remember getting goosebumps and tears in my eyes.

Then, almost without transition, the atmosphere shifts completely and the adrenaline takes over.

All the riders enter the arena to a powerful hip-hop track. The volume rises, the horses come in, and the crowd shouts, applauds and dances. Within moments, the atmosphere moves from solemn stillness to an almost explosive energy.

That contrast captures much of what I felt at the Bill Pickett. History and memory are central to the event, but they are not frozen in the past. They coexist with hip-hop, fashion, competition and a deeply contemporary Black cowboy culture.

After his ride, a cowboy walks along the edge of the arena as the crowd cheers him on at the Bill Pickett

The audience is very much part of the spectacle. Western shirts, cowboy hats and boots fill the stands: people come to watch the rodeo, but also to gather, dance, show their style and celebrate a shared culture. Throughout the event, the announcers return again and again to the history of Black cowboys and the values the Bill Pickett seeks to pass on. That history is not confined to a few lines in a programme: it is an integral part of the event.

When I ask Django what the Bill Pickett means to him, he tells me that it is about more than just rodeo: “Bill Pickett means a lot to me personally. Not just because it’s a rodeo, but because it’s a platform for us minorities to come together.”

He talks about being able to show what they can do “as a group, as a unit”, but also about having a place where he can be himself and where he feels at home.

The Outlaws Most Wanted do not compete only at Black rodeos. Django tells me they compete wherever they have the opportunity and rejects the idea that these events are a form of separation. For him, they are above all about making a heritage visible: “We just want to bring out our heritage and bring out our history and show that we are part of this history, and this is part of our history.”

Members of the Outlaws Most Wanted bronc riding team gather behind the arena

It is also about passing something on. From trail rides to rodeos, horses create a space around which families, friendships and communities are formed. For some members of the Outlaws Most Wanted, this world has even become a refuge.

When I ask Django what he hopes the young people in the stands take away from watching him ride, he does not talk about becoming a cowboy or winning competitions. Above all, he hopes to show them that another path is possible: “Do something safe, do something legal, get out the streets, keep your mind right, don’t be another statistic.”

More than a century after Black cowboys helped shape the history of the American west while remaining largely absent from its popular image, the Bill Pickett offers a space where this heritage does not belong only to the past: it continues to be lived, passed on and reinvented.

content.article_text:
From October 6, 2026, to January 6, 2027, the Cavaillon Media Library, in the Vaucluse region of southern France, will present 18 photographs by Dorothea Lange, on exceptional loan from the Musée Réattu in Arles. Among them is Migrant Mother , the American photographer’s iconic image, made in California in 1936.

This exhibition takes on particular resonance as the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art opens its doors in Los Angeles on September 22, 2026. Among the photographic works presented in its collections is Migrant Mother , now one of the most celebrated images in the history of photography.

Nearly 9,000 kilometers away, Lange’s photographs are leaving the collections of the Musée Réattu in Arles for an exceptional presentation in Cavaillon, where they will encounter a new audience. The exhibition is a rare event for the Cavaillon area. Migrant Mother is presented alongside 17 other photographs, offering a glimpse into Lange’s attentive gaze on the social and human realities of her time.

A photograph that has crossed the decades without losing its power: the face of a woman, a family and, through them, an entire era marked by the Great Depression.

The connection between Los Angeles and Cavaillon gives this presentation a particular resonance. Two institutions, two territories and two different contexts, yet sharing the same belief in photography’s ability to tell the truth of the world and the stories of human lives.

In Cavaillon, Dorothea Lange is the central figure of Le Regard en héritage , a year-long photography program taking place from September 2026 to September 2027 across the 16 municipalities of Luberon Monts de Vaucluse Agglomeration.

Supported by the French Ministry of Culture as part of the Bicentenary of Photography, the program brings together exhibitions, lectures, screenings, encounters and workshops. It creates a dialogue between documentary photography, contemporary practice, amateur photography and the transmission of photographic knowledge and skills.

Born in Oppède around the exhibition Le Verbe et l’Image , Le Regard en héritage has gradually expanded to include the municipalities and media libraries across the region. Bringing together the work of established photographers and participatory projects developed with local residents, the program explores different ways of looking: at landscapes, faces, memories, heritage and the transformations of a territory.

With Dorothea Lange as its point of departure, Le Regard en héritage places Luberon Monts de Vaucluse within the celebration of 200 years of photography, while making the photographic image a means of transmitting, questioning and renewing the way we see the world.

Dorothea Lange Exhibition From 6 October 2026 to 6 January 2027 Cavaillon Media Centre 60 rue Véran Rousset – 84300 Cavaillon Free admission Tuesday: 1 pm – 7 pm Wednesday: 10 am – 6 pm Thursday and Friday: 1 pm – 6 pm Saturday: 10 am – 6 pm Closed on Sundays and Mondays. www.mediathequeslmv.fr

JOACHIM ROMAIN — LOOKING AT WHAT OTHERS NO LONGER SEE

Joachim Romain looks at images precisely where they generally cease to interest us. Torn posters, amputated letters, anonymous faces, faded urban signs, visual debris: His domain is not that of the spectacular image, but that of what remains after it. Since his early days in street photography, he has extracted fragments from the urban environment that the ordinary gaze has learned to overlook, removing them from their status as waste and giving them another existence. For Romain, to photograph is already to displace. This gesture lies at the heart of a practice that has never fully accepted the boundaries between photography, urban art, collage, and installation. He does not regard these mediums as separate territories, but as different states of the same gaze. Photography captures, appropriation isolates, collage recomposes, and installation displaces once again. What interests him, then, is less the image itself than what it becomes when its context changes when it loses its original function and acquires a new visual charge. An advertising poster is no longer simply a poster once it has been torn; a fragment of a letter is no longer merely a sign once it becomes material; a face torn from an image can suddenly become the portrait of an era. There is a form of contemporary archaeology at work here. But it is an archaeology without nostalgia. Romain does not seek to preserve the traces of the city; he puts them into tension. He is interested in the way images appear, disappear, overlap, and ultimately generate a memory of their own. His work reveals a city that is constantly producing and destroying its own representations. Through it, he also questions our relationship to images: their omnipresence, their speed of circulation, their obsolescence, and their strange ability, despite their proliferation, to become invisible. His gaze naturally belongs to a history of urban art in which Jacques Villeglé stands as one of its defining figures. Yet with Romain, the lineage is never simply a matter of quotation. Where Villeglé turned the wall into a space of revelation, collecting the anonymous tears of public posters as signs of a collective memory, Romain works within a landscape saturated with images, where the fragment no longer comes from the street alone. It also comes from the digital realm, commerce, advertising, screens, and a new visual economy in which everything is produced, consumed, and replaced almost instantaneously.

His participation in the exhibition devoted to Jacques Villeglé at the Musée Carnavalet takes on a particular resonance in this context. It places his work within a history that continually reinvents itself: that of artists who do not necessarily create their images from nothing but know how to recognize an image that is already there, buried beneath another, and give it a second life. For Romain, this act of revelation operates as much through photography as through material, gesture, and composition. It is precisely this logic of displacement that emerges in Défragmentation at Galerie Laurent Rigail. Alongside Jacques Villeglé, Quentin DMR, and the other artists brought together for the exhibition, Romain contributes to a reflection on the fragment as artistic material: a fragment of the city, of memory, of a poster, a photograph, or a sign. Yet the exhibition’s title could almost describe his own method. To defragment is not simply to break an image into pieces. It is to alter the relationships between those pieces in order to make something else appear. This idea runs throughout his work. Even when he photographs, Romain does not simply record. He selects. He frames. He excludes. Through the choice of what he decides to look at, he is already transforming reality. “Framing one part often makes you forget the rest,” he says in this questionnaire. The phrase could serve as a key to his entire practice. Because this is precisely where his art begins: in the awareness that looking is always an act of selection and that a fragment can sometimes say more than a complete image. His relationship to photography is therefore less documentary than critical. What matters is not only what the image shows, but what it leaves outside the frame, what it conceals, and what it suddenly allows us to see. Hence his recurring attention to detail, accident, and to that which is “not there for everyone else.” Romain searches for cracks in the surface of things. He finds stories there, tensions, sometimes simply an emotion. His visual practice extends this investigation without resolving it. He transforms visual waste into material but refuses to strip it of its disorder. He does not clean up the fragment; he allows it to retain the traces of its passage. Perhaps this is where the singularity of his gaze lies. In a world where images have become instantly available, retouched, and reproducible, Romain continues to search for those that have lived for images that still bear the marks of their own disappearance.

To look at the world with Joachim Romain is therefore to accept slowing down before what we have learned to pass without seeing. A worn letter. A half-erased face. A torn poster. A fragment of the city. Nothing, apparently. And yet, within that almost nothing, the possibility of an image.
