Actu : Exhibitions : « Défragmentation » from oct 14th to nov. 14th 2026 Galerie Laurent Rigail 40, rue Volta 75003 Paris

Participation to the exhibition « Paris à l’arraché » dedicated to Jacques Villeglé at Musée Carnavalet.

What was your first photographic trigger? Joachim Romain: My father was a photographer. For my 15th birthday, he gave me a Nikon EM.

A photographic memory from your childhood? Joachim Romain: Me on the beach, photographed by my father.

The camera of your childhood? Joachim Romain: Polaroid, of course.

The one you use today? Joachim Romain: Canon 6D.

The man or woman of the image who inspired you? Joachim Romain: Brassaï.

The image you wish you had taken? Joachim Romain: The Woodstock album cover. I would have done two crazy things.

The one that moved you the most? Joachim Romain: Lee Friedlander.

And the one that made you angry? Joachim Romain: Marine mammals caught in fishing nets.

Which photograph changed the world? Joachim Romain: “Tank Man,” in Tiananmen Square.

And which photograph changed your world? Joachim Romain: A worn-out letter B and a face on a poster, photographed in Sarajevo in 2006. That image profoundly changed my photographic work and the subjects I research today.

What interests you most in an image? Joachim Romain: Its emotion.

What details do you look for in a face, a landscape, or an object? Joachim Romain: The one that isn’t there for everyone else.

Elliott Erwitt once said: “Color is descriptive. Black and white is interpretive.” Do you agree? Joachim Romain: To some extent, yes. But why choose?

Can technique sometimes take precedence over emotion in photography? Joachim Romain: For me, technique comes after the subject and the framing. But it remains a very important part, depending on the effect you want to achieve with your subject.

Is beauty in photography, for you, purely aesthetic? Joachim Romain: Absolutely not.

What can make silence visible in a photograph? Joachim Romain: A detail.

Does the uniqueness of a photograph come from the moment or from staging? Joachim Romain: The moment is unique and that’s everything.

Can a photograph be more truthful than reality? Joachim Romain: That’s where staging comes into play.

Can a photograph change our perception of an event? Joachim Romain: Clearly. Focusing on one part often makes you forget the rest.

Is photography a testimony or a form of manipulation? Joachim Romain: For me, a testimony above all.

What makes a good photograph? Joachim Romain: The emotion it gives you.

What quality is essential to being a good photographer? Joachim Romain: Going out to find your subject and waiting for the right moment.

How do you choose your projects? Joachim Romain: They are connected to my visual art practice, although originally it was the other way around: my street photography gradually gave birth to my visual art practice. Today, the two have become one body of work in which photography and visual art come together.

How would you describe your creative process? Joachim Romain: It depends on the work. With the photographic series Fast_Shop , for example, there is a whole research process beforehand, followed by a real exploration of movement and time.

An upcoming project that is particularly close to your heart? Joachim Romain: My project Made in Europe is about creating an exhibition that brings my street work, photography, and installation into dialogue.

The person you would like to photograph? Joachim Romain: my daughter, and I did it! But I’d happily do it again.

The person you would like to be photographed by? Joachim Romain: Mari Katayama or Zanele Muholi.

One essential photography book? Joachim Romain: Affichage_Libre 🙂 Otherwise, Chernobyl by Robert Polidori. And a book by Brassaï, Brassaï: Picasso and the Photographs , or Vivian Maier.

What is the last photograph you took? Joachim Romain: Portraits of artists in Turkey, in Izmir.

On social media, are you more Instagram, Facebook, or TikTok — and why? Joachim Romain: Instagram. There hasn’t been anything fun on Facebook for a while. And I’m not on TikTok at all.

What has changed in photography since the rise of social media? Joachim Romain: The quality, the framing… A bit like when digital photography arrived and everyone thought they were a photographer.

One Instagram account everyone should follow? Joachim Romain: Your friends’. The rest isn’t important.

What is your view on AI? Joachim Romain: A bit like when the first Adobe Illustrator came along: it’s a development that is difficult to avoid, but one we need to learn to master. The most important thing, in my view, is to remain the creative force, rather than simply following or letting AI do the creating for us. But, in reality, I think we won’t be in control of much for very long.

Color or black and white? Joachim Romain: Both, but with a preference for black and white.

Natural or artificial light? Joachim Romain: Natural.

Which city strikes you as the most photogenic? Joachim Romain: Marseille.

The city, country, or culture you dream of discovering? Joachim Romain: Africa.

The place you never get tired of? Joachim Romain: My bathroom 🙂 Seriously, though, definitely the Arles festival.

The image that, for you, represents the state of the world today? Joachim Romain: The photomontage of British Prime Minister Tony Blair taking a selfie against a backdrop of burning oil.

What do you think is missing from the world today? Joachim Romain: A strong movement toward nature and living together. It’s frightening right now.

If God existed, would you ask him to pose for you, or would you go for a selfie with him? Joachim Romain: That’s too disconnected from reality for me, so…

Your favorite drug? Joachim Romain: My studio.

Your best way to switch off? Joachim Romain: I haven’t found one. I dream of it.

Your latest act of madness? Joachim Romain: A Get 27–Ricard cocktail in Arles 🙂 I still have a headache.

The body of work you are particularly proud of? Joachim Romain: My Urban work, which consists of transforming what everyone considers visual waste into an art installation.

The job you would never have wanted to do? Joachim Romain: I respect people so much that saying “I wouldn’t want to do your job” feels a bit harsh 🙂

Which question throws you off the most? Joachim Romain: Who is your favorite artist?

The last thing you did for the first time? Joachim Romain: Rowing on the Olympic rowing basin in Montreal, with my family. It was great.

Your biggest regret? Joachim Romain: Not having gone to art school.

If you could start all over again? Joachim Romain: Maybe I would have taken school more seriously. But then again, I wouldn’t have had the path I’ve had, and I don’t regret it.

If I could organize your ideal dinner, who would be sitting around the table? Joachim Romain: Jim Morrison, Nina Kraviz, Jacques Villeglé, Anselm Kiefer. Music and art: everything I love.

What would you like people to say about you… afterwards? Joachim Romain: If they remember me at all, that’s already something 🙂

The one thing people absolutely need to know about you? Joachim Romain: Generous.

One last word? Joachim Romain: Together.

content.article_text:
中田友木の写真展「EMOTIONS, IN MY LIFE.」が、2026年10月20日から25日まで、大阪・南船場のギャラリー・ソラリスで開催される。自身の人生に残る怒りや悲しみといった感情の記憶を、「身体」の反応から捉え直した作品を発表する。

本展の出発点となったのは、感情と身体の関係だ。「怖いから逃げるのではない。逃げるから怖いのだ。悲しいから泣くのではない。泣くから悲しいのだ」と中田は記す。感情が先に存在し、それによって身体が反応するのではなく、身体に起こった変化を脳が察知することで感情が生じる——そうした考え方に着目し、自らの記憶を写真によって検証することを試みた。

中田が振り返るのは、これまでの人生で愚痴やぼやきとして記憶に刻まれてきた、激しい怒りや悲しみだ。それらも、もとをたどれば「ほんの些細な『身体』の反応だったかもしれない」と考え、過去の感情を生み出したであろう身体の動きを想像。カメラの前で中田自身がその動きを演じ、セルフポートレートとして写真に定着させた。それは出来事を事実として記録する一般的な自叙伝とは異なる、いわば「感情の記憶」による自画像だ。中田は「自叙伝やその記録の写真なんぞとても残す気になれない。でもこんな風な感情の記憶の写真なら残そうと思った」と語る。過去に何が起きたのかではなく、それによって身体に何が起き、どのような感情として残ったのか。身体を演じ直す行為を介して、自身の生を写真へと置き換えていく。

中田は京都府出身。2025年3月に京都芸術大学通信教育部美術科写真コースを卒業。同年4月、同大学通信制大学院の写真・映像領域へ進学し、現在は修士課程に在学している。

Artículos

Aaron Taylor-Johnson será Quicksilver en The Avengers: Age of Ultron

Julio Vélez

El protagonista de Kick-Ass ha confirmado su participación en Avengers 2 en el papel de Quicksilver. Evan Peters también lo interpretará en Days of Future Past.

The Wrap fue quien confirmó la noticia sobre que Aaron Taylor-Johnson participará en The Avengers: Age of Ultron , la nueva producción de Marvel Studios programada para el 2015, para interpretar a Quicksilver . Como recordarán, hace apenas algunos meses la misma fuente compartió que el protagonista de Kick-Ass encabezaba la lista de candidatos para el papel, pero que sus compromisos, producto de su contrato para la nueva versión de Godzilla , impedían que esto pudiera hacerse oficial. Sin embargo, ¡esto ha cambiado!

Mismo personaje, dos producciones

Esta noticia hace aún más curiosa la observación que les comentábamos antes: Taylor-Johnson será Pietro Maximoff en la segunda entrega de The Avengers de Marvel Studios, mientras que Evan Peters interpretará al mismo personaje en X-Men: Days of Future Past de Fox. ¿Ustedes recuerdan cuando ambos actores estuvieron juntos en Kick-Ass (2010)?. ¿Cuáles son sus opiniones para este giro?

Aaron Taylor Johnson se integra así a Elizabeth Olsen en el papel de Scarlet Witch y James Spader como el maligno Ultron . The Avengers: Age of Ultron se realizará bajo la dirección de Joss Whedon y el regreso de Chris Evans, Robert Downey Jr., Samuel L. Jackson, Scarlett Johansson , Chris Hemsworth y Mark Ruffalo.

Julio Vélez Colaborador en web y revista Cine PREMIERE desde 2006. Me especializo en anime/manga, comics, doblaje, tecnología y videojuegos. Mis sagas favoritas: Doctor Who, Star Trek, Dragon Ball y Star Wars. Batimaníaco, geek ochentero y hardcore gamer.

content.article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "On 21 March 1960, a crowd gathered outside a police station in a Transvaal township, part of a nationwide protest against apartheid pass laws used to control where black South Africans could live, work and travel. A young British photojournalist pushed his way to the front and took a few pictures of police across the fence who were standing atop their armoured personnel carriers. With nothing much happening, he turned back and headed for his car. content.article_text:
On 21 March 1960, a crowd gathered outside a police station in a Transvaal township, part of a nationwide protest against apartheid pass laws used to control where black South Africans could live, work and travel. A young British photojournalist pushed his way to the front and took a few pictures of police across the fence who were standing atop their armoured personnel carriers. With nothing much happening, he turned back and headed for his car. Then – without warning – there was the sound of heavy gunfire.

The photographer, Ian Berry, who has died aged 92, captured images of the carnage, which soon became known around the world as the Sharpeville massacre . Dozens of demonstrators were killed, many shot in the back as they fled, and hundreds were injured in what turned out to be a turning point in the country’s history.

Berry and his colleague, the Drum reporter Humphrey Tyler, had ignored police warnings that they would be arrested, and were the only journalists there when the shooting started. It was the first time Berry had been shot at, or seen others killed, but it would not be the last in a career that took him to the Congo crisis following independence in 1960-65, the Vietnam war, the Aberfan disaster of 1966, in which coal waste engulfed a Glamorgan village, and the six-day war between Israel and its neighbours in June 1967.

He was tenacious, but his edge was his eye for human moments, capturing the people behind the headlines, often photographing scenes that were off-centre, and yet told a story better by focusing on individuals.

In 1968, when Magnum’s Paris bureau asked if he would go to Prague as Soviet tanks encroached, he took a plane to Munich, rented a car and drove to the Czech border, only to find that journalists were being turned away. With typical guile, Berry talked his way through, persuading a Russian officer that he was on his way to an architects’ conference, which he had read about on the flight. He captured memorable images of peaceful resistance during the first days of the invasion, then smuggled them out in the hubcaps and door panels of his rented Volkswagen Beetle for publication in Paris Match.

Born in Preston, Lancashire, Ian was the son of Walter, who owned garages, and Ethel (nee McKimmings), a housewife. He was a boarder at Rossall school, on the coast at Fleetwood, and from an early age had wanderlust. A postwar assisted emigration scheme took him to South Africa in 1952, when he was 17.

In Johannesburg he worked for a family acquaintance, Roger Madden, who had recently returned home from assisting the photographer Ansel Adams in the US. Madden taught Berry to use a large-format camera and to print in the darkroom, but he would find his own path using a diminutive Leica, the camera favoured by prominent visual journalists of the day.

Berry moved on to studio work and small-town editorial assignments, and worked for the Rand Daily Mail, covering the beginnings of the treason trial in 1956 that included Nelson Mandela as a defendant. After hearing that Tom Hopkinson, the former editor of Picture Post in London, was coming to edit Drum, a newly established South African weekly aimed at a black readership, Berry persuaded him to give him a job. A few months later, Hopkinson sent him to Sharpeville.

He was called to give evidence at the trial of the wounded, who had been charged with obstruction. The pictures also brought him to wider international attention, and through Hopkinson he became acquainted with Magnum Photos, the agency with whom he remained until his death.

When Berry moved to Paris in 1962, he met Henri Cartier-Bresson , one of Magnum’s co-founders, and became a full member five years later. By then, he had left Paris for London to become a contract photographer for the Observer, travelling abroad on reportage assignments while shooting members of the British arts scene for the paper’s weekend magazine.

He photographed actors, film people and artists, including John Gielgud , Dusty Springfield , Lindsay Anderson and Henry Moore , and gained a reputation for his observational portrait stories.

Berry’s magazine assignments were accompanied by projects pursued over years, and it is for these that he will be best remembered. In 1972, the Whitechapel Gallery in London commissioned him to photograph its East End neighbourhood, and two years later, an Arts Council bursary (said to be the first ever given to a photographer) led to the publication of The English (1978), a collection that observed class, ceremony and everyday leisure activities.

That seamless transition between commissioned journalism and self-directed work reflected the Magnum model, which allowed photographers to earn a living from magazines while retaining control of their pictures and developing subjects beyond an editor’s brief.

Travel assignments for Life, Paris Match, National Geographic, Geo and others took Berry across the world, and often fed into longer studies. His continuing engagement with apartheid South Africa resulted in Black and Whites: L’Afrique du Sud (1988) and Living Apart (1996), while other projects examined changing daily life in China and the former Soviet Union.

In later years, a commission to photograph Greenland’s retreating glaciers developed into Water, an examination of how water sustains life and how its scarcity, pollution and destructive force expose humanity’s impact on the planet. Drawing on 15 years of work, it was published in 2023, accompanied by an essay by his second wife, Kathie Webber, whom he had married in 1973.

Berry’s first wife was Shirley, a South African, with whom he had a daughter, and he had a son from another relationship; both children predeceased him. He is survived by Kathie.

content.title_original: Dollywood down under: Dolly Parton fans and drag queens turn a tiny Australian town pink

She says the event was inspired by a desire to revitalise the community after a devastating drought from 2017 to 2019. It just gets our town on the map … to not write off a little town. content.article_text:
O n a sporting oval in a rural Australian town 15,000km from Knoxville, Tennessee, dozens of Dolly Partons saunter down the runway as a boisterous crowd cheers and swats away flies with their cowboy hats.

As the sun begins to set, Jim Beams are flowing and music is blaring. One lucky punter is about to be crowned this year’s best-dressed Dolly, complete with sash, trophy and bragging rights.

The Narromine Line Dancers chat before performing for the crowd

For one weekend a year, this is not the sleepy agricultural township of Narromine, 430km north-west of Sydney. This is Dollymine, home to the nation’s largest (and only) Dolly Parton festival.

Perfect pink shades

This is the fifth year the tribute festival has been running and the first to take place since the country music legend died in August. A record 1,600 tickets have been sold – equivalent to just under half of Narromine’s population.

Many in the crowd wear memorial tribute T-shirts, reading: “We will always love you, Dolly”, and “forever and always”.

Jen Ballhausen, a local resident, has volunteered on the festival’s committee since the beginning. She says the event was inspired by a desire to revitalise the community after a devastating drought from 2017 to 2019. Then Covid-19 hit and organisers had to wait until 2022 for it to run.

Juanita Kottek, who won best-dressed in 2025

“It was a fun group of people, mostly women, that had a common goal to provide something for the community, to support our community,” she says.

It was a super fan volunteer who suggested a Dolly homage, and the committee figured it was a no-brainer. “We needed a female icon,” Ballhausen says.

“The first year was overwhelming … the number of people that got dressed up, we were walking around going, ‘Holy moly, this is going to work.’

“We knew we’d set a bar, and this year has well and truly exceeded it. It just gets our town on the map … to not write off a little town. If we can at least highlight that small towns are great little communities, then we’ve won.”

Drag queen Timberlina

A town doused in rhinestones

It’s been a long day. The party starts at 9.30am in Narromine’s main street, which has undergone a metamorphosis to become a micro-Dollywood. Muted shopfronts have transformed into a sea of pink, rhinestones and butterflies. Parton’s beaming face is everywhere: plastered on to windows, on the top of cupcakes and merchandise.

There are line dancers, drag queens and children from the local primary school performing a stirring rendition of Baby I’m Burnin’, complete with pom poms.

Festivalgoers pose at a kissing booth

The temperature quickly climbs to 30C and those in Dolly-drag wipe makeup-laden sweat from their faces.

Narromine is 40km west of Dubbo and hundreds of kilometres inland – hot, flat country, and the shade awnings provide little reprieve. Some opt for tea towels to emulate Dolly’s cleavage in place of silicone to avoid overheating.

Wynonah Dove, a Dolly impersonator, grew up ‘dirt poor’ in Tennessee

Wynonah Dove, performing on Saturday evening as a Dolly impersonator, says Parton’s sudden death has made the event “especially poignant”.

“When Dolly passed, we had our first rehearsals the day after, and it was hard, I had trouble even singing the songs,” she says between tears.

“I just feel she’s here with us, any time there is love, light and inclusiveness being celebrated, she’s here in spirit.”

Dove grew up in Tennessee, from a working-class background similar to Parton’s. She recalled going a year without running water, “dirt poor”, and says that, thanks to Parton and her extensive work, the local economy exploded.

“She just wanted to make the world a better place,” she says. “None of us could afford to go on vacation, so we all went to Dollywood … Everyone felt like she was our best friend and we didn’t even know her.”

As the afternoon arrives, the crowd flocks to the local pub to re-energise with cold beers and live music. Many of the blow-ins are staying in its upstairs accommodation, which looks like a mini-tornado has passed through, leaving glitter, tasselled jackets and bottles of rosé in its wake.

Among them is Nikolaas Kostraby – AKA Dolly Delicious – who has travelled to the festival from Canberra for the past three years after a recommendation from a neighbour from Narromine. In 2023 he was crowned best-dressed Dolly. This year he’s on the committee and is a judge.

Nikolaas Kostraby as Dolly Delicious

“I was robbed the first year, however I came back the second year and cleaned up, and now every year I come back and dress up,” he says. “People are so kind out here, so respectful, there’s no judging.

“I was nervous the first time, like, I’m a man in a wig, in a regional area, but it’s been the complete opposite.”

Come 5pm, celebrations on the main stage kick off and a steady stream of people arrive at the oval armed with camping chairs and wigs. It doesn’t take long for a hoedown to occur. Couples, families and strangers link arms and twirl on the grass to the thrum of a banjo.

Lucas and his family custom-made T-shirts for the occasion, complete with their names and job titles for the “Dolly Department Company”.

Unique watches on while waiting for the best-dressed catwalk to start

His is “director of hair and volume”, while his partner, Scott, is “chief vibes officer”. The pair travelled from Sydney with Lucas’ sister and her two children.

“We decided literally a year ago to all come along together … but it’s even more special now after her passing to be able to come and celebrate,” Lucas says.

“I’m sure there’ll be many drinks and many sing-alongs tonight. It’s the soul behind her songs we love – just warming and inclusive .”

An eclectic cast of Dollys

Soon, darkness will descend, lipstick will smudge and cowboy hats may be lost. But first, a best-dressed winner must be crowned. And who better to lead the proceedings than the drag queen Timberlina, who grew up in regional New South Wales and has emceed the festival for the past five years.

Grace Wadley, 5, in costume for the best-dressed kids’ competition

In true Dolly fashion, she arrives in a vintage car and snatched rainbow dress, waving regally.

Children are judged first, then comes the best-dressed Kenny, a homage to Parton’s longtime collaborator Kenny Rogers. There are three finalists, including a man dressed as Woody from Toy Story.

Then the Dollys flock to the red carpet, as diverse and eclectic as the singer’s own career. One woman rides a blow-up horse. A small child somehow makes her way on to the stage. Fake breasts jut out of tight dresses like bowling balls waiting to be freed.

Dolly Delicious, sporting her victory sash from 2023, slowly walks among them, eventually landing on Colin Marshall – who is part of a tour group of 30 people who have travelled to Narromine from Brisbane. The tour is run by Fun Over 50 Holidays, and he isn’t the only man who has come in drag.

“It wasn’t just the look, it was the warmth, the attitude,” Dolly Delicious tells the crowd. Marshall booms: “Over 50s!”

Petina in the best-dressed competition

His wife, Leanne, crafted his outfit. He is wearing a hot pink tasselled dress, a blond wig, a cowboy hat, heels and large sunglasses, and accepts his sash as though it’s an inevitability.

For a full minute, Marshall sashays along the runway, swinging his arms with abandon. I ask him how it feels to win. “Good, great,” he replies.

“It’s hard work being a woman.”

content.article_text:
Born in London in 1975, Gareth Malone is a choirmaster and broadcaster. He began his career running youth and community choirs for the London Symphony Orchestra and first appeared on TV in 2006’s The Choir. He has since created choirs with Leicester schoolboys, Aylesbury prisoners, as well as the Military Wives, which produced the No 1 single, Wherever You Are. He lives in London with his wife and three children. His new live show, Sing-A-Long-A-Gareth: At the Movies, is on tour across the UK this autumn.

I was 15 and just coming into my own with my confidence , as you can tell by the double denim and the pose. The photo would have been taken at a party at my parents’ house in Bournemouth. When I wasn’t filling up guests’ drinks, I’d be playing some songs – it looks like I’m playing B flat major, so I suspect at this very moment it was Hey Jude.

For a few years prior to this, school had been difficult. We moved from a nice leafy part of Wimbledon to Bournemouth when I was 10, and until that point I had friends who were both girls and boys. Going to the all-boys grammar school in a new area was an aggressive gear shift and I struggled to make friends. There was no physical bullying, but it was a sustained period of ostracisation that went on for the first three years of secondary school and dribbled on into year 10. It wasn’t ever discussed. There was no “you’re being bullied. If you have a problem with any other boys, come and talk to us,” from the school. My parents probably knew because I wasn’t bringing any friends over. Instead I learned how to take care of my own problems, which was through music and theatre. My saving grace.

I feel so lucky that I had the music studio at school – a place to be expressive in a sea of business studies and maths. Playing the synthesisers started my lifelong passion for production and all-round music nerdery. We also had a piano at home and I used to sit at it and make sounds for what felt like hours.

Mum worked for Abbey Life Assurance and for the civil service. Dad worked for a bank. Neither of them were particularly career-minded – they enjoyed their life, their family and their house, hence friends often coming over. My grandparents were very important, too. Growing up as an only child made me very comfortable in my own company, but it did mean I wasn’t armed with some of the physical vocabulary that other boys had. I used to overreact when other kids were playing up. “Why are you speaking to me like that? No one speaks to me like that. Why are you behaving in this stupid way? No, I don’t want to play rough, or go and play football, because that’s what five-year-olds do.” I was far happier to sit and have a conversation. All of which is possibly why I gravitated towards the girls at school – they were a bit more sensible.

In my teens I got very into Led Zeppelin and Pink Floyd. I was singing a lot in bands – but I was also obsessed with Kenneth Branagh in Henry V, so I decided to study drama at University of East Anglia. I have fond memories of pretending to be a pig, and doing lots of clowning and mask work. Once that was over, I went on to study music at the Royal Academy of Music in London. It was a difficult transition for me – I went from that arrogant tweeny, liminal stage, as pictured, to realising that I was, actually, just fairly average compared with my peers.

After graduating, I went back to Bournemouth. I was selling ice-cream to make some money while sending out CVs. A friend got in touch and said they had seen an advert for some youth work in Poole, and thought I’d be good at it. They wanted someone young and musical to work with local children who lived on an estate with a high level of deprivation. They had a little music room with a couple of ropey instruments that I would try to teach them how to play. That’s where my passion for giving everyone opportunities – a safe space and music – came from.

I also realised that to get people to trust me, I had to be myself. I was from a totally different side of the tracks and I was wide-eyed, naive. The kids could smell the middle-classness on me, so any pretending to be cool and aloof wouldn’t work. I had to be rigorously myself.

My job is to give others confidence, but I’ve definitely gone on a journey with my own self-esteem, especially when it comes to being in front of the camera. I was working with the London Symphony Orchestra and running a choir when I first got the opportunity to be on TV. The producers of The Choir had seen that we had a high Google rating so they got in touch. The show was about starting a choir at Northolt high school in Middlesex, and throughout, I tried to apply the same method of authenticity on camera that I’d learned with the youth group. I had been given this amazing job that I’d never done before, but I was learning to do it on national television. I was being filmed constantly. The director said: “I want you when you’re angry, I want you when you’re upset, I want you when you’re happy. I won’t make you look like an idiot.” He stuck to his word, but I remember being nervous, trying to look in control, and dithering quite a lot.

after newsletter promotion

When you’re recognised it can be a great gift, but a burden when you’re, say, taking out your bins. When Military Wives got to No 1 , I was suddenly thrown into a new level of celebrity: I was meeting Simon Cowell, having tea with Gary Barlow and dinner with Andrew Lloyd Webber. My memories of that time was that it was intense – when you have a Christmas No 1, it’s like you’ve joined a weird club with people like Noddy from Slade and Shakin’ Stevens. None of the bells and whistles has ever distracted me from the reason I got into this industry in the first place 20 years ago, however. Focusing on my passion for music and the importance of art in people’s lives. There’s something so healing about music, and singing in a choir. When people come together, they are buoyed up by it. I lost a friend at the beginning of this year and before he died he said something deeply touching to me: “We never did go for that pint.” It was brutal. Such a simple thing that felt impossible as we were both absorbed in our careers. The telly, the degrees – all of those achievements are wonderful. It’s the foundation upon which a lot of my happiness is at rest. But it’s not the main thing. People and community are.

When I was 15 I had a clear vision of what I wanted with my adult life. It involved a music studio with lots of instruments in it. The teenage me would be overjoyed to know that at the end of my garden is a little den with a piano, drums, shakers, maracas, guitars, bongos, synthesisers, a computer and speakers – that there’s never a day when I’m not doing music, half of it tinkering alone, the rest making music with other people. He’d probably be confused about the amount of hot yoga I currently do. But glad to know I still like a denim shirt.

content.title_original: The Wrong Black Woman on the Fourth Plinth
content.article_blocks_json: [{"type": "heading", "text": "In this critical reflection for ART AFRICA, Ayọ̀ Akínwándé examines Tschabalala Self’s Lady in Blue (2026), installed on Trafalgar Square’s Fourth Plinth, and questions the histories, stereotypes, and expectations carried by the monumental Black female body. Beginning with a conversation between Nicole Eisenman and curator Mark Godfrey, Akínwándé considers how authorship, artistic intention, and public space shape representation, and whether celebrating Black visibility has made its images harder to question. At its centre is a provocative proposition: can one Black woman ever be expected to represent the universal “everywoman”?"}, {"type": "heading", "text": "Ayọ̀ Akínwándé"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "On 29 September 2026, I sat in the Royal Institution in London listening to Nicole Eisenman in conversation with curator Mark Godfrey. The conversation centred, in part, on Eisenman’s monumental sculpture Stack (2022), recently installed in the courtyard of the Royal Academy of Arts."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Standing more than eight metres high, Stack rises through a precarious accumulation of figures and objects. An artist carries a wine barrel. Above it sits a giant potato, then Eisenman’s cat, Edie. At the summit, the late British sculptor Phyllida Barlow balances a vase of flowers on her head. Nicole Eisenman Stack , 2022 Sculpture, Royal Academy of Arts, London ©Nicole Eisenman. Courtesy of the artist and Hauser & Wirth. Photo: Ayọ̀ Akínwándé."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artafricamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/DSC00444-687x1030.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Nicole Eisenman Stack , 2022 Sculpture, Royal Academy of Arts, London ©Nicole Eisenman. Courtesy of the artist and Hauser & Wirth. Photo: Ayọ̀ Akínwándé.", "credit": "ART AFRICA"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "During the conversation, Eisenman traced Stack to an earlier painting, Hindsight (2020), which appeared on the screen behind her. The architecture of accumulation was already there, but the figure occupying its upper reaches was different: a large, pale, naked figure, turned away from the viewer. During the question-and-answer session, a member of the audience asked whether the figure was intended to be Donald Trump. As I recall the exchange, Eisenman responded that it was not Trump, but simply a fat white man. I am paraphrasing the exchange from memory rather than quoting either speaker verbatim. Nicole Eisenman, Hindsight , 2020, Oil on canvas, 208.6 x 165.7 cm / 82 1/8 x 65 1/4 inches © Nicole Eisenman. Courtesy of the artist and Hauser & Wirth. Photo: Thomas Barratt."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artafricamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/EISEN107402-TB201120.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Nicole Eisenman, Hindsight , 2020, Oil on canvas, 208.6 x 165.7 cm / 82 1/8 x 65 1/4 inches © Nicole Eisenman. Courtesy of the artist and Hauser & Wirth. Photo: Thomas Barratt.", "credit": "ART AFRICA"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "What interested me was not whether the man was Trump. It was why he disappeared."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "As I understood Eisenman’s explanation that evening, painting offered a different kind of privacy. A painting could be made within the privacy of the studio and might eventually enter another private space, including someone’s home. Sculpture entering the public realm demanded another kind of consideration. My recollection is that Eisenman described becoming more intentional about the figure that would occupy that public space."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The anonymous man did not make that journey. Phyllida Barlow did. Barlow, who died in 2023, had been Eisenman’s friend, mentor and an important influence on her understanding of sculpture. Eisenman also spoke about allowing time after Barlow’s death before publicly presenting the work, so that the gesture could properly honour her. content.article_text:
In this critical reflection for ART AFRICA, Ayọ̀ Akínwándé examines Tschabalala Self’s Lady in Blue (2026), installed on Trafalgar Square’s Fourth Plinth, and questions the histories, stereotypes, and expectations carried by the monumental Black female body. Beginning with a conversation between Nicole Eisenman and curator Mark Godfrey, Akínwándé considers how authorship, artistic intention, and public space shape representation, and whether celebrating Black visibility has made its images harder to question. At its centre is a provocative proposition: can one Black woman ever be expected to represent the universal “everywoman”?

Ayọ̀ Akínwándé

On 29 September 2026, I sat in the Royal Institution in London listening to Nicole Eisenman in conversation with curator Mark Godfrey. The conversation centred, in part, on Eisenman’s monumental sculpture Stack (2022), recently installed in the courtyard of the Royal Academy of Arts.

Standing more than eight metres high, Stack rises through a precarious accumulation of figures and objects. An artist carries a wine barrel. Above it sits a giant potato, then Eisenman’s cat, Edie. At the summit, the late British sculptor Phyllida Barlow balances a vase of flowers on her head. Nicole Eisenman Stack , 2022 Sculpture, Royal Academy of Arts, London ©Nicole Eisenman. Courtesy of the artist and Hauser & Wirth. Photo: Ayọ̀ Akínwándé.

During the conversation, Eisenman traced Stack to an earlier painting, Hindsight (2020), which appeared on the screen behind her. The architecture of accumulation was already there, but the figure occupying its upper reaches was different: a large, pale, naked figure, turned away from the viewer. During the question-and-answer session, a member of the audience asked whether the figure was intended to be Donald Trump. As I recall the exchange, Eisenman responded that it was not Trump, but simply a fat white man. I am paraphrasing the exchange from memory rather than quoting either speaker verbatim. Nicole Eisenman, Hindsight , 2020, Oil on canvas, 208.6 x 165.7 cm / 82 1/8 x 65 1/4 inches © Nicole Eisenman. Courtesy of the artist and Hauser & Wirth. Photo: Thomas Barratt.

What interested me was not whether the man was Trump. It was why he disappeared.

As I understood Eisenman’s explanation that evening, painting offered a different kind of privacy. A painting could be made within the privacy of the studio and might eventually enter another private space, including someone’s home. Sculpture entering the public realm demanded another kind of consideration. My recollection is that Eisenman described becoming more intentional about the figure that would occupy that public space.

The anonymous man did not make that journey. Phyllida Barlow did. Barlow, who died in 2023, had been Eisenman’s friend, mentor and an important influence on her understanding of sculpture. Eisenman also spoke about allowing time after Barlow’s death before publicly presenting the work, so that the gesture could properly honour her. Members of Barlow’s family were in the room that evening. Nicole Eisenman, Hindsight , 2020, Oil on canvas, 208.6 x 165.7 cm / 82 1/8 x 65 1/4 inches © Nicole Eisenman. Courtesy of the artist and Hauser & Wirth. Photo: Thomas Barratt.

What stayed with me was the distinction Eisenman drew between making an image privately and placing a body publicly. And that who we put into public space matters. I left the Royal Institution thinking again about another monumental woman standing less than two miles away.

Tschabalala Self’s Lady in Blue (2026) has occupied the Fourth Plinth in Trafalgar Square since 10 September. More than five metres high, she is cast in bronze, dressed in intense blue, adorned with jewellery and platform shoes, and caught mid-stride as though she has somewhere to be. Tschabalala Self, Lady in Blue , 2026. Painted bronze sculpture. Fourth Plinth, Trafalgar Square, London. Commissioned through the Mayor of London’s Fourth Plinth programme. Photo: Ayọ̀ Akínwándé.

I had been thinking about her before Eisenman’s conversation. More accurately, I had been disturbed by her. Listening to Eisenman helped me understand why.

Self is a Black American woman who has achieved one of the most visible public art commissions in the world. Her sculpture also enters a public sphere in which images of Black people continue to attract racist hostility. Self knows this intimately. Her earlier public sculpture Seated (2022) was vandalised at the De La Warr Pavilion.

Since Lady in Blue appeared in Trafalgar Square, I have watched some reactions online descend quickly into racist caricature. The Black female body remains extraordinarily available for public ridicule. Perhaps that is precisely why criticism becomes difficult. But representation cannot mean suspending criticism.

Self has been explicit about the figure she intended to place in Trafalgar Square. At the unveiling, she described Lady in Blue as “an everyday person much like the many who occupy the square daily,” adding that the figure is “striding forward into our collective future with ambition, purpose and optimism.” The Fourth Plinth programme itself describes the commission as an attempt to bring a contemporary “everywoman” to the square. I take that proposition seriously. Self is asking this anonymous Black woman to operate not simply as a representation of Black womanhood, but as an everyday figure with a claim to universality.

It is a compelling question. But another sits beside it. What kind of Black woman have we chosen to make universal? Tschabalala Self, Lady in Blue , 2026. Painted bronze sculpture. Fourth Plinth, Trafalgar Square, London. Commissioned through the Mayor of London’s Fourth Plinth programme. Photo: Ayọ̀ Akínwándé.

Self’s practice has long used bodily distortion and exaggeration. Breasts expand. Hips widen. Buttocks become enormous. Bodies are constructed and reconstructed through paint, fabric, print and collage. Self knows the visual history into which these figures enter. She has spoken about the iconographic significance of the Black female body, the fantasies projected onto it, and reclaiming physical characteristics historically turned into objects of fetish and ridicule.

Kara Walker and Thomas J Price offer two useful counterpoints. Walker’s monumental A Subtlety (2014), installed inside Brooklyn’s former Domino Sugar Refinery, deliberately mobilised the mammy and the hypersexualised Black female body. The stereotype was not incidental to the work; it was part of the history Walker was forcing into view. Price takes another route. His Grounded in the Stars (2023), a twelve-foot bronze installed in Times Square in 2025, monumentalised an anonymous, large-bodied Black woman in everyday clothes. The work’s ordinariness is precisely the point: her body does not need to become heroic, exceptional or conventionally idealised to deserve monumental scale. These examples clarify what troubles me about Self. The problem is not that Lady in Blue is large, Black or female. It is whether a visual language historically entangled with the stereotyping of Black female bodies can simultaneously sustain Self’s claim to the “everywoman.”

The exaggeration is not accidental, nor is its history. The Black female body has spent centuries being made spectacular within the Western imagination. From the exhibition and exploitation of Sarah Baartman in nineteenth-century Europe to recurring fixations on Black women’s breasts, buttocks and sexuality in contemporary popular culture, bodily exaggeration has rarely been innocent. Hip hop, advertising, pornography and social media did not invent this vocabulary. They inherited and transformed it.

Self’s practice approaches that history through reclamation and self-determination. Speaking about her sustained engagement with the Black female body, she has said, “It’s the body I feel I can have the most honest conversation about because it’s my own.” Her position matters here: the body is not simply an image inherited from someone else’s gaze, but a subject through which she asserts her own intentions and aspirations.

I understand that position. But what troubles me is what happens when that strategy leaves the studio and gallery, becomes more than five metres tall and is elevated above one of Britain’s most symbolically charged public squares as an everywoman.

Trafalgar Square is not a neutral exhibition surface. It is an architectural composition of power and memory. King George IV surveys the square from his column while statues of Sir Charles James Napier and Sir Henry Havelock occupy its other plinth. The Fourth Plinth was left unresolved by that monumental scheme and has subsequently become a place where contemporary art interrupts it. Every work installed there enters into conversation with the architecture, the imperial histories around it and the thousands of bodies moving through the square below.

Scale changes an image, elevation changes it, and so does site. This is where Eisenman’s distinction keeps returning to me.

Public sculpture does not wait for us to enter it. We do not buy a ticket or choose the exhibition. It occupies our routes through the city and becomes part of the visual environment of people who may know nothing about the artist or her intentions. If the audience changes, surely the conditions of representation change with it.

I keep returning to an uncomfortable thought experiment. What if precisely this body had been designed by a white British male sculptor? What if he had exaggerated the breasts, hips and buttocks of a Black woman, put her in platform shoes and a blue dress, enlarged her to monumental scale and presented her as an everyday woman? Would we be as generous in our reading?

Authorship matters. History makes it impossible to pretend that a Black woman representing a Black female body and a white man doing so are equivalent acts. But authorship cannot become the end of looking. Otherwise, identity begins to operate as an exemption from criticism.

I think of another woman in blue when I look at Self’s sculpture. In Sophie/Elsie (2009), South African artist Mary Sibande casts her alter ego Sophie from her own body and envelops her in a spectacular blue Victorian dress. The blue emerges from the uniform associated with Black domestic workers in South Africa, a history intimately connected to Sibande’s family. Her mother, grandmother and great-grandmother worked as domestic workers. Mary Sibande, Sophie-Elsie , 2009. Life-size fibreglass figure, cotton textile, nylon, plastic button detailing and foam padding. 183 x 200 x 175 cm. Image courtesy of the artist.

Sibande allows the uniform of service to mutate. Sophie becomes aristocratic, excessive, impossible. She dreams herself beyond the position apartheid prepared for her. Mary Sibande’s blue remembers. Mary Sibande, Sophie-Elsie , 2009. Life-size fibreglass figure, cotton textile, nylon, plastic button detailing and foam padding. 183 x 200 x 175 cm. Image courtesy of the artist.

Self’s blue remembers something different. Lapis lazuli, the stone from which natural ultramarine was historically extracted, travelled from mines in Afghanistan into European painting, where its rarity and cost made blue a material of value as much as colour. It became particularly associated with the robes of the Virgin Mary. In Lady in Blue , that chromatic history of preciousness and elevation is transferred to a woman Self insists is not an idol or historic figure, but an everyday person. But standing in London, I cannot help asking what else the blue might have remembered.

Britain possesses its own vast archive of Black womanhood. Caribbean women arrived in postwar Britain and became nurses, midwives, cleaners and carers in the National Health Service. There are the women of the Windrush generation and their descendants. There are Black women in universities, corporations, hospitals, media, law, schools, government and the arts. There are women of African and Caribbean heritage whose histories cannot be compressed into a single Black British experience.

I initially wondered whether the woman on the plinth should have been one of those NHS women. There is something powerful about monumentalising the Black woman whose everyday labour has literally kept British people alive.

But that creates another problem. Why must the Black woman serve Britain before Britain permits her to become monumental? Why must she nurse, clean, migrate, struggle, mother or overcome something before she earns the pedestal?

Self is right to resist that demand. A Black woman should be able simply to exist in a blue dress, walking somewhere, without justifying her presence through sacrifice. The problem is not that Self failed to sculpt a nurse; it is the enormous representational burden contained in the word “everywoman.”

Britain already possesses a small but revealing history of Black female figuration in public sculpture. Bronze Woman (2008), conceived through Cécile Nobrega’s poem and campaign, carries histories of Caribbean migration and motherhood. Martin Jennings’s Mary Seacole (2016) stands outside St Thomas’ Hospital. Thomas J Price’s Reaching Out (2020) gives us an anonymous contemporary Black woman absorbed in her phone. Basil Watson’s National Windrush Monument (2022) places a woman within an intergenerational migrant family. Veronica Ryan avoids representing the Black body altogether in Custard Apple (Annonaceae) , Breadfruit (Moraceae) and Soursop (Annonaceae) (2021), allowing objects to carry histories of Caribbean migration and memory.

The Fourth Plinth itself offers another precedent. In 2003, Nigerian-born British sculptor Sokari Douglas Camp was shortlisted with No-o War-r No-o-War-r (2003), a group of stainless-steel protesters carrying antiwar placards in response to demonstrations that had occupied Trafalgar Square. She allowed the site’s recent history to enter the proposed sculpture.

I find myself wondering what would have happened if the plinth had refused singularity altogether. Imagine moving around it and encountering not the Black woman but Black women. Different ages, bodies and relationships to London. One might work in the city, another in the NHS, academia or the arts. Perhaps none of those professions needs to be announced. The point is not to produce a checklist of respectable Black achievement; it is to refuse the expectation that one body can carry everybody else.

I am not proposing this as the sculpture Self should have made. Artists do not owe critics the artworks we would prefer them to produce. I imagine these multiple women only to expose the contradiction within the idea of a singular Black “everywoman”: the moment one body is asked to stand for everyone, all the differences that make such universality impossible begin to appear.

There is a cruel irony here. Racist spectators look at Lady in Blue and find an opportunity to ridicule a Black body. Celebratory spectators see representation, confidence and progress. Both responses can prevent us from asking a harder question about the image itself. Perhaps representation matures when we are capable of doing something other than celebrating its arrival.

There is an African proverb frequently associated with Chinua Achebe’s thinking about history: “Until the lions have their own historians, the history of the hunt will always glorify the hunter.” Its force lies in authorship. The hunter does not only possess the weapon; he possesses the story. He decides how the hunt is remembered, who becomes heroic, and who remains merely the hunted. Who has been permitted to describe whom? Who controls the archive? Who produces the image?

For centuries, Black people have demanded the right to become authors of our own images. Contemporary culture is full of the language of finally being able to “tell our own stories,” and “speak our truth.” These are important gains. But authorship does not happen outside systems of power. The question is not only who gets to tell the story, but which stories institutions choose to commission, elevate and validate. Visibility, after all, is not the same as agency: being seen does not necessarily mean determining the conditions under which one becomes visible.

What happens, then, when the lion finally becomes the historian, but the conditions under which the story becomes visible are still shaped by the institutions that once privileged the hunter? Surely the answer cannot be that the lion’s account is beyond criticism.

Tschabalala Self has every right to put this woman into Trafalgar Square. She has every right to exaggerate her, reclaim her, dress her in blue and insist that she stands not simply for Black womanhood but for humanity. And those of us looking at her have an equal right to ask what histories arrived on the plinth with her.

Perhaps the wrong Black woman has been put on the Fourth Plinth.

Not because somewhere in Britain there is a more respectable Black woman waiting for the pedestal. Not because the woman standing there is insufficiently British, modest, heroic or accomplished.

Perhaps she is wrong because the expectation that one Black woman can become the Black everywoman was wrong in the first place. And perhaps the most meaningful consequence of finally getting the opportunity to tell the story of the hunt is not that we all agree on the story. It is that, at last, we can argue about it.

Ayọ̀ Akínwándé is a British-Nigerian artist working across painting, lens-based media, installation, sound, and performance. His work examines power, socio-political realities, and the interplay of tradition and modernity. He is also a curator, researcher, and writer, with international exhibitions and curatorial projects, including co-curating the inaugural Lagos Biennial (2017).

content.article_text:
It’s been fourteen years since screenwriter and occasional director Tony Gilroy made an original film, and he’s taking a fresh approach. The filmmaker best known for penning the Bourne films and bringing us Michael Clayton has spent most of his career in spy-coded crime and legal thrillers. (Even his take on Star Wars was procedurally stealthy.) Behemoth! sounds like it could be either, but in a shift of focus, Gilroy sets his sights on the mundane, aboveboard goings-on of a master cellist.

Described as a “love letter to the music of the movies and the people who make it,” Behemoth! presents more of a winding, tangenting letter than a cohesive narrative, similar to the way reading a series of diary entries might amount to a character study. We follow Alex Serian (Pedro Pascal), a principal cellist in the Chicago Symphony who’s returned to L.A. to look after his dying mother, get back into session work on orchestral film scores, and break free from an ex that gives overbearing a new name.

Deranged former lover and institutional string-puller Carol Spedding (Olivia Wilde) bears the spirit of a behemoth herself, lending the movie a sharp comedic edge every time she apepars onscreen. In her third extraordinary performance of 2026, Wilde is outrageous as Carol, a top-shelf patron of the Chicago Symphony and a jump scare of eccentricities that can be found popping out of lurking SUVs and marching through restricted areas to hunt Alex down. By the time we meet her, she’s a bona fide stalker, but no one can stop her, and she has no regard for boundaries. When she finally catches up to him (i.e., waits outside his house in L.A.), Alex threatens to call the cops. “My driver is an off-duty sheriff,” she retorts with disgust, offended by the suggestion she’s bound by the law.

The pace is electric for how commonplace the developments in Alex’s life are (new flings, work troubles, people dying), largely because Gilroy plays the metatextual scoring instrument as assuredly as the virtuoso at the heart of his story plays the cello. He transforms what starts as diegetic music in a scoring session for a fictional film into the non-diegetic score of a memory the music triggered for Alex (and vice versa, from the non-diegetic suddenly back into the recording studio). It’s the never-ending magic trick that simply never gets old.

Behemoth! is laced with scoring sessions aplenty, which is where most of the characters in Alex’s life come from. As the grouchy pros tune up to set the mood for a new crime thriller or aching romance that rolls on screens around them, they talk about their personal lives, industry drama, etc., and eventually start recording. For the sake of the film we’re watching, Gilroy makes most of the scoring sessions thrilling or thick with drama, Alex and co. chugging cellos and strings while winds follow suit in an ethereal register, timpanis booming and horns pumping all around them. They seamlessly transition from conversation to complicated composition at the drop of a hat like it’s nothing, merely second nature.

As Alex’s body goes on autopilot, his mind tends to wander, leading us back into periods of his life set in Boston, Dallas, and Chicago. He wrestles with the memories of what happened in each city as he dodges those who want his attention in L.A. in the present. You’d think Alex Serian was Barack Obama or Scarlett Johansson with how desperately everyone is trying to get his time, but no matter how much they claim to love him or have his best interest at heart, Alex isn’t having it. He’ll escape through the underground staff tunnel if he needs to. The constant chase of it all, while mostly comedic, has a classic Gilroy thriller tone embedded in it, meant for spies and three-letter agencies.

Naturally, Behemoth! ’s score is a mosaic of pieces provided by a supergroup of cinema’s best composers: Michael Giacchino, James Newton Howard, Alan Silvestri, Henry Jackman, Michael Abels, Emily Bear, Lukas Frank, Nami Melumad, and Brandon Roberts. Their work is spread across four fake movies being scored throughout the film, cello practice etudes, fictional TV theme songs, Alex’s father’s compositions, and more. Alongside the metatextual moves, it’s Gilroy’s best idea across the whole film, and it sings with the bravado of a concert of maestros.

It’s fitting that the fictional Behemoth! (one of the four fake movies) is covertly titled Open World in post-production. Gilroy’s diaristic dramedy has an exploratory open-world feel, as if we’re in a third-person video game à la Grand Theft Auto , watching player one check off objective after objective—“Escape Carol Spedding,” “Train Underling,” “Watch Video of Dad,” “Hit All Marks in Studio Session,” “Visit Nadia”—to complete the main quest.

Not all of these objectives are compelling to watch, which gives Behemoth! a dullness at times. On top of that, one can’t help wondering what organic charisma a different leading man might’ve brought to the table. But the rest of the stellar supporting cast (Alia Shawkat, Hank Azaria, Will Arnett, Eva Victor, Thomas Kretschmann) holds the film’s weight. And Gilroy’s vision to bring the scoring process to life through some central to its operation still ends up being a relatively riveting watch.

Behemoth! premiered at the 64th New York Film Festival and opens on December 4.

content.article_text:
Animals and their people: country shows across the UK – in pictures

Photographer Irina Werning, who grew up in rural Argentina surrounded by animals, has spent the summer photographing animals and their people at county and agricultural shows across the UK, from Essex and Kent to Surrey, Gloucestershire and Buckinghamshire, a project she began in Argentina.

‘As animals become less visible in the countryside, I’ve turned to agricultural shows – places where people still gather to see and celebrate them. For the past four years, I’ve photographed these fairs in Argentina and the UK, exploring our changing relationship with animals. I see them as a kind of Darwinian theatre, looking for moments when humans and animals unexpectedly mirror each other’

Photographs by Irina Werning

Sun 11 Oct 2026 07.00 BST

写真家・松尾修の新作写真集『Other Shore』が刊行された。松尾が生まれ育った長崎県佐世保市を舞台に、2023年から2026年にかけて撮影した身近な人々と風景78点をモノクロームで収録する。

米海軍が駐留する基地の街であり、日本の高度経済成長を支えた造船の街でもある佐世保。松尾は商業写真家として東京で活動する一方、長年にわたって故郷へ通い、そこに暮らす人々や風景を撮影してきた。代表的な連作「サセボプロジェクト」をはじめ、その制作では一貫して「写真」と「写真を残そうとする人間の心」を見つめている。

タイトルの「Other Shore＝向こう岸」が示唆するように、本作で松尾は東京と佐世保、過去と現在、虚と実、そして写真の「向こう側」と「こちら側」とを往還する。カメラの前に確かに存在したはずの身近な人物や風景は、写真として定着された瞬間、「いたかもしれない人々」へと姿を変えていく。そこから浮かび上がるのは、記録でありながら現実そのものではないという、写真というメディアが本来的に抱える不可思議さだ。

巻末には、松尾自身によるエッセイ「滅びの予感」を日本語と英語で収録。佐世保という街の歴史と、写真というメディアの本質をめぐる作家の思索が、写真群と呼応する。また、布張りの上製本による表紙には、「向こう側の世界」を象徴するミラープレートを貼り込み、写真集そのものの造本にも作品のコンセプトを反映させた。装丁はThere Thereの渡辺和音が担当している。

松尾は1970年、長崎県佐世保市生まれ、東京在住。これまでに『他人のアルバム』『写真論』のほか、「サセボプロジェクト」として『坂道とクレーン』『誰かのアイドル』『HEAVY METAL』『17』などを刊行している。

松尾修『Other Shore』 価格：6600円（税込） 発行：CLOCK Inc.

content.article_text:
Cine

La isla olvidada – Crítica de la película

Gerardo Frías

Una animación con un mensaje importante sobre la amistad, que no cae en el cinismo o la fórmula fácil y genérica.

Entré a la sala sin ninguna expectativa. De lo poco que sabía de la película La isla olvidada , esperaba una aventura animada más, bonita a la vista y olvidable al día siguiente. Me llevé una sorpresa: pocas veces una película infantil reciente se anima a decir algo tan sincero sobre la amistad sin caer en el cinismo o la fórmula fácil y genérica.

Ambientada en Filipinas en los años noventa, la historia sigue a Jo y Raissa, mejores amigas desde niñas que, justo cuando Raissa se prepara para irse a estudiar a Estados Unidos, terminan varadas en Nakali, un mundo fantástico poblado por criaturas de la mitología filipina que habían querido conocer desde pequeñas. El truco cruel de Nakali es que el poder volver a casa podría costarles, literalmente, olvidarse la una a la otra. Es una manera muy inteligente de ponerle imágenes al miedo, tan real, de perder a tu mejor amiga cuando la vida las empieza a separar.

DreamWorks Animation vuelve a demostrar que sabe construir personajes profundamente específicos: Jo y Raissa no se sienten genéricas, se sienten genuinas de verdad. Con un entorno, un humor y una manera de quererse que se nota trabajada con cariño, se sienten reales y eso hace que podamos identificarnos con alguna de las dos. Ese cuidado se extiende al terreno visual, que retoma el estilo pictórico que Joel Crawford ya había explorado en El gato con botas: el último deseo , pero va más allá. Durante los flashbacks , la animación cambia a un estilo 2D inspirado en el anime (esto recordándome bastante a Kill Bill ). Estas secuencias además fueron animadas por Snipple Animation, un estudio con sede en Manila. Que la película le dé crédito visible a las manos filipinas detrás de esas escenas, en lugar de tratarlas como mano de obra anónima, dice mucho de las intenciones reales detrás del proyecto.

Ahora, mi única reserva, y es una que cada vez tengo más seguido con este tipo de cine familiar: se nota que está hecha para una generación acostumbrada al ritmo de las redes y el video corto. Todo el tiempo sucede algo, todo el tiempo hay una explosión de color, un personaje en movimiento constante, una música estruendosa de fondo. Es un festival de dopamina que, para cuando termina la hora con treinta y ocho minutos, te deja un poco agotado, casi con los efectos secundarios de tanta sobreestimulación.

Por eso se agradece tanto que la película sepa bajarle el ritmo justo cuando más importa. El cierre es genuinamente emotivo, y más todavía los créditos: ver al equipo detrás de la cinta compartir, uno por uno, lo que la amistad significa para ellos es un gesto pequeño pero precioso, la prueba de que esta es una película hecha con el corazón por delante y con toda la intención de dejarle algo al espectador.

No es una cinta que le pondría a niños muy pequeños, pero es hermosísima para niños más grandes y adolescentes, y un recordatorio muy necesario de que el cine infantil todavía puede decir algo bonito sin tener miedo de que se le note el corazón.

Gerardo Frías

content.article_text:
El terror vuelve a poner sus ojos en una de las franquicias más emblemáticas de la historia del cine. Más de cinco décadas después del estreno de la película original de William Friedkin, El Exorcista prepara una nueva entrega , esta vez de la mano de Mike Flanagan, uno de los directores más reconocidos del género contemporáneo.

La nueva producción, conocida como El Exorcista: Mártires , busca recuperar el espíritu inquietante de la película de 1973 y ofrecer una historia diferente dentro de este universo.

Mike Flanagan, el director elegido para revivir El Exorcista

Después de películas como Doctor Sueño , Oculus y El juego de Gerald , y series como La maldición de Hill House y Misa de medianoche , Mike Flanagan asumió el desafío de trabajar con una de las propiedades más reconocidas del cine de terror.

El realizador se caracteriza por combinar elementos sobrenaturales con historias atravesadas por el trauma, la culpa, la pérdida y los vínculos familiares.

Su incorporación al proyecto despertó expectativas entre los fanáticos, especialmente después de la recepción dividida que tuvo El Exorcista: Creyentes en 2023. A diferencia de aquella producción, la nueva película no está planteada como una continuación directa, sino como una historia independiente ambientada en el universo de El Exorcista .

Scarlett Johansson protagonizará la nueva película de “El Exorcista”

Las películas de terror que ayudan a quemar calorías, según la ciencia

Scarlett Johansson protagoniza la nueva película

Uno de los grandes atractivos del proyecto es la participación de Scarlett Johansson , quien encabezará el elenco junto a Chiwetel Ejiofor .

Para Johansson, la película representa una nueva incursión en el cine de terror sobrenatural, después de una carrera que incluye producciones tan diferentes como Lost in Translation , Historia de un matrimonio , Under the Skin y el universo cinematográfico de Marvel.

Por su parte, Ejiofor ya trabajó con Flanagan en La vida de Chuck , por lo que esta película marcará un nuevo encuentro entre ambos.

Aunque los detalles de la trama permanecen bajo reserva, se espera que la historia explore nuevamente los temas de la posesión demoníaca, la fe y el enfrentamiento con fuerzas sobrenaturales.

El desafío de recuperar una saga histórica

Estrenada en 1973, El Exorcista se convirtió en un fenómeno cultural que transformó para siempre el cine de terror. Dirigida por William Friedkin y basada en la novela de William Peter Blatty, la película narraba la posesión de una niña y los intentos desesperados de dos sacerdotes por salvarla.

Su impacto fue extraordinario: consiguió diez nominaciones al Oscar, ganó dos estatuillas y se convirtió en una de las películas más influyentes del género. Sin embargo, sus continuaciones no siempre consiguieron repetir ese éxito.

La entrega más reciente, El Exorcista: Creyentes , dirigida por David Gordon Green, intentó recuperar la franquicia con el regreso de Ellen Burstyn, pero recibió críticas mayormente negativas.

Ahora, con Flanagan detrás de cámara, la saga tendrá una nueva oportunidad de reinventarse.

Mirá el trailer acá

¿Cuándo se estrena la nueva película de El Exorcista?

La nueva película forma parte de los proyectos de Universal Pictures y Blumhouse para recuperar una de las franquicias más reconocidas del terror.

El regreso de El Exorcista promete convertirse en uno de los estrenos más esperados por los fanáticos del género, especialmente por la combinación de un director especializado en terror psicológico y un elenco encabezado por figuras de Hollywood.

Con Mike Flanagan al frente, la pregunta es inevitable: ¿podrá esta nueva versión recuperar el impacto que tuvo la película original hace más de 50 años?

content.article_text:
A franquia aposta em um novo casal, mas o humor previsível e os conflitos pouco explorados limitam a tentativa de renovação.

Transferir a troca de corpos de “Se Eu Fosse Você” para uma nova geração oferece à franquia a possibilidade de explorar outros desacordos conjugais. A premissa continua fértil para uma comédia sobre intimidade. Contudo, é na dificuldade de desenvolver esse novo casal que “ Se Eu Fosse Você 3 ” encontra sua maior limitação.

Bia (Cléo Pires), filha de Cláudio (Tony Ramos) e Helena (Glória Pires), trabalha como chefe de cozinha e enfrenta uma crise no relacionamento com Aquiles (Rafael Infante), guia de esportes radicais. A possibilidade de ter filhos se mostra um dos maiores desacordos, pois ele deseja ser pai, enquanto ela se considera satisfeita com a maternidade de Maria Clara (Valentina Daniel), que teve aos dezessete anos. Quando os dois trocam misteriosamente de corpos, precisam assumir também as responsabilidades profissionais um do outro. Uma avaliação gastronômica e uma competição esportiva tornam especialmente inconveniente a descoberta de que conhecer a rotina do parceiro não significa saber executá-la.

A divergência sobre a maternidade oferece ao filme uma oportunidade de conflito, uma vez que Bia já passou por uma experiência que Aquiles ainda idealiza, e viver no corpo do outro poderia tornar mais concreta a diferença entre desejar uma mudança e arcar com suas consequências. O roteiro, porém, dedica mais atenção à administração dos compromissos do que ao que esse impasse revela sobre o casal. A necessidade de desenvolver empatia orienta a trama desde o início, mas as situações se mostram escolhidas pela facilidade com que podem encaminhar esse aprendizado.

Isso não impede que a comédia encontre alguns bons momentos, sobretudo com Rafael Infante. O ator distingue o Aquiles apresentado no início da Bia que passa a ocupar seu corpo, alterando a energia da interpretação de maneira perceptível. Existe prazer em acompanhar essa mudança porque ela dá a impressão — sem tanto apoio do roteiro — de uma pessoa tentando funcionar sob condições que escapam ao seu controle. Infante sustenta, assim, passagens que, no papel, pouco se afastam do esperado.

Cléo trabalha numa direção complementar, assumindo uma postura mais largada e desajeitada para representar Aquiles. A composição funciona melhor nas cenas em que Aquiles precisa executar procedimentos da cozinha que não domina. Em outros momentos, a caracterização depende demais de sinais convencionais de masculinidade. No conjunto, falta compreender com maior clareza o que mantém Bia e Aquiles juntos, para que a crise desperte interesse e a futura reconciliação também ganhe relevância.

A avaliação dos críticos gastronômicos torna claro o que Bia arrisca ao deixar a cozinha nas mãos de Aquiles, cuja falta de domínio também provoca atritos entre os dois. Já a competição de esportes radicais recebe uma construção bem menos convincente, sem estabelecer a dimensão do que está em jogo na carreira dele. Os dois ambientes e as responsabilidades profissionais acabam tendo pesos diferentes na experiência de conhecer o parceiro.

A iluminação uniforme e as cores saturadas aproximam o tratamento da cozinha e das atividades ao ar livre, apesar das diferentes pressões que cada espaço impõe aos personagens. No geral, fica a sensação de que os espaços não passam de acomodações para as situações do roteiro. Não se trata de exigir realismo de uma comédia sobre troca de corpos, mas falta explorar essas diferenças para que assumir o trabalho do parceiro tenha também uma expressão visual. Isso foi feito com bem mais cuidado, por exemplo, com a agência de Cláudio e o coral de Helena no primeiro filme, estabelecidos com tempo e calma e contribuindo para o humor e o andamento da narrativa.

A passagem dos pais de Bia pela história acaba concentrando outro problema dessa renovação. Creditados como participações especiais, Tony Ramos e Glória Pires aparecem brevemente, enquanto uma viagem à China justifica seu afastamento. A caracterização superficial do destino reforça a impressão de que a segunda lua de mel (citada desde o longa anterior) serviu apenas para liberar o caminho ao novo casal. A continuação evita se resumir a uma sequência de citações aos filmes anteriores, mas a história pouco aproveita a experiência de Cláudio e Helena na trajetória da filha.

“Se Eu Fosse Você 3” não precisava reproduzir a dinâmica de Tony Ramos e Glória Pires para justificar sua existência. Precisava dar ao novo casal uma relação capaz de sustentar o interesse para além dos constrangimentos da troca. Rafael Infante consegue tornar parte do percurso divertida, mas a continuação termina sem fazer de Bia e Aquiles uma dupla que desperte a mesma vontade de um reencontro.

Artículos

Una familia al instante: Sean Anders y su historia real de adopción

Cine PREMIERE

Sean Anders nos platicó la verdadera historia detrás de Una familia al instante y es aún más emotiva que la trama de la película.

La historia verídica del director Sean Anders, y la representación de ella en forma de comedia dramática en su película Una familia al instante (2018), es una pequeña muestra del proceso de adopción en Estados Unidos.

A pesar de ser el país con mayor índice de adopción en el mundo –y de contar con el apoyo de grandes estrellas de Hollywood, como Sandra Bullock o Viola Davis–, ha disminuido un 72% en la última década. Historias como ésta, sin embargo, podrían ayudar a que ese índice regrese a lo que era a inicios del mileni

“Cualquier niño que entra a tu casa sin ser tu hijo biológico pasa por algunos problemas. Esa es la realidad”, nos platicó en entrevista el también director de Guerra de papás y Cómo matar a tu jefe 2 . “Pero de lo que nadie habla es que hay beneficios que vienen con estos niños”.

La familia Anders

Una familia al instante cuenta la historia real sobre cómo Anders y su esposa empezaron su familia. La pareja de 40 años de edad se debatía si tener hijos era una opción viable, ya que no querían ser esos papás viejos cuando sus hijos cumplieran 15. Cierto día, Anders –de nombre Pete en la cinta, interpretado por Mark Walhberg – bromeó con su esposa (interpretada por Rose Byrne):“Deberíamos adoptar a un niño de 5 años y así sería como si lo hubiéramos tenido hace cinco años y no seremos tan viejos”. Nunca esperó que ella lo tomara en serio: después de pensarlo, adoptaron a tres niños. Una familia al instante retrata ese proceso de ajuste.

Anders se identificó con sus personajes desde la primera entrega de Guerra de papás , donde un padrastro se esfuerza por ganar el cariño de dos pequeños.

«Desde entonces quise retratar la inseguridad, miedo y amor que un padre siente por sus niños en la película, porque me siento identificado con eso».

Esta comedia toca temas como el racismo y el prejuicio hacia las madres solteras y las parejas homosexuales durante el proceso de adopción, sin perder el respeto a ninguno. Según el director, en gran parte se debe al trabajo de las mujeres. “Una cosa que ayudó tremendamente fueron las mujeres. Rozemary Domínguez, quien interpreta a la madre biológica que pierde a sus hijos por drogadicción, logra subrayar esa parte que yo no conocía. Lo hizo tan maravilloso en su papel, de una manera tan enfática. Mientras que la trabajadora social, interpretada por Tig Notaro, realmente tuvo que ejercer esa profesión para poder representar la situación de su personaje”.

¡No hay pretexto! Podrás ver una de las historias más emotivas de la filmografía de Sean Anders al 2 x 1 pagando con tu tarjeta Mastercard en Cinemex .

content.article_text:
Artículos

Bad Boys 3… ¿sin Michael Bay pero con Will Smith?

Julio Vélez

Jerry Bruckheimer, Will Smith y Martin Lawrence podrían regresar para la segunda secuela de Policías rebeldes. ¿Pesará la ausencia de Michael Bay?

Deadline reveló que Sony Pictures tiene intenciones de revivir la franquicia policíaca de Dos policías rebeldes , anteriormente dirigida por Michael Bay, con la nueva entrega Bad Boys 3. Para esta, se habla sobre el posible regreso de Will Smith y Martin Lawrence como protagonistas.

Los estudios ya se encuentran en charlas con David Guggenheim ( Protegiendo al enemigo , 2012) para que escriba la historia. Sin embargo, lo que más llama la atención es que parece que el director Michael Bay , quien dirigió las primeras dos películas de la saga en 1995 y 2003, no está vinculado de forma alguna con este proyecto.

Quien sí regresa como productor, una vez concluida su relación con Disney , es Jerry Bruckheimer , aunque intriga saber cómo lo hará ya que recientemente firmó un contrato con Paramount .

¿Qué opinan? ¿Creen que sea buena idea traer de vuelta a estos personajes? Más de $100 millones de dólares en ganancias con la secuela en 2003 parecen ser una buena razón para Sony.

Julio Vélez Colaborador en web y revista Cine PREMIERE desde 2006. Me especializo en anime/manga, comics, doblaje, tecnología y videojuegos. Mis sagas favoritas: Doctor Who, Star Trek, Dragon Ball y Star Wars. Batimaníaco, geek ochentero y hardcore gamer.
