content.article_text:
The family-friendly noir pastiche is now just as much of a throwback as Who Framed Roger Rabbit? was to the genre’s old Hollywood heyday, and the spirit of Robert Zemeckis’ madcap riff on that hard-boiled style is alive and well in the year’s best animated films. First there was Coyote vs. Acme , the Looney Tunes legal conspiracy thriller that bore more similarities to the Zemeckis classic than simply featuring a roll call of cartoon icons, updating its mystery narrative with a darker satirical bent against late-capitalist America that ensured it couldn’t be seen as a cozy echo of an earlier canonized blockbuster. Now we have Brad Bird’s decades-in-the-making passion project Ray Gunn , a private-detective adventure set in a retrofuturistic metropolis where humans and aliens co-exist, flying cars and Blade Runner -style holograms sit alongside Art Deco skyscrapers, and a stinging rebuke of our current age of tech hides in plain sight.

After the big-budget whiff of Tomorrowland and hugely successful but underwhelming Incredibles sequel, Bird’s latest is a return to the inventive, hilarious form of his first three animated efforts, albeit with some distracting narrative decisions along the way that undermine the intelligence of his family audience. For example: it takes an hour to reveal one character has a dual identity, which anybody can immediately work out from the famous, distinct voice two characters share, but is staged as something of a grand reveal. The film doesn’t have the number of twists and double-crosses the most stereotypical noir would, and that’s the most glaring of several plot beats that feel like an unwarranted concession to the genre’s reliance on shocks and rug pulls.

With that one quibble noted, Bird and co-screenwriter Matthew Robbins––a veteran collaborator of Steven Spielberg––have otherwise crafted an impeccable script, the kind where every small world-building detail they introduce pays off by the finale, with the relentless, chaotic energy of the story hiding just how neatly, meticulously constructed it all is. Sam Rockwell voices the titular private detective, one of the least-grizzled gumshoes to ever appear onscreen; he’s racked with debts so can’t pay his only employee (the alien Eyera, voiced by Tom Waits), but has an aversion to playing dirty to make those ends meet. He hates violence, and will return any cash he makes if he discovers he was hired for a sinister motive. Most movie PIs are haunted by their troubled past; he seems overly cautious to avoid making any trouble for himself to start with. It’s an effective, against-type use of Rockwell, allowing him the rare chance to excel as the straight man in a filmography where his best-known roles are violent, eccentric, or both.

Ray and Eyera get their most high-profile gig yet when hired by Arnold (Bobby Cannavale), the fourth husband of pop superstar Venus Nova (Scarlett Johansson), who is worried that she’s having an affair. The pair soon discover it was all a ruse so he had a reason to divorce her on the eve of a new album tracking to flop; this puts them in touch with her manager Barry Vogel (Alan Tudyk), who hires them with the simple assignment of watching over the star for the rest of her release week. She’s a high-tempered tabloid fixture with a tendency to overshadow her album rollouts with relationship breakdowns and self-inflicted controversy. All they need to do is ensure she remains safe and out of the spotlight for another day. Unfortunately, they soon discover she’s being blackmailed over a potentially career-ruining secret by a kingpin in the alien underworld (Matt Berry), and various people from her personal life start winding up dead: staying out of trouble stops being an available option.

Although he’s rebuked the criticism several times, there is ammunition within Ray Gunn for anybody looking for further evidence Bird shares the objectivist sympathies of Ayn Rand. This time, however, the director seems conscious of this, and Nova’s character arc appears to be in direct conversation with this very idea; she’s a superstar with a very distinct persona, yet her fame has hidden her “true voice” from the public, her art all compromised and impersonal. Bird’s prior movies have focused on characters forced to hide their identities to conform, but the arguments they shared were considered Randian because their talents were for society’s greater good, and that they were held back from utilizing them.

Nova, on the other hand, already has a platform she doesn’t want if it means maintaining a lack of authenticity, which complicates the idea that Bird is singularly fixated on protagonists who are held back by ungrateful bureaucracy and creates a fascinating tension. The movie doesn’t fully rebuke the criticisms of this storytelling preoccupation, but does succeed in complicating them, which adds greater intrigue to an adventure that’s already plenty of fun on its surface.

It’s further complicated by how this clashes with timely themes designed as overt allegories for our current world of tech intrusion, with later stages of the movie presenting ideas of a surveillance state being weaponized for marketing, and the replacement of artists with AI—all of which are natural to criticize, yet when contextualized in this director’s work, criticizing them starts to line up comfortably with the broadest Randian sympathies. Think real human artists should be elevated instead of computer-programmed mediocrity, and you should be able to live free of constant oversight from devices that monitor your every conversation? Of course you do, and Bird subtly twists the knife on his critics by introducing perhaps the only progressive ideas that align with the author’s worldview into the core of his story. The movie ending with a “Produced by David Ellison” credit does, admittedly, make it a little harder to give him the benefit of the doubt on the movie’s political leanings, but we may have to start getting used to overlooking that insidious billionaire’s involvement in many great films for years to come.

The fact that a throwback adventure like Ray Gunn can inspire this level of internal debate should hopefully convince you that this is Bird back at his best, with rich and thorny ideas hidden beneath a joyously crowd-pleasing adventure. Any debate it causes will struggle to overshadow just how much fun it is.

Ray Gunn premiered at the 2026 BFI London Film Festival and will open in theaters on December 4 and arrive on Netflix on December 18.

content.article_text:
In her essay The Oppositional Gaze: Black Female Spectators, writer and philosopher bell hooks explains that the relationship between Black people and the act of “looking” has been traumatic since slavery. Black people, many of whom are still subject to the constant surveillance that originated during enslavement, have historically been punished with severe consequences, such as lynching, for looking back at those who subjugate them. Despite these risks, hooks writes, they rebelled by secretly looking at white people, as well as their surroundings, rejecting the white gaze as the singular framework of reality. We can, as bell hooks writes, “interrogate the gaze of the Other but also look back, and at one another, naming what we see”.

I thought of this analysis when I visited Edge Control, artist Deana Lawson’s latest photography exhibition at the Gagosian gallery in New York City. Edge control refers to the gels and pomades that slick the hairs along the edges of a Black woman’s hairline, but in Lawson’s exhibit, the phrase takes on an additional meaning. It’s at once a styling product for Black haircare devotees as well as a tool to examine the beauty industry, consumerism and how surveillance and race intersect.

To explore these intersections, Lawson uses photos of alleged beauty supply store shoplifters, presented in large scale and outside their original contexts. As a warning to customers, many beauty supply stores post surveillance photos of alleged shoplifters caught in the act of stealing products. The stores, which almost exclusively sell Black haircare products within Black neighborhoods, are rarely owned by Black people. The small, indistinct images tend to fade in the background amid the various colors of shampoo bottles and hair accessories.

Lawson’s images, however, are large portraits framed by mirrors, forcing the onlooker to simultaneously see themselves looking at these shoplifters. The viewer is small and narrow while the shoplifters are life-size, and what was once quiet, passive spectatorship immediately becomes active participation. This evolution is further emphasized once a viewer moves to the middle of the gallery room where two holograms stand, revealing Black women’s bodies that shift depending on the viewer’s angle. These pieces demonstrate how Lawson manipulates perception: these alleged shoplifters are not frozen in time, they are in motion, just as the viewers are.

The notion of wrongdoing is questionable as the exhibition becomes a house of mirrors exploring who is and is not being watched. Lawson accomplishes exactly what bell hooks wrote about – the rebellious gaze – by looking at her subjects, challenging viewers to evaluate them, and therefore exploring how perception functions within a space full of unequal power relations.

The exhibit’s official description proclaims that Lawson does not intend to cast moral judgment over these images, but rather “foregrounds the implications of agency and transformative potential of beauty products within our late capitalist society”. Lawson is not trying to villainize or glorify these shoplifters, but she does protect them. The shoplifter photos are evasive – the original images are low resolution, some of the shoplifters are masked and a few of the photos are so blurry that the viewer is unable to make out the subject’s face. Lawson’s deliberate refusal to clarify these images causes the viewer to contemplate what or who they are looking at. Who is the regular customer and who is the criminal?

She aims for neutrality in the depiction of her subjects by making the artistic decision to show them in stark contrast to other Black people whose images were not gathered from surveillance cameras. On the right wall opposite Lawson’s shoplifter images, the photographer’s signature style portraits hang: lush images of Black men and women in very private settings.

In all these artworks, the subjects’ gaze always meets the viewers’, reinforcing their humanity and leveling the playing field. In fact, due to their size, the subjects seem to be looking down at you. In the early 20th century, Black photographers would immortalize their Black subjects in suits, nuns’ habits or graduate gowns to usher in a new form of race pride – and respectability – into the mainstream. Lawson’s subjects are casually dressed – if at all. She’s not interested in a dignified kind of Blackness, but rather the beauty of Blackness within the mundane. By placing all of these images together within the same space, Lawson forces the viewers to view Blackness through a continuum of life in all of its contradictions, rather than a flat binary of good and bad behavior.

The relationship between the Black subjects on both sides of the room is contingent upon the viewer’s own judgment. How different is the Black female shoplifter near the braid extensions aisle from the naked Black woman squatting with her knees apart? How different is the Black male shoplifter from the Black man with a busted eye posing with others in a living room? However the viewer judges these subjects reveals their own biases. But in this exhibition, one’s biases are not private, inconsequential flaws. They’re ideological constraints that must be confronted.

Edge Control succeeds at capturing the extreme vulnerability of people who are being surveilled without their knowledge in active pursuit of beauty. At the same time, Lawson narrows the gap between spectator and participant as the viewer is confronted with multiple gazes–including their own–so that no one person is valued differently than the other. With power being briefly reassembled, parity is achieved.

content.article_text:
Walking home after dropping his little girl at school, Peter Crome sensed he was being watched. A former professional ballet dancer now living in London, he had supplemented his income with photography work for 20 years. “But since having my daughter, my Nikon gear has sat idly by,” he says. “I got so used to lugging my heavy equipment around with me, it’s been quite refreshing to go somewhere just with a phone and still come back with wonderful pictures. My iPhone has also been a blessing for keeping in touch with family back home in Sydney,” Crome adds.

The cause of his disquiet that day was, to his happy surprise, these two dogs. “It was such a comical moment,” he says. “They looked like two curtain-twitchers, though not very subtle ones. I liked how they were perfectly framed with the different layers of window frames, and the brickwork and hedge provided some pleasing textures, but it was the disapproving expression on their faces that made the photo for me.”

Crome waited for a while as the dogs watched other passersby, turning their heads in unison. He crossed the road to draw their attention, then took a single photo on his iPhone 14 Pro. “This is the sort of picture I would have sent my mum before she passed away a couple of years ago. I think this one would have really tickled her,” Crome says.

Weekly Newsletter

Long Live Generation 6-7

Lucy Ives reviews the Krasner-Pollock show at The Met, the L train burlesque arrives in Manhattan, photos from the student protests in France, and an interview with outgoing Yaddo President Elaina Richardson.

You try to get the latest news about the inspiring student protests in France but a snarky reporter on the New York Times podcast tells you that the country’s problem is providing “too generous” pension plans and parental leaves.

These welfare benefits saddle the country with debt, he says, scolding the government for not making France more competitive in the marketplace.

You turn off the podcast because you can’t listen to any more of this evil idiocy.

You finally finish reading a much-hyped new novel and wonder why you made yourself go through such torture. You return to Marcel Proust’s In Search of Lost Time to cleanse your mind’s palette. “When one is in love one has no love left for anyone.”

You go to a gala dinner and remind yourself of the golden rule at these events: always go with the steak because you never know with chicken. You feel snazzy in your new tuxedo and remember that the last time you wore one was during the Arab Spring.

You meet with Algerian-French artist Kader Attia in a Tunisian restaurant in Manhattan for an interview about a show he’s curating in India. His face full of wisdom and passion, he encourages you to wear your wounds on your sleeve.

In the cold morning breeze, you see two doves perching on the wing of an eagle sculpture on a tall column. You think about how all good art has some connection to music, and how houses always look good when they’re painted green. Nina Simone sings “Tomorrow will be the 22nd century” in your ears. Meanwhile, generation 6-7 is remaking May 68.

—Hakim Bishara, editor-in-chief

The Met’s Krasner and Pollock Show Is a Breathtaking Upending

I was married to an artist once. It was not a good experience, although calling it “an experience” makes it sound like a unified, parsable thing, and it wasn’t that, either. We’re all adults here, is what I’m getting at — so no one should imagine that anyone has bulletproof insight into anyone else’s romantic relationship, much less their own.

Certainly, once a relationship is over, it becomes a moving target in permanence: the good, the bad, and the ugly all trading places, each a microcosm in which various genres of chaos and ecstasy hold sway. And whatever we may think of other people’s marriages, we must take care. What we believe we know is almost always something we meant to say about ourselves. The phone call is coming from inside the building. If you see something, well, see something. | Lucy Ives

佐内正史の初めての写真集『生きている』が復刊を遂げる。本書は1997年4月に刊行されたが、当時、決定的瞬間ではない、私写真でもない、誰も見たことがなかった写真群は大きな反響を呼び、新たな才能を世の中が知るところとなった。その衝撃は次世代の写真家にも影響を与え、新しい写真の潮流を生み、写真史的にもエポックな出来事として記憶されている。その後『生きている』は版を重ねたものの、写真集の本文に使っていた用紙が生産中止となったことで、2007年の重版を最後に今では手に入れられなくなった写真集となっていた。

そんな中、2025年10月に創立30周年を迎えた青幻舎のメモリアルイヤースペシャル企画として、もう手に入らなくなった本の復刊プロジェクトが立ち上がる。読者からのリクエストによって、この『生きている』が晴れて復刊を遂げることとなった。

復刊には、初版『生きている』のブックデザインを手がけた造本家の町口覚氏監修の元、新たな本文用紙選定のための印刷テストを重ね、ようやくオリジナルの代わりとなる用紙に辿り着いたことで進んでいった。印刷は当時の方法に拘り、製版フィルムを使用して版を焼き、油性インクで印刷されている。一方、装丁は表紙のイメージをアップデートし、復刊として生まれ変わった新たな仕上がりとなった。刊行から29年、写真の歴史に新たなページが加わる。

さらに復刊記念として、福岡を皮切りに京都、名古屋、盛岡、広島を巡る 刊行記念展や会期中トークイベント の開催も。東京では10月11日、青山ブックセンター本店での佐内と町口によるトークイベントが予定されている。この機会をお見逃しなく。

content.article_text:
Le Premi Fotografia Femenina Fisheye x InCadaqués 2026 a récompensé Julie Peiffer pour Renversement , une série où la nature fragile croise quelques portraits. Cette dernière est à découvrir pendant cette dixième édition du festival espagnol, qui s’achèvera le 25 octobre prochain.

Le festival InCadaqués a lancé sa dixième édition en Catalogne, en Espagne. Jusqu’au 25 octobre 2026, le public peut y découvrir 25 expositions portées par 40 photographes venus du monde entier. Parmi eux se trouve notamment Julie Peiffer, lauréate du Premi Fotografia Femenina 2026, un prix en partenariat avec Fisheye qui célèbre le regard féminin au sein du 8e art. Au fil de projets marqués par le temps long, l’artiste française sonde les liens qui unissent le corps, la mémoire et le territoire. Elle porte un intérêt particulier à ce qui ne se voit pas forcément, mais laisse une empreinte pérenne.

Saisir des déséquilibres discrets

« Un matin, le chant d’un oiseau m’a semblé un cri, explique Julie Peiffer en introduction à sa série . Ce désordre a bouleversé ma manière de percevoir notre milieu : sa lumière, sa densité, sa vibration, la promesse même des saisons. Enfant, je croyais que mon père pouvait arrêter le vent ; cette croyance disait la confiance absolue que j’avais dans la permanence du monde. Aujourd’hui, je vois les chaleurs écraser nos étés, les forêts se taire, la pluie ronger nos repères ; le monde m’apparaît traversé par une matière invisible. Mes photographies cherchent à en révéler la trace, dans l’épaisseur même de l’image. » Face aux métamorphoses constantes du territoire, l’artiste utilise son médium pour saisir des déséquilibres encore discrets. Pour les matérialiser, elle inverse le sens des tirages, les transforme en négatifs et les retravaille jusqu’à faire émerger « une matière instable, vulnérable » . « Renversement ne propose ni constat ni réponse. C’est un espace de coexistence fragile. Un lieu où le paysage n’est plus regardé, mais éprouvé » , conclut-elle.

Intime

Partenaire

Intime

content.article_text:
This summer marked 15 years since the death of British singer-songwriter Amy Winehouse, but her spirit lives on. Now, her life and influence are the subject of “Nothing Personal,” a just-opened exhibition by artist Alex Margo Arden spread across three rooms of the Nicoletta Fiorucci Foundation in London .

For the exhibition, Arden has created hundreds of simulacra of Winehouse’s personal items, recreating a pair of ballet slippers signed by fans left outside the singer’s home after her death and a birthday card from the music producer Mark Ronson and Adele that Winehouse never received. To round out this display, Arden purchased exact copies of books found in Winehouse’s library, the makeup and perfume she used, and boardgames and decorative items like mirrors that dotted her house. The display can at times feel like you’re surreptitiously browsing the most intimate parts of someone’s home. Since 2021, Arden has been forensically dissecting pixelated images of Winehouse she’s found online, in catalogues, newspapers and magazines, to determine which items she would need to track down.

Related Articles

The Zaha Hadid Foundation Is Reopening the Late Architect's Former HQ as a Public Arts Space

Both London's Sid Motion and Beers Galleries Are Closing, Citing Economic Pressures

“This show is a really personal insight into Amy,” Arden told ARTnews , describing what’s on view as “parallel objects.” She feels that the hundred books on display create an intimate atmosphere and add historical value, more so than if she actually had presented just one or two authentic items from Winehouse’s estate.

The sensitivity to detail across the project is striking. At one point during this five-year scavenger hunt, Arden wound up with 20 versions of the same book; she wanted to compare each copy’s spine and cover to make sure she had the correct one. The bulk of this labor is showcased in Library (2026), containing dozens of tomes from Vladimir Nabokov’s Speak Memory next to the cookbook The New Classic 1000 Recipes , which is not far from a book on marriage. There are also biographies of David Beckham, Bob Dylan, Carole King, Marilyn Monroe, and Audrey Hepburn.

“What I’m proposing in the artwork is that as a collection, this gives us really good insight” into Winehouse’s life, Arden said, warning against zeroing in on any one book. She pointed to a Weight Watchers book, which some might relate to Winehouse’s history of eating disorders, which were put under a microscope by the British tabloids. “In isolation, these objects can be used to really push specific narratives about her,” she explained.

In the next room, Arden presents Same Otherwise (2026), a recreation of the fireplace in Winehouse’s home at 2 Jeffrey’s Place, where she wrote her Grammy Award–winning album Back to Black . Just as Winehouse once had it, Arden has positioned framed issues of British Vogue , comic book pages from Betty and Veronica , and a mirror with a picture of Marilyn Monroe over the mantel. But the artist has left gaps where the musician had personal photos of friends and family framed. “The gaps speak to the feeling of things being present and missing always,” she said.

As we spoke, I became captivated by a scent in the gallery. At first I thought it was Arden’s perfume, but the fragrance was, in fact, an artwork, Perfume said to have belonged to Amy Winehouse [I-IV] (2024–26). The Chanel No.5 I was smelling had been emitted from a custom dispenser by Arden. Throughout the exhibition’s run, the Chanel No.5 will be exchanged for other perfumes that Winehouse is said to have worn. Arden wouldn’t disclose which ones would feature, but various accounts by fashion publications previously reported that Winehouse also wore Alien by Thierry Mugler, Vera Wang Princess, and Givenchy’s Hot Couture. The work was a touching reminder of Winehouse’s tangible presence, wafting through the galleries.

The exhibition also includes more intimate works that at times get overshadowed. Jigsaws (2026), for example, is a stack of those titular puzzles of scenes of the Beatles, The Simpsons , and Casablanca . The patience required to piece them together paints Winehouse as an introspective woman as opposed to her party girl that the tabloids portrayed her as. Sent Otherwise (2026) is the recreation of the aforementioned birthday card that was only discovered years later, a poignant reminder that even a decade and a half after Winehouse’s death, her life is still being excavated. Taken together, they act as clever tidbits into Winehouse’s short-lived life.

To her tribute to Winehouse, Arden also adds a piece of herself, via Display Identification Cubes (2026), an artwork made up of a thousand acrylic ice cubes that resemble the placards that are typically used in museum vitrines to match an object to its corresponding label. This numbering methodology recurs across Arden’s oeuvre. In All Clear (2022), these numbers appear as print-outs affixed next to items such as a broom, a ladder, and a woven basket, perhaps evoking the objects found at a crime scene, the mundane taking on a more sinister connotation.

But in “Nothing Personal,” on view through January 23, the plastic numbers serve as pieces that Arden hasn’t discovered about Winehouse yet—and maybe never will. “They draw attention to spaces where things are absent, but they also mark spaces where things have once been,” she said.

content.title_original: Remember Me review – narrow view of two photographic centuries is like a history of food in three ham sarnies
content.article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "‘B eware … of assuming the sterile attitude of the spectator, for life is not a spectacle” scream the words of Aimé Césaire – writ large and bold by Barbara Kruger, in a giant installation, The History of Tears, that fills Bourse de Commerce’s spectacular Rotunda. Kruger’s angry, menacing, viscerally charged work – words as images, and large-scale video clips of people seething with self-hate – is a thrilling setup for Remember Me, an exhibition that promises a take on 200 years of photography through 700 works by more than 70 artists drawn from the collection of the French billionaire François Pinault. That excitement quickly dissipates as the exhibition moves on."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "This is the biggest photography show ever held at the Bourse de Commerce. Remember Me has two main problems: first, it tries to say too much with too few artists. For a start, nearly 450 of the 700 or so works are by Irving Penn . It leans heavily on classical, conventional approaches, styles and familiar names, and that creates a very obvious skew in the perception of what photography is, does, and how it is presented.", "links": [{"text": "Irving Penn", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign/irving-penn"}]}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/0aa4517cc7a38f53bb3fd53926e830477afa9ff6/0_0_4000_2667/master/4000.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "A man takes in numerous black and white photographs as they’re displayed on a curving wall", "caption": "Like waves … Remember Me", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The organisation makes no real sense. There are two main spaces, in addition to Kruger’s installation, dedicated exclusively to one artist. Penn is one of them. The installation looks undeniably beautiful: following the curving Ando architecture, the works have been hung like waves, expanding in undulating lines across the walls, without chronology or theme, flowing freely into the space. However, when you look closely at the works themselves, this configuration becomes very problematic. There are a large number of colonial-style portraits taken in a temporary tent studio by Penn when he travelled in Cameroon and Benin. Many of the pictures depict men and women in traditional tribal dress, and were taken as a commission for Vogue. These nations were actively negotiating independence from France at that time. When you compare them with portraits by Malick Sidibé or Seydou Keïta of the same time, they look even more like anthropological, ethnographic, extractive images by a westerner who couldn’t even communicate with his subjects.", "links": [{"text": "Malick Sidibé", "url": "https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malick_Sidib%C3%A9"}, {"text": "Seydou Keïta", "url": "https://www.seydoukeitaphotographer.com/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“Primitive subjects respond more to tone than to obscure words,” Penn stated of how he directed the people who appear in these photographs. content.article_text:
‘B eware … of assuming the sterile attitude of the spectator, for life is not a spectacle” scream the words of Aimé Césaire – writ large and bold by Barbara Kruger, in a giant installation, The History of Tears, that fills Bourse de Commerce’s spectacular Rotunda. Kruger’s angry, menacing, viscerally charged work – words as images, and large-scale video clips of people seething with self-hate – is a thrilling setup for Remember Me, an exhibition that promises a take on 200 years of photography through 700 works by more than 70 artists drawn from the collection of the French billionaire François Pinault. That excitement quickly dissipates as the exhibition moves on.

This is the biggest photography show ever held at the Bourse de Commerce. Remember Me has two main problems: first, it tries to say too much with too few artists. For a start, nearly 450 of the 700 or so works are by Irving Penn . It leans heavily on classical, conventional approaches, styles and familiar names, and that creates a very obvious skew in the perception of what photography is, does, and how it is presented.

The organisation makes no real sense. There are two main spaces, in addition to Kruger’s installation, dedicated exclusively to one artist. Penn is one of them. The installation looks undeniably beautiful: following the curving Ando architecture, the works have been hung like waves, expanding in undulating lines across the walls, without chronology or theme, flowing freely into the space. However, when you look closely at the works themselves, this configuration becomes very problematic. There are a large number of colonial-style portraits taken in a temporary tent studio by Penn when he travelled in Cameroon and Benin. Many of the pictures depict men and women in traditional tribal dress, and were taken as a commission for Vogue. These nations were actively negotiating independence from France at that time. When you compare them with portraits by Malick Sidibé or Seydou Keïta of the same time, they look even more like anthropological, ethnographic, extractive images by a westerner who couldn’t even communicate with his subjects.

“Primitive subjects respond more to tone than to obscure words,” Penn stated of how he directed the people who appear in these photographs. To me, that says everything about his perspective on African bodies and culture. Then you notice the rest of it: the glamorous white women who appear as pristine models of passive beauty, while all the men are mediocre-looking and wear suits. Still lifes are woven through – presumably to undo the idea of hierarchy between subjects. So, a man who looks at a vase or a plate of fruit the same way he looks at people. The camera has been instrumental in colonialism, and in cultural extraction and appropriation – including in the fashion industry, of which Penn was part. But there’s no attempt to tackle that here, to counter these visions with other perspectives.

It’s not the last you’ll see of Penn, unfortunately – his works keep popping up through the upper floor, where various major names reappear in different sections that each try to heavy-handedly explain and demystify, in an annoyingly didactic way, what photography is and how it’s made. We jump between sections on composition, abstraction, portrait and seriality, to nudes – where the women have gorgeous bums and breasts turned alluringly to the camera, and the men are small and, so we’re told to think, weak and vulnerable, with very large penises. My biggest issue here was why the sumptuous, elegant nude portrait of Zanele Muholi (by the artist themself, but not technically a self-portrait) needed a lengthy wall text, justifying the work via the western painting tradition – where none of the nudes of white women seemed to warrant one. Yet a quirky series of small 1933 nude shots by Man Ray – an erotic performance featuring the younger artist Méret Oppenheim, unclothed, and Man Ray in a suit and bowler hat – are left with no explanation about the power dynamics of the camera and male surrealism’s issues with women.

This is a show that’s too afraid to let people think for themselves. We’re told Richard Avedon’s trio of 1963 portraits of William Casby, a former enslaved person who was 106 when Avedon photographed him, elevate his subject, giving him back his dignity. They’re glaringly close and unflattering photographs that resemble mug shots. Compare them with Avedon’s smaller, slightly blurred, portrait of Malcolm X. Decide for yourself what Avedon felt, whose image is claimed and whose is handed to them.

Once the exhibition lets go of the binaries, the anxiety to overexplain, or to adhere to the techniques of photography, when it allows active participation or just to be with the work, it gets better. The looser, thematic unions between images are intelligible and interesting, such as sections on “hands” and a glorious room exploring photographs of the sea. These rooms make you feel something, and reflect photographic resonances through history in a more meaningful way. By the Sea, for example, moves seamlessly from the 19th century in Gustave Le Gray’s painterly wet collodion prints, where he spliced two negatives together, one for the sea and one for the sky, to create his perfect vision of a seascape, to Hiroshi Sugimoto and Wolfgang Tillmans’ elegiac and laconic black and white ruminations. I think about why artists keep returning to look at the sea, looking for the infinite, for continuity, for obliteration and enormity. This room captures the feeling of gazing out at the sea, the ocean’s soothing violence and impervious calm.

Photography is an inherently accessible medium, and they take it seriously in France. This show feels fumbling, and an unnecessary dumbing-down. Trying to bend two centuries of one of the most prolific mediums around these particular artists is like trying to tell the history of food through three ham sandwiches. There are more than 8,000 photographs in the wider collection: perhaps it’s more varied in perspective than appears in this show – but as it is, it shirks the responsibility of retelling photography’s history with nuance and multiplicity. Remember Me forgets Kruger’s invocation at the start.

Remember Me is at Bourse de Commerce, Paris, until 18 January

content.article_text:
神戸のアートブック書店THE BOOK ENDにて、10月8日（木）より小島康敬による写真展「中今 | ベルリン」を開催している。

写真家・小島康敬が提示するのは、私たちが知る歴史や記憶から乖離し、時空間をも通り抜けたような、どこでもない「ベルリン」。 最先端の量子理論や、時間と空間の中心を指す古神道の概念「中今（Naka-ima）」に着想を得て制作された本シリーズは、過去・現在・未来が同時に存在する「立体的な今」を静かに捉え引き出す試みだ。

東京、ニューヨークを経てたどり着いた目線の高さによる平面的でミニマルな画面構成。 特定の場所や歴史的表象を削ぎ落とした作品群は、ロラン・バルトが称した「空虚な記号」のように中心を空虚に保ち、観る者に意味の解釈をそっと委ねる。 撮影された瞬間の「かつてあった」一瞬の奥に流れる時間と距離、そしてどこか静けさを纏った円環する時間の深みを、ぜひ会場でご体験いただきたい。

小島康敬「中今 | ベルリン」

THE BOOK END（兵庫県神戸市中央区海岸通3-1-5海岸ビルヂング 302 ）

2026年10月8日（木）〜11月9日（日）

11:00〜18:00

火、水曜

無料

content.article_text:
Interview

Raven Chacon Sounds the History of the Land

The Pulitzer Prize-winning Diné artist talks about his recent performances at the Park Avenue Armory, the freedom of improvisation, and the privilege of “deep listening.”

On Wednesday and Thursday night, sound mixers, synthesizers, pedals, speakers, whistles, a turkey call, and a ceramic horn sat on a table at the center of the Veterans Room in Manhattan’s Park Avenue Armory . Serving as the stage for Raven Chacon’s hour-long improvisation sessions for the Armory’s Artists Studio series, the table also offered audiences the rare opportunity to see the prolific artist at play.

During his performance on October 8, the Diné artist, composer, and Pulitzer Prize-winner used each object on the table to surprising and often discomfiting ends. He rigorously blew a whistle into a microphone, looping the sound and layering it atop a rising drone, which he intermittently cut to make room for the electronic transmission of the breath he recorded moments earlier. He mixed screeches over the whistles, eventually transforming the former into an oscillating, metallic sound redolent of the extraterrestrial signals in a sci-fi film. When the composition strayed too far into speculative abstraction, he’d snap it back with a clear, often frightening reminder of the world outside. Chacon ended the session by playing recordings of the wind through a hyperdirectional speaker that he moved in a circle around himself. He swept the sound of the wind over a new part of the room with each turn, transmitting with it the geography of alternative worlds much less violent than those sounded by the cars blaring up and down Park Avenue immediately outside, but whose continued existence depends upon our choosing to listen.

I talked with Chacon over the phone between his performances at the Armory about the role of location in his work, his repurposing of tools associated with colonial violence, and his turn to science fiction for an upcoming show at the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art .

Hyperallergic: For your Arts and Letters show, you were working with both local naturalist histories and the Lenape culture and history of New York. How do you bring site-specificity to a work like this that's entirely improvised?

Raven Chacon: I wish I could say I was responding to the Armory [ laughs ]. When I’m playing in the city, I tend to bring in more field recordings of the outdoors, of wind and other sounds from other places. A lot of these were gathered where I'm from in New Mexico. While not site-specific to the Armory in this case, I find myself incorporating those more indoors, amongst the other things that encroach upon the interior of the space. It’s unavoidable that we might hear sirens and traffic outside, and those usually become part of the soundtrack of what I’m working with.

H: Those sounds can have a different effect just based on the setting. We recently published a review of a group show you were in at the Hammer that likens your sound piece to a “ California earthquake ,” which is the type of resonance that you wouldn't get in New York.

RC: That was certainly a consideration. Also, with that show, there were a lot of works about the actual ground. That installation was situated at the entry, but immediately, you have works by Edgar Calel, Ana Mendieta, these works that involve soil and dirt. I wanted to reference that with that piece. And as you move through, you have these different interactions with different materials and visual concepts happening throughout the show.

content.article_text:
Art Review

Truman Lowe Listens to the Water

In his first major retrospective, the Hoocąk artist transforms natural materials into fluid sculptures that carry the memory of place, ancestry, and cultural survival.

Hyperallergic )

WASHINGTON, DC — Hoocąk (Ho-Chunk) artist Truman Lowe’s first major retrospective opens with “Ottawa” (1992), a billowing sculpture of pine and peeled willow saplings that brings together the tributary currents of the rivers that marked the aquatic realms of his childhood. The form undulates with an audacious disregard for the material’s inherent fixed state; each bend, movement, and ripple echoes Lowe’s unwavering ethos that wood is water.

Throughout Water’s Edge: The Art of Truman Lowe at the National Museum of the American Indian, Lowe resonates with Toni Morrison’s sentiment that “all water has a perfect memory and is forever trying to get back to where it was.” The works are arranged around four themes of moving water: Landscape and Place, Woodland Structures, Memory, and Shared Knowledge.

In Hoocąk culture, the number four holds reverence, history, and the recognition that repetition signifies permanence. This durability appears in multiple works by Lowe, such as “Mimi” (1979), a sculpture composed of four peeled willow branches, four groupings of blue jay feathers, and collections of red beads in sequences of four that cocoon the four strips of leather.
content.excerpt_original: In his first major retrospective, the Hoocąk artist transforms natural materials into fluid sculptures that carry the memory of place, ancestry, and cultural survival.

content.article_text:
The latest attempt to halt the impending construction of President Donald Trump’s 250-foot-tall triumphal arch involves a local government body. The five-member Arlington County Board filed a lawsuit Thursday in the Eastern District of Virginia, related to the project’s questionable review process.

Democracy Forward, the advocacy group representing the Board, along with the Arlington County attorney’s office, referred to the proposal as a “vanity project” that would be “massively intrusive and harmful.” Democracy Forward notes November 5 as the date of the National Capital Planning Commission’s next meeting, at which point the committee could “rubber stamp” the start of construction.

Related Articles

After Resignation of Advisory Council, American Institute of Architects Weigh in on Trump's Arch

Vietnam Veterans File Restraining Order to Block Progress on Trump's 250-Foot Triumphal Arch

The County Board is asking the court to prevent any demolition or construction until a full environmental review is completed. In early September , Interior Secretary Doug Burgum posted on X that “after a very long wait (over 125 years!), we are preparing to start, over the next two-week period, the excavation work necessary for the Great Triumphal Arch and Military Observation Deck …” (Though that was posted more than a month ago, the groundbreaking has yet to occur.)

The proposed site for the arch is Memorial Circle at the end of the Arlington Memorial Bridge. One of the most serious complaints about the arch’s impact on dozens of surrounding monuments is that it would “directly obstruct the line of sight between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery that was deliberately created to symbolize the nation’s post-Civil War reunification,” according to the lawsuit.

Matt de Ferranti, chair of the Arlington County Board, said in a statement that Arlington’s community “has the most to lose from this egregious and unlawful proposed project.” He added, “Enough is enough. We will do all we can to hold this administration accountable and to protect and serve the best interests of our community.”

The lawsuit , which lists as defendants Bergum, the National Park Service, and Jessica Bowron, acting director of the NPS, accuses the administration of not complying with the National Environmental Policy Act and glossing over the ways it will negatively impact its surroundings, specifically pointing out the impact on emergency services and the increase in noise and air pollution.

“Using the Arch to store large stockpiles of ammunition and as a staging point for drones and snipers, so close to commuters and tourists,” the lawsuit warns, “will dramatically worsen these public-safety harms and the risk of accidents.”
content.excerpt_original: In the latest attempt to halt construction of President Donald Trump’s triumphal arch, the Arlington County Board filed a lawsuit on Thursday.

content.article_text:
Guide

7 New York Exhibitions That Embody Indigenous Survivance

In shows coinciding with Indigenous Peoples' Day, artists including Jeremy Dennis, Shelley Niro, and Sarah Sense chart Native history and futurity.

To commemorate Indigenous Peoples' Day here in New York, we have highlighted seven ongoing exhibitions of Native art and history in Manhattan, the Hessel Museum of Art at Bard College, and the Long Island Museum in Stony Brook. Across solo and group presentations, the featured artists, who represent a diverse tapestry of Indigenous populations across Turtle Island, embody survivance by tracing and rejecting narratives of dispossession and irrelevance, upending and satirizing stereotypes, preserving and reinventing traditional art forms, and bringing underrepresented histories out from the margins.

Some of these sites are closed in observance of the occasion, and some of you have not been afforded the three-day weekend commanding this period of reflection, so rest assured that the following programs will be available from the last week of October through next spring.

Cannupa Hanska Luger: American Traditional

Garth Greenan Gallery , 10 Greene Street, SoHo, Manhattan Through Oct. 24

Inaugurating the gallery's new space, Cannupa Hanska Luger's (Mandan, Hidatsa, Arikara, and Lakota) American Traditional exchanges the artist's typically colorful verve for a series of uniform matte-black works born from ironstone clay, sumi ink, and direct flame. The titular work presents a striated sculpture of a skinned bison with a bifurcated skull sitting on a standard colonial-fashion dining table. Encoded in tautly wrapped yarn, this distortion manifests throughout Luger's wall hangings and pedestals of other animal skulls and carcasses, which are embellished with railroad spikes, Pulaski axes, and vintage “American Traditional” furniture associated with the westward settler expansion. Per the artist, the work emphasizes the “bizarre and horrific history of colonialism,” and the motifs of mutilation and mutation speak to the manipulation of collective memory in the retelling and neglect of certain perspectives.

Shelley Niro: In Her Lifetime

Hales Gallery , 547 West 20th Street, Chelsea, Manhattan Through Oct. 31

Turtle Clan of the Kanyen’kehá:ka (Mohawk) Nation artist and filmmaker Shelley Niro celebrates her second solo show with Hales New York in a tight selection of mixed-media photographic works spanning decades of her career. In Her Lifetime , which takes its name from Niro's 1992 black-and-white picture sequence of her sister with overlaid text, emphasizes the artist's use of humor and accessible references in her personal reflections on identity, nationhood, collective memory, and stereotypes through an Indigenous perspective. For this exhibition, Niro also reinterprets a variety of her iconic photos from the early 1990s, embellishing them with hand-painted elements and decorative patterns that, in the context of Indigenous womanhood, add a certain cheeky assertiveness to her family portrayals.
content.excerpt_original: In shows coinciding with Indigenous Peoples' Day, artists including Jeremy Dennis, Shelley Niro, and Sarah Sense chart Native history and futurity.

content.article_text:
News

Gochman Collection of Indigenous Art to Open Katonah Space in November

The new home in New York, known as Branchline, will display selections from the family’s trove of over 800 contemporary Native artworks.

Branchline, a permanent exhibition space for the Gochman Family Collection, will open on November 6 in Katonah, New York, functioning as a new home for the renowned trove of contemporary Native art.

Building on the private collection's focus on Indigenous and anti-colonial art, Branchline will present rotating exhibitions of the over 800 works by contemporary Native artists in the Gochman Collection and provide residential and studio spaces for artists. Deriving its name from the network of rail lines that connect Katonah to surrounding areas like Manhattan and Upstate New York, Branchline also encompasses the ancestral and historical lineages informing the featured art.

"We imagine this as a flexible space to not only more broadly share the Collection, but to also create opportunities for varied audiences of artists, scholars, students, families, and our neighbors to spend time together," Laura Phipps, who became the collection's director in March , told Hyperallergic .

content.title_original: Between Legacy and Discovery: Rebekah Sherman-Myntti on the 2026 Downtown Festival
content.article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "In a city like New York, what’s another film festival? When one can crop up in any neighborhood, keeping track is neither possible nor desirable. So if I might’ve accordingly raised an eyebrow to hear of the Downtown Festival upon its appearance in 2024, allow me a moment of judging a book by its cover.", "links": [{"text": "the Downtown Festival", "url": "https://www.thedowntownfestival.com/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Coming to know the festival and its founder, Rebekah Sherman-Myntti, has disavowed any wonky feelings. Downtown, now in its third year, is further and further proving itself a valuable companion to New York’s larger festivals: a repository for debut filmmakers, low-budget fare, or (speaking for myself and a small group of friends) an undistributed TV pilot that was shot in our apartments and serves as something of an all-male Girls riff. It’s a place that makes artists feel welcome and comfortable, allowing them to tailor a world premiere to their desires without excluding them from a larger flux."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Sherman-Myntti and I spoke about Downtown’s third year , which commences tonight with Paul Schrader’s The Basics of Philosophy , a film she says exemplifies the festival’s balance between legacy and discovery.", "links": [{"text": "Downtown’s third year", "url": "https://www.thedowntownfestival.com/program"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Let’s start with a basic question: can you tell me how the third edition of The Downtown Festival separates itself from predecessors?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I think this year feels quite a bit different. The first two editions were really about establishing the festival’s identity and proving the concept. In 2024, I wanted to see if this seemingly crazy idea could actually work and be pulled off. In 2025, it was really about realizing how much of an appetite there was for something like this to exist, which was super exciting. With the third edition this year, the scale is much bigger, the program is more ambitious, and the relationships between film, music, artist talks, and nightlife feel way more intertwined."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "At the same time, the core idea of the festival hasn’t changed. It’s still artists-for-artists, deeply rooted in discovery, and focused on creating real exchanges between filmmakers, musicians, and various other disciplines. I’m always thinking about the kind of festival experience I’d genuinely want as a filmmaker… one where people feel supported, connected to their fellow artists as well as audiences, and part of something that can continue beyond a single event. We haven’t even announced half of our non-film programming yet! So stay tuned."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/EVE_RIGHT_4-1200x648.jpeg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "The Film Stage"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The Story of Eve by Alexandra Cabral"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The program is impressive, albeit not comprising much that is even the least-bit known. I’m curious, also, about the distinction between programming a number of first-time filmmakers—exactly the kind of group that would struggle to be prioritized by programmers—and films that are plainly worthwhile, regardless of author. Do you see yourself prioritizing one while still hoping to serve another?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I definitely don’t prioritize first-time filmmakers just because they’re first-time filmmakers. I like to prioritize work that feels incredibly specific and like it has a real point of view. There has to be a certain aliveness to it. With films, we’re always looking for ones that feel deeply personal, where you can really sense that the filmmaker had to make this film in this way. Rather than something that could have been made by anyone or that feels like it’s trying to fit into an existing mold."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "That said: I do feel really strongly about making space for artists who haven’t already been “validated” by the usual systems. If someone has made something amazing and doesn’t yet have representation, press, institutional support, or a recognizable name attached to them, that makes me more interested. I think festivals can play a meaningful role in helping people discover work they might not otherwise know about and in giving that work a context that helps audiences understand why it’s cool or important."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "At the Downtown Festival, you can have a true legend like Paul Schrader showing work alongside a visual artist making her first feature, like Ondine Viñao, and have both works taken equally seriously. You can also have someone like Paul Tschinkel, whose work is so beautifully tied to an older New York art world and to documenting artists from that era, sitting alongside much newer and younger voices. I love those kinds of juxtapositions because they break down the hierarchy a bit. The work gets to speak for itself and our audience can experience someone they already know alongside someone they may be discovering for the very first time. That tension between legacy and discovery is super fascinating to me and it’s a huge part of what makes programming exciting and fun for me and Briana. There’s so much value in putting artists who helped shape a particular cultural moment in direct conversation with people who are reinterpreting or challenging it now."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "How much do you see yourself as separate from the elite New York pack of ND/NF, Tribeca, and NYFF? Is there anything you actively seek to do differently?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I definitely see us as separate, but not in an antagonistic way. Those festivals have their own incredible histories, scales, and institutional roles. I really enjoy going to screenings at them. I would say that The Downtown Festival is something very different! The biggest differentiating factor is probably that we are truly multidisciplinary. Film is a huge part of it, but it exists alongside music, artist talks, performances, and other one-night-only events. I’m interested in what happens when all of those worlds actually overlap rather than being treated as separate cultural lanes. The festival is also very multigenerational and very explicitly artists-for-artists. I want somebody making their first film to feel as meaningfully included as somebody who has been making work for forty years. We’re much less interested in reinforcing traditional hierarchies around who is already considered “important” enough to deserve attention."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "And structurally, we’re an extremely tiny team and we don’t have a huge institution or infrastructure behind us. That limitation has actually shaped the festival in a way I really value because it keeps things super personal and close to the artists. I also like the flexibility and organized chaos because with that comes the freedom of spontaneity! content.article_text:
In a city like New York, what’s another film festival? When one can crop up in any neighborhood, keeping track is neither possible nor desirable. So if I might’ve accordingly raised an eyebrow to hear of the Downtown Festival upon its appearance in 2024, allow me a moment of judging a book by its cover.

Coming to know the festival and its founder, Rebekah Sherman-Myntti, has disavowed any wonky feelings. Downtown, now in its third year, is further and further proving itself a valuable companion to New York’s larger festivals: a repository for debut filmmakers, low-budget fare, or (speaking for myself and a small group of friends) an undistributed TV pilot that was shot in our apartments and serves as something of an all-male Girls riff. It’s a place that makes artists feel welcome and comfortable, allowing them to tailor a world premiere to their desires without excluding them from a larger flux.

Sherman-Myntti and I spoke about Downtown’s third year , which commences tonight with Paul Schrader’s The Basics of Philosophy , a film she says exemplifies the festival’s balance between legacy and discovery.

Let’s start with a basic question: can you tell me how the third edition of The Downtown Festival separates itself from predecessors?

I think this year feels quite a bit different. The first two editions were really about establishing the festival’s identity and proving the concept. In 2024, I wanted to see if this seemingly crazy idea could actually work and be pulled off. In 2025, it was really about realizing how much of an appetite there was for something like this to exist, which was super exciting. With the third edition this year, the scale is much bigger, the program is more ambitious, and the relationships between film, music, artist talks, and nightlife feel way more intertwined.

At the same time, the core idea of the festival hasn’t changed. It’s still artists-for-artists, deeply rooted in discovery, and focused on creating real exchanges between filmmakers, musicians, and various other disciplines. I’m always thinking about the kind of festival experience I’d genuinely want as a filmmaker… one where people feel supported, connected to their fellow artists as well as audiences, and part of something that can continue beyond a single event. We haven’t even announced half of our non-film programming yet! So stay tuned.

The Story of Eve by Alexandra Cabral

The program is impressive, albeit not comprising much that is even the least-bit known. I’m curious, also, about the distinction between programming a number of first-time filmmakers—exactly the kind of group that would struggle to be prioritized by programmers—and films that are plainly worthwhile, regardless of author. Do you see yourself prioritizing one while still hoping to serve another?

I definitely don’t prioritize first-time filmmakers just because they’re first-time filmmakers. I like to prioritize work that feels incredibly specific and like it has a real point of view. There has to be a certain aliveness to it. With films, we’re always looking for ones that feel deeply personal, where you can really sense that the filmmaker had to make this film in this way. Rather than something that could have been made by anyone or that feels like it’s trying to fit into an existing mold.

That said: I do feel really strongly about making space for artists who haven’t already been “validated” by the usual systems. If someone has made something amazing and doesn’t yet have representation, press, institutional support, or a recognizable name attached to them, that makes me more interested. I think festivals can play a meaningful role in helping people discover work they might not otherwise know about and in giving that work a context that helps audiences understand why it’s cool or important.

At the Downtown Festival, you can have a true legend like Paul Schrader showing work alongside a visual artist making her first feature, like Ondine Viñao, and have both works taken equally seriously. You can also have someone like Paul Tschinkel, whose work is so beautifully tied to an older New York art world and to documenting artists from that era, sitting alongside much newer and younger voices. I love those kinds of juxtapositions because they break down the hierarchy a bit. The work gets to speak for itself and our audience can experience someone they already know alongside someone they may be discovering for the very first time. That tension between legacy and discovery is super fascinating to me and it’s a huge part of what makes programming exciting and fun for me and Briana. There’s so much value in putting artists who helped shape a particular cultural moment in direct conversation with people who are reinterpreting or challenging it now.

How much do you see yourself as separate from the elite New York pack of ND/NF, Tribeca, and NYFF? Is there anything you actively seek to do differently?

I definitely see us as separate, but not in an antagonistic way. Those festivals have their own incredible histories, scales, and institutional roles. I really enjoy going to screenings at them. I would say that The Downtown Festival is something very different! The biggest differentiating factor is probably that we are truly multidisciplinary. Film is a huge part of it, but it exists alongside music, artist talks, performances, and other one-night-only events. I’m interested in what happens when all of those worlds actually overlap rather than being treated as separate cultural lanes. The festival is also very multigenerational and very explicitly artists-for-artists. I want somebody making their first film to feel as meaningfully included as somebody who has been making work for forty years. We’re much less interested in reinforcing traditional hierarchies around who is already considered “important” enough to deserve attention.

And structurally, we’re an extremely tiny team and we don’t have a huge institution or infrastructure behind us. That limitation has actually shaped the festival in a way I really value because it keeps things super personal and close to the artists. I also like the flexibility and organized chaos because with that comes the freedom of spontaneity! It’s great to have the independence to occasionally make decisions quickly or very last-minute and sometimes build programs around conversations and relationships rather than around a preexisting institutional framework or schedule.

With our film program, we’re interested not only in the film and the screening itself, but in everything that forms around it: who is in the room, who engages with the work, artists meeting each other, what conversations continue afterward, and what kinds of relationships or collaborations might emerge from that experience. For me, the festival is as much about creating the conditions for genuine artistic exchange as it is about presenting a slate of films.

It’s notable that this is not The Downtown Film Festival. You have a music showcase and events sponsored by MFNY. Do you see these as in any way linked to cinema? I won’t try to force some idea of “live concerts are actually cinema,” but there’s an interesting intersection of a communal vibe to screenings and actual communal events that aren’t screenings.

Very much so. The point was never to build a film festival that just happened to have a few side events. The multidisciplinary aspect is fundamental to what The Downtown Festival is, and for me, the connective tissue is the artists and the audience. Film, music, art, performance, and nightlife all create communal experiences in different ways, and I love what happens when those artists and audiences collide. Historically, downtown New York culture wasn’t neatly divided into disciplines. Filmmakers were hanging out with musicians, visual artists were acting in and making films, musicians were making movies, and everyone was ending up in the same clubs. There was a real fluidity to it.

I’m much more interested in that kind of cross-pollination than keeping everything professionally siloed, which I think happens far too often now. Especially in a festival context. I really don’t believe in “staying in your lane.” The festival is about creating a space where those different worlds can come together naturally. And a big shoutout to MFNY for supporting that vision this year!

Without asking you to give away too much, what do you see as an expansion in future years?

I’d love for The Downtown Festival to become a true home base for artists from around the world who are making work that doesn’t fit into established categories and who are looking for a genuine community around what they make. A huge part of that is continuing to bring different generations into direct conversation with one another. I want artists to be able to show work alongside people they might never otherwise be programmed with—for those combinations to create unexpected connections between the work, the artists, and our audience. I also want to expand the festival’s footprint across downtown New York, taking over more spaces and neighborhoods all throughout Lower Manhattan. Ultimately, I see the festival as part of a much larger artistic ecosystem. I’m also a filmmaker and producer working on a few projects that connect to that broader “Downtown” world. I can’t say too much yet but there’s more coming soon.

Do you prioritize anything in particular when programming short films and music videos? Or, say, a TV pilot?

Point of view above everything. With shorts especially, I’m very resistant to the idea that they’re simply calling cards or proof-of-concepts for features. A short should justify its own form, you know? It should feel like the artist chose that length because it was exactly the right container for the idea. With a TV pilot, I’m looking for the same thing: specificity, meaning, and whether the work creates a world I want to spend time in, or at least one that feels unmistakably its own. In the case of Fellas , you guys created a world that genuinely makes me laugh, but also has a lot of heart. I’m so excited for you to share it with our audience.

Fellas by Matthew Danger Lippman

The Roxy is an interesting space to hold a festival. As a single-screen theater, there’s a big bleed-through of the crowd for something that just ended and something that’s just beginning—you genuinely can’t tell who’s who. I fear I’m answering my own question, but can you tell me what you especially like about hosting a festival there?

They have been incredible hosts of The Downtown Festival’s film program! And after a few days, Roxy Cinema starts to feel like our little clubhouse—it’s the best. I love the setup and energy there because there’s so much natural crossover. People come out of one screening and run into someone arriving for the next, filmmakers stay for other films. Everyone ends up catching up in the lobby or green room. I’ve seen real deals get made and really awesome collaborations begin there. Remind me to tell you the story about Abel [Ferrara] yelling to Susan Seidelman’s husband from inside the cinema because he wanted to stay for Abel’s film but Susan had made a dinner reservation and they needed to leave ASAP. Hilarious.

Illyse Singer, the cinema’s director, has been incredibly, incredibly supportive of me on the filmmaking side of things as well as with the festival. I love her very much. The cinema’s projectionists Mitchell [Mailloux Glidden] and Dillon [Friend] really hold it down with all of the files (a massive undertaking) and the rest of the staff are amazing. It’s also just a beautiful place to watch a movie—like watching a film inside a jewel box. It’s a very intimate setting, which is different from some larger festivals where you’re in a massive theater watching a filmmaker speak on a stage that feels very far away—physically and emotionally!

Like any proper festival director, you have a great sense of style. What do you prioritize for Downtown fits?

[Laughs] That’s really nice of you. My go-to is sequins and leather pants—I basically spend the entire festival running around dressed like Michael Jackson.

The Downtown Festival is now underway.

content.article_text:
There’s a lot going on in the opening scene of Everything Else is Noise , but director Nicolás Pereda hardly has to move his camera. It just sits there, gazing out the window and onto a Mexico City intersection as a traffic jam forms from construction. In one long, continuous shot, vehicles accumulate and block the box, forcing oncoming drivers to make dangerous maneuvers that instigate horns and sirens—a soundtrack supplemented by the sustained notes of a cello coming from inside. The cacophony of noise is enough for a new father downstairs to knock on the door and ask his cellist neighbor, Tere (Teresita Sanchez), to quiet down. She’s already made a similar pact with another bothered tenant, but this request seems absurd considering the blaring noise outside. As Tere will be reminded throughout the rest of this wry, knowing, minimalist comedy of manners, she’s always at the mercy of other men’s schedules, preferences, and selective ears.

Pereda ( Lazaro at Night ), a veteran Mexican filmmaker whose films frequently dabble between fantasy and reality, stays inside Tere’s plant-filled apartment for the rest of the movie. There’s too much activity to leave, anyway. On this loud morning, Tere has lent her living space to her friend Rosa (Rosa Estela Juárez Vargas), another cellist and fellow composer, so she can film a cable-television interview about her craft. When the interviewer Lázaro (Lázaro G. Rodríguez, Pereda’s longtime collaborator), and his cameraman, Paco (Francisco Barreiro), show up to record, the power shuts off, the camera’s audio malfunctions, and the next-door dog won’t stop barking—among several hiccups that turn this shoot into a cursed, comical experience.

Between the humorous fits and starts, the pair interrogate Rosa with some basic questions that she entertains in short, slightly stubborn answers. The stilted rapport builds a stuffy atmosphere, and at times it seems Lázaro and Paco are mailing in their questions like a group homework project. This gives Tere—and later, her daughter Luisa (Luisa Pardo), lurking in the corner of the room—a chance to interject with her own answers (and force Paco to mic her up) about the trio’s work in a male-dominated field, even relaying a fantastical story about how the scent of rat influenced her to become a composer. Lázaro can’t tell she’s fibbing (or, at least, partially fibbing) and proceeds to take her seriously, yet asks none of the follow-up questions that such a revelation would warrant. He’s just there to collect material he needs.

About halfway through Noise , Pereda adds some stylistic flourishes that don’t announce themselves so much as sneak up on you. When Lázaro and Paco step outside, waiting for the power to return, Pereda stays keyed into their conversation while the camera remains on the three women. It’s an eerie, effective juxtaposition, like you’re eavesdropping without any visual reference. The pair exchange small talk until Lázaro explains that this messy, all-day interview might have real merit only because of the fact that Luisa’s father (and Tere’s one-time lover) is the legendary composer Estevez (José Rodríguez López). Upon their return, Lázaro brings up the maestro and recedes into an easy corner of questioning. “What was his influence on you?” he asks Rosa, as though nobody in the room might have their own source of inspiration.

Pereda and his co-writer Juan Francisco Maldonado nestle into this subtly ingrained groove of sexism (including an awkward scene in which Paco attempts to ascertain Lusia’s number for a movie he’s directing) throughout the rest of the 70 minutes, a runtime that cuts off opportunity for a deeper examination of the complicated family dynamics at its core—namely the relationship between Tere and Luisa, which boils into a frustrated third-person conversation about their generational insecurities. Still, there’s enough to infer in the way Luisa spats about her mother having her at 18 and losing her independence or Tere believing her daughter hasn’t to terms with her lack of vocation. They have history and musical gifts and a shared understanding that will never be given due credit.

What binds them is the patriarch, the maestro that Lázaro seems to care more about anyway—all the more evident when Estevez stops by at night and captures the interviewer’s full attention. As they rabble under candlelight, Tere and Luisa listen to his self-congratulatory list of accomplishments and projects and the predicted talking points that never change. They can’t handle the reality of this chaotic day and this secondary existence, but can at least indulge in its preposterousness. “You’ve spent your whole life doing what other people want,” Luisa advises her mother. “Stop caring so much.” What better way than to laugh?

Everything Else is Noise screened at the 64th New York Film Festival and will be released by Pragda.

content.title_original: Tenzing review – reconstruction of first summit of Everest puts Sherpa at the centre of the story
content.article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "H ere is a well intentioned, watchable, if sometimes soft-edged film with some NatGeo production values on high mountain peaks. The subject is the triumphant Mount Everest expedition of 1953, in which the ultimate ascent was achieved by Sherpa mountaineer Tenzing Norgay and New Zealander Edmund Hillary.", "links": [{"text": "Mount Everest", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/world/everest"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Tenzing, a former guide whose unparalleled knowledge of the mountain and exemplary climbing skills earned him promotion to full team member, is played here by Genden Phuntsok, a Chinese actor of Tibetan descent, while Hillary is robustly portrayed by Tom Hiddleston. Screenwriter Luke Davies and director Jennifer Peedom have the decent aim of restoring Tenzing’s achievement to the centre of the narrative, a tale which at the time was resoundingly claimed for Hillary and the British empire: a glorious redemption of Scott’s Antarctic ordeal 41 years earlier and a sign of divine approval for the imminent coronation of Queen Elizabeth II."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "For years, many assumed that Tenzing was somehow Hillary’s servant or military-style batman, a Sancho Panza figure to whom Hillary had just been sentimentally loyal. But Tenzing is the hero of this story, and the narrative of the great climb with Hillary and expedition leader John Hunt (Willem Dafoe) is interspersed with flashbacks to his early life – not Hillary’s – starting with his awestruck childhood encounter with the legendary British alpinist George Mallory, played in cameo by Johnny Flynn. He starts as an eager boy, passionate about the mountain, for which he uses the Tibetan name Chomolungma (though the name “Mount Everest” is not here stigmatised like “Ayers Rock” or “Snowdon”). His biddable good nature and instinctive mastery of the terrain make him indispensable to other countries’ expeditions (although these are not featured in the flashback sections) and, finally, to the British."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "There are vertiginous moments of peril in the climb, but this is not exactly a bromance between Tenzing and Hillary; it is more a romance between Tenzing and the mountain. Nor is it specifically a rebuke to British imperial arrogance; both men were in their way outsiders to the stiff-upper-lip British club. content.article_text:
H ere is a well intentioned, watchable, if sometimes soft-edged film with some NatGeo production values on high mountain peaks. The subject is the triumphant Mount Everest expedition of 1953, in which the ultimate ascent was achieved by Sherpa mountaineer Tenzing Norgay and New Zealander Edmund Hillary.

Tenzing, a former guide whose unparalleled knowledge of the mountain and exemplary climbing skills earned him promotion to full team member, is played here by Genden Phuntsok, a Chinese actor of Tibetan descent, while Hillary is robustly portrayed by Tom Hiddleston. Screenwriter Luke Davies and director Jennifer Peedom have the decent aim of restoring Tenzing’s achievement to the centre of the narrative, a tale which at the time was resoundingly claimed for Hillary and the British empire: a glorious redemption of Scott’s Antarctic ordeal 41 years earlier and a sign of divine approval for the imminent coronation of Queen Elizabeth II.

For years, many assumed that Tenzing was somehow Hillary’s servant or military-style batman, a Sancho Panza figure to whom Hillary had just been sentimentally loyal. But Tenzing is the hero of this story, and the narrative of the great climb with Hillary and expedition leader John Hunt (Willem Dafoe) is interspersed with flashbacks to his early life – not Hillary’s – starting with his awestruck childhood encounter with the legendary British alpinist George Mallory, played in cameo by Johnny Flynn. He starts as an eager boy, passionate about the mountain, for which he uses the Tibetan name Chomolungma (though the name “Mount Everest” is not here stigmatised like “Ayers Rock” or “Snowdon”). His biddable good nature and instinctive mastery of the terrain make him indispensable to other countries’ expeditions (although these are not featured in the flashback sections) and, finally, to the British.

There are vertiginous moments of peril in the climb, but this is not exactly a bromance between Tenzing and Hillary; it is more a romance between Tenzing and the mountain. Nor is it specifically a rebuke to British imperial arrogance; both men were in their way outsiders to the stiff-upper-lip British club. Hiddleston plays Hillary as frank, thoughtful, practical, with no side to him; Phuntsok maintains Tenzing’s boyish innocence. Would a Tibetan film-maker have immersed us even more thoroughly in Tenzing’s world and excluded the British more? Maybe. At any rate, Genden Phuntsok’s charm carries the picture.

Tenzing is in UK and US cinemas from 9 October and Australian cinemas from 16 October, and on Apple TV from 16 October.
