content.article_text:
Del regreso de Carrie a una historia criminal ambientada en Los Ángeles, estas son las cinco series que recomendamos para disfrutar este fin de semana en las principales plataformas de streaming.

Si estás buscando algo nuevo para ver este fin de semana, las plataformas de streaming renuevan sus catálogos con propuestas para todos los gustos. Desde el terror y el suspenso hasta la comedia dramática, hay cinco series que merecen un lugar en tu lista. En Cinéfilos, repasamos qué ver en Netflix , Prime Video , Apple TV+ , Disney+ y HBO Max .

Carrie – Prime Video

La nueva adaptación de Carrie , basada en la novela de Stephen King, llega con una propuesta que traslada la historia de terror a los tiempos actuales. Desarrollada por Mike Flanagan, esta versión presenta a una joven que debe enfrentarse al despiadado ecosistema de su instituto tras la repentina muerte de su padre.

Interpretada por Summer H. Howell, Carrie atraviesa una etapa marcada por la presión constante, la crueldad de sus compañeros y el impacto de las redes sociales. A medida que despiertan sus misteriosos poderes telequinéticos, la adolescente deberá lidiar con una situación que amenaza con cambiarlo todo.

Con Mike Flanagan al frente, la producción propone una nueva mirada sobre uno de los relatos más conocidos de Stephen King, con el terror adolescente como eje central.

Bajo la superficie – Netflix

Para quienes buscan una historia de misterio con elementos de terror, Bajo la superficie ( Below ) es una alternativa para tener en cuenta. La miniserie canadiense cuenta con seis episodios y presenta una amenaza inesperada en un pequeño pueblo de Terranova.

Te puede interesar

Mike Flanagan se refirió a las comparativas entre Carrie y Stranger Things: “Para mí, no tiene sentido…”

Qué ver este fin de semana: 4 películas y series que son tendencia en Netflix, HBO Max, Prime Video y Disney+

La tranquilidad de sus habitantes se ve alterada cuando una misteriosa criatura marina comienza a sembrar el terror. En medio de la incertidumbre, un curtido pescador y su familia se convierten en la única esperanza de sus vecinos.

Con Josh Hartnett, Mackenzie Davis y Charlie Heaton entre sus protagonistas, la producción combina suspenso, intriga y monstruos en una historia que pone a prueba a toda una comunidad.

Pequeños profetas – Apple TV+

Si preferís una propuesta que combine comedia y drama con un toque fantástico, Pequeños profetas ( Small Prophets ) puede ser una buena elección. La serie sigue a Michael Sleep, un hombre excéntrico que lleva una vida aparentemente ordinaria mientras continúa aferrado a la esperanza de reencontrarse con Clea, su pareja desaparecida hace siete años.

Su rutina cambia cuando decide experimentar con una antigua receta que combina agua de lluvia, estiércol de caballo y bastante alquimia. El objetivo es crear homúnculos, pequeños seres mágicos capaces de predecir el futuro.

Con la esperanza de encontrar una respuesta sobre el paradero de Clea, Michael se embarca en una búsqueda tan insólita como personal. Creada y protagonizada por Mackenzie Crook, la ficción británica mezcla humor, fantasía y una historia atravesada por la pérdida y la incertidumbre. Además, ya fue renovada para una segunda temporada.

The Drop: Una saga de Snowfall – Disney+

El universo criminal de Snowfall se expande con The Drop: Una saga de Snowfall , una serie ambientada en Los Ángeles durante la década de 1990, cuando el crack transformaba las calles y redefinía el poder en distintos barrios de la ciudad.

La historia pone el foco en los territorios controlados por los Bloods y los Crips, que se convierten en el epicentro de una escena musical emergente en South Central. En ese contexto, el crimen organizado, las disputas territoriales y la cultura urbana se entrecruzan en un relato que explora una etapa decisiva para la ciudad.

Con una propuesta que combina drama y crimen, la ficción busca ampliar el universo de Snowfall y ofrecer una nueva perspectiva sobre el entorno social y cultural que marcó aquella época.

Youth – HBO Max

Para cerrar las recomendaciones, Youth propone una comedia dramática británica centrada en las complicaciones de la vida adulta y los vínculos familiares. La serie sigue a una mujer divorciada de 50 años que intenta encontrar un equilibrio entre su vida amorosa, el cuidado de sus padres y las responsabilidades que implica acompañar a su hijo adulto.

Con Sharon Horgan y Rupert Friend entre sus protagonistas, la ficción aborda las dificultades de reorganizar la propia vida cuando las obligaciones familiares y los deseos personales parecen avanzar en direcciones opuestas.

A través de situaciones cotidianas, la producción explora las relaciones, las segundas oportunidades y los desafíos de una etapa en la que volver a empezar puede resultar tan complicado como necesario

content.article_text:
Announcement

New Art Books from the Quarto Group

From art history to instruction, Quarto publishes visually-rich books for artists of all mediums and skill levels.

Quarto publishes visually-rich books for artists of all mediums and skill levels. Explore highlights from the 2026 collection!

Light & Color in the Watercolor Landscape

By Vladislav Yeliseyev Discover the secrets to capturing depth, atmosphere, and emotion in your watercolor landscapes with Light and Color in the Watercolor Landscape . Acclaimed artist and instructor Vladislav Yeliseyev shares his proven techniques for harnessing light and shadow, creating luminous colors, and refining compositions to enhance realism and impact.

Frida Kahlo at Home

By Suzanne Barbezat Discover the intimate spaces that shaped one of the world’s most iconic artists. This compelling visual biography traces Kahlo’s life through the places she loved, from her childhood in Coyoacán and her student years in Mexico City, to her time in the United States, and her final return to La Casa Azul. Drawing on archival photographs, family images, personal artefacts, and Frida’s own paintings, the book uncovers how home was not merely a backdrop but a central force in her art and self‑expression.

New Lessons in Landscape Painting

By Mitchell Albala Refine and expand your landscape painting skills with this next-level guide by award-winning painter and bestselling author Mitchell Albala. New Lessons in Landscape Painting builds on the success of the bestselling The Landscape Painter’s Workbook , with new topics, step-by-step exercises, demonstrations, and in-depth painting analyses. Each is designed to build stronger skills in the core practices of landscape painting: shape interpretation, composition, and color.

The Wild Magic of Iceland

By Norris Niman For centuries, the breathtaking waterfalls, fierce volcanoes, and sweeping green hills of Iceland have captivated travelers’ imaginations. In The Wild Magic of Iceland , acclaimed photographer and adventurer Norris Niman transports you to these and more picturesque sites on a visual adventure through the seasons, featuring 100+ dazzling photographs.

Paul Nicklen: A Photography Masterclass

By Paul Nicklen Join Paul Nicklen – renowned conservationist, wildlife and art photographer – for a rare, tell-all masterclass in photography. Drawing on more than three decades of experience, including 20 years of shooting for National Geographic, Nicklen distils his craft into 20 key lessons, each with a clear and simple takeaway.

Art of the New York Subway

By Adrian Brune Step into the world’s largest underground art museum with Art of the New York Subway , a stunning tribute to the artistry that transforms the New York subway from a transit system into a cultural landmark. Tracing nearly 200 stations of the subway, this book celebrates the fusion of architecture, design and public art that defines New York’s identity.

Wanderlust Ink

By Ollie Smither Wanderlust Ink is a stunning collection of fine-line tattoo designs that amaze and inspire. These thoughtful, hand-drawn designs by popular artist and designer Ollie Smither (@os.illustration) demonstrate a passion for travel, adventure, nature, and connectivity of all kinds.

The Art of the Unknown

By S. Elizabeth The Art of the Unknown is an enthralling journey for anyone fascinated by mystery and the esoteric, inviting you to look again at the forces that persist just beyond the threshold of ordinary reality, and to discover how artists have long attempted to make the invisible visible.

Learn more at quarto.com

content.article_text:
Art Review

A Felix Gonzalez-Torres Exhibition Forgets What He Was Fighting For

“Sweet Revenge” at the Reina Sofía gives the impression of a showcase of a second-generation Minimalist artist, emphasizing form over anything else.

Hyperallergic )

MADRID — The long-awaited exhibition Felix Gonzalez-Torres: Sweet Revenge at the Museo Reina Sofía opens with an emphasis on Madrid’s role in the artist's life. Gonzalez-Torres briefly lived here as a Cuban child refugee in 1971 before moving on to Puerto Rico and New York. While this marks his first large-scale solo exhibition in the Spanish capital, it follows a landmark show at the Centro Galego de Arte Contemporánea in Santiago de Compostela in 1995, just before his death from AIDS-related complications; a 2000 group show ( No es sólo lo que ves: Pervirtiendo el Minimalismo) at the Reina Sofía itself; and a 2021 exhibition at the Museu d’Art Contemporani de Barcelona framed by the COVID-19 pandemic. By centering his brief history as a refugee, the present exhibition challenges our traditional understanding of Gonzalez-Torres's trajectory. Why, though, are many of his most politically charged works missing?

The exhibition unfolds across seven galleries on the first floor of the Sabatini Building, featuring more than 50 works by Gonzalez-Torres: his iconic candy spills, text portraits, puzzles, beaded curtains, paper stacks, and photographs, alongside quotes by the artist printed on the gallery walls. Strikingly, there is no chronological framework. The exhibition was curated by artist Alejandro Cesarco and Nancy Spector, the former Guggenheim artistic director and chief curator who organized Gonzalez-Torres's definitive 1995 retrospective in New York. They drew inspiration for the show's title and central theme from the blue candy spill “‘ Untitled’ (Revenge) ” (1991), a work the artist created after returning to Madrid as an adult. He would later reflect on the personal significance of the visit: “I returned to Madrid nearly twenty years later — sweet revenge.” According to a wall text, being sent to Madrid as a child refugee “was a traumatic experience, one that heavily informed his preoccupations with memory and repetition.”

Felix Gonzalez-Torres: Sweet Revenge with "'Untitled' (Revenge)" (1991) (photo Roberto Ruiz, courtesy Museo Reina Sofía)

Adopting “Sweet Revenge” as their operational framework, the curators highlight the ambiguity and complexity of Gonzalez-Torres’s works, which often oscillate between aesthetic beauty and critical engagement. They present a parallel text titled "Methodology" in the entrance hall, outlining the principles, instructions, and responsibilities that guide the exhibition. This text explains the logistics behind the replenishable candy piles, paper stacks, and alterable text portraits, detailing how they are to be presented and expanded upon. Ultimately, the curators seem to focus more on the mechanics of Gonzalez-Torres's works than on what he was trying to say.

content.article_text:
Moving work by artists from two generations is evocatively installed at Japan House

In London for Frieze? Luckily you can still see Kyotographie: Kawada Kikuji x Iwane Ai , on show at Japan House London until 18 October. Organised by the celebrated Japanese photography festival, the exhibition brings together two image-makers whose work resonates with shared concerns about how we place ourselves in the world, how we travel through life, and how photography can represent both.

Kawada presents works from the 1950s until today, including his series Chizu (The Map) ; published as a book in 1965, exactly 20 years after the US dropped an atomic bomb on Hiroshima, it records munitions bunkers, Special Forces soldiers, and survivors with facial scars. It also shows Lucky Strike cigarettes and Coca-Cola bottles, American consumer goods Kawada found in the wrecked city.

Kawada came to prominence in the 1960s, after founding the VIVO collective with image-makers such as Eikoh Hosoe and Shōmei Tōmatsu; eschewing the quasi-objective documentary photograph they embraced an “are-bure-boke” – “blurry and out-of-focus” – approach that evoked a deeper reality. “I don’t start out with a title or theme in mind,” Kawada says in a video made with Kyotographie. “But then suddenly, unexpectedly, something really not logically, but intuitively, appears out of nowhere. That’s how it works.”

His installation also includes a projection room, flicking through shots he recently posted on Instagram; Kawada continues to play with his medium, still restlessly experimental though he’s now nearing 100 years old. “Since photography inevitably cuts out a single moment, that also means you can reconstruct time in any way you like,” he says. “When various layers of time overlap, then human psychology, the atmosphere of an era, the state of society, even my own mental state – all these emerge. That’s why I always take this approach.”

“I don’t start out with a title or theme in mind. But then suddenly, unexpectedly, something really not logically, but intuitively, appears out of nowhere.” Kawada Kikuji

Born in 1975, Iwane is from a different generation yet testing limits runs through her practice too. She’s showing a work titled Kipuka , which she shot in 2018; focusing on Japanese immigrant communities in Hawaii, it centres on the o-bon, a festival for honouring the ancestors and the dead. The festival includes a circular dance, and a particular song, the ‘Fukushima Ondo’, originally from the area devastated by the 2011 earthquake, tsunami, and nuclear accident.

Using a rotating panoramic camera – traditionally used by these communities to photograph funerals – Iwane gathers the many individuals at the festival, and displays the resulting long prints as curling walkways. The visitor must walk in between, immersing themselves in the crowd. Her images also include panoramic shots of cemeteries, and of the destruction wrought on quiet streets, by a nature that’s beyond human control.

Iwane is also showing her series A New River, shot during the Covid pandemic in 2020. It shows cherry trees in bloom, something celebrated in Japan with outdoor parties which include family and friends but also a bittersweet sense of transience; Iwane includes figures from Japanese folklore too, suggesting a respect for nature and spirituality that photography, and the scientific worldview from which it emerged, tried to sideline. A New River is also underpinned by a very personal grief, because Iwane was under a blossoming cherry tree when she found out that her sister had died. Images of her sister also feature, in a moving projection of shots gathered after her death.

“It was a very hard time for me for a long time, and I kept thinking about her every day,” says Iwane, in a video made by Kyotographie. “Maybe after one or a couple of years, there was the day that I realised ‘Oh today I never thought about her’. So during the making of A New River, I recalled the day that I realised I forgot about her and I thought ‘Maybe I will forget about this strange time of the state of emergency’, and about how easily people can forget about things. So then I started to search for photographs that I have taken of my sister and my family, because I won’t be able to photograph my sister or anyone who has passed but the picture and the memory stay.”

Kyotographie festival is noted for its innovative approach to installation and the exhibition at Japan House is no exception; made with the help of spatial designer Hiromitsu Konishi, it includes the circle as a motif. A round table gathers Kawada’s publications in a room devoted to his The Last Cosmology, for example, which features celestial phenomena such as eclipses. In Iwane’s show, the panoramic shots snake through the gallery, while images from A New River hang in concentric waves round the visitor.

Throughout, the exhibition is darkly-lit, spotlights picking out the photographs; the viewer’s first-hand reality is thrown into shadow and the world of the images surfaces, but this is less photography as observation, and more evocation of emotion.

Kyotographie: Kawada Kikuji x Iwane Ai is on show at Japan House London until 18 October. www.japanhouselondon.uk

content.article_text:
Announcement

Over $100,000 in Prizes and New Public Art Opportunities at 2027 ArtFields Festival

Southern artists can apply now to show in Lake City, SC, where the whole town becomes a gallery April 15 - May 1, 2027.

A small town in South Carolina may not be the first place you think of when it comes to the Southʼs art scene, but each spring Lake City proves otherwise. For three weeks, storefronts, restaurants, and galleries become a town-wide exhibition during the ArtFields Festival, which returns April 15 – May 1, 2027 .

Now celebrating its 15th year, ArtFields invites emerging and established artists from across the Southeast to apply . From now through November 1, 2026, artists working in any medium and living in Alabama, Arkansas, Florida, Georgia, Kentucky, Louisiana, Mississippi, North Carolina, South Carolina, Tennessee, Virginia, or West Virginia can submit one 2D or 3D work to the festivalʼs signature juried competition. Around 400 works are selected for exhibition, competing for more than $100,000 in cash prizes, including a $50,000 Grand Prize. The entry fee is $25.

For the first time, ArtFields is also accepting public art proposals during the same window. Artists with an idea for an outdoor, large-scale, site-specific installation —the kind of project that needs more room than a gallery wall— can propose it for the streets and spaces of Lake City by the same November 1 deadline. There is no fee to apply.

Since 2013, ArtFields has grown from a bold idea to elevate artists living and working in the South into a year-round arts organization, awarding more than $1 million in prize money along the way. The festival also features a live portrait contest, plein air painting, and more, with details available on the ArtFields website .

For more information and to apply, visit artfieldssc.org .

content.article_text:
Lee Friedlander, Maria and Erik, New City, New York , 1961

Reviews - October 9, 2026

Piper French

Lee and Maria Friedlander recount the beginning of their long life together in much the same way. After running into her at the Sports Illustrated offices, where she worked as an assistant—women weren’t allowed to write for the magazine in 1958—Lee called Maria up and asked her to a Count Basie show at the jazz club Birdland. “I went and—it never stopped,” she told the gallerist Jeffrey Fraenkel in 2019. In Lee’s telling, they went to see Basie—“And that was it.” First date, rest of life. They have now been married sixty-eight years.

For each of those years, Lee has taken portraits of his wife: Maria caught in profile; Maria by Lee’s side; Maria holding their infant son; Maria at the wheel; Maria dozing off in the grass; Maria in Paris, Santa Fe, or Wales; Maria doing the crossword with their now adult daughter; Maria reading the funny pages with her daughter’s young son.

Wales , 1992

Maria and Giancarlo, New City , 2001

The photographs, currently on display at San Francisco’s Fraenkel Gallery, are clearly “Friedlanders.” They have a formal rigor to them. They are all monochrome. Lee, the original selfie king, is often present—sometimes only obliquely, his shadow stamped onto Maria; always in the clarity of his vision. But these pictures are also more intimate than much of Lee’s work. A 1974 photograph taken on a camping trip in Colorado is an apt spatial rendering of the family dynamic, with its uneasy miasma of romantic and domestic love. In the right half of the image, the couple’s children occupy themselves at the picnic table; on its left, Maria, in dishabille, meets Lee’s gaze from the back of the camper, a look of sly complicity creasing her face. These portraits document the relentless etchings of time: Maria’s cheeks hollow; a furrow appears in her forehead; her mane of black hair lightens and one day reappears cropped short. Later images of her reclining, legs splayed, or reviewing documents in her underwear are discomfiting, and forceful, in their rare combination of aging, eroticism, and the mundane.

Maria, New City, New York , 1971

The word muse does not seem quite right here: Lee felt the compulsion to make photographs long before he met Maria, and he would have gone on doing so if there had been no Sports Illustrated encounter, no Basie show. (“What’s in front of me starts to get photographed. And Maria has been in front of me a lot,” he told one interviewer, characteristically unsentimental.) But his portraits evince a steady desire to keep looking and an awareness of what they cannot see, two qualities that seem essential to the tenacity of a marriage. Consider Maria’s appraisal of why their sometimes troubled relationship endured: “No matter what was going on, we always did what we said we were going to do.” “I’m certainly curious about Maria,” Lee said, more than thirty years in. “I still am.”

Maria, Las Vegas , 1970

In some of these images, Maria revels in Lee’s gaze, preening like a rock star or a fashion icon; in others, she seems to reluctantly tolerate it, or merely looks back at him, inscrutable. Who knows what she’s thinking? She has compared the experience of looking back at Lee’s pictures of their shared past to “rereading a private journal.” Unlike Lee, who is often comically taciturn when asked about his work, Maria’s essays and interviews allow us a degree of access into that hidden world. They reveal a life not merely documented by her husband’s camera but also molded by it. She recalls her discomfort, in the years after his late ’70s Nudes series, when women they knew socially would brazenly ask him to shoot them naked. Photographs Lee took in 1979 of a then unknown Madonna later put their children through college; Lee and Maria went to the theater to see Desperately Seeking Susan and realized that his former nude model was now a famous singer and actress. Other luminaries appear, at decidedly human scale. (Maria is drily hilarious on the topic of Garry Winogrand, Lee’s contemporary: “Garry seemed happy as he said his third ‘I do’”; “Garry never punched anyone in our house.”) Lee made his first portrait of Maria with Walker Evans’s camera.

New City, New York , 1962

All photographs © the artist and courtesy Fraenkel Gallery, San Francisco and Luhring Augustine, New York

Maria’s Shadow, New City, New York , 2012

Maria has written about the emotional whiplash of seeing the arc of her family’s life represented in book form. The passage of decades can seem to collapse in on itself: There she and Lee are with their young children, and a few pages later, those same children have grown up and are holding babies of their own. Fraenkel’s visual presentation achieves the same effect. The photographs on the main wall of the gallery balloon outward in the fullness of midlife, then taper. The final portrait shows the couple’s shadows, shoulders touching. You feel the weight of life and its ephemerality; the endless span of days, weeks, months, and the speed with which, looking back, it has vanished.

In 2019, when Fraenkel interviewed Maria for a Friedlander retrospective, she spoke bluntly about the vicissitudes of old age. Her eyesight was failing, robbing her of “one of the greatest pleasures of my life.” Lee, meanwhile, had whittled down the substance of his own life, retreating into his work: “The darkroom has become his cupola.” Nearly everything has gone, but Lee and Maria are still there, together. And so is Lee’s camera.

content.article_text:
Dayanita Singh at ARCHIVIO , Archivio di Stato, Venice, 2026 Photograph by Mark Henley

Interviews - October 9, 2026

Earlier this year, the artist Dayanita Singh staged an unusual exhibition in Venice. She wanted to present a project during the Venice Biennale but to avoid the enormous financial and practical costs associated with the world’s most famous art extravaganza. Singh, who has photographed archives in Italy for more than a decade—and whose own voluminous archive has been the subject of many inventive installations—worked with the national archives at the Archivio di Stato, which provided an airy, double-height storage room (otherwise closed to the public) where shelves were lined with boxes of official documents. Singh’s own black-and-white photographs were arranged on fifteen four-sided, freestanding (but collapsible) wooden structures, inviting visitors into a choreographic experience arranged with minimal shipping expenses. Students served as docents in exchange for Singh’s mentorship, part of what she calls the “friendship economy” she relied upon to produce ARCHIVIO . In June, I visited the space with Singh, who told me why she considerers herself an archivist and how photography can democratize the art world.

ARCHIVIO , Archivio di Stato, Venice, 2026. All photographs by Luca Girardini

Sarah Meister: How did your ARCHIVIO exhibition come about? And how did you learn about the Archivio di Stato?

Dayanita Singh: In 2002, I was an artist in residence at the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum in Boston. And I was photographing chairs, because at the Gardner Museum, what can you do, right? So that’s where my chair obsession started. And then, Pieranna Cavalchini, the curator of contemporary art, said, “If you’re going to focus on chairs, you have to photograph some Renaissance chairs.”

So, she brought me to Florence, to Fausto Calderai, who’s a furniture historian, who also introduced me to chairs, but he also introduced me to his friend who looked after the Corsini Archive. When I went to the Corsini Archive, my jaw dropped. A little bit like when I first went to the Vespa factory in India.

Meister: That’s an amazing archive.

Singh: But then, as you know, I did a lot of work with archives in India. Later, around 2013 and 2014, Pieranna introduced me to Barbara Bianchini and Luigi Vigevani, who have an apartment in Venice. They’re professors in Milan, and they offered to let me to stay there. I walk into the apartment, and they had acquired work from my Hamburger Bahnhof show in 2003. So they said, “Stay.” [ laughs ]

I had been in the Venice Biennale in 2011 and in 2013, so I was familiar with Venice. My friend Massimo Warglien, a professor at Ca’ Foscari University, said that they’re doing a project with Archivio Stato with IBM. He thought it would be interesting for me to see this archive. So, it was because of Massimo that I got permission to come to the archive. This was maybe 2015. And from then on, every time I could come to Venice, I came because of this archive.

I’ve been photographing in this room for ten years, and then the director of the archive invites me to do a show here, about a year and a half ago. And I said, “Of course. It’s a dream. I would love to.”

Meister: One of the things that I think you and I both love about photography is how it helps us catalog and understand the world around us. I just saw the Spanish Pavilion, where Oriol Vilanova installed thousands of postcards. The space where you have been working is a space where the impulse to catalog is functioning almost on a municipal level. How do photographs and memories move from that institutional idea into something else for you?

Singh: You know what it’s made me realize is that for all the things I’m not—I’m not a photographer, I’m not this, I’m not that. I am an archivist. And I think that’s what I’ve done my whole life, is to archive places, people that I’ve been drawn to. So, of course, it’s a completely subjective archive. It was impossible to make these pillars just with images of the archives, so instead I started to excavate my own archive of twenty-five years.

Meister: All in Italy.

Singh: Yeah, all in Italy. Because, because of this friendship network that got set up.

Meister: These institutional archives are organized according to a certain municipal function. But the archives in your own home are different. How do you approach that? Because I’ve seen you sort and re-sort and re-sort.

Singh: So, the archive keeps shifting, much to the annoyance of anyone who might want to look through it. These were cataloged as chairs, and there’s a chairs folder. For ARCHIVIO , we have cities—Palermo, Naples—and that made it the most direct connection to this show. But I’m not sure. I mean, here is Rome. Other than say the Colosseum there, you don’t see Rome. You don’t see Palermo. And yet friends from Rome tell me this is more Rome than any big image of Rome. So, I went from my cataloging things like glass or statues to places. The other thing was to try and think of the form.

Meister: I do feel for whoever is responsible for your archive eventually, because they’re bound to wonder, “Was she thinking about stone? Was she thinking about place?”

Singh: Yeah. But every time I look at my archive, it changes, you know?

Meister: Andrea Anastasio described your work as a “relational cartography,” which I thought just beautifully captured the idea of the human centeredness but also the expansiveness. It’s a cartography of the world. What do you think of that idea?

Singh: I loved that he saw it was a human cartography—such a lovely word.

Meister: One of the interesting things around archives I think is the question of access. I’m curious how you approach that in your work?

Singh: For one, it was to make this space accessible so that people who live in the neighborhood, you know, it’s the first time those doors have been opened to the public.

For me, art is dissemination. So, when I call myself an offset artist, it’s not just the printing. It’s the dissemination.

Meister: And when they pulled them open, it was monumental.

Singh: Exactly. One of the main intentions of ARCHIVIO was to make the archive accessible in some form. People can’t go everywhere else, but at least they can see one cloister, and the room. And the work doesn’t even feel like an exhibition, because to me, it feels like it just grew out of the floor.

An interesting thing comes up in talking to the director of the archive and archivists. See, when I go to an archive, I don’t really open up anything. I don’t ask them. The archivist said, “You’ve never asked me to look at any document.” It’s the way archivists work, because in a lifetime you might only go through one shelf.

But you have to be able to read the code of the archive. And I thought that’s so much like my photography, where I have a certain map with which I enter a place. So, if I was coming to see you in Texas, I would first find out if there was a house museum there because that tells me something about a place. You know, people go to markets, people go to museums. This idea of the archivist photographer has become quite an important thought for me.

Meister: I think preservation is such an interesting thing. And there are different ways of thinking about preservation. I remember so fondly when you were at MoMA and all you wanted was for people to be able to touch your work.

Singh: Yeah.

Meister: I’d love to hear you speak about how you navigated the question of preservation here, from touching to organizing to temperature.

Singh: What I did here was I made exhibition copies. Because one of the things I don’t like about photography is that it’s so sensitive. That it has to be dark. You couldn’t be showing in a museum, you couldn’t have this kind of light for four months. And so I made exhibition copies.

Meister: I chuckled when I read Aruna D’Souza’s review in The New York Times , where she wrote, “What if I told you the most compelling art show in Venice right now consisted of black-and-white photos of Italian archives?” I love that what seems so incredible to the art world of course feels very natural.

Singh: Yes.

Meister: Would you talk about a few of the ways in which ARCHIVIO was so different from any other kind of installation in Venice now?

Singh: Well, mainly there was no sponsor. And I analyzed the costs involved in Venice. It would be about 150,000 euros, not for making the work, but just for various things. And each of those became a challenge for me. If I wanted docents for six months, 25,000 euros. Instead, we made a collaboration with Ca’ Foscari, and the Italian Cultural Institute in Delhi covered the shipping. I have docents here from Ca’ Foscari and Iuav University of Venice. They get credit. I mentor them.

Then I was told that lighting here would be 10,000 euros to light a show like this. And I said, “I’m perfectly happy with it.” But they said, “It’ll become dark early.” So, I said, “We’ll close the show early. We don’t have to have it till November. I’m not connected to this biennale.” And in fact, I didn’t open with the biennale. I opened with the literature festival to make that point. And that is the strength of photography, that it can go into so many different areas, no?

Meister: I agree. I’d be interested to hear you just share a little bit about where you see the democracy of photography, where you see its frailty, its edges, its constraints. Both how they’re operating here and about a way they might function, let’s say, in a space like Aperture in New York.

Singh: I think, I think going forward, it’s going to be the wall book for me. A wall book is that delicious space between being a print on the wall and a book in your bookshelf. I want to make a book that can be displayed on the wall as you would a watercolor, but still remain true to the book.

Meister: Are they different sizes?

Singh: No. It’s all the same size. They have sixty images and sixty different covers. And that’s all that would be available at one time. So, if you want this one, you have to get there in time.

Meister: Because otherwise there are only fifty-nine images left.

Singh: Yeah. Otherwise, you can get this one.

Meister: The work is the book. The covers are what vary and they reflect each of the pages of what’s inside. But the interiors of the books are the same.

Singh: Exactly. Like the Museum of Chance .

Meister: Everyone ultimately has access to the same thing.

Singh: And photography can really democratize the art world. But instead, we’ve gone the same route, right? With larger, larger prints, smaller, smaller editions—I’m part of that world—and higher prices. I think with the book object, everybody will find their own forms for it. I come from photography. For me, art is dissemination. So, when I call myself an offset artist, it’s not just the printing. It’s the dissemination.

ARCHIVIO was presented at the Archivio di Stato, Venice, from April 17–July 31, 2026, and is on view at the Museo Nazionale Etrusco di Villa Giulia, Rome, through January 3, 2027.

content.article_text:
Marguerite dans Le Théorème de Marguerite (2023) de Anna Novion Ella elle l’a ! C’est ce film qui a valu à Ella Rumpf sa statuette du meilleur espoir féminin aux Césars en 2024 (ainsi que celle du meilleur espoir féminin pour son coéquipier Julien Frison). Peut-être l’une des rares fois où les mathématiques ont inspiré avec autant de ferveur le cinéma, mettant en scène la quête obsessionnelle de Marguerite, étudiante nerd avec ses lunettes cerclées de fer un tantinet cliché, pour prouver la fameuse conjecture de Goldbach (nous non plus on n’y comprend pas grand chose). Attachante et brillante, Ella Rumpf apporte à son personnage une trajectoire nuancée – d’abord d’une nature réservée, elle évolue vers une ténacité impressionnante.

Céline dans Des preuves d’amour (2025) de Alice Douard Avec le délicat Des preuves d’amour , Ella Rumpf trouve un rôle à la hauteur de sa complexité et de sa profondeur. Elle y joue, Céline, amoureuse de Nadia (interprétée par notre québécoise chouchou Monia Chokri), qui accompagne sa femme dans les trois derniers mois d’un processus long et fastidieux de PMA à deux. La future maman cherche sa place dans un espace confiné aux yeux de la loi, de sa mère et de ses amis. Un espace gracieusement rempli par la comédienne, tout en parcimonie, qui évoque la direction d’acteurs de Jeanne Herry (laquelle y joue d’ailleurs le rôle d’une avocate). Résultat : ce couple aussi doux qu’imparfait touche en plein coeur.

Alexia dans Grave (2016), de Julia Ducournau Dans le premier film de Julia Ducournau (« Titane », « Alpha »), Ella Rumpf est Alexia, la soeur de Justine (interprétée par Garance Mariller), toutes deux en école de véto lorsqu’un bizutage que l’aînée inflige à sa cadette, mène cette dernière à des pulsions cannibales sidérantes. L’actrice, presque punk avec sa mèche brune sur le côté et son air gravement supérieur, adopte pour ce film un masque impassible, avec ses injonctions de grande soeur plutôt badass… Jusqu’à ce qu’elle ne puisse (presque) plus lever le petit doigt.

Angèle dans Coutures (2025) de Alice Winocour La réalisatrice de Revoir Paris (2022) invite Ella Rumpf au sein d’un trio insoupçonné de femmes, formé par Angelina Jolie et Anyier Anei. Dans ce drame sous haute couture signé Alice Winocour, l’actrice franco-suisse incarne un personnage de maquilleuse en galère, avec son col roulé et sa coupe en pagaille, propulsée en pleine Fashion Week, cachant derrière ses pinceaux un goût affirmé pour l’écriture… Un personnage tout en finesse qui aspire au beau, à la création, et nous dit qu’abandonner ses rêves n’est pas une option.

Stéphane dans L’Espèce explosive (2026) de Sarah Arnold Pour son premier film, faux thriller riche en épisodes rocambolesques et en dérision, Sarah Arnold transforme Ella Rumpf en psy du travail au bord du burn-out, et elle le fait bien. Stéphane est complexe, désorientée, tout en cherchant à recentrer ceux qui gravitent autour d’elle et en particulier Fulda (Alexis Manenti), ce brigadier un peu barré. Une fine équipe, en somme. La comédienne a tout l’air d’être aussi imprévisible que son personnage, et c’est sûrement ce qui fait qu’on aime la voir à l’écran. Avec ce choix de rôle, Ella Rumpf vise juste et ajoute une nouvelle couleur à sa palette de personnages, tous plus singuliers les uns que les autres.

Exhibition of the week

Tarek Atoui Sound art inspired by everyday objects and the eerie harmonies of history provides the latest artistic intervention in Tate Modern’s biggest space. Read more here . Turbine Hall, Tate Modern, London, from 13 October to 11 April

Also showing

Frieze London and Frieze Masters The colossal art fairs offering a luxurious view of the new, the old and everything in between. Regent’s Park, London, from 14-18 October

Cindy Sherman The latest surreal self-fashionings from this pioneer of the fantastic and grotesque. Hauser & Wirth, London, from 13 October until 23 December

Isaac Julien Julien’s film about 19th-century anti-slavery campaigner Frederick Douglass comes to a Scottish city where he delivered four of his inspiring speeches. Perth Museum, from 9 October until 11 April

Georg Baselitz: The Heroes Perhaps the most powerful and unforgettable works of the German artist who died this year. Thaddaeus Ropac, London, from 13 October until 18 December

Image of the week

Shopfront, scaffolding, throbbing car bodies … 37 artists take the temperature of the nation in a show which demonstrates the breadth and eccentricity of British identity. Read more about British Art Show 10: A Chorus of Strangers .

What we learned

Tate Britain missed the mark with breathlessly superficial exhibition of 90s art and fashion

Why children have always adored taking pictures – and what their images can tell us

Whether your brain can handle a show that only has white paintings

The Greek goddess Aphrodite was thrown on the rubbish heap in Oxford

Australia’s historic theatres and cinemas are the stuff of ritzy glamour

A £110m gallery can still run the risk of looking like a fashion mag

after newsletter promotion

Tories could be in hot water after using Stanley Chow’s cartoon portrait of Andy ‘Bottler’ Burnham without consent

Masterpiece of the week

An Angel in Red With a Lute by Giovanni Ambrogio de Predis, c 1495–1499

Leonardo da Vinci is said to have been sent to the court of Milan by Lorenzo de’ Medici to play on a bizarre stringed instrument of his own invention. His drawings do include inventions for novel musical devices. This painting is closely influenced by Leonardo: not only does it imitate his shadowed, dreamy style but it was originally part of the same altarpiece in Milan as his National Gallery masterpiece The Virgin of the Rocks. Leonardo, De Predis and every other Renaissance artist associated music with the mathematics of Pythagoras and the harmony of the universe: the angel here is playing, could we but hear it, such heavenly music. But it is the lute that suggests a very direct influence by Leonardo. The precise and detailed, entrancing way that De Predis depicts its nine strings and the angel’s highly realistic fingering echo Leonardo’s fascination with machinery and technology – in this case the sweet machinery of music. Painted under the hypnotic sway of the Tuscan polymath who was Milan’s court artist, this painting holds you charmed and soothed by the sound of silence. National Gallery, London

Looking for what to see in theaters? Our feature, updated weekly, highlights our top recommendations for films currently in theaters, from new releases to restorations receiving a proper theatrical run.

While we already provide extensive monthly new-release recommendations and weekly streaming recommendations , as distributors’ roll-outs can vary, this is a one-stop list to share the essential films that may be on a screen near you.

American Doctor (Poh Si Teng)

Poh Si Teng’s American Doctor is a harrowing, heartbreaking portrait of Palestinian, Jewish, and Zoroastrian doctors who are risking their lives to tend to the overwhelming victims of the ongoing genocide in Gaza and speak the truth in any way they can. Dan Mecca said in his Sundance review , “When will this end? When will this bloodshed stop? And when will the United States of America stop supporting it? Filmmaker Poh Si Teng offers a clear-eyed, unrelenting look at the genocide in Gaza with her documentary American Doctor . It follows three doctors––Dr. Feroze Sidhwa, Dr. Thaer Ahmad, and Dr. Mark Perlmutter––that are consistently trying to save lives in the Gaza Strip. On some trips they are approved to enter. On others they are denied for specious reasons. Dr. Perlmutter is Jewish, Dr. Sidhwa is Zoroastrian, and Dr. Ahmad is Palestinian. Their mission is the mission of all medical professionals: to heal everyone they can.”

Chronovisor (Kevin Walker and Jack Auen)

In a year of remarkable debuts, one of the most formally astounding comes with Kevin Walker and Jack Auen’s unclassifiable, riveting detective-meet-academia tale, Chronovisor . As Leonardo Goi said in our Rotterdam review , “Ostensibly set in the present, Chronovisor keeps jamming your temporal bearings. Save for the occasional smartphone, the ‘action,’ such as it is, unfolds in a world frozen in time (when Béatrice tries to contact one of Ernetti’s surviving relatives, it isn’t an email she sends but a typed letter). The focus gradually moves from the academic-turned-detective toward the media she consults: we hear recordings of a lecture Ernetti gave about his creation, watch old TV footage concerning the man and others who sought to communicate with the dead, but mostly we read . Chronovisor is so enamored with the written word that close-ups of books and articles comprise most of its runtime—with English translations of their various languages dished out not as subtitles but placed directly over the original text on the page. There’s nothing precious about the choice: Auen and Walker want you to read along with Béatrice, and what’s so fascinating about their film is the way it tries to combine two different art forms (literature and cinema) and different actions (reading and watching) all while adjusting its pace to the time needed to perform both.”

Fjord (Cristian Mungiu)

As with R.M.N. , Mungiu is in top-shelf operation. Fjord is a triumphant film that tugs at the spiritual and soulful in all of us, regardless of nation, creed, faith, or the rejection of all three. What the court will rule in both cases, and whether or not the Gheorghius will get back their kids, pulses with a pregnant tension as the nearly two-and-a-half-hour film proceeds in what seems 30 minutes. And its end will have you falling off the edge of your seat. – Luke H. ( full review )

Ha-Chan, Shake Your Booty! (Josef Kubota Wladyka)

One of the breakouts of the Sundance Film Festival this year, where it picked up the U.S. Dramatic Directing award, Josef Kubota Wladyka’s stylish and moving Ha-chan, Shake Your Booty! is coming this fall. Blake Simons said in his review , “In dance, you have to lead with confidence. Your partner looks to you for guidance, and they require you to look back at them responsively, to move instinctually without faltering. There’s need for surefootedness, consistency, and impeccable timing. Luckily for us, Josef Kubota Wladyka’s fun and deceptively frothy third feature Ha-chan, Shake Your Booty! has all of these qualities in spades.”

The History of Concrete (John Wilson)

Like a movie tie-in, John Wilson’s debut documentary feature, The History of Concrete , picks up immediately where his HBO series How To with John Wilson left off after three seasons. An elevated public profile does not lead to the next bigger, better project. Instead it’s illustrated via Wilson stumbling upon an empty bag of weed featuring an unauthorized branding of his likeness. The full-sized crew afforded by his show now absent, Wilson is forced back to his roots, filming the day-to-day scenes of New York City life solo. – Caleb H. ( full review )

If They Go Will They Miss Me (Walter Thompson-Hernández)

Finding poetic beauty in the quotidian, Walter Thompson-Hernández’s If I Go Will They Miss Me centers on coming of age in housing projects of southern Los Angeles. It’s a way of life often depicted with a grittiness that favors do-or-die intensity, yet this emerging director of great promise takes an opposite approach. One where dreams of flight are always on the mind as the planes coming in and out of nearby LAX are constantly passing above. Greek gods, as studied in school, give purpose to a higher calling. An affection and adoration for and from its ensemble (many non-professionals, in this case) form a portrait of a living, loving community that rises above hardship. Just as his characters draw grand personal inspiration, Thompson-Hernández is greatly indebted to a variety of renowned directors, including Barry Jenkins, RaMell Ross, Charles Burnett, and Spike Lee, with the end result a film greater than the sum of its recognizable influences. – Jordan R. ( full review )

My Undesirable Friends: Part II – Exile (Julia Loktev)

With My Undesirable Friends: Part I – Last Air in Moscow winning the 2025 Indie Film Site Network Advocate Award , the most-anticipated sequel of the year may be Julia Loktev’s My Undesirable Friends: Part II – Exile , which expands its scope by tracking the journalists who were forced out of Russia and now continue their work across the globe. As Savina Petkova said in our Critic’s Pick review out of Venice , “As Julia Loktev follows her protagonists in exile to Turkey, Georgia, Latvia, the Czech Republic, Poland, and the United States, what in any other film could be a chronicle of homes and places becomes a cartography of grief and displacement. Exile tastes as bitter as the collective responsibility of its protagonists, whose acute sense of accountability (‘we let this happen’ are words uttered by several people) clashes with the ambivalence of being Russian today. Still, the strength of their convictions is the driving force behind My Undesirable Friends , the urge to never forget that history is made here and now.”

NAZA (Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor)

In a sobering wake-up call to anyone somehow not paying attention to the genocide Israel is enacting, as well as the most essential documentary of the year, No Other Land directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor have returned with NAZA . Luke Hicks said in his review , “Very, very few films, no matter how great or important, are actually urgent. You’ll get around to it eventually; it’ll be stuck in time waiting for you. But NAZA is urgent, an essential film, a living document in conversation with the most pressing issue in the world right now. And it’s the new foremost authority on what’s happening on a granular, behind-the-scenes level in Israel’s crusade against Gaza. It’s much harder to question or deny a genocide that’s happening when the people perpetrating it in real time call it genocide themselves.”

Primetime (Lance Oppenheim)

Robert Pattinson was born to play Chris Hansen. In the opening shot of Lance Oppenheim’s Primetime —the documentary savant’s first foray into fiction, this one based on a true story—we immediately see the popular To Catch a Predator host as the menace Oppenheim and first-time screenwriter Ajon Singh want us to understand him as. He’s cast in a devilish red light, swallowed by shadow, displayed through an eerie mini-DV grain, and reciting the lines “I will undress you and you will undress me” over and over in Hansen’s trademark brassy, rehearsed, does-he-really-sound-like-that (yes, he does) tone. The chilling music of the haunted fairytale score glitches in and out while children’s-show chimes ring ominously. – Luke H. ( full review )

Resident Evil (Zach Cregger)

Resident Evil , as a game series, has always borrowed heavily from cinema, whether it be the fixed angles and Kiyoshi Kurosawa inspirations of the first title to the Texas Chainsaw riffs in the 7th. It’s less about the zombies, more the feeling of powerlessness and weird puzzles. Zach Cregger understands this on a deep level. His follow-up to Weapons may not be a pitch-perfect adaptation of the long-running lore, but it perfectly captures the spirit of Resident Evil as a whole, not to mention what it’s like to play it. The perfect title might actually have been Biohazard . – Devan S. ( full review )

The Scout (Paula González-Nasser)

Premiering at last year’s Tribeca Festival to much acclaim, Paula González-Nasser’s debut The Scout follows a day in the life of an NYC location scout. Michael Frank said in his Tribeca review , “González-Nasser invites an openness from these characters, each given one scene with Sofia, to banter with her, make her uncomfortable, or some combination of the two. And the young location scout just takes it all in stride, as though she’s been in these situations countless times, as each apartment is a part of her job she doesn’t love, but also doesn’t mind. She might even relish it on one or two occasions, the opportunity to sit on someone’s couch and hear their story or to find a new hack to delete her mountain of parking tickets.”

The Weight (Padraic McKinley)

Gold is such an apt metaphor for greed. It’s shiny, it’s heavy, it’s superficial, and it’s obtained through someone’s hard labor. That labor is carried on the backs of the downtrodden and desperate while its benefactors maintain a comfortable distance. Gold prices are currently at an all-time high, a testament to the timelessness of its corrupting allure, while life isn’t getting any easier for those on the bottom of the economic totem pole. Every day, we see news stories about more people struggling to make ends meet or afford healthcare. It’s a devastating sign of the times which director Padraic McKinley taps into in his debut feature, The Weight. – Kent M. W. ( full review )

Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother (Bassam Tariq)

Latif (Mahershala Ali) is a righteous man. A religious man. He sees himself in a holy war to cleanse the world of his people’s enemies by picking up where the law ends. Those who know about his work justifiably condemn it, whether that be his Imam (Giancarlo Esposito’s Abdul Malik) or his wife. They don’t, however, condemn him . Because they understand his struggle. They know his pain. Why add to it? So, they grant him mercy instead. They accept him and hope he will one day find his way back. – Jared M. ( full review )

content.article_text:
Note: This review was originally published as part of our 2026 Cannes coverage. The film opens in theaters on October 9.

A soft upright piano playing “Amazing Grace” drapes in warmly over the opening image of Fjord : a powder-blue-hued glacial mountain towering over the glistening Norwegian fjord around which Lisbet (Renate Reinsve) and Mihai Gheorghiu (Sebastian Stan) have resettled their seven-person family. Lisbet, a Norwegian nurse, and Mihai, a Romanian aeronautical engineer, just moved to the idyllic seaside village in Norway from Bucharest, where their devout evangelical Christian faith held a much better reputation in the conservative home country of writer-director Cristian Mungiu, who’s aimed his last two features ( Graduation , R.M.N. ) at the pitfalls of its uber-traditional society.

The Gheorghius don’t necessarily come across as a good hang. They spend all their free time singing worship songs and reading scripture, and insist their children do the same. The two teenage eldest of the five, chronic rule-followers Elia (Vanessa Ceban) and Emmanuel (Jonathan Ciprian Breazu), have no access to the internet, much less YouTube. When she sees an electric piano at school, Elia can’t help but play a hymn, just like her father did when he was touring the campus. Both are lightly reprimanded by the Norwegians near them. “We don’t do evangelism at school,” Mats, their neighbor, tells Elia with a smile. Even their outfits are conservative: long, unflattering grey skirts and Mennonite-esque hair tied up for Lisbet, turtlenecks and blazers for Mihai.

Their poised stance against homosexuality is abominable, their casual tendency to spank their children a reprehensible relic of generations past. Both are anachronisms in a modern global age that sees the backwards ideological strongholds as thought crimes—in Norway, actual crimes. So much so that, in the middle of the afternoon, after a teacher develops reason to believe they’ve been spanked, Child Protective Services arrive unannounced to take the children into custody while they investigate the situation. But, like anyone else, the Gheorghius deserve their liberties and a proper defense in court from the iron-fisted Norwegian powers that have gone so far left that they’ve come back around to the right—flown the country so close to the sun of liberalism that they’ve begun to burn the minorities who live there. (“They never had communism,” Mihai remarks critically.)

Several key questions run through the veins of Fjord . The first is whether or not the Gheorghius are physically abusing their children. But when they openly admit to occasionally spanking them, and the children say the same, the question transforms: should parents be allowed to do this? If not, what should be the punishment for parents? Should their children be legally seized for the remainder of their youth? Another question, one the film refuses to weigh in on for its audience, hangs in the balance: at what point does spanking become beating or physical abuse?

Civil and criminal trials hang over Lisbet and Mihai’s baffled heads like a spectre of familial death as they prepare for their internationally publicized civil trial, which CPS keeps postponing in hopes of the criminal trial taking place first—one that will almost certainly find the Gheorghius guilty per Norwegian legislation. In a culture-versus-law showdown for the ages, the Gheorghius ask Mia (Lisa Carlehed)—a liberal atheist neighbor whose wrist-cutting, fuck-saying, and rule-breaking daughter becomes an influence on Elia and Emmanuel—to represent them. Mia agrees, finding the state’s stance harsh and damaging to the children in light of something as minor as spanking when the kids want to go home, the Gheorghius have promised never to do it again, and they clearly didn’t know they were committing a crime in the first place. Together, they take a religious-persecution angle that suggests the Gheorghius are facing discrimination.

Avalanches cascade in the background of the western Norwegian port town, a visual metaphor for the impenetrable layers of icy, inhuman behavior that characterizes most Norwegians in the film (save Mia, who considers the situation with reason and beyond its legal precedent). The CPS representative who first tells Lisbet what’s going on is so clinical in her responses that it’s as if they were programmed ahead of time, not an ounce of empathy or discerning logic in her bones. Yet she acts on behalf of the state, in the name of principles with which almost anyone would agree. Among them: “You shouldn’t hit your kids.”

The original lawyer who represents them takes on the same unblinking, robotic tone before she bails on them as calmly as she signed up simply because they’re upset. There’s an irony to a rationalism that doesn’t consider the human soul. Take, for instance, a CPS representative insisting there’s no evidence that suggests children are better off with non-abusive biological parents than a set of foster parents if the kids and new parents get along—an idea that requires no research to debunk.

Up against the cold, overbearing, soulless characterization of a Norwegian CPS operating in the name of reducing risk, the Gheorghius’ strict, silly rules for their children come across as something they’ll merely have to mature past when they’re older and opposed to something that will ruin their lives. Mungiu accentuates the lack of rigidity by showing how easy it is for Elia and Emmanuel to break their parents’ rules when peer-pressured by Noora (Henrikke Lund Olsen), a reality anyone who grew up in a religious home knows is true.

As progressive as Norway’s ideals may be, and however much one might agree with them on paper, Mungiu draws out the maltreatment in forcing someone to conform to laws of a society that are against their relatively harmless beliefs. The one thing the Norwegian state does have is an absolutely gobstopping courtroom that hovers over the fjord with floor-to-ceiling windows brandishing the celestial glow of the mountainous region in the background of every shot.

Cinematographer Tudor Vladimir Panduru and colorist Andu Radu once again wed their efforts to create the most aesthetically pleasing film of Cannes thus far, as they did with R.M.N. in 2022—a chilly sky blue masks the region in a beauty that’s hard to appreciate amidst the operation of its society. Reinsve and Stan are terrific, playing the conservative matriarch and patriarch with a gentle, hushed desperation, quaking in the wake of losing their five children forever as if they already have.

As with R.M.N. , Mungiu is in top-shelf operation. Fjord is a triumphant film that tugs at the spiritual and soulful in all of us, regardless of nation, creed, faith, or the rejection of all three. What the court will rule in both cases, and whether or not the Gheorghius will get back their kids, pulses with a pregnant tension as the nearly two-and-a-half-hour film proceeds in what seems 30 minutes. And its end will have you falling off the edge of your seat.

Fjord premiered at the 2026 Cannes Film Festival and will be released by NEON.

content.article_text:
Note: This review was originally published as part of our 2026 Venice coverage. The film opens in theaters on October 9.

Day 1,645 of Russia’s full-scale war in Ukraine also brings us the world premiere of Julia Loktev’s My Undesirable Friends: Part II – Exile, the follow-up to My Undesirable Friends: Part I – Last Air in Moscow (2024). War time is even more elastic than peace time, even though it’s only accessible to those living through it. For us, viewers huddled in the screening rooms or hunched over the laptops if we’re streaming, this concept remains abstract. Instead we count film time in hours and minutes, the only measure we can access directly: Last Air in Moscow clocked in at 324 minutes, and Exile is longer at 355. But how precious is our viewing time, really, in comparison to what the total 12 hours of My Undesirable Friends depicts, the fascistic suffocation of truth in real time?

The first film began in autumn 2021, when independent journalists—our protagonists—were being declared “foreign agents” by Putin’s regime. In four months’ time they were fleeing the country as Russia started a full-scale war in Ukraine, making their journalistic work punishable with jail time. Exile starts only two days after the events depicted in Last Air in Moscow, circa March 2022, providing the continuity we need for history to make sense. There is no gap between Parts I and II, yet they are worlds apart—for those we see onscreen and us watching real time unfold with a three-year delay.

What we’re seeing are brave, resourceful young women who are no less scared, shocked, and trying to plan their next move out of Russia. However, it’s a relief to see all of them alive and well. Regardless of whether or not you’ve already spent hours with Anya (Anna Nemzer, credited as co-director), Lera (Valeria Ratnikova), Ksyusha (Ksenia Mironova), Lena (Elena Kostyucheko), Ira (Irina Dolinina), Alesya (Marokhovskaya), and Sonya (Groysman), Loktev’s affection is palpable from behind the camera. Shooting on an iPhone allows her, like in Part I , to stay close and bottle the intimacy shared, which in this case it feels even more precious to preserve.

When Last Air in Moscow premiered, critics remarked on Loktev’s transition from fiction to documentary as a novelty, yet were somewhat unsurprised to find the same delicate framing and attention to faces, flushed with emotion, one sees in the director’s works of fiction. A nimble camera staying close by, attending to every word each of the film’s multiple protagonists utters, taking in the surroundings as the final glimpses of Moscow for each and every one of them—streets, apartments, workplaces. Stylistically, Exile is no different, but watching it feels more claustrophobic, the camerawork more propulsive and shaky, as if it too is trying to make sense of that new, exilic reality. All those who worked together at TV Rain as one of the last (and very few) oppositional media in Russia have scattered—some fled to Europe via Turkey, others to Georgia—and splintered. Now that the media has shut down, it’s Loktev and her film keeping them close. But that uniting role is neither overstated nor forced. It’s welcome, and the trust between filmmaker and subjects is clearly felt in every second of screen time—including the “new faces” like Yana (Kuchina, partner of Lena) and the Ukrainian-Russian journalist couple Peter Ruzavin and Nataliya Gumenyuk, who also fit right in the constellation of fearless protagonists with their impressive work and sweet humor.

Like its predecessor, My Undesirable Friends: Part II — Exile shows history in the making by documenting fragments of its peoples’ lives, reflections, and struggles against the authoritarian state, but also exceeds the expectations of your regular observational documentary. Loktev has described the approach as a “fly in the soup” more than “fly on the wall,” but by staying with her protagonists, she extends the act of care so crucial for the genre beyond any time and space of shooting. She translates her care to the audience as one of bearing witness, actively with her own voice in dialogue with a protagonist, or more discreetly by just being there. Unlike them, Loktev may be free to travel, but that asymmetry doesn’t make her presence any less reassuring—filming, as an act and a process, becomes the only source of stability for all, it seems.

Exile also crystallizes history’s relationship to the present tense and time in general. Despite offering clear timestamps and contextual information in the inter-titles, the film inadvertently places viewers in a state of dissonance. Not a cognitive one, but temporal—and by extension, mnemonic—dissonance where the present is past, yet still present. While there is a chronological narrative of sorts, moving from March 2022 to early 2026, the emotional timeline is anything but linear. Loktev’s editing bookends every scene with a black frame and inter-titles containing a place, time, and protagonist, yet the mosaic of trauma and resistance defies the sense of linear time. We, as viewers, get to experience again the first news of Bucha, Irpin, and Mariupol, mass graves, and accounts of torture by the Russian army—all squashed in our memory by the innumerable atrocities of war committed ever since.

As Julia Loktev follows her protagonists in exile to Turkey, Georgia, Latvia, the Czech Republic, Poland, and the United States, what in any other film could be a chronicle of homes and places becomes a cartography of grief and displacement. Exile tastes as bitter as the collective responsibility of its protagonists, whose acute sense of accountability (“we let this happen” are words uttered by several people) clashes with the ambivalence of being Russian today. Still, the strength of their convictions is the driving force behind My Undesirable Friends , the urge to never forget that history is made here and now.

My Undesirable Friends: Part II — Exile premiered at the 2026 Venice Film Festival and opens on October 9.

content.article_text:
Each week we highlight the noteworthy titles that have recently hit streaming platforms in the United States. Check out this week’s selections below and past round-ups here .

Barrio Triste (Stillz)

At barely two years old, Harmony Korine’s “post-cinema” company EDGLRD is already branching out. After directing AGGRO DR1FT and Baby Invasion , Korine takes on a producer role for Barrio Triste , the feature debut of Colombian-American artist Stillz. It’s a good match of talents, given Stillz’s background as a music video director for artists like Bad Bunny and Rosalia, and while Barrio Triste takes a vibes-based approach à la Korine’s last two features it’s an entirely different beast. Exhilarating, tense, personal, and enigmatic, Barrio Triste is a compelling look at a lost generation in search of salvation, and among this year’s best first features. – C.J. P. ( full review )

Where to Stream: VOD

Colony (Yeon Sang-ho)

Ten years ago, Train to Busan pitted passengers against zombies on high-speed rails. Driven by a canny script and propulsive editing, Yeon Sang-ho’s film became a worldwide hit. In Yeon’s latest, Colony , an experimental serum unleashes hordes of zombies into a downtown Seoul office complex. The difference this time is that they can communicate instantaneously, evolving in a sort of hive mentality. Helped by Jun Ji-hyun in her first screen role in over a decade, Colony was a box-office hit when it opened this May in South Korea. Along with The King’s Warden , Yeon’s movie helped resurrect Korean moviegoing after a long, fallow stretch. I spoke with Yeon and Jun at the New York Asian Film Festival for the North American premiere of Colony . Read the full interview . – Daniel E.

Where to Stream: VOD

Disclosure Day (Steven Spielberg)

Certain beliefs unite all of humanity. Take, for example, the idea that the extraordinary is possible. Or, even more, that the impossible is possible. Steven Spielberg isn’t shy about believing in extraterrestrial life, and he doesn’t think you should be either. He’s so sincere about this aloof-yet-sky-high-stakes concept that he’s returning to it again with a very simple profundity in tow: “Empathy is the core of animate existence–our evolutionary advantage.” And he intends to remind us of our capacity for such. – Luke H. ( full review )

Where to Stream: Peacock

Late Fame (Kent Jones)

It is early into Kent Jones’ Late Fame when Ed Saxberger (Willem Dafoe) joins a coterie of twenty-something wannabe intellectuals for a drink in the Village. This is Saxberger’s scene––better yet, was . A one-time poet, he hasn’t written anything after his first and only book came out in the late 1970s, whereupon he retreated into anonymity, serving as a different man of letters at NYC’s post office for almost 40 years. But when a budding writer one-third his age shows up at his doorstep to beat the drum for his forgotten literary endeavor, Way Past Go , Ed doesn’t quite know how to react. “It’s as if the poems were written yesterday,” Meyers (Edmund Donovan) croons, before inviting the grizzled bard to a drink with his new fans (a token of “inspirationally motivated gratitude”). Ed hesitates; when he finally caves, Jones lingers on Dafoe’s face as the meeting with a rapt audience rekindles something in him. Call that a re-self-discovery: surrounded by a gaggle of youngsters who treat him with reverential respect, Ed is suddenly reminded of who he was, who he still is. Stunned by this epiphany, Dafoe smiles, and the film smiles with him. – Leonardo G. ( full review )

Where to Stream: VOD

Oasis: Don’t Look Back in Anger (Will Lovelace and Dylan Southern)

Directed by Meet Me in the Bathroom documentarians Will Lovelace and Dylan Southern and written by Peaky Blinders creator Steven Knight, Don’t Look Back in Anger offers something quite unique in the music documentary genre: a literal backstage / rehearsal-room glimpse of a musical reunion. We’ve witnessed endings in films such as The Last Waltz and Let It Be . To see a band reunite—two brothers, no less—is a far different experience. There have certainly been other shocking musical reunions; the Eagles called their mid-90s tour “Hell Freezes Over” for a reason, while individuals as combative as the members of Guns N’ Roses, Simon and Garfunkel, and Fleetwood Mac have managed to reconnect for hefty paydays. Sometimes these reformations sputter out (see: Jane’s Addiction). And occasionally the result is literally a one-time deal, like Pink Floyd at Live 8 or Led Zeppelin’s 2007 London performance. – Christopher S. ( full review )

Where to Stream: Disney+ , Hulu

Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma (Jane Schoenbrun)

Jane Schoenbrun’s I Saw the TV Glow follow-up Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma is a wildly entertaining exploration of the slasher film, erotic pleasure, and everything in between. Led by Hannah Einbinder and Gillian Anderson, Rory O’Connor said in his Critic’s Pick review from Cannes , “Shot masterfully by their regular cinematographer Eric Yue (Alex G also makes a welcome return as composer), the movie-within-the-movie’s formative kill scene is so mesmerizing that you’ll welcome Schoenbrun’s decision to play it again and again––all the better to get a feel for how Kris’ obsessions have led them to the movie’s climax, and perhaps their own. Yue and Schoenbrun’s approaches also perfectly align when capturing actresses’ faces, often in achingly beautiful close-ups that only occasionally allow for a flicker of menace. ‘There’s a hole at the bottom of the lake,’ Billy explains to Kris in one of those moments, setting off a sequence that is quickly becoming Schoenbrun’s signature—that churning sense of movie spiraling a drain as it drags you down with it.”

Where to Stream: MUBI

It’s a drama uninterested in its own stakes. It’s a comedy unconcerned with making us laugh. The longer you watch it, the more it seems to only exist as a platform for writer-director Chris Rock’s most hateful impulses. The titular actress is a cipher, shepherded from scene to scene by plot mechanisms alone. Rosalind Eleazar plays Misty Green with energy and commitment, but the narrative has no real respect for her as a woman. The real star of the film is Rock himself, who plays a hapless director mysteriously named Jordan Green. He even shares his name with Misty’s mentally ill brother, referred to as Jay presumably to lessen confusion. But like most of the problems in the film, this needless misunderstanding can be attributed to Rock’s shocking lack of imagination. Going by Rock’s script, the most important thing to know about Misty Green is that she lets men down."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "But who is Misty? Misty has an Emmy for Best Supporting Actress in a Drama for her role in Red Eye , a fictional Shondaland series that used to come on after Scandal in the 2010s. Since then she has been financially supporting her brother while (presumably) spending the rest of her network checks on clothes, shoes, bags, and partying. When we meet her, she’s living in an apartment bought for her by a married man. It’s a year after his death and the widow (Amy Landecker) has come to seize the property. This dilemma gives Misty a ticking clock that she immediately ignores, partying with Zach (Adam Driver) the night before her audition. When she arrives late and unprepared the next morning, she ducks into a bathroom for a bump."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Making this situation all the more bleak is that Misty seems, at no point, to ever have any fun in her wild life. She’s a lonely, pathetic character for seemingly no other reason than Rock needing her to be. It’s as if she’s based on a woman Rock fell for years ago but never really got to know. Perhaps he, like his director avatar, sees himself as a good man constantly set aside for reasons he’ll never fully understand. Regardless of how little Rock knows Misty, he knows her well enough to believe she should be punished.
