Misty Green is a disaster on all fronts. It’s a film that seems to hate its characters, the audience, and Black cinema in general. It’s a Hollywood satire with no insight. It’s a character study with no character. It’s a drama uninterested in its own stakes. It’s a comedy unconcerned with making us laugh. The longer you watch it, the more it seems to only exist as a platform for writer-director Chris Rock’s most hateful impulses. The titular actress is a cipher, shepherded from scene to scene by plot mechanisms alone. Rosalind Eleazar plays Misty Green with energy and commitment, but the narrative has no real respect for her as a woman. The real star of the film is Rock himself, who plays a hapless director mysteriously named Jordan Green. He even shares his name with Misty’s mentally ill brother, referred to as Jay presumably to lessen confusion. But like most of the problems in the film, this needless misunderstanding can be attributed to Rock’s shocking lack of imagination. Going by Rock’s script, the most important thing to know about Misty Green is that she lets men down.

But who is Misty? The film never tells us, but it does provide some first-draft details. She grew up with a white mother and absent Black father. Her brother Jay (Daniel Kaluuya) isn’t her mother’s son, but she took him in anyway, and the three lived together unhappily. Misty has an Emmy for Best Supporting Actress in a Drama for her role in Red Eye , a fictional Shondaland series that used to come on after Scandal in the 2010s. Since then she has been financially supporting her brother while (presumably) spending the rest of her network checks on clothes, shoes, bags, and partying. When we meet her, she’s living in an apartment bought for her by a married man. It’s a year after his death and the widow (Amy Landecker) has come to seize the property. This dilemma gives Misty a ticking clock that she immediately ignores, partying with Zach (Adam Driver) the night before her audition. When she arrives late and unprepared the next morning, she ducks into a bathroom for a bump.

Making this situation all the more bleak is that Misty seems, at no point, to ever have any fun in her wild life. Everything she does is framed as a form of self-harm. Her only sex scene—with Zach—is passionless, her eyes looking forward as he hammers into her. She’s a lonely, pathetic character for seemingly no other reason than Rock needing her to be. It’s as if she’s based on a woman Rock fell for years ago but never really got to know. Perhaps he, like his director avatar, sees himself as a good man constantly set aside for reasons he’ll never fully understand. Regardless of how little Rock knows Misty, he knows her well enough to believe she should be punished. His film is the chronicle of a downfall unmotivated by any narrative truth beyond the fact that it’s what he wanted to film.

Throughout Misty Green , people ask Eleazar’s character if she knows any personal details about the people she considers friends. These repeated exchanges are meant to illustrate that Misty is a brat who only cares about herself. She struts through life in sexy clothes, Birkin bag in hand, with big eyes that always seem to be asking for a favor. She drinks only to get drunk. Her energy seems to come solely from cocaine. She smokes weed and cigarettes, rarely eats, and never seems to get enough sleep. The only healthy practice Misty manages to keep up with is going to her local gym with her best friend Naomi (Anna Kendrick). But even that is framed as an extension of Misty’s constant pursuit of unbridled vanity. Rock structures her story as a grim procession of humbling encounters, meant to bring her back down to Earth. It’s made all the more obvious by Rock’s constant onscreen presence, his character functioning as both a love interest and paternal figure. Misty Green is a woman’s story told entirely in a man’s voice, and that voice seems to hate her on a level that feels intensely personal and perverse.

Misty Green has no interest in the plight of Black women in Hollywood or their work, handwaving sexism and racism as if they’re both beside the point. This is also exemplified in the roles we see Misty read for and discuss. She is, for some reason, auditioning for the role played by N’Bushe Wright in the 1994 crime film Fresh . The sides she reads are direct quotes. If it were a reboot, why is the script the same? Later, we see an old clip of Misty reading for Anne Hathaway’s role in The Devil Wears Prada , which seems unrealistic based on her fame level. Throughout the journey we also hear about an ill-fated Cinderella reboot that brings to mind the 1997 version with Brandy Norwood and the late Whitney Houston. Then we hear about Misty being in Shaft —presumably the 2019 version, based on her age. But the biggest indication of Rock’s limited knowledge of recent roles for Black women is the part Misty chases the most throughout the film: Deena in Dreamgirls , last played in the 2006 film by Beyoncé. Though it is normal to reboot a film 20 years later, it seems unlikely that a television actress would be reading for a role previously played by one of the biggest singers on the planet.

If this suggests nitpicking, the laziness is distracting. The film’s one true invention, Red Eye , is a show no one takes the time to describe. Did Rock choose a title and immediately move on? Misty has an Emmy for playing a popular character, but no one mentions who that character was or even what she did on the show. The film is more concerned with the men in Misty’s life—especially her brother—and the many ways she has let them all down. As Misty’s life implodes around her, Rock pulls focus towards the unhoused residents of Los Angeles. Characters express disgust at having to see them on a constant basis, living in tents and asking for change. These moments, coupled with Misty’s money troubles, seem to function as a narrative threat. It’s as if Rock is saying that holding onto money is everything, and if you lose it, you become a nuisance and drain on society. The ending is especially tasteless in that regard. But perhaps California Governor Gavin Newsom will enjoy it.

Many will laud the work of Eleazar, who simply isn’t given a real character to play here. We never get into Misty’s head beyond flashbacks involving her brother. She often looks at a framed photograph of them with her mother, each close-up emptier than the last. Eleazar moves through every scene stiffly, her clothes fitting perfectly, her hair thick and luminous, her eyes begging for one more shot. But she never seems comfortable in the role, delivering her lines unconvincingly; audition and performance scenes are distinctly unnatural. This becomes especially clear in her scenes with Kendrick, who makes a meal out of a deeply troubled, darkly funny character. As for Kaluuya: he does the best he can with a poorly written role that turns him into a walking plot device. But it’s Rock’s performance as a scumbag deluded enough to think he’s a good guy that truly dooms the film. There is no good here. Misty Green is a black hole.

Misty Green screened at the 64th New York Film Festival and opens in theaters on October 9.

content.article_text:
Jusqu’au 25 octobre 2026, la Galerie du Jour agnès b. présente Le Chant des villes , une exposition collective aux écritures contrastées se réunissant pour révéler les nuances d’un territoire commun : la ville.

C’est à la Fab, au cœur du 13e arrondissement que se déploie Le Chant des villes , un dialogue entre les langages de dix artistes et un collectif dans une seule et même pièce. L’espace y est blanc, neutre. Il sert à se faire oublier pour accueillir les narrations portées par Aristide Barraud, Nicolas Boulben, Etienne Boissier, Alexandre Dupeyron, Flore Faucheux, Sinae Lee, Claire Nicolet, Mandy Payne, Julie Rochereau, Chloe Sharrock et le Solar Collective . Autant de voyages d’une urbanité à l’autre, de Marseille à Séoul, tantôt sombres et mystérieux, tantôt drôles et insolites. Photographie, peinture, dessin et même céramique s’y croisent comme pour nous pousser à dérégler notre regard, à prêter attention aux textures, aux surfaces, aux ombres et lumières des villes dans lesquelles nous évoluons – comme pour en convoquer leurs âmes. Pourtant, au détour des œuvres, très peu de traces humaines. Si celles-ci percent, çà et là, elles semblent rester au service d’un récit plus large : celui de la construction d’un intime dans un territoire partagé par tous·tes. Une ruine révélée par l’éclat d’un soleil en monochrome, des flous vertigineux décomposant les sommets des gratte-ciels, un trognon de pomme géant aussi gros qu’un camion-poubelle dans une rue déserte… Sur les murs, ce sont moins les métropoles que les émotions qui les traversent qui règnent.

Perdre tout repère

Alexandre Dupeyron nous propose l’une des premières errances de l’exposition. Passant du bleu au noir et blanc, il convoque un lieu poétique aux frontières floues, comme pour nous ouvrir les portes d’un rêve. Spectrales, ses compositions plongent des détails dans la pénombre pour ne révéler que des silhouettes, humaines ou non, corps égarés, anonymes, ou architectures gargantuesques mangées par le grain. Une immersion vibrante dans une ville où la nuit a noyé le jour, où nos yeux cherchent – et perdent – tout repère.

Au détour d’un autre mur, la Galerie du Jour accueille un diptyque de Chloe Sharrock, photojournaliste et membre de MYOP – deux images prises en zone de conflit que l’autrice retravaille au charbon et au fusain. Face à nous, une étrange impression de calme, dans ce lieu de ruines noires révélées par des éclats blancs. Rien ne bouge, on ne peut contempler que la destruction soulignée par le clair-obscur. Une sélection d’œuvres poignantes : en distordant ainsi ses clichés, Chloe Sharrock leur offre une nouvelle matérialité tout en interrogeant le caractère répétitif de l’iconographie de guerre et notre rapport à celle-ci. Les surconsommer nous a-t-il insensibilisé·es à leur violence ?

Enfin, entre Paris et Séoul, Sinae Lee illumine l’une des cimaises de flashs puissants, d’images effet cartes postales et de textes aux allures de journaux intimes. Une réflexion tendre et amusante autour de son expérience en tant qu’étrangère en France. S’y croisent pigeons et feux d’artifice dans une tentative de donner du sens à un quotidien ancré dans une forme d’altérité. Une belle manière de conclure ce voyage aux écritures multiples dans une ville tout aussi plurielle.

content.article_text:
写真家、映像作家、音楽家として活動する中野道の写真展「めいめつ」が、2026年10月9日から22日まで東京・代官山のSISON GALLERyで開催される。自身の時間のなかに現れては消えていった人や風景を見つめながら、「記録」と「記憶」のあいだをたどる展覧会だ。

アメリカ・ノースカロライナ州に生まれ、長野県松本市で育った中野。幼少期を過ごした松本の野山、写真との出会い、身近な人との別れなど、自身の経験や記憶を起点として写真や映像、音楽による表現を続けてきた。中野は「写真は、記録であり、記憶でもある」と語る。シャッターを切った瞬間、そこに存在していた時間は過去へと変わり、写真だけが残される。しかし写真を見返すことで、フレームには写っていない前後の時間や当時の感情までもが立ち上がり、記憶そのものが更新されていくという。

本展で中野がたどるのは、写真に残すことのできたものと、その周縁に存在する「残せなかったもの」だ。かつて共に過ごした人々、すでに戻ることのできない時間、見えているものと見えなくなったもの。それらを写真によって往還しながら、自身が過ごしてきた時間にひとつの区切りをつけようとする。

背景にあるのは、老いや喪失に対する意識の変化だ。自身の白髪、飼っていた犬の死、祖父の葬儀、年齢を重ねた祖母や母の姿。かつて永遠に続くと思っていた時間が失われていくなか、中野は「僕が集めていたのは、自分がもう戻れなくなる時間だった」と記す。展覧会タイトルの「めいめつ」は、消えていくものと、それでもまだ残っている光を見つめようとする眼差しを示している。

中野自身、本展について「自分の青春にさよならするようなもの」と位置づける。過去を保存するためだけではなく、失われていくことを受け入れながら、それでもなお光っている時間を写真にとどめる。その行為を通して、記憶、時間、喪失という中野が継続してきたテーマに向き合う。

中野は上智大学大学院文学研究科修士課程修了後、2015年から写真と映像を中心に制作活動を開始。2020年に写真集『あかつき』、2023年に『Days in Between』を刊行した。現在は東京とニューヨークを拠点に活動し、音楽ではバンドModern Jazz Warのフロントマンも務めている。

content.translated_excerpt_zh: 作为摄影师、摄像师和音乐家而活跃的中野道的摄影展“Meimetsu”将于 2026 年 10 月 9 日至 22 日在东京代官山的 SISON GALLERy 举办。一边观看在自己的时代出现和消失的人和风景，

content.title_original: Jean-Pierre et Luc Dardenne : « On a toujours le désir de filmer comme si c’était la première fois que ce que nous filmons apparaît. »

content.article_text:
Comment s’est présentée cette opération d’acquisition de droits de vos films par mk2 ?

Luc Dardenne : Nous travaillons avec Denis Freyd, fondateur de la société de production Archipel 35, depuis notre film Le Fils en 2001 [ mk2 films a racheté cette société de production et son catalogue de trente-deux films, dont certains sont signés Patricia Mazuy, Pierre Schoeller, Laurent Cantet, Pascale Ferran, Ursula Meier ou encore Abderrahmane Sissako, ndlr ]. Et il a coproduit tous nos films depuis. mk2 vient donc d’un côté de racheter les droits producteurs de nos films à Archipel 35 et d’un autre côté les droits de nos autres films à notre propre société, Les Films du Fleuve. Nous avons ainsi cédé nos droits producteurs à mk2 également pour les films que nous avions réalisés avant 2001, ce qui inclut tous nos documentaires faits dans les années 1970 et 1980 et nos premiers films de fiction comme Je pense à vous, La Promesse et Rosetta [ cela représente vingt-trois films au total, ndlr ].

Jean-Pierre Dardenne : Denis Freyd nous a dit qu’il allait vendre sa société et nous a demandé si on voulait racheter la partie des droits producteurs qu’il possède de nos films. Il nous a aussi dit qu’on pourrait éventuellement vendre à l’inverse les droits producteurs de tous nos autres films. On en a discuté avec Luc et on s’est dit que, vu notre âge [ Jean-Pierre Dardenne a 75 ans, et Luc Dardenne trois ans de moins, ndlr ] et vu que notre société de production n’a pas les épaules assez larges pour donner une visibilité à nos films au niveau européen et international, c’était une belle opportunité de les confier à mk2.

Il s’agit donc de la transmission et la perpétuation de votre œuvre . Avez-vous à ce titre l’habitude de suivre la carrière de vos films après leurs sorties en salle ?

L.D. : On fait ça tout le temps ! La Cinémathèque de Bruxelles va par exemple repasser Le Fils parce qu’Emmanuel Marre [ réalisateur de Notre salut , ndlr ] a choisi ce film pour sa carte blanche. On va faire un débat avec lui devant le public. Nous allons aussi dans des ciné-clubs ou des associations où l’on discute avec les spectatrices et spectateurs. Quand on a commencé nos documentaires à la fin des années 1970, on allait déjà avec notre lecteur de bobines montrer nos films partout où on nous le demandait. Et aujourd’hui, on fait encore beaucoup de projections pour les écoles où l’on échange avec des lycéens.

Avez-vous le sentiment que certains de vos films ont eu un fort impact politique et qu’ils conserveront au fil des années cette capacité à faire changer le regard ?

J-P. D. : C’est une vaste question. Parce qu’un film s’adresse à chaque spectatrice et chaque spectateur qui le voit. Notre première pensée a toujours été celle-là. On croit dans le cinéma, non pas comme outil de propagande, mais comme une conversation de chaque personne avec le film. On a assisté en 2025 à la Cinémathèque de Bologne à la projection d’un de nos premiers documentaires [ le court-métrage Lorsque le bateau de Léon M. descendit la Meuse pour la première fois, réalisé en 1979, ndlr ], consacré à un ancien militant syndical qui raconte son parcours, ses désillusions et ses combats. Je craignais que cette histoire qui se passe à Liège dans les années 1970 n’intéresse pas le public de Bologne mais les gens ont été passionnés. Car le film raconte un morceau de l’Histoire de l’Europe en même temps que la fin de l’industrie et de la métallurgie. Et cela passe à travers le récit qu’un homme fait de sa vie. J’étais très ému de voir ça. Quand on s’intéresse vraiment à l’individu, c’est universel.

Après votre passage du documentaire à la fiction, La Promesse est vraiment le film qui a lancé votre carrière en 1996. Avez-vous décidé de toujours garder les mêmes principes de mise en scène depuis ? On a l’impression que vous êtes restés fidèles à une même ligne.

L.D. : J’espère que c’est une ligne vivante ! C’est vrai qu’avec La Promesse, on a trouvé notre méthode : travailler avec une équipe proche de nous, tourner avec des acteurs pas nécessairement connus ni professionnels, filmer dans des décors de la région de Liège/Seraing… Pour les moyens techniques, on s’est un peu adapté avec le temps, et on a tourné en 16mm, en Super 16, en 35mm, en image numérique. Au début, c’était lié à nos moyens financiers car c’était moins cher de tourner en 16mm. On tournait avec la caméra la plus légère possible mais cela correspondait aussi à notre volonté d’avoir peu de médiation entre les acteurs et nous. C’est pour ça qu’on a éliminé les travellings, la machinerie, les grues… On est toujours restés fidèles à ça, de même que pour la mise en scène on a gardé notre manière de filmer en plans-séquences, qui donne le rythme d’une scène en se rapprochant et en allant chercher dans l’image un détail sans couper. On a, ceci dit, remarqué qu’il fallait être vigilants nous-mêmes afin de ne pas refaire toujours la même chose. Par exemple, on n’arrive pas à utiliser de la musique. On n’a rien contre, mais c’est chez nous une sorte d’incapacité. Mais quand on a réalisé Le Gamin au vélo [2011, ndlr] , on a cherché une manière à nous de mettre de la musique à un moment donné dans le film. On a aussi besoin du regard de la critique et du public pour voir si on arrive à ne pas trop refaire la même chose.

Après La Promesse, vous avez réalisé Rosetta , portrait d’une jeune femme confrontée à une précarité extrême qui a remporté la Palme d’or au Festival de Cannes en 1999. Comment avez-vous réussi à gérer un tel tournant dans votre carrière ?

J-P. D. : C’est d’abord une immense joie, pour les gens qui ont travaillé avec nous, pour les comédiennes et les comédiens – je pense à Émilie Dequenne [ actrice principale de Rosetta et lauréate pour ce film du Prix d’interprétation féminine à Cannes. L’actrice est décédée en 2025, des suites d’un cancer, ndlr ]. Et c’est évidemment une reconnaissance de notre travail de cinéastes. Notre tante maternelle nous a d’ailleurs tout de suite dit après la Palme de Rosetta : « Les enfants, faites attention. Parce que plus on monte, plus la chute est terrible ! » Le fait qu’on soit deux nous a probablement aidés à rester ceux qu’on était avant. Le film qui a suivi Rosetta fut ainsi Le Fils [sur la relation complexe qui se tisse entre un formateur en menuiserie dans un centre de réinsertion et un adolescent accueilli dans ce centre, dont il apprend qu’il a tué son fils, ndlr], car on avait promis à Olivier Gourmet de faire un film dont il serait le personnage principal. Cela a vite été notre obsession : que Rosetta ne devienne pas le module à l’intérieur duquel nous allions nous déplacer et que la vitalité qu’on cherche dans nos films ne se transforme pas en attitude.

▌ À LIRE AUSSI :

Émilie Dequenne en 7 rôles sublimes

Est-ce que le fait d’avoir progressivement fait tourner un casting plus connu, comme Cécile de France dans Le Gamin au vélo ou Marion Cotillard dans Deux jours, une nuit, venait d’une même volonté de se renouveler à tout prix ?

J-P. D. : On s’est dit à un moment que ce serait bien de voir si on trouvait des personnes intéressées pour entrer dans notre famille de cinéma et travailler de la manière dont on l’entend. Et Cécile de France et Marion Cotillard ont totalement répondu à ces espoirs. Nous, on fait quand même beaucoup de répétitions. Pendant quatre ou cinq semaines quotidiennement avant de tourner avec l’équipe, on répète dans les décors avec le casting principal. Ce ne sont pas des répétitions autour d’une table et d’un texte, mais vraiment avec une caméra, car c’est là qu’on trouve la forme de ce que sera le film. Et on a travaillé avec Cécile et Marion exactement comme nous avons travaillé avec Émilie Dequenne ou avec les cinq jeunes filles qui ont tourné dans Jeunes mères [dernier film en date des frères Dardenne, Prix du scénario à Cannes en 2025, sur cinq adolescentes accueillies dans une maison maternelle de Liège, face aux défis de la maternité, ndlr].

L.D. : Pour nous, faire un gros plan du visage de Marion Cotillard, ce n’était pas comme faire un gros plan du visage d’Émilie Dequenne dans Rosetta quand elle était inconnue et faisait son premier film. Avec Émilie on était dans une spontanéité, le plan prenait vie avec elle et on ne se posait pas la question de savoir si on répétait des codes. Mais quand on fait un gros plan du visage de Marion, on se dit qu’elle vient déjà avec une histoire de cinéma et un visage connu. Que faire ? On devait trouver une manière de la filmer et on se disait qu’il fallait la « désicôniser », enlever son côté icône. Et Marion a été géniale car elle a été vraiment présente de façon singulière. On a toujours le désir de filmer comme si c’était la première fois que ce que nous filmons apparaît. Il faut arriver à ce que le plan qu’on est en train de faire semble tout à fait neuf. Nous pensons que c’est la vocation du cinéma : filmer le visage humain, ses réactions, son regard, ses égarements, ses fixations.

Et vous ne craignez pas que le cinéma disparaisse face à l’IA et autres technologies ?

L.D. : L’inquiétude a toujours été là. Quand on avait quinze ou vingt ans, on entendait déjà que le cinéma allait mourir. L’idée s’exprimait avec Wim Wenders, avec la fin de la Nouvelle Vague…. Alors le cinéma s’apprêtait peut-être à mourir, mais c’était pour renaître autrement.

J-P. D. : Le contexte n’est plus le même qu’il y a encore vingt ans, car il y a aujourd’hui toute la question de la fabrication du faux qui circule. Qui fait encore quoi dans l’écriture ? Dans un film, beaucoup de choses – dont les pires – sont possibles. Mais tant qu’il y aura des personnes qui ont l’envie de faire le grand saut de la création, le cinéma subsistera. L’IA peut certes être un outil de travail mais les cinéastes qui se trouvent derrière un film continueront à compter. Je pense que le public ne sera pas dupe et saura participer à cette aventure vieille de plus de cent ans.

Cela nous renvoie aussi à cette nécessité de faire perdurer les œuvres artistiques à travers le temps, dont nous parlions au début de l’entretien…

L.D. : Pour ce qui est de la transmission future de nos films, on trouve formidable que mk2 soit un acteur indépendant. La première fois qu’on a collaboré avec mk2, c’est parce qu’on faisait le commentaire DVD des Temps Modernes de Charlie Chaplin. Et on a été séduits par cette politique d’indépendance. Dans la mesure où mk2 a différents supports de diffusion et un logiciel pour ses films, si une association, une école ou une rétrospective de festival veut montrer un de nos films, elle y aura accès immédiatement. Cela rejoint notre conception du cinéma qui est fait pour être vu partout.

content.excerpt_original: Ils ont reçu sept prix à Cannes, dont deux Palmes d’or (pour « Rosetta » en 1999 et « L’Enfant » en 2005). Figures incontournables du cinéma européen et auteurs d’une filmographie engagée et sensible, les frères Jean-Pierre et Luc Dardenne peuvent se targuer d’avoir un sacré…

content.article_text:
Week in wildlife: a friendly seal, a furious goldcrest and ‘the swanfather’

This week’s best wildlife photographs from around the world

Fri 9 Oct 2026 08.00 BST

Comedy Wildlife Photography awards 2026 . Wittmer said: “During my photo trip to the island of Helgoland, Germany, I encountered a goldcrest for the first time – and it was love at first sight. Europe’s smallest bird wandered right in front of me, presumably searching for food. To get a perspective at eye level, I placed my camera on the ground. My heart was pounding and my finger was glued to the shutter as the tiny bird darted back and forth. Suddenly, it came to a stop and looked straight at the camera”Photograph: Jan Wittmer/Comedy Wildlife awards 2026

Living Planet report , the World Wildlife Fund writes: “In 2010, only around 3,200 wild tigers remained, and the species seemed to be sliding toward extinction. By 2025, the population had grown to roughly 5,700, an increase of more than 70%”Photograph: Andy Rouse/WWF/PA

wētāpunga , the world’s heaviest insect, in New Zealand. The flightless cricket, which can be up to 10cm (4in) long, used to be found across the North Island, but by the 1990s had retreated to a few smaller islands. However, a new breeding programme has released 11,000 wētāpunga into the wild – grounds for hope for the species’ futurePhotograph: Anton Sorokin/Alamy

parrots were seized by customs staff at the port of Pozzallo, Sicily, Italy. They were found in a car about to board a catamaran bound for Malta. The driver of the car, rather ambitiously, had hoped to smuggle out 300 tortoises and 77 parrots, many of which were protected species. The animals are now in the care of a breeding facilityPhotograph: Guardia Di Finanza - Ragusa

content.title_original: ‘Old-timey fascism was kept secret. Now you don’t have to hide it’: Martin McDonagh, John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell on Wild Horse Nine
content.article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "‘E armuffs!” says Sam Rockwell, pausing his gushing tribute mid-flow and turning to face John Malkovich on the couch. Rockwell loves Malkovich and has been discussing his work at some length. Malkovich, he says, is charismatic and dangerous, half masculine, half feminine; a unique combination and the perfect sparring partner. He’s one of the world’s finest actors and annoyingly modest to boot. “Earmuffs!” says Rockwell and pivots back towards me. “He hates hearing all this. That’s why I keep saying ‘earmuffs’.”", "links": [{"text": "John Malkovich", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/film/john-malkovich"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Malkovich frowns. “I don’t mind it,” he says."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“Hates it,” says Rockwell. “He truly hates all this stuff.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In Martin McDonagh’s Wild Horse Nine , Malkovich and Rockwell play bickering CIA agents who may also be the best of friends. Chris and Lee are fresh from plotting the 1973 coup in Chile and are spinning their wheels on Rapa Nui, amid the crashing waves and the moai statues. They’ve seen too much and sinned too greatly and now Chris has cancer, which is hardly helping his mood. So he takes Lee aside and asks for one last big favour.", "links": [{"text": "Wild Horse Nine", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/sep/03/wild-horse-nine-review-sam-rockwell-john-malkovich-martin-mcdonagh"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Ahead of the film’s premiere, the production team commandeer suites at an opulent Venice hotel and hand out hats and T-shirts to each new arrival. The lobby becomes a sea of merch. The harried concierge has to raise his voice to be heard. He says: “Second floor for the Six White Horses press interviews.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "McDonagh makes films that are playful and volatile, spring-loaded with violence and spiced with absurdist black comedy. Wild Horse Nine nods to In Bruges and The Banshees of Inisherin with its odd-couple antics and explosive side notes. But its mood is more mournful, death-haunted, with one eye on the past. McDonagh – once the upstart enfant terrible of London theatre – is now a silver-haired 56-year-old who comes at life from a different angle. “I’m getting older,” he says. “Maybe this is my first old-man movie.”", "links": [{"text": "The Banshees of Inisherin", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/film/2022/sep/05/the-banshees-of-inisherin-review-martin-mcdonagh"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "On sitting down to script Wild Horse Nine, the film-maker wrote GUILT and REGRET at the top of page one, as though setting his course with a compass and sextant. His film opens in Santiago before relocating to the South Pacific. From there it homes in on Malkovich’s CIA veteran, a leaky repository of cold war horror with his memories of the Bay of Pigs and Dealey Plaza. Chris is likely dying and wants to go out with a bang. He claims that he knows who killed JFK and is about to spill the beans."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/75e54c6d11e2efd3b35c48ab015459349e896632/0_0_3000_2001/master/3000.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "Sam Rockwell and John Malkovich in Wild Horse Nine.", "caption": "In focus … Sam Rockwell as Lee and John Malkovich as Chris in Wild Horse Nine. Photograph: Diego Araya Corvalán/Searchlight Pictures", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The Kennedy assassination is the God particle of conspiracy theories. It marked the loss of US innocence, or the start of the rot of disinformation and fake news. McDonagh knows the official version and remains breezily unconvinced. “I definitely think there was something going on,” he says. “I’m definitely a believer in the conspiracy. Exactly what that was, we’ll never really know. Was Lee Harvey Oswald involved? More than likely. Was he the lone gunman? I don’t believe that for a second.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "He’s made several pictures with Woody Harrelson. Wasn’t Harrelson’s father once rumoured to have been involved in the killing? McDonagh sits up and mimes zipping his lip. “I know nothing,” he says."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Wild Horse Nine was never intended as a comment on the present-day United States. Except that history has a tendency to repeat and the shoot coincided with Donald Trump’s strike on Venezuela. Operations like that used to be more covert, conducted via proxies, whereas now they seem brazen, the equivalent of a smash-and-grab raid. “But I don’t think Trump is the worst president that we’ve had,” he says. “I don’t even think he’s the worst in the past 60-years. Nixon was more of a fascist pig. George W Bush probably killed more people than Trump. And then if you look at Vietnam, there’s Johnson. The difference is that with old-timey fascism, you at least had to keep it secret. These days you don’t have to hide it any more. Is that more fucked? Or is it more honest?”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "McDonagh sits behind one closed door; Rockwell and Malkovich behind another. On-screen or off, the two actors have different energies, different speeds, so that the interview feels like a private performance: the Energizer Bunny versus the all-seeing Sphinx. One of these men has left his sunglasses on the floor. Inevitably it is Rockwell, who is altogether more bouncy and heedless. “My Guccis,” he cries. “Oh man, I would have stepped on those.”"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/7f06a0a1804df5bccc8f8c8105370a2230fd987b/0_0_3000_2001/master/3000.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "Martin McDonagh gestures with his arms to John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell next to vintage cars with mountains in the background", "caption": "On location … the director Martin McDonagh with John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell in Rapa Nui. Photograph: Diego Araya Corvalán/Searchlight Pictures", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Rockwell won an Oscar for playing the bumptious small-town deputy in McDonagh’s Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri . Malkovich may well follow suit thanks to Wild Horse Nine, which goes on to receive a rapturous 13-minute ovation at the premiere. The 72-year-old is on fabulously flavourful form as Chris, a tragicomic monster who is simultaneously melting down and seeing the light, lashing out and making amends. The character plays to the actor’s natural strengths, mining his innate theatricality and enigmatic air. But he explains that the role required some heavy lifting as well. Endless rehearsals and hours of line-readings, he says. “Sam and I did each scene at least a thousand times.”", "links": [{"text": "Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/film/2018/jan/12/three-billboards-outside-ebbing-missouri-review-frances-mcdormand"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "A thousand? Malkovich is so self-contained and unblinking, it’s hard to know when he’s joking."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Rockwell chips in. “Yeah, about a thousand times. We ran it on the weekends. John’s a workhorse.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“You are, too,” Malkovich says. It’s good to have a co-star to rehearse with, he adds, although every good actor has their own way of working. Clint Eastwood, for instance, prefers to hit the ground running. “You have to be a slick talker to get more than two takes out of Clint. You have to be pretty convincing, because he doesn’t take that lightly. As I know from experience.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "They were on Rapa Nui for six weeks, which helped with the process. “I have two granddaughters, so it was a long time away from them,” he says. “I don’t like being away from my grandchildren. But it’s a great place to shoot because there’s nothing else to do. You can swim with the turtles but that’s about it. Your work days are long. You’re always prepping for tomorrow. If it weren’t for a movie, I’d probably go nuts.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Rockwell enjoyed it. “We had a great time,” he says. “Every night we had a little Chile wine and some rum. And there was a drink made with sugarcane, what the hell was it called? They put an egg-white in it.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "His partner, the actor Leslie Bibb, has materialised in the doorway. “Pisco sour,” she says."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“Pisco sour!” He’s delighted to see her and glad of the intel. Bibb has swung by to check when Rockwell breaks for lunch. He introduces her to me and indicates Malkovich on the couch. “But you can’t miss John,” he says. “Look at him, he’s beautiful.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Marooned on his island, Chris plans to write his memoirs and come clean. His bosses are terrified he’ll mention “the Dallas parts” of his story. Some secrets, they feel, must be taken to the grave."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Malkovich has played heroes and villains. He’s been Tom Ripley, Biff Loman and the Vicomte de Valmont. But his career has been long and he’s covered this particular topic before. In 1994, he adapted and directed a stage version of Libra, Don DeLillo’s novel about Lee Harvey Oswald. He studied the Zapruder footage of JFK’s final moments and wandered down several conspiracy rabbit holes. The Warren Commission’s findings, he concluded, were either flawed or a lie. And if that makes him a crank, he’s hardly in the minority."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“Well, I think 60% of the American public don’t believe it,” he says. “Could the official story be true? Yeah, I guess. So could Keebler elves. The government tells us all kinds of things. Some of them may be true but not the majority of them, that’s my experience.”"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/e1e936dc82ccb65e023ae750c2fbb32956678ea0/0_0_3000_2001/master/3000.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell sat in long grass next to two moai statues", "caption": "Heading for trouble? John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell. Photograph: Entertainment Pictures/Alamy", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I’ve read that he hasn’t voted since the 1972 presidential election, when the liberal George McGovern lost in a landslide to Nixon. He nods; this is true. “I’m not a believer,” he says."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Not a believer in what? Democracy? Malkovich shrugs. “In the whole thing, really. As they say in France: ‘Je ne pratique pas’, I’m not practising. I remember the night McGovern lost. I was talking to my father on the phone and I said: ‘Well, I’m done.’ He said: ‘My God, John, you can’t be done.’ I was 19 years old but that was it, I was done. I concentrate on what I can make and leave it at that.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "What about Rockwell? Is he still practising? “Yeah, well, I vote,” he says glumly. “I vote with faint hope. Hoping Obama will come back.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The publicist sticks her head around the door. She reports that lunch is almost ready, which means that we’ve reached the last question. Rockwell perks up. “No pressure,” he says."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Let’s finish with death. That’s where the whole film is leading. Chris has decided he wants to die on Rapa Nui. Then he changes his mind and opts for Venice instead. Assuming that a death can be scripted like a film, where in the world would be the ideal place to bow out?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Malkovich thinks for a moment. “Probably on stage,” he says. “About 15 years ago I toured with a new opera based on Casanova’s memoirs. It started with Casanova chasing a chambermaid around the stage, as he was known to do, and then he has a heart attack. The play stops and people come out with a stretcher and then everyone breaks into song. Before the performance, I always made sure to tell all my friends: ‘It’s just the beginning of the play. I fake a heart attack. Don’t pay any attention.’ But forgot to tell my then-agent and I don’t think she has ever forgiven me.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "A few nights after that, he made the exact same mistake. “I have a friend, Barbara Sturm, who is a knee doctor in Düsseldorf. She came to see me and I suddenly realised I hadn’t warned her either. So I tried to text from the dressing room but of course she already had her phone switched off, being a well-mannered person. content.article_text:
‘E armuffs!” says Sam Rockwell, pausing his gushing tribute mid-flow and turning to face John Malkovich on the couch. Rockwell loves Malkovich and has been discussing his work at some length. Malkovich, he says, is charismatic and dangerous, half masculine, half feminine; a unique combination and the perfect sparring partner. He’s one of the world’s finest actors and annoyingly modest to boot. “Earmuffs!” says Rockwell and pivots back towards me. “He hates hearing all this. That’s why I keep saying ‘earmuffs’.”

Malkovich frowns. “I don’t mind it,” he says.

“Hates it,” says Rockwell. “He truly hates all this stuff.”

In Martin McDonagh’s Wild Horse Nine , Malkovich and Rockwell play bickering CIA agents who may also be the best of friends. Chris and Lee are fresh from plotting the 1973 coup in Chile and are spinning their wheels on Rapa Nui, amid the crashing waves and the moai statues. They’ve seen too much and sinned too greatly and now Chris has cancer, which is hardly helping his mood. So he takes Lee aside and asks for one last big favour.

Ahead of the film’s premiere, the production team commandeer suites at an opulent Venice hotel and hand out hats and T-shirts to each new arrival. The lobby becomes a sea of merch. The harried concierge has to raise his voice to be heard. He says: “Second floor for the Six White Horses press interviews.”

McDonagh makes films that are playful and volatile, spring-loaded with violence and spiced with absurdist black comedy. Wild Horse Nine nods to In Bruges and The Banshees of Inisherin with its odd-couple antics and explosive side notes. But its mood is more mournful, death-haunted, with one eye on the past. McDonagh – once the upstart enfant terrible of London theatre – is now a silver-haired 56-year-old who comes at life from a different angle. “I’m getting older,” he says. “Maybe this is my first old-man movie.”

On sitting down to script Wild Horse Nine, the film-maker wrote GUILT and REGRET at the top of page one, as though setting his course with a compass and sextant. His film opens in Santiago before relocating to the South Pacific. From there it homes in on Malkovich’s CIA veteran, a leaky repository of cold war horror with his memories of the Bay of Pigs and Dealey Plaza. Chris is likely dying and wants to go out with a bang. He claims that he knows who killed JFK and is about to spill the beans.

The Kennedy assassination is the God particle of conspiracy theories. It marked the loss of US innocence, or the start of the rot of disinformation and fake news. McDonagh knows the official version and remains breezily unconvinced. “I definitely think there was something going on,” he says. “I’m definitely a believer in the conspiracy. Exactly what that was, we’ll never really know. Was Lee Harvey Oswald involved? More than likely. Was he the lone gunman? I don’t believe that for a second.”

He’s made several pictures with Woody Harrelson. Wasn’t Harrelson’s father once rumoured to have been involved in the killing? McDonagh sits up and mimes zipping his lip. “I know nothing,” he says.

Wild Horse Nine was never intended as a comment on the present-day United States. Except that history has a tendency to repeat and the shoot coincided with Donald Trump’s strike on Venezuela. Operations like that used to be more covert, conducted via proxies, whereas now they seem brazen, the equivalent of a smash-and-grab raid. “But I don’t think Trump is the worst president that we’ve had,” he says. “I don’t even think he’s the worst in the past 60-years. Nixon was more of a fascist pig. George W Bush probably killed more people than Trump. And then if you look at Vietnam, there’s Johnson. The difference is that with old-timey fascism, you at least had to keep it secret. These days you don’t have to hide it any more. Is that more fucked? Or is it more honest?”

McDonagh sits behind one closed door; Rockwell and Malkovich behind another. On-screen or off, the two actors have different energies, different speeds, so that the interview feels like a private performance: the Energizer Bunny versus the all-seeing Sphinx. One of these men has left his sunglasses on the floor. Inevitably it is Rockwell, who is altogether more bouncy and heedless. “My Guccis,” he cries. “Oh man, I would have stepped on those.”

Rockwell won an Oscar for playing the bumptious small-town deputy in McDonagh’s Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri . Malkovich may well follow suit thanks to Wild Horse Nine, which goes on to receive a rapturous 13-minute ovation at the premiere. The 72-year-old is on fabulously flavourful form as Chris, a tragicomic monster who is simultaneously melting down and seeing the light, lashing out and making amends. The character plays to the actor’s natural strengths, mining his innate theatricality and enigmatic air. But he explains that the role required some heavy lifting as well. Endless rehearsals and hours of line-readings, he says. “Sam and I did each scene at least a thousand times.”

A thousand? Malkovich is so self-contained and unblinking, it’s hard to know when he’s joking.

Rockwell chips in. “Yeah, about a thousand times. We ran it on the weekends. John’s a workhorse.”

“You are, too,” Malkovich says. It’s good to have a co-star to rehearse with, he adds, although every good actor has their own way of working. Clint Eastwood, for instance, prefers to hit the ground running. “You have to be a slick talker to get more than two takes out of Clint. You have to be pretty convincing, because he doesn’t take that lightly. As I know from experience.”

They were on Rapa Nui for six weeks, which helped with the process. “I have two granddaughters, so it was a long time away from them,” he says. “I don’t like being away from my grandchildren. But it’s a great place to shoot because there’s nothing else to do. You can swim with the turtles but that’s about it. Your work days are long. You’re always prepping for tomorrow. If it weren’t for a movie, I’d probably go nuts.”

Rockwell enjoyed it. “We had a great time,” he says. “Every night we had a little Chile wine and some rum. And there was a drink made with sugarcane, what the hell was it called? They put an egg-white in it.”

His partner, the actor Leslie Bibb, has materialised in the doorway. “Pisco sour,” she says.

“Pisco sour!” He’s delighted to see her and glad of the intel. Bibb has swung by to check when Rockwell breaks for lunch. He introduces her to me and indicates Malkovich on the couch. “But you can’t miss John,” he says. “Look at him, he’s beautiful.”

Marooned on his island, Chris plans to write his memoirs and come clean. His bosses are terrified he’ll mention “the Dallas parts” of his story. Some secrets, they feel, must be taken to the grave.

Malkovich has played heroes and villains. He’s been Tom Ripley, Biff Loman and the Vicomte de Valmont. But his career has been long and he’s covered this particular topic before. In 1994, he adapted and directed a stage version of Libra, Don DeLillo’s novel about Lee Harvey Oswald. He studied the Zapruder footage of JFK’s final moments and wandered down several conspiracy rabbit holes. The Warren Commission’s findings, he concluded, were either flawed or a lie. And if that makes him a crank, he’s hardly in the minority.

“Well, I think 60% of the American public don’t believe it,” he says. “Could the official story be true? Yeah, I guess. So could Keebler elves. The government tells us all kinds of things. Some of them may be true but not the majority of them, that’s my experience.”

I’ve read that he hasn’t voted since the 1972 presidential election, when the liberal George McGovern lost in a landslide to Nixon. He nods; this is true. “I’m not a believer,” he says.

Not a believer in what? Democracy? Malkovich shrugs. “In the whole thing, really. As they say in France: ‘Je ne pratique pas’, I’m not practising. I remember the night McGovern lost. I was talking to my father on the phone and I said: ‘Well, I’m done.’ He said: ‘My God, John, you can’t be done.’ I was 19 years old but that was it, I was done. I concentrate on what I can make and leave it at that.”

What about Rockwell? Is he still practising? “Yeah, well, I vote,” he says glumly. “I vote with faint hope. Hoping Obama will come back.”

The publicist sticks her head around the door. She reports that lunch is almost ready, which means that we’ve reached the last question. Rockwell perks up. “No pressure,” he says.

Let’s finish with death. That’s where the whole film is leading. Chris has decided he wants to die on Rapa Nui. Then he changes his mind and opts for Venice instead. Assuming that a death can be scripted like a film, where in the world would be the ideal place to bow out?

Malkovich thinks for a moment. “Probably on stage,” he says. “About 15 years ago I toured with a new opera based on Casanova’s memoirs. It started with Casanova chasing a chambermaid around the stage, as he was known to do, and then he has a heart attack. The play stops and people come out with a stretcher and then everyone breaks into song. Before the performance, I always made sure to tell all my friends: ‘It’s just the beginning of the play. I fake a heart attack. Don’t pay any attention.’ But forgot to tell my then-agent and I don’t think she has ever forgiven me.”

A few nights after that, he made the exact same mistake. “I have a friend, Barbara Sturm, who is a knee doctor in Düsseldorf. She came to see me and I suddenly realised I hadn’t warned her either. So I tried to text from the dressing room but of course she already had her phone switched off, being a well-mannered person. And so blah-blah-blah, the whole thing happened again.”

The production was pure chaos, but it was also rather funny. Every night he’d fake a coronary and see the panic sweep through the audience like wildfire. “As many as 20 people would run up to the stage. You’d have the doctors and a stretcher and then everybody starts singing.”

Rockwell is laughing. “That’s good acting,” he says.

“Well no, it’s terrible,” says Malkovich. “But still, it wouldn’t be the worst way to go.”

content.article_text:
10月9日より、 OVERCOAT TOKYOの旗艦店にてOVERCOAT Fall Winter 2026のポップアップイベントが開催される。 会期中は、 今シーズンのルックブックの舞台となったNYの非営利の写真出版社・文化団体『Aperture』と関係の深いアーティスト4名の作品が店内に展示される。このコラボレーションは、『Aperture』現編集長のマイケル・ファミゲッティとデザイナー大丸隆平がNY渡米時からの旧友であり、出会いから約20年の時を経て実現したものだ。

さらに、会期初日とその翌日には、デザイナー大丸とのパーソナルセッションが予定されている。セッションに参加すれば、今回OVERCOATが提示するFWコレクションにより深く 触れられるだろう。Fall Winter 2026のフルコレクションとともに、OVERCOATとApertureが描く空間とビジュアルの世界を、実際の店頭に赴いて堪能したい。秋の深まるこの季節ぜひ出掛けてみたい。

content.article_text:
De la mano de Rob Savage, con Jessica Chastain, Other Mommy arribó a los cines este 8 de octubre.

Other Mommy es una adaptación de la novela de Josh Malerman, Incidents Around the House . Cuando uno acude a la sala con la expectativa de que la producción estuvo a cargo de James Wan y Jason Blum, detrás de Atomic Monster y Blumhouse Productions, estima que la cinta estará a la altura: comienza a toda orquesta y se va desinflando con el paso de las escenas.

La historia sigue a Bela ( Arabella Olivia Clark ), una niña de siete años cuya vida se modifica cuando un ente sobrenatural llamado la “Otra Mamá” se manifiesta en su cuarto. La criatura “cobra vida” en la forma de su madre, Úrsula ( Jessica Chastain ), y al principio se presenta como una figura cercana y curiosa, aunque pronto revela su verdadera intención: obtener el corazón de Bela. La tercera pata de la familia es Russ ( Jay Duplass ), quien se muestra como un padre muy cercano a la niña, pero con poco desempeño para las tareas domésticas.

La premisa plantea un escenario con potencial para explorar el miedo infantil, la identidad materna y la fragilidad de la confianza, pero nunca desarrolla ese mismo potencial debido a que abusa de los jump scares y los movimientos repentinos con cambios de sonido. Rob Savage mantiene buenos planos, como en sus películas anteriores, pero no logra cautivar al espectador durante varias escenas, debido a que la intensidad brindada no condice con el desarrollo demostrado: nunca se llega a construir una verdadera atmósfera de tensión y terror.

El CGI, una deuda en la cinta

La visualización a través de los efectos especiales es poco convincente, por lo que no muestra lo que debería. A su vez, el espectador puede sumergirse por momentos en la historia, pero, en otros, verá que no hay demasiada cohesión en la historia.

A su vez, esta historia muestra la fragilidad de lo infantil y también de las relaciones intrafamiliares, pero ambas socavan siempre ante los intentos de sorprender al espectador con una nueva escena de persecución o aparición de la entidad, que deja todo a mitad de camino.

Te puede interesar

La aparición de “especialistas” de conjuros, de una abuela materna que da consejos y un final un poco absurdo terminan sepultando una cinta que tenía muchísimo más potencial del que terminó demostrando a través de 1 hora y media.

Calificación: 5/10.

content.article_text:
Just because you are invited into the room does not mean you decide where you stand.

At La Biennale di Venezia, visibility has its own geography, and not every country enters it on equal terms. For African and global African diaspora pavilions, the question is not simply who is present, but who gets seen, how they are seen, and what determines the difference. The Senegalese Pavilion. Image courtesy of Brendon Bell-Roberts

At La Biennale di Venezia, some countries have the privilege of being discovered; others have to persuade you to look for them. Walk through the Giardini and the Arsenale and national pavilions appear one after another, introducing visitors to artists and art histories they may never have intended to see. Beyond these venues, discovery becomes less assured. Some pavilions remain on routes visitors naturally take, while others require a conscious decision to find them. This creates a hierarchy of attention: some countries benefit from passing visitors, while others depend on visitors who already know enough to seek them out.

For countries whose artists and art histories have been marginalised by Western-dominated narratives of art history, this matters. Venice offers an opportunity to challenge that imbalance and bring their own histories to new audiences. But participation alone cannot guarantee that their pavilions will be encountered, that their artists will receive meaningful attention, or that greater visibility will continue beyond the Biennale.

Here, the geography of visibility begins.

In 2026, one hundred countries are taking part: twenty-nine at the Giardini, twenty-five at the Arsenale and forty-six elsewhere in Venice. Seven nations are exhibiting for the first time, four of them from Africa: Guinea, Equatorial Guinea, Sierra Leone and Somalia. Although these countries have the same official status, their situations regarding access, attention, and representation differ.

Egypt’s Silence Pavilion: Between the Tangible and the Intangible , by Armen Agop, and Brazil’s Comigo ninguém pode , by Rosana Paulino and Adriana Varejão, occupy permanent pavilions in the Giardini, while Morocco’s Asǝṭṭa , by Amina Agueznay, is located in the Arsenale. South Africa too has a long-term presence at the Arsenale, even though it did not take part this year. These locations sit within the routes where Biennale attention is already concentrated, allowing visitors to encounter the pavilions without deliberately seeking them out. Countries without permanent sites face a different challenge: they must establish their presence elsewhere in Venice and attract visitors to a location that may change with each participation. Permanent pavilions also acquire familiarity over time, becoming part of the geography returning visitors already know, while countries that move between venues must make themselves visible in a new place each time. Egyptian artist Armen Agop outside the Egyptian Pavilion. Image courtesy of Brendon Bell-Roberts

A pavilion situated outside the Giardini or the Arsenale doesn’t necessarily mean it is peripheral. Senegal’s WURUS and Uganda’s Kampala are in adjacent locations right on the Riva degli Schiavoni. Cuba’s Hombres Libres / Free Men , which is on Via Garibaldi, is also in a similar position along the main pedestrian route leading to the Giardini and the Arsenale. The Democratic Republic of the Congo’s first pavilion, Simba Moto! Seize the Fire! Saisis le feu!, is also conveniently located on a busy square in Castello. These pavilions sit along paths Biennale visitors are likely to follow and can therefore see without having to look for them specifically.

Guinea’s first National Participation, Le Son de l’Art: l’Écho de la Matière , occupies a very different geography. Located on the island of San Servolo, it cannot be reached simply by turning down another Venetian street. Visitors have to decide to go there, allow time for the journey and pay for a vaporetto, turning a pavilion visit into a destination in itself.

Mere proximity can also be misleading. The exhibitions Ethiopia’s Shapes of Silence , by Tegene Kunbi and curated by Abebaw Ayalew, and Zimbabwe’s Second Nature | Manyonga , curated by Fadzai Veronica Muchemwa, were both held at Castello, near the Giardini, Arsenale, Senegal, and Uganda. Yet finding them revealed how easily visibility can change within a few metres. Official Biennale signage on the Riva degli Schiavoni directed visitors down the alley towards both Ethiopia and Zimbabwe, but where the route divided, only Ethiopia was clearly signposted. We had deliberately set out to visit both and still struggled to find Zimbabwe. On a map, the difference was negligible; on foot, a missing sign made one pavilion considerably easier to find than the other.

Financial resources also shape visibility. Countries without permanent pavilions must secure temporary venues, often long before the Biennale opens, so budget size and timing can determine which spaces remain available. Funding can influence the kind of art that can be brought to Venice and exhibited, as well as the resources available for communications and for artists and curators to be present during the crucial opening days. The consequences are visible throughout: in where a pavilion is located, what audiences encounter when they arrive, who is there to speak about the work and how effectively the exhibition attracts attention beyond its doors.

ART AFRICA encountered the consequences firsthand. We were in Venice specifically to report on the African and global African diaspora pavilions, yet received no communication from Haiti, Tanzania, Uganda, Guinea, or New Guinea: no press releases, invitations, or approaches to arrange interviews. We then repeatedly emailed the media contacts listed for these pavilions in the official press material from La Biennale di Venezia, but received no response and, months later, still have not heard from them. The Cuban Pavilion. Image courtesy of Brendon Bell-Roberts

We cannot know why, nor does this mean that these pavilions received no publicity elsewhere. But if specialist media actively seeking to cover them could not make contact through the official channels provided, how effectively were they reaching audiences who did not already know they were there?

But visibility is only one part of the question. Once a pavilion has been found, another issue remains: who has been chosen to represent the country, who made those choices, and what version of the country is being made visible? Sierra Leone, Guinea, Somalia and Equatorial Guinea, all participating for the first time, bring these questions into sharp focus.

Sierra Leone’s first participation makes this question particularly relevant. Mondi Presenti / Worlds of Today , curated by Italians Sandro Orlandi Stagl and Willy Montini, brings together sixteen artists: four from Sierra Leone, four from other ECOWAS countries (the Economic Community of West African States)—Senegal, Togo, Benin, and Nigeria—seven from Italy, and one from Mexico. The curatorial statement places the pavilion within the context of ECOWAS while also referring to a history of exchange between Africa and Italy. The inclusion of artists from neighbouring West African countries therefore clearly relates to that framework. Less clear is why seven Italian artists make up almost half of Sierra Leone’s first national presentation, how the Mexican artist fits within the curatorial concept, and ultimately who determines the version of Sierra Leone that enters the Biennale’s official record.

Guinea’s inaugural Le Son de l’Art: l’Écho de la Matière , curated by Italian curator Carlo Stragapede, raises the stakes further. The exhibition brings together roughly 66 artists, including a significant number of Italians, while only a small minority appear to be Guinean. The issue is not simply who was selected, but what informed those choices and how such a large international exhibition comes to represent Guinea on its first national platform at the Biennale. Whose understanding of the country and its contemporary cultural community is being presented in its name?

Also participating for the first time, Equatorial Guinea’s The Forest The Undergrowth , curated by Catalan curator Joan Abelló, makes the issue even more explicit. Its 23 exhibitors include artists from Italy, Spain, China, Romania, Finland, Albania, Cameroon, Cyprus, Germany and Israel, alongside only one clearly identified Equatoguinean artist, Fernando Nguema Madja. The pavilion also includes Catalan-born Modest Gené Roig, who lived and worked in Equatorial Guinea. Here the question of representation has already been challenged from within the country’s cultural community. Before the Biennale opened, a group of Equatoguinean cultural practitioners publicly argued that contemporary voices from the country were largely absent and called for local artists and cultural professionals to be included in the curatorial process. The Giardini. Image courtesy of Brendon Bell-Roberts

Somalia’s first National Participation has prompted an even more direct debate over who gets to represent a country in Venice. SADDEXLEEY , featuring Ayan Farah, Asmaa Jama and Warsan Shire, is curated by Stockholm-based Mohamed Mire and Italian project manager Fabio Scrivanti. The Somali Arts Foundation has publicly criticised the pavilion for what it describes as a lack of meaningful consultation with artists and arts organisations based in Somalia, while the Somali collective Warbixinta Cidda has called for Scrivanti’s removal, questioning the appointment of an Italian co-curator given Italy’s colonial history in Somalia. An open letter subsequently drew on both statements and called for a boycott if its demands were not addressed. The dispute adds another dimension to the question of representation: not simply which artists are selected, but who is consulted, who participates in making those decisions and whose understanding of the country is ultimately presented in its name.

Taken together, these four inaugural pavilions raise a broader question of curatorial authority. The issue is not the curator’s nationality, nor must an African national pavilion be curated by someone from that country or continent. What matters is who has the authority to represent a country, what knowledge and relationships inform their choices, how its artists and cultural practitioners participate in that process, and ultimately who determines what becomes visible in the country’s name.

These questions are nothing new; the Kenya pavilion of 2013, curated by two Italians, included eight Chinese artists, one Italian, and two Kenyans. When comparable concerns were raised about the country’s representation in 2015, Kenyan artists objected, and the government then withdrew its support. The first Namibian pavilion in 2022, A Bridge to the Desert , also attracted similar criticism. Curated by Italian Marco Furio Ferrario and featuring the anonymous artist RENN, this exhibition drew objections from Namibia’s arts community over the country’s representation; the Namibian government subsequently withdrew its support, although the exhibition took place.

The controversies showed the difference between official participation and cultural legitimacy; a national pavilion makes visible not only a country but a specific representation of it, so it matters as much who has the authority to construct that representation as it does that the country is seen at all. The Bahamas Pavilion, installation view. Image courtesy of Brendon Bell-Roberts.

Visibility is also influenced by the professional networks that come together in Venice, particularly during the opening week, when museum directors, curators, collectors, foundations, galleries, and the press stay for a few intense days; having an established relationship with an artist, a curator, or an institution can help make a pavilion into a destination, while those who do not have such connections depend more on drawing attention outside of their current networks.

For journalists, those few days are often the only chance to interview artists and curators while in Venice, since time is limited and the city is expensive. So many events compete for attention—namely the Giardini, the Arsenale, the 100 National Participations, the collateral events, and the various exhibitions—that harder-to-find pavilions must put in extra time and effort. Moreover, geography and professional networks can interact: a pavilion off the main routes must work harder to enter the channels through which professional attention flows.

Yet a pavilion’s audience is not limited to the people who walk through its doors. Media coverage can take an exhibition far beyond Venice, reaching readers and viewers who will never attend the Biennale. Reviews, interviews, photographs, videos, podcasts, newsletters and specialist publications can introduce artists and their work to entirely new audiences, while an interview might bring an artist to the attention of a curator who never saw the exhibition in Venice. This coverage also gives the pavilion life beyond the months of the Biennale, creating a record that can circulate long after the exhibition has closed. In this sense, what happens beyond the pavilion can become as important as what happens inside it.

International media coverage is not necessarily more valuable than national, regional, or specialist coverage, which can offer the backgrounds and contexts that general reporting tends to ignore. What matters is how far the coverage reaches, whether it introduces the artists and their work to people who were not already familiar with them, and whether the attention results in anything beyond Venice.

Being highly visible doesn’t necessarily mean having a real impact. Image courtesy of Brendon Bell-Roberts

It is important when considering the reasons why countries choose to invest in Venice, since taking part requires a great deal of financial and institutional resources and therefore high numbers of visitors do not necessarily indicate that the investment has been worthwhile; a pavilion that is crowded may bring about some degree of exposure without achieving any real results, while fewer interactions could result in exhibitions, acquisitions, commissions, publications, or in the establishment of long-term institutional relationships.

No single criterion can judge success, since there shouldn’t be one. However, participation alone cannot measure success.

If international exposure is one reason for taking part in the Biennale, then more significant questions arise once the pavilion has opened. Has it brought the artists and their respective art histories to the attention of people who are not already familiar with them? Has anyone written about, interviewed, or exhibited their work in other institutional contexts? Have the artists obtained new opportunities? Have any relationships persisted after Venice?

The geographical aspect of visibility therefore extends beyond Venice; it affects the chances of discovery, directs professional interest, shapes the kind of content linked to a country’s name, and influences how far that representation will extend afterwards.

For African countries and the global African diaspora, the stakes are particularly high. La Biennale di Venezia can bring artists and art histories long marginalised by Western-dominated narratives to wider attention, opening doors to audiences, institutions and conversations that might otherwise remain out of reach. But an official place within the Biennale does not guarantee an equal chance of being discovered, nor does it necessarily give artists and cultural communities greater authority over how their countries and histories are presented.

The differences begin long before the doors open and can continue long after they close.

Presence, then, is only the beginning. If nobody was looking for you, did Venice make them look — and when they did, who decided what they would see?

Paris Photo and Aperture are pleased to announce the shortlist for the 2026 Paris Photo–Aperture PhotoBook Awards—an annual celebration of the photobook’s enduring role within the narrative of photography. Now in its fourteenth year, the awards recognize excellence in three major categories of photobook publishing: First PhotoBook, PhotoBook of the Year, and Photography Catalog of the Year.

This year, Paris Photo–Aperture PhotoBook Awards received a record number of books from fifty-six countries around the world, including standout entries from Armenia, Iran, Morocco, Venezuela, and more. On September 22–24, the 2026 shortlist jury met in New York for three concentrated days of review and deliberation by an international team: Alejandro Cartagena , artist; Alexandra Cunningham Cameron , director of design, Judd Foundation; Michael Famighetti , editor in chief, Aperture; Anna Planas , artistic director, Paris Photo; and Anshika Varma , curator and founder, Offset Projects.

“Reviewing the many submissions from around the globe underscores how photography books are a quietly powerful medium with endless possibilities for design, storytelling, and reflection on human experience,” says Michael Famighetti. Anna Planas adds, “The jury brings together different perspectives on photography and publishing. Through the selection presented at Paris Photo, we aim to highlight the photobook as a space for experimentation and to celebrate its importance within photography today.”

The shortlisted books will be exhibited at Paris Photo, open to the public from November 11 through November 15, followed by an international tour, including in Dublin at PhotoIreland, December 2026, New York at Printed Matter, January 2027, and other venues to be announced.

On Thursday, November 12, a ﬁnal jury composed of ﬁve members will meet in Paris to select the winners for all three prizes, which will be revealed on Friday, November 13, at 3:00 p.m. (CET), at a ceremony at Paris Photo, and announced on Aperture.org and Parisphoto.com.

Below, see the thirty-five selected titles for the 2026 PhotoBook Awards shortlist.

content.article_text:
Ce portrait a été initialement publié en 2024, lors de la sortie du folm,

Dans son salon, la lumière passe à travers des fenêtres en vitrail typiques de la Belle Époque. Derrière le canapé en velours sur lequel on discute, il y a un personnage de Disney (le vilain Jafar, dans Aladdin) en carton, fabriqué par son enfant, et, tout autour, des dessins, croquis, peintures ou photos, disposés dans une sorte de bazar ordonné. À mi-chemin entre un appartement et un atelier, l’intérieur de l’habitation de Louise Bourgoin, zen et chaleureuse, atteste d’une chose : ici, pas de hiérarchie entre l’art classique, les dessins de nus et les gribouillages enfantins. Dans Bis repetita d’Émilie Noblet, il y a une combinaison tout aussi grisante entre totems antiques et culture pop (on apprend les rudiments du latin en écoutant sur YouTube une version traduite en latin de « Pour que tu m’aimes encore » , le hit sentimental de Céline Dion).

L’actrice y campe avec une jubilation contagieuse Delphine, une prof démissionnaire d’un lycée d’Angers. Pas très à cheval sur la déontologie, celle-ci scrolle les offres de fringues sur des applications face à des élèves désintéressés au possible. Les deux parties ont passé un contrat : contre des 19 sur 20 dans les bulletins de notes pipés, les élèves laissent leur prof tranquille. Tout ce beau monde blasé doit remettre le pied à l’étrier quand la directrice (la géniale Noémie Lvovsky), les croyant surdoués, inscrit les élèves au championnat international de latin, à Naples.

Hasard du calendrier : en moins d’un an, Louise Bourgoin a campé deux profs au bout du rouleau, d’abord dans un registre plus grave chez Thomas Lilti, dans Un métier sérieux , et maintenant chez Émilie Noblet. Si elle interprète si bien ces enseignantes au bord de la crise de nerfs, c’est aussi parce qu’elle connaît par cœur et intimement ce milieu.

« Un métier sérieux » de Thomas Lilti : l’école au corps

AU PREMIER RANG

L’actrice, qui arbore une marinière (comme un subtil clin d’œil à ses origines bretonnes, elle qui est née à Rennes en 1981), avait tout pour être une enfant de la balle : sa mère était prof de lettres modernes ; son père, de philosophie. En grandissant, elle les a vus trimer : « Ils étaient régulièrement épuisés par leur travail. Et j’ai grandi dans les années 1990-2000, donc ce n’est pas un phénomène nouveau, même si on en parle plus aujourd’hui. C’est un métier extrêmement peu considéré en France, difficile, sous-payé. C’était une grande responsabilité de l’incarner à l’écran. »

Pas vraiment du genre dissipée à l’école ( « j’avais quand même la pression pour ne pas redoubler, ça aurait été horrible pour mes parents » ) ni dégoûtée par ce métier, la future actrice, attirée par les arts plastiques, cherche d’abord à marcher dans les pas de sa famille. Elle suit des études aux Beaux-Arts. Elle tente de rentrer dans le moule familial en s’inscrivant comme prof stagiaire à l’Institut universitaire de formation des maîtres, en vue de passer son CAPES. C’est après avoir échoué au concours qu’elle décide de passer des castings pour la télé et le cinéma.

Rétrospectivement, ce lancement dans le jeu sans filet ni formation a provoqué un complexe durable chez elle. « C’est un métier un peu magique parce que quelqu’un comme moi, qui n’a pas pris de cours, peut démarrer avec un premier rôle. Mais j’ai un sentiment d’illégitimité, je culpabilise de ne pas avoir fait le Conservatoire. » La première fois que le public la découvre, c’est sur le plateau du Grand Journal de Canal+, en 2006, où elle officie comme Miss météo.

Xavier Lacaille : « Quand je n’arrive pas à mettre mon masque social, ça me tord profondément »

Face caméra, elle lit des textes drôles, osés, malins et décalés, tout en entrant dans la peau d’une animatrice sexy, avec les limites et la stéréotypisation que ce rôle peut engendrer. Louise Bourgoin ne renie pas du tout cette expérience à la télévision – là encore, pas de hiérarchie, et peu de jugement. Il faut dire que ses performances télévisuelles ont eu le mérite de montrer que cette bonne élève, qui apprend ses textes longtemps avant le tournage et avec méthode (elle les recopie, puis mémorise les répliques en inversant les mots dans les phrases), excelle paradoxalement à incarner une forme d’irrévérence à l’écran.

STATUES VIVANTES « C’est une artiste qui m’a beaucoup marquée » , nous dit Louise Bourgoin quand on l’interroge sur son rapport à Louise Bourgeois, artiste française célèbre et provocante, dont elle s’est inspirée pour trouver son pseudonyme d’actrice. « Je l’ai découverte à mes 17 ans, puis j’ai regardé un documentaire dans lequel elle épluche une orange et parle de façon étonnante de son travail. Elle joue la naïve en disant que ses immenses phallus en albâtre sont des petites filles avec des cols roulés. Elle se moque des spectateurs et a une insolence dans son discours sur ses œuvres. »

Dans une scène de Bis repetita , les élèves et leur prof visitent les ruines napolitaines et bloquent sur des sculptures antiques de nus, avec un air mi-choqué, mi-amusé. Hors plateau, le nu passionne justement Louise Bourgoin. En 2012, elle a coécrit avec Edwart Minot Orsay mis à nu , livre dans lequel elle commente les plus belles œuvres déshabillées du musée d’Orsay. « J’ai toujours adoré dessiner des corps entremêlés, enlacés. Je n’aime pas dessiner des vêtements, parce que ça date une œuvre. Dans le livre, je me suis penchée sur des œuvres de la fin du xixe et du début du xxe siècle, avec peu de peintres femmes mais beaucoup plus de modèles féminins nus que masculins. »

Peinture et cinéma, même combat ? Longtemps cantonnée sur le grand écran à des rôles de muses (des personnages de séductrices ou d’amoureuses), l’actrice, qui aime jouer « des personnes pas très reluisantes, qui trichent, qui mentent » et qui a été chamboulée plus jeune par les films de Larry Clark ou Gregg Araki, semble enfin avoir droit à des rôles à la hauteur de son aura (voir la série Hippocrate de Thomas Lilti, dans laquelle elle incarne une interne en médecine brillante et ambitieuse) et de sa puissance comique (voir ses scènes alcoolisées dans Bis repetita , anthologiques).

Loin d’être en crise, la quadra atteint a contrario une forme de plénitude artistique – elle a osé exposer pour la première fois ses œuvres à la galerie Laura Pecheur, en 2022. Elle espère secrètement se lancer dans l’arène de films d’action (elle fait de la boxe française) : « J’aime beaucoup la violence féminine au cinéma, elle est encore trop rare. » À voir son visage anguleux et son regard féroce lorsqu’elle ne sourit pas, on se dit qu’elle pourrait tout pulvériser.

Bis repetita d’Émilie Noblet, Le Pacte (1h26), sortie le 20 mars.
