Daidō Moriyama: Ink ★★★★☆

If it’s a crime to have a crush on an elderly avant garde Japanese street photographer then lock me up and throw away the key, because I have some seriously strong feelings for Daidō Moriyama . His ultra-confrontational, high contrast, aggressive take on photography just gets me blushing, what can I say.

This little exhibition is Moriyama at his artiest and strangest. In the 1960s he discovered Warhol and became obsessed. The works here find him playing with repetition and silk screening, printing up ghostly, painterly, effervescent monochrome images of stacks of soft drinks, neon lit crosswalks and peep show adverts. This is the grim, gritty side of Japanese urbanity, but you can see American capitalism creeping in and taking hold, slowly suffocating the streets.

He repeats an image of lips like Warhol’s Marilyn Monroe, duplicates a photo of people walking down a street, their bodies becoming indistinguishable from the adverts hanging from the high rises around them. Then he snaps a woman lifting her skirt, another stomping down the road in thigh-high boots. It’s like Warhol without the pretence, and with added filth. Hamiltons Gallery, London, until 14 November

Jenkin van Zyl: Enclosure ★★★★☆

Jenkin van Zyl is hellbent on cementing their place as English art’s ultimate hyper-camp weirdo, and their new show at Somerset House Studios is a pretty persuasive argument.

The exhibition is centred on a speculative sci-fi movie about some bleak company where tourists can inhabit other people’s bodies. But when the central character, a starlet called Mercy, comes to end the lease on her body, the line between reality and fiction starts getting anxiously blurry. Who is the real Mercy, and who is the clone? Who controls your identity? Who has access to what makes you you ?

Its grubby atmosphere is reinforced by an immersive installation that replicates the film set as you walk in, with broken automatons, flickering lights and piles of rubbish, all bathed in a pink glow. It’s an unsettling, uncomfortable, dirty, dystopian bit of art cinema – like an overblown, fetishistic take on Terry Gilliam’s Brazil . Van Zyl has a singular aesthetic, and this is pretty much as watchable as this kind of art film gets. It stays with you long after you’ve escaped its unnerving clutches.

The gallery handout wants to make out like this is about technological advancement and ideas of authorship. But like all good sci-fi, this feels more obviously allegorical than that. It’s about identity, the versions of ourselves that we present and preserve online, or in public, and how easy it is to lose your grip on the true you. Like a lot of artists these days who grew up with the internet and reality TV turning their brain into gloop, Van Zyl is trying to make sense of a post-reality world, a place where identity can be constructed, but never fully controlled. Somerset House, London, until 29 November

George Shaw: Albion Groans Part Two ★★★★☆

There’s nothing all that pleasant, or even particularly green, about the England of George Shaw’s paintings. There are no rolling hills or quiet pub afternoons here in this excellent show of small works by the 60-year-old artist. Instead, there are endless potholes, crumbling masonry, darkened alleys and damp, muddy, miserable, mid-winter landscapes. This is the England of council estates left to rot.

His landscapes – always based on his native Coventry – are devoid of life. There are no humans here, only the places they’re desperate to escape. Every sky is overcast, every tree barren, every path sodden with puddles. A union jack has been left crumpled on the pavement near an empty bottle of booze in one, endless knobs have been crudely graffitied on garage doors in another. There’s a painting of a single cloud blighting a blue sky, another of a robin lying dead on its side. Suburbia has leached into the countryside like a toxic spill.

They are gorgeously painted, especially the smaller works: sticky with enamel, glossy and horrifyingly alluring, like staring at a car crash.

But the car crash here is England itself. Sure, Shaw has been painting the same views of the same bit of Coventry for 30 years, but in that time the country has continued to erode. His whole career is a living portrait of England’s slow collapse. This time it doesn’t just feel like perpetual decline – it’s terminal. Anthony Wilkinson Gallery, London, until 7 November

after newsletter promotion

Tanoa Sasraku: Tropical Ken ★★★☆☆

The thing that’s so good about the main work in Tanoa Sasraku’s Turner prize installation – open now at Mima in Middlesbrough – is how perfectly it marries image with idea. Sasraku’s collection of corporate paperweights from oil companies acts as a horrifying symbol of the greed of that vile industry. Perfect.

Here at Vardaxoglou, Sasraku is showing works from another series, some of which are also on show at Mima, that don’t quite hit the same dopamine receptors. They’re all paper cut into the form of torsos, held together with clips. She places acetates of military camouflage on top of them and then pops them in a tanning bed, leaving behind the faintest impressions of the patterns.

They’re meant to evoke warfare, weapons crates and fruit boxes, all while alluding to Ken dolls, but they just look a bit like tea-stained gilets. The gap between image and idea, between the concept and its ability to communicate itself visually, is just a bit too wide. Vardaxoglou, London, until 31 October

content.article_text:
P aul Greengrass has in fact already made his “uprising” film: United 93 , the gut-wrenching 2006 masterpiece about the passengers onboard United Airlines flight 93 who rose up against the 9/11 hijackers and prevented them from hitting their destination and causing fatalities – except, that is, for those onboard the plane. Greengrass’s new movie, shot in his distinctive handheld, docu-reportage style, is notionally about the 1381 Peasants’ Revolt, in which Wat Tyler and John Ball became legendary for leading an insurrection against the cruel poll tax of Richard II. Or at least … it sort of is. Because the film, in a disconcertingly silly way, imagines the uprising as an origin myth for Robin Hood, or at least someone who’s supposed to be more or less Robin Hood – because that’s not what he’s called and the dates don’t quite match up.

Ex-soldier Tyler and radical preacher Ball, capably played by Cosmo Jarvis and Jamie Bell, are joined by a third fictional hero, apparently destined later to canter through the forest with a wealth-redistribution plan. He is a ploughman, known simply as “Ploughman”, played by Andrew Garfield; grieving the loss of his wife and children to the plague and sickened by the tax collectors’ greed and brutality, he instigates an insurrection that soon merges into other outbreaks of revolutionary rage. This involves rivers of smudgy-faced folk in rough clothes descending on the capital from all directions, to demand concessions from the king to whom they are still loyal and believe to have been misled by advisers.

The appearance of the well-bathed royal overlords themselves may remind you of the immortal line from Monty Python and the Holy Grail about how to tell if someone is a king. Tom Hollander gives a very enjoyable performance as his majesty’s evil adviser Sir Robert Hales, and Katherine Waterston is typically stylish and composed as Joan of Kent, the king’s mother, while Woody Norman has a sinister moon-faced blankness as the young Richard II himself. There are moments to enjoy in all the overclass performances, and indeed to respect in those of the doomed uprisers, whose heroism nonetheless is supposed to create a historic legacy of fighting against bullies and tyrants.

That, it seems, is the point of it all. Which brings us to the coda; I wondered if Greengrass would boldly hit us with an immersive scene from London’s 1990 poll tax riots. But no. It’s Garfield emerging from the dense forest with his un-merry men like a gag-free episode of Blackadder, and being oddly lenient with the ermine-clad VIPs that they catch. It’s a bit of letdown.

H ollywood is sending a clear message: it’s a friend of tech. Netflix is no longer a lone disruptor: historic studio MGM is now the property of Amazon’s Jeff Bezos; David Ellison’s takeover of Paramount and subsequent Warner Bros merger was supported by his tech giant father; and Apple TV has acted as a patron for multiple film-maker passion projects. Everyone, including trendy auteur-factory A24, is tying themselves financially to AI.

The enormous pull of the tech industry – including its many trillions of dollars, oversized influence on politics and heavily pushed algorithms and AI products – means Hollywood is not alone in courting its wealth, but it has intensified the historic tension between art and commerce in the entertainment business. Technology that augments the human experience may be a compelling narrative subject, but this year brings a trio of films about the gurus responsible for the industry’s false promises.

Starring Jeremy Strong as Mark Zuckerberg, The Social Reckoning is Aaron Sorkin’s pseudo-sequel to The Social Network, about Facebook employee Frances Haugen (Mikey Madison) blowing the whistle on her employer for building an algorithm that radicalised the “alt-right” and damaged teen mental health. This week, two further films receive their UK premiere at the BFI London film festival – Musk is a four-hour study of the SpaceX CEO from Alex Gibney, the documentarian who previously tackled the Enron bankruptcy scandal and Theranos founder and fraudster Elizabeth Holmes. Luca Guadagnino’s Artificial stars Andrew Garfield (whose breakout role was as Zuckerberg’s ex-bestie in The Social Network) as OpenAI co-founder Sam Altman, who was fired and rehired by his own board a year after the release of ChatGPT.

All three projects come with a degree of buzz that goes beyond their directors’ credentials. We are long overdue a meaningful, mainstream critical rebuke of the volatile and egocentric “great men” rewarded by our tech-obsessed culture. Zuckerberg, Musk and Altman are among the biggest names in tech, and all three recently aligned with President Trump to protect their companies’ interests. Seeing major if unrelated film projects taking them to task gives the impression of a united front of tech scepticism. But how strongly can a major motion picture attack big tech? In the case of Artificial, there may be a cost to biting the hand that feeds you, as Amazon decided to not distribute the film, after announcing a $50bn (£38bn) “strategic partnership” with OpenAI.

Certain contextual details lend the films an edge of legitimacy and danger: a distributor suddenly unloading a hot-button project; Sony hiring an outside law firm to vet every fact in The Social Reckoning ; or TikTok and X blocking trailer advertisements for Musk. These anecdotes are cleanly rolled into the films’ marketing, fanning the audience’s desire to see something damning and damaging behind the curtain of Silicon Valley – but they are likely more useful in Oscar campaigns than as a challenge to big tech impunity.

Time will tell how severely these films will affect the credibility of their subjects, but recent surveys indicate young Americans are already turning on giants such as Zuckerberg, Musk, and Altman. It seems as if these projects are taking advantage of a rising tide of tech scepticism rather than forging it themselves. What’s more noteworthy is how the films coincide with the widespread devaluing of films as art by corporations and their products.

There’s an inconvenience to watching a two-hour film that rankles the compulsively tech-obsessed: its pleasures are better redistributed into short-form clips on Instagram, TikTok and YouTube, all of which handily drive traffic as part of users’ infinite scroll. You may not see any ads for Musk on X or TikTok, but some enterprising grifter is welcome to package up clips from Gibney’s doc for engagement farming once it’s released. Clips from The Social Reckoning will go nicely with the thousand other snippets of Sorkin’s verbal duels from The West Wing and The Newsroom on Meta’s platforms.

What’s more, the hype around GenAI has proven tech elites want to disrupt production and distribution – to their benefit. In light of tech’s accelerating entanglement with Hollywood, entire filmographies may soon used en masse to train image and video generation tools. Meta, OpenAI and Musk’s xAI have a head start, having already “scraped” scripts and books without permission to train their models. In 2025, Disney and Universal filed a suit against AI firm Midjourney for stealing their copyrighted works in this manner (Midjourney denies liability, arguing that its platform operates on transformative fair use). But don’t jump to defend their anti-AI integrity, Disney recently invested $1bn in OpenAI – they want a slice of the pie.

The triple release of The Social Reckoning, Musk and Artificial is less a clear political stance, more like movie studio opportunism. But as the industry grows more eager to placate big tech, studios are more likely to censor films like these getting made. Still, history is on the side of artists who take swipes at powerful moguls. When newspaper tycoon William Randolph Hearst found out Orson Welles’ Citizen Kane was based on him, he called on his network of columnists and producers to sabotage the film’s release – behaviour that is not beneath Elon Musk, if his posts are anything to go by . It’s surprising to learn that tech moguls – whether they’re protected by a cult of personality or not – still get seriously riled up by any narrative they don’t control.

content.article_text:
H ere is a film for all those people who solemnly deplore social media in conversation but haven’t quite got round to deleting their accounts. Sixteen years have gone by since The Social Network , written by Aaron Sorkin and directed by David Fincher; this was the addictive, obsessive-compulsive movie about the birth of Facebook in Harvard’s macho-competitive cauldron of student sexism and nerdy self-pity, starring Jesse Eisenberg as the fast-talking, arrogant, not-necessarily-evil genius Mark Zuckerberg. Now Sorkin is back with a sequel of sorts, directing his own script – and now Zuckerberg is basically evil, but also weirdly slow talking, as if all the zinging, smart-alecky Sorkinesque dialogue energy of the first film has been siphoned away in early middle age and dispersed among the insurgents in the new cast.

Sorkin’s jittery, funny, syncopated style is unmistakable, as distinctive in its way as David Mamet, although he has one joke about “spatula” being a Yiddish word that he has borrowed from Philip Roth’s Portnoy’s Complaint . It is the story of how in 2021, Zuckerberg’s Facebook empire was challenged by courageous whistleblower-employee Frances Haugen and Wall Street Journal investigative reporter Jeff Horwitz, who were on a mission to tell the world how Zuckerberg, scared by falling revenue, changed the algorithm so that engagement was supercharged by rage bait and hate speech, malice and envy. Facebook, moreover, didn’t factcheck political ads, thus driving a huge, nationwide surge in extremist groups and teen bullying and becoming a major player in the Capitol riots. (Having said that, this film does not say aloud the word “Trump” and rather cravenly declines to specify Maga activity.)

Mikey Madison sympathetically plays the unhappy, principled, supersmart Haugen, who is dismissed as a “disrupter” – and Sorkin leaves it to us to notice that this in other circumstances is what oligarchs smugly call themselves. Jeremy Allen White does a capable, unflashy, unrisky job as Horwitz, a stolid performance that perhaps, in sync with the film, tells us about the diligent professionalism of old-school print journalism. And Zuckerberg? Well, we were all hoping and expecting it would be Jesse Eisenberg again. (You’ve heard of Richard Linklater’s Boyhood; this would be Aaron Sorkin’s Techbrohood.) But no: it is Jeremy Strong, who does a very interesting Zuckerberg impersonation, standing and sitting like a Thunderbird puppet, modifying the torpid sadness of his Kendall Roy in TV’s Succession, making this the unhurried contempt of someone simultaneously burdened and energised by knowing he’s richer and therefore smarter than everyone else. (A famous line in The Social Network was “A million dollars isn’t cool. You know what’s cool? A billion dollars.” This film starts by telling us that Facebook is worth a trillion dollars.)

Zuckerberg, though, is almost a cameo, with no equals with whom he can exchange dialogue, only employees – although the film imagines one former investor-turned-critic called Charlie (Bill Burr) who heckles Zuckerberg’s practice performance before a confessional hearing, with Zuckerberg amusingly having to be told how to smile. Charlie is the angry, unheeded voice of conscience.

The resulting drama rattles along at an entertaining clip, although there are false notes. When Frances has secret meetings with Horwitz in a hotel, the film has her wearing a slinky evening dress, supposedly as a kind of disguise, so that if recognised it would seem like she was out on a date. Hmm, really? Or is it so that the movie’s female lead has scenes where she looks glamorous? Later, Horwitz affectionately tells her to be less “mean”. But she is not “mean”. She just speaks Sorkinspeak. So does Horwitz. The ubiquity of Sorkinspeak effaces the difference between all the characters.

The most disturbing scene comes at the very beginning, showing a drunk woman livestreaming her racist abuse of traffic cops; this is the woman whom Haugen recognises as an acquaintance of hers, radicalised by Facebook . Towards the end we glimpse her again, looking ambiguously appalled by what she has become. But would she be appalled in reality? Or is this just the film-makers’ wish fulfilment? The closing-credit titles – usually the platform for a film to promote and summarise its heroes’ achievements – concedes that Facebook still isn’t checking political ads. Plus, of course, the film is set at the start of the Trump interregnum of 2020-24, when it seemed as if the Capitol riots were the ultimate wake-up call and moderation had returned. Nowadays Trump and his tech bro courtiers are more vainglorious than ever, and the values of investigative journalism have been thrown out at the Washington Post by its owner Jeff Bezos. This is a film which doesn’t reckon with the future we’re living in.

content.article_text:
Dans son ouvrage Blinded by the Grace , publié chez Loose Joints, Sarah Chaplin Espenon s’intéresse aux femmes chasseuses de tornades. Une pratique traditionnellement masculine que l’éditrice française explore au cœur d’un récit délicat aux noirs et blancs menaçants.

Les images sont granuleuses, obscures, elles disent l’agitation, la panique, le déferlement des éléments. À l’horizon – un horizon dramatiquement proche – on voit des tornades, tourbillons gigantesques aux tubes monstrueux. Les nuages s’y jettent, le ciel est sombre – il menace, lui aussi. Dans les cadres, quelques détails s’ajoutent : l’éclair qui s’abat non loin d’un toit, l’herbe qui se tasse contre le sol des champs, les branches qui ploient sous la force des vents… Et quelques silhouettes féminines, cheveux emmêlés, sourires triomphants, regards rivés vers la tempête qui approche, prêtes à saisir leur magnificence, malgré le danger, malgré la peur.

Pour réaliser Blinded by your Grace , Sarah Chaplin Espenon, éditrice de cofondatrice de Loose Joints, s’est intéressée à ces femmes qui chassent les tornades, fascinées par leur intensité. Entre recherches et collaborations directes avec ces aventurières, elle propose une relecture des images qui restent de ces face-à-face aussi périlleux qu’exaltants : harmonisées dans un monochromes rugueux, où les noirs et blancs se mangent, comme pour convoquer la hâte et l’excitation de l’instant, elle imagine un récit reposant sur les sensations.

Le rapport genré au danger

Les pages sont fines, presque friables, presque déchirables. Les tornades s’y déplacent, d’une feuille à l’autre, dans un alignement vertigineux. Loin du documentaire, ce que Sarah Chaplin Espenon donne à voir, dans cet ouvrage, c’est l’abandon de ces femmes, celles qui acceptent le risque – celui d’être détruites par dévouement, par passion. Dans ces paysages ébranlés, il n’est pas question de chercher un simple frisson, mais plutôt de choisir la vulnérabilité. Une vulnérabilité qui ne peut naître qu’en parallèle d’une intense concentration.

En filigrane, l’éditrice interroge cette pratique, traditionnellement masculine, et le rapport genré au danger. Pourquoi est-ce socialement plus convenable pour un homme de s’y intéresser ? Comment s’approcher volontairement d’une menace lorsqu’on est une femme et qu’on nous apprend à fuir plutôt qu’à nous attarder ? La prise de risque n’est-elle jugée saine d’esprit que quand un individu masculin choisit de l’entreprendre ? Peut-elle être perçue comme un droit universel ? Au cœur des débris et des ciels tumultueux, les chasseuses-autrices publiées dans Blinded by your Grace semblent nous proposer une narration complexe aux nuances délicates. Là, entre les orages et les grondements célestes, dans le noir le plus profond des tourbillons, elles laissent apparaître les lignes de crêtes sur lesquelles elles avancent, entre attirance et tension, entre prudence et conquête.

Curiosité

content.article_text:
10月8日より、BOOK AND SONSで小平雅尋による写真集『Videre Videor』刊行を記念した写真展が開催される。

小平は直感的な撮影行為を続けながら、いかにして対象を認識しシャッターを切るに到るのかについて、省察を続けてきた。本シリーズのタイトル「Videre Videor」は、ルネ・デカルトのコギト命題「われ思う、ゆえにわれあり」へと至る一文、「私は確かに見えると思われ（videre videor）、聞くと思われ（audire videor）、熱を感じると思われる（calescare videor）」を端緒としており、写真に取り組み始めてから約30年、撮り続けてきた本シリーズにおいて、小平はこれらの問いを再考。直感的な撮影を通して個人と世界の根源的な関係性を探る、一種の帰着点を提している。

本展では、1Fと2Fのスペースを使用して24点の作品が展示される。会期に合わせて写真集の先行販売されるほか、初日にはレセプション、10月10日には関連イベントとしてトークイベントも開催されるので会期中に訪れてみてはいかが。

「もし『無意識が見た風景』を写真にするならば、写真家は何をすべきだろうか。 小平雅尋の写真制作は、この問いに対する一つの答えである」 -若山満大（東京ステーションギャラリー学芸員）による寄稿文より

Reseña de “Border”: Un romance monstruoso entre lo bizarro y lo sublime

Border: La película de fantasía nórdica que tenés que ver

Te contamos porqué debes ver “Border”, la extraña y atrapante película de Ali Abassi

Border (también conocida como Gräns ) irrumpió en la pantalla en el año 2018 bajo la dirección de Ali Abbasi. Esta extraordinaria rareza sueca, inspirada en un cuento homónimo de John Ajvide Lindqvist (“Déjame entrar”), te transporta a un mundo parecido al nuestro, pero del que seguro vas a dudar. Es un territorio donde el drama, la fantasía y el suspenso se entrelazan de manera visceral, fusionando el realismo mágico y el folklore nórdico para crear una experiencia que atrae y aterra al mismo tiempo.

¿De qué va?

La historia sigue a Tina, una agente de aduanas que trabaja en un puesto fronterizo y posee un don único: puede oler las emociones de las personas. Un día, durante un control de seguridad, interroga a un hombre de traje. Revisa minuciosamente su bolso, pero no encuentra ningún objeto prohibido. Entonces le pide que saque su teléfono. Lo toma y comienza a olerlo. Algo no está bien: percibe algo oscuro. Decide seguir interrogándolo y, finalmente, descubren una tarjeta de memoria escondida en la funda. Dentro hay videos de crímenes. Una vez más, su olfato no se había equivocado. A lo largo de su vida, Tina ha sido discriminada por su apariencia y aprendió a mantenerse alejada de los demás, refugiándose en la soledad del bosque. Pero todo cambia cuando conoce a Vore, un hombre con características muy similares a las suyas.

A partir de ese encuentro, comienza a descubrir que hay mucho más detrás de su apariencia y de sus extrañas habilidades.

La nueva adaptación de Carrie, dirigida por Mike Flanagan, llega a Prime Video y vuelve a poner sobre la mesa las similitudes entre el personaje de Stephen King y Once, de Stranger Things. El director explicó por qué la comparación debe entenderse en otro sentido.

Mike Flanagan llega a Prime Video con una nueva adaptación de Carrie , la clásica novela de Stephen King publicada en 1974. La historia vuelve a centrarse en Carrie White , una adolescente con poderes telequinéticos que debe enfrentarse al acoso de sus compañeros y a una vida familiar marcada por el fanatismo religioso. Sin embargo, desde que se conocieron los primeros detalles de la serie, las redes sociales comenzaron a encontrar similitudes entre Carrie y Stranger Things , especialmente por la presencia de una protagonista con poderes sobrenaturales. Para Flanagan, la comparación tiene un punto de partida equivocado.

La razón es sencilla: Carrie apareció mucho antes que la serie creada por los hermanos Duffer. De hecho, Stephen King publicó su primera novela más de cuatro décadas antes del estreno de Stranger Things en Netflix , en 2016.

La influencia de Carrie sobre la cultura popular tampoco es nueva. El personaje de King marcó a numerosas historias posteriores que exploraron la adolescencia, el aislamiento, el bullying y el despertar de poderes sobrenaturales. Stranger Things no es una excepción.

Mike Flanagan habló sobre las comparaciones entre Carrie y Stranger Things

Durante una entrevista con Screen Rant, Mike Flanagan fue consultado por las comparaciones que comenzaron a surgir entre Carrie y Stranger Things. El director explicó que, a la hora de desarrollar esta nueva adaptación, tuvieron en cuenta las distintas versiones que ya existen de la historia, pero también aquellos personajes que fueron influenciados por la creación de Stephen King.

“Para mí, no tiene sentido intentar hacer un remake y repetir lo que ya se ha hecho. Eso implicaba tener en cuenta no solo las adaptaciones anteriores, sino también, como bien dices, a Once y a otros personajes que, obviamente, están fuertemente influenciados por Carrie White”.

De esta manera, Flanagan dejó claro que Once no representa una referencia previa a Carrie, sino todo lo contrario. El personaje interpretado por Millie Bobby Brown forma parte de una larga lista de protagonistas que, de una u otra manera, recibieron la influencia de Carrie White.

La comparación tampoco resulta extraña desde el punto de vista visual o conceptual. Ambas historias presentan a jóvenes con habilidades sobrenaturales que deben aprender a lidiar con sus poderes mientras atraviesan situaciones de violencia y aislamiento. La diferencia fundamental está en el origen de esos poderes y, por supuesto, en el contexto de cada relato.

Carrie, una historia que sigue influyendo décadas después

Publicada en 1974, Carrie fue la primera novela publicada de Stephen King y rápidamente se convirtió en uno de los títulos más importantes de su carrera. Dos años después, Brian De Palma llevó la historia al cine con una película protagonizada por Sissy Spacek, considerada hasta hoy como una de las grandes adaptaciones de la obra del escritor.

Desde entonces, Carrie tuvo nuevas versiones y continuó dejando su huella en el género. Su influencia también puede encontrarse en numerosas producciones posteriores que abordaron el acoso escolar, la adolescencia y personajes jóvenes con capacidades extraordinarias.

En el caso de Stranger Things, los propios hermanos Duffer han reconocido en distintas oportunidades la influencia de Stephen King en su trabajo. La serie de Netflix combina además diferentes elementos del cine y la literatura de terror y ciencia ficción de las décadas de 1970 y 1980.

Por eso, para Flanagan, el desafío de esta nueva versión de Carrie no consiste en ignorar esas influencias, sino en reconocerlas y encontrar una manera diferente de contar una historia que ya forma parte de la cultura popular.

La nueva serie de Carrie llegará a Prime Video este miércoles 7 de octubre , con Mike Flanagan al frente de una nueva interpretación del clásico de Stephen King.

クラシック音楽を香りに編曲するフレグランスブランド、「La Nuit parfum（ラニュイ パルファン）」が、ブランド設立5周年を記念して発表した新作オードパルファン5種のムエットに、国内外の写真家、アーティストによる作品を採用した。香りを試すための消耗品として扱われることの多いムエットを、音楽、香り、写真という3つの表現をつなぐメディアとして展開する。

2026年の新作は、フランツ・シュミット《7つの封印の書》、シェーンベルク《グレの歌》《浄められた夜》、ベルリオーズ《幻想交響曲》、チャイコフスキー《くるみ割り人形》の5作品。それぞれの楽曲を世界的指揮者ファビオ・ルイージ、ドイツの調香師ヨシカ・クレー、フランスのスタジオFLAIRが嗅覚へと翻訳した。各30mL、1万9800円（税込）で、10月7日から伊勢丹新宿店サロン ド パルファン 2026で先行発売される。

今回、それぞれの香りに対応するムエット（試香紙）も独立したビジュアル作品として制作。《7つの封印の書》には在本彌生、《グレの歌》には柏田テツヲ、《幻想交響曲》には山谷佑介、《くるみ割り人形》にはmanimaniumを起用。そして《浄められた夜》には、フランスを拠点に活動する現代美術家Marie Gueydon de Dives（マリー・ゲドン・ド・ディヴ）の作品が採用された。

世界を旅する在本は終末から新世界が生まれる曲に合わせ、光が差す希望を感じさせる1枚。山谷は野湯を撮ったONSENシリーズから、サイケデリックな作品を提供。柏田はウードを使用した叙事詩的に楽曲に神話的な屋久島の森を撮った。manimaniumは代表作である「ケーキでエロ本作れるし」シリーズのような官能的なデザートを撮影。Marieはダークな曲と香りに合わせて夜の森のシリーズをペアリングしている。

La Nuit parfumは、2021年のブランド誕生以来、クラシック音楽を単に香水の商品名として引用するのではなく、楽曲の構造や物語、感情の推移そのものを香りへと置き換えることを試みてきた。今回のムエットでは、その方法論をさらに視覚表現へと拡張。ひとつの楽曲から「音楽→香り→写真」という異なる感覚への翻訳を重ねることで、香水を嗅ぐ体験そのものをひとつの複合的な作品へと近づけている。

Photographers and visual artists worldwide are invited to submit single images and photographic series for the third edition of the Chennai Photo Biennale International Photography Open Call, offering selected artists the opportunity to exhibit their work publicly in Chennai, India.

Open Call:

Submissions are open for Edition 3, 2026–27 of the Chennai Photo Biennale International Photography Open Call, an annual platform inviting photographers and artists worldwide to submit work for consideration by an international jury.

The call is open to anyone, from anywhere, working on any subject, with entries accepted across a wide range of photographic approaches. Applicants may submit either individual photographs or a cohesive photo series. Selected finalists will have their work produced and presented as part of a public exhibition in Chennai.

Institutional Context:

The CPB Foundation, a registered non-profit public trust based in Chennai, India, organises the International Photography Open Call and is dedicated to expanding engagement with photography and the photographic medium.

The Foundation also organises the Chennai Photo Biennale, an international photography festival held every two years in Chennai. Through exhibitions, education and public programmes, its activities create opportunities for photographers and audiences to engage with contemporary photographic practices from India and around the world.

Eligibility and Criteria:

The open call welcomes photographers of any age and from anywhere in the world, from amateur to professional practitioners. Applicants under 18 must provide consent from a parent or guardian. Individual artists, collaborative teams and groups may apply.

Submissions may explore fine art, documentary, portraiture, landscape, conceptual, experimental and other approaches to photography. Work that has previously been exhibited or published is eligible, provided the applicant holds the necessary rights.

Applicants may submit unlimited entries. Photo series must contain a minimum of 10 and a maximum of 20 images and should function as a cohesive body of work. Each submission must be accompanied by a concept note and/or captions.

AI-generated images are not accepted and will be disqualified. Video submissions are also not eligible.

Evaluation Process:

A diverse international jury of photographers, artists, curators, editors, and cultural professionals will review every submission.

The jury assesses entries on artistic merit, originality, technical excellence, and relevance to contemporary photographic discourse.

The 2026–27 jury includes practitioners and cultural figures such as Carine Dolek, Charan Singh, Yumi Goto, Danit Ariel, Katy Hundertmark, Ronny Sen, Sadaf Raza, Aditya Arya, Ana Casas Broda, Bhavna Kakar, Emmeline Yong, Senthil Kumaran, Umah Jacob, Ushmita Sahu, Venket Ram and Vineet Vohra, among others.

Successful applicants are expected to be notified in late December 2026.

Practical Information:

Selected finalists will receive print production and exhibition of their work in Chennai, alongside promotion through CPB’s digital campaigns, social media, email communications and print and digital partnerships. Selected artists will also receive a dedicated online feature through the Open Call website and CPB’s social channels.

Selected works may also be considered for travelling exhibitions and digital presentations at partner festivals. An extended shortlist will be presented digitally at the Open Call exhibition venue.

Submission fees vary according to location and entry type. For residents of India and South Asia, the fee is ₹300 for a single image and ₹700 for a photo series. For applicants from the rest of the world, the listed fees are €8 for a single image and €15 for a photo series. Students in India can apply at reduced rates: ₹100 for a single image and ₹200 for a photo series.

Applicants retain copyright and ownership of their work, while shortlisted and selected participants grant the organisers non-exclusive usage rights for purposes connected to the Open Call, the exhibition, the Chennai Photo Biennale, and related promotion.

Applications and Queries:

Submit applications through the Chennai Photo Biennale International Photography Open Call online platform by 31 October 2026.

Submit images according to the technical specifications in the official rules. Upload single-image entries as JPEG files, and submit photo series as a single ZIP file. Shortlisted photographers will subsequently be asked to provide original camera files and full-resolution processed TIFF files for printing.

For more information, please refer to the official website .

content.article_text:
A.I.R. Gallery invites emerging women and non-binary visual artists based in New York City to apply for its year-long Fellowship Program, which offers six artists mentorship, professional development, curatorial support, a $3,000 stipend, and their first solo exhibition in New York City.

Open Call:

Applications are open for the 2027–2028 A.I.R. Fellowship Program, a 12-month professional development opportunity for emerging and underrepresented women and non-binary visual artists based in New York City.

Running from September 2027 to August 2028, the programme selects six artists annually. It provides each Fellow with professional development workshops, mentorship, studio visits, curatorial support, and a solo exhibition at A.I.R. Gallery in spring or summer 2028. Each Fellow also receives a $3,000 stipend.

Institutional Context:

Established in 1993 by artist Stephanie Bernheim, the A.I.R. Fellowship Program has supported more than 130 artists in realising their first solo exhibition in New York City. The programme helps artists develop sustainable practices while creating opportunities for experimentation, professional exchange, and intergenerational dialogue.

A.I.R. Gallery is a longstanding feminist arts organisation founded in New York in 1972. The Fellowship forms part of its broader commitment to supporting women and non-binary artists and addressing underrepresentation within the contemporary art landscape.

Since 2009, the youngest annual recipient has held the Emma Bee Bernstein Fellowship seat. Since 2024, A.I.R. has also named one participant annually as the Louise H. McCagg Fellow.

Eligibility and Criteria:

Applicants must be women or non-binary visual artists working in any medium and must be aged 18 or older.

Artists must reside in one of New York City’s five boroughs, Manhattan, Queens, Brooklyn, the Bronx or Staten Island, for the full duration of the Fellowship. Applicants do not need to be American citizens, but A.I.R. cannot provide visa sponsorship.

Applicants must not have had a solo exhibition at a permanent venue in New York City during the previous ten years. Exhibitions at temporary or pop-up spaces, art fairs and non-art venues do not make an applicant ineligible.

Artists must not be enrolled in a degree-granting programme or participating in a comparable fellowship, residency or professional development programme during the Fellowship period. Current A.I.R. members, employees, and board members; previous A.I.R. Fellowship recipients; and artists who have previously had a solo exhibition at A.I.R. are not eligible.

Collaborative artist teams may apply, provided they demonstrate an established history of working together and propose a collaborative exhibition.

Evaluation Process:

The selection process is completely anonymous and takes place across three rounds. A three-person external panel of curators, critics, and established artists reviews applications.

Artists are assessed according to the quality of and commitment to their work, as well as their potential to benefit significantly from the Fellowship’s support. A.I.R. members and staff conduct final interviews and selections, with six artists ultimately awarded Fellowships.

The 2027–2028 selection panel comprises Ada Potter, Joey Tang and Mindy Seu. Successful applicants will be notified in April 2027.

Practical Information:

The Fellowship runs from September 2027 to August 2028.

Each selected artist receives:

• A $3,000 stipend • A solo exhibition at A.I.R. Gallery in spring or summer 2028 • Four to five professional development workshops during fall 2027 • An A.I.R. artist mentor for the duration of the programme • A one-on-one studio visit with a selection panellist • Ongoing studio visits and support from A.I.R. staff

Fellows are expected to participate actively in the A.I.R. community and attend programme activities in person. Mandatory requirements include presenting the solo exhibition, holding a group discussion during the exhibition and participating in the programme’s professional development workshops.

Applications and Queries:

Applications close on 10 November 2026 at 11:59 PM ET. A free online information session will take place on 29 October 2026 at 6:30 PM ET, and a recording will be available for applicants unable to attend.

Applications are submitted online through Submittable. Applicants should provide examples of their strongest and most representative work created within the past three years rather than sketches or works in progress.

Importantly, the application process is anonymous. Applicants must ensure their name does not appear anywhere in submitted materials, including filenames, images, statements, CVs or other documents. Applications containing the artist’s name will be disqualified.

Deadline: 10 November 2026, 11:59 PM ET Notification: April 2027 Programme: September 2027 to August 2028 Location: New York City, USA Fellowships available: Six Stipend: $3,000 Information session: 29 October 2026, 6:30 PM ET Queries: info@airgallery.org

For more information, please refer to the official website .

content.article_text:
The Image Centre in Toronto invites Canadian and international scholars, researchers and artists to apply for six fellowships supporting original research across its extensive photography collections, with opportunities ranging from artistic research to postdoctoral study.

Open Call:

Applications are open for The Image Centre’s 2027 Research Fellowships, offering researchers and artists the opportunity to work directly with significant photographic collections and archives in Toronto, Canada.

Six competitive fellowships are available for 2027, accommodating applicants at different stages of academic and artistic practice. Research may draw on The Image Centre’s holdings and, where relevant, the collections of Toronto Metropolitan University Archives and Special Collections.

The opportunities include the IMC/AMC Postdoctoral Fellowship, Nadir Mohamed Postdoctoral Fellowship, Penny Rubinoff Fellowship, Elaine Ling Fellowship, Howard Tanenbaum Fellowship for Artistic Research, and Wendy Snyder MacNeil Research Fellowship.

Institutional Context:

Since 2014, the Image Centre at Toronto Metropolitan University has offered fellowships supporting photography-related research.

Its holdings include the acclaimed Black Star Collection, comprising more than a quarter-million photojournalistic prints spanning the twentieth century, alongside historic and fine art photography collections and archives devoted to photographers including Werner Wolff, Jo Spence, Wendy Snyder MacNeil, Berenice Abbott, Minna Keene, Violet Keene Perinchief and Richard Harrington.

The 2027 programme also introduces the IMC/AMC Postdoctoral Fellowship, developed with the Archive of Modern Conflict, which enables research across internationally significant photographic collections in Toronto and London.

Eligibility and Criteria:

All six fellowships are open to Canadian and international applicants, although individual eligibility requirements vary.

The IMC/AMC Postdoctoral Fellowship requires a PhD and provides a full-time, one-year research opportunity.

The Nadir Mohamed Postdoctoral Fellowship is open to applicants holding a PhD.

The Penny Rubinoff Fellowship requires a master’s degree. Current PhD students and candidates may apply, but applicants who already hold a PhD and postdoctoral researchers are not eligible.

The Elaine Ling Fellowship is intended for current master’s students and recent master’s graduates. Doctoral students, PhD holders and postdoctoral researchers are ineligible.

The Howard Tanenbaum Fellowship for Artistic Research is open to applicants at any level of education, including independent artists with relevant experience and demonstrated interests. Artists seeking to conduct artistic research within the collections are specifically encouraged to apply for this fellowship.

The Wendy Snyder MacNeil Research Fellowship is open to applicants who hold or are working towards at least an undergraduate degree and/or are photo-based artists. Research should contribute new perspectives on women photographers, including Wendy Snyder MacNeil.

Evaluation Process:

Applications are evaluated according to the clarity and strength of the proposed research plan, originality and creativity, engagement with primary sources in The Image Centre’s collections, the applicant’s ability to undertake the research, and the specificity of the proposed research outcomes.

The selection committee includes representatives from The Image Centre and Toronto Metropolitan University, alongside an external curator or scholar.

Applicants must apply for the fellowship appropriate to their research and eligibility. Blanket applications for multiple fellowships will not be considered. Previous recipients of an Image Centre Fellowship may not reapply for five years following submission of their previous final report.

Practical Information:

Funding and residency periods vary by fellowship.

IMC/AMC Postdoctoral Fellowship: $70,000 CAD annual salary plus benefits. The full-time fellowship runs from 1 July 2027 to 30 June 2028 and includes additional research funding for work in London.

Nadir Mohamed Postdoctoral Fellowship: $10,000 CAD. Research period of one to three months.

Penny Rubinoff Fellowship: $5,000 CAD. Research period of two to six weeks.

Elaine Ling Fellowship: $4,000 CAD. Research period of one to four weeks.

Howard Tanenbaum Fellowship for Artistic Research: $4,000 CAD. Research period of one to four weeks.

Wendy Snyder MacNeil Research Fellowship: $4,000 CAD. Research period of one to four weeks.

Except for the IMC/AMC Postdoctoral Fellowship, research residencies take place between 15 February and 15 December 2027 . Fellows are responsible for travel and accommodation expenses, and the fellowship stipends are intended to help offset these costs. International fellows are responsible for obtaining any required visas.

Applications and Queries:

For the Nadir Mohamed, Penny Rubinoff, Elaine Ling, Howard Tanenbaum and Wendy Snyder MacNeil Fellowships, applicants must submit a research proposal of approximately 1,000 words, a CV, a writing sample of up to 20 pages and one letter of recommendation. Artists applying for the Howard Tanenbaum Fellowship may submit a portfolio of up to ten images or film or video work of up to ten minutes instead of a writing sample.

Applications and reference letters must be received by 18 October 2026 at 11:59 p.m. EST .

Deadline: 18 October 2026, 11:59 p.m. EST Location: Toronto, Canada Programme: The Image Centre Research Fellowships 2027 Number of fellowships: Six Eligibility: Canadian and international applicants Funding: From $4,000 CAD to $70,000 CAD plus benefits, depending on fellowship Applications and general enquiries: imagecentre.research@torontomu.ca Collection enquiries: imagecentre.collects@torontomu.ca

For more information, please refer to the official website .

content.article_text:
Elsinore

This film puts Andrew Scott in line to become the first out gay man to win the best actor Oscar . He plays Ian Charleson, who became a star in Chariots of Fire and in 1989 took on the role of Hamlet at London’s National Theatre when Daniel Day-Lewis withdrew, despite being desperately ill with Aids, knowing that the strain would accelerate his illness. For Charleson, the play’s themes of life and death, truth and falsehood, justice and injustice, were all too real.

7 Miles Out

Fans of Manchester, Manchesterism and indie British film-maker Carol Morley will relish the thought of her much anticipated new movie, adapted from her autobiographical novel of the same title. The lead character, Ann, based on Morley herself, experiences an emotional crisis as a teen and takes refuge in the thrilling new Manchester music scene, featuring bands including Joy Division, New Order and Magazine. Lucy Halliday is Ann and her mum and dad are played by Gemma Whelan and Aidan Gillen.

Fatherland

Polish film-maker Paweł Pawlikowski has created a brilliantly poised, superbly performed historical vignette in black-and-white whose brevity and control can hardly contain its characters’ anguish. Hanns Zischler and Sandra Hüller play Thomas and Erika Mann – that is, the great Nobel-winning German author and his daughter. After the war and the destruction of the Nazis, whose tyranny he escaped by fleeing to the US, Mann returns to Germany with daughter in tow, to accept prizes in the fatherland’s capitalist West and communist East. But he is in denial about a terrible family crisis.

La Gradiva

Surely the year’s best debut feature? French cinematographer turned director Marine Atlan tells a gripping story of a school trip to Pompeii: an emotionally troubled teacher has to keep an emotionally troubled bunch of kids in line. Perhaps the most difficult is a boy called Toni, who has always believed a story told him by his mum that he has aristocratic lineage from a Pompeii nobleman whose castle was reduced to rubble by southern Italy’s 1980 earthquake, an event he thinks is thrillingly analogous to the Pompeii disaster. He’s heading for his own emotional earthquake.

I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning

Birmingham is the setting for this absorbing and moving social realist picture from film-maker Clio Barnard , featuring terrific performances from its young cast. It’s a home town drama about a city to which the characters are fundamentally loyal while simultaneously longing to escape; as they approach the end of their 20s, they must come to terms with decisions and life choices. Joe Cole, Daryl McCormack, Lola Petticrew, Anthony Boyle and Jay Lycurgo are the cast-members bursting with energy, tenderness and vulnerability.

A Long Winter

Andrew Haigh’s mysterious and beautiful new film is adapted by him from a story by Colm Tóibín: a poignant, subversive study of grief and desire, and the terrible, infantilised loneliness of men without women. A family living a tough existence in remote 1950s Colorado are traumatised when the troubled mother of the household, played by Caitriona Balfe, disappears one winter and the menfolk, having decided that the search can only resume once the snows have melted, enter into a strange new period of bachelor freedom.

The Blood Countess

It’s the part she was born to play. Isabelle Huppert is Countess Elizabeth Báthory, a 16th-century Hungarian noblewoman and serial killer, legendary for having the blood of hundreds of young girls on her hands, and indeed all over the rest of her body, in an attempt to attain eternal youth. Her Báthory is a vampire who has returned to present-day Vienna, the historical seat of the Austro-Hungarian empire, seen initially gliding through its sewers as if on a royal barge, making her way far more coolly than Harry Lime in The Third Man.

I Love Boosters

Chicago rapper and film-maker Boots Riley , the comic bard of black anxiety and white privilege, returns with a hyperactive romp about a bandit group of fashion influencers who deal with the issue of price by simply “boosting” clothes from stores. This group of outlaws includes Naomi Ackie and Taylour Paige, and the resentful fashionista ice-queen whose wares are being sticky-fingered in this way is played by Demi Moore.

Gentle Monster

Here is a coldly eloquent and disquieting drama starring Léa Seydoux about women who find themselves imprisoned by a duty of care and loyalty to the men in their lives. Seydoux plays Lucy, an acclaimed musician with a TV director husband and three-year-old child; one day, the police show up at their door to take away the husband’s computers, tablets and smartphones. The husband replies unconvincingly to Lucy’s desperate questions as to what this is all about, and her ordeal is her need to believe him, to twist and contort what she sees so it will fit into the husband’s shapeshifting explanations.

The Debut

Jesse Eisenberg follows up his excellent drama A Real Pain with this much admired and widely enjoyed dramedy about community theatre, for which Julianne Moore may be once again in the Oscar conversation. She plays a neglected housewife, going mad with boredom and emotional neglect in her Stepford prison; she tries out for a local amateur troupe’s production of a musical (whose hokey songs Eisenberg has himself written). Needless to say, she transforms from a suburban doormat into a Bette Davis-level diva.

My Notes on Mars

Hungarian film-maker Lili Horvát has always had a taste for the inexplicable; now she makes her English-language debut with a film that fuses romance, science fiction and mystery. Mackenzie Davis is Margot, a scientist with emotional problems who vanishes while on a hiking trip with her husband Sam, played by Rupert Friend. Much later, at her memorial service, Margot sensationally reappears, with no memory of what happened, but a determination to destroy her notes on Mars. Is that where’s she’s … gulp … been?

Tender Loving Care

Is this Mike Leigh’s final film ? Let’s hope not. It’s a tender, poignant drama that is also candid and forthright, muscular in its effects. It’s an intergenerational story about the friendship of two women from west London, Rosie and Amy, who share a flat and work in social care. The film gives a complex, interrelated pattern of scenes showing their personal and professional lives and the people close to them. It is a lovely film.

In ‘Sacred Vessels ‘ , Tasanee Durrett brings architecture, material and personal history into conversation, asking how memory is held, transformed and carried across generations.

For Tasanee Durrett, the body is both structure and vessel, a place where memory, identity and lived experience accumulate. In her solo exhibition ‘Sacred Vessels: Healing and Memory in the Black Diaspora ‘ , the artist and architect works with acrylic, raffia, salt and silkworm cocoons to explore transformation, inheritance and repair. Moving between personal experiences of rebuilding and the wider histories of the Black diaspora, Durrett considers how memory survives rupture and how materials can carry histories of their own. In conversation with ART AFRICA , she discusses architecture as a way of thinking, the Atlantic as a site of both trauma and possibility, and what it means to make healing visible without suggesting that it is ever fully resolved. Tasanee Durrett, ‘ Crab Hands In Deep Waters ‘, 2026. Image Courtesy of Artist.

Suzette Bell-Roberts: ‘Sacred Vessels’ brings together healing, memory, and the Black diaspora. Within the exhibition, what does a “vessel” mean, and how did it become the framework for these works?

Tasanee Durett: To me, a vessel is what holds our emotions, experiences, and stories. That is why, in my figurative work, I mostly paint and draw from the neck up. I see the head as the true vessel. From the neck down, our bodies are largely the same. But the head is different for every one of us, whatever our background or race. It holds our identity, our memories, and everything we have lived through. The eyes matter to me too. Biologically, they grow out of the brain itself, so I feel that when we look into someone’s eyes, we’re looking at the mind. The neck is what carries that vessel. It holds up the mind and the psyche. Tasanee Durrett, ‘ Endure Endure Endure ‘, 2024. Image Courtesy of Artist.

Your practice moves between architecture and painting. How has your architectural training shaped your thinking about space, structure, and the body?

Architecture taught me to think with my hands before I think in words, and that instinct never left me. My continuous, unbroken line comes directly from that training, thinking while drawing rather than drawing what I’ve already decided. That same logic carries into how I think about the body, as a structure with load, grain, and thresholds, not just a subject to depict. When I’m building a piece, I’m asking the same questions an architect asks about a room: what does this space need to hold, where does weight need to be carried, where is the opening? The body in my work functions the same way. Tasanee Durrett, ‘ I Am, We Are Agave ‘, 2024. Image Courtesy of Artist.

Raffia, salt, and silkworm cocoons appear throughout your work, each carrying particular histories and associations. How do you approach material as memory and storytelling?

I try to let the material tell me what it already knows before I ask it to say anything else. Raffia carries a West African textile and hair tradition in its fibre, so when I work with it I’m not inventing a meaning; I’m continuing one. I press salt into the wet paint as a reminder that we are salt people. Salt is in our blood, our sweat, and our tears, and it has its own long history in healing traditions around the world. Silkworm cocoons hold the physical proof of transformation in how something enters one state and leaves in another. None of these is symbols I chose from the outside. They’ve become materials with their own inherited stories and histories, and my job is to build with that history intact rather than erase it. Tasanee Durrett, ‘ The Oyster King Lives On ‘, 2025. Image Courtesy of Artist.

Physically and conceptually, transformation appears in your materials, particularly through silkworm cocoons. In ‘Sacred Vessels’, how does transformation operate?

Silkworm cocoons are transformation you can literally hold in your hand, and it’s fascinating! Like the silkworm, I see us as human beings going into something as one form and coming out changed. But unlike the silkworm, we don’t transform just once. We do it again and again over a lifetime as our bodies age, as we grow wiser, and as we rediscover who we are and where we come from. That is what I want Sacred Vessels to do too: not solely represent healing, but allow those who experience the show to undergo their own transformation. Tasanee Durrett, ‘ Shorelines of the Spirit ‘, 2026. Image Courtesy of Artist.

Alongside questions of identity and lineage, the exhibition considers psychological healing within the Black diaspora. How do you relate personal memory to diasporic history?

My own path through rupture and rebuilding, coming out of an eight-year abusive relationship and finding my way back to myself, shows up in the work less as subject and more as method. Repair is how I make things now. When I connect that to diasporic history, I’m not claiming my story stands in for a larger one; I’m noticing that the pattern is the same and that when something is broken, knowledge or memory gets interrupted, and then, generations or years later, it resurfaces and gets rebuilt into something new. Sacred Vessels holds both scales at once, my own healing and the diaspora’s, because I don’t think they operate on different logic. Tasanee Durrett, ‘ Tethered Waters ‘, 2025. Image Courtesy of Artist.

Your ongoing Black Maritime Collection engages with the Atlantic as a space shaped by trauma, knowledge, movement, and ancestral memory. How does the ocean shape your thinking about the histories and experiences in ‘Sacred Vessels ’ ?

The Atlantic is where a huge amount of Black history was carried, interrupted, and rewritten, all at once. Trauma, knowledge, movement, and ancestral memory all moved through the same water. When people think of Black history and the ocean, they usually stop at the Middle Passage. I never want to forget that. But the Black Maritime Collection also tells the stories that get left out: Black sailors, whalers, ship captains, lifesavers, and fishing communities who built lives, wealth, and freedom on that same water. Captain William T. Shorey began as a cabin worker and became one of the most respected and well-known Black whaling captains on the Pacific coast in the 1800s. His story belongs in the same ocean as the Middle Passage. The ocean was a place of loss, and for many of us it was also a place of skill, independence, and pride. I want to honour both. Working on the Black Maritime Collection alongside ‘Sacred Vessels’ reminds me that water doesn’t only separate. It also holds. It carries things across distance without destroying them completely. That’s what I ask of myself and my materials too. The ocean taught me that memory can travel through rupture and still arrive somewhere, carrying the pain and the triumph together. That duality is the throughline between the two bodies of work. Tasanee Durrett, ‘ Oceanic Origins ‘, 2025. Image Courtesy of Artist.

Your works are built through layering and embedding materials into painted surfaces. What role does this construction play in meaning in each work?

As an architect, I coordinate and construct commercial buildings, and I paint the same way I approach construction. I see each painting as a problem to solve. I build it up layer by layer, and every part has to work with the others, the way a building’s systems come together into one working whole. Each coat of acrylic and each place I press raffia, cocoons, or salt into the wet paint is part of that structure. By the end, the painting works like a machine that tells a story. I see buildings as living things. They tell the stories of the people inside them, and those people shape the building in return. My paintings work the same way. I tell a story as I build each piece, but once someone stands in front of it, they bring their own experiences. Every viewer pulls out their own threads, so the story keeps growing beyond what I put into it. Tasanee Durrett, ‘ Access To Water For Brown Bodies II ‘, 2026. Image Courtesy of Artist.

As audiences encounter ‘Sacred Vessels ’ , what questions about memory, inheritance, and healing do you continue to explore through the exhibition?

I keep coming back to what it actually takes for something to be inherited well, not just passed down but received in a way that can be carried forward. And I keep asking what healing looks like when it’s not resolved, when the wound and the repair are both still visible in the same piece. ‘Sacred Vessels’ doesn’t answer those questions so much as it holds space for them, the way I hope people also see each other, and other cultures, through the visual stories in the work.

This exhibition is on view at the Hannibal Square Heritage Center in Florida until 13 December 2026.

content.article_text:
Jusqu’au 7 novembre, la commune de Fontenay-sous-Bois accueille la première édition de FLASH, festival social et citoyen qui dresse un portrait des périphéries, urbaines, sociales ou intimes, à travers des images d’archives et contemporaines. Plusieurs artistes ont été invité·es à explorer cette thématique, notamment Carolina Arantes , Léa Rivera-Hadjes ou encore Mohamed Bourouissa , qui présente son film documentaire expérimental Noubia .

Fontenay-sous-Bois a cette particularité de se raconter à travers sa topographie. Construite sur deux versants, la commune juxtapose des réalités sociales qui se côtoient sans toujours se rencontrer : d’un côté, des quartiers plus aisés tournés vers Paris et le bois de Vincennes ; de l’autre, autour de Val-de-Fontenay, des ensembles sortis de terre entre les années 1950 et 1970.

C’est précisément ce désir de créer du lien entre les différentes composantes de la ville qui est au cœur de FLASH. Pour sa première édition, le festival s’est installé à la Halle Roublot, ancien marché couvert transformé en pôle artistique. Un lieu où Émilie Chazelle et Margaux Hannart ont imaginé un projet qui dépasse le seul cadre de l’exposition pour faire de la photographie un catalyseur de rencontres, de transmission et de mise en relation : « FLASH est avant tout un festival social et citoyen, qui utilise le médium photographique comme outil d ’interrogation et de valorisation des territoires et populations périphériques. »

Une périphérie envisagée au-delà de sa dimension géographique

Toutes deux ont grandi autour de Cergy-Pontoise, dans une banlieue dont elles retiennent autant la richesse de la mixité sociale et culturelle que le manque de représentation. Avec FLASH, elles entendent déplacer le regard vers ces territoires, leurs habitant·es et leurs histoires à travers trois volets : une exposition réunissant des artistes contemporain·es dont les œuvres explorent cette idée de marge ; un volet plus historique imaginé à partir d’archives photographiques liées à Fontenay-sous-Bois ; et enfin un troisième, essentiellement participatif, issu d’un travail collaboratif avec la population locale.

Au cœur de FLASH, Émilie Chazelle et Margaux Hannart placent une conception élargie de la périphérie, envisagée au-delà de sa seule dimension géographique, dans ses aspects sociaux ou intimes : « Il y a notamment ce sentiment d’être à la marge de la société, d ’une communauté, voire de soi-mê me. » Pour elles, l’intime est résolument politique.

C’est ce qu’illustre l’exposition Trajectoire(s) , qui réunit douze artistes contemporain·es explorant les différentes formes de marginalité à travers la photographie, le film, la sculpture, le livre ou l’installation. Plusieurs projets sont consacrés à la jeunesse et à la quête de soi. Avec La Vie immé diate , Sandra Rocha livre ainsi un journal intime collectif dans lequel des adolescent·es livrent leur perception de l’avenir. Leurs mots dialoguent avec des clichés transfigurés par des jeux de collage. Plus loin, dans des images en noir et blanc où affleure une poésie toute en retenue, Gil Lesage documente la transition de genre de son enfant.

D’autres séries, comme celle d’Anne Mocaër, s’intéressent à la manière dont les transformations urbaines affectent celles et ceux qui habitent la ville. Avec Avenue Royale , la photographe donne un visage aux habitant·es d’un quartier de Casablanca pris depuis plus de trente ans dans un vaste projet de réaménagement, entre démolitions annoncées et promesses de relogement. Hicham Gardaf et Rio Saito observent quant à eux des formes de vie façonnées par la ville et ses mutations : le premier filme à Tanger les vendeurs de Javel, métier voué à disparaître face à l’urbanisation accélérée ; le second s’intéresse aux habitant·es de la périphérie du Caire qui traversent chaque jour le Ring Road au péril de leur vie pour rejoindre le centre-ville. Les trajectoires féminines et les questions d’émancipation traversent également les travaux de Mohamed Bourouissa, Sabrina Belouaar ou encore Laïs Decaster. Cette dernière prend pour décor le Car Wash , une station de lavage où sa sœur, tout en nettoyant sa voiture, raconte le rapport d’indépendance, de séduction et de liberté qu’elle entretient avec celle-ci.

Plus loin, les expositions Fragments d ’une histoire collective et Banlieue en fête ! racontent Fontenay-sous-Bois à travers ses célébrations collectives pour la première, qui puise dans les archives municipales de la commune, et intimes pour la seconde, imaginée à partir des clichés personnels des Fontenaisien·nes. Une exposition qui cristallise l’ambition du festival de devenir une plateforme collaborative et participative. Les nombreux partenariats et ateliers organisés autour de FLASH prolongent cette volonté. Si le festival a été pensé comme une biennale, les ateliers se poursuivront tout au long de l’année afin de maintenir un lien avec la population locale. À terme, FLASH ambitionne de se développer et d’investir d’autres lieux de la ville. De quoi, surtout, inscrire durablement la photographie dans un territoire où elle était jusqu’ici peu présente.

content.article_blocks_json: [{"type": "heading", "text": "Now extended until the end of October, Jillian Edelstein’s retrospective at Stills Gallery, Edinburgh shows her deep engagement with people, from those at South Africa’s Truth and Reconciliation to swimmers at Hampstead Heath"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Born in Cape Town, Jillian Edelstein is best-known for her work on South Africa’s Truth and Reconciliation Commission. Photographing perpetrators, victims, and other individuals involved in the public hearings which grappled with the country’s Apartheid history from 1996-2002 – and some of the landscapes involved – Edelstein worked on the project for four years. When she published it as a book in 2002, Truth and Lies included endorsements from Archbishop Desmond Tutu, Gillian Slovo and Pumla Gobodo-Madikizela (Research Chair in Studies in Historical Trauma and Transformation at Stellenbosch University in South Africa), plus extensive text and reflections written by Edelstein."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "But though Truth and Lies is important, it’s also not the only thing Edelstein has made. In fact when she made it she wasn’t living in South Africa any more; she has now been a UK resident for much longer than she lived in Africa. Edelstein’s retrospective at Stills Gallery includes Truth and Lies , but it also includes other projects from across her five decades of work. Curated by Tracey Marshall-Grant, it’s titled Jillian Edelstein – Among People to mark the photographer’s commitment to individuals from many different communities, and includes early images from Johannesburg and Cape Town, and from an anthropological project in Portugal, right up to recent work from 2020-22, showing the community of swimmers who use Hampstead Heath’s ponds."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.1854.photography/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/4.Jillian-Edelstein_WaterRats.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Nicky  leaves  Hampstead Heath, 2021. Edelstein has also made work about male suicide, migration, the West Bank, and poverty in the UK, and has shot portraits for publications such as The New York Times Magazine, The FT Weekend Magazine, Vogue, GQ, and Esquire . The National Portrait Gallery holds more than 100 of her prints."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "She has shot people from wildly different communities and walks of life, in fact, from those immersed in wealth to those facing very hard times. “It’s a privilege, because people are people and you can learn from everyone,” says Edelstein. “I try to treat everyone with equality, I think that can show something really powerful…In South Africa I remember thinking how fascinating it was that the perpetrators put themselves forward to be captured, in a vain kind of way. That was very striking. I think there is quantifiable experience, and you have to face that and think how to portray it.”"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.1854.photography/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Jillian-Edelstein_Kalk-Bay_Fisherman.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Local fisherman at Kalk Bay harbour, Cape Town, from Jillian Edelstein's earliest project on the fishing community of the area, 1980-83 © Jillian Edelstein", "credit": "British Journal of Photography"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.1854.photography/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Jillian-Edelstein_Western-Cape.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Local resident walking his dogs. content.article_text:
Now extended until the end of October, Jillian Edelstein’s retrospective at Stills Gallery, Edinburgh shows her deep engagement with people, from those at South Africa’s Truth and Reconciliation to swimmers at Hampstead Heath

Born in Cape Town, Jillian Edelstein is best-known for her work on South Africa’s Truth and Reconciliation Commission. Photographing perpetrators, victims, and other individuals involved in the public hearings which grappled with the country’s Apartheid history from 1996-2002 – and some of the landscapes involved – Edelstein worked on the project for four years. When she published it as a book in 2002, Truth and Lies included endorsements from Archbishop Desmond Tutu, Gillian Slovo and Pumla Gobodo-Madikizela (Research Chair in Studies in Historical Trauma and Transformation at Stellenbosch University in South Africa), plus extensive text and reflections written by Edelstein.

But though Truth and Lies is important, it’s also not the only thing Edelstein has made. In fact when she made it she wasn’t living in South Africa any more; she has now been a UK resident for much longer than she lived in Africa. Edelstein’s retrospective at Stills Gallery includes Truth and Lies , but it also includes other projects from across her five decades of work. Curated by Tracey Marshall-Grant, it’s titled Jillian Edelstein – Among People to mark the photographer’s commitment to individuals from many different communities, and includes early images from Johannesburg and Cape Town, and from an anthropological project in Portugal, right up to recent work from 2020-22, showing the community of swimmers who use Hampstead Heath’s ponds.

“ People are people and you can learn from everyone. I try to treat everyone with equality.” Jillian Edelstein

It also includes images from Edelstein’s long-running portrait series Affinities , which explores creative partnerships; her long term project on the Sangoma, traditional healers on the Lesotho-South African border; and portraits taken from Ukraine, from her book Here and There: An Expedition of Sorts , published by GOST in 2024. Edelstein has also made work about male suicide, migration, the West Bank, and poverty in the UK, and has shot portraits for publications such as The New York Times Magazine, The FT Weekend Magazine, Vogue, GQ, and Esquire . The National Portrait Gallery holds more than 100 of her prints.

She has shot people from wildly different communities and walks of life, in fact, from those immersed in wealth to those facing very hard times. “It’s a privilege, because people are people and you can learn from everyone,” says Edelstein. “I try to treat everyone with equality, I think that can show something really powerful…In South Africa I remember thinking how fascinating it was that the perpetrators put themselves forward to be captured, in a vain kind of way. That was very striking. I think there is quantifiable experience, and you have to face that and think how to portray it.”

Born in 1958, Edelstein originally studied social work rather than photography; her first job was at the National Institute for the Crime and Rehabilitation of Offenders in Cape Town, where she worked with mainly men who were in prison, or had recently been released. There was energy and compassion in this work, but she had discovered photography at university and soon decided that shooting documentary and portrait images was a way to continue social work “without having to write out the case report”, she says.

Working as an assistant during the week, which allowed her to learn technical skills as well as how to use lights and print, she started to work as a press photographer at a time of great unrest in South Africa, as people struggled to overthrow Apartheid. Eventually she became a photojournalist, working for The Rand Daily Mail in 1982–83, and The Star newspaper in 1984. She worked alongside Black colleagues and was well aware of her privilege compared to them, she says; she was able to take greater risks as a White, “because the costs for them would have been so much higher, they had to keep in line”.

Edelstein won awards for her work but in 1985 decided to leave to formally study documentary photography at the London College of Printing [now the London College of Communication]. She lasted six months before Michael Cranmer, then-picture editor of The Sunday Times , came to do a guest lecture and saw some of her work. “He said ‘What are you doing here?!’” Edelstein laughs. “He gave me a commission and then Andrew Neil [then-editor of The Sunday Times ] saw the portrait and said ‘Offer her a contract’. It was sort of extraordinary even then.”

Edelstein says she is grateful to have been a press photographer then though, when staff jobs did exist and commissions were more generous; she could support herself with this work, and the commissions also helped her access to hard-to-reach individuals. Many of her personal projects include commissioned elements, such as the portrait of Nelson Mandela in Truth and Lies , or the comedians French and Saunders in Affinities.

But her success also wasn’t just down to luck or the structures of the day; working in an extremely male-dominated environment – and as a single mother – she still tried to leverage her work to help others. In fact she’s acutely aware of power, and how it’s unfairly brought to bear. “Looking back across these photographs, I’m struck by how much my work has been shaped by my early engagements or interactions with inequality and subjugation,” she states in Stills’ press material, “one asserting an unjust superiority over another”.

She tells me that her training in social work, anthropology, psychology and sociology helped her refine these insights; she thinks about power at both a macro and micro level, in terms of the interpersonal and the societal. There’s the delicate balance between directing a shoot and giving her subjects space, for example, but then there’s also authority and how it plays out. She tells me an anecdote about photographing five members of the security police in South Africa, for example, who were testifying before the Truth Commission for the murder of one of their Black colleagues, who they had decided was informing on them to the ANC; it was a difficult, intimidating shoot but a few days later she saw one of the men on his own in the airport, lacking all the bravado of his strength-in-numbers.

Edelstein is also well-attuned to the role of photography and observation, however, the negative ways in which the gaze can be used, and she can therefore be implicated. In Truth and Lies she writes about the bright lights which illuminated the townships in the 1970s and 80s, the ‘eye of the state’ which kept residents under surveillance. In the West Bank she noted something similar in the turnstiles, she says, which allows Israeli soldiers to control peoples’ movements. “This practical handiwork that autocratic governments put in place, it operates and it’s horrifying,” she says.

Edelstein is also saddened by the current state of the world, the fact that terrible things happen and that “no matter how present the camera is, it hasn’t stopped them”. Even so, she’s still enthusiastic about her current work, which includes a commission photographing women who have survived sexual violence and abuse. “It’s the challenge of photographing someone, the dance that you have to do,” she says. “What you give is what you get back.” Then she smiles and asks me about myself.

Jillian Edelstein – Among People is on show at Stills until 31 October https://stills.org/exhibitions/exhibition-jillian-edelstein/

content.article_text:
T he children were never lost; if a baby goes missing, the police get called, social services become involved. The babies born at the mother and baby home run by nuns in the town of Tuam in County Galway were discarded: up to 796 tiny bodies thrown away, some in an old sewage tank. The amateur historian who uncovered the horror of the mass graves at the St Mary’s mother and baby home is Catherine Corless, superbly played here by Monica Dolan. Produced by Liam Neeson, and based on a 2017 New York Times article , The Lost Children of Tuam is a painful, devastating film. It feels scraped clean of anything unnecessary that might trivialise, fiction-ise or movie-ise what happened at St Mary’s, home to thousands of unmarried women and children between 1925 and 1961.

“It gets me out of the house,” Corless says when she starts a course in local history. She turns detective after becoming interested in the children from St Mary’s, and what she uncovers is that babies died at a rate of nearly one a fortnight at the home – from whooping cough, measles, malnutrition and other childhood illnesses. Eventually, she obtains nearly 800 death certificates, but cannot find burial records for the babies. There are no graves.

It is usual to say that a film like The Lost Children of Tuam is a difficult watch – but in fact it’s the opposite: hard to look away. Dolan is excellent as Corless, who does most of her research at her kitchen table, and is ill at ease in the spotlight when the media finally picks up the story. Just as compelling are the actors playing the survivors – neglected and abused by nuns as children, now in their late middle age. Some only appear for a matter of moments, but their faces stayed with me. It’s a deeply serious film; there’s no exhilaration at the end, no comforting sense of closure, just pain.

ファッションフォトグラファー、クレイグ・マクディーン（Craig McDean）の写真展が、東京・千駄ヶ谷のUNDER R TOKYOで開催される。会期は2026年10月23日から11月6日まで。マクディーンが伝説的なDucatiのモーターサイクルを撮り下ろした新作を展示するほか、同名写真集の発売、UNDER Rとのコラボレーションによるアパレルコレクションも展開される。

1990年代初頭、『i-D』や『The Face』といったカルチャー誌で頭角を現したマクディーン。その後はシャネル、ジル サンダ－、カルバン・クラインをはじめとするブランドの広告キャンペーンやエディトリアルを数多く手がけ、現代のファッションフォトグラフィーを代表する写真家のひとりとして活動してきた。

今回、マクディーンがカメラを向けたのは、Ducatiを象徴する歴史的モデル「750 Supersport Green Frame」。1970年代初頭、同社のチーフデザイナー、ファビオ・タリオーニによって開発された750cc Vツインエンジン搭載のレーシングマシンをルーツとし、1972年のイモラ200マイルレースではデビュー戦で1位と2位を独占。その後、市販モデルとしてわずか401台が生産され、現在も世界のコレクターを魅了する存在となっている。

マクディーンは本プロジェクトで、希少な2台のDucatiと向き合い、そのフォルムやディテール、機械としての構造とクラフトマンシップを写真として記録した。ファッションにおいて身体や衣服、プロダクトを独自の視覚言語へと変換してきた写真家が、モーターサイクルという工業製品をどのようなイメージへと昇華させるのか。写真、デザイン、ファッション、モーターカルチャーが交差する展示となる。

さらにUNDER Rとのコラボレーションアイテムとして、マクディーンの写真を配したTシャツ（8800円）とロングスリーブTシャツ（1万2100円）も登場。
