content.article_text:
Pour sa deuxième édition, le prix du Livre Robert Delpire a récompensé le projet Caty, la vie, la mort , de Caty Jan et Mat Jacob. L’ouvrage sortira chez Delpire en fin d’année 2027.

« Le Prix a été attribué à une œuvre unique, singulière et tragique. Un travail à quatre mains et en deux volumes, le premier, inédit, le second, intime et hanté. Caty, la vie, la mort , le titre le dit avec souffrance et tremblement » , déclare Sarah Moon dans le communiqué diffusé à l’occasion de la remise du prix du Livre Robert Delpire. La photographe en présidait le jury composé de Quentin Bajac , directeur du Jeu de Paume, José Chidlovsky, réalisateur, Michel Christolhomme, président de Pour que l’esprit vive, Héloïse Conesa, chargée de la collection de photographie contemporaine au département des Estampes et de la Photographie de la BnF, Emmanuelle Kouchner, directrice des éditions Delpire, Wajdi Mouawad, metteur en scène et écrivain, et Natacha Wolinski, écrivaine et critique. Chacun des membres a proposé et défendu un projet de livre avant de s’accorder sur celui Caty Jan et Mat Jacob, qui devient ainsi le deuxième à obtenir la récompense.

Un regard sur l’existence

Caty, la vie, la mort se distingue par sa genèse poignante. Caty Jan et Mat Jacob se sont rencontrés en 1989. Animés par une passion commune pour le 8e art, ils se lient d’une amitié qui deviendra une histoire d’amour et donnera naissance à un enfant. Aux côtés d’autres photographes, ils cofondent le collectif Tendance Floue , en 1991, et multiplient les projets. Seulement, en 2003, Caty Jan est victime d’un accident vasculaire cérébral. « Elle perd l’usage de la parole, se retrouve emmurée dans un corps accidenté. Elle ne photographiera plus. Elle garde cependant une extrême lucidité, une sensibilité, et son regard sur la vie » , explique Mat Jacob dans sa note d’intention.

Dans le souvenir de sa compagne, disparue en novembre 2025, celui-ci a imaginé ce projet présenté au prix du Livre Robert Delpire. « Depuis qu’elle est partie, avec la force qu’ont les défunts de résister à l’absence, le projet de composer un livre à quatre mains, les siennes, les miennes, ne me quitte pas. Un livre sur les liens qui nous définissent, qui nous obligent, les chemins que nous empruntons, la fragilité, la création, la liberté et le temps qui passe » , poursuit-il. Mêlant textes et images, Caty, la vie, la mort témoignera du parcours de l’autrice, de son œuvre comme de son existence. Il s’agira de son premier ouvrage.

content.article_text:
Bringing together more than 80 artists and authors, ‘Mientras seamos salvajes’ examines how colonial histories constructed the boundaries between civilisation and barbarism, and how those categories continue to shape bodies, territories and knowledge.

At TEA Tenerife Espacio de las Artes, ‘Mientras seamos salvajes ’ brings historical material into conversation with contemporary art to reconsider the systems that have classified cultures and people. Spanning artworks, films, photographs, documents, and objects, the exhibition connects the Canary Islands with Africa, Europe, the Caribbean, and Latin America through histories of colonial expansion, migration, and exchange.

Curated by Alejandro Castañeda, Néstor Delgado, Katya García-Antón, Roberto Gil, Narelys Hernández, Joel Peláez and Sergio Rubira, the exhibition features more than 80 artists and authors, including Sammy Baloji, Yto Barrada, Ana Mendieta, Wifredo Lam, Abdoulaye Konaté, Coco Fusco and Carlos Motta.

Across five interconnected sections, ‘Mientras seamos salvajes’ explores representations of Indigenous peoples, the divide between the so-called “wild” and “civilised”, alternative systems of knowledge, labour and extractivism, and the museum’s role in producing historical narratives. Rather than simply dismantling inherited categories, the exhibition asks what other relationships, forms of knowledge and futures might emerge beyond them.

This exhibition is on view at TEA Tenerife Espacio de las Artes in Santa Cruz until 24 January 2027.

content.article_text:
Jean-Jacques Annaud , director

I read an article about a curious book that had great reviews in Italy, a murder mystery about monks in the middle ages fighting for the fictional missing part of Aristotle’s Poetics. I said: “This is for me.” Since childhood, I had been fascinated with medieval and religious architecture, and Aristotle’s Poetics is my favourite literary work.

I learned that Umberto Eco, the author, was going to be in France for one night and agreed to meet me at his hotel and that I would drive him to Charles de Gaulle airport. The first thing I saw was his shadow on the hotel staircase, which looked like the silhouette of Sherlock Holmes – Umberto was a man of great humour, and he met me wearing a deerstalker, with a pipe in his mouth. In the car, I asked questions: what sort of shoes would the Franciscans have been wearing? Would the monks have had beards? What colour would the pigs have been? He said: “I don’t know, I didn’t have to write any of that.” I ended up hiring medievalist Jacques Le Goff and seven of his colleagues to make sure we got all the details right – costumes, architecture, liturgy and so on.

I wanted an unknown to play William of Baskerville, the friar who investigates the deaths, and travelled the world to watch plays featuring great actors in their 50s. Meanwhile, agent Mike Ovitz kept calling, saying: “Sean Connery would love to make this movie.” Eventually, there was a knock on my door and I opened it to find Sean with the screenplay under his arm. He said, “Listen, boy …” and started reading. I had goose bumps. The way he said the dialogue was exactly what I’d been hearing in my head while reading the book.

I flew to Vienna to look at paintings by Bruegel the Elder . I wanted to be inspired by the real people of the period, people who had no dentists or doctors, but I did cast some good-looking monks, too. Christian Slater turned up to audition for the young novice, Adso, and said: “I didn’t learn the lines, I got drunk.” The casting director, Mary Jo, was furious and tried to send him away, but he was the one I wanted. He was only 16, but looked 14. It turned out he was Mary Jo’s son. I had three women selected to audition for the part of the nameless girl from the village, but Christian fell in love with the first, Valentina Vargas, as soon as he did a screen test with her, so I never saw the other two.

We built a vast set on a hilltop near Rome for the monastery and village. During the scene at the end where the library tower burns, Sean’s cowl briefly caught fire, and a big piece of real timber fell on Feodor Chaliapin Jr, who played the blind monk, knocking him to the ground. “I’m 80 years old,” he said, “I don’t mind dying. Was the take good?” He went to hospital and we had to change the schedule because he then had a scar.

After four months in Rome, I went back to my production office in Munich and couldn’t find it. I discovered the film’s producer, Bernd Eichinger, in the cellar with his feet on a table. He said, “JJ, I didn’t want to disturb you during the shoot, but I sold the building to help pay for the movie.”

Ron Perlman , played Salvatore

My very first film, Quest for Fire, was directed by Jean-Jacques. I played a caveman. Transforming myself into something completely foreign was an incredibly rewarding exercise and a phenomenal introduction to the world of cinema, so when I read that Jean-Jacques had attached himself to The Name of the Rose, I went through the book and found a character named Salvatore – an intellectually challenged hunchback who spoke in a jumble of seven languages – who would embody a similar challenge. I told Jean-Jacques that this part would be a dream come true.

Jean-Jacques gave me complete freedom to figure out my dialogue. The Name of the Rose had been published in 80 languages, so I got copies in the seven that Umberto Eco has Salvatore referencing, and circled every time Salvatore spoke. Then I just went, “Eenie, meenie, miny, moe – OK, this word is Latin, this word is Spanish, this word is Italian …” and so on. That was the genesis of Salvatore’s communicative skills.

I worked with a dialect coach who was also a historian with particular knowledge of the period. He suggested the lullaby that Salvatore sings when he’s burned at the stake. Jean-Jacques had this idea that Salvatore was so out of touch with reality that he was initially amused to be in that situation. The lullaby gave a sense of childlike wonder at the fact he’s involved in this ceremony, but doesn’t realise he’s about to lose his life.

I only had to wear the prosthetic hump once, filming the scene where Salvatore is about to be tortured by F Murray Abraham as the inquisitor, Bernardo Gui. I was in the makeup chair for more than 13 hours and by the time I got to set, they had almost run out of time. My hair was shaved so it looked like I had mange. They said: “Good luck with your personal life, my friend.”

I spent every moment I could with Sean Connery, watching him act and listening to his stories. He was my hero, the real deal. When it came to the scene where I had to spit in his eye, I just couldn’t do it. Sean took me aside, and said: “Ron, if you don’t actually spit in my face, we’ll be here all fucking day.” So I finally just let one fly. The problem was, you don’t film from just one angle, you have to recreate in profile, medium shot, closeup, over-the-shoulder … I must have spat in Sean Connery’s face 16 times that day.

content.article_text:
Museum Ludwig traces the overlooked connections between the Black diaspora and European modernism, revealing a transatlantic history shaped by movement, exchange and resistance.

What happens to modernism when you view its history across the Atlantic? Marking Museum Ludwig’s 50th anniversary, ‘Along the Color Line: Traces of a Transatlantic Modernism’ brings modern and contemporary artists of the Black diaspora into dialogue with works from the museum’s collection.

Taking its title from the writings of African American sociologist W. E. B. Du Bois, the exhibition examines the cultural exchanges, migrations and encounters that connected Black artistic practice with European modernism. Painting, sculpture, drawing, literature and music reveal a history shaped by movements including the Harlem Renaissance and Négritude.

Curated by Eboa Itondo, the exhibition also confronts the historic absence of Black artists within European museum collections. Artists including Mildred Thompson, Herbert Gentry and Iba Ndiaye offer alternative perspectives on modernism, while James Gregory Atkinson’s nonlinear archive connects early twentieth-century histories with contemporary Black diasporic experience.

Moving between continents and generations, ‘Along the Colour Line’ reveals the intercultural relationships often obscured in established art histories, inviting audiences to reconsider modernism through questions of identity, community, migration, and belonging.

This exhibition is on view at the Museum Ludwig in Cologne until 7 March 2027.

content.article_text:
At the Yemisi Shyllon Museum of Art, ‘What Is Given ’ brings together four artists from Nigeria and Ghana to consider how memory, material and inheritance can be received, questioned and remade.

Curated by Ugonna Ibe-Ejiogu, ‘What Is Given’ marks the inaugural Myma Art Prize exhibition at the Yemisi Shyllon Museum of Art, Pan-Atlantic University. Bringing together Omolola Coker, Emmanuel Ellis, Vincent Frimpong and Edward Prah, the exhibition asks a deceptively simple question: what do we make of what has been given to us?

Across painting, photography, sculpture and installation, materials arrive already carrying histories. Adiré, family photographs, second-hand objects, symbolic impressions, memory and place become starting points through which the artists explore identity, labour, cultural meaning and exchange. Rather than approaching inheritance as fixed, each artist tests, transforms and returns what they have received in new forms.

The exhibition unfolds across two interconnected presentations. Alongside the four Myma Art Prize artists, The Belo-Osagie Collection: Practice & Time draws from Dr Myma Belo-Osagie’s personal collection, tracing years of engagement with Nigerian and Ghanaian art.

Together, these perspectives expand the idea of inheritance beyond objects and traditions. ‘What Is Given’ considers artistic legacy as an ongoing exchange, shaped equally by making, remembering, collecting and the sustained act of paying attention.

This exhibition is on view at the Yemisi Shyllon Museum of Art until 21 October 2026.

content.article_text:
La lauréate et les finalistes du prix de Photographie Marc Ladreit de Lacharrière ont été dévoilés. Voici le palmarès de cette édition 2026 !

Le jury du prix de Photographie Marc Ladreit de Lacharrière s’est réuni ce 10 septembre au palais de l’Institut de France pour examiner 21 candidatures présélectionnées. Il a désigné Sophie Zénon lauréate de l’édition 2026 pour son projet Odyssée végétale . Elle remporte une dotation de 30 000 euros et son travail sera présenté au Pavillon Comtesse de Caen de l’Académie des beaux-arts à l’automne 2028. Céline Croze , Grégoire Eloy et Alain Nzuzi Polo sont, quant à eux, les finalistes de cette 16e édition. Le prix de Photographie Marc Ladreit de Lacharrière permet d’aider les photographes confirmés, français ou étrangers, travaillant en France. Depuis 2018, il soutient le projet d’un artiste tout en lui laissant la liberté de choisir son thème. Le travail primé est restitué sous la forme d’une exposition. À partir du 8 octobre, retrouvez Ukraine, le mal qui reste de Guillaume Herbaut , lauréat 2024.

Faire coexister les plantes et les hommes

Avec son projet Odyssée végétale , Sophie Zénon travaille sur les thèmes de la temporalité, la présence dans l’absence et la fragilité de nos existences humaines et non humaines. Elle explore également les ressorts de la mémoire, de l’exil et de l’identité. De sa pratique naissent des œuvres organiques, vibrantes et poétiques. Son projet nous invite tous à explorer les paysages et les luxueux jardins guadeloupéens et martiniquais auxquels la photographe est très sensible. Un vrai travail où elle fait coexister les plantes et les hommes à travers le prisme des migrations. « Dans mon travail, le végétal dans ses différentes expressions (arbres, plantes, fleurs, racines) constitue un fil conducteur. Il n’y est pas seulement un motif décoratif, mais le lieu d’une réflexion et d’engagements plus profonds, historiques, écologiques et philosophiques, ouvrant à la construction de nouveaux récits, à des espaces d’imaginaire et de perception sensible » , explique-t-elle dans son projet.

Témoigner du monde

Trois finalistes ont été mis en lumière. Les purs , de Celine Croze, est un projet qui naît d’une nécessité : comprendre ce qui insiste. L’artiste s’intéresse à ce qui se transmet sans bruit, aux héritages invisibles mais aussi aux répétitions et aux chemins de transformation. Elle utilise les codes cinématographiques pour transgresser le monde qui l’entoure. Pour ce projet, elle prend son inspiration en Ariège, chez sa grand-mère, pour ensuite s’en détacher et se concentrer sur la notion de l’héritage. Grégoire Eloy présente son projet Les Sentinelles, Botaniques des lisières glacières. Son travail est celui d’une enquête qu’il mène avec des techniques et des approches photographiques diverses. Il utilise les expérimentations analogiques et des outils scientifiques pour étudier ce qui nous entoure. Son enjeu est de regarder ce qu’il y a de proche, tout autour de nous, plutôt que de se tourner vers un horizon lointain. Avec L’archéologie de l’inavouable, Alain Nzuzi Polo cherche à réactiver et mettre en lumière une expression queer née à Kinshasa dès les années 2000, encore largement invisibilisée, fragilisée ou exposée à des formes de répression. Le photographe cherche à se positionner comme archéologue de sa propre mémoire pour faire ressurgir, dans ses photos, les artefacts, pour arracher ses vécus queer à l’effacement et pouvoir témoigner de ces présences historiques et contemporaine.

Intime

content.article_text:
I feel for film critics, I really do. Tom Cruise’s latest film Digger put them in an impossible position: you can’t really talk about it without spoiling what makes it, in my eyes, a masterpiece. Or completely terrible – as many, many critics have argued over the last week, without being fully free to say why.

That is not their fault: media screenings around the world opened with a plea from Warner Bros to not spoil the film’s central reveal . This seems like it may have been a misstep, because curiosity and Cruise alone were clearly not enough to get bums on seats. Digger is now projected to lose around $150m , after taking a paltry $20m globally in its opening weekend. Warner Bros is trying to make the best of a bad situation, first crowing about the stinker reviews – “insufferable” and “smug” have been repeated a lot – then pivoting to a new sell: the Yanks don’t get it, so it must be good .

Which is a shame, because I think Digger is a remarkable film and I am going to spoil the reveal to say why – so stop reading here if you don’t want to know.

Despite the marketing, Tom Cruise isn’t really playing Digger Rockwell, a fictional, swaggering oil tycoon who is tasked with saving the world after his oil rig explodes in Greenland, causing an enormous glacier to hurtle towards Europe and guaranteed climate disaster. Cruise plays Curtis Markson, an actor who is portraying Digger onstage in a didactic, satirical play decades after the rig really exploded and left the world in ruins. The big-budget play, titled Fossil Fools, is directed and adapted by Hannah (Sophie Wilde) and funded by Rockwell’s nephew Kenny (Jesse Plemons), in what seems to be a tiny act of philanthropic penance to offset his family’s terrible legacy.

I have seen Digger twice already, and I think it is brilliantly audacious. Alejandro G Iñárritu’s film is the best fictional work about the climate crisis that I have seen yet, because it is also about the inability of art to speak to this moment truthfully. It is about perception and reality. And it is about our inability to distinguish the two, and how that leaves us vulnerable to the loudest, most charismatic voices in a room.

Cruise’s Curtis Markson is frustrated by Fossil Fools, complaining that he is being made to play a “cartoon” version of Rockwell so Hannah can “make some statement”. Fossil Fools is objectively terrible: the grotesque and pathetic US president (John Goodman) constantly moans about having “cancer of the asshole” for laughs, while his top brass, all gorillas, demand the chance to bomb the glacier and “blow that frozen cunt up”. One literally eats popcorn while watching Europe go underwater. And when Digger finally stands before the world to answer for his crime, he pins the blame on them; it was their demand for oil that led to disaster, all so they could have “two-day delivery of shit you don’t need”. “You want freedom to live your unsustainable lives,” he shouts. “You love oil. Let’s cut the bullshit.”

The real Digger Rockwell was a “composed, frightening, seductive psychopath”, but Curtis is being ordered to play him like a rootin’-tootin’ clown in a ten-gallon hat. “What the fuck is happening? What are we doing?” he shouts at Hannah. The two argue it out: is this meant to be a satire? Is it a farce? Is it revenge on Digger? Or is it just a bad telling of a true story, one that was never meant to go beyond the “shitty little theatre in London” where Kenny first saw it, then saved it with his big wallet and his guilty conscience?

But then Kenny steps in to deliver a speech that, in my eyes, embodies the film’s true point. “It really doesn’t matter. Satire, comedy, farce, drama – it doesn’t matter,” he tells Curtis and Hannah. “You’re both right. We’re all right. Now what?”

“Now what” is what stayed with me. I don’t think many of us need a film to tell us that climate change is a terrifying, maddening thing to live through, or that political bloviating will probably block viable solutions, or that greed is degrading us and the planet. But I do love that a blockbuster film packed with enormous stars has posed the question: what does art mean at the end of the world? And, if we are honest with ourselves, do we just want art that tells us the truth, or reinforces what we already think?

Iñárritu’s answer is the latter; we’d probably settle for a middling play with a bad title if it gave us two hours of distraction and someone to blame. We like our US presidents stupid and laughable, not stupid and terrifying. A play written at the literal end of the world, about the literal end of the world, would very likely be didactic, plodding and annoying. Did you see Don’t Look Up? We are not above Fossil Fools.

Art will never be the thing that saves us from existential threat, Digger argues – but it can give us catharsis. In the end, Curtis plays Digger as a clown and gets a euphoric standing ovation. Then an alarm goes off, signalling some horrifying reality outside – and the audience put on their gas masks and file out the theatre.

It is almost poetic that so many critics are arguing that all of Iñárritu’s metatextual postmodern faff is a lazy defence against the criticism they want to dish out: the acting/script/accent in Fossil Fools is supposed to be bad, so we can’t say Digger is bad! But I don’t think this is quite honest and it seems like every single critic has found plenty of creative ways to say Digger is bad. So many reviews seem unable to distinguish between what is Fossil Fools and what is Digger; perception and reality. Perhaps the one truth we can settle on is: you should probably go see it yourself.

content.article_text:
I n the early 1960s, when Peter Zumthor was a teenage apprentice in his father’s cabinet-making workshop, he designed his first cupboard. He later recalled the satisfaction of fitting the door so perfectly that it closed “with a special sucking sound”, saying his father instilled in him “the Basel pride in the well-built object” .

Six decades on, with a fleet of globally celebrated projects to his name, the 83-year-old Swiss architect is back in Basel, beaming with the same local pride. He is gazing out at his latest well-built object, which is also his first project here: a monolithic new gallery that looks chiselled from the earth, its layers of pale crumbly concrete hammered into shape, its big oak and bronze doors – their handles wrapped with leather cord – closing with that same satisfyingly expensive Swiss swoosh.

“It was an old feeling,” Zumthor tells me, describing working in his home town to build the £110m addition to the Beyeler Foundation . “I encountered craftspeople who remembered my father, who had this special knowledge of how to make things. They weren’t surprised if something had to be custom-made.”

It was quite a change from his previous building site. Fresh from the recent opening of the tortuous, two-decade-long, $724m addition to the Los Angeles County Museum of Art , Zumthor is visibly relieved to be back on home turf. “The normal American architect is used to sourcing products, not looking for somebody who can make something custom-made,” he says, with a furrowed brow. “Their buildings are an assembly of products.”

Not so in Switzerland . From the pear wood handrails to the leather benches and blown glass lamps, every piece of his new gallery has been meticulously handmade. But is the sum of these bespoke parts a worthy companion to one of the country’s – if not the world’s – most beloved art museums?

Designed by Italian architect Renzo Piano, the Beyeler Foundation was hailed as a model of elegant restraint when it opened in October 1997 – the same month as Frank Gehry’s billowing Bilbao Guggenheim – praised as a sober foil to the “iconic” tendencies of the time. Sited in Riehen, just outside Basel, in the grounds of an 18th-century villa, the museum was commissioned by Ernst Beyeler, Europe’s pre-eminent modern art dealer and co-founder of Art Basel, and his wife Hildy, to house their staggering collection of Monets and Mirós, Matisses and Picassos.

A long, low, temple-like shed nestled in a garden, the foundation contains within its porphyry walls a luminous sequence of galleries, with daylight flooding through slender rooftop louvers. Piano took his hi-tech fetish and wrapped it in a luxurious stone skin, foreshadowing his bigger museums to come. But it was too small right from the day it opened. Two years later, it was extended by 12 metres and soon became the most visited art museum in the country, receiving 500,000 visitors a year. The challenge was how to extend a museum already deemed perfect by its art world patrons.

“They wanted something completely different,” says Zumthor, who was selected from a shortlist of 11 architects in 2016, after 100 were approached for their ideas. “Renzo’s building is more industrial, whereas mine is almost domestic. It is the villa that this garden was missing.”

The foundation acquired the Iselin-Weber park, a formerly private woodland adjacent to the museum campus, which now doubles its size, and where Zumthor’s gallery rises like a rocky outcrop. It is one of three new structures he has designed, along with a five-storey, timber-clad office and art-handling block, and an auditorium pavilion, conceived as an open public lounge – a particularly appealing space that can be accessed without a ticket. “Ninety per cent of the time,” says the foundation’s director, Sam Keller, “museum auditoriums are dead spaces. So we’ve turned it into a social space for people to come and hang out, read books, listen to podcasts or do some work, a real extension of the park.”

The three buildings stand as an eclectic ensemble on either side of a lane, framing a public square of sorts, where a new drinking fountain trickles into a big stone trough, as in a traditional mountain village, welcoming art pilgrims to Zumthor-ville. Stone benches built into the museum facade greet weary wanderers. “A building is something you ought to be able to lean against every now and then,” says the architect, as Maurizio Cattelan’s unnerving sculpture of a drummer boy perches perilously on the parapet overhead, intermittently hammering his drum from the rooftop.

The chance for Zumthor to finally build in Basel, a few kilometres from his birthplace, clearly brought back fond memories. In a schmaltzy new two-hour documentary by Wim Wenders called From Inside Out, the misty-eyed architect explains that this “intimate building” has “a lot to do with me growing up here”. He recounts that Jura limestone was “the stone of my youth”, describing how the village fountains and the cattle troughs “all glowed”. He wanted his own building to glow, too, so he mixed Jura stone into the concrete, and had workers tamp the dry mixture by hand, laying it at a rate of no more than 45cm a day. This is all filmed with a stirring musical backdrop. He wanted the wobbly joints between each day’s work left visible, like strata of sedimentary rock.

“I call it ‘farmer concrete’,” he says. “You see it everywhere in the mountains. They make it themselves, and they don’t vibrate the mixture, so it looks rough like this. You can see the building has a history, that hands have worked on it. It’s nice if you can see those traces. If it’s too slick, you just look like a fashion magazine.”

Zumthor’s rugged brand of “rammed concrete” has become one of his highly published trademarks (and has indeed featured in fashion magazines ). There is a sense of him bringing his greatest hits to the Beyeler ensemble. He used the technique for the Bruder Klaus field chapel in rural Germany and a holiday house in Devon for Alain de Botton’s Living Architecture company. The admin block, meanwhile, bears a distinct resemblance to his atelier building in Haldenstein , also in Switzerland, its elegant oak facade (masking a concrete frame) crowned with a slender corrugated canopy.

And the pavilion draws on yet another language. It’s like a warm wooden womb that’s been dug into the landscape, surrounded by walls of glass and topped with a low upholstered acoustic ceiling, full of armchairs encouraging visitors to lounge awhile. Zumthor had to wait so long for a commission in his home town, he has turned one project into three.

The galleries themselves are quite a departure from Piano’s top-lit white cubes. After the gleaming stone exterior, the interior feels almost cave-like, Monet’s waterlilies looking muddier than ever in the ground-floor gloom. Things get brighter upstairs, with large picture windows framing pastoral views in different directions as you ascend the three floors, looking towards the Black Forest on one side and the Jura mountains on the other. Limestone terrazzo floors, lime-washed walls and pale concrete ceilings create an all-encompassing world of beige, which somehow flattens the work on show, relieved only by dark timber-lined nooks for loos and lifts.

Lozenge-shaped glass lamps (“made by the only two men in Italy who have the lung capacity to do it”, I am told) provide some ambient light, while spots highlight particular works. But you might find yourself pining for the celestial top-light of Piano’s galleries next door. Despite the architect’s protestations, it oozes the aura of a luxury boutique. As one visiting Angelino noted: “It feels like a new Skims store .”

The creamy promenade culminates in a roof terrace, with more views of pretty Swiss countryside, before visitors are shuttled down a pharaonic external stairway between the concrete walls, punched with triangular openings on one side, giving glimpses of the park and a mature ginkgo tree, around which the arms of the Y-shaped building extend. Questioned about the need for all this concrete, and its attendant carbon footprint, Zumthor is adamant. “I could not make a wooden museum,” he says. “I think it is not good for art. This kind of classical art needs more substance.”

He might have questioned his own assumptions. When it first opened, the Beyeler was praised for its brave departure from the fashions of the time. Thirty years on, Zumthor, for all his talk of sensitivity to place, has created something that feels as globally ubiquitous as the Louise Bourgeois spider that crouches in the garden outside. Like the menagerie of buildings by noted architects at the Vitra campus nearby, the foundation has succeeded in adding another familiar collectible to its haul of prized works.

content.article_text:
写真家・相澤有紀が、新たなZINEシリーズ「MONOCHROMES」を創刊する。これを記念した展覧会「MONOCHROMES Launch Exhibition」が、2026年10月16日から18日まで、東京・世田谷区代沢のフリースペースDoeで開催される。

「MONOCHROMES」は、相澤が旅や日々の生活のなかで撮影した写真をまとめていくモノクロフィルムの写真集シリーズ。季節ごとに編み、年間4冊の発行を予定している。今回の創刊では「ISSUE FOR SUMMER 2025」と「Vol.01 ISSUE FOR WINTER 2025」の2冊を発表する。

相澤は、2023年に写真集「TOKYO MONOCHROMES」を刊行後、約2年間メルボルンに滞在。今回発表する夏号は、帰国前のメルボルンでの日々や、ヨーロッパを旅するなかで撮影した写真を中心に構成される。制作の軸となるのは、モノクロームによって日常のなかの光を捉えることだ。相澤はこれまで、目の前の光景に現れる模様や形状を見つめながら撮影を続けてきた。「MONOCHROMES」でもその視点を引き継ぎつつ、旅先や日常で出会う光景を季節ごとに編み直し、時間の蓄積を一冊のZINEへと定着させていく。

ローンチ展では、2冊のZINEの販売とモノクロプリントを展示。あわせて、新作「TOKYO MONOCHROMES」のデザインも手がけたMikuto MurayamaによるデザインのスクリーンプリントTシャツも販売する。

相澤は1990年、東京都生まれ。写真家、アーティスト写真やアルバムジャケット、ファッション、広告などの撮影を手がける一方、旅や日々の生活のなかで撮影を続けている。2023年に写真集「TOKYO MONOCHROMES」を刊行し、同年より約2年間メルボルンに滞在。写真集やZINE、展示を通して作品を発表している。

「MONOCHROMES Launch Exhibition」

content.article_text:
Anne Hathaway se destaca, mas a adaptação do livro de Colleen Hoover acumula revelações sem dar consistência aos personagens ou tensão aos seus segredos.

Uma revelação pode mudar tudo numa história sem mudar muita coisa para quem a acompanha. Michael Showalter acumula surpresas em “ Verity ”, mas esquece que é preciso conhecer os personagens para sentir o peso do que cada descoberta ameaça destruir. Em vez disso, o diretor prefere organizar o suspense em torno da próxima informação escondida, deixando de lado a desconfiança que deveria tornar a espera angustiante.

Lowen Ashleigh (Dakota Johnson) enfrenta dificuldades financeiras depois da morte da mãe quando recebe a proposta de finalizar os livros de Verity Crawford (Anne Hathaway), incapacitada após um acidente de carro. Instalada na casa da escritora, ela examina anotações e rascunhos até encontrar um manuscrito autobiográfico com confissões perturbadoras. Ainda tentando compreender o que leu, Lowen acaba se aproximando de Jeremy (Josh Hartnett), marido de Verity, passando a desejar uma vida da qual tem cada vez mais motivos para desconfiar.

O roteiro de Nick Antosca, adaptado do livro de Colleen Hoover, tenta estabelecer razões para essa atração, mas fornece pouca consistência à protagonista. O luto, a insegurança profissional e a possibilidade de conforto material tornam a proposta tentadora. Porém, falta conhecer os valores que Lowen estaria disposta a comprometer para ocupar aquele espaço. É perceptível ainda a ausência de uma progressão convincente entre essa vulnerabilidade do início e as escolhas que Lowen faz após se envolver com a família.

A própria escrita, responsável por levá-la até ali, recebe um tratamento superficial. Há pouco interesse pelo que significa ser romancista para Lowen ou por como essa experiência poderia interferir na interpretação do manuscrito. Ela funciona principalmente como alguém que recebe as descobertas junto do público. Dakota Johnson acentua essa limitação com uma atuação de pouquíssimo alcance expressivo. A voz baixa e a postura contida variam pouco diante da curiosidade, do desejo ou do medo, reduzindo drasticamente as diferenças entre reações que deveriam marcar mudanças na relação de Lowen com os demais personagens.

As longas passagens de leitura tornam essa limitação ainda mais evidente. Enquanto Verity assume a narração do manuscrito, a direção retorna insistentemente a Lowen lendo, aos seus olhos ou ao papel em suas mãos. A situação já está compreendida, mas o filme continua reafirmando quem lê, sem encontrar nesses retornos uma reação que transforme o sentido do relato ou explore o efeito daquelas palavras sobre a protagonista.

Os enquadramentos são simplistas demais, e a direção pouco explora o espaço e aquilo que permanece fora de vista, além de recorrer a jump scares previsíveis. Nem os clichês típicos do gênero, como o lago claramente associado a um segredo, contribuem para criar um clima de apreensão. O público percebe que há algo escondido, mas não sente a inquietude em torno da descoberta.

Quando as reviravoltas conseguem registrar uma nota de surpresa, vêm acompanhadas de explicações cada vez menos convincentes. Um material com essas características poderia funcionar sob uma condução mais abertamente melodramática ou sustentar um suspense sério. “Verity”, porém, não encontra um tom que dê força aos excessos nem constrói a tensão necessária para torná-los ameaçadores.

Anne Hathaway oferece a atuação mais densa do elenco, dando presença à personagem mesmo quando o roteiro impõe limites e mudanças difíceis de sustentar. Seu comprometimento produz momentos de interesse que a direção não consegue prolongar ou integrar ao conjunto. Josh Hartnett, por sua vez, recebe a figura previsível do marido sedutor, com um percurso que pouco se afasta do esperado. O próprio ator desempenhou um papel semelhante em “Armadilha” , em que o uso do charme para influenciar os outros se repete, mas com muito mais nuances de personalidade.

A fragilidade se torna mais evidente quando o filme tenta reconsiderar o sentido da confissão escrita. A nova explicação é tão difícil de aceitar quanto os acontecimentos que pretende esclarecer, e a dúvida passa a depender da possibilidade de qualquer informação ser desmentida. Essa ambiguidade poderia enriquecer a relação entre o desejo de Lowen e aquilo em que ela escolhe acreditar. Aqui, porém, sua caracterização é insuficiente para sustentar essa leitura, deixando a reviravolta com mais responsabilidade do que consegue assumir.

Ao fim, “Verity” exige mais disposição para aceitar suas explicações do que oferece motivos para se envolver com seus personagens. A expectativa pela próxima descoberta vai cedendo ao cansaço de acompanhar uma história que trata cada nova versão dos fatos como suficiente para renovar o interesse. Tudo pode mudar a qualquer momento, mas quase nada chega a importar.

content.article_text:
1960年代の日本で巻き起こった前衛芸術のムーブメントを、当事者たちの証言と貴重なアーカイブからひもとくドキュメンタリー映画『日本前衛派の開拓者』が、11月7日より渋谷・シアター・イメージフォーラムほか全国で順次公開される。

監督を務めたのは、ロンドンを拠点に活動するフランス人監督アメリー・ラヴァレック。6年の歳月をかけ、細江英公、森山大道、荒木経惟、川田喜久治、石内都、横尾忠則、田名網敬一らへのインタビューを敢行。さらに寺山修司や土方巽らの膨大な映像・写真資料を交え、既成の価値観やジャンルの境界を越えて独自の表現を切り拓いた日本の前衛芸術家たちの実像に迫る。

映画は「第二次世界大戦」「戦後日本」「写真」「川田喜久治」「三島由紀夫」「PROVOKE」「森山大道」「荒木経惟」「緊縛」「暗黒舞踏」「パフォーマンスアート」「寺山修司」「アングラ」「横尾忠則」「田名網敬一」などの章で構成。個々の作家や運動の独自性を追いながら、それらを貫く時代精神や共通項を浮かび上がらせる。ニューヨークのグッゲンハイム美術館やロンドンのテート・モダンのキュレーターをはじめとする専門家の証言も収録されている。

公開された予告編は、戦後日本美術とアジア現代美術研究で知られるキュレーター、美術史家のアレクサンドラ・マンローの証言からスタート。寺山修司は大学闘争が始まろうとしていた1960年代の社会状況を振り返り、森山大道は自らの世代について、それぞれが自身のジャンルや世界、政治的なものに対する「アンチ」の姿勢を持っていたと語る。田名網敬一、川田喜久治、荒木経惟、細江英公、横尾忠則らの言葉も次々と登場し、当時の作品とともに前衛表現が生まれた背景を映し出していく。

戦後の写真、美術、グラフィック、舞踏、演劇、パフォーマンスなどを横断しながら、日本の1960年代を世界の芸術史の中に位置づけ直そうとする本作。2025年にイギリスとフランスで製作され、上映時間は105分。公開に合わせ、ラヴァレック監督の来日と関連イベントも予定されている。

content.article_text:
Cette année, le Salon Photo & Vidéo se tiendra du 8 au 11 octobre à la grande halle de La Villette. Il s’intéressera autant à l’image animée qu’aux évolutions technologiques et artistiques du médium au cours de ces deux siècles passés.

En 2026, le Salon de la Photo change de nom et devient le Salon Photo & Vidéo. Dans son communiqué, l’événement explique ce changement par l’intérêt croissant pour ce second médium : « Aujourd’hui, la vidéo s’impose comme un langage universel et créatif. De nouveaux acteurs se sont installés sur le marché, des formats innovants apparaissent chaque jour, et les créateurs multiplient les expériences immersives. Qu’il s’agisse de vlog, de courts-métrages, de contenus pour les réseaux sociaux ou de projets artistiques ambitieux, la vidéo est désormais incontournable pour tous les passionnés d’image. » Du 8 au 11 octobre, les visiteurs pourront découvrir 114 exposants et 180 marques, ainsi que des expositions dont certaines feront la part belle à la vidéo. À cela s’ajoutent différentes rencontres avec des réalisateurs, des vidéastes et des créateurs de contenu qui témoigneront de leur approche créative. Ces quatre jours seront également rythmés par des ateliers, des lectures de portfolio et des conférences.

À l’occasion du Bicentenaire de la Photographie , la Grande Exposition du salon s’intéressera aux évolutions technologiques et artistiques du médium. Intitulée Deux siècles d’appareils photographiques (1826-2026) et organisée en partenariat avec le musée Nicéphore Niépce, elle proposera un parcours culturel et pédagogique. Vous pourrez y découvrir une collection unique de boîtiers, allant des débuts de la photographie à nos jours, de même que des tirages d’époque ou des reproductions. Différents procédés seront à l’honneur. Parmi eux se comptent l’héliographie, le daguerréotype, le calotype, le collodion, l’ambrotype ou encore le ferrotype. Ce projet inédit a par ailleurs été labellisé par le ministère de la Culture.

Une conférence, une chasse au trésor et d’autres surprises signées Fisheye

Comme chaque année, les équipes de Fisheye seront présentes sur place et vous proposeront notamment une conférence sur le livre photo à l’heure des réseaux sociaux. Celle-ci aura lieu le vendredi 9 octobre, de 18h à 18h30, et sera animée par Théo Gosselin et Boby . Ce dernier organisera également une chasse au trésor, en partenariat avec Sandisk™, dans la grande halle de La Villette. Au total, vingt enveloppes seront cachées. Toutes vous feront remporter un produit Sandisk™ et cinq d’entre elles, les Gold, vous permettront d’obtenir un exemplaire de Croisette 3000 , de Boby, à sa sortie. Tous les lots seront à récupérer à notre stand. Enfin, grâce à notre code promo FSEYE26, vous pourrez avoir des billets d’entrée gratuits au Salon Photo & Vidéo. Nous vous y attendons nombreux !

content.article_text:
フォトグラファーMARCOによる個展「still blue」が、2026年10月7日（水）から25日（日）まで、東京・代官山のSPEAK FOR WALLで開催される。MARCOにとって約5年ぶりとなる都内での個展で、ライフワークとして制作を続けてきた水中写真シリーズの新たな展開を披露する。

ファッション写真やアーティストのポートレートなどを数多く手がけ、独特の色彩感覚とアイデア、軽やかなフットワークで知られるMARCO。ファインダー越しに人物を風景として捉える一方、その背後にある物語だけでなく、裏側に潜む社会的な情報にも眼差しを向けてきた。一方、2016年頃からは水中写真によるオリジナル作品を発表。旅先で海に潜り、波に舞い上がる砂やきらめく光彩などを捉えながら、海中で見つけた宇宙を表現してきた。2021年の写真集『lost in the blue』では、あえて色を排除することで海中世界をモノクロームで描き出している。

「still blue」では、そうした水中写真の現在地を提示。モノクロのシリーズに加え、透明フィルムを用いたコラージュ作品約7点を発表する。さらに、水中の風景写真を居住空間に調和させる試みとして、軸装作品も都内では初めて展示・販売。写真作品と掛け軸のサイズや生地を組み合わせ、会場でセミオーダーすることもできるという。

MARCOは長野県生まれ。慶應義塾大学在学中から蜷川実花に師事し、2008年よりフリーランスのフォトグラファーとして活動。エディトリアルや広告、ポートレート撮影のほか、個展やウェブなどで作品を発表している。写真集に『PARCO de MARCO』『lost in the blue』『SOMEWHERE NOWHERE』など。

content.article_text:
La nueva serie animada de fantasía deportiva Messi y los Gigantes presentó un adelanto en San Diego Comic-Con Málaga y estrenará en Disney+ en 2027 .

Durante San Diego Comic-Con Málaga, en España, la nueva serie animada Messi y los gigantes hizo vibrar el escenario del Hall M, donde se presentó el adelanto de la esperada serie producida ejecutivamente por Lionel Messi ante una audiencia de más de 3.000 fanáticos, ansiosos por conocer más sobre esta épica serie de fantasía deportiva.

Los productores ejecutivos Lacey Stanton y Bryan Korn (Sony Pictures Television), el director Dan Creteur (Atlantis Studios) y Sergi Reitg (Sony Music Vision) revelaron nuevos detalles sobre la épica mitología original de la serie, sus audaces personajes y su extraordinaria música.

¿De qué va?

El adelanto oficial presenta la nueva canción original de la serie, “Vamos, Vamos, Vamos” , interpretada por el argentino Luck Ra. El actor argentino Milo Burgess-Webb será quien le ponga voz al personaje de Leo en la serie.

Messi y los gigantes es una serie animada infantil de fantasía deportiva que sigue a Leo, un niño de 12 años que queda atrapado en una realidad alternativa gobernada por gigantes. Para regresar a casa, deberá competir en batallas de alto riesgo, similares al fútbol, utilizando poderosas “esferas”, derrotar a gigantes legendarios y restaurar los reinos fracturados de Iko. A diferencia de los demás, Leo no puede utilizar los poderes de este mundo para potenciar su juego, por lo que deberá confiar en sus verdaderas fortalezas: su habilidad, el trabajo en equipo y la determinación. Así, la historia se convierte en una aventura protagonizada por un héroe que lucha contra las adversidades y que destaca el valor, la perseverancia y la importancia de creer en uno mismo.

View this post on Instagram

Messi y los gigantes estrenará globalmente en Disney+ en 2027.

content.article_text:
Après les Conversations photographiques lancées à Arles l’été passé, Sandisk™ et Fisheye s’associent de nouveau et proposent des balades visuelles. Pensées comme des ateliers de création collective, celles-ci auront lieu au cœur de La Villette, à l’occasion du Salon Photo & Vidéo.

Sandisk™ s’associe de nouveau à Fisheye et présente ses balades visuelles, dont voici les deux formulaires d’inscription . Au nombre de quatre et accueillant cinq à six participants, elles auront lieu les 10 et 11 octobre 2026, à 14h et 17h , lors du Salon Photo & Vidéo, à La Villette, auquel vous pourrez accéder gratuitement grâce au code FSEYE26. Celles du samedi s’articuleront autour de la vidéo et seront animées par Lucas Troadec , photographe et vidéaste qui interroge comment les espaces façonnent l’identité. Celles du dimanche feront la part belle à la photographie et seront portées par Diane Moyssan, photographe qui travaille notamment dans les univers du luxe, de la mode et du lifestyle . Toutes seront néanmoins traversées par un thème commun : le mouvement.

Concevoir une œuvre commune

Au début de ces ateliers d’une durée de 1h30, les participants rencontreront leur animateur qui les aidera à régler le boîtier qu’ils apporteront afin d’optimiser la prise de vue. Il leur donnera également des conseils artistiques pour mieux aborder la thématique. Après cela, ils sillonneront librement le parc de la Villette dans lequel ils utiliseront les modes les plus exigeants de leur appareil, à savoir la rafale haute vitesse en RAW et le slow motion haute fréquence d’images et 4K. S’ils nécessitent un matériel performant, ils requièrent tout autant de cartes fiables et adaptées, qui correspondent justement à celles développées par Sandisk™ et qui leur seront prêtées pour l’événement.

À l’issue de cette déambulation, toutes et tous se réuniront pour immortaliser une zone commune, au même moment, selon un angle différent. À la manière de Barbara Probst, les images seront ensuite assemblées, puis projetées sur un écran installé au stand Fisheye . Les co-créations pourront être relayées sur nos plateformes.

Pour vous inscrire, il suffit de cliquer sur ce lien pour le samedi ou celui-ci pour le dimanche , et d’indiquer le modèle de votre boîtier. En participant à l’un de ces ateliers, vous bénéficierez d’un code promo exclusif de 20 % de réduction sur l’ensemble des cartes du site Sandisk™, dans la limite de 500 € d’achat maximum. En outre, Sandisk™ et Fisheye organisent le jeu-concours gratuit Lucky Scan. Ce dernier consiste en un tirage au sort qui aura lieu à la fin du salon et permettra de remporter des produits Sandisk™. Au cours de cette édition du Salon Photo & Vidéo, vous pourrez également participer à une chasse au trésor de Boby.

content.article_text:
Na Hong-jin regresa con una película tan ambiciosa como despareja, donde el terror, la acción y la ciencia ficción conviven a puro exceso.

Después de casi diez años, Na Hong-jin , director de The Chaser, The Yellow Sea y The Wailing, vuelve al cine con Hope , una gigantesca producción surcoreana que mezcla monstruos, ciencia ficción, acción, terror y humor negro.

Con 160 minutos de duración, la película es tan ambiciosa como irregular. Tiene momentos extraordinarios y otros en los que su exceso termina jugando en contra, pero pocas veces deja de resultar interesante.

Un misterio que se transforma en pesadilla

La historia comienza en un pequeño pueblo cercano a la frontera entre Corea del Sur y Corea del Norte. Después de encontrar una vaca brutalmente mutilada, el jefe de policía Bum-seok (Hwang Jung-min) comienza a investigar lo ocurrido.

Lo que inicialmente parece el ataque de un animal salvaje rápidamente se transforma en algo mucho más extraño. Una criatura desconocida comienza a atacar a los habitantes y el pueblo queda atrapado en una situación que nadie comprende.

Uno de los grandes aciertos de Na Hong-jin está en retrasar la aparición del monstruo. Durante buena parte de la primera hora, la amenaza permanece prácticamente fuera de campo y el director construye el suspenso a través de edificios destruidos, vehículos destrozados, disparos y cuerpos.

Border, la extraña y atrapante joya del cine escandinavo

La decisión funciona: antes de mostrar a la criatura, Hope consigue que el espectador imagine algo mucho peor.

Acción a toda velocidad

Cuando la película decide convertirse definitivamente en una producción de monstruos, Na Hong-jin despliega una enorme cantidad de recursos.

Las persecuciones y escenas de acción son uno de los grandes puntos fuertes. Hay vehículos, explosiones, enfrentamientos y secuencias filmadas con una energía impresionante, acompañadas por la fotografía de Hong Kyung-pyo, responsable de Parasite y Burning.

La cámara se mueve constantemente y consigue transmitir una sensación de caos controlado. A eso se suma la música de Michael Abels, que aporta tensión y convierte varias escenas en auténticos momentos de espectáculo.

Hoyeon se roba la película

El reparto es otro de los atractivos de Hope. Hwang Jung-min funciona muy bien como un policía que intenta sobrevivir a una situación que lo supera, mientras que Zo In-sung aporta una presencia más cercana al héroe tradicional.

Pero la gran sorpresa es Hoyeon.

La actriz demuestra un enorme dominio de las escenas de acción y, además, aprovecha el humor negro del guion para construir uno de los personajes más carismáticos de la película. Sus intervenciones aportan una energía particular y le permiten destacarse dentro de un elenco cargado de nombres internacionales.

El problema: cuando aparece el monstruo

Hope funciona especialmente bien mientras mantiene el misterio. Una vez que explica demasiado sobre sus criaturas y su origen, parte de la tensión inicial comienza a desaparecer.

Los efectos visuales tampoco son completamente consistentes. Algunas escenas resultan impresionantes, mientras que determinados momentos digitales tienen una apariencia demasiado artificial y contrastan con la espectacularidad de las secuencias prácticas.

El guion también deja personajes algo desdibujados y una segunda mitad que puede sentirse más larga de lo necesario.

Una película sobre el miedo al otro

Debajo de todo el espectáculo, Na Hong-jin introduce una lectura relacionada con el miedo a lo desconocido y la necesidad humana de encontrar un enemigo.

La cinta juega con la idea de que una comunidad puede reaccionar con violencia frente a aquello que no comprende. No es un concepto desarrollado con la profundidad de The Wailing, pero le aporta una capa interesante a una historia que, en principio, parece enfocada únicamente en monstruos y destrucción.

¿Vale la pena ver Hope?

Hope es una película excesiva, ambiciosa y bastante irregular. Su duración puede jugarle en contra y sus efectos visuales no siempre están a la altura de sus extraordinarias escenas de acción.

Pero también es una película con personalidad. Na Hong-jin vuelve con una propuesta que no tiene miedo de mezclar géneros, romper el tono y llevar el cine de monstruos hacia lugares inesperados.

Su primera hora es especialmente potente, Hoyeon se convierte en una de sus grandes revelaciones y algunas de sus secuencias de acción justifican por sí solas verla en pantalla grande.

Hope no es una película perfecta, pero sí una experiencia cinematográfica difícil de olvidar. Una enorme, extraña y desquiciada apuesta de Na Hong-jin que seguramente dará mucho de qué hablar.

Calificación: 7.5/10. Estreno: 8 de octubre en cines, luego en MUBI .

content.article_text:
Cuatro propuestas imperdibles para disfrutar el fin de semana, con dramas, acción, suspenso y animación en las principales plataformas.

Este fin de semana, las plataformas ofrecen opciones para todos los gustos: una gran adaptación literaria en Netflix , un intenso drama en HBO Max , acción y suspenso en Prime Video y el regreso de una de las franquicias animadas más queridas en Disney+ .

Al este del Edén – Netflix

La nueva adaptación de la novela de John Steinbeck llega como una miniserie de siete episodios protagonizada por Florence Pugh , Christopher Abbott y Mike Faist . La historia sigue a los hermanos Adam y Charles Trask y a Cathy Ames, una mujer que irrumpe en sus vidas y desencadena una saga familiar marcada por secretos, conflictos y traiciones. Con Zoe Kazan como creadora, esta versión apuesta por un tono más oscuro y contemporáneo y pone especial atención en Cathy, uno de los personajes más complejos de la obra original.

War – HBO Max

Dominic West y Sienna Miller encabezan este nuevo drama legal que combina conflictos familiares, poder y estrategias judiciales. La historia comienza cuando Martin Henderson, un poderoso empresario tecnológico, y Carla Duval, una reconocida estrella de cine, se enfrentan en un complicado divorcio. En medio de la batalla legal aparece Johnny Warren, un joven abogado que busca demostrar su talento mientras queda atrapado en una disputa mucho más grande de lo que imaginaba. La serie suma tensión, secretos y giros desde sus primeros episodios.

Normal – Prime Video

Bob Odenkirk se mete en la piel de Ulysses, un sheriff que llega al tranquilo pueblo de Normal buscando empezar de nuevo después de atravesar problemas personales y una lesión sufrida en servicio. Sin embargo, la aparente calma del lugar se rompe cuando un robo a un banco expone un oscuro secreto y convierte al pueblo en el escenario de una violenta cadena de acontecimientos. La película, de 2026 y con una duración de 1 hora y 31 minutos, combina acción, suspenso y humor negro, con Henry Winkler y Lena Headey completando el elenco.

Toy Story 5 – Disney+

Woody, Buzz, Jessie y el resto de los juguetes están de regreso para una nueva aventura de Disney y Pixar. Esta vez, el principal desafío llega desde la tecnología: una nueva tableta llamada Lilypad aparece en la vida de Bonnie y pone en peligro el lugar de los juguetes en la hora de juego. Dirigida por Andrew Stanton, la quinta película de la saga vuelve a combinar aventura, humor y emoción, mientras plantea una nueva batalla por mantener vivo el juego tradicional frente a las nuevas formas de entretenimiento.

content.title_original: The Photographers Who Shaped Our Picture of New York
content.article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "The inaugural installation at Aperture’s new space, Aperture Loves New York pays tribute to photographers who have shaped—and been shaped by—the city. Showcasing artists anchored in Aperture’s publishing history, the presentation brings together photographs alongside corresponding Aperture books that have advanced the medium of photography and captured the complex spirit of New York. Organized by Sarah Meister, Executive Director, the installation features photographs by more than twenty artists ranging from past to present—including Diane Arbus, Awol Erizku, Robert Frank, Justine Kurland, Stephen Shore, and more.", "links": [{"text": "Aperture Loves New York", "url": "https://aperture.org/exhibitions/aperture-loves-new-york/"}]}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://aperture.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Tina-barney-the-reception-1985.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Tina Barney, The Reception , 1985, from Family Ties (2024) Courtesy the artist and Olney Gleason, New York", "credit": "Aperture"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Tina Barney"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "As she so often does, Tina Barney stages a familiar social ritual as a quiet psychological drama. In a wood-paneled room hung with paintings and ornamented with flowers, figures in formal dress seem gathered for celebration. Yet their gazes slide away from one another, and the seating arrangement feels oddly tense. What is happening beyond the frame that the women are paying attention to?", "links": [{"text": "Tina Barney stages a familiar social ritual", "url": "https://store.aperture.org/collections/aperture-loves-new-york/products/tina-barney-family-ties"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Barney is known for large-scale color photographs that look effortless but are carefully constructed, often using the language of the family portrait to reveal what manners can conceal: hierarchy, intimacy, impatience. Made in New York in the mid-1980s—an era of sharpened wealth, display, and social choreography—this picture turns privilege into a subject, and the “nice” occasion into something charged and unsettled."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://aperture.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Ernest-cole-untitled-harlem-1968-scaled.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Ernest Cole, Harlem, ca. 1968, from The True America (2024) © Ernest Cole Family Trust", "credit": "Aperture"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Ernest Cole"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Ernest Cole captures the city in motion: two women stride through the frame in bright patterned clothing, their faces crisp against a gentle smear of traffic and storefront signs. The slight blur of the street behind them and the one woman’s knowing look make Harlem feel fast, lived-in, charged. The neighborhood offers public space as both a backdrop and a pulse."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Cole had arrived in New York only a short time earlier, after fleeing South Africa in 1966 to publish House of Bondage (1967), his devastating photobook on apartheid (reissued by Aperture in 2022). Living in exile, he turned his camera toward Black life in America , attentive to style, dignity, and the everyday theater of the sidewalk. Seen in the turbulent late 1960s—after civil rights victories, at the height of the Black Power movement, yet amid ongoing struggle—this photograph suggests both joy and urgency.", "links": [{"text": "House of Bondage", "url": "https://store.aperture.org/products/ernest-cole-house-of-bondage"}, {"text": "turned his camera toward Black life in America", "url": "https://store.aperture.org/collections/aperture-loves-new-york/products/ernest-cole-the-true-america"}]}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://aperture.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Awol-erizku-malcolm-x-2018-scaled.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Awol Erizku, Ruth E. Carter’s costume design, from Malcolm X , two embroidered kufis for Elijah Muhammad, Malcolm X’s sometime mentor, and one kufi for an assistant of Muhammad’s. The New Yorker , from Mystic Parallax (2023) Courtesy the artist and Sean Kelly, New York", "credit": "Aperture"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Awol Erizku"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In this image made for The New Yorker , Awol Erizku depicts three kufis designed by Ruth E. Carter for Spike Lee’s Malcolm X . Set against a roiling, clouded backdrop, the hats read like small constellations: carefully patterned, slightly luminous, and charged with the weight of history carried by everyday objects. The figures appear in profile, as if the camera has caught a passing formation rather than a posed tableau.", "links": [{"text": "Awol Erizku", "url": "https://store.aperture.org/collections/aperture-loves-new-york/products/awol-erizku-mystic-parallax"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Erizku moves fluidly between editorial commissions and a studio practice that quotes and reroutes art-historical forms, pop vernacular, and spiritual iconography. He may be best known for his 2017 portrait of Beyoncé announcing her twin pregnancy, in which almost archetypal symbols—the pose, the flowers, the veil—make contemporary fame feel like a myth already living in our collective imagination."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://aperture.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Aperture_Frank_Americans_plot-dragged-scaled.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Robert Frank, New York, 1955–65, from The Americans (1968/2024) © and courtesy The Robert Frank Foundation", "credit": "Aperture"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Robert Frank"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In this image, Robert Frank turns a street corner into a study of attitude. Three young people lean against what may be a storefront; one meets the camera head-on, one half-hides behind a hand, and one looks caught between performance and fatigue. Behind them, a sign warns “DON’T MISS,” as if the city itself were constantly advertising the next spectacle, while spikes on the railing in front of them hint that the spectacle could have an edge."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Frank, a Swiss-born photographer living in New York, made this picture while developing the restless, off-kilter style that would permeate his 1958 book The Americans and reshape documentary photography. (The book was published in English the following year, and first published by Aperture in 1968.) He gravitated toward everyday scenes, recasting them as part of a searching, unsentimental portrait of the country. In the mid‑1950s, the Lower East Side was a dense, immigrant neighborhood, where life played out on stoops, sidewalks, and thresholds like this one. As Frank said in a 2015 interview, “When I was young, I could walk around, day after day, and hunt for pictures.”", "links": [{"text": "The Americans", "url": "https://store.aperture.org/collections/aperture-loves-new-york/products/robert-frank-the-americans"}]}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://aperture.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Nan-goldin-trixie-on-the-cot-new-york-city-1979.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Nan Goldin, Trixie on the cot , New York City, 1979, from The Ballad of Sexual Dependency (1986/2021) Courtesy the artist", "credit": "Aperture"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Nan Goldin"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In Trixie on the cot (1979), Nan Goldin photographs a room with startling directness: a hard overhead light, a bar cot, and a figure resting on it in a dress and heels. The cluttered floor and improvised furnishings carry the atmosphere of hardscrabble downtown life: makeshift, intimate, often inscrutable to outsiders."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Goldin began photographing as a teenager and developed her approach within the subcultures she lived alongside—first in and around Boston, then in New York after moving there in 1978. Rather than looking in from the outside, she made pictures from within a “chosen family” of friends and lovers, recording desire, tenderness, glamour, and collapse with the immediacy of lived experience. Those pictures were turned into slideshows that were accompanied by music, and later into her landmark book The Ballad of Sexual Dependency , a visual diary that helped redefine documentary intimacy.", "links": [{"text": "The Ballad of Sexual Dependency", "url": "https://store.aperture.org/products/the-ballad-of-sexual-dependency"}]}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://aperture.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Justine-kurland-playground-1998.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Justine Kurland, Playground , 1998, from Girl Pictures (2020) Courtesy the artist", "credit": "Aperture"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Justine Kurland"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In Playground (1998), Justine Kurland turns an everyday New York scene into something quietly cinematic: a small group of girls clustered around the swings, one in motion, the others seemingly engaged in the serious, shifting politics of attention and belonging. content.article_text:
The inaugural installation at Aperture’s new space, Aperture Loves New York pays tribute to photographers who have shaped—and been shaped by—the city. Showcasing artists anchored in Aperture’s publishing history, the presentation brings together photographs alongside corresponding Aperture books that have advanced the medium of photography and captured the complex spirit of New York. Organized by Sarah Meister, Executive Director, the installation features photographs by more than twenty artists ranging from past to present—including Diane Arbus, Awol Erizku, Robert Frank, Justine Kurland, Stephen Shore, and more.

Tina Barney

As she so often does, Tina Barney stages a familiar social ritual as a quiet psychological drama. In a wood-paneled room hung with paintings and ornamented with flowers, figures in formal dress seem gathered for celebration. Yet their gazes slide away from one another, and the seating arrangement feels oddly tense. What is happening beyond the frame that the women are paying attention to?

Barney is known for large-scale color photographs that look effortless but are carefully constructed, often using the language of the family portrait to reveal what manners can conceal: hierarchy, intimacy, impatience. Made in New York in the mid-1980s—an era of sharpened wealth, display, and social choreography—this picture turns privilege into a subject, and the “nice” occasion into something charged and unsettled.

Ernest Cole

Ernest Cole captures the city in motion: two women stride through the frame in bright patterned clothing, their faces crisp against a gentle smear of traffic and storefront signs. The slight blur of the street behind them and the one woman’s knowing look make Harlem feel fast, lived-in, charged. The neighborhood offers public space as both a backdrop and a pulse.

Cole had arrived in New York only a short time earlier, after fleeing South Africa in 1966 to publish House of Bondage (1967), his devastating photobook on apartheid (reissued by Aperture in 2022). Living in exile, he turned his camera toward Black life in America , attentive to style, dignity, and the everyday theater of the sidewalk. Seen in the turbulent late 1960s—after civil rights victories, at the height of the Black Power movement, yet amid ongoing struggle—this photograph suggests both joy and urgency.

Awol Erizku

In this image made for The New Yorker , Awol Erizku depicts three kufis designed by Ruth E. Carter for Spike Lee’s Malcolm X . Set against a roiling, clouded backdrop, the hats read like small constellations: carefully patterned, slightly luminous, and charged with the weight of history carried by everyday objects. The figures appear in profile, as if the camera has caught a passing formation rather than a posed tableau.

Erizku moves fluidly between editorial commissions and a studio practice that quotes and reroutes art-historical forms, pop vernacular, and spiritual iconography. He may be best known for his 2017 portrait of Beyoncé announcing her twin pregnancy, in which almost archetypal symbols—the pose, the flowers, the veil—make contemporary fame feel like a myth already living in our collective imagination.

Robert Frank

In this image, Robert Frank turns a street corner into a study of attitude. Three young people lean against what may be a storefront; one meets the camera head-on, one half-hides behind a hand, and one looks caught between performance and fatigue. Behind them, a sign warns “DON’T MISS,” as if the city itself were constantly advertising the next spectacle, while spikes on the railing in front of them hint that the spectacle could have an edge.

Frank, a Swiss-born photographer living in New York, made this picture while developing the restless, off-kilter style that would permeate his 1958 book The Americans and reshape documentary photography. (The book was published in English the following year, and first published by Aperture in 1968.) He gravitated toward everyday scenes, recasting them as part of a searching, unsentimental portrait of the country. In the mid‑1950s, the Lower East Side was a dense, immigrant neighborhood, where life played out on stoops, sidewalks, and thresholds like this one. As Frank said in a 2015 interview, “When I was young, I could walk around, day after day, and hunt for pictures.”

Nan Goldin

In Trixie on the cot (1979), Nan Goldin photographs a room with startling directness: a hard overhead light, a bar cot, and a figure resting on it in a dress and heels. The cluttered floor and improvised furnishings carry the atmosphere of hardscrabble downtown life: makeshift, intimate, often inscrutable to outsiders.

Goldin began photographing as a teenager and developed her approach within the subcultures she lived alongside—first in and around Boston, then in New York after moving there in 1978. Rather than looking in from the outside, she made pictures from within a “chosen family” of friends and lovers, recording desire, tenderness, glamour, and collapse with the immediacy of lived experience. Those pictures were turned into slideshows that were accompanied by music, and later into her landmark book The Ballad of Sexual Dependency , a visual diary that helped redefine documentary intimacy.

Justine Kurland

In Playground (1998), Justine Kurland turns an everyday New York scene into something quietly cinematic: a small group of girls clustered around the swings, one in motion, the others seemingly engaged in the serious, shifting politics of attention and belonging. The picture is a familiar city space, but it also hints at a world the girls control—they’re watched, but not fully available.

This image appears in Girl Pictures (Aperture, 2020), which gathers the artist’s now-iconic series made between 1997 and 2002. What began with a single teenage collaborator became trenchant social commentary, overturning the kinds of adventure stories that typically feature boys. As Kurland put it, “I staged the girls as a standing army of teenaged runaways in resistance to patriarchal ideals.”

Danny Lyon

In this scene, Danny Lyon photographs Lower Manhattan as it’s being emptied out—cast-iron facades still upright, streets suddenly wide with absence, demolition debris gathering at the edges. A lone figure crosses the frame as if passing through a city that’s already becoming a memory.

Lyon, who was born in New York, in 1942, is one of the key postwar American documentary photographers. He has consistently been drawn to communities and places under pressure. Here he chronicled the “slum clearance” demanded by vast civic projects like the original World Trade Center, making pictures that feel like both record and eulogy. Aperture’s 2020 facsimile The Destruction of Lower Manhattan returns to Lyon’s original 1969 photobook, bringing its acts of witness before new audiences and reminding us of the downtown architecture this city once had.

Sophie Rivera

In this picture, Sophie Rivera photographs a server front-on, framed tightly against a dark wall so that the crisp bow tie, jacket lapels, and white apron read almost like a costume. The sitter’s expression is steady but hard to place—professional, guarded, a little weary—while the flash fixes them in a moment of work that might otherwise pass unnoticed. Made in New York as Rivera was developing a photography rooted in Nuyorican life, the picture turns everyday labor into a direct encounter. The image sits within a wider body of portraits and street photographs shaped by feminist and political consciousness, insisting that dignity, complexity, and self-definition can begin in ordinary rooms and routines.

Coreen Simpson

Coreen Simpson photographs four young champions as if they were a single unit—lined up shoulder-to-shoulder, knees bent, ready. The jump rope cuts across the frame like a drawn line, tightening the composition further. Matching uniforms and headbands signal pride and discipline, but what really holds your attention is the girls’ attitude: each face meets the camera with a different mix of cool, focus, and challenge.

Simpson made images like this while covering New York’s cultural life from the late 1970s onward, bringing the tools of editorial photography to scenes that mainstream coverage often overlooked. Here, the uniforms and headbands are part of the performance. The picture also captures an important New York continuum—girls’ games and street culture alongside the early hip-hop era’s emphasis on crew, stance, and self-making in public.

Aperture Loves New York is on view at Aperture through November 1, 2026.

content.article_text:
Walker Evans was given a major exhibition at the Museum of Modern Art in 1971. That same year, Evans and his friend Leslie George Katz, publisher of Eakins Press, collaborated on an extensive interview. At this retrospective moment of his life, Evans wanted to record his thoughts on photography, his work, and the influences on him. He wanted to codify his legacy. In addition to the interview, Evans selected and commented on eight photographs that spanned the arc of his life’s work. While the interview and the photographs appeared at the time in Art in America , the project didn’t see book form until 1995, when Eakins Press published Walker Evans: Incognito . Charles Baudelaire, one of Evans’s greatest influences, wrote, “The observer is a prince enjoying his incognito wherever he goes.” This suggests that the observer, like a prince traveling in disguise, has a privileged position: They can move through the world anonymously, seeing everything while remaining unseen themselves.

The picture of a gutter was the most recent and least-known photograph in Evans’s selection. It is from 40 Studies of Street Debris, Manhole Covers, and Trash Bins, New York City (ca. 1968). Here is Evans’s accompanying text:

While removed from nature, this picture of a gutter is in a sense very human. It is Baudelairean. I wish Baudelaire was alive to see it. The secret of photography is, the camera takes on the character and the personality of the handler. The mind works on the machine.

When Evans wrote “Baudelairean,” he was referring to this paragraph, describing a chiffonnier , a ragpicker, from Baudelaire’s essay “On Wine and Hashish”:

Here is a man whose task it is to pick up all the rubbish produced on one day in the capital. All that the great city has thrown out, all that it has lost, all that it has disdained, all that it has broken, he catalogues and collects. He consults the archives of debauchery, works through the lumber-room of rubbish. He sorts things out and makes a selection, chooses astutely; like a miser, he collects the muck which, once more digested by the Gods of Commerce, will become objects of utility or pleasure.

Aperture Magazine Subscription

Like the ragpicker, a photographer “catalogues and collects”—a photographer “sorts things out” and “chooses astutely.” Here, Evans looks at a city’s debris, a most common and lowly subject, and in the image he offers a taste of his mind. As Evans elaborated in the interview, “The mind works on the machine—through it, rather.”

Writing now in my late seventies, I know that a time may come when a person reviews their past actions and experiences and recontextualizes them in the light of the perspective of a lifetime. In his interview with Katz, Evans looked back on the experience of his hot streak in the 1930s. He called the experience “a very exciting, heady thing,” adding that “it goes like magic” and “I use the word transcendent .” Evans is describing what I call a gift state. Many artists and writers have the feeling, for a period of time, of something taking over, of something working through them. Evans was now connecting the transcendence of his experience making the work with the transcendence conveyed by the images. They were imprinted with a quality of his mind.

Focus is the nexus that connects the photograph, the world, and the mind. It is the door to the passage from the surface to the interior.

The only time I had the opportunity to hear Evans speak was at a lecture he gave at the Museum of Modern Art in the early 1970s. He showed Corrugated Tin Façade (1936)—a deadpan photograph of a dilapidated contractor’s office in Alabama, sunlight shimmering off the corrugation—and, by my recollection, called it a “transcendent document.” I knew that he had previously described “documentary style” as having the qualities of “severity, rigor, simplicity, clarity . . . without artistic pretension.” I was not expecting him to describe his work as transcendent. He was now indicating that below the surface of a “document” could lie an interior depth. He chose Matisse’s quote “L’exactitude n’est pas la vérité” (Exactitude is not truth) as the epigraph for his book Message from the Interior (1966). He is saying not to mistake the surface exactitude of documentary style for truth, but to look beneath the surface. Truth may be buried in its interior, the message from the interior. Truth can reside beneath the surface of the mundane, the quotidian. This recalls an Arab maxim, “The apparent is the bridge to the real.”

An Evans photograph in which I feel this depth, this undercurrent, an image that moves me most deeply, is Breakfast Room at Belle Grove Plantation , from March 1935. In an early act of urban exploration, Evans, accompanied by his future wife Jane Ninas and her friend Christine Fairchild, broke into the Belle Grove mansion. They shared a picnic breakfast in this space he would later call the “breakfast room.” Before making the photograph, Evans arranged the shutters in the center of the picture, allowing just a crack of light to seep through.

The Belle Grove Plantation in White Castle, Louisiana, was built by the sugar planter John Andrews in 1857. The seventy-five-room Greek Revival mansion was one of the largest residential buildings in the American South during the antebellum period. Belle Grove exemplified the grand architectural ambitions of Louisiana’s sugar aristocracy and stood as a testament to the economic power generated by the brutal system of enslaved labor that perpetuated this culture. Without enslaved labor, the plantation could not be sustained. It changed hands several times after the Civil War and was eventually abandoned. By the early twentieth century, the mansion had fallen into serious disrepair.

When I see the decaying Corinthian columns in the breakfast room, I think of Giulio Romano’s Sala dei Giganti (Hall of the Giants) in the Palazzo Te. Here the giants are trying in vain to hold up crumbling columns, massive columns tilting and breaking apart, the classical world disintegrating around them, as Zeus and the gods crush the giants for their hubris.

Look at the photograph Breakfast Room at Belle Grove Plantation . Slowly, deliberately, move your attention, your focus, along the side walls to the columns, then to the floor of the small vestibule, and then to the shutters. Notice the depth of space from the columns, across the vestibule, to the shutters. Do you have a sensation of your eyes changing focus? Do you sense Evans’s experience? Do you have a taste of Evans’s mind?

Focus is the nexus that connects the photograph, the world, and the mind. It is the door to the passage from the surface to the interior. It is a way of connecting with the mind that works through the machine.

This article originally appeared in Aperture No. 264, “Stop Time,” guest edited by Hiroshi Sugimoto, under the column Notebook.

content.article_text:
武蔵野美術大学 造形構想専攻 映像・写真コースの菅沼比呂志ゼミによる展覧会「写真、その複数形 ～写真をめぐるいくつもの入口」が、武蔵野美術大学市ヶ谷キャンパス1/Mで開催されている。会期は2026年9月26日から10月4日まで。

本展には、学部4年生から大学院、博士課程まで計22人が参加。21歳から35歳までと年齢層も幅広く、そのうち15人を海外からの留学生が占める。大学で初めて写真を学んだ学生から、デザインなど別領域を経て写真へと進んだ学生、社会人経験後に大学院で学び直す学生まで、それぞれ異なる背景を持つ。

展覧会のタイトルにある「複数形」が示すように、焦点となるのは単一の写真観ではない。プリント、写真集、スクリーン、言葉などさまざまな形式を通して、写真を見るとは何か、写真を介して何を見るのかを22人それぞれの実践から問い直す。完成された答えを提示するのではなく、作品を「句点」「読点」「クエスチョンマーク」「イコール」「ダッシュ」にたとえながら、写真について考えるための複数の「入口」をつくり出すことが展覧会の試みだ。

そのアプローチも多岐にわたる。内藤翼の「FACTA」は、フェイクニュースと物理的に操作された写真を同一紙面上で交差させ、虚構から「現実らしさ」が生成される構造を検証。生成AIをはじめイメージの真正性が揺らぐ現在において、「現実とは何か、リアルとは何か」という問題を写真とメディアの双方から問いかける。

一方、寺井雅也の「注がれた景色」は、街の廃材だったやかんをピンホールカメラへと転換した作品。像が定着される以前の光学現象に着目し、やかんの内部へ反転して投影される風景そのものを鑑賞者が覗き込めるよう構成する。写真が「写真」になる以前の状態へと遡り、メディウムの原理そのものを体験へと変換する試みだ。

ほかにも、故郷や土地の歴史、記憶、都市、家族、身体、時間など、学生たちの関心は広範囲に及ぶ。中国東北部の土地と「満洲」という名称に刻まれた歴史を見つめる葛苡辰の「北満ノ森」や、日本で暮らすなかで自身と場所との距離を考察する郭暁頴の「ひとつにはならない」、幼少期の家族写真を思い出の場所へ投影し、過去と現在を一枚の写真上で交差させる陳泓毅の「記憶の面影」など、写真を「記録」に限定しない実践が並ぶ。

会期終盤にはゲストを迎えたトークイベントも実施。10月3日13時から批評家のきりとりめでる、10月4日13時から写真家の野口里佳が登壇し、学生たちの作品について講評する。
