content.article_text:
HBO Max renueva su catálogo en octubre con nuevas series, películas, documentales, realities y una programación especial de terror por Halloween.

Octubre llega a HBO Max con una programación cargada de series, películas, documentales, realities y propuestas especiales para Halloween. Entre las principales novedades aparecen producciones originales, historias basadas en hechos reales y varios títulos de terror.

El mes también tendrá un estreno muy especial para la plataforma: Epitafios , la primera producción original de HBO realizada en América Latina, regresa en una versión remasterizada para celebrar los 35 años de HBO en la región.

Series

Guerra – 1 de octubre

Archie Renaux, Dominic West y Sienna Miller protagonizan este drama legal ambientado en el mundo de los grandes abogados de Londres. La historia enfrenta a dos prestigiosos estudios jurídicos mientras un joven abogado queda atrapado en una batalla marcada por la ambición, el poder y la traición.

Estado de Furia – Temporada 2 – 9 de octubre

La segunda temporada presenta nuevas historias protagonizadas por mujeres que quedan atrapadas en un sistema donde las situaciones extremas pueden transformarse en un espectáculo. Maribel Verdú, Carmen Maura, María León y Cecilia Suárez forman parte del elenco.

Epitafios – versión remasterizada – 15 de octubre

Para celebrar sus 35 años en América Latina, HBO recupera su primera producción original realizada en la región. Julio Chávez, Paola Krum, Antonio Birabent y Cecilia Roth protagonizan esta historia policial sobre una serie de asesinatos conectados con una antigua tragedia.

Te puede interesar

Qué ver este fin de semana: 4 películas y series que son tendencia en Netflix, HBO Max, Prime Video y Disney+

Recomendaciones de finde: 4 títulos para ver en streaming

El colombiano de Keko – 22 de octubre

Juan Cruz, Christian Tappan y Juan Pablo Raba protagonizan este drama basado en hechos reales. Andrés Ballesteros viaja a Tanzania en busca del amor, pero termina encarcelado injustamente por una acusación de narcotráfico y pasa ocho años intentando regresar a su hogar.

Documentales y true crime

Tragedia en el Estadio de La Corregidora – 15 de octubre

Este documental de HBO reconstruye los violentos acontecimientos ocurridos durante un partido entre Querétaro y Atlas en 2022. A través de testimonios inéditos y material nunca antes visto, la producción vuelve sobre las dudas y controversias que quedaron alrededor de aquella jornada.

Poeta Caníbal – octubre

El documental se mete en la historia de José Luis Calva Zepeda, conocido como “El Poeta Caníbal”, y reconstruye el caso a partir de testimonios exclusivos y una investigación sobre los crímenes que conmocionaron a México.

La Masacre de Flores – octubre

La serie documental reconstruye uno de los casos criminales más impactantes de Argentina a través de la historia de Matías Bagnato, único sobreviviente del incendio que terminó con la vida de sus padres, sus dos hermanos y un amigo en 1994.

Películas

Los domingos – 16 de octubre

Ainara tiene 17 años y, mientras su familia espera que decida qué carrera universitaria estudiar, la joven sorprende a todos al revelar que quiere convertirse en monja de clausura. La decisión pone a prueba los vínculos familiares. El elenco incluye a Blanca Soroa, Patricia López Arnaiz y Juan Minujín.

The Moment – 30 de octubre

Charli xcx protagoniza esta película sobre una estrella emergente del pop que debe enfrentarse a las presiones de la fama y de la industria musical mientras prepara su primera gira en grandes estadios. También participan Rosanna Arquette, Kate Berlant, Kylie Jenner y Rachel Sennott.

Realities

MasterChef: Profesionales Brasil – Temporada 6 – 9 de octubre

La versión brasileña del popular reality culinario vuelve con nuevos cocineros profesionales que deberán convencer a tres reconocidos chefs para quedarse con la victoria. El jurado está integrado por Erick Jacquin, Helena Rizzo y Henrique Fogaça.

Supervivencia al Desnudo: Brasil – Temporada 4 – 18 de octubre

Diez participantes intentarán sobrevivir en una región de Sudáfrica atravesada por una histórica sequía y poblada por animales peligrosos, entre ellos búfalos y mambas negras.

Comedia

Kate Berlant: Parmesano – 23 de octubre

La comediante Kate Berlant llega con un especial de HBO Original en el que aborda con humor y sarcasmo temas como la tecnología, la sexualidad y las contradicciones de la vida moderna.

Animación infantil

Hora de Aventura: Misiones Secundarias – 5 de octubre

Finn y Jake regresan a los primeros días de sus aventuras en una nueva serie de episodios autoconclusivos que recupera a varios personajes clásicos de la franquicia, incluido el Rey Helado.

Especial de Halloween

HBO Max también prepara una programación especial para octubre con varias propuestas de terror.

Evil Dead: En llamas – 9 de octubre

Una reunión familiar en una casa aislada se transforma en una pesadilla cuando sus integrantes comienzan a convertirse en Deadites . La película está dirigida por Sébastien Vaniček y cuenta con Souheila Yacoub y Hunter Doohan en su elenco.

Mother Mary – 23 de octubre

Anne Hathaway y Michaela Coel protagonizan esta película dirigida por David Lowery. La historia sigue a una icónica estrella del pop que se reencuentra con su antigua amiga y diseñadora de vestuario antes de regresar a los escenarios.

La herencia de Hope Hill – 23 de octubre

Una joven abogada viaja a Jamaica para investigar una disputa por una herencia, pero descubre que la propiedad involucrada está relacionada con las pesadillas que la persiguen y con un oscuro pasado familiar.

Devorador de almas – 23 de octubre

Un viaje de fin de semana a una mansión aislada en Irlanda se convierte en una pesadilla cuando una antigua criatura de la mitología irlandesa despierta y comienza a infectar a los protagonistas.

Además, durante octubre se suman otros títulos de terror como No te sueltes, Fear Factor: la casa del miedo, Junji Ito: Historias Extrañas para Noches de Insomnio, El Tormento, Noche Infernal, Cacería, Spree: Viaje Desenfrenado, Campeonato de Reposteros: Halloween, A Ciegas, El Carnicero y Los Cazamuertos .

Más estrenos de HBO Max en octubre

Series: La Favorita 1922 T2 (2/10), The Paper T2 (próximamente), Tip Toe (16/10, fecha por confirmar) y Georgie y Mandy – Su Primer Matrimonio T3 (22/10).

Películas: Un Pastel para el Presidente (2/10), Vieja Loca (2/10), Ninotchka (7/10), El Bazar de las Sorpresas (7/10), Maridos (7/10) y ¡Súper Agente Hitpig! (16/10).

Documentales y docuseries: Miller Night Football (3/10), Revista People investiga: sobreviviendo al asesino T2 (6/10), Mi relación con un asesino serial (7/10), Cuando Nadie me ve (9/10), Tierra de Crimen (12/10), Epic: Elvis Presley in Concert (16/10), Narco Hack (23/10), Sister Wives T14 (26/10) y Kordell: Slash & Burn (31/10), entre otros.

Animación: El Maravillosamente Extraño Mundo de Gumball T2 (9/10), Solo Necesitas Matar (9/10), Tom and Jerry Gokko Compilation-2 (23/10), Regular Show Presents: Terror Tales of the Park VII Halloween (4/10), Get Jiro (3/10), Gachiakuta (12/10) y Dragon Ball Beerus (16/10).

content.article_text:
20. Document of the Dead (1985)

Behind-the-scenes footage from Dawn of the Dead is the highlight of this aficionados-only affair, which follows the 1979 satirical zombie horror all the way through to distribution. Director George A Romero, makeup maestro Tom Savini and the occasional zombie actor shoot the breeze in the deserted shopping mall that provides the movie with its incongruous central location.

19. The Death of “Superman Lives”: What Happened? (2015)

Imagining what might have been if Tim Burton’s Superman Lives had got off the ground, documentary maker Jon Schnepp cosies up on screen with his interviewees and insinuates himself unforgivably into the story. The material is almost good enough to transcend his vanity: there is test footage of lead actor Nicolas Cage in his Man of Steel duds, plus interviews with Burton, original screenwriter Kevin Smith and producer Jon Peters, who was adamant that Superman should fight polar bears and a giant spider.

18. Becoming Bulletproof (2014)

A group of actors with disabilities form the bulk of the cast of the short western Bulletproof, shot in the California desert courtesy of the inclusive arts project Zeno Mountain Farm. Crucially, Bulletproof itself isn’t about disability, but rather an attempt to highlight the lack of on-screen representation – and plug the gap. This affectionate documentary tracks the film from preproduction to premiere.

17. They’ll Love Me When I’m Dead (2018)

Orson Welles spent five years shooting what became his final film, The Other Side of the Wind, with three years elapsing before its star – director and sometime actor John Huston – even stepped in front of the camera. After all that, the footage ended up impounded by the Iranian revolutionary government. A version eventually premiered in 2018 and is now on Netflix, along with this scattershot documentary, presented by Alan Cumming, which strings together archive footage, new interviews and typically Wellesian stories of on-set bluffs, tomfoolery and procrastination.

16. Filmmaker: A Diary by George Lucas (1968)

A half-hour snapshot by Lucas of his new buddy Francis Ford Coppola, who is hard at work on his fourth film, The Rain People, and not too shy to argue with his lead actor, Shirley Knight. Contains one choice detail: in preparation for driving across the country shooting this road movie, all the men on the crew, Coppola included, shave off their beards to look more presentable for any hippy-hating officials they might encounter along the way.

15. Boorman and the Devil (2025)

In declining The Exorcist but taking on Exorcist II: The Heretic, John Boorman perhaps displayed a preference for poisoned chalices over champagne flutes. He is candid and good-humoured, if still a little shell-shocked, as he recounts the experience of filming the sequel once derided as “the stupidest major movie ever made”, and the despair that led him to contemplate self-immolation on Hollywood Boulevard. Sand-related illness, a sozzled Richard Burton, locusts and tap-dancing: this has it all.

14. Doomed! The Untold Story of Roger Corman’s The Fantastic Four (2015)

Filmed in a rat-infested studio on sets recycled from the Jurassic Park rip-off Carnosaur, with special effects entrusted to a local outfit called Mr Film, this cheapo superhero adventure was made in a rush to prevent the rights to The Fantastic Four reverting from producer Bernd Eichinger to Marvel. (“That movie was never supposed to be shown to anybody,” said Stan Lee.) This heartening documentary, which shows the crestfallen cast refusing to let their film die, feels even more pertinent after Warner Bros recently shelved some movies as tax write-offs, including Batgirl and Coyote Vs Acme, the latter rescued only by the skin of its teeth.

13. Jodorowsky’s Dune (2013)

In trying to adapt Frank Herbert’s Dune in the mid-1970s, cinematic shaman Alejandro Jodorowsky (Santa Sangre, El Topo) bit off more than he could chew, just as David Lynch would when his version came to painful fruition in 1984. But Frank Pavich’s documentary proves that Jodorowsky’s intention to make “a film that gives LSD hallucinations without taking LSD” was not too fanciful. Among those in his corner were the artist HR Giger, who went on to design the monsters in Alien, and a cast including Salvador Dalí, Mick Jagger and Orson Welles, with the latter being bribed to take part with the promise of having his favourite chef on set.

12. Lost Soul: The Doomed Journey of Richard Stanley’s Island of Dr Moreau (2014)

When the studio New Line tried to ditch South African director Richard Stanley from his own HG Wells adaptation, he asked a warlock called Skip to pull some cosmic strings. That did the trick for a while, helping Stanley to charm the film’s star, Marlon Brando. But black magic was no match for cast member Val Kilmer, who demanded a 40% reduction in his own shooting days, then spent his time on set playing power games. There was nature to contend with, too, in the form of wild animals (a puma pisses on Stanley’s tailored suit) and a hurricane that ravages the location in Cairns, Queensland. Finally replaced by curmudgeonly veteran John Frankenheimer, Stanley refuses to leave Australia, which is when things go from mad to worse.

11. No Frank in Lumberton (1988) / Blue Velvet Revisited (2016)

Two behind-the-scenes Blue Velvet documentaries from one director. Peter Braatz was still a film student when David Lynch, with whom he had been corresponding for several years, invited him to Wilmington, North Carolina in 1985 to chart the making of what would become his twisted masterpiece. Braatz marshalled just under an hour of the resulting Super-8 material into his 1988 documentary, which straddled the line between orthodox and experimental. He then reshaped it into a full-on ambient head-trip for the 86-minute 2016 version, which mixes flickering footage and crisp black-and-white photographs with a woozy score and the voices of Lynch, Dennis Hopper and others to form an ethereal audiovisual collage.

10. The Sweatbox (2002)

Disney had high hopes for Kingdom of the Sun, a Prince and the Pauper-style animated musical drama set in the Inca empire. The studio sent Lion King co-director Roger Allers on a research trip to Peru and commissioned a suite of new songs by Sting. But it was back to the drawing board after a calamitous screening of an early rough cut; Allers and Sting were given the heave-ho, and the movie was retooled as the larky comedy The Emperor’s New Groove. Sting’s wife, Trudie Styler, charts every disastrous step in a documentary that Disney has done its darnedest to suppress .

9. From Darkness to Light (2024)

A 10-a-penny title for an account of a once-in-a-lifetime film-making folly: Jerry Lewis’s abandoned, incomplete 1972 Holocaust drama The Day The Clown Cried . Directing himself as a former clown who entertains children in a concentration camp, Lewis made a misguided bid to be taken seriously. “It was bad work,” he admits here. It wasn’t only the dubious material that defeated the former Nutty Professor: unbeknown to him, the option on the script had expired, rendering the entire project illegal. It was his decision, though, to hire a repentant former concentration camp guard as part of the crew. “He was a human being!” Lewis protests.

8. Poultry in Motion: Truth Is Stranger Than Chicken (2008)

Seventy-odd fans of horror exploitation studio Troma worked unpaid on Poultrygeist: Night of the Chicken Dead while living in a deserted church in a rundown corner of Buffalo, New York, with one cold shower between them. Meanwhile, the chicken-themed zombie flick was shot at a nearby abandoned McDonald’s. This documentary captures all the on-set horror, from the sexually disinhibited auditions to the hourly cast-and-crew bust-ups. Actors walk off, burst into tears and throw punches; a zombie extra accidentally sets himself on fire; and bilious co-director and Troma boss Lloyd Kaufman proves both lackadaisical and tyrannical.

7. Shirkers (2018)

When budding film-maker Sandi Tan met the enigmatic Georges Cardona, he cited Fitzcarraldo as his inspiration and claimed to know crew members from Apocalypse Now. Those pictures – famously troubled productions that spawned their own jaw-dropping documentaries – look like red flags considering what came next: Cardona directed Tan’s indie road movie Shirkers, swallowing up $10,000 of her savings when he ran out of money, then vanished with the resulting 70 reels of unprocessed film. She didn’t see the footage until decades later, when those reels were returned to her by Cardona’s widow. Tan’s sobering 2018 documentary attempts to make sense of the betrayal.

6. The Peddler (2010)

“Good film directors will notice many mistakes,” says prolific camcorder auteur and 67-year-old Santa Claus lookalike Daniel Burmeister. “But I like what I do: making hand-crafted films.” In exchange for a month’s food and accommodation, Burmeister sets up shop in a remote Argentinian village to bring the community together by shooting a movie from one of his own scripts. His budget may be nonexistent but his resourcefulness is boundless: in place of a dolly shot, for instance, he sits on a blanket, camera on his shoulder, while being dragged across the floor. This delightful, deeply humanistic portrait of grassroots DIY cinema has all the charm and idiosyncrasies of a Jared Hess comedy.

5. Lost in La Mancha (2002)

Terry Gilliam was happy to have documentary makers Keith Fulton and Louis Pepe on set for The Man Who Killed Don Quixote after being impressed by The Hamster Factor, their behind-the-scenes film on the making of his earlier 12 Monkeys. The anguished result shows exactly why Quixote was abandoned after six days’ shooting in Spain in September 2000. Takes were rendered unusable by the roar of F16s from a nearby Nato base; Jean Rochefort, co-lead opposite Johnny Depp, fell seriously ill; and the equipment was destroyed by a merciless storm. Gilliam’s on-set catchphrase sums it up: “We’re fucked!” (When Quixote was eventually made in 2018, Fulton and Pepe documented that shoot, too, in He Dreams of Giants .)

4. Henri-Georges Clouzot’s Inferno (2009)

The subgenre of documentaries about unfinished films stretches back to the BBC’s 1965 The Epic That Never Was, which investigated Josef von Sternberg’s planned version of I, Claudius starring Charles Laughton and Merle Oberon. But it reached its apotheosis with Henri-Georges Clouzot’s Inferno, Ruxandra Medrea and Serge Bromberg’s ravishing reflection on an early-1960s Proustian psychological drama from the director of Les Diaboliques. Lavishly funded by Columbia, Clouzot’s vision was impossibly ambitious, with three crews and a trippy array of complicated in-camera special effects. The director, who could not be dissuaded from shooting time-consuming test footage, suffered a heart attack three weeks into the 18-week shoot. The fragments of his vision, cherrypicked here from 15 hours of unseen footage, are intoxicating: where else can you see Romy Schneider covered in glitter, cellophane and olive oil?

3. Burden of Dreams (1982)

Deep in the rainforests of South America, Werner Herzog battles mud and misery, along with his leading man Klaus Kinski, to make Fitzcarraldo, about one man’s dream of building an opera house in the Amazon. Les Blank’s documentary, which is arguably more compelling than the movie it’s about, enables us to watch in disbelief as a film about a lunatic mission turns into one itself. Herzog’s initial footage has to be abandoned when the lead actor, Jason Robards, falls ill with amoebic dysentery and co-star Mick Jagger is needed on a world tour. Up and running again, the production is forced to relocate more than 1,000 miles away due to a border war, while Herzog’s plans to move a steamship up a hillside provide a textbook example of madness eclipsing method.

2. American Movie (1999)

Mark Borchardt, a Milwaukee junkyard poet with a mullet and plateglass specs, may be best suited to factory work or serial killing, according to his brother, but he positively glows with a passion for cinema. Lacking the funds to finish his feature debut, he instead tries to complete a short horror film, Coven, undaunted by his inability to pronounce the title. More Wiseau than Welles, he has optimism and indefatigability to burn. Not to mention a crew of colourful collaborators, including his mother, whom he enlists as an extra despite her protestations that she needs to go shopping; his bleary, poodle-haired pal and former acid-head Mike; and the gnarled, trailer-dwelling Uncle Bill, who needs 30 takes to deliver four lines. Director Chris Smith (who later made the priceless Fyre festival documentary ) rightly portrays Mark as one of cinema’s most inspiring heroes – even if he still hasn’t finished his first feature.

1. Hearts of Darkness: A Filmmaker’s Apocalypse (1991)

Megadoc, the forthcoming behind-the-scenes film about Francis Ford Coppola’s $120m passion project Megalopolis , is directed by Mike Figgis, though earlier Coppola-related documentaries tended to be family affairs. The director’s late wife, Eleanor, was responsible for Making Marie Antoinette, released later this month, about their daughter Sofia’s 2006 historical fantasia. And it was Eleanor, too, who co-directed the extraordinary Hearts of Darkness, which draws on her 60 hours of footage and 40 hours of audio recordings, as well as her own diaries, all from the turbulent 238-day shooting of Apocalypse Now. The film reveals her husband arguing on set with Dennis Hopper, frantically typing new scenes just moments before the cameras roll, and negotiating with Marlon Brando, who has piled on the pounds but neglected to learn his lines. “I’m thinking of shooting myself,” the director confides. “This is one crisis I can’t pull myself out of.”

content.article_text:
Realising that the experiences of a whole generation of British-Bangladeshis will soon be lost – and motivated by celebrating the community in the midst of a rising far right – Seema Khalique built a multi-faceted piece of history now on show in London’s Bethnal Green

Seema Khalique’s father Abdul arrived in the UK from Bangladesh in 1956; her mother, Gulnehar, arrived in 1973, after the Bangladesh Liberation War. Abdul Khalique was in the restaurant business, and the family moved to Croydon in the 1970s after buying a restaurant there; later they moved to Eltham, once again following work. It’s a story that speaks of graft and determination, the sheer grit required to start a new life in a new country. But there are also gaps in the narrative. As Khalique’s father grew older, she realised she knew little about his early London years, or what it had been like to arrive in the UK. She realised that he and a whole generation of British Bangladeshis would soon pass away, and with them these experiences would be lost.

And so connecting with 12 individuals – many linked to her father – Khalique spent hours with each of them from 2021 on, listening to their stories, collaborating on their portraits, and looking through their archives. The result is Londoni Memoirs , a still on-going project supported by the National Lottery Heritage Fund, which gathers oral history, archive photos, ephemera, and new images to document Bangaldeshis who settled in Britain in the 1950s-70s. Some, like Khalique, are based in London, others are further afield, landing by luck and the work that was available when they migrated.

“Generally all the participants moved where there was work, so if that meant going to Birmingham, because of the factory trade there, they were in Birmingham,” says Khalique. “There was a massive community in the East End because of the factories there, and that created opportunities for women working from home – they could do sewing and tailoring, and be with the kids. Everyone had a sewing machine. Most people worked six days a week. One of the participants lived in St Albans and his general pattern, when he worked, was to work from four in the morning until four in the afternoon at a factory, then the evening shift at a restaurant.”

By working at this level people managed to set themselves up, says Khalique; many were also sending money to Bangladesh, particularly during the war [in 1971]. “Many people spoke about feeling that they had helped Bangladesh survive,” she says. “Family members didn’t starve because they were able to provide.”

Londoni Memoirs collects some heartbreaking stories, tales of people fleeing burning villages – the only ones to escape – and returning years later, not knowing who they would find alive. Few of the participants had spoken publicly about these experiences before, says Khalique, preferring to move on “though they still carry the trauma”. But Londoni Memoirs also records happier times, Khalique determined not to flatten a range of experiences into a monotone, or many testimonies into a single lumpen mass.

“One participant came from a very affluent family, he came to the UK to study law and his father basically funded him,” she points out. “He lived on the same road as The Beatles, and had these crazy stories about parties where the police would chase everyone away. Others spoke about squatting in London, as a solution to the housing crisis. It was interesting to hear about the parallel lives that were lived at that time, and to hear about not just the struggles that we associate with migration, but the enjoyment that comes from it. Experiencing cold weather, snowball fights, all of it.”

Khalique’s sensitivity shows in her portraits, which she made collaboratively. There’s a sweet photograph of her mother in her garden, wearing a green sari matching the foliage of a Bangladeshi Marrow Plant “which the Bangladeshi grow with pride in the summer months”. Some of the women preferred not to be shown looking straight at the camera though, wary of the sin of idolatry; Khalique has also collected other images, which present other images and do other things. There’s a formal studio portrait of Rajia Yaqub and family, for example, a snap of Makhlisur Rahman standing with his house and a smart car; often taken to send back home, these shots present carefully-constructed images of happiness and prosperity, not everyday trials or tribulations.

Khalique has also collected passport photos and official documentation, including an amazingly glamorous photograph of her mother in a passport due to expire in 1977, and a receipt from the Pakistan Relief Fund for £5, dated in pre-independence 1965 [when £5 was worth about £125 today]. Khalique’s exhibition at Four Corners includes 10-minute videos of the participants speaking; she’s also created transcripts of the videos, and published them in a newspaper. “I know not everyone will sit and watch all the videos,” she says. “So the newspaper was important, and then it can also travel.”

The location of the gallery is important too because, though Khalique still lives in South East London, she wanted to show the work somewhere close to the British-Bangladeshi community; Four Corners is in East London, near the long-standing Banglatown in Whitechapel and Brick Lane. Few of the participants could come to the opening night, as they’re now elderly and some in poor health, but ten were able to come for a special afternoon, and for Khalique that was deeply rewarding. They were wowed by seeing their portraits and archive photographs on the walls, she says, adding she had framed these images to ensure they felt properly honoured.

Khalique also arranged a family workshop in the gallery, allowing children to find out more about British, Bangladeshi, and British-Bangladeshi history, plus issues of representation; these issues have become more important to her, she says, because of hardening far right attitudes, and because she now has kids of her own. “I grew up in a very multicultural area, growing up I never felt racially different,” she says. “It’s only since becoming a mother I’ve realised that, and only in the last few years I’ve experienced it. And that pains me because, while I can fight for myself, my children can’t fight for themselves. So I felt I had to do it for them. I wanted to make work that would celebrate this community.”

Londoni Memoirs by Seema Khalique is on show at Four Corners until 10 October www.fourcornersfilm.co.uk www.seemakhalique.com

content.title_original: ‘A saving gesture’: the art exhibition spotlighting US prisoners’ creations
content.article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "W ith nearly 2 million people behind bars, America is the global leader in incarceration. When you look at it per capita, we have the highest rate of incarceration of any independent democracy and rank fourth overall in the world, just behind El Salvador, Cuba and Turkmenistan."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Despite these troubling numbers, mass imprisonment is largely invisible. “Our carceral system is something we as a society try to separate out from the everyday,” observes Terra Warren, an associate curator at Grand Rapids Art Museum, Michigan , who alongside curator Jennifer Wcisel brings audiences three solo shows from artists Julie Green, Gary Tyler and Ray Materson. They collectively aim to make us examine more closely just what prisons are doing to our society – and how art can prove transformative to those incarcerated.", "links": [{"text": "Grand Rapids Art Museum, Michigan", "url": "https://www.artmuseumgr.org/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In a major feat, Green’s show collects the artist’s work The Last Supper, rarely exhibited in full. This masterpiece took 22 years to complete and comprises nearly 1,000 plates, each depicting the final meal requested by an individual on death row before their execution. Poignantly, many of the plates are simply inscribed with the word “none”, indicating when an inmate opted not to eat a final meal. One imagines it would be hard to find an appetite under such conditions."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/9699f7550d3d04e8fef2567819ed51e7e3ceb6f1/0_360_3600_2880/master/3600.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "White plate with the word “none” painted in the center", "caption": "Julie Green, The Last Supper [Texas 22 May 2002], 2021. Paint on found ceramic plates. Diameter: 6in. Photograph: Courtesy of Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art, Bentonville, Arkansas. Gift of The Last Supper Irrevocable Trust", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In centering breaking bread, a practice that’s a cornerstone of our shared humanity, The Last Supper forces audiences to reckon with the contradictions of a system that at once gives the pleasure of consuming a fine meal, yet also dehumanizes and even puts to death those within its grasp. Additionally, the piece opens space for compassion and understanding by giving us a window into the lives of those who are rarely represented in any meaningful way at all."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“There’s one in particular where a prisoner opted to eat vending machine food with their family,” Warren says, recalling plates that particularly stood put in her memory. “There’s another whose mother was allowed to come in and cook their last meal.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Some of the plates also underscore the fact that the state will put to death individuals who are not even aware of what’s happening; one plate indicates that an inmate chose to save some of their last meal for later, not understanding that there would not be a chance to ever eat again. “One of the plates details that a person with an IQ of 61 was executed,” said Warren, indicating someone was put to death in spite of serious mental impairments."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "D eath row figures prominently in the life of Gary Tyler, an author and artist, who in 1974 was charged with the murder of a white teenager when Tyler was 16 years old. When he was convicted by an all-white jury and sentenced to death, he became the youngest person on death row in the United States. The case was marred by police misconduct, and Tyler is now widely considered to have been wrongfully imprisoned."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/1b071f0a91607e5d1e1ad3c9240e3a404aa7e9b8/38_0_1125_900/master/1125.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "Quilting fabric embroidered with image of butterfly on open hand", "caption": "Gary Tyler, Fernanda’s Touch, 2025. Quilting fabric, thread and battling. 64in x 68.25in. Photograph: Courtesy of the artist and Grand Rapids Art Museum", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Although Tyler was never formally exonerated, he was freed in 2016 following the supreme court ruling in the 2012 Miller v Alabama case, where the court held that it was unconstitutional to adjudicate mandatory sentences of life imprisonment for juvenile defendants.", "links": [{"text": "unconstitutional", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/law/2014/jun/24/minors-life-sentences-despite-us-supreme-court-ban"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "While serving four decades in the infamous Angola state prison – known as the Alcatraz of the south and currently the largest maximum-security prison in the United States – Tyler began to make quilts to comfort inmates dying in the prison’s hospice. At first reluctant to work with textiles, he soon saw just how valued his creations were. “I saw that I could help the men in the hospice, so it was something that I warmed up to,” Tyler said. “I realized we were doing something that would last for generations in the family. content.article_text:
W ith nearly 2 million people behind bars, America is the global leader in incarceration. When you look at it per capita, we have the highest rate of incarceration of any independent democracy and rank fourth overall in the world, just behind El Salvador, Cuba and Turkmenistan.

Despite these troubling numbers, mass imprisonment is largely invisible. “Our carceral system is something we as a society try to separate out from the everyday,” observes Terra Warren, an associate curator at Grand Rapids Art Museum, Michigan , who alongside curator Jennifer Wcisel brings audiences three solo shows from artists Julie Green, Gary Tyler and Ray Materson. They collectively aim to make us examine more closely just what prisons are doing to our society – and how art can prove transformative to those incarcerated.

In a major feat, Green’s show collects the artist’s work The Last Supper, rarely exhibited in full. This masterpiece took 22 years to complete and comprises nearly 1,000 plates, each depicting the final meal requested by an individual on death row before their execution. Poignantly, many of the plates are simply inscribed with the word “none”, indicating when an inmate opted not to eat a final meal. One imagines it would be hard to find an appetite under such conditions.

In centering breaking bread, a practice that’s a cornerstone of our shared humanity, The Last Supper forces audiences to reckon with the contradictions of a system that at once gives the pleasure of consuming a fine meal, yet also dehumanizes and even puts to death those within its grasp. Additionally, the piece opens space for compassion and understanding by giving us a window into the lives of those who are rarely represented in any meaningful way at all.

“There’s one in particular where a prisoner opted to eat vending machine food with their family,” Warren says, recalling plates that particularly stood put in her memory. “There’s another whose mother was allowed to come in and cook their last meal.”

Some of the plates also underscore the fact that the state will put to death individuals who are not even aware of what’s happening; one plate indicates that an inmate chose to save some of their last meal for later, not understanding that there would not be a chance to ever eat again. “One of the plates details that a person with an IQ of 61 was executed,” said Warren, indicating someone was put to death in spite of serious mental impairments.

D eath row figures prominently in the life of Gary Tyler, an author and artist, who in 1974 was charged with the murder of a white teenager when Tyler was 16 years old. When he was convicted by an all-white jury and sentenced to death, he became the youngest person on death row in the United States. The case was marred by police misconduct, and Tyler is now widely considered to have been wrongfully imprisoned.

Although Tyler was never formally exonerated, he was freed in 2016 following the supreme court ruling in the 2012 Miller v Alabama case, where the court held that it was unconstitutional to adjudicate mandatory sentences of life imprisonment for juvenile defendants.

While serving four decades in the infamous Angola state prison – known as the Alcatraz of the south and currently the largest maximum-security prison in the United States – Tyler began to make quilts to comfort inmates dying in the prison’s hospice. At first reluctant to work with textiles, he soon saw just how valued his creations were. “I saw that I could help the men in the hospice, so it was something that I warmed up to,” Tyler said. “I realized we were doing something that would last for generations in the family. When our patients passed, the quilt was passed into their family, and it was really moving for me.”

As Tyler continued making quilts for dying inmates, he developed a perspective that would later inform his transition to making textile art, and that would help him be able to tell his own story through the intricate quilts that he had made for years as an artist. “You realize that that could be you, and it will be you eventually, you’re just as human as the individual you’re taking care of,” he says. “Being a hospital volunteer was one of the greatest things in my life. I never would have thought that I had the creative gene in me.”

Tyler’s quilts tend to be backgrounded by static colors shot through with rich texture and repeating motifs – flowers in one, abstract tear shapes in another. The scenes they depict are vivid and powerful: a bull smacking over a red table, a man literally struggling under the weight of the world, a child in shackles with their back turned to us.

One work that stands out in Tyler’s mind depicts a moment from the trial, when he was being led away from the courthouse in handcuffs by an escort of police, while a crowd of supporters cheered for him. “I got this surge of energy,” he says. “I wanted to raise my hands in a fist, but I had handcuffs on, with deputies holding my arms, but I still managed to show defiance, that despite what happened I would continue to fight.”

T he Grand Rapids trio is rounded out by a comprehensive museum survey of Ray Materson, the outsider embroidery artist, who developed his signature technique of working with unraveled socks by necessity while serving seven years in prison due to drug addiction.

While boxer shorts and bedsheets could supply Materson with plenty of white thread, socks were of special importance to him, as they gave him the colors that he required in order to create intricate scenes. He would spend hours and hours simply getting the dearly needed materials. “Ray said to me one time: ‘Your biggest enemy in prison is the clock,’” said Warren. “For him to be able to spend days and days in this meditative act was such a saving gesture.”

Materson’s skills quickly became known to the other inmates, who soon began asking him to make embroidery of loved ones or items such as national flags with great symbolic meaning. These pieces gave Materson a purpose and allowed the men he created for to experience a sense of identity and selfhood in a profoundly dehumanizing environment.

Life in prison has stuck with Materson, who to this day sources vintage socks like the ones he used while in jail in the 1980s. “Their nylon has the stretchability that he needs in order to work,” explained Warren. His work tends to depict intense scenes, often derived from the likes of Shakespeare, Ibsen and Chekhov, as well as royalty like Queen Victoria and Catherine the Great. While small, often measuring just 2in x 3in, the works are filled with pathos and are a wonder to behold.

“This show brings a lot of shock at the facts of what’s the reality for a lot of people, but they also bring a lot of hope,” said Warren, sharing her hopes that the art on display can both humanize and inspire, as well as show audiences that artistic creation can be transformative for them too. “Ray was on a track of death through his addiction, but because of art his life turned around into something defined by creativity and giving.”

Julie Green: The Last Supper; Gary Tyler: Rebirth and Ray Materson: Metamorphosis are all at Grand Rapids Art Museum from 3 October 2026 until 24 October 2027 (Green) and 3 January 2027 (Tyler, Materson)

ビックリするほど当たるためIMA御用達の占い師・マコが、12星座の今をタロット1枚で運気予報！フォトグラファー清水はるみによるファンタスティックな星座＆大アルカナのヴィジュアルと共に、明るい未来の指針を毎月前・後半でお届けします。

10月前半に思うこと

「床を拭いて運気を2トーン上げる魔法」

10月に入り、秋風が心地よく部屋を吹き抜ける季節になりました。今回のテーマは「お掃除で開運」です！

​我が家にも文明の利器「掃除ロボット」が鎮座しておりますが、秋の運気を一気にブーストさせたい時に私が絶対に譲れない儀式。それは「手作業の雑巾がけ」です。

​便利家電も最高ですが、自分の手で四つん 這いになって床を丁寧に拭き上げると、嘘みたいにその空間が途端に2トーン明るくなった気がするから不思議！​特に力が入るのが、全ての運気がなだれ込んでくる玄関です。

​ここで登場するのが、前回ご紹介したあの最強アイテム。そう、レモンとローズマリーを煮出した特製ハーブ液！そこに塩を勢いよくぶち込んで（ここ大事！）雑巾を絞り、一心不乱に玄関のたたきを拭き上げるのです。

​邪気を弾き飛ばすレモン、トラウマや停滞感を断ち切るローズマリー、そして強力な祓いパワーを持つ塩。この「開運・三種の神器」をしみ込ませた雑巾で磨き上げると、玄関に溜まった澱んだ気が一瞬で吹き飛び、空間の密度が変わるのを肌で感じます。

​仕上げのポイントはしっかり乾拭きすること！水分を残さないことで、ツヤと良い気がバチッと定着します。

​占いでも運は足元から入ると言いますが、床や玄関を磨くことは、自分自身の土台を整えることそのもの。

​秋の夜長、お気に入りのハーブ塩水で玄関を磨き上げて、明るくなったお家で最高にツイてる秋を迎えに行きませんか？

La actriz de Verity reveló una tierna anécdota familiar y explicó por qué Lionel Messi es “un puente hacia tantas cosas maravillosas”.

Lionel Messi volvió a aparecer en una historia inesperada que llega desde Hollywood. Esta vez, el protagonista indirecto fue el hijo de Anne Hathaway , quien encontró en el capitán argentino la clave para romper el hielo y comenzar una nueva amistad.

La actriz contó la divertida anécdota durante una entrevista realizada en el marco de la promoción de Verity , el thriller psicológico que protagoniza junto a Dakota Johnson y Josh Hartnett .

La pregunta sobre el astro que cambió todo

Hathaway explicó que su hijo estaba conociendo a otro niño, pero ninguno de los dos encontraba la manera de comenzar una conversación. “Los chicos pueden ser tímidos alrededor de otros. Son solo niños y no saben de qué hablar”, contó la actriz al recordar la situación.

Fue entonces cuando decidió intervenir con una pregunta que, inesperadamente, funcionó a la perfección: “¿Te gusta Messi?” . La respuesta fue afirmativa. El otro niño dijo que sí y el hijo de Hathaway rápidamente se sumó: “Me encanta Messi” .

A partir de ese momento, todo cambió. Según relató la actriz, los dos chicos encontraron un punto en común y terminaron convirtiéndose en grandes amigos. Para Hathaway, la historia demuestra el enorme poder que tiene la figura del futbolista argentino incluso entre los más chicos.

Lionel Messi y ¿su guiño? a Harry Potter en su despedida de la selección Argentina

¿Quién es quién en La Odisea de Christopher Nolan?

“ Es un puente hacia tantas cosas. Un puente para tantas cosas maravillosas ” , expresó la actriz al hablar del futbolista.

La actriz lo destacó como embajador

La anécdota surgió después de que Hathaway comenzara a hablar sobre su vínculo con la Argentina.

Durante la entrevista, la actriz recordó también su encuentro con Joaquín Furriel en Shanghái. Ambos coincidieron en 2024 durante un evento de Moncler, marca de lujo de la que son embajadores. En aquella oportunidad, Furriel había aprovechado para hablarle sobre la Argentina e incluso invitarla a conocer el país.

Cuando le preguntaron si el actor había hecho un buen trabajo promocionando nuestro país, Hathaway respondió que la Argentina tiene “tantos embajadores increíbles”. Entre ellos mencionó al polista Nacho Figueras y, naturalmente, al fútbol argentino. “Tienen a su equipo de fútbol entero. Tienen a Messi” , destacó la actriz.

La referencia al rosarino derivó entonces en la particular historia de su hijo, que terminó demostrando de una manera muy sencilla el alcance internacional de la figura del capitán argentino.

También habló de la Argentina

No es la primera vez que Hathaway tiene un acercamiento público con la cultura argentina y latinoamericana.

Durante la promoción de El diablo viste a la moda 2 , la actriz protagonizó junto a Meryl Streep un divertido momento en México al bailar Cómo te voy a olvidar , uno de los grandes clásicos de Los Ángeles Azules.

Ahora, con Verity como nuevo proyecto, volvió a referirse a la Argentina y a algunas de sus figuras más reconocidas. En la misma entrevista, Dakota Johnson también habló de Buenos Aires y contó que visitó la ciudad en varias oportunidades. Josh Hartnett , en cambio, reconoció que todavía no conoce el país, aunque manifestó sus ganas de hacerlo.

content.article_text:
田中久貴による写真展「大廈 The Buildings, Mansions.」が、2026年10月13日から18日まで大阪・心斎橋のギャラリー・ソラリスで開催される。

タイトルの「大廈」とは、中国語でビルや大きな建物を意味する言葉。本作で田中が向き合ったのは、2025年8月の香港だ。地下鉄やトラムを乗り継ぎ、高温多湿の街を歩きながら、建て増しと積層を繰り返す高層住宅や、その窓から突き出すエアコンの室外機、ベランダのない窓辺に干された洗濯物など、都市に刻まれた日常の光景を撮影した。かつて香港のイメージを形づくっていた無数のネオンサインは減少し、九龍寨城は公園となり、啓徳空港もすでに閉鎖されている。田中がカメラを向けるのは、そうした過去の香港へのノスタルジーというより、変貌を続ける都市の現在だ。隙間なく林立する巨大な集合住宅を見上げながら、そのスケールとは裏腹に感じられる「せせこましさ」や、建築の表面から漏れ出す生活の痕跡をモノクロームの画面へと取り込んでいく。

田中はステートメントで、大廈から「冷徹な眼で凝視」される感覚について記している。都市を一方的に観察するのではなく、自らもまた都市から見返される存在として身を置き、そこへ飛び込んでくる「日常としての香港」を受け入れる。その視線の往復から、建築物そのものだけでなく、そこに暮らす人々の存在や時間が浮かび上がる。

本作は2026年、文芸社「写真集大賞」で最優秀賞を受賞。同名写真集『大廈』として9月15日に刊行された。本展では写真集に収められた作品から16点を展示する。

content.article_text:
音楽家・渋谷慶一郎によるポートレート連載「Humanity」第2回。舞台は、渋谷が東京とともに拠点とするパリへ。街で出会い、時間をともにする人々をコンタックスT3で写し出す。モノクロームの柔らかなイメージの中に、パリに生きる人々の飾らない表情がこぼれ落ちる。

写真・文＝渋谷慶一郎

目次

Mae Mei Lapres（マエ・メイ・ラプレ、モデル／ヴィンテージ・コレクター）

Claude Gassian（クロード・ガシアン、写真家）

Justine Emard（ジュスティーヌ・エマール、ヴィジュアル・アーティスト）

Takami Nakamoto（タカミ・ナカモト、Nonotak共同ファウンダー／アーティスト／サウンド・アーティスト）

Noemi Schipfer（ノエミ・シプフェ、Nonotak共同ファウンダー／アーティスト）

Mae Mei Lapres（マエ・メイ・ラプレ、モデル／ヴィンテージ・コレクター）

グッチ時代のアレッサンドロ・ミケーレのミューズで、ルイ・ヴィトン、ミュウミュウなど多くのブランドのランウェイやキャンペーンを制覇しながらパリのクリニャンクールのテナントをDIYして、自分のヴィンテージショップ「MeiMei Vintage」を運営している。マイペースで自分を曲げない、わがままなところが僕と似ている。家で飼っている2羽のオウムにはすっかり懐かれている。

Claude Gassian（クロード・ガシアン、写真家）

この前パリで、今年11月にリリースするアルバム『Thereshold』のジャケットを撮影してもらった。今までにジミヘン、マドンナ、プリンス、パティ・スミスなど数多くのミュージシャンを撮影しているけど、特にミック・ジャガーとデヴィッド・ボウイはパリでは彼にしか撮らせなかったという伝説があるらしい。撮影の日はアシスタントも付けず自分でカメラと照明をイーストパックのキャリーで持ってきて、700枚撮影して颯爽と帰って行った76歳。日本のカメラマンも見習った方がいい。

Justine Emard（ジュスティーヌ・エマール、ヴィジュアル・アーティスト）

10年以上、僕と色んなコラボレーションをしてきたけど、僕が英語を話せるようになったのは彼女のおかげ。最近は大阪万博のフランス館のアーティスティック・ディレクターを務めたり、すっかり偉くなっていて嬉しい。ちなみにアンドロイド・オペラの映像もここ数年は彼女が担当している。フランス人離れした真面目さが面白い時がある。

Takami Nakamoto（タカミ・ナカモト、Nonotak共同ファウンダー／アーティスト／サウンド・アーティスト）

10年くらい前にパリで知り合ったけど、去年から僕の家が近所になったから特に仲良くなってよく家に遊びにくる。時間をかけて仲良くなったから、話しているとリラックス出来て非常に良い。Nonotakの作品が元々好きだからいつか一緒に仕事も出来たらと思う。とか書いているけど、普段は悪いことばかり話しているからここに書けることが少なくて困っている（笑）。

Noemi Schipfer（ノエミ・シプフェ、Nonotak共同ファウンダー／アーティスト）

Takamiと一緒にNonotakをやっていて、彼と同様に家にもよく遊びに来る。この前は「陰謀論とか言われていることは大概、人々の無知によるもので、そもそも世の中陰謀だらけ」ということで意気投合した。タトゥーのデザインもやっていて、それを見た時にNonotakのデザインのエッセンスを見た気がした。

渋谷慶一郎（しぶや・けいいちろう） 音楽家。1973年東京生まれ。東京藝術大学作曲科卒業。2002年に音楽レーベルATAK設立。先鋭的な電子音楽作品からピアノソロ、オペラ、映画音楽、サウンド・インスタレーションまで、幅広い領域で活動を行う。東京とパリを拠点に国内外で作品を発表し、人間とテクノロジー、生と死の境界領域を作品を通して問いかけている。 http://atak.jp/

content.article_text:
写真家・藤澤一の写真展「A Light, A Live, A Life」が、2026年10月9日から18日まで、東京・神宮前のgallery&bar ニニニ・ニーで開催される。藤澤は1994年神戸市生まれ。コロナ禍をきっかけに写真を始め、人物撮影を中心に活動。これまで300人以上を撮影してきたという。本展では、同い年の俳優・大原海輝を約1年間にわたって撮影した作品を発表する。

2人が出会ったのは、藤澤が上京して間もない頃。初めての撮影で大原から掛けられた「人をちゃんと『人間』として撮れる写真家に久しぶりに出会った」という言葉が、今回の展覧会を構想するひとつの原点となった。

藤澤がテーマに掲げるのは、「人を写す」こと。ポートレートに写るのは、その人物の容姿だけなのか。同じ人物、場所、服という条件をそろえても、同じ写真は二度と生まれない。そこには撮影された日の感情や人生の断片、被写体の生き方、さらにはシャッターを切る写真家との関係までが入り込むと藤澤は考える。撮影は、朝5時の激しい雨が降る海から、気温マイナス20度の雪原、ベトナムの街角まで、さまざまな環境で行われた。藤澤は一連の作品について、「写り手と撮り手が剥き出しの命でぶつかり合った、生のエネルギーの記録」と表現する。

被写体となった大原は、俳優として映画、舞台、ドラマ、ミュージックビデオなどに出演する一方、プロデュースや脚本、演出にも活動領域を広げてきた。2025年からは今回の会場でもあるgallery&bar ニニニ・ニーのオーナー代表を務め、異なるカルチャーや表現をつなぐ活動にも取り組んでいる。写真家と俳優という「撮る側／撮られる側」の関係を1年間継続することで、その間に何が写真へ刻み込まれていったのか。「A Light, A Live, A Life」は、一人の人物のポートレートであると同時に、写真を介して向き合った2人の時間を提示する試みとなる。

会期中には藤澤と大原によるトークショーも開催予定。

content.title_original: Bristol Photo Festival 2026 enters the Time Machine
content.article_blocks_json: [{"type": "heading", "text": "Bristol Photo Festival’s third edition creates a palimpsest of past, present and future, explains festival director Alejandro Acín"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In Castle Park, central Bristol, there is a plaque paying tribute to men from the city who joined the fight against fascism in the Spanish Civil War. “It’s always been in my mind,” says Bristol Photo Festival director Alejandro Acín. This year marks 90 years since the Spanish Civil War but, with authoritarian governments and far-right activism rising across the globe, that moment now feels uncomfortably close."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "It is a reminder that the past has a way of shapeshifting into the present, and this idea reverberates through the 2026 Bristol Photo Festival. Themed Time Machine , it includes a show taking place in a cave not far from the park featuring three artists exploring the contemporary resonance of the Spanish Civil War – Anna Jorné, Julián Barón and Natasha Christia. content.article_text:
Bristol Photo Festival’s third edition creates a palimpsest of past, present and future, explains festival director Alejandro Acín

In Castle Park, central Bristol, there is a plaque paying tribute to men from the city who joined the fight against fascism in the Spanish Civil War. “It’s always been in my mind,” says Bristol Photo Festival director Alejandro Acín. This year marks 90 years since the Spanish Civil War but, with authoritarian governments and far-right activism rising across the globe, that moment now feels uncomfortably close.

It is a reminder that the past has a way of shapeshifting into the present, and this idea reverberates through the 2026 Bristol Photo Festival. Themed Time Machine , it includes a show taking place in a cave not far from the park featuring three artists exploring the contemporary resonance of the Spanish Civil War – Anna Jorné, Julián Barón and Natasha Christia. Their work is part of a city-wide programme of exhibitions in which photography is not simply a recording of the past, but an articulation of our non-linear experience of time. Memory of what has been and speculation about the future meet in the present day.

“Often the works that we bring explore historical events but from contemporary approaches, or vice versa, so there’s always this kind of entanglement of time that happens,” Acín notes, adding that Time Machine follows two previous editions focusing on movement (in 2024) and place (in 2021). “We can look at the three editions as almost a trilogy,” he explains.

“Culture this year is more political than ever. We are fighting to keep spaces that allow people to think, talk and look at the world differently” – Alejandro Acín

This year a show by Goa-based artist Akshay Mahajan responds to the British Empire and Commonwealth Collection held in Bristol, drawing on Indian folklore to consider how the ghosts of colonialism still haunt the border between India and Pakistan. Italian photojournalist Giulio Di Sturco’s Anthropocosmos invites viewers into constructed spaces designed by scientists and engineers, meanwhile, to test out space conditions. His images show how humans are preparing for a potential – as yet unrealised – future beyond Earth.

There is also an exhibition presented by Kegham Djeghalian, the son of the late Kegham Avedis Garabet Djeghalian – an Armenian-Palestinian photographer who set up Gaza’s first photographic studio. Djeghalian Senior’s images are a portal to a flourishing pre-Nakba Palestine, which stands in stark contrast to the horrifying images of destruction of recent years. Elsewhere Annie Wang’s Mother as a Creator charts the Taiwanese artist’s journey into pregnancy, through motherhood, and on to the shifting, overlapping terrain she now occupies between her maternal and creative roles.

This edition of Bristol Photo Festival is Acín’s second as director (after a stint as director of education and engagement for the first edition); alongside it he runs IC Visual Lab with co-director Ben GJ Thomas and designer/producer Safia Belhaj. ICVL is based in the middle of the city, in the one-time home of the South African Resource Centre and curator Christine Eyene is drawing on the building’s radical history for an exhibition there, featuring work by George Hallett. An award-winning South African photographer, Hallett was exiled to London in the 1970s and made portraits of anti-apartheid creatives, writers, artists and musicians.

The festival includes a busy opening week from 14 to 18 October, featuring parties, openings and a symposium; it will also include an ‘education weekend’ in its five-week run, featuring masterclasses led by photographers and industry insiders. “It’s about building relationships where participants can continue developing their work,” says Acín.

The 2024 festival was a resounding success. Amak Mahmoodian’s exhibition in it, One Hundred and Twenty Minutes , went on to earn a Deutsche Börse Photography Foundation Prize nomination, while some 40 per cent of those who went to the Bristol Museum and Art Gallery during its run were visiting the institution for the first time. “We had visitors from every postcode in Bristol, so on a local level we had pretty good engagement,” says Acín.

However, since then much has changed in Bristol (and beyond), with arts organisations facing a tougher funding landscape than ever. Bristol Photo Festival consists of curated exhibitions – rather than depending on an open call – which provides an income for some; this puts more financial pressure on the festival, and more onus on partnership. The closure of the Royal Photographic Society’s gallery has also had an impact, as it was previously a key venue – although some new spaces have come on board.

The festival, along with the wider photography community, is also still mourning the loss of Martin Parr in December 2025, a long-term Bristol resident and keen advocate of the programme. “It was very sad,” says Acín. “Martin was part of the board and he was always helpful with contacts, interested and supportive of the festival.” The festival maintains close ties with the Martin Parr Foundation, whose group exhibition Dark Tales: British Documentary Photography and the Gothic will be on show during its run; the popular Books on Photography will also return to MPF on 17 and 18 October.

Acín is open about the difficulties, believing it is important for organisations to speak up about the impact of massive cuts to public arts in the UK, and the loss of access to EU funding post-Brexit. “It’s a reality that’s very palpable, very tangible,” he says. “Culture this year is more political than ever. We are fighting to keep spaces that allow people to think, talk and look at the world differently.”

Bristol Photo Festival takes place from 14 October–15 November 2026. BOP is the weekend of 17–18 October 2026.

Rachel Segal Hamilton is a freelance writer and editor, specialising in photography and visual culture, for art magazines, book publishers, national press, awards, agencies and brands. Since 2018, she’s been contributing editor for the Royal Photographic Society Journal, is a regular writer for Aesthetica and author of Unseen London, published by Hoxton Mini Press.

content.title_original: Restoring the fractured archive: SWANA collective memory at BredaPhoto Festival
content.article_blocks_json: [{"type": "heading", "text": "Held within the wider BredaPhoto Festival, a strand of exhibitions by artists from the SWANA region dismantles flat media-driven narratives to present richer, more nuanced perspectives"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "For decades, the visual vocabulary assigned to the Southwest Asia and North Africa (SWANA) region by the international world of photography has been an exercise in transactional observation. A hyper-visible taxonomy of ruin, anchored in flattened and anonymised rage and grief, manufactures a state of perpetual exception, flattening complex social topographies into spectacles that court Western pity while burying structural truth. Within global institutions, regional image-makers are mined for local authenticity but systematically stripped of political urgency; international editors sanitise symbols of local resistance to satisfy detached audiences, while treating practitioners’ lived experiences as barely compensated raw material."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Yet a slow but steady shift in lens-based practices is gaining momentum, even in traditional and so-called apolitical spaces. Rather than seeking to correct the distorted mirrors held up by so many foreign photographers, or bending to the restrictive mandates of international gatekeepers, an emerging generation of image-makers, researchers, and storytellers is choosing to bypass these institutions, or only engage with them on their own terms. They are constructing what can be termed a “counter-archive”, not as a nostalgic retreat into a static past, but as an intentional, self-authored historical record of perpetual survival towards ultimate liberation."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "This critical reclamation underpins a strand of the exhibitions in the current BredaPhoto Festival, which is themed Our Songs Came Through . Co-curated by Mohamed Somji, Ileana L. Selejan, and Astrid Hulsmann, the biennial explores how individuals and communities find solace and comfort (or “troost” in Dutch) and how intimate imagery and memory can puncture institutional erasure. These questions are key in the SWANA context."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.1854.photography/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/abdulmughni02.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Huda Abdulmughni's work on show at BredaPhoto Festival", "credit": "British Journal of Photography"}, {"type": "quote", "text": "“ This kind of work gives us the tools to crack open a radical collective imagination.” Noor Abed"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Somji’s curatorial approach is characterised by a rigorous push towards self-authored storytelling, honed through his experience programming at Gulf Photo Plus, including at its popular Slidefest evenings. There developing regional practitioners are given the space to express their grievances and interrogate their motivations, away from the Western gaze. Inherited hierarchies of recognition are consistently broken down. But manifesting this dialogue in an exhibition in a Western institution can be challenging."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“When we started talking about this theme toward the end of the last festival, I was skeptical about how easily it could become very kumbaya – a superficial ‘let’s all go into the mountains, cleanse our world, and come back’ approach, while mass killing and active displacement are unfolding in Palestine, Lebanon, Yemen, Sudan, Iran and elsewhere,” says Somji. “We went back and forth on the texts and the selections of artists, work, and more, to make sure the structural, political reality was firmly addressed."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“Through GPP, we’ve spent years building an infrastructure for self-authored stories, because we know the damage of institutional erasure,” he continues. “The artists featured here aren’t just capturing conflict, they are archiving the poetry, the domestic resistance, and the psychological architectures that endure when people insist on surviving on their own terms.”"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.1854.photography/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Also-Video-Still-Noor-Abed-2.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Video still © Noor Abed", "credit": "British Journal of Photography"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.1854.photography/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/This-NoorAbed_00_18_41_06.Still024.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Video still © Noor Abed", "credit": "British Journal of Photography"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Palestinian artist Noor Abed’s specially-commissioned video installation, we walk in our sleep , presents a poetic blueprint of Palestinian realities, for example, subverting the clinical approaches of mainstream media and military occupation. Outsiders’ depictions of Palestine have often relied on the iconography of the barrier – checkpoints, watchtowers, concrete walls, and actively-restricted freedom. This centres the occupier’s gaze, defining Palestinian life entirely by that which restricts it. Abed adamantly refuses this framework."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Working in close collaboration with her family and neighbours, she turns the lens inward to examine how land is claimed, remembered, and mythologised through collective, physical ritual. we walk in our sleep moves through a series of vignettes, showing people whose gestures hover between ancient agrarian labor and contemporary performance art. Synchronised figures moving across open hillsides, the subtle positions of their heads and hands invoke histories that predate violent colonial sketches. Projected in a completely darkened, small room with only a tiny bench to sit on, the film is difficult to categorise; it’s overwhelming, in a way that feels necessary."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Abed was initially inspired to make the film when she noticed people muttering to themselves on the streets of her hometown; after many sleepless nights of contemplation, she connected this phenomenon to something else she had already zoned in on, the sacred space between the living and the dead. Abed believes that the martyrs walk among us."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“For many, many years now, I’ve been contemplating the wide range of rituals around mourning and death, which is something we witness every day,” Abed explains. “In the last few years, it started to become physical. The dead are among us, I truly believe that. So for me, it’s almost like carving into this space, the air around me. It became an exercise of listening to and being close to the martyrs [those who have been unjustly killed].”"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.1854.photography/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Video-Still-Noor-Abed-1.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Video still © Noor Abed", "credit": "British Journal of Photography"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Abed’s work maps a psychological landscape that remains inaccessible to the colonial apparatus; a checkpoint can bisect a road, but it cannot erase the collective memory of a community that has walked, sung, and lived on that land for thousands of years. She refuses to use folklore as mere nostalgia, but positions it as a perpetual tool of survival, demonstrating its inherent political utility. Her lens is patient and meditative, a direct rejection of the high-velocity aesthetic of breaking news stories disseminated in a 24-hour cycle; instead it asserts an invisible, unbreakable network of spatial permanence."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“For me, it’s a work of deliberate digging, of continuous searching – instead of considering the past as framed and fixed,” she says. “Because this is very dangerous, particularly in the context of Palestine. Once the past is turned into mere symbols, there is a risk of not being able to breathe anymore. It becomes empty. And for me, the collective memory is all about the embodied practices, knowledge, our rituals and the visceral connection to our land – whether in joy or in loss, in a funeral for a martyr that turns into celebration.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Abed insists on the preservation of memories, by transforming them and keeping them connected to the present. “To simply lean on the past in this utopian way, with distance, there is no resistance for that in me,” she says. “This kind of work gives us the tools to crack open a radical collective imagination, that gives us both the hope and the means to rehearse liberation. Because there is no future other than liberation.”"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.1854.photography/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/hallak04.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Fouad Hallak’s work on show at BredaPhoto Festival", "credit": "British Journal of Photography"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "While Abed maps the deep roots of connection to the land, Fouad Hallak’s A Mind in the Past, Eyes on Tomorrow addresses the fractured geometries of exile and return. Born in Syria, Hallak fled the country on a migrant vessel to claim asylum in the Netherlands; his work shifts away from diasporic trauma towards an internalised psychogeography. His recent documentation tracks his return to his homeland, in transition following the fall of Assad, capturing the fragile space between historical devastation and actualised hope."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“After the fall of the Assad regime, I noticed that people often looked at what happened in two different ways – some stories were bright, and others were painful,” Hallak reflects. “But these feelings can exist at the same time. When I went back, I was not an outsider. I was part of the story. I see this in the photograph of Khaled, who protested and fought against the regime. He carries his history with him and still moves forward… Before, this possibility did not exist. Now it does. For me, that is hope.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Fascinated by old studio portraiture, and saddened by its disappearance due to war, Hallak created a temporary mobile setup in the streets of Damascus. Inviting residents to have their portraits taken, he constructed a new archive of Syrian presence with his series, Studio Damascus."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“When survival becomes part of everyday life, the simple act of having a portrait taken becomes difficult,” he says. “I believe that having a portrait taken with your family can be a sign of stability. When I direct people in front of the camera, the connection creates a moment in which they can step away from their instability. Studio Damascus explores reunion, memory, belonging, and the human need for stability.” Hallak refuses to flatten the reality of a community navigating a shattered state. “After all these years, I still feel there is a desire to make these realities easier to understand,” he concludes. “I don’t think the problem is misunderstanding. This is what I search for in my practice – a language that comes from human feeling. Something emotional, intimate, and perhaps even spiritual.”"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.1854.photography/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/This-FouadHallak_DSF7988.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "© Fouad Hallak", "credit": "British Journal of Photography"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Meanwhile photographer and filmmaker Fatima Joumaa turns the counter-archive towards the structural realities of South Lebanon (Al-Janoub) and Beirut’s southern suburbs (Dahiyeh). In her intimate project From My Mother’s Novel: Returning to South Lebanon , she weaves images through her mother Layla’s old notes and sketches, creating a meditation on grief, memory, and women as keepers of history. Joumaa combines analogue photography, poetic video essays, and first-hand local testimonies to directly challenge the usual media representations of war."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Whenever life in Lebanon is ruptured – and there have been many compounding crises over the past seven years alone, long before Israel’s current genocidal assault and occupation of the South – global image-makers flood the streets, capturing the immediate violence and debris, the grief and rage, before equally swiftly departing. This high-velocity reportage leaves what Joumaa calls an “after-image” in its wake, a concept she has developed into a series for independent Lebanese magazine The Public Source ."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Shifting her gaze toward the quiet, slow-burning aftermath and complex interiorities that unfold after the intrusive cameras leave, she fights the persistent clichés that reduce entire neighbourhoods and their inhabitants to passive sites of devastation. “I was always aware of how much the image is treated as an extractable resource, whether moving or still,” she says. “And often, when international media or institutions approach us, they want the image because it carries a kind of authenticity – but they want to decide what that authenticity is allowed to contain."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“I have been asked to remove flags, portraits of martyrs, political signs, or anything that might make the image appear too political to them, as if there’s anything that isn’t political,” she continues. “And I refuse to portray my people only as victims.”"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.1854.photography/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/This-FatimaJomaa_FromMyMothersNovel_03.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "From My Mother's Novel © Fatima Joumaa", "credit": "British Journal of Photography"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Joumaa argues these signifiers are at the core of this landscape, not mere additions to it – and that removing them does not render the image more neutral. Quite the opposite. “It produces another complete image, one that is more comfortable for the institution,” she says. “To them, it simply checks a box of exclusivity [paying lip-service to local perspectives] rather than talking about what is fundamentally happening.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "For Joumaa, the Israeli assault on South Lebanon, and its systematic violent occupation and genocidal destruction of almost all of the land in the region, is an everyday reality. She could not return to her village in Janoub to bury her grandmother, as is the reality for many families in South Lebanon. But by integrating first-person local testimonies into her video essays, she ensures that the voices of the community dictate the narrative arc of the work; the record of survival is written in the smallest, most intimate – most often overlooked – pockets of human existence."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Centring the camera on home-bound networks of care, Joumaa suggests that sovereignty is maintained through everyday acts of defiance, not on a grand geopolitical stage. And her insistence on documenting the unseen, foundational rhythms of community forms a natural bridge to Kuwaiti photographer and researcher Huda Abdulmughni, whose work focuses on the ancestral landscape."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.1854.photography/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/this-Huda-Abdulmughni-Nowruz-Sayadeen-2.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "From Nowruz Sayadeen © Huda Abdulmughni", "credit": "British Journal of Photography"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Where Joumaa’s lens operates as an almost forensic instrument within the targeted spaces of her land and people, Abdulmughni focuses on a different kind of survival – one grounded in ecological harmony and collective memory. Abdulmughni’s Nowruz Sayadeen documents the annual fisherman’s New Year on the Iranian island of Qeshm, for example, in which the village’s primary source of income is paused, out of respect for nature’s seasonal bounty. Using both analogue and digital media, Abdulmughni captures the highly-stylised, almost mythical cast of characters populating the shores, including the iconic shushis – figures adorned with white face paint and palm leaves."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "But rather than presenting the figures as exotic subjects, performing in costume once a year, Abdulmughni captures a world that relies on ancestral knowledge of the seas. Depicting traditions passed down through the generations, outside the strict categories preferred by Western ethnography, Abdulmughni’s work demonstrates that regional sovereignty is preserved through seasonal rhythms and ancestral ecological care. But her work also shows that this is also a world increasingly impacted by climate change due to geopolitical conflict, in which the community’s harmony with the earth may be devastated."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The biennial takes a devastating turn to remind us of the stakes raised when gentle rhythms are severed by colonial violence, including a posthumous show by Majd Arandas, A Memorial in Fragments . Arandas’ work brings the viewer face-to-face with the realities of active elimination; born in Gaza in 1994, he was killed in an Israeli airstrike near his home in Deir al-Balah on 01 November 2023. Arandas had long ago been forced to sell his professional camera to survive the Israeli blockade, but continued to document with his mobile phone, and his archive has been retrieved and preserved by his brother."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Somji wanted to honour Arandas’ work and life, but also show the networks of solidarity that surrounded him, and now surround his archive. “Whether it’s a beautiful exchange between Majd and a friend about the plants in his beloved grandmother’s garden, or a photographer friend exchanging cat photos with him, it shows how communities find ways to bond together, and provide solace, despite everything that’s against them, despite the challenges of neoliberal worlds and neo-colonialist regimes,” Somji says."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Arandas’ surviving images testify to what it means to create an archive when your existence is being contested in real-time. But he photographed Gaza with luminous tenderness, his images capturing quiet gestures of affection, subtle exchanges of care, and the warm, amber lights of temporary shelters. His work refuses to let his people be remembered solely by their erasure, insisting instead on the profound beauty and unyielding right to exist that defined their daily survival."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.1854.photography/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/also-Majd-Arandas-dress.jpeg", "alt": "", "caption": "© Majd Arandas", "credit": "British Journal of Photography"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "These exhibitions help make Our Songs Came Through a significant biennale; they also surface the often behind-the-scenes negotiations required to present these images within a Western framework. Organising exhibitions of work by independent SWANA practitioners in a European institution is a change, even in an institution known for pushing the envelope; more than that, it is a linguistic, bureaucratic, and geopolitical battleground. A violent manifestation of this gatekeeping is the European Visa system, for example, which prevented Libyan artist Amera Elnaal from entering the Netherlands to attend her own exhibition."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Our Songs Came Through is an intervention in the contemporary photography landscape, gathering an eclectic group of somehow connected artists to move far beyond the tokenism that often plagues Western institutions’ attempts to showcase art from the SWANA region. Rather than grouping these artists under a banner of shared trauma, it highlights their shared commitment to visual sovereignty, formal experimentation, and archival repair. The artists gathered here demonstrate that, to restore a fractured archive, one cannot simply add more images. Rather, we must fundamentally reinvent the methodology of image-making."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Collectively, the SWANA artists exhibiting at BredaPhoto are dismantling the familiar, flat, media-driven narratives.
