content.article_text:
Held within the wider BredaPhoto Festival, a strand of exhibitions by artists from the SWANA region dismantles flat media-driven narratives to present richer, more nuanced perspectives

For decades, the visual vocabulary assigned to the Southwest Asia and North Africa (SWANA) region by the international world of photography has been an exercise in transactional observation. A hyper-visible taxonomy of ruin, anchored in flattened and anonymised rage and grief, manufactures a state of perpetual exception, flattening complex social topographies into spectacles that court Western pity while burying structural truth. Within global institutions, regional image-makers are mined for local authenticity but systematically stripped of political urgency; international editors sanitise symbols of local resistance to satisfy detached audiences, while treating practitioners’ lived experiences as barely compensated raw material.

Yet a slow but steady shift in lens-based practices is gaining momentum, even in traditional and so-called apolitical spaces. Rather than seeking to correct the distorted mirrors held up by so many foreign photographers, or bending to the restrictive mandates of international gatekeepers, an emerging generation of image-makers, researchers, and storytellers is choosing to bypass these institutions, or only engage with them on their own terms. They are constructing what can be termed a “counter-archive”, not as a nostalgic retreat into a static past, but as an intentional, self-authored historical record of perpetual survival towards ultimate liberation.

This critical reclamation underpins a strand of the exhibitions in the current BredaPhoto Festival, which is themed Our Songs Came Through . Co-curated by Mohamed Somji, Ileana L. Selejan, and Astrid Hulsmann, the biennial explores how individuals and communities find solace and comfort (or “troost” in Dutch) and how intimate imagery and memory can puncture institutional erasure. These questions are key in the SWANA context.

“ This kind of work gives us the tools to crack open a radical collective imagination.” Noor Abed

Somji’s curatorial approach is characterised by a rigorous push towards self-authored storytelling, honed through his experience programming at Gulf Photo Plus, including at its popular Slidefest evenings. There developing regional practitioners are given the space to express their grievances and interrogate their motivations, away from the Western gaze. Inherited hierarchies of recognition are consistently broken down. But manifesting this dialogue in an exhibition in a Western institution can be challenging.

“When we started talking about this theme toward the end of the last festival, I was skeptical about how easily it could become very kumbaya – a superficial ‘let’s all go into the mountains, cleanse our world, and come back’ approach, while mass killing and active displacement are unfolding in Palestine, Lebanon, Yemen, Sudan, Iran and elsewhere,” says Somji. “We went back and forth on the texts and the selections of artists, work, and more, to make sure the structural, political reality was firmly addressed.

“Through GPP, we’ve spent years building an infrastructure for self-authored stories, because we know the damage of institutional erasure,” he continues. “The artists featured here aren’t just capturing conflict, they are archiving the poetry, the domestic resistance, and the psychological architectures that endure when people insist on surviving on their own terms.”

Palestinian artist Noor Abed’s specially-commissioned video installation, we walk in our sleep , presents a poetic blueprint of Palestinian realities, for example, subverting the clinical approaches of mainstream media and military occupation. Outsiders’ depictions of Palestine have often relied on the iconography of the barrier – checkpoints, watchtowers, concrete walls, and actively-restricted freedom. This centres the occupier’s gaze, defining Palestinian life entirely by that which restricts it. Abed adamantly refuses this framework.

Working in close collaboration with her family and neighbours, she turns the lens inward to examine how land is claimed, remembered, and mythologised through collective, physical ritual. we walk in our sleep moves through a series of vignettes, showing people whose gestures hover between ancient agrarian labor and contemporary performance art. Synchronised figures moving across open hillsides, the subtle positions of their heads and hands invoke histories that predate violent colonial sketches. Projected in a completely darkened, small room with only a tiny bench to sit on, the film is difficult to categorise; it’s overwhelming, in a way that feels necessary.

Abed was initially inspired to make the film when she noticed people muttering to themselves on the streets of her hometown; after many sleepless nights of contemplation, she connected this phenomenon to something else she had already zoned in on, the sacred space between the living and the dead. Abed believes that the martyrs walk among us.

“For many, many years now, I’ve been contemplating the wide range of rituals around mourning and death, which is something we witness every day,” Abed explains. “In the last few years, it started to become physical. The dead are among us, I truly believe that. So for me, it’s almost like carving into this space, the air around me. It became an exercise of listening to and being close to the martyrs [those who have been unjustly killed].”

Abed’s work maps a psychological landscape that remains inaccessible to the colonial apparatus; a checkpoint can bisect a road, but it cannot erase the collective memory of a community that has walked, sung, and lived on that land for thousands of years. She refuses to use folklore as mere nostalgia, but positions it as a perpetual tool of survival, demonstrating its inherent political utility. Her lens is patient and meditative, a direct rejection of the high-velocity aesthetic of breaking news stories disseminated in a 24-hour cycle; instead it asserts an invisible, unbreakable network of spatial permanence.

“For me, it’s a work of deliberate digging, of continuous searching – instead of considering the past as framed and fixed,” she says. “Because this is very dangerous, particularly in the context of Palestine. Once the past is turned into mere symbols, there is a risk of not being able to breathe anymore. It becomes empty. And for me, the collective memory is all about the embodied practices, knowledge, our rituals and the visceral connection to our land – whether in joy or in loss, in a funeral for a martyr that turns into celebration.”

Abed insists on the preservation of memories, by transforming them and keeping them connected to the present. “To simply lean on the past in this utopian way, with distance, there is no resistance for that in me,” she says. “This kind of work gives us the tools to crack open a radical collective imagination, that gives us both the hope and the means to rehearse liberation. Because there is no future other than liberation.”

While Abed maps the deep roots of connection to the land, Fouad Hallak’s A Mind in the Past, Eyes on Tomorrow addresses the fractured geometries of exile and return. Born in Syria, Hallak fled the country on a migrant vessel to claim asylum in the Netherlands; his work shifts away from diasporic trauma towards an internalised psychogeography. His recent documentation tracks his return to his homeland, in transition following the fall of Assad, capturing the fragile space between historical devastation and actualised hope.

“After the fall of the Assad regime, I noticed that people often looked at what happened in two different ways – some stories were bright, and others were painful,” Hallak reflects. “But these feelings can exist at the same time. When I went back, I was not an outsider. I was part of the story. I see this in the photograph of Khaled, who protested and fought against the regime. He carries his history with him and still moves forward… Before, this possibility did not exist. Now it does. For me, that is hope.”

Fascinated by old studio portraiture, and saddened by its disappearance due to war, Hallak created a temporary mobile setup in the streets of Damascus. Inviting residents to have their portraits taken, he constructed a new archive of Syrian presence with his series, Studio Damascus.

“When survival becomes part of everyday life, the simple act of having a portrait taken becomes difficult,” he says. “I believe that having a portrait taken with your family can be a sign of stability. When I direct people in front of the camera, the connection creates a moment in which they can step away from their instability. Studio Damascus explores reunion, memory, belonging, and the human need for stability.” Hallak refuses to flatten the reality of a community navigating a shattered state. “After all these years, I still feel there is a desire to make these realities easier to understand,” he concludes. “I don’t think the problem is misunderstanding. This is what I search for in my practice – a language that comes from human feeling. Something emotional, intimate, and perhaps even spiritual.”

Meanwhile photographer and filmmaker Fatima Joumaa turns the counter-archive towards the structural realities of South Lebanon (Al-Janoub) and Beirut’s southern suburbs (Dahiyeh). In her intimate project From My Mother’s Novel: Returning to South Lebanon , she weaves images through her mother Layla’s old notes and sketches, creating a meditation on grief, memory, and women as keepers of history. Joumaa combines analogue photography, poetic video essays, and first-hand local testimonies to directly challenge the usual media representations of war.

Whenever life in Lebanon is ruptured – and there have been many compounding crises over the past seven years alone, long before Israel’s current genocidal assault and occupation of the South – global image-makers flood the streets, capturing the immediate violence and debris, the grief and rage, before equally swiftly departing. This high-velocity reportage leaves what Joumaa calls an “after-image” in its wake, a concept she has developed into a series for independent Lebanese magazine The Public Source .

Shifting her gaze toward the quiet, slow-burning aftermath and complex interiorities that unfold after the intrusive cameras leave, she fights the persistent clichés that reduce entire neighbourhoods and their inhabitants to passive sites of devastation. “I was always aware of how much the image is treated as an extractable resource, whether moving or still,” she says. “And often, when international media or institutions approach us, they want the image because it carries a kind of authenticity – but they want to decide what that authenticity is allowed to contain.

“I have been asked to remove flags, portraits of martyrs, political signs, or anything that might make the image appear too political to them, as if there’s anything that isn’t political,” she continues. “And I refuse to portray my people only as victims.”

Joumaa argues these signifiers are at the core of this landscape, not mere additions to it – and that removing them does not render the image more neutral. Quite the opposite. “It produces another complete image, one that is more comfortable for the institution,” she says. “To them, it simply checks a box of exclusivity [paying lip-service to local perspectives] rather than talking about what is fundamentally happening.”

For Joumaa, the Israeli assault on South Lebanon, and its systematic violent occupation and genocidal destruction of almost all of the land in the region, is an everyday reality. She could not return to her village in Janoub to bury her grandmother, as is the reality for many families in South Lebanon. But by integrating first-person local testimonies into her video essays, she ensures that the voices of the community dictate the narrative arc of the work; the record of survival is written in the smallest, most intimate – most often overlooked – pockets of human existence.

Centring the camera on home-bound networks of care, Joumaa suggests that sovereignty is maintained through everyday acts of defiance, not on a grand geopolitical stage. And her insistence on documenting the unseen, foundational rhythms of community forms a natural bridge to Kuwaiti photographer and researcher Huda Abdulmughni, whose work focuses on the ancestral landscape.

Where Joumaa’s lens operates as an almost forensic instrument within the targeted spaces of her land and people, Abdulmughni focuses on a different kind of survival – one grounded in ecological harmony and collective memory. Abdulmughni’s Nowruz Sayadeen documents the annual fisherman’s New Year on the Iranian island of Qeshm, for example, in which the village’s primary source of income is paused, out of respect for nature’s seasonal bounty. Using both analogue and digital media, Abdulmughni captures the highly-stylised, almost mythical cast of characters populating the shores, including the iconic shushis – figures adorned with white face paint and palm leaves.

But rather than presenting the figures as exotic subjects, performing in costume once a year, Abdulmughni captures a world that relies on ancestral knowledge of the seas. Depicting traditions passed down through the generations, outside the strict categories preferred by Western ethnography, Abdulmughni’s work demonstrates that regional sovereignty is preserved through seasonal rhythms and ancestral ecological care. But her work also shows that this is also a world increasingly impacted by climate change due to geopolitical conflict, in which the community’s harmony with the earth may be devastated.

The biennial takes a devastating turn to remind us of the stakes raised when gentle rhythms are severed by colonial violence, including a posthumous show by Majd Arandas, A Memorial in Fragments . Arandas’ work brings the viewer face-to-face with the realities of active elimination; born in Gaza in 1994, he was killed in an Israeli airstrike near his home in Deir al-Balah on 01 November 2023. Arandas had long ago been forced to sell his professional camera to survive the Israeli blockade, but continued to document with his mobile phone, and his archive has been retrieved and preserved by his brother.

Somji wanted to honour Arandas’ work and life, but also show the networks of solidarity that surrounded him, and now surround his archive. “Whether it’s a beautiful exchange between Majd and a friend about the plants in his beloved grandmother’s garden, or a photographer friend exchanging cat photos with him, it shows how communities find ways to bond together, and provide solace, despite everything that’s against them, despite the challenges of neoliberal worlds and neo-colonialist regimes,” Somji says.

Arandas’ surviving images testify to what it means to create an archive when your existence is being contested in real-time. But he photographed Gaza with luminous tenderness, his images capturing quiet gestures of affection, subtle exchanges of care, and the warm, amber lights of temporary shelters. His work refuses to let his people be remembered solely by their erasure, insisting instead on the profound beauty and unyielding right to exist that defined their daily survival.

These exhibitions help make Our Songs Came Through a significant biennale; they also surface the often behind-the-scenes negotiations required to present these images within a Western framework. Organising exhibitions of work by independent SWANA practitioners in a European institution is a change, even in an institution known for pushing the envelope; more than that, it is a linguistic, bureaucratic, and geopolitical battleground. A violent manifestation of this gatekeeping is the European Visa system, for example, which prevented Libyan artist Amera Elnaal from entering the Netherlands to attend her own exhibition.

Our Songs Came Through is an intervention in the contemporary photography landscape, gathering an eclectic group of somehow connected artists to move far beyond the tokenism that often plagues Western institutions’ attempts to showcase art from the SWANA region. Rather than grouping these artists under a banner of shared trauma, it highlights their shared commitment to visual sovereignty, formal experimentation, and archival repair. The artists gathered here demonstrate that, to restore a fractured archive, one cannot simply add more images. Rather, we must fundamentally reinvent the methodology of image-making.

Collectively, the SWANA artists exhibiting at BredaPhoto are dismantling the familiar, flat, media-driven narratives. They remind us that history is not merely written by the victors, even those who wield a camera; it is unobtrusively and persistently preserved in the songs that survive, the rituals that map, and the communities which refuse to be forgotten. The fractured archive is reimagined as a site of radical agency, resistance, and complexity, and it honours the nuances of daily human survival.

BredaPhoto Festival 2026, Our Songs Came Through, is open until 25 October https://bredaphoto.nl

Farah-Silvana Kanaan is a Lebanese-Italian-Dutch writer, editor and creative consultant based between Amsterdam and Beirut. Her words have appeared in Kinfolk, Dazed, Rolling Stone, Discontent, Middle East Eye, and elsewhere.

content.article_text:
写真家パスカル・グレコによるトークイベントが、渋谷の404 Not Foundにて開催される。グレコは、ビデオゲーム内の仮想空間を写真として捉える「インゲームフォトグラフィー」に取り組んできた写真家。建築や都市、風景を撮影してきたこれまでの視点をゲーム空間に持ち込み、仮想世界のイメージと現実の風景写真、記憶との関係を問い続けている。

本トークイベントは、9月25日から10月4日まで同会場で開催される写真・映像展「PHOTOGRAPHING THE VIRTUAL IN THE AGE OF ANIMA LUDENS」にあわせて企画されたもの。会期中の10月2日には、写真家の小林健太に、編集者、クリエイティブディレクター、アートプロデューサーの後藤繁雄を迎え、グレコを交えた三者によるトークを行う。デジタル環境のなかで「写真を撮る」とはどのような行為なのか。グレコの実践を写真史・現代写真の文脈から読み解き、現実と仮想空間を横断する今日の写真の可能性を考える機会となる。

なお本展では、グレコがビデオゲームの風景を撮影した写真シリーズ「Photography, Video Game, Landscape」に連なる作品と映像作品を紹介する。ぜひ会場に足をお運びいただきたい。

404 Not Found（東京都渋谷区桜丘町1-4 Shibuya Sakura Stage SHIBUYA SIDE 4F）

2026年10月2日（金）

18:30〜20:00

content.article_text:
写真家・早川勝夫による「pendulum Art Book & Fine Art Photo Exhibition」が、11月13日から18日まで、せんだいメディアテークで開催される。雪によって風景が消え、再び現れる現象を通して、写真が持つ「固定する力」と、絶えず変化する世界との関係を見つめるプロジェクトだ。

「雪に風景が消え、また現れる」。本作の起点にあるのは、雪がもたらす圧倒的な美しさと、視界を奪われる恐ろしさだ。降り積もる雪は風景の輪郭を覆い、距離や奥行きを曖昧にする。さらにホワイトアウトのなかでは、そこに存在しているはずのものさえ見えなくなり、「何を見ているのか」という知覚そのものが揺らぎ始める。

早川はこうした雪の性質と、一瞬を一枚の像として定着させる写真の性質を対置する。確かな輪郭を持っていた世界が白の中へ溶け、やがて再び姿を現す。その「見える／見えない」「存在する／消失する」という往還を、早川は「存在の還流」と呼ぶ。タイトルの「pendulum＝振り子」も、固定と揺らぎ、可視と不可視、存在と消失のあいだを行き来する運動に由来している。

本展の特徴は、展示とアートブックを一つの作品として構想していることにもある。アートブック『pendulum』は全270ページに62点を収録し、半透明のトレーシングペーパーを採用。ページをめくると、前の写真の気配を残しながら次の像が透過して現れ、重なり、そして消えていく。「見る」「触れる」「めくる」「待つ」という行為そのものによって、写真に内在する時間を体験させる仕掛けだ。

一方、会場では62点の作品から32点を選び、5つの章の流れを再構成するように大判プリントで展示。アルポリック板にマウントした作品をフローティングフレームに収め、壁面に固定されながらもわずかに「浮遊」するような状態を生み出す。ページをめくることで時間の中に現れるアートブックと、身体を移動させながら空間の中で像と向き合う展示。二つの異なる体験を往還することで、「pendulum」の世界を立ち上げる。

アートブック『pendulum』は2026年12月、Inunicより刊行予定。

content.article_text:
Star Wars | Jon Watts, da trilogia Homem-Aranha do MCU, vai dirigir primeiro filme de nova trilogia

Escrito por Simon Kinberg, nova trilogia é especulada como o próximo capítulo na Saga Skywalker.

(Imagens: Getty Images, Lucasfilm)

Os Skywalker estão de volta. Segundo o THR , Jon Watts vai dirigir um novo filme de “ Star Wars “, que será o primeiro de uma nova trilogia.

O cineasta Simon Kinberg vem trabalhando na criação de uma nova trilogia para a Lucasfilm desde o final de 2024. Ao que tudo indica, o projeto deve servir como o próximo capítulo na chamada Saga Skywalker, que é composta pelos nove filmes entre “Star Wars: Episódio I — A Ameaça Fantasma” e “Star Wars: Episódio IX — A Ascensão Skywalker”. Rey Skywalker, a jovem Jedi interpretada por Daisy Ridley na trilogia lançada pela Disney entre 2015 e 2019, deve retornar na trilogia de Kinberg.

Para Watts, trata-se na verdade de seu segundo projeto da franquia. Em 2024, ele cocriou e dirigiu parte da série “Skeleton Crew”, que acompanha um grupo de crianças que se perde pela galáxia tão, tão distante em uma aventura à la “Os Goonies”. Watts é mais conhecido também por dirigir a trilogia principal de filmes do Homem-Aranha de Tom Holland para a Marvel, incluindo “Homem-Aranha: Sem Volta Para Casa”.

Segundo o relato, o projeto ainda está em desenvolvimento e não recebeu sinal verde da Disney, embora pareça ser o projeto mais avançado em produção pela Lucasfilm depois de “Star Wars: Starfighter”, estrelado por Ryan Gosling e dirigido por Shawn Levy. A princípio, também seguem em desenvolvimento os filmes de Sharmeen Obaid-Chinoy, focado em Rey Skywalker, e o de James Mangold sobre a origem da Ordem Jedi.

“Star Wars: Starfighter” tem estreia prevista para 27 de maio de 2027, coincidindo com o aniversário de 50 anos da franquia.

content.article_text:
作品集 『日高理恵子 空間と、自然光と、絵と、』 がtorch pressより刊行される。本書は、画家・日高理恵子が自然光のもとで作品を展示した2つの展覧会を鈴木理策が撮り下ろした写真と、美術評論家の椹木野衣が書いた2つの文章で構成された作品集。

この本の始まりは、2023年多摩美術大学 アートテークギャラリーで開催された「家村ゼミ展 2023 空間に、自然光だけで、日高理恵子の絵画を置く」。本展ではひとつの空間に、ほぼ1作品を自然光の中で展示するという試みがされた。この体験をもとに、2025年に同ギャラリーで退任展が開催された。この2つの展覧会を、自身の作品で常に「見ること」について問いかけてきた写真家・鈴木理策が撮り下ろした写真で構成。椹木はその体験を自身の身体、知覚とともに、単に文章を寄せるにとどまらない、実験的な2稿で日高の絵画に、展示に、対峙した。

本書のデザインを須山悠里が手がけ、展覧会を須山自身が見、体験し、感じたことを、いわゆる展覧会の記録という枠組みを超えてまとめあげている。「本」という場で、絵画と、写真と、文のそれぞれ自立し、かつ関係しあう、他に類を見ない一冊が生まれている。

また、9月26日より小山登美夫ギャラリー京橋・六本木の2会場で、 「日高理恵子」展 が同時開催される。会期中は トークイベント も予定されており、10月10日には椹木野衣、10月31日は鈴木理策と須山悠里がゲストに招いて日高とのトークが行われる。日高の絵画と空間を味わいながら本を手に取り、作品世界を堪能したい。

Sabrina Carpenter e Margaret Qualley se juntam a Tom Holland em cinebiografia de Fred Astaire

Filme terá direção de Paul King, de "As Aventuras de Paddington".

(Imagens: reprodução)

A próxima grande cinebiografia de Hollywood está tomando forma. Sabrina Carpenter e Margaret Qualley se juntaram a Tom Holland no elenco do filme sobre a vida de Fred Astaire (via Deadline ).

Qualley interpretará Adele Astaire, irmã de Fred, e Carpenter interpretará Ginger Rogers. Fred e Adele foram grandes estrelas da Broadway e do West End em Londres antes de Fred Astaire se tornar uma das maiores estrelas do cinema ao lado de sua parceira de dança, Rogers. O desdobramento ocorre quase cinco anos depois de Holland revelar, pela primeira vez, que lideraria o projeto.

Paul King, de “As Aventuras de Paddington”, dirige o filme e assina o roteiro junto a Steven Levenson, baseando-se no livro “The Astaires: Fred & Adele”, de Kathleen Riley. Riley também atua como consultora de roteiro e história no filme, que tem ainda o apoio de Ava Astaire McKenzie, filha de Fred; seu filho, Tyler McKenzie, é consultor e coprodutor do filme.

Ainda não há previsão de estreia para a cinebiografia de Fred Astaire.

content.article_text:
JFK Jr. is back on television, everyone is wearing straight-leg jeans, and carrying an analog camera around your neck is no longer seen as an affectation of hipster-dom. It’s 2026, and the perpetually online masses are sighing as they romanticize how great it must have been to be young in 1996, with lives yet to be suffocated by social media. But what so much of this current 1990s nostalgia overlooks is the anger and restlessness of those growing up in that era of seismic change—their cynicism and disdain for capitalist avarice and their inviolable distrust of corporations, just before everything was corporatized. To the then-teenage Gen Xers who were becoming adults in the 1990s, “selling out”—now a shameless imperative—was an unforgivable sin.

It was this moral compass that, in 1994, led a twenty-two-year-old musician from Montreal named Melissa Auf der Maur to reject the Smashing Pumpkins frontman Billy Corgan’s initial attempt to recruit her to Hole following the death of their bassist Kristen Pfaff. So skeptical was Auf der Maur of success and celebrity that she hesitated for a while aboutjoining the band—abrasively antiestablishment but signed to a major label—until Courtney Love (affectionately) bullied her into acquiescence. A photography student at Concordia University, Auf der Maur had taught herself how to use a camera by photographing herself nude in her bedroom from different angles. At most, she thought that she would end up a working photographer with some involvement in music. “That’s sort of what I assumed my job would be in life, because it seemed more realistic than a musician,” she told me.

Despite her modest ambitions, she went on to spend nearly a decade traveling and performing on stages across the world as the bass player for Hole and the Smashing Pumpkins, two of the biggest alternative rock bands of the 1990s. Determined to continue her photography, she became a relentless documentarian of her life, relying on a 28mm point-and-shoot Nikon and the occasional one-hour photo lab whenever she could find one in between tour stops. During that period, she took nearly ten thousand photographs, most of which have languished in her attic in upstate New York—until now.

Aperture Magazine Subscription

This September, the exhibition Melissa Auf der Maur: My ’90s Rock Photographs opened at the Art Gallery of Ontario (AGO), where two hundred photographs from her personal archive will be on display. The show comes on the heels of Auf der Maur’s memoir, Even the Good Girls Will Cry: A ’90s Rock Memoir , published this past March. In 2020, when Auf der Maur began working on her memoir, she revisited the photographs for the first time and was struck by how she’d managed to capture an almost inconceivable dissonance in time and culture, back when the massive public fame that rock musicians experienced hadn’t entirely been subsumed by corporate machinery and the demands of the platform economy. “Even though from the outside my generation looked like disaster and self-destruction, on the inside it was so delicate and human,” she said. “These were armies of misunderstood people taken hostage by a corporate, digitizing, greedy world.” Youth culture was undergoing a “brutal loss of innocence,” she added. “It was death, death, death, plus fame, fame, fame. I was shocked by their shock.”

So much 1990s nostalgia overlooks the anger and restlessness of those growing up in an era of seismic change.

In tour buses, hotel rooms, dressing rooms, sets, stadiums, and arenas—where thousands of people convulsed around her electric presence onstage—Auf der Maur photographed her life as a musician and the people in it with a raw spontaneity and irreverence. In a hazy self-portrait, she curls her lip in a mock come-hither expression, ginger ringlets cascading around her face, as she’s playfully jostled by Love, a tender moment between two girls—except that they happen to be members of one of the most successful bands in the world. Behind her, an arm attends to a drooping frond, which we now know will be set on fire, since Auf der Maur snapped this selfie avant la lettre on the set of the photoshoot for the cover of Hole’s album Celebrity Skin (1998), which features the band posed against a conflagrant tree. The infamous blazing billboard and palm trees of Hole’s “Malibu” music video also make an appearance in an off-hand behind-the-scenes photograph of the band on set (the fires were all real).

In a photograph dated 1999, a disheveled Love lounges on a tarmac in an anonymous location while a plane idles in the background. Tinted a toxic green, the picture seems to have been taken at some ungodly hour—could be midnight, could be morning. Such is life for musicians on the road. Auf der Maur captures her bandmate in a rare moment of vulnerability, the belligerence of her onstage (and offstage) persona set aside in favor of what Sophie Hackett, AGO’s curator of photography, calls Love’s “playfulness, quietude, and tenderness.” Here, Love looks a little drowsy: cigarette in hand, headphones on, flip-flopped, rummaging in her handbag, exuding an air of unguarded exhaustion.

Sometimes painterly, sometimes full of mischief, Auf der Maur’s photographs treat both the musicians and their fans—and the relationship between them—with a deep compassion, revealing the human and fallible faces of what was a generation-defining phenomenon. “Because the corporate greed of the ’90s music scene was so fast rising, I was also capturing the magic while it still lasted,” she said. To those of us who have only ever known fandom dictated by algorithms, overpriced concert tickets as Amex exclusives, and self-portraits referred to as “selfies,” the photographs are proof that there was, in fact, a brief moment in time when you could be famous but still have the freedom to revel in all your ugliness, both internal and external; when your imperfections, filth, and mess were not meant to be swept away but were proof of a full life while it was being lived. But that was 1996. Thirty years later, in Auf der Maur’s own words, “Our world is on fire, and our minds are melting.”

This article originally appeared in Aperture No. 264, “Stop Time,” under the column Redux.

content.article_text:
Jurandir Filho , Rogério Montanare , Thiago Siqueira e Fernanda Bermoltz conversam sobre a trajetória brilhante de Meryl Streep . Existe alguma atriz maior que ela? Dona de uma carreira extraordinária, recordista de indicações ao Oscar e responsável por algumas das atuações mais marcantes da história do cinema, ela é simplesmente a GOAT! Mas, entre tantos personagens inesquecíveis, qual é o MELHOR filme de Meryl Streep?

Neste episódio do RapaduraCast , revisitamos toda a trajetória dessa lenda de Hollywood! Dos primeiros sucessos aos grandes clássicos, passando por “Kramer vs. Kramer”, “A Escolha de Sofia”, “Dúvida”, “As Pontes de Madison”, “O Diabo Veste Prada”, “Mamma Mia!” e tantos outros. Relembramos suas maiores atuações, os prêmios, as transformações, as curiosidades e os momentos que fizeram dela uma das artistas mais respeitadas de todos os tempos.

content.article_text:
Exhibition of the week

Turner prize Kira Freije creates a waste land peopled by Rodinesque ghosts in the machine, Simeon Barclay meditates on masculinity, Tanoa Sasraku takes on big oil and Marguerite Humeau gets lost in wonderland in the most exciting Turner prize in years. MIMA, Middlesbrough, from26 September until 29 March

Also showing

Korea A survey of 2,000 years of Korean art, belief and philosophy – but will it be as big as Bayeux? British Museum, London, from 1 October until 31 January

Fail We May, Sail We Must Artists from Salvador Dalí to the 18th-century British painter George Romney star in another eclectic dip into artist Glenn Brown’s impressive collection. Brown Collection, London, until 7 August

Mark Wallinger: Circling the Square Paintings and a film from the Turner prize winner, that explore abstraction and the vitality of nature with a nod to Dylan Thomas. Paul Stolper Gallery, London, until 24 October

William Kentridge: A Nicely Built City A new animated film by this artist who takes drawing into new dimensions gets its world premiere. Goodman Gallery, London, until 7 November

Image of the week

Goons in the military fatigues and wraparound shades beloved of ICE agents ride around in a clown car – a pretty clear comment on contemporary US. Elsewhere a solitary figure amid the ruins of Stonehenge is overwhelmed by the universe – are we now lost in in cosmic speculation? Welcome to the abstract, humorous yet deeply unsettling world of Nicole Eisenman. Read our review here .

What we learned

101-year-old art warrior Ce Roser has had an amazing life

Sophie Calle has stalked people, posed as a hotel maid to get into rooms and filmed her mother’s last breath in the name of art, but she has no regrets

Dutch sculptor Magali Reus reimagines rubbish into vast versions of sardine tins and fishing lures

A new Magritte exhibition showcases his surrealist brilliance and his occasional trash

The Greek PM has said a deal to return Parthenon marbles could still be reached

Beverly Buchanan’s ramshackle mini barns memorialise the survival of enslaved people

after newsletter promotion

Rachel Kneebone’s porcelain sculptures are edgy and marvellous

Masterpiece of the week

An Elderly Man as Saint Paul by Rembrandt, probably 1659

You can see he’s wearing archaic garments and has religious trappings that identify him as the early Christian Paul, but all that slips your mind compared with this man’s incredibly real, suffering face. Paul, who set out some of the Church’s most severe views on matters including sexuality, doesn’t usually come across as anything like as doubtful or hesitant as this pensive soul. He is surrounded by the shadows of evening, or night, or death, and in his eyes you see a world of cares and regrets. Rembrandt has no respect for the conventions of art or storytelling that would make this a picture of Paul and allow us to move on after recognising that: instead he wants you to be shocked into recognition of the human predicament. You are held by this face, dragged behind the painting, into the man’s mind or soul or whatever we call the essence of the human. Nothing else, for Rembrandt, is worth making art about. National Gallery, London

content.article_text:
Apesar do esforço do elenco, longa reduz o trauma de sua protagonista a um mistério pouco envolvente e desperdiça a tensão do confinamento numa base polar.

Uma estação de pesquisa isolada no gelo é o cenário ideal para um longa de crime e investigação. A distância de qualquer ajuda e a necessidade de continuar dividindo espaços com um possível agressor poderiam alimentar o suspense e tornar a convivência insuportável. “ Antártida ” aproveita bem pouco dessa situação. À medida que a narrativa se concentra em identificar o responsável pelo estupro de Inês (Marina Ruy Barbosa), a personagem perde presença, e o trauma passa a servir quase exclusivamente à movimentação do mistério.

A subcomandante Elisabeth (Andrea Beltrão) surge como a figura responsável por assumir a investigação, interrogando os possíveis culpados enquanto o roteiro apresenta segredos e novas situações de violência entre os integrantes da base. A gravidade dessas descobertas, porém, não encontra uma construção dramática à altura. Trata-se de revelações sobre pessoas que o filme mal nos permitiu conhecer, sem desenvolvimento suficiente para que as descobertas provoquem surpresa ou mexam com a percepção do público.

O roteiro de Cláudia Jouvin tenta ampliar a denúncia reunindo diferentes manifestações de abuso e machismo que se acumulam e prejudicam o aprofundamento. O passado de Marina (Leandra Leal), por exemplo, é significativo por se tratar de outro caso de abuso cujo agressor também está na base, mas recebe uma atenção desproporcionalmente pequena diante do peso que poderia ter. Os diálogos procuram compensar essa pressa explicando os conflitos e as intenções, como se deixar a mensagem clara substituísse o impacto de sentir as consequências de fato.

O caso de Inês se mostra ainda mais problemático ao vermos a personagem sendo mantida distante e enclausurada enquanto os demais discutem o crime — ela deixa de conduzir a perspectiva sobre o que lhe aconteceu. Outros personagens falam por ela, e a narrativa acompanha essas conversas com mais interesse do que acompanha seu estado emocional. A situação por si só já poderia expor a maneira como uma vítima é privada de autonomia mesmo por quem afirma ajudá-la, mas o filme pouco explora essa possibilidade, e a investigação prossegue sem que sua ausência se torne uma questão.

Mesmo com essa prioridade, o mistério também não se sustenta com firmeza. A demora em considerar as câmeras de segurança, seguida da falta de iniciativa para obter as imagens, é apenas um exemplo do esforço do roteiro para adiar respostas. Romances acessórios e novas ameaças acrescentam desvios a uma trama já sobrecarregada, e nada chega a tornar a busca mais intrigante.

Algo que se destaca é a recriação da neve e da paisagem polar, que convence na maior parte do tempo. A direção de Bruno Safadi, contudo, tira pouco proveito desse cenário. A câmera foca quase a todo momento no registro das atuações, sem nos permitir conhecer a base ou sentir o desconforto de compartilhar aqueles espaços. A montagem acentua essa distância ao interromper conversas intensas com imagens externas do gelo — transições repetidas que funcionam como meras pausas genéricas entre acontecimentos, sem intensificar a sensação de confinamento.

O elenco ainda se esforça para encontrar algo humano no material, sobretudo Andrea Beltrão, Leandra Leal e Lázaro Ramos. Já Marina Ruy Barbosa sustenta Inês mesmo com o espaço progressivamente reduzido. Apesar de consistentes, as interpretações não conseguem criar sozinhas a continuidade e o peso emocional que faltam às cenas. Surge uma sensação estranha de acompanhar bons atores tentando dar vida a figuras que o roteiro mantém vazias.

Com a pretensão de discutir a violência contra a mulher, “Antártida” organiza sua narrativa de um modo que enfraquece a própria denúncia. Já como um filme whodunnit, falta força ao mistério e, acima de tudo, capacidade de usar a ambientação e o isolamento a favor da tensão. Todos querem descobrir o que aconteceu com Inês, mas o filme mal se preocupa em perguntar como ela está.

content.article_text:
A new exhibition and the THEA space in Groningen, Netherlands, use art to think through technology and human experience, explains curator and director Roosje Klap

Last year the Nooderlicht Biennale was themed Machine Entanglements and, including exhibitions by 75 artists across the northern Dutch city of Groningen, explored “how we now live, eat, sleep, dream and even date through technology,” says Roosje Klap, director of Nooderlicht, the platform for photography and lens-based media. The shows in one venue, THEA, focused on extraction – the “ugly monster” which makes technology, as Klap puts it – and, working in the building, she was called to reception one day. “There was this guy, maybe about 55, and he was very emotional because he had seen all this for the first time,” she explains.

“He had known about it, but this was the first time he had really seen it. That was very important for me, very touching, but then he asked, ‘Is there any hope? Because I don’t see any hope, only sadness and terrible feelings’. And that’s when I started to wonder, what’s the way out? There must be a way out, how can we escape, or what’s the antidote?” That insight led to the latest exhibition at THEA, Thinking Hands , which explores how embodied knowledge endures in our ever-more technological age.

Curated by Klap with Musoke Nalwoga, Thinking Hands includes both still and moving work, and finds quirky, thought-provoking twists on the theme. There’s Paul Kooiker’s series Talking Hands , for example, a playful look at body language, and there’s Martina Bacigalupo’s found series Gulu Real Art Studio – a series of studio portraits, in which the heads had been clipped out of the image to make passport photos. Removing the face as a point of focus, Gulu Real Art Studio throws the attention on the sitters’ hands and postures, and what they express.

Andi Gáldi Vinkó’s Sorry I Gave Birth I Disappeared But Now I’m Back explores the deeply embodied experience of early motherhood, a time in which the baby is technically separate but is often ‘joined at the hip’; Martha Rosler’s Semiotics of the Kitchen, from the generation before Gáldi Vinkó, rethinks cookery skills as enforced, internalised physical socialisation. Laure Prouvost’s Taking Care (Love letter to a fellow art work) depicts the artist as art handler, talking to a viewer as if he or she is a painting or object; Requiem for an Exit by Kvam/Oldereid shows an eerie armless robot, whose disembodied projected face and AI-generated voice speak of genocide and human displacement.

“All the thinking that is somehow stored within the body, all the knowledge that isn’t necessarily in the head, that’s what makes us human.” Roosje Klap

Klap takes me on a virtual tour, walking me through the space via her laptop; we’re 300 miles apart but she’s warm and funny, cracking jokes through cyberspace. “All the thinking that is somehow stored within the body, all the knowledge that isn’t necessarily in the head, that’s what makes us human,” she smiles, turning the laptop back to herself and reflecting on how instinctively we now use technology. And photography, of course, is part of that process.

“The apparatus is part of the body, and the decision to make that photo – yes or no – is also an embodied decision,” Klap muses. “I think it is really a mind/body-correlative decision, and I feel that’s very much at the basis of what’s at stake now [as technology expands], because we are taking ourselves out of that whole system.”

And her lively engagement with technology is important because, as well as being director of Noorderlicht, Klap is now Cultural Development Lead at Niemeyer. The Niemeyer is a former tobacco factory now being developed into a public culture and tech hub and THEA has some 8000 square metres of space in it, spread over three floors; THEA is backed by the Mondriaan Fund and support from the City of Groningen, and its mission is to explore the impact of technology via art and culture. The project is a two-year startup so far but, says Klap, she’s “here to stay”, and she is co-developing THEA with Rosa Wevers, an independent curator and senior researcher in Art & Technology at Hanze University.

THEA is also developing alongside the other initiatives at the Niemeyer, which include projects such as the AI Factory; part of an EU-backed network of projects using AI to help research healthcare and agriculture, the AI Factory aims to rethink the technology with privacy, security, and digital sovereignty in mind. “The AI Factories are being put into place as alternatives to big tech, so they are interesting and important,” says Klap. “But that’s where THEA is important too.

“That work is all happening in computers; we can help make it more visible. We can also be a critical little sister to Big Brother and the tech bros. THEA and the tech companies [which are moving into Niemeyer] are an integral part of each other.”

In fact THEA is named after a rebellious female figure; Theodora Niemeyer was the daughter of tobacco company founder Theodorus Niemeyer but, rather than pursuing the bourgeois life into which she was born in 1912, went to the Hague and became a painter. She used her inheritance to create an art fund. “I wanted to honour her, and so the programme is divided into three areas,” says Klap. “It’s a combination of making, doing and talking about art, so there’s art and technology; care and technology, which includes symposia and critical thinking; and make and technology, which for example includes hackerspace.”

THEA will be a key venue for the Noorderlicht Biennale next summer, which will be themed PLAY; the theme suggests latitude to explore computer games and gaming culture, and while Klap – who will be artistic lead – is keen to embrace these forms, she’s also thinking less literally. She wants to include Debi Cornwall’s Necessary Fictions / Model Citizens , for example, which explore Hollywood film tropes and their impact on people’s perceptions, the stereotypes which inform our reactions without us being consciously aware of them.

As before the biennale will be spread over six or seven locations across Groningen, both the city and the wider province; Klap was born in Amsterdam and studied in the Gerrit Rietveld Academie, but moved to Groningen two years ago and says it’s a traditionally radical city. “Groningen is known as the red heart of the Netherlands,” says Klap, who I interviewed shortly before far right clashes in The Hague. “Something I find really great here is that I don’t have to explain to politicians that culture is important for society.”

Thinking Hands is on show at THEA, Groningen until 01 November noorderlicht.com/en/whats-on/thinking-hands

content.article_text:
渋谷のアートブック書店、東塔堂にて原田直宏の写真展「2」が開催される。

本展では、2009年から2011年にかけて撮影された東京の道行く人々を撮影した作品「Drifting」と、2018年から2021年にかけて、東京の道で魚をファッションモデルのように撮影した「Tokyo Fishgraphs」の２つのシリーズの作品を展開。どちらも前作のセレクションで選ばれなかった未公開写真の中から、新たに選ばれた写真を中心に展示が構成されている。

写真展の「2」というタイトルには、続編の意味が込められており、初作と続編の関係性、時間を経て選び直されたイメージ等、普段取り上げられることの少ないアートブックの続編が出来上がる経緯や意味を考察できる内容となっている。2つの旧作の未公開写真を通して、アートにおける「続編」とは何かを考える機会となるだろう。

会期中にはアーティストトークも予定されており、これまでのアーティスト活動、制作のきっかけ、海外出版社との仕事等について語られる。

content.article_text:
“I t’s like a film set. Like it’s not real,” the bemused Uber driver says as we pass through a succession of silent rural villages washed with milky sunlight. He’s right: signs of human life are weirdly absent during our windy journey through the Alentejo. I’m making my way to Ai Weiwei’s secluded farm, nestled deep in the Portuguese countryside, where arguably the world’s best known living artist has quietly lived for the last six years.

When I arrive, I am ushered inside a vast cathedral of a building, a replica of Ai’s erstwhile, and controversially demolished , studio in Shanghai. The space is cavernous. It’s gridded by huge wooden columns and its dizzyingly high ceilings are webbed with beams. There is no artwork on the walls, nor are there any obvious signs of production or activity.

“People say, what is this building for? For what? Fuck that. Maybe it’s for nothing,” Ai tells me with a shrug. “It’s empty. And emptiness, people cannot accept.”

Ai has been busy filling other vacant spaces: I’m visiting him to chat about the unveiling of his latest work, Mushrooms, this year’s Neil Balnaves Tallawoladah Lawn Commission outside Sydney’s Museum of Contemporary Art. Characteristically epic, elliptical and urgent, this installation is 40 metres in length, and consists of 500 identical cast iron sculptures of combat helmets on an elevated platform. The title alludes to the visual rhyme between mushroom caps and the shape of the helmets – as well as the fungal associations with decay, death and the fragility of life, brutally exposed by armed conflict.

“Curiosity” and “boredom” generally shape Ai’s creativity, and the origins of this particular commission are “very simple”. In 2015, Ai began work on Human Flow , his documentary on the migrant crisis for which he and his team travelled to 23 countries. The process of producing this film led him to reflect more deeply on the causes of these perilous mass movements across the globe: war – or more specifically, the mechanics and munitions involved in contemporary warfare.

“I studied for two years to understand the military, arsenals, who designs bombs, and how they are used. Then, when Russia threatened Ukraine and Ukraine asked for help from Germany, the German chancellor offered them 5,000 helmets . I laughed,” Ai says. “I thought, wow, that’s interesting. So, at the beginning of the conflict, you can say Germany or Europe did not understand the nature of the war.”

Last year, Ai also visited Ukrainian soldiers on the frontline four times. He scrolls through his iPhone and shows me pictures and footage he took during his time there: Ai being taught how to use a rifle, the troops sporting uniforms he had embroidered with motifs of sunflowers. He plans to use these clips in an upcoming film.

But he is keen that I do not simply see these experiences and this background as research for the new MCA piece. “I never prepare my life so I can make an artwork – or create artwork for my life,” he says. Mushrooms was also shaped by its future home, “a beautiful location” that he has visited several times, with a dramatic view of the Sydney Opera House. That interested him too: “That building represents rational, peaceful enjoyment … but at the same time we have to re-announce that there are wars going on and peace is essential for any civilised society.”

His choice of words – “re-announce” – is striking. Throughout our conversation, over green tea, Ai seems despairing about a collective and cold amnesia about the parlous state of our geopolitics; if not amnesia, our deliberate refusal to truly engage with the doomed state of our world. “We cannot be blind, we cannot say I don’t know the situation,” he says. “You know the situation and you just pretend you don’t know it.” When speaking about the genocide in Gaza, he seems, too, deeply concerned about the lack of connectedness within modernity, our failure to understand that “if injustice happens to one person, it happens to the whole of humanity as well”. Much of his art, not least his trip to the battlefields of Kharkiv , seems an attempt to reestablish a connection and commitment to other human beings, however difficult and dangerous that might be.

Can art play some role in offering him hope about the future of humanity? No, he says, typically pugnacious and plain speaking: “Art today is very corrupted – 90% of what we see in most institutions, or in so-called artistic circles, I think is just garbage. Real art questions the existing order. Art is not about representing so-called beauty, but rather to question the existing judgment about everything in politics, in life, in personal relations, in individual judgment – but this kind of art is never encouraged. People want you to behave, want you to be a nice guy, pleasant, cheerful, enjoying your life. And so most work we see in the museums is very decorative and sentimental, rather than having any relations to human struggle and our reality.”

The Chinese word for mushroom is 蘑菇 or mógū, a term often associated with slowness, delay and dawdling. While our discussion regularly returned to Ai’s dissatisfaction with the tardy pace of societal and institutional progress, the conversation itself was leisurely. Despite describing himself as “the most interviewed human being” and claiming to have been interviewed “more than 1,000 times”, he is generous, fleetingly mischievous – and often startlingly wise. I’m curious, after Mushrooms, where his interests might take him next. But his existence is not so teleological: he has no “goals”.

“The only thing we should try to do,” he says, “is live a life which can naturally capture the light.”

Ai Weiwei’s Mushrooms is free to visit now on the Tallawoladah Lawn at the Museum of Contemporary Art in Sydney

content.article_text:
Jason Statham protagoniza boas cenas de ação, mas o roteiro se acomoda em personagens previsíveis e intrigas que tornam cansativa uma simples vingança.

Jason Statham construiu uma carreira sustentando histórias de ação banais com sua presença, apostando no porte físico e na segurança com que interpreta homens capazes de enfrentar qualquer adversário. “ Código: Vingança ”, porém, depende tanto dessa familiaridade que é praticamente incapaz de distinguir seu protagonista dos personagens anteriores do ator. Statham ainda convence, mas está cercado por personagens e conflitos que repetem a fórmula sem encontrar muito o que fazer com ela.

O protagonista da vez é Cole Reed, um veterano das Forças Especiais e ex-policial de Nova York que trabalha como motorista e segurança particular. O assassinato do seu empregador numa emboscada o coloca em uma busca por vingança que envolve um navio utilizado para o tráfico humano. A base remete bem à franquia “Duro de Matar” , com essa combinação de um homem preparado para o combate e os adversários concentrados em um espaço delimitado. Porém, o roteiro complica o que poderia ser simples, adicionando conspirações, traições e revelações sem desenvolver as pessoas envolvidas o suficiente para tornar as descobertas interessantes.

O passado militar de Reed e sua tradição familiar na polícia existem para reafirmar a competência e os princípios que a própria presença de Statham já sugere com facilidade. Isso acaba não trazendo ao protagonista algo que, de fato, o torne diferente de tantos outros personagens do ator. Também é notável a ironia (para dizer o mínimo) de ver que a morte do chefe bilionário parece mobilizá-lo bem mais do que a situação das vítimas de tráfico. O crime serve muito mais para estabelecer a crueldade dos adversários, enquanto a vingança permanece presa à perda do patrão.

Não é surpresa que o restante do elenco receba pouquíssimo espaço para compensar as limitações. Annabelle Wallis interpreta uma personagem com possibilidades ligadas à sua família, mas sem desenvolvimento suficiente para ser mais que um mecanismo de roteiro. Surgem outras figuras previsíveis, além de diálogos sem muita personalidade que acrescentam informações sem aumentar o interesse pelo conflito. Essa fragilidade pesa ainda mais nos intervalos entre as lutas, quando o longa depende justamente das relações e da investigação para manter a atenção.

Nas cenas de ação, a execução finalmente encontra alguma força no material. O diretor Jean-François Richet conta com vários filmes de ação no currículo, incluindo “Herança de Sangue” e o mais recente “Alerta Máximo” . Richet é competente ao filmar e montar os confrontos com clareza e preservar o impacto dos golpes, além de explorar bem a capacidade física de Statham. As sequências são sangrentas, com algumas figurando entre as mais satisfatórias dos trabalhos recentes do ator. São momentos que demonstram como o clichê pode funcionar quando há cuidado em sua realização.

A escassez desses respiros pesa ainda mais porque as relações, a investigação e tudo o mais que não é luta não funcionam. Não é necessário preencher os 95 minutos com combates, mas as sucessivas explicações e cenas esticadas não constroem tensão suficiente, fazendo o longa parecer arrastado mesmo com a curta duração. Para um filme que precisava apenas deixar Statham fazer o que faz de melhor, “Código: Vingança” sofre até para seguir a própria receita.

content.article_text:
A-POC（エイポック）とは、A Piece of Cloth＝「一枚の布」の意味。1998年に三宅一生がパリで発表したA-POCは、新しい概念で服作りのプロセスを変革し、時代を見つめながら進化を遂げてきた。そうした思想を受け継ぎながら、異分野や異業種との協業によって新たな可能性を探るA-POC ABLE ISSEY MIYAKE（以下、A-POC ABLE）が、東京・南青山の店舗を移転リニューアルし、9月4日、同じフロム・ファースト・ビル内に、国内最大となる3フロアの旗艦店「A-POC ABLE ISSEY MIYAKE / AOYAMA」をオープンした。

撮影＝今津聡子 取材・文＝IMA編集部

目次

ファッション写真とは違うアプローチで

テクノロジーが進化しても「手」が主役

伝えることもデザインの一部

ファッション写真とは違うアプローチで

新設されたギャラリー空間「A-POC SPACE」は、A-POC ABLEが共鳴するアートやデザイン、テクノロジー、伝統芸能など、さまざまな領域のクリエイションが発信する場所となる。そのオープニングを飾るのが、パリを拠点に活動する写真家・梅本健太による 「PORTRAITS：HANDS」展 である。

A-POC ABLEと梅本の取り組みは今回が初めてではない。きっかけとなったのは、梅本が長年取り組んできた花のシリーズ《FLŌRA》だった。

梅本の作品に惹かれたA-POC ABLE ISSEY MIYAKEデザイナーの宮前義之は、2022年に一時帰国した梅本と初めて対面する。その後パリでも交流を重ね、2024年には《FLŌRA》を起点に「TYPE-VIII Kenta Umemoto project」が実現した。

梅本が新たに撮り下ろした花のイメージと、A-POC ABLE独自のSteam Stretch技法を掛け合わせ、写真をそのまま衣服に転写するのではなく、互いの表現をぶつけ合いながら未知のアウトプットへと変換していった。

「手を動かしながら、抽象的なイメージを少しずつ形にしていきました。梅本さんとのやりとりはジャズセッションのような感覚でした」と宮前は振り返る。最初から完成形を描くのではなく、それぞれがアイデアを投げ、受け取り、また返す。予定調和ではない瞬発力こそが、協業の醍醐味だったという。

そして今回、宮前が梅本に投げかけたのは、さらにシンプルな依頼だった。「ブランドが大切にしている思想を、ファッションフォトとは異なるアプローチで表現したい」。より普遍的なテーマと向き合うことによって、梅本がそこからどんな表現を生み出すのかを見てみたかった。

《FLŌRA》の次に浮かび上がったキーワードは、「手」のポートレイトだった。

テクノロジーが進化しても「手」が主役

「PORTRAITS：HANDS」展風景

A-POCという言葉から、私たちは最先端のテクノロジーを連想する。コンピュータープログラムによって一枚の布の中に服の構造を織り込み、素材と技術の可能性を拡張してきたその方法論は、確かに未来的だ。しかし宮前は、そのイメージだけが先行することへの違和感も抱いていたという。

「私たちが大切にしていることは、いつも“手”の感覚なのです」

素材に触れ、その感触から何かを感じ、試し、考え、つくる。どれほどテクノロジーが進化しても、その出発点には人間の身体と手がある。それはA-POC ABLEに限らない。伝統工芸、建築、アート——異なる領域で新しいことに挑み続ける人々にも、それぞれの「手」がある。

今回、梅本がカメラを向けたのは、横尾忠則をはじめ、A-POC ABLEと関わりを持ち、同時代を生きるさまざまな分野の表現者たちだ。写されるのは顔と手。そこでは「手が顔であり、顔もまた手である」かのように、一人の人間の存在と、その人が何をつくり、どのように世界と関わってきたのかが二つのポートレイトによって浮かび上がる。

「花に続く何かを考えた時に『人物』が出てきたんです。同時代に生きている人、何かを創造している人」。梅本はそう発想したという。

宮前も即座に共感した。「創作というのは一人では成り立たない。A-POC ABLEはさまざまな方と一緒に考え、手を動かしながらものづくりを続けています。お互いが共鳴することで、また次の創造へとつながっていく。そうした連なりを伝えたいと思った時に、『ポートレイト』『手』というキーワードはふさわしかった。服を着た人を見せるのではなく、そこにいる人と、その人の「手」を主役にしたかったんです。

素材を触って、インスピレーションをつかんで、ものが生まれていくのがものづくりの本質です。分野は違っても、新しいことに挑戦をしている人たちがいる。私自身、そういう人たちから多くのインスピレーションを受けています。そういう人たちの存在や、その「手」から生まれるものを伝えることが大切だと思っています」

彼らが身につけているのはA-POC ABLEの服だが、写真の中でプロダクトが主役になることはない（どころか、ほとんど写っていない写真も多い）。服を見せるためではなく、さまざまな表現者の「手」が連なることでそこには写らないストーリーが立ち現れる。広告的なキャンペーンフォトとは異なる方法で、A-POC ABLEが何を考え、何を大切にしているのかといった思想を伝える試みでもある。

その思想は、プリントにも貫かれている。梅本はデジタルとマニュアルな工程を行き来しながら、意図的にズレや偶発性を取り込む。完全に制御するのではなく、手を介することで生じる予測不能な出来事を受け入れ、そこから新しい質感を探していく。それは、緻密なプログラムとフィジカルな揺らぎを共存させてきたA-POC ABLEのものづくりとも響き合う。

左から宮前義之、梅本健太

「人選は、身近にいる関係性がある人たちから始まりました。多くは表現者です。普遍的なテーマなので、タイムレスに残るものをと考え、私なりに新しい印刷方法を取り入れました。UVプリンターを使用し、一枚一枚手作業でオリジナルのプリントを作っています」。そう語る梅本の作品からは、手、ポートレイトというありきたりな被写体ながら、見たことのないビジュアルが生まれている。

伝えることもデザインの一部

写真とファッション。テクノロジーと手仕事。精密さと偶然性。一見相反するものを分けるのではなく、その間にある領域から新しいものを生み出す。そこに両者の共通する姿勢がある。

そして「PORTRAITS：HANDS」は、新しいA-POC SPACEの最初の展覧会でもある。

宮前がこの場所に期待するのは、完成した商品を届けるだけの店舗ではない。スマートフォンの画面では伝わらない素材の質感やスケールを身体で感じて体験する。さまざまな対話を通じて、その背景にあるストーリーを知る。「一枚の布」の可能性を探究しながら、宇宙や医療、建築、工芸、アートといった異分野の知性と接続する。そこで生まれた会話が、また次のクリエイションへと連なっていく。

A-POC ABLE ISSEY MIYAKE / AOYAMA店内

A-POC ABLE ISSEY MIYAKE / AOYAMA店内

A-POC ABLE ISSEY MIYAKE / AOYAMA店内

「つくることだけではなく、それをどう相手に届けるかまでがデザインの仕事だと思っています。写真を通してどう伝えるかを考えることも、デザインの一部です。ファッションの世界だけを見ていても、新しいものはなかなか生まれない。一枚の布ができるまでにも、その背景にはさまざまな技術や知恵があります。だから写真に限らず、宇宙や医療など、一見ファッションとは遠くにある分野の人たちとも出会い、考えや技術を結びつけてみる。そこから、自分たちだけでは想像できなかったものが生まれることを大切にしています。

このA-POC SPACEはスマホの画面だけでは伝わらないことを、実際にここに来て感じてもらえる場所にしたい。ブランドの背景にある人や技術、ものづくりのプロセスまで含めて、体験してもらいたいんです」。宮前は、服のその先を見ている。

三宅一生もまた、さまざまな領域の表現者たちと交流し、互いに刺激を与えながらクリエイションを育んできた。その精神を受け継ぐように、A-POC SPACEは、人と人、異なる領域が出会い、まだ名前のない何かが生まれるための場所になろうとしている。

衣服とは、人間の身体に最も近い存在である。だからこそ、テクノロジーがどれほど進化しても、その中心にいるのは人間なのだ。新しい場所の最初の物語は、「手」から始まった。

「PORTRAITS：HANDS by KENTA UMEMOTO」

A-POC ABLE ISSEY MIYAKE / AOYAMA「A-POC SPACE」（東京都港区南青山5-3-10 FROM-1st）

2026年9月4日（金）〜10月28日（水）

11:00〜20:00

無休

無料

https://www.isseymiyake.com/blogs/a-poc_space/18780

梅本健太 パリを拠点として活動している日本人写真家。明治大学在学中に大学の講義で写真と出会い、その後、日本の伝統的な着物の会社や資生堂の化粧品のスティルライフの撮影を始める。ビューティー、ボタニカル、ランドスケープへと興味の対象は広がり、インスピレーションの源泉である日本の浮世絵や漫画の独特な色使いから影響を受け、写真と絵画的な表現を融合させた独自の作風を発展させている。

宮前義之 A-POC ABLE ISSEY MIYAKE デザイナー。1976年東京生まれ。2001年 三宅デザイン事務所に入社し、三宅一生が率いたA-POCの企画チームに参加。その後ISSEY MIYAKEの企画チームに加わり、2011年から2019年までISSEY MIYAKEのデザイナーを務めた。2021年にスタートしたブランドA-POC ABLE ISSEY MIYAKEでは、エンジニアリングチームを率いて、A-POCの更なる研究開発に取り組む。

content.article_text:
F rantically and even stroboscopically over-energised, this big new movie from DreamWorks about best friends for ever seems to me another example of exhausting AI-type content production in animation. You could make the same argument against plenty of live-action films of course, but it is in animation that this kind of soulless blitzkrieg tends to predominate. Forgotten Island is over-controlled and over-determined, a movie that never, or hardly ever, takes its pedal from the metal, never takes a breath or a moment to let its characters come to life. At times it seems to be aping the world of Japanese anime, but without its sense of character or capacity for calm.

The story, weirdly reminiscent of The Hangover of all things, is set in the Philippines in the pre-social media 90s. Jo, voiced by R&B star HER, is a lonely and super-imaginative teen always in trouble at school; like Moana she has a wise grandma who guides her to her ancestral destiny and has captivated Jo with stories of her culture and identity – stories of the forgotten island of Nakali. Jo makes friends with similarly lonely Raissa (Liza Soberano) who like Jo is smart but with a much more focused sense of academic discipline.

Their alliance is pledged and a friendship bracelet woven, but as the years go by, poor Jo winds up with a loser’s job in a fast food joint, whereas Raissa feels guilty about leaving Jo behind as she heads for college at Caltech in the glamorous world of America. (The moment when she tells Jo she is leaving – effectively breaking up with her – is a rare moment of silence in which real emotions emerge and something is recognisably at stake.) But it is now that Jo discovers a mystical portal into the magical forgotten island of Nakali and semi-accidentally makes Raissa tumble down through this portal with her; they awaken 12 hours later to discover they have already done things here of which they have no memory and need to find out what. They also need to discover the portal which will take them back.

This Hangover-style amnesia facilitates a quest narrative, in the course of which they meet a goofy pal in the form of a wacky shapeshifting dog called Raww (Dave Franco) and a scary batibat, or memory demon, resembling Jabba the Hutt called Batiba (Jenny Slate) to whom they may have to surrender precious memories in return for freedom. They also encounter the terrifying figure of Manang (Lea Salonga) who, like Batiba may have relatable vulnerabilities that we don’t yet appreciate. And so it continues, developing and resolving with algorithmic efficiency. It leaves you with a strange sense of emptiness.

content.article_text:
CREATIVE CLASS PHOTO EXHIBITION「CCPE」が、2026年9月25日から27日まで東京・杉並のstudio behind by sceneryで開催される。

「CCPE」は、デジタルクリエイティブ領域で活躍するクリエイターから直接フィードバックを受けられるオンラインスクール「CREATIVE CLASS supported by iDID」のフォトディレクションコースから生まれた初の合同写真展。同コースでは、写真家／ビジュアルディレクターのshuntaroがマスターを務めている。

今回参加するのは、アルファ／Alfa、Chiharu Kodama、Nenpa_、Syuheiinoue、木村洋達、トム・イシカワ、中村和貴、間宮真介の8名。会場となるのは、shuntaro率いるクリエイティブスタジオbird and insectの撮影スタジオ、studio behind by sceneryだ。

展覧会の中心となるのは、受講生それぞれが企画から装丁まで一貫して制作したオリジナル写真集。完成した写真を壁面に並べるだけでなく、一冊の本として写真を編集し、ストーリーを構築するところまでを作品として提示する。来場者は実際に写真集を手に取って閲覧できる。

さらに、それぞれの写真集が持つ世界観を会場空間へと展開。セレクトされた写真のパネル展示も行い、本という二次元のメディアと展示空間を往来しながら作品を体験できる構成となる。会場ではオリジナルグッズや写真集の販売も予定している。

content.article_text:
写真家YUTARO SAITOによる展覧会「72 CLUB TOUR」が、2026年9月18日から10月2日まで、東京・板橋のCOPY CENTER GALLERYで開催されている。

SAITOは2021年より、「NOT PLASTIC FASHION」をコンセプトに高齢者のファッションを撮影してきた。衣服がイメージとして大量に流通する現代において、彼がカメラを向けるのは、その背後にある身体と個人の時間だ。高齢者の装いを通して、「着る」という日常的な行為のなかに蓄積された記憶や習慣を掘り起こしている。

本展は、新たに刊行される写真集『72 CLUB CALENDAR』に合わせ、国内主要ブックフェアでの販売と全国各地での展示を行う巡回プロジェクト。同書は、これまでNOTEやFASHIONSNAPなどで発表してきた高齢男性へのファッションインタビューに、未発表作品を加えて再構成したものだ。

特徴的なのは、高齢者の装いが持つ「機能性」に着目していること。『72 CLUB CALENDAR』自体も、一般的な写真集にとどまらず、カレンダーであり、写真集であり、さらには展示物でもあるという複数の機能を併せ持つ。本展では同書とともに、高齢男性を写したポートレート作品や衣服、「NOT PLASTIC FASHION(2030)」シリーズからポスター作品を展示する。

流行や新しさが絶えず更新されるファッションの世界に対し、長い年月をかけて身体になじみ、生活の一部となった服は何を物語るのか。SAITOの写真は、装うことを表層的なスタイルとしてではなく、一人ひとりが生きてきた時間や身体の記録として捉え直している。

content.article_text:
O ne man and his dog have an amazing adventure in this survivalist drama starring Brad Pitt, from screenwriter Cameron Alexander and director David Ayer, for which the first and last words of the title have been carefully chosen to signal a mix of sentimentality and thrills. It’s an entertaining anthro-canine-mance, with man and dog relating to each other on a deep level … kind of like Owen Wilson in Marley & Me , only without Jennifer Aniston, or Bernie Winters and Schnorbitz, only without the devastating melancholy.

Pitt, who last worked with Ayer on the second world war action thriller Fury , plays a US military special forces veteran called Belmont, tough, self-reliant and laconically good-humoured in the classic Pitt manner, now spending his retirement roaming the breathtaking remote landscape of Alaska in his seaplane. He is accompanied by his beloved service dog Odin, or Odey (played by four different German shepherds), who saw action with Belmont in various fuzzily imagined flashback combat sequences. Odin took retirement with Belmont and is now his best and only pal. Whether or not Belmont ever had a human partner is never revealed.

Their lives together look heavenly, but a heartstoppingly dramatic event means that Belmont must make an extraordinary journey across rough and hostile terrain, on foot, during which he must look after Odin and Odin must look after him. And the dog is no mere passenger in this ordeal; at one stage Odin gets into a stare-out contest with a digital bear, and a mano-a-mano fight with some digital wolves. Visual effects work, however top-drawer it is, always slightly undermines the feeling of real jeopardy, which here is otherwise expertly maintained. Among the humans they encounter is a grizzled old former goldminer played by JK Simmons (channelling Walter Huston), and Anna Lambe as a young woman who fatefully enters the story at its very beginning.

The idea of a man and a dog having no one in this world but each other is an engagingly bittersweet idea; as well as calling up the hardihood of Jack London, it speaks of loneliness and companionship at the same time. Yet weirdly, Belmont is not unlike Pitt’s stuntman character Cliff Booth in Tarantino’s Once Upon a Time in Hollywood, living in a trailer all on his own except for his loyal pitbull Brandy, a dog which can go into terrifying attack mode on a prearranged signal. (Belmont has the same setup with Odin.) Booth and Brandy are Mr Hyde to Belmont and Odin’s Dr Jekyll.

As for Pitt himself, his acting chops are tested when he has to sob and then laugh with joy when it looks wrongly as if Odin has been fatally wounded – but extravagant emoting is not why we love him. Heart of the Beast is a bit cheesy and the final moments will test your credulity, but Pitt is the right guy in the right film.

content.article_blocks_json: [{"type": "heading", "text": "As Aperture moves to the Upper West Side, and puts a renewed focus on reaching out, executive director Sarah Meister reflects on its ‘tentacular’ past and future"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Nothing says “killing it” like buying real estate in an outlandishly expensive culture-rich metropolitan hub. Aperture, the nonprofit publisher of sleek photobooks and the esteemed magazine, has done just that, purchasing and settling in a new permanent home that’s just opened to the public."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The 74-year-old organisation now occupies two floors of a New York City building dating back to 1886, refurbished by architecture practice Levenbetts (which was also behind the Queens Museum and five New York Public Libraries). “Because it was a residential building, it has an intimacy to it,” says Aperture’s executive director Sarah Meister, and the ground-floor entrance boasts street-level visibility to appeal more widely to passers-by, not just to photography devotees. (“Serious photographers will find you on the fourth floor of a side street in Chelsea,” Meister notes.)"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Aperture’s new home is on the Upper West Side, which might seem unexpected given the centripetal force of New York’s downtown art scene. But “trendy arts neighbourhoods… move with fashion,” Meister reasons. As Aperture moves to the Upper West Side, and puts a renewed focus on reaching out, executive director Sarah Meister reflects on its ‘tentacular’ past and future

Nothing says “killing it” like buying real estate in an outlandishly expensive culture-rich metropolitan hub. Aperture, the nonprofit publisher of sleek photobooks and the esteemed magazine, has done just that, purchasing and settling in a new permanent home that’s just opened to the public.

The 74-year-old organisation now occupies two floors of a New York City building dating back to 1886, refurbished by architecture practice Levenbetts (which was also behind the Queens Museum and five New York Public Libraries). “Because it was a residential building, it has an intimacy to it,” says Aperture’s executive director Sarah Meister, and the ground-floor entrance boasts street-level visibility to appeal more widely to passers-by, not just to photography devotees. (“Serious photographers will find you on the fourth floor of a side street in Chelsea,” Meister notes.)

Aperture’s new home is on the Upper West Side, which might seem unexpected given the centripetal force of New York’s downtown art scene. But “trendy arts neighbourhoods… move with fashion,” Meister reasons. By contrast, Aperture’s new neighbours are institutions such as the American Museum of Natural History and the New York Historical, and Central Park is just a stone’s throw away. They – and it – aren’t going anywhere.

Moreover, the singularity of the real estate gives it cachet. Meister points out that “it has 140-year-old load-bearing masonry, and it just has a great feel to it”, and Aperture was able to make the purchase through funding from private individuals such as Judy Glickman Lauder and Jon Stryker, as well as grants from New York State Council on the Arts and the New York City Department of Cultural Affairs.

“ It’s not a white box, and it never will be.” Sarah Meister

Inside the entrance – and past a Majestic Photobooth – the bookstore features Aperture’s output, which includes four issues of the magazine plus 12 books per year, and a backlist which unfurls as far back as the mid-1960s. It also features a pop-up collaboration with Dashwood Books, New York City’s de facto photobook purveyor; founder David Strettell will present a savvy selection of titles to sit alongside Aperture’s publications, and some of his knowledgeable staff will move uptown. “It’s just a smarter way of being,” Meister says, “rather than us trying to do what they do, because they do it so well.”

Aperture will host book launches in the shop, including for a new monograph by Elle Pérez, and for the Catherine Opie edition of The Photography Workshop Series; the Aperture PhotoBook Club will also create an opportunity for follow-up discussions. The shop features some lighthearted collaborations on merch too – there are Vik Muniz printed umbrellas, for example, and placemats printed with images from Stephen Shore’s American Surfaces . There are also baseball caps and tote bags, branded with the Aperture logo.

“There’ll be a handful of things in the store in collaboration with artists or people whose design sensibility we really respect,” Meister enthuses. “So we hope you come in for the books and the magazine, but there will be other fun things to buy too.”

The building’s two levels – one is half below street-level, and one is half above – give visitors views into key work areas, providing a behind-the-scenes peek into Aperture’s activities. The magazine team, the production team, and the book team are visibly present. “You can see in, and we’re happy about that. I think it’s going to give us a new understanding of our audience,” Meister says. Staff are encouraged to sit at a table in the bookstore, and listen and talk to people walking by.

The building also features a dedicated gallery space and the inaugural exhibition, which was curated by Meister, spotlights photographers who have been integral to depicting New York City, including Diane Arbus, Tina Barney, Dawoud Bey, Awol Erizku, Lee Friedlander, Nan Goldin, Deana Lawson, and Carrie Mae Weems. There’s a print loaned from the Robert Frank Foundation; some artists made new 8x10s.

Temporary exhibitions will generally be on view in the space for six to eight week stretches, though Meister says “we don’t want to become too rigid”. That ethos will run through the shows too, with most works leant on a picture rail on a shelf, rather than hung, leaving the original exposed brick undisturbed. “That lack of preciousness is very intentional,” Meister explains. “A little bit of informality feels like a nice thing. Our wall text is going to be printed on an 11×17 sheet with magnets on a beautiful little metal panel: very simple.”

In the longer term, Aperture is working with artists to develop different configurations for the space, allowing each individual to use it in their own way. “It’s not a white box, and it never will be,” Meister affirms, adding that Alex Webb, Dionne Lee, and Angélica Dass will be showing there in future.

Aperture will run public events in the gallery, with a series of conversations “between pairs of people who either know one another or one another’s work well”. Stephen Shore and Lucy Gallun, curator in the Department of Photography at the Museum of Modern Art , will speak together on 03 October, for example, then Gillian Laub and Jil Weinstock, director of Baxter St, on 14 October; Coreen Simpson and Rujeko Hockley, curator at the Whitney Museum of American Art , will be in conversation on 21 October. Aperture will also continue to organise large-scale touring exhibitions.

Aperture also offers an educational program, with online curricula offered free of charge to public school teachers and kids. As Meister says: “Somebody once described Aperture as tentacular, which I love – not just because it rhymes with spectacular! It captures the breadth of what we do.”

Aperture, 380 Columbus Avenue, New York, NY 10024 aperture.org

Sarah Moroz is a Franco-American journalist and translator based in Paris. Her words have been published in the International New York Times, the Guardian, Vogue, NYLON, and others.

Avant-garments: the wild world of wearable art – in pictures

Each year international designers gather in New Zealand for World of WearableArt – a festival in Wellington where art, design, fashion and theatre collide. It culminates in a competition where designers show off their creations, from gowns resembling birds, fish and telephones to surreal garments inspired by cultural heritage and the natural world.

New Zealand artist Kayla Christensen took out 2026 top prize – the Supreme Wow award – for Sacred Nightfall, an intricately stitched tapestry that summons a night goddess from the native forests of Aotearoa

写真家 若林満による写真展「Dérive（漂流）」がライカギャラリー京都にて開催される。

街を歩くなかで、ふと目に留まる風景。若林満は、そうした一瞬を写真に残してきた。そこにあるのは、特別な場所や劇的な瞬間を探し求めることではない。何気なく過ぎていく日常のなかで、ある風景に目が留まり、シャッターを切る。その小さな偶然の積み重ねが、若林の写真を形づくっている。

本展のタイトル「Dérive（デリヴ）」は、フランス語で「漂流」を意味する言葉。この概念は、移動というものを目的地へ向かう手段としてではなく、歩くことを通して環境や感覚を体験する実践として捉えたものだ。若林が「Dérive」という言葉に出会ったのは、自身がすでに長く続けてきた撮影のあり方を振り返るなかでのことだった。なぜその場所で足を止めたのか、そのときには自分でもわからない。けれども行く先を定めずに街を歩き、目の前に現れるものを受け入れていく感覚は、まさに「Dérive」という言葉によって捉え直すことができるものであった。

本展では、日々の歩みのなかで出会い、撮り続けてきた風景を通して、ひとりの写真家が「見る」という行為とどのように向き合ってきたのかを紹介していく。 若林の写真を通して、いつもの風景にもう一度目を向ける機会になれば幸いだ。

また、本展と同名の写真集『Dérive』を 2026年秋に刊行予定。詳細は公式サイトに更新されるので、是非ともチェックしていただきたい。 https://mitsuruwakabayashi.com/photo-book/
