content.article_text:
Zach Cregger traduz a tensão e o humor dos jogos em uma aventura que envolve o espectador pelas escolhas de câmera e pelas decisões desastrosas de seu protagonista.

A discussão sobre adaptações de jogos para o cinema costuma dedicar tanta atenção à fidelidade narrativa que uma exigência tão básica quanto “ser um bom filme” pode ficar em segundo plano. Reconhecer personagens e referências faz parte do prazer, mas pouco adianta quando a obra não encontra uma maneira própria de envolver o público. Felizmente, o diretor Zach Cregger compreende essa prioridade no novo “ Resident Evil ” e faz dela o caminho para adaptar a experiência dos games.

O longa acompanha Bryan (Austin Abrams), um sujeito completamente despreparado para a noite que terá pela frente. Sua jornada se resume a chegar a um lugar, descobrir como prosseguir e escapar do que aparecer pelo caminho. Essa simplicidade permite que Cregger concentre a narrativa no percurso e nas dificuldades que se apresentam. Objetivos aparentemente próximos por vezes exigem uma sequência de improvisos e decisões questionáveis que tornam o deslocamento até mais importante do que o que o espera no destino.

Essa estrutura oferece a base necessária para a adaptação trabalhar com liberdade. Os personagens reconhecíveis dos jogos estão ausentes, enquanto Umbrella e Raccoon City servem como breves referências para localizar os fãs, sem assumir qualquer responsabilidade de sustentar a história. O diretor utiliza o universo para construir uma aventura própria, sem gastar boa parte da duração preparando acontecimentos conhecidos ou explicando como cada elemento se encaixa na cronologia. O vínculo com o material original se estabelece pela experiência de atravessar aquele mundo.

Essa escolha reconhece uma diferença fundamental entre as duas mídias — há uma razão para o produto final se chamar “adaptação”, não “transcrição”. No jogo, avançar depende de quem está diante da tela, inclusive quando a vontade é apenas permanecer parado ou desligar a plataforma para evitar o próximo susto. No cinema, o percurso continua independentemente dessa disposição. Cregger busca recriar esse envolvimento exercitando constantemente a atenção do público durante a exploração dos ambientes, e as escolhas de câmera concretizam essa intenção.

Os enquadramentos mantêm vários pontos sob suspeita e estimulam a busca por ameaças. Há sempre alguma parte que ainda precisa ser vista, e a direção prolonga essa descoberta o suficiente para tornar a exploração desconfortável. Já as cenas em primeira pessoa restringem a visão, aproximando o olhar do espectador da perspectiva do protagonista. Cada movimento de câmera revela uma área e abandona outra, alimentando a tensão de que o perigo esteja justamente onde não dá para ver. Não é possível decidir por Bryan, claro, mas é possível avaliar (e julgar) seus caminhos, antecipar os riscos e sofrer (ou rir) quando ele faz exatamente o que parecia ser uma péssima ideia.

Embora sejam frequentes, os sustos repentinos se beneficiam dessa atmosfera que já deixou o público atento a qualquer mudança no quadro. Cregger sabe que a expectativa de uma aparição pode sustentar o desconforto por mais tempo do que a aparição em si. As criaturas rompem a espera com movimentos agressivos e violência suficientes para desestabilizar a percepção de como enfrentá-las. Mas essa experiência também comporta o absurdo, e é no acúmulo de problemas que o filme encontra sua característica mais divertida. O roteiro constrói uma espécie de progressão da desgraça na qual Bryan é incapaz de concluir uma dificuldade sem descobrir outra ainda pior. A mesma lógica que mantém a narrativa em movimento produz comédia.

É inegável o quanto Bryan contribui para piorar as próprias circunstâncias. Sua falta de preparo está longe de servir como ponto de partida para a descoberta de um heroísmo escondido. Ele faz besteira o tempo todo, e o filme tem plena consciência disso. Algumas decisões já parecem ruins antes mesmo de serem colocadas em prática (como as hilárias e irritantes sequências com os cadeados), enquanto outras só revelam a extensão do desastre quando já não há muito a fazer (como abraçar uma garotinha para lá de infectada). Cregger encontra humor tanto na antecipação do erro quanto na reação ao resultado.

Dessa forma, o bom trabalho de Austin Abrams é indispensável para equilibrar tudo. O ator se mostra capaz de retratar esse descompasso entre o ritmo frenético dos acontecimentos e a capacidade de Bryan compreendê-los, como se o personagem ainda estivesse tentando processar o problema anterior quando o seguinte já exige uma resposta. Seu espanto e a maneira de lidar com tudo rendem alguns dos melhores momentos, e a situação em que ele se coloca é tão absurda que é difícil não torcer para ele concluir sua missão — mesmo quando se comporta como um idiota.

É interessante observar que o humor participa ativamente da construção do protagonista e do ritmo da aventura. Uma reação pode aliviar a tensão por alguns segundos sem tornar o ambiente mais seguro, assim como uma escolha engraçada pode produzir consequências violentas logo depois. Essa simbiose impede que o filme se acomode num revezamento previsível entre a hora do susto e a hora da piada porque, muitas vezes, os dois efeitos pertencem à mesma situação. O espectador ri do tamanho do problema enquanto continua preocupado com a possibilidade de Bryan não conseguir sair dele.

Com 1h35 de duração, o longa mantém essa dinâmica sem precisar expandir a história para justificar a importância da propriedade intelectual que está adaptando. A progressão quase em tempo real favorece bastante a sensação de que os acontecimentos não são etapas de uma explicação maior sobre aquele universo, e sim dificuldades que precisam ser resolvidas agora.

Essa concentração também expõe algumas limitações. No ato final, esse mecanismo de acumular obstáculos para o protagonista já está bem evidente, e a sucessão de desafios acaba perdendo parte do impacto. Além disso, a tentativa de desenvolver uma trajetória dramática para Bryan acrescentando uma preocupação com a paternidade recebe bem pouco espaço para amadurecer. Essa camada acaba parecendo dispensável, afinal, o vínculo com o personagem já era convincente por outros meios, sobretudo pela atuação e pela convivência com sua sucessão de calamidades.

“Resident Evil” reconhece que a passagem de uma mídia para outra exige reconstruir o envolvimento do público. Para isso, Cregger aposta nas ferramentas do cinema (principalmente o uso da câmera) para recriar o sentimento de jogar um terror de sobrevivência. O resultado é tenso e muito divertido, sendo capaz de preservar a aflição e o prazer inexplicável de atravessar um lugar hostil, mesmo sem oferecer qualquer controle sobre o percurso. Bryan se encarrega de tornar essa jornada o mais desastrosa possível.

content.article_text:
写真家・伊丹豪の個展「a plan for all things」が、2026年10月3日から27日まで、東京・神楽坂のCAVE-AYUMI GALLERYで開催される。本展では、すべて自身の自宅で撮影した新作を発表。会場デザインを建築家の板坂留五が手がける。

伊丹はこれまで、画面内のすべてにピントを合わせる「全焦点」の写真を通して、写真を「見ること」と「撮ること」の関係を考察してきた。被写体の一つだけを際立たせるのではなく、画面に存在するものを等しく鮮明に写すことで、鑑賞者の視線に無意識のうちに生まれるヒエラルキーを揺さぶる。一方、その写真は鮮やかな色彩や大胆な構図にも特徴があり、鑑賞者は視覚的な面白さに引き込まれながら、次第に「何が意図され、何が偶然なのか」という問いへと導かれていく。

今回、伊丹が被写体とするのは、自宅にある家具や日用品など、ごく身近なものだ。それらを選び、動かし、配置することで画面を構成していく。その背景には、過去に見てきた写真や絵画、美術の構造を、生活空間に存在する物の配置へと置き換える行為がある。撮影を終えれば配置は解体され、実際の空間から消えてしまう。写真の中にだけ、そこに存在した物と、すでに存在しない一時的な関係性が残される。

展覧会タイトルの「a plan for all things」には、「plan＝計画」と「plane＝平面」という二つの意味が重ねられている。物を選び、配置して撮影するという「計画」と、それらすべてが同じ密度で定着される写真という「平面」。美術からの引用も日用品も、作為も偶然も、一枚の表面では等価な存在として並ぶ。

「写真は目の前を複製することしか出来ない」と伊丹は語る。だからこそ、何を写し、どのように配置し、どの技術によって複製するのか。その選択の積み重ねに、写真を撮る行為の誠実さを見いだしている。作品の中で何が重要なのか、何が偶然なのかという答えはあえて明示されない。判断は見る側へと委ねられ、「何を見るか」という行為そのものが、私たち自身の価値判断を浮かび上がらせていく。

さらに本展では、これまでも建築家やデザイナーらとの協働を行ってきた伊丹の姿勢を引き継ぎ、板坂留五が展示空間を設計する。板坂は新たな造形を加えるのではなく、「しんとした空気の部屋」をつくり、鑑賞者が写真へゆっくりと近づいていける空間を構想。ギャラリーにもともと存在する壁や床、躯体の凹凸と伊丹の写真を組み合わせることで、写真に表れる独特の物の捉え方を空間へと拡張する。

伊丹豪「a plan for all things」

2026年10月3日（土）〜27日（火）

content.article_text:
Aperture Opens at 380 Columbus Avenue

The new home for photography, now open to the public as of September 18

Aperture Ribbon Cutting, New York, September 2026. Photo by Lloyd McCullough

Aperture News - September 18, 2026

To mark the momentous opening of Aperture’s permanent home in New York’s Upper West Side, supporters, artists, and neighbors gathered for a ceremonial ribbon cutting on the morning of September 18, following festive celebrations the evening before. The opening events toasted Aperture’s new chapter at 380 Columbus Avenue—a dedicated space for “serious photographers and creative people everywhere,” as its founders envisioned seventy-four years ago.

Honoring Aperture’s past and future, more than thirty artists gathered to take a group photograph, marking the significance of the occasion. Other artists in attendance included Emmet Gowin, Richard Renaldi, Sable Elyse Smith, Naima Green, Philip Montgomery, Edward Burtynsky, and Carlos Jaramillo.

Cathy Kaplan, Chair of Aperture’s Board of Trustees, welcomed guests and recognized the many funders and organizations whose steadfast support made the new home possible. Public officials, including New York City Council Member Gale A. Brewer; Erika Mallin, Executive Director of the New York State Council on the Arts; Diya Vij, Commissioner of the New York City Department of Cultural Affairs; Miesha Smith, Deputy Borough President for Manhattan; and Erik Bottcher, New York State Senator, joined to celebrate Aperture’s contributions to New York’s arts and culture landscape.

Just before the ribbon-cutting moment, Aperture Executive Director Sarah Meister expressed deep appreciation and emphasized the significance of 380 Columbus Avenue as a welcoming forum to gather, share ideas, and engage with photography. “Just like each brick in the beautiful arches of this load-bearing masonry building needs its neighbor to serve its function, each of us has played an essential role in making this historic moment possible,” said Meister, in thanks to the supporters, staff, and community.

At the celebrations, guests previewed the bookstore, stocked with new and classic Aperture publications along with titles in collaboration with Dashwood Books, New York, and Offset Projects, New Delhi, and visited the gallery space featuring the inaugural installation Aperture Loves New York , which showcases artists anchored in Aperture’s publishing history with photographs and corresponding Aperture books that have advanced the medium of photography and captured the complex spirit of New York itself. Guests also stopped by the new photo booth, which will remain available for visitors. Now open to the public, Aperture hosts a full season of artist talks, panel discussions, and book celebrations.

Aperture thanks and Zabar’s for their generous support of the opening celebrations, with champagne provided by Ruinart and wine provided by Massican. Promotional support for Aperture Loves New York is provided in part by the New York City Tourism Foundation.

Aperture’s capital campaign to date includes transformative gifts from Judy Glickman Lauder, Melissa and James O’Shaughnessy, Vasant Nayak, Thomas R. Schiff, and Jon Stryker and Slobodan Randjelović, as well as from Michael Hoeh and the Thompson Family Foundation. Aperture received significant grants from New York State Council on the Arts; and City of New York, including the Manhattan Borough President, New York City Council, and New York City Department of Cultural Affairs. Support for the campaign reflects the full participation of Aperture’s Board of Trustees, along with generous contributions from other individuals and foundations. The acquisition of the new space was led by Cathy M. Kaplan, Chair of Aperture’s Board; Helen Nitkin, Chair of the Board’s Real Estate Committee; and Sarah Meister, Executive Director. Financing has been provided by LISC NY, a nonprofit community development institution.

Jurandir Filho , Rogério Montanare e Thiago Siqueira batem um papo sobre os personagens que aparecem quando tudo já deu errado. Quando o plano saiu do controle, alguém precisa desaparecer, uma cena precisa ser limpa ou um problema precisa ser resolvido sem fazer muitas perguntas. É aí que entram os fixers : os grandes “resolvedores de problemas” da cultura pop .

Neste RapaduraCast, falamos sobre alguns dos personagens mais eficientes, perigosos e carismáticos desse arquétipo. De Mike Ehrmantraut, o veterano metódico de “Breaking Bad” e “Better Call Saul”, ao lendário Winston Wolf, o Mr. Wolf de “Pulp Fiction”, chamado quando Vincent e Jules precisam desesperadamente de alguém que saiba exatamente o que fazer. Também passamos por Harry Da Souza, de “Terra da Máfia”, e outros personagens que construíram suas reputações justamente fazendo o trabalho que ninguém mais consegue fazer.

|| OFERECIMENTO – A guerra entre os Harrigan está só começando. Tom Hardy, Helen Mirren e Pierce Brosnan voltam em “ Terra da Máfia “, série de Guy Ricthie, em um universo ainda mais caótico e eletrizante, onde não dá pra confiar em ninguém. A nova temporada estreia hoje, dia 18 de setembro, só no Paramount+ . Assista e entre nessa guerra! 👉 https://bit.ly/4y2PVFM

content.article_text:
This week, Aperture opens the doors of its new home at 380 Columbus Avenue in New York City. Situated on the first two floors of a historic building on the Upper West Side, the bookstore and gallery is a place to gather, share ideas, and engage with photography, and will be a platform for a dynamic series of public programs .

Design for Aperture’s new home has been led by the award-winning architecture practice LEVENBETTS. Here, Stella Betts and David Leven dive into five lesser-known facts about our new space, from embracing the building’s history to the nickname “Aperture Gray.”

History of the Building

David Leven: The building is historical; it was built in the 1880s or so as a residential building called The Evelyn. It was designed by an architect named Emile Gruwe in a kind of Renaissance Revival fashion. During our research, we discovered that part of Aperture’s space was originally dining and kitchen areas for multiple apartments. It would have been a place for cooking and dining for residents who may not have had kitchens in their own apartments, alongside communal fireplaces and so on. It was a social space. The entry we have created for Aperture is located in this area. We were interested in this idea of socialness and community, which has now been carried from the past to the present, but reinterpreted in a new way within the architecture.

Bookstore & Gallery

Stella Betts: The bookstore space is really about celebrating the books and the magazine that Aperture does. It’s the public face, and it was vital that you really see it when you’re on the street, and that there’s a visibility as soon as you enter from the lobby.

Leven: As soon as you come in, you’re seeing bookshelves and the public space. There will be talks and events that happen in this space, where we’re able to bring in chairs and a projector screen that comes down.

The shelving in the store has very thin lines, as a kind of juxtaposition to the roughness of the brick walls. We took into consideration how thin and minimal they could be and still carry the weight of all the books that are going to go in here.

There was also a lot of discussion with Sarah Meister, Aperture’s director, about whether to paint the gallery and programs area white, or how much do we leave or take away, what gets cleaned or left. In the end, we all decided that we really wanted to keep the markings and the character of the original building. And I think that that still works well with the photography that will be shown here, almost becoming in dialogue with the building itself.

Emphasizing the Existing Materials

Betts: When we were initially looking at potential spaces for Aperture’s future home, I think the idea of moving to the Upper West Side was a little bit of a leap. For the past twenty years or so Aperture had been located in Chelsea and had even set its sights on SoHo and other neighborhoods. What we all fell in love with about this space and location is the character, the history. And we wanted to continue to capture a downtown loft feeling—what David calls “the rawness of the space.”

To do this, we made an effort to leave a sort of history of the building. That’s also a really important thing for us in terms of what we love about photography, it’s about telling stories. What was significant with this project was to tell the story of the building and to not remove that history.

Leven: We’ve had so many great conversations about how much do we leave, how much do we take away, what gets cleaned, what gets preserved. There are steel lintels holding up thousands of pounds. There are original archways and markings and brickwork throughout. It all goes back to this idea of the history and story.

Betts: A big part of the design process was cataloging every single wall. We photo-documented each wall and made decisions in terms of to what degree certain things were going to be cleaned. For example, many of the walls retain so-called imperfections that in other projects would be removed.

Aperture Gray

Betts: We took this approach of what we are calling “insertions,” where we’re adding to the space and making it distinct from the existing space. These insertions were created in a palette that we affectionately named “Aperture Gray,” which was partially based on the photography Zone System.

Leven: This was also in order to not add too many other elements within the palettes and things you see. The light Aperture Gray color recedes into the space, but it’s also omnipresent throughout: the doorframes are all the same color. The bookshelves are all the same color. The desks pick up that color.

Betts: The books themselves will animate the space, and there’ll be photography in the gallery as well. So, the idea for us was to let the building be present with the photography and books, and the additions that we’ve made are in this neutral Aperture Gray.

Equity of Light

Betts: Aperture’s home has a split between two floors, so you need light for both the lower level and the upper level, and we really wanted to have all areas have some degree of shared light or direct light—an equity of light. The idea of transparency also was really important.

Downstairs there are some very thick, heavy stone foundation walls that have beautiful texture. Although there are windows, the lower level doesn’t get the same amount of light as the upper floor. In order for the light to bounce, we decided to paint the entire downstairs white—while keeping that original texture. When we had conversations during the design process it was very much like seeking a kind of Robert Ryman white-on-white painting where you get just a single palette color, but you get to enjoy the texture of the wall itself. It all goes back to the character of the building.

content.article_text:
A couple walks side by side across a sun-bleached desert. The taller, male figure rests his hand on the shoulders of his female companion, who glances off to one side, lips parted, as though she’s about to remark on some distant curiosity. Seemingly unconcerned by the volcano erupting in the background, they might pass for a pair of flaneurs strolling the streets of Paris—if they weren’t naked and covered in long shaggy hair. Their faces are apelike, with heavy brows, flat noses, and jutting prognathic jaws.

Earliest Human Relatives (1994) by Hiroshi Sugimoto is a bewildering photograph. At first glance, it might seem as though the hirsute figures are models wearing the latest in simian prosthetics, posing for the artist in some remote volcanic region. Or they could be extras from 2001: A Space Odyssey caught sneaking off set for a cigarette break.

But something’s not quite right. The flock of birds pecking the dirt under a nearby tree looks flat and vaguely cartoonish on close inspection. So does the miniscule herd of horses even farther away. There’s something unconvincing about the scene, even as our brains tell us the prehistoric figures are tangibly real.

Sugimoto’s enigmatic photograph depicts a bygone diorama at New York’s American Museum of Natural History. The figures—sculptural reconstructions of Lucy, the famous fossil representative of Australopithecus afarensis from Ethiopia, and a male counterpart—once stood on a patch of artificial dirt, before a painted background, behind a large pane of glass. I grew up with this tableau, fascinated by the primordial world (and, yes, the nakedness) it depicted. Transporting though it was, the figures were clearly sculptures, the landscape a mural. In Sugimoto’s deadpan photograph, the diorama appears far more uncanny than it did in life. With his camera, he’s completed the illusion.

When Sugimoto made Earliest Human Relatives , he’d been photographing dioramas for nearly twenty years. The series, the artist’s first and most sustained mature body of work, began soon after he moved to New York, in 1974.

Although it’s tempting to imagine Sugimoto—whose interest in science has since led him to photograph fossils, mathematical models, and the optical effects of prisms—making an immediate beeline for the museum, it wasn’t his first stop. In fact, it was the very last on a list of great institutions he visited to find his bearings in a new city.

Aperture Magazine Subscription

And yet it was there, not in the city’s great art collections, that Sugimoto’s career began. Wandering the darkened halls of wildlife dioramas, he made a startling discovery. These displays, with their taxidermy animals, artificial plants, and painted backgrounds, looked “utterly fake” to the young artist, but when he closed one eye, simulating the way a single-lens camera perceives the world, they suddenly looked real. The seams between the three-dimensional foregrounds and painted walls became undetectable. Instead of static displays inside an urban museum, his photographs seemed to show living creatures in exotic habitats.

In 1975, Sugimoto returned to the museum with an 8-by-10-inch camera. When a security guard asked him if he had permission for the photoshoot, the artist said he did. Technically, this was true. Sugimoto had told museum officials he was a tourist and secured permission to take photographs—he’d neglected to mention he would be constructing makeshift tents around the dioramas to block reflections on the glass or that the exposures would last around twenty minutes.

Sugimoto’s desire to resurrect the lifeless animals on display is the same desire that motivated museum staff to fabricate them in the first place.

The artist photographed two dioramas on that first expedition. One depicts a rowdy flock of vultures tearing into a zebra carcass. In the other, a polar bear stands over a bloody seal on a stark expanse of ice. “My life as an artist began the moment I saw with my own eyes that I had succeeded in bringing the bear back to life on film,” he later wrote.

Sugimoto’s desire to resurrect the lifeless animals on display is the same desire that motivated museum staff to fabricate them in the first place. The dioramas were the cries of naturalists lamenting the environmental devastation of the early twentieth century.

“As civilization advances in Africa, the extinction of the elephant is being accomplished slowly but quite as surely as that of the American buffalo two generations ago,” wrote Carl Akeley, the pioneering taxidermist, big game hunter, and namesake of the museum’s Akeley Hall of African Mammals. Akeley mourned the destructive impact of Europeans and Americans on the African wilderness even though (or largely because) he’d known the continent when it was a paradise for Great White Hunters.

By presenting audiences with spectacular wild scenes, Akeley hoped to rally support for conservation among urbanites who’d likely never experience these places firsthand. Although his preservationist ideals and destructive appetites may be difficult for contemporary readers to reconcile, they weren’t paradoxical for him or the many wealthy sportsmen who championed conservation at the time.

Dioramas themselves have recently become endangered species. Few public museums could afford the costly collecting expeditions and painstaking artistry of the old dioramas today, even if they wanted to. Major institutions have even destroyed their antique dioramas in recent years, replacing them with sleeker, more modern displays equipped with touch screens, animatronics, and other whiz-bang attractions. Although the American Museum of Natural History has largely resisted this trend, Lucy and her companion barely survived a revamp that claimed their volcanic desert environment. Today, the couple stands inside a glass vitrine, surrounded by glowing screens. Over the past fifty years, Sugimoto has inadvertently created an archive of a disappearing art.

Museum staff who once bristled at Sugimoto’s claim that the dioramas look more “real” in his photographs than they do in life have since come around. “He really does, through his work, honor the dioramas as the fine art that they are,” said Stephen Quinn, an authority on dioramas who built and restored them at the museum for nearly forty years. Now, Sugimoto says, the series is almost complete. He took his last photographs at the American Museum of Natural History in the fall of 2025. How did he feel about finishing a body of work he began as a young man? “Relief,” he said, seated in his New York studio. “Fifty years is enough.”

For this final photoshoot, Sugimoto used color film—a first for the series. He returned to a diorama he shot before, in black and white, depicting a path winding through a bird sanctuary on Long Island. Although dozens of birds perch and flit through the blooming trees, in gray scale they’re difficult to spot, their bodies well camouflaged. In color, the scene resembles an Impressionist painting: a scarlet tanager, practically invisible in the earlier print, is a shock of red among the dappled patches of pink, white, and green.

Over time, Sugimoto has increasingly trained his lens on overlooked dioramas showing ecosystems devoid of central, spectacular subjects. In these serene landscapes, the artist sees prophetic visions of a posthuman world.

“Humans should be punished by nature,” Sugimoto told me recently, gesturing at a nearby window. “These skyscrapers—so unnatural.” Years ago, the artist could see the George Washington Bridge, about nine miles north of Chelsea. Now, glossy spires block the view.

Sugimoto takes comfort in the thought that humans aren’t long for this world. “Nature will survive,” he said. The artist likes to imagine vines and wild grass overtaking the natural history museum uptown, its roof collapsing on the dioramas, and even his own Odawara Art Foundation in Japan in ruins. Thousands of years from now, he says, the stones will still look beautiful.

This article originally appeared in Aperture No. 264, “Stop Time,” guest edited by Hiroshi Sugimoto.

content.article_text:
T here is absolutely nothing unexpected about this Netflix comedy set in the world of rival Bollywood dance groups on American campuses. Each plot twist is instantly familiar, every character recognisable, the essential formula untweaked from a dozen previous college comedies. But it’s funny and snappy, and directed with infectious energy by Lena Khan, one of the few Muslim female film-makers working in Hollywood. The scriptwriters are Hasan Minhaj and Prashanth Venkataramanujam, a pair of millennial comedians who look as if they’ve done enough research on the inner workings of gen Z behaviour to write a PhD.

Maya (Maitreyi Ramakrishnan) and Anjali (Priyanka Kedia) star as lifelong best friends who enrol together at UCLA. Maya is the clever difficult one; Anjali is the nice pretty one. (It goes without saying Maya is also a total babe.) During freshers’ week they join the college’s Bollywood dance club where, predictably, Maya locks horns with leader Ronak (Ankur Rathee) over the choreography. He wants to base their new-season routine on Bollywood weddings, which, as Maya points out, is a bit trad. If they are going to beat their rivals they will need to come up with something modern and fresh.

No prizes for guessing where this is headed. But the comedy is whip-fast, with plenty of second-generation in jokes. When Anjali’s mum slaps her in full view of the dorm house, Maya jokes that the white kids looked like they wanted to call the police. And it ends brilliantly with a choreography that has a plotline involving a heist of the Koh-i-Noor – the diamond now in the crown jewels. The sequence manages to say something about young future-facing south Asians and diaspora communities while also including a celebration of traditional dance. It’s a high note that will leave you thinking this is up there with the best.

content.article_text:
写真家・篠田優の個展「Garden」が、2026年9月18日から30日まで、東京・高田馬場のAlt_Mediumで開催される。本展で篠田が向き合うのは、親交のあった写真家・飯田鉄（1948–2023）が遺したフィルムと、その記憶だ。

展示される作品は、すべてモノクロームのフィルムで撮影されたもの。そのフィルム自体が、生前の飯田から篠田へと譲られたものだという。篠田はそれを用いて、飯田が撮影地として愛着を持っていた場所の風景と、飯田が自身の蔵書として集め、のちに篠田が受け継いだ書籍を撮影した。

写されるのは、すでに本人が不在となった場所と物。しかし、撮影地、蔵書、そしてフィルムという複数の痕跡を重ね合わせることで、写真の中には飯田という写真家の存在が間接的に立ち現れる。誰かの姿を直接撮るのではなく、その人物が見ていた風景や手にしていた本、残した素材を介して、その人の輪郭へと近づいていく試みだ。

1986年長野県生まれの篠田は、写真やヴィデオを主なメディウムとして、「記録」の実践とその再考をテーマに制作を続けてきた。消えつつあるものを記録する一方で、記録するという行為に不可避的に伴う恣意性や限界にも目を向け、その不完全さの先に生まれる可能性を探っている。

content.article_text:
グローバル・ラグジュアリー・グループのケリングが、2026年10月27日、第39回東京国際映画祭 提携企画として「ウーマン・イン・モーション」トークを開催する。プログラム創設から11年目、日本での開催は9年目を迎える。現在9月30日まで観覧者を募集中だ。

今年は、映画監督・是枝裕和によるオープニング・スピーチに続き、アカデミー・ミュージアム・オブ・モーション・ピクチャーズ館長兼プレジデントで、アカデミー・コレクション統括責任者のエイミー・ホンマ、歌手・俳優の二宮和也、映画『国宝』（2025）の企画・プロデュースを手がけた映画プロデューサーの村田千恵子が登壇。

世界の映画文化を俯瞰するホンマ、日本映画を世界へ届けてきた村田、国内外の映画制作現場を経験してきた二宮。それぞれ「映画文化を継承・発信する立場」「作品を生み出す立場」「作品を体現する立場」から、日本映画の魅力や可能性、世界から見た現在地、次世代へ向けた映画文化のあり方について議論する。さらに、ジェンダー、多様性、アライシップの観点から、創造性を育む環境についても考える。

ホンマは2024年、アカデミー賞を主催する映画芸術科学アカデミーがロサンゼルスに設立したアカデミー・ミュージアムの館長兼プレジデントに就任。現在は同館の展覧会や上映、教育プログラムなどに加え、5200万点を超えるアカデミー・コレクションを統括している。

二宮はクリント・イーストウッド監督『硫黄島からの手紙』（2006）への出演をはじめ、第78回カンヌ国際映画祭でワールドプレミアされた『8番出口』（2025）に主演するなど、国内外で俳優として活動。村田は『キングダム』（2019）などの製作を経て、2025年公開の『国宝』を企画・プロデュースした。同作はカンヌ国際映画祭「監督週間」でワールドプレミアされ、第98回アカデミー賞メイクアップ＆ヘアスタイリング部門にノミネートされた。

トーク終了後には、ホンマが自身に影響を与えた画期的なアメリカ実写映画のひとつとして選んだ、ルル・ワン監督『フェアウェル』（2019）を特別上映。中国系アメリカ人監督であるワン自身の体験をもとに、アジア系移民のアイデンティティと家族を描いた作品だ。

ケリング「ウーマン・イン・モーション」は2015年、カンヌ国際映画祭とのパートナーシップのもと、映画界でカメラの前後を問わず活躍する女性の創造性と功績に光を当てるプログラムとしてスタート。現在ではジェンダーだけでなく、文化的背景や人種などを含む多様な声へと視点を広げ、よりインクルーシブな文化環境を目指す国際的な取り組みへ発展している。

content.article_text:
Pentax Auto 110, Yoko Kusano

Toyo Field 45CF, Daisuke Yokota

横田大輔、濵本奏、宇田川直寛、古田直人、草野庸子、渡邊聖子の6名の写真家によるグループ展「soft room」が、2026年9月17日から27日まで、東京・代田橋のflotsam booksで開催される。2023年にSprout Curationで開催された「幽霊の道具」展以来、3年ぶりとなる展覧会だ。

本展が着目するのは、完成した写真作品だけではなく、それを生み出す「カメラの側」。一般的なカメラ紹介と作例紹介という形式をあえて用いながら、作品や展覧会という完成形からはこぼれ落ちてしまう機材、撮影プロセス、物質、行為へと視線を向ける。そこから、通常は記述されることのない文化や存在、現象が複雑に絡み合う場を「部屋」として捉え直す。

写真を見るとき、鑑賞者の意識は往々にして「何が写っているか」や「写真家が何を表現したのか」に向けられる。しかし写真は、カメラやレンズ、フィルム、デジタル機器といった道具、さらには撮影や現像、プリントなど複数のプロセスを経て生み出されるメディアでもある。「soft room」はそうした写真を成立させる周縁的な要素を表舞台へと引き出し、作品と制作環境の関係を考える試みとなる。

展示に合わせ、6名それぞれの作品を構成するカメラや機材、撮影プロセスの詳細を収録したアンソロジー冊子『soft room』も刊行。展示作品だけでは見えてこない各写真家の「部屋」を、制作の方法論や道具から読み解くことができる。価格は2,000円。

また会期中には、参加作家6名による写真集やZineなどを販売するブックフェア「FancyshopDrivein」を実施。9月19日と26日には、30歳以下の表現者を対象としたポートフォリオレビュー「Standin」も開催される。一般的な講評会ではなく、ポートフォリオと、可能であれば実際に使用しているカメラを持ち寄り、参加作家との対話から、まだ形になっていない作品を言語化・具体化するための手がかりを探る。

content.article_text:
T ypically horror fans react to blatant on-screen stupidity with vocal derision. Don’t go in there! Girl, get out of the house! Guys, ignore that distress signal! But genre aficionados may find themselves falling a little bit in love with Bryan (Austin Abrams), the hapless de facto hero of the new horror film Resident Evil . It’s not that Bryan is traditionally hunky, or even a caricatured version of a square-jawed warrior, like Bruce Campbell in his later Evil Dead outings. But Abrams is in possession of a Campbell-ish charm, even in the face of his character’s repeated blundering, as well as an everyman relatability that makes this wild carnival-ride movie play a little closer to the ground.

Bryan is a courier – a glorified Postmates driver, in his own estimation – who postpones the end of his shift to take one last night-time run, driving an important item from one hospital to another in a snowstorm without the proper tires or four-wheel drive. After all, the distance and urgency means double pay. When he hits a mysterious woman who emerges suddenly on to a slick road, he’s drawn into a hellish outbreak that will look familiar to fans of the Resident Evil video game series (or maybe the previous six-movie Milla Jovovich franchise, which apparently drifted afield from the games’ storylines).

The key to Abrams’s winning performance as a perpetual loser is in how the actor and cowriter-director Zach Cregger take care to show Bryan stumbling his way through sloppy versions of doing the right thing. When he hits the clearly zonked woman, Bryan attempts to take her along on his hospital run. When he’s quickly pulled over by a cop, he makes little attempt to weasel out of his situation, attempting to prioritize his medical task. The man tries, even if some of his efforts in certain areas are lamentably weak (supporting his unseen girlfriend in a non-outbreak-related couple crisis) or understandably incompetent (wielding a firearm against undead creatures). His oscillations between overconfidence and panic make him a particularly fresh point-of-view character for a zombie/monster movie.

In short, he’s not unlike a guy who’s been dropped into a video game before learning the proper controls – in keeping with Cregger’s reported desire to replicate the experience of the game without adapting any of its stories directly. Abrams manages to humanize this unspoken and potentially arch conceit of an avatar learning the rules as he goes. It’s tempting to compare his many scenes without other human characters to silent comedy – only he’s not quiet enough to qualify, unleashing a hilarious symphony of profane and frustrated muttering. At one point, well after his life has been endangered multiple times, he can be heard complaining about his wet socks.

Good as Abrams is, alone and when playing opposite skeleton-crew supporting cast, he’s not exactly a one-man show, either; the guy behind the camera is his constant scene partner. Cregger, who has become a horror brand name on the strength of the similarly inventive Barbarian and Weapons, orchestrates the mayhem with expert command of pacing, comic-horrific timing, and even that old standby, the lowly jumpscare. (There’s at least one genuinely masterful version here.) The movie’s comic side isn’t quite Sam Raimi broad (or bold), but Cregger’s sketch-comedy roots are just as delightfully visible here as they were in Barbarian, without the aid of that movie’s clever shifts in timeline or perspective.

Indeed, Resident Evil has a streamlined single-mindedness, and as it barrels through its gamified plot, the tension and entertainment value never flag. Cregger only falters in the tail end, and it’s more a sin of omission than a big misstep. Resident Evil flirts with becoming a full-on monster movie where its cinematic predecessors tended to keep circling back to zombie action (at least in terms of their horror elements; let’s not discount Jovovich’s action bona fides). Cregger’s monster-mashier shift is a welcome one, and presumably closer in spirit to the games. But he doesn’t bring the movie close enough to whatever line separates monstrousness and the humanity that might be lurking underneath.

It could be that there’s not supposed to be any – in which case the movie more or less just screeches to a halt before it gets too thorny. Weapons had a creepy, evocative aversion to simple metaphorical reads that ultimately increased its effectiveness; the same isn’t quite true here. Resident Evil foregrounds one obvious bit of character change for Bryan, but after doing a great job making us care about him for more than 90 minutes, Cregger seems to abandon him a few steps shy of completing any real journey. Is he awaiting a level up that never arrives? Hard to say. But maybe bringing a video game sensibility to the big screen while keeping any gamer cheesiness on the margins is journey enough.

Resident Evil is in cinemas on 18 September

ビックリするほど当たるためIMA御用達の占い師・マコが、12星座の今をタロット1枚で運気予報！フォトグラファー清水はるみによるファンタスティックな星座＆大アルカナのヴィジュアルと共に、明るい未来の指針を毎月前・後半でお届けします。

9月後半に思うこと

「瀬戸内グリーンレモンに恋した理由」

それは、滋賀の日吉大社、奈良の橿原神宮、そして天河大弁財天社を巡る聖地巡礼の旅から始まった。神聖な空気に触れ、心身が大きく震えた直後、私はなぜか「塩レモン」に強烈に取り憑かれることになったのだ。

気になって仕方がなくなり取り寄せたのは、今しか手に入らない瀬戸内のグリーンレモン「璃の香」。形はいびつで傷もある「訳ありレモン」だ。しかし、見栄えの良いエリートよりも、野生の生命力が詰まったその姿に愛おしさが爆発。さらにレモンの輪切りにローズマリーとバニラエッセンスを合わせて火にかけ、じっくりと煮出してみる。部屋中に広がるすっきりと鋭いハーブの香りと、すべてを包み込むような甘い香り。その贅沢な香りを胸いっぱいに吸い込んでいる時間が何より心地良かった。

実はこの衝動、単なる料理ブームではない。私は今、人間関係を軽くし、過去の恐怖を克服して、新しいことに挑戦したい！という人生の転換期に立っている。この時、私が出合えた3つの素材は、私の決意を支えるスピリチュアルメッセージが隠されていた。青々と香る「ローズマリー」は古来より「記憶」と「トラウマの解消」を司る聖なるハーブだ、過去の恐怖を整理しメンタルを強く保つための戦士のような強さを授けてくれる。鋭い光を放つ「レモン」は澱んだエネルギーを強烈に弾き飛ばす」邪気払い」の象徴。特に今回選んだ「グリーンレモン」はハートチャクラを癒やし、未熟な状態からステップアップする「リスタート」のサイン。最後に、甘く漂う「バニラ」は、過去の恐怖で傷つき、固くなっていた内なる子供の心（インナーチャイルド）を「もう大丈夫だよ」と優しく抱きしめる「絶対的な安心感と自愛」をもたらす。

過去の恐怖を克服しようとする時、心は大きなエネルギーを消費する。ローズマリーで過去を断ち切り、レモンで道を拓き、バニラで自分を最大に愛するという「魔法の調合」なのだ。そこに祓いの代表「塩」が加わり私は最強になれるのです！

自分で仕込んだ塩レモンを、玉ねぎセロリ麹、ニンニクと合わせて豚しゃぶでいただく夜。レモンが瓶の中でじっくりと発酵していくように私の新しい人生もまた、ここから力強く豊かに熟成を始めていく。ハズ……。

content.article_text:
Joel Crawford e Januel Mercado articulam experimentação visual e intimidade em uma animação sobre preservar lembranças e continuar na vida de alguém.

É emocionante ver Jo e Raissa prometerem permanecer juntas para sempre antes de terem ideia do que isso significaria. Ao terminarem o ensino médio, a mudança de Raissa para os Estados Unidos coloca essa certeza em dúvida. A amizade continua, mas a rotina próxima e intensa que permitiu construí-la está prestes a acabar. “ A Ilha Esquecida ” se encontra nesse intervalo, representando bem esse medo de deixar de fazer parte do cotidiano de alguém e isso se tornar o começo do desaparecerimento da vida dessa pessoa.

Ambientado nas Filipinas dos anos 1990, o longa acompanha a última noite das amigas antes da mudança. A despedida toma outro rumo quando um portal transporta ambas para Nakali, uma ilha habitada pelas criaturas das histórias que ouviam durante a infância. Quando descobrem que voltar para casa pode custar a memória da própria amizade, a aventura reforça ainda mais a urgência que já estava estabelecida pela iminente separação da dupla.

Os diretores Joel Crawford e Januel Mercado, de “Gato de Botas 2: O Último Pedido” , desenvolvem a relação das protagonistas com bastante carinho e atenção aos detalhes — antes de colocá-la em perigo. A sequência que acompanha Jo e Raissa desde o primeiro encontro até o presente aproveita uma linguagem típica dos animes, e a formação da amizade se torna uma epopeia frenética. A montagem atravessa os anos com poucos diálogos, construindo a intimidade nas pequenas expressões e na maneira como as duas compartilham as situações. Quando a ilha começa a ameaçar essa história, já nos importamos o suficiente para temer o que está para ser perdido.

Esse compromisso de colocar a imagem a serviço da narrativa orienta a concepção visual de todo o filme. Ainda na cidade natal das protagonistas, proporções exageradas e cores vivas estabelecem um mundo que responde à energia das duas. A chegada a Nakali extrapola essa liberdade, com criaturas e paisagens que alteram constantemente a percepção de escala. Uma galinha pode ocupar o espaço com a imponência de um monstro, enquanto a aparição de um Cãobizomem parece perfeitamente aceitável. A opção da direção de arte é claramente recusar que o extraordinário possibilitado pelo gênero se comporte de maneira discreta.

Essa liberdade visual se aproxima daquela que “Aranhaverso” , “A Família Mitchell” , “As Tartarugas Ninja” e o próprio “Gato de Botas 2” ajudaram a consolidar na animação comercial. Crawford e Mercado exploram essa possibilidade para construir uma linguagem bastante adequada à história. O trabalho em 3D convive com passagens em 2D, sobretudo nos relatos sobre o passado, cujos estilos variam conforme o personagem da vez. Isso faz com que as lembranças também sejam novas formas de contar histórias, cada uma com uma aparência particular, em vez de receber um tratamento padrão apenas para indicar que se trata de um flashback. Em um filme sobre aquilo que as pessoas carregam consigo, essa escolha dá às memórias uma identidade que vai além de sua utilidade para explicar a trama.

A própria organização da aventura também se beneficia disso. Parte do percurso envolve reconstituir os acontecimentos que levaram as protagonistas àquela situação, no melhor estilo “Se Beber, Não Case!” . O recurso alimenta o humor e permite que novas revelações e informações incertas reorganizem o sentido de momentos anteriores, além de colocar o ato de lembrar no centro da ação. Jo e Raissa precisam recuperar o passado para decidir o próximo passo, enquanto tentam proteger uma história compartilhada que corre o risco de deixar de existir.

Nem sempre, porém, o filme administra bem a quantidade de coisas que coloca no caminho. O segundo ato acumula encontros com personagens cuja função inicial parece se limitar a apresentar uma nova excentricidade e render algumas piadas. Vários deles são divertidos, mas o tempo dedicado às apresentações enfraquece momentaneamente a urgência da fuga. É curioso que uma animação tão movimentada e frenética consiga parecer parada em certos momentos, enquanto o conflito das protagonistas espera sua vez de avançar.

A expressividade dos personagens e o contraste entre suas reações e o absurdo das situações produzem excelentes sequências, mas algumas gags insistem além do necessário, acrescentando exageros a cenas que já funcionavam. Ter um estilo com muitos estímulos não é, por si só, um problema. É que, por vezes, essa escolha acaba interrompendo uma aproximação emocional ou prolongando um encontro sem acrescentar muito ao que já havia sido estabelecido.

Essa distribuição desigual de atenção também prejudica a vilã. Sua presença salpicada pela história mantém a sensação de perigo, mas seu desenvolvimento não corresponde ao destaque que recebe na vida das protagonistas no primeiro ato, das referências em um trabalho escolar à fantasia usada pelas duas amigas. O filme não hesita em encontrar tempo para desvios cômicos e figuras passageiras, enquanto sua principal antagonista merecia um pouco mais de espaço para tornar seu conflito mais envolvente.

Quando os elementos apresentados ao longo da jornada finalmente se encontram, “A Ilha Esquecida” dá um peso emocional ainda maior à promessa que abre o filme. Perder as lembranças uma da outra significa também perder uma parte de si próprias. Apesar dos desvios, a aventura consegue transformar o medo da separação em algo igualmente íntimo e fantástico. Algumas amizades continuam fazendo parte de quem somos, mesmo quando já não fazem parte dos nossos dias.

content.article_text:
写真家・蓮井元彦と倉島水生による二人展「故郷」が、2026年9月16日から10月5日まで、東京・御徒町の229GALLERYで開催される。二人がそれぞれ自身の故郷を撮影し、土地と記憶、家族、そして時間の経過によって変化していく「故郷」のあり方を見つめる。

本展の原点となったのは、約2年前に二人が制作したZINE「故郷」。今回の展覧会に向け、蓮井の故郷である東京・国分寺と、倉島の故郷である岐阜・飛騨高山を、二人と229GALLERYのメンバーがともに訪れた。普段は一人で撮影することの多い二人が、他者とともに故郷を歩き、かつて過ごした場所やそこにまつわる記憶を語る。その経験は、2年前とは異なる距離から故郷を捉え直す機会にもなったという。

蓮井にとって国分寺は、家族も実家もなくなったことで「少し閉じかけていた」場所だった。今回、仲間とともに小学校や図書館、神社、中学校、昔住んでいた家の周辺などを歩き、35年間通うラーメン店で食事をする。その翌日には偶然、中学時代の同窓会への誘いが届き、28年ぶりに同級生たちと再会した。過去の記憶によって成立していた故郷に、新しい人間関係と記憶が書き加えられる。蓮井はその変化を「僕の故郷は第二章へと進んだのかな」と綴っている。

一方、倉島は2年前のZINEで、「故郷とは家や土地であり、それは人間が完全に所有できるものではなく、本当のところは故郷なんてないのかもしれない」と記した。その言葉をきっかけに、高山で暮らす母親から届いたのが、自身にとって現在の住まいこそ、子どもたちとの喜怒哀楽の記憶が息づく「HOME」なのだという言葉だった。

その後の5年間で家族の形は変化し、近づいたり離れたり、ときには血縁者さえ他人のように感じたりするなかで、倉島自身の「故郷」や「家族」に対する考え方も変わり続けてきた。血がつながっているからといって、すべてを理解し合えるわけではない。それでも母や姉たちが健やかに日々を送っていること自体を幸福だと感じる。故郷を特定の土地や家に固定するのではなく、人との関係や記憶の変化から捉え直している。

二人の写真から浮かび上がるのは、「帰る場所」として固定された故郷ではない。そこから離れ、時間が経ち、人間関係や自分自身が変化することで、その意味もまた書き換えられていく。かつての記憶を記録するだけではなく、現在から過去を見返し、さらに新しい記憶を重ねていくこと。蓮井と倉島、それぞれ異なる二つの「故郷」を通して、鑑賞者自身が自らの帰る場所や、そこから現在まで続く時間について考える展覧会となる。

content.article_text:
アクネ ストゥディオズが、ブランド創立30周年を記念したキャンペーンを発表した。撮影を手がけたのは、アメリカを代表する写真家ナン・ゴールディン。ブランドの原点である「デニム」をテーマに、これまでアクネ ストゥディオズと関係を築いてきたクリエイターたちをポートレートに収めている。

アクネ ストゥディオズの歴史は1996年、ストックホルムで制作された100本のローデニムジーンズから始まった。「Ambition to Create Novel Expressions（新しい表現を創造する野望）」の頭文字を取った「Acne」として活動を開始し、ジーンズを地元のアーティストやクリエイター、友人たちへ贈ったことがブランドの出発点だった。2006年に現在の名称へ変更し、ファッション、アート、カルチャーを横断するブランドへと発展してきた。

30周年を迎え、共同創設者兼クリエイティブ・ディレクターのジョニー・ヨハンソンが改めて目を向けたのが、その原点であるデニム。ブランドにとって初のコラボレーションとなるゴールディンは、過去30年間を象徴するデニムの現行モデルやアーカイブ、復刻モデルをまとった人々を、親密かつダイレクトなポートレートとして撮影した。

被写体となったのは、ミュージシャンのエリー・ロウゼル、モデル兼写真家のグィネヴィア・ヴァン・シーナス、アーティストのジョナサン・リンドン・チェイス、写真家ジョーダン・ヘミングウェイ、俳優兼ミュージシャンのジュリエット・ルイス、アーティストのピーター・シュレシンジャー、俳優兼モデルのラヤ・マルティニー、俳優の福島リラ、アーティストのサンドラ・ポールソンら。いずれも過去のコラボレーションや対話を通して、ブランドの現在を形づくってきた人物たちだ。

「モデルとしてではなく、友人として出演してもらいたかった」とヨハンソンが語るように、今回のキャンペーンはスターを並べることよりも、ブランドと人との関係性に焦点を当てている。長年、友人や恋人、アーティストたちの私生活を親密な距離から撮り続けてきたゴールディンの写真と、コミュニティとの対話を重視してきたアクネ ストゥディオズ。その両者の姿勢が重なり合うプロジェクトとなった。

content.article_text:
東京・銀座のArt Gallery M84でベッティナ・ランスの写真展「密室」No.12が2026年10月5日から17日まで開催される。同ギャラリーでは12回目となるランスの個展で、代表作「Chambre Close（シャンブル・クローズ／密室）」を中心に約30点を展示する。

1952年パリ生まれのランスは、1970年代後半から写真家として活動。ストリッパーやダンサー、娼婦などを被写体としたポートレートやヌードで頭角を現し、1980年代には『VOGUE』『Figaro』などの雑誌や広告へと活動の場を広げた。女性を主要な被写体としながら、華やかさや儚さ、美しさと苦悩、憂いといった相反する感情を写真に捉えてきた。

本展の核となる「Chambre Close」は、作家・セルジュ・ブラムリーとのコラボレーションによって1990年から92年にかけて制作されたシリーズだ。パリの女性たちを親密な距離から撮影したヌード作品は、その大胆なポーズと濃密な色彩で注目を集め、同名写真集はヨーロッパのみならずアメリカ、日本、韓国、オーストラリアなど各国で広く知られることとなった。

「Chambre Close」は、ランスにとって初めて本格的にカラー写真に取り組んだシリーズでもある。室内の鮮やかな壁や家具、衣服といった背景を積極的に画面へ取り込みながら、モデルの身体や視線を演出。代表作「Chambre Close Octobre I, Paris.」でも、赤を基調とした室内と女性の肌、黒い衣服が強いコントラストを生み、私的な空間を覗き込むような親密さと緊張感が共存している。

ランスはその後も、ジェンダーやセクシュアリティ、身体をめぐる表現を展開。1995年にはフランス大統領の公式カメラマンを務め、1998年にはイエスの生涯を現代に置き換えて撮影した「I.N.R.I.」を発表するなど、ファッションとアートの領域を横断して活動してきた。

今回の展示では、ランスが女性の身体とその内面をどのように写真へと変換してきたのかを約30点からたどる。モデルの視線や身振り、室内の色彩、写真家と被写体の距離。閉ざされた「密室」のなかで交わされる視線を通して、1990年代を代表するランスの写真表現を改めて検証する機会となる。

content.article_text:
L atif, the solemn hitman played soulfully by Mahershala Ali , carries diapers in his kill kit. I can’t tell if that’s because they come in handy when soaking up pools of blood on the fly; or because at a moment’s notice the hitman has to switch over from his brutal occupation to daddy duties. Or perhaps it’s both for this contract killer who comes armed with a blade and baby wipes, who takes lives and nurtures them, whose life is composed of jarring and poetic contradictions, much like the movie he’s in.

Those contradictions are on full striking display in Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother’s opening moments, an explosive close-quarters brawl in a restroom, after which Latif uses the baby wipes to clean up the mess he made with that blade. It’s a lovely image, in a film filled with so many, cutting right through the tension within this character. It also feels like a wink to the audience from Ali and writer/director Bassam Tariq, a way for them to acknowledge right off the top the distracting mess made by that other Blade.

Tariq and Ali were collaborating on Marvel’s Blade reboot . Ali was announced to star as the vampire-slayer formerly played by Wesley Snipes all the way back in 2019. Tariq signed on to write and direct in 2021 but departed a year later. Ali recently revealed that, after being strung along for seven years in development, the reboot was not happening. It’s easy to assume that some of the ideas Tariq and Ali had for Blade made their way into this new collaboration, in which Ali gets to finally wield a blade and John Cho, of Harold and Kumar fame, stuns as a vampiric foe. The echoes and parallels are there but minimal, perhaps even coincidental.

Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother is its own beautiful singular thing, partly a stylish and pulpy neo-western thriller about a father racked with guilt, navigating violence that comes heavy and uneasy, but first and foremost a drama about a family reconciling their Muslim faith with their actions, their environments and their grief.

Both Tariq and Ali are Muslims. The former’s debut, Mogul Mowgli, and his directing work on the Prime Video series Bait, both starring Riz Ahmed, were about young British-Pakistani men who internalize hostility towards their faith. In Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother, Tariq builds an even more nuanced portrait of faith around Ali, who seizes the rare opportunity to explore his religion onscreen.

Ali’s Latif, who once taught kids at prayer school, fashions himself as a righteous killer with a code, meting out justice to those who offend Islam. Getting paid for it is beside the point, he argues, when a supportive but critical Imam played by Giancarlo Esposito takes Latif to task.

As the film opens, when Latif is bashing that victim’s head against a bathroom sink and unceremoniously tying up his corpse, his own wife (Shakirah DeMesier) lies there dying, her body delicately cared for by their community in Houston (the movie was shot in Atlanta). That leaves Latif a widower who, alongside his eldest, Fatiha (Adia, quietly mesmerizing), cares for a curious young son (Jahleel Kamara) and infant daughter who won’t take formula.

So much of Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother is propelled by Latif’s frantic search for breast milk, inspired by the writer and director’s own ordeal when his wife fell ill. Ali is especially breathtaking in these moments, with Latif looking weathered and exasperated, but fighting to maintain his wits and composure, as he’s turned away from a milk bank that requires a prescription and accosted by a doctor in the family (Tramell Tillman) when seeking help. Latif finally has to square the assistance he gets from a breastfeeding sex worker (Tiffany Boone) with his at times rigid and hypocritical moral and religious code.

Those negotiations are constant and granular. At every turn, Latif and Fatiha figure out how to make their Islamic faith work for who they are and the situations they’re in. How important is fasting when your frantic ordeals make you forget to eat altogether? How do we grapple with scriptures that limit growth and empathy, but not ignore the profound lessons also found in those texts? In the grand scheme of things, does it matter that your adolescent daughter is using the Mormon neighbour’s wifi to watch Furry porn, which must be all kinds of Haram? These are the questions that make Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother so grounded, compassionate, and, dare I say, divine.

That spiritual journey is also the bridge between the intimate family story and the thriller plot. Latif finds himself caught in a beef between his employer’s son, a producer of “Habibi porn” (Abubakr Ali) who tests what the former stands for, and Cho’s Pastor Hwan Yoon. The latter, captivating in a gold grill, cowboy hat and southern drawl, is an Iraq war veteran who turned evangelical after he supposedly rose back from the dead on the battlefield. His heel turn towards religious fanaticism means surrounding himself with tooled-up mercenaries and preaching about Christ at gunpoint.

Tariq deftly navigates the divide between Latif and Pastor Hwan, setting up binaries and conflicts that could easily give in to Muslim versus Christian sensationalism. But his approach is soulful and considered, allowing everyone their convictions and bandwidth for the mercy and grace the movie ultimately preaches about.

Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother isn’t just interrogating faith. It’s embracing and appreciating those jarring and poetic contradictions that come with the territory.

Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother is premiering at the Toronto film festival and opens in select theaters in New York City and Los Angeles on 25 September, following a wider release on 2 October and 9 October. It is released in the UK on 20 November

シャネル・ネクサス・ホールにて、「Icons and Image Makers ナショナルポートレートギャラリー展」が開催される。

本展ではロンドンのナショナルポートレートギャラリーが所蔵する世界屈指の写真コレクションから、 英国のファッション、音楽、映画界を象徴するアイコンたちのポートレートを厳選して紹介。国際的に高い評価を受ける写真家たちの作品を通して、英国カルチャーを彩った人物像と、時代を映し出すポートレート写真の魅力に迫る。

ポートレートの中には、私たちの視覚文化に深く刻まれ、時代を象徴するイメージとなったものがある。その一方で、公のイメージの背後にある、一人の人間としての姿が捉えられたこともあった。こうした魅力的な肖像は、ナショナルポートレートギャラリーのコレクションの核心にある問いを投げかける。——イメージとアイデンティティはどこで交差するのか？——本展は、英国文化を牽引してきた アイコンたち、そして彼らの姿を形づくってきた写真家たちのクリエイティビティを称える展覧会である。

また会期初日には、ナショナルポートレートギャラリーのアシスタントキュレーターによるガイドイベントが開催されるなど、関連イベントも実施予定。この機会にぜひ足をお運びいただきたい。

content.article_text:
ジル サンダーが2026年秋冬キャンペーンを発表した。シモーネ・ベロッティによるクリエイティブ・ディレクションのもと、フォトグラファー／ディレクターのモニ・ホーワースが撮影。モデルにはエディ・キャンベルとウエダ ダイスケを起用している。

舞台となるのは、自家用飛行場の滑走路。そこにはラテックスで覆われたテーブルやアルミ箔に包まれたソファなど、本来は室内にあるはずの家具が野外に配置されている。明確な間取りも壁もなく、「住まい」という概念だけが断片的に残された空間。離陸と着陸の両方を受け入れる滑走路を、何かが始まる場所として描き出した。

ベロッティが追求したのは、ジル サンダーの根幹にある研ぎ澄まされた抑制美と「力強いシンプルさ」に、わずかな違和感を差し込むことだ。「余剰」が不可欠なものへと変わり、「加える」行為が「取り除く」行為と呼応する。相反する要素を共存させることで、断片的かつ緊張感に満ちた視覚的な物語を構築している。

物語には明確な筋書きが用意されていない。ヒッチコックやライナー・ヴェルナー・ファスビンダーを思わせる気配を漂わせながら、見る者がその空白を自由に補完できるよう意図的に抽象性を残した。キャンベルとウエダは、滑走路で暮らしているのか。これから旅立つのか、それとも到着したばかりなのか。その判然としない状況そのものが、キャンペーンのサスペンスを生み出している。

ビジュアルは、ホーワースが手がけたショートムービーから切り出されたスチールで構成。ざらついたテクスチャーと色褪せたVHSを思わせる色調によって、緊張や高揚、自己の内面と向き合う瞬間を捉えている。さらにSpace Afrika feat. Deuénによる「If This Is Hell」が、映像の断片性と不穏な空気を増幅させる。

「最小限の手法で、緊張感と驚きを表現したかった」とベロッティ。ジル サンダーらしい「少ない要素でより多くを表現する」という美学を保ちながら、今回はそこから一歩踏み込み、影と官能性を帯びた世界を構築した。エレガンスと不穏さ、抑制と官能。完全には解読できない相反する感覚のあいだに、ベロッティ率いる新たなジル サンダーのイメージが浮かび上がる。

content.article_text:
Eileen Perrier, Untitled, Afro Hair and Beauty Show , 1998 © the artist

Featured - September 11, 2026

The Editors

Hometown , 2018

Courtesy the artist

Hailun Ma — Amsterdam

It was only after moving to New York to study fashion photography that Hailun Ma began to recognize the artistic potential of her native Xinjiang—China’s westernmost region, home to twenty-five million people and more than forty ethnic groups, many of them Muslim majority. “If you search for images of Xinjiang online, you get these very National Geographic images,” she once told Vogue . “I wanted to present a younger perspective of what is happening.” Her first major solo show outside of China gathers photographs that delight in the everyday traditions and style of Uyghur teenagers, Kazakh cowboys, and other communities sidelined in mainstream depictions of the country.

Hailun Ma at Foam, Amsterdam, September 18, 2026–January 20, 2027

Let’s Take Back Our Space: “Female” and “Male” Body

Language as a Result of Patriarchal Structures , 1977

© 2026 Marianne Wex Estate and courtesy The Museum of Modern Art, New York, Committee on Photography Fund, and The Modern Women’s Fund

Taking Back Our Space — New York

From 1972 to 1977, Marianne Wex collected thousands of images tracing the connection between gesture and gender. The result, Let’s Take Back Our Space , juxtaposes Wex’s own snapshots of body language from the streets of Hamburg with sources reaching back to antiquity—showing, say, how the pose of a manspreader on a park bench descends from the uninhibited contrapposto of Doryphoros . In this exhibition, Wex’s opus, arrayed across systematized panels à la Aby Warburg, is paired with work by contemporary artists such as Nona Faustine, K8 Hardy, and Wendy Red Star, who extend observation of everyday public space into defiant acts of reclamation.

Taking Back Our Space: Photographic Perspectives at the Museum of Modern Art, New York, September 20, 2026–May 2, 2027

There’s no start or finish (detail), 2026

Courtesy the artist

Taryn Simon — New York

For over two decades, Taryn Simon has mined the hidden systems of power and influence that covertly order our lives. Father Country I Do Love You will be the largest debut of a new work ever at the Guggenheim, and the first single-artist exhibition by a photographer in the rotunda. Across forty-two works of photographs, text, video, and sculpture, Simon traces the life of a real, unnamed federal agent, examining how his individual decisions reverberated across lives and nations in ways he never knew. It’s Simon’s most personal project yet, as the work lives in the shadow her own father, who traveled the globe for the US government before transitioning into a career selling arcade games. “America is the best story on earth,” he once told her, “if you could find someone to tell it.”

Taryn Simon: Father Country I Do Love You at the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, New York, September 18, 2026–March 14, 2027

Couple dancing , 1956

© The Estate of Roy DeCarava

Roy DeCarava — Los Angeles

Listening, for Roy DeCarava, was far from a passive act. For his series the sound i saw , he tuned his camera to the rhythms of midcentury New York’s jazz world, immortalizing titans—Trane, Count, Duke, Lady—in his signature palette of charcoal and smoke. He also captured peripheral scenes: tender embraces, dancehall silhouettes, quiet moments of downtime. The result is a deeply personal exploration of how American life, as Ralph Ellison once wrote, “comes to focus” through jazz. Curated by Ebony L. Haynes, this exhibition brings together 130 photographs from the series, accompanied by a listening room inspired by the records DeCarava cherished most.

Roy DeCarava: the sound i saw at David Zwirner, Los Angeles, September 19–October 31, 2026

Young Pink Kate London 1998

© the artist

The 90s: Art and Fashion — London

Hoist the Union Jack: The 90s: Art and Fashion looks back at a decade when Britain’s irreverent cultural renaissance ruled the runways, airwaves, museums, and magazines. Curated by Edward Enninful, The 90s will bring together fashion by Vivienne Westwood, John Galliano, and Alexander McQueen; works by the (formerly) Young British Artists; and, of course, photographs by the likes of Corinne Day, David Sims, and Juergen Teller, who chronicled a new era of Swinging London in the pages of i-D and The Face .

The 90s: Art and Fashion at Tate Britain, London, October 8, 2026–February 14, 2027

Edge Control_edv c, 2023–

© the artist

Deana Lawson — New York

Diane Arbus has always been a north star for Deana Lawson, the artist renowned for her regal photographs of Black people she meets in various scenarios, often pictured in domestic settings and bestowed with a transcendent, otherworldly, yet sometimes strangely specific presence. Like Arbus, Lawson can astonish and unnerve. For her first solo exhibition with Gagosian since signing with the gallery in 2022, Lawson presents recent portraits that gesture to vernacular photography and Old Master painting, together with a new series called Edge Control , about the phenomenon of surveillance in beauty supply shops, where shoplifters are tracked on cameras and their likenesses posted to store windows to deter theft. Beauty—and scrutiny—is in the eye of the beholder.

Deana Lawson at Gagosian, New York, September 10–October 24, 2026

KEYHOLE 12-3 (IMPROVED CRYSTAL)

Optical Reconnaissance Satellite Near Scorpio (USA 129), 2007

Courtesy the artist and Fellowship, Jessica Silverman Gallery, San Francisco, and Pace Gallery, New York

FotoFocus — Cincinnati

FotoFocus returns with its eighth edition, The Long View , offering seventy-four exhibitions in sixty-five venues throughout Greater Cincinnati, Dayton, Columbus, and Northern Kentucky. The “long view” of the title refers, in part, to the quarter-millennium of the United States, inviting artists and viewers to contend with the nation’s past, present, and possible futures. Standouts include exhibitions by Paul Mpagi Sepuya, Nancy Rexroth, and Trevor Paglen, whose work—spanning facial recognition technologies, alternate-reality games, and AI rabbit holes—probes the dark infrastructures of surveillance and power that govern how we see the world, and how it sees us.

FotoFocus Biennial 2026: The Long View , Cincinnati, Ohio, October 1–31, 2026

Le Coup de Fil Sportif (The athletic phone call) , 1998

© the artist and Tezeta and courtesy David Hill Gallery

Sanlé Sory — London

Sanlé Sory cut his teeth photographing car crashes for newspapers. When he acquired his own equipment, in 1960, he opened the Volta Photo studio and turned to a more celebratory subject: the vibrant youth culture of newly independent Upper Volta (now Burkina Faso). Like his better-known peers Malick Sidibé and Seydou Keïta, Sory redefined the photography of West Africa by portraying its people on their own terms. This show focuses on his rarely exhibited color portraits—images of irrepressible panache made during the restive 1980s and ’90s, when his country sought a new identity focused on anti-imperialism and self-reliance.

Sanlé Sory: Colour Years at the Photographers’ Gallery, London, October 14, 2026–February 21, 2027

Untitled (Teenagers at soda fountain) , c. 1950

© President and Fellows of Harvard College and courtesy Harvard Art Museums

Barbara Norfleet — Cambridge, MA

In the 1970s, the sociologist and curator Barbara P. Norfleet began assembling a vast archive of images from the 1930s to 1960s taken by photographers working on commission across the United States. Consisting of over twenty-thousand photographs depicting social rituals from weddings to corporate gatherings, the archive formed what Norfleet called a “unique and valuable record of American life.” This fall, the Harvard Art Museum stages the exhibition The Way We Never Were , drawn from Norfleet’s archive. Thematic sections ranging from the rise of suburbia and cultural conformity to growing struggles for equal rights centers the role of the professional photographer and commissioned image in shaping how midcentury America came to define itself.

The Way We Never Were: The American Professional Photographers Collection at Harvard Art Museum, Cambridge, Massachusetts, through May 9, 2027.

Hostage Situation , 1979

© the artist

Flashback — Baltimore

In Paula Gillen’s Hostage Situation (1979), a young, masked child yanks a woman’s leg—clad in fishnets and yellow peep-toe heels—protruding through an unfinished ceiling. It’s one of countless gems in Flashback , an unprecedented survey of Baltimore photography spanning almost two hundred years, from daguerreotypes of Frederick Douglass, to A. Aubrey Bodine’s deadline-driven pictorialism, to the zany world of John Waters (that dangling leg belongs to Susan Lowe, a regular in Waters’s films), to younger talents such as Devin Allen and Gioncarlo Valentine who are shaping the city’s photographic landscape today.

Flashback: Two Centuries of Baltimore Photography at the Baltimore Museum of Art, October 4, 2026–February 7, 2027

23 Wall Street , 1977

© the artist and courtesy Howard Greenberg Gallery and Hunters Point Press

Baldwin Lee — New York

Raised in New York’s Chinatown, Baldwin Lee studied with Walker Evans at Yale in the early 1970s. He would return to New York in the following years to photograph the city’s empty, early-morning streets with a 4-by-5 camera. These images, which resonate with German photographer Thomas Struth’s similarly unpeopled streetscapes from the same era, were printed in 2025 for this exhibition at Howard Greenberg Gallery, which previously presented Lee’s now-celebrated large-format portraits made in the 1980s on road trips through the American South. Lee’s portrayal of New York shows how both the skyline and the sidewalk have changed, as in his image of seemingly abandoned Financial Center lofts beneath the Twin Towers of the World Trade Center—a monument to a bygone era.

Baldwin Lee: New York at Howard Greenberg Gallery, New York, September 18–October 31, 2026

Pledge of Allegiance, 1899 , 2017

Courtesy the artist and Gladstone

Arthur Jafa — New York

Named for the pioneering jazz drummer Tony Williams, Arthur Jafa’s exhibition I Am Tony presents video installations, paintings, photographs, and sculptures across two floors of the recently expanded New Museum. Renowned for his trenchant explorations of race and American culture, the artist will premiere new works alongside searing video montages including Love Is the Message, The Message Is Death (2016) and The White Album (2019), as well as early works such as the photograph Monster (1988), an unflinching self-portrait of the artist as a young man.

Arthur Jafa: I Am Tony at the New Museum, New York, September 24, 2026–January 3, 2027

Untitled , 2004, from the series

the eyes the ears

Courtesy the artist

Japanese Women Photographers — New York

A much-needed counterpoint to the male-centric canon of Japanese photography, I’m So Happy You Are Here: Japanese Women Photographers from the 1950s to Now reframes the history of the medium through the work of twenty-eight intergenerational artists. Presented in partnership with Aperture in conjunction with the 2024 monograph , this exhibition is curated by the book’s editors, Pauline Vermare, Lesley A. Martin, and Takeuchi Mariko. I’m So Happy spans the medium from installations to photobooks, providing an indispensable introduction to the contributions of Japanese women to photography by showcasing intimate observations of everyday life, critical perspectives on history, and radical experiments with form.

I’m So Happy You Are Here: Japanese Women Photographers from the 1950s to Now at International Center of Photography, New York, October 15, 2026–January 11, 2027.

Crosby Street and Grand Street, New York, New York ,

February 24, 1974 , from

Uncommon Places (Aperture, 1982)

© the artist and courtesy 303 Gallery, New York

Aperture Loves New York — New York

Aperture Loves New York pays tribute to photographers who have shaped—and been shaped by—the city. Showcasing artists long championed by Aperture and anchored in our publishing history, the presentation brings together important and memorable photographs with corresponding Aperture books that have advanced the medium of photography and captured the complex spirit of New York City. Organized by Aperture’s executive director, Sarah Meister, the installation features photographs by more than twenty artists ranging from past to present—including Diane Arbus, Deana Lawson, Stephen Shore, Awol Erizku, and more.

Aperture Loves New York at Aperture, New York, September 18–November 1, 2026.

content.article_text:
Jurandir Filho , Rogério Montanare , Thiago Siqueira e Fernanda Bermoltz batem um papo nostálgico sobre o ano de 1996 nos cinemas!! Esse podcast é mais uma edição da série We Have to Go Back , onde voltamos no tempo e revisitamos os grandes filmes de um ano específico. Além disso, é um programa nostálgico, pois relembramos os acontecimentos desse ano, as músicas, as evoluções tecnológicas, os jogos de videogames, as curiosidades, os costumes e muito mais!!

Falamos sobre “Um Drink no Inferno”, “Twister”, “O Corcunda de Notre Dame”, “Missão-Impossível”, “Matilda”, “Independence Day”, “Pânico”, “A Rocha”, “Jerry Maguire”, “101 Dálmatas”, “Space Jam”, “Trainspotting”, “Romeu + Julieta” e muito mais.

content.article_text:
ギンザ・グラフィック・ギャラリーにて、第416回企画展「田中義久 ARCHIVE / ACHIEVE」が開催されている。本展では、グラフィックデザイナーの田中義久がこれまで手がけてきた仕事を振り返りながら、クライアントとの継続的な協働を通して取り組んできた視覚言語のあり方を紹介するとともに、一過性にとどまらないデザインの形式そのものに目を向ける。

グラフィックデザインは、社会のなかで使われ、流通し、時に役目を終えながらも、その時代の視覚文化や技術、思想をとどめる重要な資料だ。会場では、DNP文化振興財団の所蔵するコレクションをはじめ、企業や大学機関に保存されたデザイン資料を手がかりに、デザインの過程や印刷物がどのように保存され、分類され、展示されていくのかを検証していく。その一環として、田中義久が継続して研究してきた和紙を用いた保存容器や展示什器、資料を包むための構造を新たに制作。アーカイブを支える箱、紙、台紙、分類、展示台といった、通常は表に現れにくい要素を、グラフィックデザインの実践として捉え直す。

アーカイブとは、過去を閉じ込めるための場所ではなく、未来に向けて開かれるための仕組みでもある。本展は、グラフィックデザインの成果を展示するだけでなく、それらを残し、受け渡していく行為が、次の時代にどのような文化的価値をもたらすのかを考える試みだ。

会期中にはギャラリートークも開催予定。詳細は決まり次第ギャラリーのホームページに掲載されるので、そちらをご確認いただきたい。

content.article_text:
東京を拠点に活動する写真家ヨーガン・アクセルバル（Jörgen Axelvall）が、写真と言葉による回想録『Art Rat』を刊行した。約3万7000語、全30章からなる本書は、写真家として制作してきた作品世界を散文や詩的な記述によって拡張する、250ページの一冊だ。

『Art Rat』でアクセルバルが振り返るのは、自身の人生の30年。ニューヨークで過ごした15年間と、現在まで東京で過ごしてきた15年間をつなぎながら、1990年代から2000年代のニューヨークでの記憶、HIVへの感染、その後のステージ4の癌の診断、パートナーとともに直面した困難を一人称で綴っている。深刻な経験を扱いながらも、語りには時折ユーモアが差し込まれ、個人的な記憶と病をめぐる経験がテンポのあるノンフィクションとして展開される。

執筆を始めたのは2019年。当時アクセルバルは、代替的なホリスティック療法によってHIVが抑制されていると考えていた。しかし2020年に癌と診断されると病状は急速に悪化し、生命の危機に直面。執筆はいったん中断され、それまで信じていた価値観が揺らぐなかで、科学的治療を回復への道として受け入れることになる。4年間の寛解を経て執筆を再開したとき、当初構想していた物語とその意図もまた、大きく変化していたという。

本書を特徴づけるのが、文章と写真を並列させた構成だ。30章それぞれの間には見開き2ページのイメージページが設けられ、写真とともに詩句や警句、格言、詩などを収録。掲載される61点の写真は、アナログフィルム、インスタントフィルム、ポラロイド、デジタル写真と多岐にわたり、30年にわたって蓄積されたアクセルバル自身のアーカイブから選ばれている。

『Art Rat』において写真は、文章を説明するための図版ではない。過去に撮られた像と、現在から過去を振り返って書かれた言葉が同じ時間軸の上で交差することで、写真家の個人的な歴史を複数の視点から組み立て直していく。レンズを通して世界と向き合ってきたアクセルバルが、その実践を「書く」という行為へと拡張した作品でもある。

病と回復、ニューヨークと東京、過去の写真と現在の言葉。30年という時間を一つの直線的な自伝に閉じ込めるのではなく、異なる時代の像と言葉を行き来しながら、自らの生を再編集する『Art Rat』。200部限定の著者版として2026年7月に刊行された。

刊行を記念し、9月12日には渋谷のNONLECTURE books/artsでトークイベント「『Art Rat』ができるまで──写真と言葉で綴る30年の記憶」が開催される。アクセルバルと、本書のデザインを手がけたアガ・デ・ロス・サントスが登壇し、ARTnews JAPAN編集長の名古摩耶をモデレーターに、30年にわたる記憶を写真と言葉によって一冊の本へと編み上げた制作の背景を語る。

出版記念トーク「『Art Rat』ができるまで──写真と言葉で綴る30年の記憶」 日時：2026年9月12日（土）16:00〜17:00 会場：NONLECTURE books/arts（渋谷） 登壇者：ヨーガン・アクセルバル、アガ・デ・ロス・サントス モデレーター：名古摩耶（ARTnews JAPAN） 参加費：1,000円＋1ドリンク代
content.excerpt_original: 東京を拠点に活動する写真家ヨーガン・アクセルバル（Jörgen Axelvall）が、写真と言葉による回想録『Art Rat』を刊行した。約3万7000語、全30章からなる本書は、写真家として制作してきた作品世界を散文や詩的な記

content.article_text:
X-Men | Asa Germann, de Gen V e The Boys, será o Anjo no novo filme da Marvel

Novo “X-Men” tem estreia prevista para 5 de maio de 2028.

(Imagens: Getty Images, Marvel)

Um novo mutante se junta ao Instituto Xavier. O ator Asa Germann se juntou ao elenco do novo “ X-Men ” no papel de Warren Worthington III, mais conhecido como Anjo (via THR ).

Germann é mais conhecido por seu trabalho nas séries “Gen V” e “The Boys”, onde interpretava o jovem super Sam Riordan, um dos aliados do Capitão Pátria na Universidade Godolkin. Ele também esteve em “Pânico 7” recentemente, no papel de Lucas Bowen. Segundo o relato, Germann fez testes para o papel de Scott Summers, o Ciclope, em “X-Men”, mas foi escolhido para o papel do Anjo.

O Anjo foi criado por Stan Lee e Jack Kirby, sendo apresentado logo na primeira edição de “X-Men” em 1963. Sua mutação consiste em asas emplumadas nas costas que lhe permitem voar. Em certo momento de sua trajetória, o Anjo foi mutilado e teve suas asas substituídas por asas metálicas capazes de disparar projéteis, uma alteração feita pelo vilão Apocalipse. Nos cinemas, o personagem foi vivido por Ben Foster em “X-Men: O Confronto Final” e Ben Hardy em “X-Men: Apocalipse”.

Germann se junta ao elenco que já conta com Sadie Sink como Jean Grey, Kit Connor como o Ciclope, Inde Navarrette como a Vampira, Maya Boyd como a Tempestade e Christopher Abbott como Charles Xavier, o Professor X. Entre os vilões, Samara Weaving será Emma Frost, com Adam Driver interpretando Nathaniel Milbury, o Sr. Sinistro.

Jake Schreier assume a direção do novo “X-Men” após o sucesso de “Thunderbolts*”. O roteiro fica a cargo de Lee Sung Jin, que já trabalhou com Schreier na série “Beef”, e de Joanna Calo.

O novo “X-Men” tem estreia prevista para 5 de maio de 2028.

Saiba Mais: Asa Germann , Marvel , X-Men

content.article_text:
Andrew Scott conduz um drama histórico que troca campos de batalha por mapas e previsões, encontrando tensão na espera, mas nem sempre força dramática.

“ Pressão ” acompanha o meteorologista James Stagg (Andrew Scott) nas 72 horas anteriores ao Dia D, quando as forças aliadas precisam decidir se as condições climáticas permitem a invasão da Normandia. Uma premissa que prevê homens reunidos analisando mapas e comparando previsões pode não parecer muito cinematográfica. Contudo, o diretor Anthony Maras tem plena ciência do impacto que é colocar uma decisão irreversível nas mãos de pessoas que sabem exatamente o que está em jogo. Esse nível de tensão independe de qualquer batalha.

No começo, sistemas meteorológicos e previsões divergentes parecem se distanciar de qualquer urgência. Aos poucos, porém, a ciência atmosférica evolui de um assunto técnico para um grande problema moral. Stagg precisa defender sua previsão diante de autoridades que desejam uma resposta definitiva, enquanto o comandante supremo Eisenhower (Brendan Fraser) precisa decidir se confia nela. Avançar pode colocar milhares de vidas em risco. Esperar pode comprometer uma operação capaz de mudar o rumo da guerra. Não existe alternativa segura.

Andrew Scott evita retratar Stagg como um herói convencional, carregando a tensão de alguém consciente de que um erro de cálculo pode ter consequências históricas. Sua atuação funciona melhor nos momentos em que a pressão aparece por meio de hesitações e confrontos profissionais. Brendan Fraser oferece o contraponto necessário, interpretando um comandante que precisa ouvir especialistas sem transferir a eles a responsabilidade pelas decisões. A tentativa constante de humanizá-lo (inclusive na insistência em tratá-lo como “Ike”) soa ufanista em excesso, deixando a sensação de que alguém naquele posto e naquela situação dificilmente seria tão “compreensivo”.

O restante do elenco é competente, por mais que o roteiro não dê a todos a mesma atenção. Kerry Condon busca extrair algo do pouco material que tem disponível, mas sua personagem soa por vezes despropositada, o que é uma pena diante da oportunidade de explorar os desafios de ser a única mulher em posição de destaque naquele ambiente. Já Damian Lewis tem um pouco mais de tempo de tela como o veterano general Bernard Montgomery, mas a severidade constante acaba tornando-o unidimensional.

Maras sabe que o suspense mais impactante reside na espera, e aposta nisso também na montagem. As discussões avançam enquanto o relógio se aproxima da decisão, e cada nova previsão mexe diretamente com os ânimos dentro da sala. A fotografia também trabalha a favor dessa proposta, contornando as limitações dos espaços fechados com algumas cenas exteriores que criam uma alternância entre confinamento e amplitude. A trilha sonora completa esse mecanismo aumentando a pressão sem ser invasiva ou querer forçar uma sensação de grandiosidade onde não é necessário.

Adaptado a partir de uma peça de teatro, o filme preserva uma estrutura muito concentrada em diálogos e confrontos verbais. Nessa transposição do palco para o cinema, algumas sequências soam esticadas além do necessário. O filme é curto o suficiente para não perder completamente o controle. Porém, nem sempre possui material dramático suficiente para sustentar a urgência constante que procura impor, sobretudo quando insere um drama familiar com pouquíssimo desenvolvimento.

Também há momentos em que o roteiro reorganiza situações e personalidades para criar um conflito mais acessível ao público, e algumas reações acabam soando calculadas demais. Quem conhece os acontecimentos históricos pode perceber com facilidade quais conflitos foram ampliados para criar suspense. Isso não invalida a proposta, mas diminui a naturalidade das atuações.

Curiosamente, essa redução na escala também é o que diferencia “Pressão” de muitos dramas da Segunda Guerra Mundial. O Dia D aparece como consequência de uma cadeia de decisões tomadas por pessoas que trabalham com informações incertas. O verdadeiro conflito está na responsabilidade de escolher quando agir e aceitar que nenhuma informação será suficiente para eliminar a possibilidade de erro.

Nesse sentido, o longa também assume com tranquilidade a posição de um típico “filme de pai”. Além do contexto histórico em que está inserida a história, some a presença de homens discutindo estratégia em salas fechadas, as figuras históricas conhecidas e a trama baseada em decisões militares praticamente e você vai praticamente gabaritar o checklist — e isso não necessariamente é um defeito. O filme sabe exatamente qual público pretende alcançar e oferece a esse espectador um drama histórico tecnicamente bem executado e fácil de digerir.

“Pressão” não está interessado em reinventar o drama de guerra, tampouco em oferecer a visão definitiva do Dia D. Sua força está em transformar uma decisão técnica em um dilema humano e construir tensão a partir disso. O resultado é funcional e bem conduzido, ainda que a narrativa não alcance todo o peso emocional de um acontecimento histórico dessa dimensão.

代官山ヒルサイドテラス・ヒルサイドフォーラムで2026年9月23日から10月4日まで、写真展「『いつでもいま ― ガラスに映す光』柿本ケンサク写真展」が開催される。映画やドラマ、広告映像を手がける一方、国内外で写真・現代美術作品を発表してきた柿本が、ガラス作家・三嶋りつ惠の透明なガラスを通した光を、新作「Hikari」シリーズとして提示する。

柿本にとってヒルサイドテラスは、写真家としての活動における重要な場所でもある。2016年に同会場で「TRANSLATOR」を開催し、2021年の「TRANSFORMATION」では時間と記憶をめぐる実験を展開。2026年、三度同じ場所に戻り、今回は写真を「光の記憶」として捉え直す。

本展の核となるのは、「写真は光を固定する。ガラスは光を揺らす」という二つのメディアの性質だ。柿本は三嶋による10点のガラス作品を、いわば光を描くためのレンズとして使用。ガラスの位置を数ミリずつ動かし、角度を変えながら、そこを通過する光を撮影した。目の前の風景を忠実に写すのではなく、偶然に生まれる光の屈折や揺らぎと対話しながらシャッターを切ることで、時間の流れや季節の空気、身体の動き、ガラスそれぞれの個体差までを写真の中に定着させている。

写真とガラスという異なるメディアが交差することで立ち上がるのは、「固定」と「流動」、「定着」と「融解」、「点」と「線」のあいだにある緊張関係だ。点として固定された光が時間のなかで線へとほどけ、曖昧になった記憶が見る者のなかでもう一度像を結ぶ。作品は、光を記録する写真というメディアそのものの性質を改めて問い直す。

資料に掲載された「Hikari」シリーズでは、花や水辺、都市風景などがガラス越しの光によってにじみ、歪み、時に抽象的な色面へと変化している。被写体の輪郭を明確に示すというより、光によって世界が別の像へと移り変わる瞬間そのものが写し出されている。

三嶋は1962年京都生まれ。ヴェネツィアと京都を拠点に、ムラーノ島の職人との協働によって無色透明のガラス作品を制作してきた。周囲の光や空気を取り込み、空間のなかに光の輪郭を生み出す作品で知られる。本展では、三嶋のガラスが単なる被写体ではなく、光と風景を変容させる装置として柿本の写真表現に組み込まれている。

会期中の10月3日16時には、柿本と三嶋によるトークイベントも開催（1000円、1ドリンク付き）。それぞれが写真とガラスを通して向き合ってきた「光」と「時間」をテーマに語り合う。また、南青山のLUMIX BASE TOKYOでは、本展と連動し、LUMIX L10で撮影した別作品群による写真展「いつでもいま」も同時開催される。

Digger | Tom Cruise é um bilionário excêntrico que precisa salvar o mundo no trailer do novo filme de Alejandro Iñárritu

Filme chega aos cinemas nacionals em 1 de outubro.

(Imagens: Warner Bros.)

Foi divulgado o trailer final de “ Digger “, novo filme de Tom Cruise dirigido por Alejandro González Iñárritu . Assista acima à versão legendada e abaixo à dublada.

Foi divulgado também o novo cartaz nacional do filme, abaixo.

No filme, Cruise interpreta Digger Rockwell, um barão do petróleo que desencadeia um enorme desastre ecológico global graças aos anos de exploração. Ele é o único capaz de resolver o que parece ser uma crise de derretimento acelerado de icebergs, e recebe ordens do atual presidente dos EUA para agir e evitar o fim do mundo.

Além de Cruise, compõem o elenco Riz Ahmed, John Goodman, Sandra Hüller, Michael Stuhlbarg e Jesse Plemons.

“Digger” chega aos cinemas brasileiros em 1 de outubro.

Saiba Mais: Alejandro G. Iñárritu , Digger , Tom Cruise
